### [1] [Fine-Grained Emotion Classification from Mobile App Reviews: An Empirical Study with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03802)
*Quim Motger,Carlota Catot,Marc Oriol*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates how large language models can perform fine-grained, multi-label emotion classification on imbalanced mobile app review data and proposes strategies that make encoder models competitive with decoder LLM prompting at much lower latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Polarity-based sentiment analysis (positive/negative) on app reviews is too coarse for many requirements engineering tasks, such as prioritizing issues by user frustration or analyzing feedback per feature. Fine-grained emotion detection could provide richer signals but has been understudied for app reviews and is challenging due to many emotion classes and severe imbalance, especially for rare emotions.

Method: Using an existing human-labeled dataset based on Plutchik’s emotion taxonomy, the authors systematically compare: (1) encoder-only models fine-tuned for multi-label classification or as a binary ensemble of one-vs-rest classifiers; (2) decoder-only LLMs used via zero-shot and few-shot prompting (both open-source and proprietary); and (3) several imbalance mitigation methods for encoders, including loss reweighting, resampling, and generative data augmentation. Synthetic review generation and prompting strategies are automatically chosen based on an intrinsic ranking of augmentation utility.

Result: Decoder-only LLMs with few-shot prompting achieve the best performance, with a macro-F1 of 0.642. Baseline fine-tuned encoders perform much worse (0.387 for multi-label, 0.450 for binary-ensemble). However, combining the best multi-label encoder with generative data augmentation and positive-class weighted loss improves macro-F1 by 0.204, substantially narrowing the gap with LLM prompting while offering up to three orders of magnitude lower inference latency. The improvements are most pronounced on rare emotions, where F1 increases from zero to up to +0.501.

Conclusion: Fine-grained, multi-label emotion classification of app reviews is practically achievable with large language models, yielding modest but useful macro-F1 scores for integration into requirements engineering workflows. Decoder LLM prompting currently gives the highest accuracy, but appropriately optimized and augmented encoder models can approach this performance far more efficiently. The optimal setup depends on the model backbone and problem formulation. The authors publicly release their pipeline, synthetic datasets, and fine-tuned models to support replication and application.

Abstract: Context: Fine-grained emotion classification of mobile app reviews enables requirements engineering activities that go beyond polarity-based opinion mining, including emotionally informed issue prioritisation and feature-oriented feedback analysis. However, automatic fine-grained emotion extraction from app reviews remains understudied. Objectives: Building on a previously published annotation framework and human-labelled ground truth adapted from Plutchik's taxonomy, this paper investigates how large language models can be leveraged for automatic multi-label emotion classification under severe class imbalance. Methods: We compare encoder-only fine-tuning under multi-label and binary-ensemble formulations, decoder-only zero- and few-shot prompting across open-source and proprietary models, and a catalogue of imbalance mitigation strategies (loss reweighting, resampling, generative data augmentation), with the synthetic-review generator and prompting strategy selected via an intrinsic augmentation-utility ranking. Results: Fine-tuned encoders trail the best decoder-only few-shot prompting (macro-F1 0.642) by a wide margin at baseline (multi-label: 0.387; binary ensemble: 0.450); pairing the best multi-label encoder with generative data augmentation and positive-weighted loss closes most of this gap (+0.204) at up to three orders of magnitude lower inference latency than the decoders, with the largest gains on the rarest emotions, from undetected to gains of up to +0.501 F1. Conclusion: Large language models make fine-grained, multi-label emotion classification of app reviews feasible for requirements engineering pipelines, with modest macro-F1, and the best formulation and mitigation strategy are backbone- and formulation-dependent. We release the experimental pipeline, synthetic corpora, and fine-tuned checkpoints for replication and reuse.

</details>


### [2] [Same Output, Different Gold: Measuring How Reference Choice Moves a Multilingual Benchmark Score](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03825)
*Parth Kulshreshtha,Shivali Dalmia,Abhishek Mukherji*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They study how sensitive benchmark scores are to which annotation reference is used, showing that changing the reference can significantly alter F1 scores and system rankings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Benchmark evaluation usually focuses on system outputs and treats the reference labels as fixed ground truth, but real benchmarks are built from noisy, multi-annotator data, and the choice of reference variant can bias scores and even favor particular systems.

Method: Using a six-language PII benchmark that retains two independent annotators, an aggregated gold, and a separate expert reviewer sample, they recompute F1 scores while holding system outputs fixed and varying which annotation record is used as the reference, then quantify how scores and system comparisons change, including confidence intervals and multiple-testing correction. They further analyze the construction process and an aggregation default that copied one annotator in many cases, partially aligning the reference with one system’s outputs.

Result: Changing only the reference labels shifts F1 scores by up to ~5 points for one system and ~2 for another, with CIs showing the effects are statistically reliable and reaching 7.55 points in the worst language; system-vs-system comparison also changes, with a statistically significant reference–system interaction of about +2.95 points that even flips the margin in one language, traced to an undocumented aggregation behavior that effectively made the benchmark partially tailored to one system.

Conclusion: Benchmark scores can be strongly reference-sensitive; when multiple annotation records exist, different plausible gold standards can yield meaningfully different scores and system rankings. They propose computing a reference-sensitivity band from the annotation record for any benchmark and reporting this band alongside point scores to make evaluation uncertainty visible and reduce hidden biases from annotation aggregation choices.

Abstract: A benchmark score compares a system output against a reference, and methodological attention falls almost entirely on the first term. We measure the second. The retained annotation record of a six-language benchmark for personally identifiable information contains two independent annotator labellings, the aggregate shipped as gold, and a reviewer gold from independent expert re-annotation of a sample. Using it, we hold the scored output fixed and exchange the reference. The score moves by 4.95 F1 points for one output and 2.00 for the other (95% CIs [3.23, 6.27] and [0.26, 3.37]), and by 7.55 in the worst language. The comparison between two outputs moves as well: the paired interaction between reference and system is +2.95 points (CI [+1.97, +3.87]), survives correction for multiple testing, and changes one language's margin outright. The cause is an undocumented aggregation default that usually kept one annotator when adjudication did not fire, making the shipped reference a partial copy of an output being scored. We report the resulting reference-sensitivity band, show how to compute one from any retained annotation record, and argue that the quantity belongs beside the score.

</details>


### [3] [The Score Is Not the Structure: Brain Alignment and Cross-Lingual Transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03827)
*Saman Rahbar*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper examines similarity scores used to claim structural correspondence between models, brains, and languages, showing that much of the reported signal can persist even when true correspondence is absent or the measurement tool fails.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Similarity scores between models and brains or across languages are often taken as evidence of shared underlying structure. However, it is unclear what these scores look like when there is no genuine correspondence or when the probing tools are unreliable. The paper aims to critically evaluate how much of the observed similarity is actually specific to true structural correspondence versus arising from methodological artifacts, tool failure, or statistical miscounting.

Method: The authors analyze three empirical setups. (1) Cross-lingual transfer of a grammaticality probe: they evaluate how a probe trained in one language transfers to others and whether the probe itself maintains above-chance performance in each language, then assess how excluding non-functioning probes affects the relationship with language distance and how different ways of counting samples (language pairs vs. languages) change p-values. (2) Brain-model similarity: they train a language model to predict human brain responses, measure the change in similarity score relative to a ceiling, and compare this with a model trained on brain targets whose correspondence to true brain data has been intentionally destroyed, quantifying how much of the gain is actually specific to brain structure. They also examine the similarity floor that exists even with no model due to rank-based effects. (3) Directional steering of languages: they test how steering linguistic representations along a language’s own direction versus a random direction affects performance across languages and whether such effects correlate with language distance.

Result: (1) In cross-lingual probing, probes perform at chance in 4 of 17 languages. As a result, 64 of 272 language pairs are evaluated with non-working tools. Removing those languages halves the observed relationship between transfer performance and language distance, and correctly treating the 17 languages (rather than the 272 pairs) as independent units changes the p-value from 0.0006 to 0.155, undermining the claimed significance. (2) For brain similarity, training a language model on real brain responses raises the similarity score from 0.10 to 0.34 (ceiling 0.54). However, a model trained on destroyed (non-corresponding) brain targets still reaches 0.31, implying that only about 0.028–0.068 of the improvement is specific to actual brain structure. Moreover, even with no model, a destroyed target has a baseline similarity of 0.204 to the real brain data, determined largely by rank/number-of-sentences effects. (3) Steering each language along its own direction consistently outperforms steering along a random direction (+6.2 in 16/17 languages) but shows no modulation by language distance, contradicting expectations that structural similarity should vary with distance.

Conclusion: Apparent similarities between models, brains, and languages can remain surprisingly high even when real structural correspondence is absent or when the measuring probe is effectively non-functional. Mis-specified statistical units and floors inherent in the metrics further inflate perceived effects. Therefore, researchers should first quantify how much of a similarity score would persist under a broken or irrelevant correspondence before interpreting such scores as evidence of shared structure or functional alignment.

Abstract: Researchers often support the claim that a model shares structure with the brain, or across languages, by reporting a similarity score. We ask what such a score reads when the shared structure is absent, or when the tool that measures it does not work. We check two settings, and in both the score is not what it appears. First, a probe trained to tell grammatical from ungrammatical sentences in one language transfers worse to more distant languages, the usual evidence for shared structure. But the probe itself gets worse along the same axis: in four of seventeen languages it performs at chance, so 64 of 272 language pairs are scored with a tool that does not work. Dropping those languages halves the strength of the relationship, but they are also the most distant, and this design cannot separate the two effects. Counting matters too: the same data give p = 0.0006 when the 272 pairs are treated as independent and p = 0.155 when the seventeen languages are, which is the correct unit. Second, training a language model to match human brain responses raises its similarity score from 0.10 to 0.34, against a ceiling of 0.54. A model trained on a target whose correspondence to the brain was destroyed still scores 0.31, so only 0.028 to 0.068 of the rise is specific to the brain. With no model at all, a destroyed target already sits at 0.204 from the real one, a floor that tracks the target's rank divided by the number of sentences. Finally, steering a language along its own direction works (+6.2 over a random direction in sixteen of seventeen languages) yet shows no effect that varies with language distance. Before asking whether a correspondence helps, ask how much of the score would survive without it.

</details>


### [4] [OncoNoteBERT: A Foundation Representation Model for Natural Language Processing of Real-World Outpatient Oncology Notes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03829)
*Wuraola Oyewusi,Eliana Vasquez Osorio,Goran Nenadic,Gareth Price*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper builds oncology-specific BERT-style language models from a large UK outpatient oncology notes corpus and shows that both continued pretraining of existing models and training from scratch with a bespoke tokenizer outperform adjacent-domain encoders, each offering distinct advantages in fit and tokenization efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: General biomedical or radiology/pathology language models do not capture the specialised terminology, staging language, treatment and toxicity expressions, and local de-identification markers found in real-world oncology outpatient notes. This mismatch leads to poor language modelling fit and suboptimal tokenisation (fragmentation of important clinical terms and placeholders), which can harm downstream oncology NLP tasks. The authors are motivated to understand whether local adaptation of existing models or training new oncology-specific encoders with a tailored tokenizer can better represent this domain.

Method: They assembled a governed UK outpatient oncology corpus of 290,026 notes from 21,564 lung and head-and-neck cancer patients. They compared two existing encoders, RadBERT and PathologyBERT, with two local models: (1) OncoNote-RadBERT, created via continued masked language model pretraining of RadBERT on the oncology corpus; and (2) OncoNoteBERT, trained from scratch using an oncology-specific WordPiece tokenizer. They evaluated models on multiple axes: masked language modelling loss and perplexity on a validation set, tokenizer fragmentation metrics (subword fertility, normalized sequence length), tokenization behaviour for clinical terms, a set of 13 masked-token “cloze” probes reflecting clinical reasoning, and exploratory analysis of learned representations (including handling of institutional placeholder tokens).

Result: Zero-shot, the external domain-adjacent models fit the oncology corpus poorly (perplexity 113.04 for RadBERT and 2035.03 for PathologyBERT). Continued pretraining of RadBERT yielded OncoNote-RadBERT with the best corpus-level fit (perplexity 2.10). OncoNoteBERT, trained from scratch with a bespoke oncology tokenizer, achieved slightly worse perplexity (2.83) but much more efficient tokenization: lower subword fertility and shorter normalized sequence length. In masked-token probe tasks, OncoNoteBERT gave clinically acceptable predictions in 12/13 cases, outperforming OncoNote-RadBERT’s 7/13, despite its higher perplexity. Both locally developed models learned to represent an institutional placeholder as a single, coherent token.

Conclusion: Domain-adjacent biomedical encoders (e.g., radiology or pathology BERT models) do not transfer well to specialised oncology outpatient notes without adaptation. Two complementary strategies help: (1) continued pretraining of an existing model yields superior global language modelling fit, while (2) training a new model with a bespoke oncology tokenizer improves tokenization efficiency and clinical behaviour on targeted probes. The apparent discrepancy between corpus-level metrics and probe performance is partly driven by tokenizer fragmentation rather than pure semantic learning. Careful tokenizer and representation-layer design, alongside continued adaptation, is therefore crucial before applying external encoders to oncology NLP tasks.

Abstract: Real-world outpatient oncology notes contain specialised terminology, tumour staging expressions, treatment names, toxicity descriptions, and institution-specific de-identification markers that may not be represented efficiently by general biomedical or adjacent clinical language models. We developed and evaluated oncology-specific BERT-style encoders using a governed UK outpatient oncology corpus comprising 290,026 notes from 21,564 patients treated for lung and head-and-neck cancer. We compared RadBERT and PathologyBERT with two local strategies: OncoNote-RadBERT, produced by continued masked language model pretraining, and OncoNoteBERT, trained from scratch with an oncology WordPiece tokenizer. Models were evaluated using masked language modelling loss and perplexity on the validation set, tokenizer fragmentation metrics, clinical term tokenisation, masked-token probes, and exploratory representation analysis. Both external encoders fit the oncology corpus poorly in zero-shot evaluation (perplexity 113.04 for RadBERT; 2035.03 for PathologyBERT), while continued pretraining produced the strongest fit (2.10 for OncoNote-RadBERT). OncoNoteBERT achieved perplexity 2.83 but produced the most efficient tokenisation, with lower subword fertility and shorter normalised sequence length. It also returned a clinically acceptable prediction for 12 of 13 masked-token probes, compared with 7 of 13 for OncoNote-RadBERT. This divergence between corpus-level fit and masked-token performance was partly attributable to tokenizer fragmentation rather than learned semantics alone. Both locally developed models represented the institutional placeholder as a single learnable token. These findings show that continued adaptation and bespoke tokenisation provide complementary benefits, and that representation-layer design matters before adjacent-domain encoders are applied to oncology NLP.

</details>


### [5] [SYNLAT: Syntax-Aligned Text-Latent Compression for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03839)
*Yifeng Zhao,Hongjun Yu,Shibo Wang,Yunjiao Zhou,Zixiao Zhu,Zhipeng Ning,Kezhi Mao,Junlang Qian*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes SynLat, a syntax-aware framework to compress chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning while preserving answer-critical information, achieving better accuracy than baselines at various compression levels on Qwen3 models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long CoT outputs are costly in terms of tokens. Under token budgets, we need to compress reasoning traces without losing information that is crucial for correct answers. Existing compression schemes often cut at token or fixed lengths, which can split meaningful linguistic or logical units, or use step-level units that mix content needing different compression treatments. The authors aim to design a compression framework that chooses boundaries more intelligently so that important reasoning is preserved while reducing output length.

Method: They introduce SynLat, a text-latent CoT framework organized around Syntax-Aligned Units (SAUs), which are non-overlapping units aligned to syntactic structure (e.g., phrases, clauses). A Teacher model, conditioned on the answer, creates supervision in the form of KEEP/LATENT labels for these units at multiple compression levels, effectively defining what should remain explicit text and what can be treated as latent (compressed away). A single Student model is then trained with this supervision and a compression control variable, so at inference it can generate mixed explicit/latent reasoning conditioned only on the question and desired compression level. This is evaluated across two sizes of Qwen3 Students, multiple task groups (Standard-CoT and Long-CoT), and three compression settings.

Result: Across all combinations of model size (Qwen3-8B/14B), task group (Standard-CoT vs Long-CoT), and compression level, SynLat matches or outperforms the strongest baselines in all 12 aggregate evaluations and is strictly better in 11 of them when comparing at similar achieved compression ratios. The performance gains are more pronounced at higher compression: up to +3.6 and +2.6 points at a medium compression level and +7.0 and +5.5 points at high compression for Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B, respectively, with especially large improvements for tasks requiring Long-CoT.

Conclusion: Aligning CoT compression boundaries with syntactic structure via Syntax-Aligned Units enables more effective token reduction without sacrificing, and often improving, task performance. A unified Student model conditioned on compression level can reliably generate partially latent reasoning traces using only the question at inference. SynLat scales across model sizes and task types, and its benefits grow with stronger compression and longer reasoning traces, suggesting syntax-aware boundary design is a key ingredient for efficient CoT compression.

Abstract: Long chain-of-thought (CoT) traces impose substantial output-token costs. Under constrained budgets, compression must preserve answer-critical information, making boundary placement central. Token-level and fixed-length boundaries can fragment coherent spans such as phrases, formulas, and local derivations, whereas step-level boundaries can bind content requiring different compression actions. We introduce SynLat, a text-latent CoT framework that aligns compression boundaries with syntactic structure through non-overlapping Syntax-Aligned Units (SAUs). An answer-conditioned Teacher constructs progressive KEEP/LATENT targets for a single compression-conditioned Student, which generates mixed reasoning from only the question and requested compression level at inference. Across two Qwen3 Student scales, Standard-CoT and Long-CoT groups, and three compression levels, SynLat matches or exceeds the strongest evaluated baseline in all 12 task-group aggregates and strictly leads in 11 under the reported achieved-CR selection protocol. Overall gains reach 3.6/2.6 points at MEDIUM and 7.0/5.5 points at HIGH for Qwen3-8B/14B, with larger advantages under stronger compression, particularly on Long-CoT groups.

</details>


### [6] [When Evidence Changes: Evaluating Memory Repair and Re-reading in Language-Model Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03902)
*Wenhui Chu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates how AI agents should handle memory when supporting documents are revoked or replaced: repair stored memory or re-read all evidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents often build and cache structured memories (e.g., medication lists) from source documents. When some sources are later revoked, updated, or replaced, it is unclear whether it is more efficient and reliable to incrementally repair these memories or to discard them and re-read the original evidence. There is a lack of empirical evaluation of memory-revision strategies versus simple re-reading, especially under realistic clinical workloads and token costs.

Method: The authors design an evidence-revision benchmark using medication- and problem-list extraction tasks from public ICU records. They simulate three event types—revocation, replacement, and controls—then compare different strategies: (1) full re-reading of all documents, (2) source-filtered re-reading (only reading sources relevant to the current state), and memory-based approaches including (3) caching prior extractions, (4) rebuilding structured memory from scratch, and (5) graph-local repair that only updates affected parts of memory. They run these strategies on two 7B-parameter models, compute token costs for ingestion, revision, and every subsequent use, and analyze performance and cost under both short and extended (~10k token) record settings. They also include a pre-specified small development sweep and statistical tests, particularly in a replacement-study setting.

Result: For short clinical records, graph-local repair reduces revision token usage dramatically—5–10× fewer revision tokens than rebuilding from scratch. However, across held-out conditions, every memory-based pipeline still costs at least twice as much as full re-reading when considering the entire pipeline (ingest, revision, and uses). In a development setting where ineligible documents are added to extend records to about 10,000 tokens, the average cumulative cost of using memory becomes lower than full re-reading after 2–14 uses, helped by truncated extraction, but source-filtered re-reading remains the cheapest strategy overall. In the replacement-focused study, none of the four main confirmatory statistical tests produced significant differences between methods.

Conclusion: Incremental memory repair can be token-efficient for the revision step itself but may not be cost-effective when the full lifecycle costs are counted, especially on short records. Memory approaches only begin to outperform full re-reading in long-document, multi-use scenarios, and even then, simple source-filtered re-reading can remain the cheapest solution. The study concludes that evaluations of agent memory under evidence revision must compare against strong re-reading baselines—particularly source-filtered re-reading—over the complete pipeline rather than just the revision phase, cautioning against assuming that complex memory-repair mechanisms are always beneficial.

Abstract: When documents supporting an agent's derived facts are revoked or replaced, should it repair memory or re-read current evidence? We introduce an evidence-revision evaluation on medication- and problem-list tasks from public ICU records. Under revocation, replacement and control events, we compare full and source-filtered re-reading with caching, rebuilding and graph-local repair across two 7B models. Memory is supplied in full without retrieval, and costs include ingest, revision and every use. On short records, local repair uses 5-10$\times$ fewer revision tokens than rebuilding, yet every memory pipeline costs at least twice full re-reading in held-out conditions. In a small pre-specified development sweep, adding task-ineligible documents extended records to about 10,000 tokens; at that length, memory's mean cumulative cost fell below full re-reading's after 2-14 uses, partly through truncated extraction, while source-filtered re-reading remained cheapest. In the replacement study, none of the four primary confirmatory tests reached statistical significance. These results show why the cost of agent memory after evidence revision must be assessed against source-filtered re-reading over the full pipeline.

</details>


### [7] [General Decision Models: Benchmarking and Insights Beyond Jev](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03935)
*Feiyu Duan,Jiayu Lin,Jia Wang,Jun Xiang,Jialiang Wu,Xinnong Zhang,Hanqi Yan,Siyuan Wang,Zhongyu Wei*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: JEVal benchmark evaluates when specialized decision models like Jev are reliable, and shows they work well for evidence-based single decisions but struggle with uncertainty, long-horizon systems, and social simulations, while a new distilled family (InnerJev) approaches Jev’s performance with very low latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: General decision models (like Jev) are emerging as cheaper, faster alternatives to full generative LLMs for tasks that boil down to choosing among options or making structured judgments. However, it is unclear: (a) which decision types they handle reliably, (b) how their local decision quality scales to complex, multi-step systems, and (c) how they compare to LLMs in realistic, large-scale environments like social simulations. The paper aims to fill this gap by providing a broad benchmark and systematic comparison, and by exploring ways to distill LLM reasoning into fast one-shot decision models.

Method: 1) Build JEVal, a bilingual benchmark of 11,257 instances from 36 datasets across 10 domains, designed to test many decision types. 2) Evaluate 25 model configurations, including general decision models (e.g., Jev) and standard generative LLMs, on this benchmark. 3) Analyze behavior in more realistic, dynamic settings: (a) long-horizon, multi-step interaction tasks (τ-bench) to see how local errors accumulate into system-level failures; (b) large-scale social simulation, comparing individual response prediction, user profiling, and aggregate statistics. 4) Propose InnerJev-4B and InnerJev-27B, which compress an open-weight LLM’s chain-of-thought reasoning into a single-pass, first-token decision using Reasoning-to-Readout Self-Distillation, and evaluate them against Jev on JEVal and timing metrics.

Result: 1) On JEVal, decision models are strong when decisions can be made from explicit evidence; they degrade on tasks needing expert knowledge or calibrated uncertainty, often picking the right outcome but assigning overconfident probabilities. 2) On τ-bench, local speed advantages translate into shorter episodes, but accumulated decision errors reduce overall task success in long trajectories. 3) In large-scale social simulations, decision models nearly match powerful LLMs in predicting single responses at lower inference cost, but are worse at user profiling and produce larger errors and systematic biases in aggregate estimates. 4) InnerJev-27B achieves performance comparable to Jev on JEVal while answering typical queries in ~0.1 seconds, showing that LLM reasoning can be effectively distilled into fast one-shot decision models.

Conclusion: General decision models are attractive for fast, low-cost structured decisions when evidence is sufficient and tasks are relatively local, but they are less reliable when expert knowledge, uncertainty calibration, long-horizon planning, or nuanced social modeling are required. System-level performance can degrade as local errors accumulate, and in social simulations they show notable aggregate bias and weaker profiling despite good per-step predictions. The proposed InnerJev models demonstrate that LLM-style reasoning can be distilled into efficient one-pass decision models—InnerJev-27B matches Jev’s benchmark performance with very low latency—yet the broader limitations identified suggest that careful evaluation and system design remain crucial when deploying such models in complex decision pipelines.

Abstract: General decision models, such as Jev, have recently emerged as efficient alternatives to LLMs for structured judgment and selection. But what kinds of decisions can these models reliably make, and how does their behavior change when individual decisions are composed into larger systems? To study this, we introduce JEVal, a bilingual benchmark comprising 11,257 instances from 36 datasets across 10 application domains, and evaluate 25 model configurations spanning general decision models and generative LLMs. Our results show that (1) general decision models are most competitive when decisions can be resolved from available evidence, but weaken when they require specialist knowledge or faithful uncertainty estimation: they can often identify the most likely outcome while substantially overstating its probability. (2) In more dynamic and realistic systems involving long-horizon, multi-step interactions, the advantages of fast local decision making are offset by reliability failures at the system level. on $τ$-bench, faster local decisions reduce median episode time but lower task success as decision errors accumulate over long trajectories. (3) In large-scale social simulation, decision models approach strong generative LLMs on individual response prediction at substantially lower inference cost, yet remain weaker in user profiling and exhibit larger aggregate estimation errors and systematic bias. Finally, we propose InnerJev-4B and InnerJev-27B, which internalize an open-weight LLM's own reasoning into a single-pass first-token decision through Reasoning-to-Readout Self-Distillation, with InnerJev-27B performing on par with Jev on JEVal while answering a typical query in about 0.1 s.

</details>


### [8] [A Step Towards Forgetting: Optimiser History and the Loss of Answer Mass](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03940)
*Valeria Ruscio,Seth Nabarro,Keiran Thompson*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper analyzes how optimizer momentum (especially in Adam) contributes to catastrophic forgetting in language models, showing that stored gradient history can reduce probability mass on previously learned answers even when current gradients try to preserve them.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Catastrophic forgetting in continual or multi-task training of language models is common, but most analyses focus on current gradients or data rather than the optimizer’s internal state. Momentum-based optimizers accumulate gradient history, which may unintentionally push parameters in directions that hurt performance on older tasks. The authors aim to understand and quantify how this optimizer memory specifically causes degradation of previously learned behaviors.

Method: The authors study fine-tuning of multiple language-model families with momentum-based optimizers (notably Adam). They decompose old-task loss into two components: (1) confusion, i.e., mis-ranking among old answers, and (2) leakage, i.e., loss of total probability mass on the old answer set. They further decompose Adam updates into the contribution from the current gradient and from accumulated history, examining how each affects answer mass and discrimination. They analyze history contributions by age (old vs. recent gradients) and by orientation relative to old-task gradients. They perform interventions that reset momentum while keeping the initial update norm fixed, and integrate loss changes along parameter update trajectories, using local projections and curvature analyses to capture large loss increases.

Result: Across three language-model families, they find that probability mass on old answers systematically declines during new-task training, even as the model’s ability to discriminate among the old answers typically improves. Decomposition of Adam updates shows that gradient history tends to push probability mass away from the old answers (increasing leakage), while the current gradient often counteracts this effect. Older stored gradients from the new task are most responsible for harmful leakage, whereas recent gradients more often protect old answers. The impact of history is largely determined by how its direction aligns or misaligns with the old-task gradient. Momentum-reset interventions demonstrate that removing optimizer memory improves retention and lowers final old-task loss, primarily by restoring answer mass. Path integration reveals that most large loss spikes are predictable from local projections, though curvature along the history direction can amplify some events.

Conclusion: Optimizer momentum, via accumulated gradient history, is a key driver of forgetting in fine-tuned language models. Even when current gradients favour preserving old-task performance, stored history can erode probability assigned to previously learned answers, especially through leakage of answer mass outside the original answer set. Resetting or controlling momentum can mitigate forgetting, indicating that managing optimizer memory is crucial for stable continual learning in language models.

Abstract: During fine-tuning, a language model can assign less probability to previously learned answers even when the current gradient acts to preserve that probability. With momentum, each update also carries gradients computed at earlier model states, and these stored contributions can push the model in the opposite direction. We investigate how this optimiser memory contributes to forgetting by separating old-task loss into confusion among its answers and leakage of probability outside the answer set. Across three language-model families, answer mass consistently declines while discrimination among old answers usually improves: the model becomes less likely to produce answers that it can still distinguish correctly. Decomposing Adam updates reveals opposing contributions to this loss of answer mass. Over training, accumulated history favours leakage, while the current gradient opposes it. Resolving history by age shows that the harmful contributions come mainly from older gradients of the new task, whereas recent gradients tend to protect the old answers. Changes in history's effect are dominated by its orientation relative to the old-task gradient. Interventions that reset momentum while matching the initial update norm establish that stored history affects retention, with state-dependent immediate effects and lower final old-task loss over longer Adam continuations, mainly through recovered answer mass. Finally, integration along finite updates shows that most sampled large loss increases are captured by local projections, while curvature along history amplifies some events. Together, these findings reveal how an optimiser's memory can erode learned behaviour even as its current gradient acts to preserve it.

</details>


### [9] [BAIBAICHUCHU at the NTCIR-19 FinArg-3 Task: When Is Maximum Possible Profit Predictable from Investor Text?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03962)
*Zong-Han Bai,Po-Yen Chu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper analyzes the BAIBAICHUCHU team’s system for ranking Chinese investor posts by Maximum Possible Profit (MPP) in the NTCIR-19 FinArg-3 task, diagnosing why development performance did not carry over to official runs and decomposing predictability into text, volatility, horizon, and pair structure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors want to understand why their seemingly strong development results (0.734) failed to translate into equally strong official test performance (best run 0.517), and more broadly to clarify what components of financial return predictability come from text vs. market conditions. They also seek to test whether stock-return predictability might be near-random or if structural factors (e.g., volatility and horizon) matter, and to propose better evaluation practices for financial argument mining and profit-based ranking tasks.

Method: They build a three-track ensemble: (1) lexical-feature-based models, (2) a MacBERT ranker further fine-tuned on FinArg-2 data, and (3) an LLM-based judge combining signals. They then perform a post-hoc audit of the LLM judge, discovering a long-only rule misapplied to bearish posts. Beyond model debugging, they decompose the ranking task into separate components: direction (bullish/bearish text), volatility and time horizon (σ√T scaling via a running-extremum model), and pairwise margin between posts. Using a separate July 2026 dataset of 502 price-aligned posts, they quantify how pre-event volatility scaled by observation horizon relates to a truncated-horizon MPP proxy and analyze correlations (Spearman ρ) and pairwise ordering accuracy. They also examine how prediction reliability changes with the labeled MPP gap and reference prior benchmark results (ERAI) to rule out trivial explanations like universal unpredictability.

Result: On development data, their three-track ensemble reaches 0.734 when posts are grouped, but official submissions only reach 0.4598–0.5402, with their best at 0.517 and a unanimous three-track subset at 0.500. Fixing the LLM judge’s long-only treatment of bearish posts changes 28 of 87 official predictions without affecting official accuracy, but it reduces development accuracy from 0.680 to 0.622, showing that an incorrect, regime-specific shortcut had overfit the validation regime. In the July 2026 dataset, pre-posting volatility scaled by post-specific horizon (σ_pre,20√N_i) shows moderate correlation with a later truncated-horizon MPP proxy (Spearman ρ=0.320 with ticker-cluster 95% CI [0.133,0.466]) and correctly orders 61.4% of unequal-outcome pairs. Transferred text-based signals have almost no correlation with July outcomes (ρ=0.055) and add little predictive power once volatility-based scoring and stance are known. Reliability of development predictions increases from about 0.60 to 0.93 as the labeled MPP gap between posts increases. A prior ERAI score of 0.6207 suggests that pure unpredictability cannot fully explain performance levels.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that financial return predictability in this setting is driven more by market-structure features—volatility, horizon, and pair composition—than by transferred textual features alone, and that superficially strong validation performance can hide regime-specific shortcuts such as long-only assumptions. They argue that evaluation for MPP-style ranking tasks must jointly consider text signals, market regime, historical volatility, horizon, and the composition of post pairs, rather than attributing performance solely to text models. The observed σ√T scaling and nontrivial volatility-based predictability also suggest that the task is not universally unpredictable, so careful task design and diagnostics are crucial to avoid misinterpreting model performance.

Abstract: The BAIBAICHUCHU team participated in the Social Media Subtask of NTCIR-19 FinArg-3, ranking Chinese investor posts by Maximum Possible Profit (MPP). A three-track ensemble of lexical features, a FinArg-2-pre-finetuned MacBERT ranker, and an LLM judge reaches 0.734 in post-grouped development evaluation, but our best official run scores 0.517. All twelve submitted runs lie between 0.4598 and 0.5402, and our 26 unanimous three-track pairs score 0.500.
  A post-hoc audit finds that the submitted judge applied a long-only rule to bearish posts although MPP is stance-aware. Correcting it changes 28 of 87 official predictions without changing accuracy, yet lowers development accuracy from 0.680 to 0.622: a regime-specific semantic shortcut improved validation fit.
  We decompose ranking into directional text, volatility and horizon, and pairwise margin. A running-extremum model predicts $σ\sqrt{T}$ scaling, observed ex post in 502 price-aligned posts from a separate July 2026 collection. Pre-posting volatility scaled by the post-specific observation horizon, $σ_{\mathrm{pre},20}\sqrt{N_i}$, is associated with a later truncated-horizon MPP proxy (Spearman $ρ=0.320$; ticker-cluster 95% CI [0.133,0.466]) and correctly orders 61.4% of unequal-outcome pairs. Transferred text is nearly uncorrelated with the July outcome ($ρ=0.055$) and adds little conditional on this score and stance. Development reliability rises from about 0.60 to 0.93 as the labeled MPP gap widens. An earlier ERAI result of 0.6207 rules out universal unpredictability as a simple explanation. Evaluation should jointly consider text, market regime, historical volatility, horizon, and pair composition.

</details>


### [10] [Do Language Models Need a Trainable Input Embedding Table? Fixed Minimal Token Codes at 1.7B-Class Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04002)
*A. Bochkov*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper tests whether trainable token embeddings are actually necessary for strong language modeling, by replacing them with fixed code-based inputs and comparing performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard language models use a learned embedding vector for each token, which adds many parameters and assumes token-specific vectors are essential. The authors want to know if this design choice is truly required for good performance, or if a shared Transformer can learn effectively even when tokens are represented only by fixed, non-trainable codes.

Method: Train three decoder-only language models from scratch under matched conditions (same tokenizer, Transformer backbone, untied output head, training data and recipe, and ~100B training tokens). They vary only the input interface: (1) a standard learned embedding table, (2) fixed canonical 16‑bit token ID codes, and (3) a fixed invertible recoding over GF(2). For the fixed-code models, these codes are tiled to match model width without any extra trainable input projection. They then evaluate all models on benchmarks like HellaSwag, PIQA, and LAMBADA.

Result: Both fixed-code models achieve substantial performance, e.g., canonical codes reach 52.40% normalized accuracy on HellaSwag, 70.51% on PIQA, and 42.75% on LAMBADA. However, the learned-embedding model still performs better on several evaluations. Using fixed codes removes about 100.7M trainable parameters, yielding 1.711B-parameter models, but this parameter saving is secondary to the main finding.

Conclusion: Independently trainable token-specific input embeddings are not architecturally necessary for the observed level of language-modeling capabilities: a Transformer can learn well from immutable token codes. The advantage of learned embeddings appears empirical rather than fundamental. Fixed identity-style interfaces also offer a clean setting to study how internal representations and capabilities arise downstream of a frozen, non-trainable input layer.

Abstract: A trainable input embedding table assigns each vocabulary item an independently adjustable vector. We investigate whether this token-specific parameterization is required for substantial language-modeling capability, or whether a shared Transformer can learn from fixed token identities. We compare three decoder-only language models trained from scratch with the same tokenizer, contextual backbone, untied output-head architecture, and training recipe, with a target budget of 100 billion prediction tokens per model. Their input interfaces are a learned table, canonical 16-bit token-ID codes, and one fixed invertible recoding over GF(2). The fixed codes are repeated to model width without an additional trainable input projection. Both fixed-code models acquire substantial capabilities: canonical codes achieve 52.40\% HellaSwag normalized accuracy, 70.51\% PIQA accuracy, and 42.75\% LAMBADA accuracy. The learned-input control performs better on several evaluations, including HellaSwag and LAMBADA, so these results establish viability rather than performance parity. The fixed interfaces remove 100.7 million trainable parameters, yielding 1.711B-parameter models, but parameter reduction is not the central result. These single-run experiments distinguish architectural necessity from empirical utility: independently trainable token-specific input vectors are not required for the observed capabilities. A fixed identity interface also provides a controlled setting for studying representation learning downstream of an immutable input, without establishing where particular capabilities are localized.

</details>


### [11] [Periscope: Extending Frozen Language Models Beyond Their Context Window](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04047)
*Mohamed Eltahir,Anas Obayd,Raed Rashid,Abdulrahman Alghamdi,Abdulrahman Mousa,Abdallah Ahmed,Tanveer Hussain,Naeemullah Khan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Periscope, a training-free inference method that lets frozen language models handle very long texts efficiently by probing carefully chosen subsets instead of processing the entire sequence in one quadratic pass.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard transformer language models suffer from quadratic cost and degraded accuracy as input length grows, even before hitting the context window limit. This makes long-context tasks—like finding relevant documents, supported options, or key evidence passages—both expensive and unreliable, especially for very long inputs reaching hundreds of thousands or millions of tokens. The authors want to know if, for decision problems over a finite set of options, the long read can be factorized into cheaper probes that still let the model identify the right answer and evidence location.

Method: They propose Periscope, a training-free inference procedure that works with a frozen LLM. The text is split into N chunks and laid out on a K×K grid with K = ceil(sqrt(N)). The model is queried on 2K spans: K local spans of consecutive chunks and K strided spans that sample across the whole text. For each candidate answer, they read off log-odds at a single token position from each probe. An answer’s score is the best among its local and strided scores. Each chunk inherits scores from its associated local and strided spans, producing an evidence map over chunks without extra passes. The highest-scoring chunk is taken as the evidence behind the answer. Probes involve about sqrt(sc) tokens for a text of s tokens and chunk size c, so with a context window W the method can effectively cover W^2/c tokens, incurring about s^1.5 cost instead of s^2. They then restrict full reading to only the top-K chunks selected by the evidence map.

Result: On LongBench v2, the approach that reads only the K highest-ranked chunks (about 9k tokens) matches the performance of the same model doing its best single-window read across windows from 32k up to 1M tokens. On InfiniteBench, whose median context length is 150k tokens, Periscope outperforms the best windowed reading baselines by 5 points. For BRIGHT long-document ranking tasks, the evidence map yields the best NDCG@10 among six compared methods. Memory-wise, because each forward call caches only one probe, a 27B-parameter model can process 4.5M-token contexts on a single 80GB GPU, whereas a conventional single-pass attention over that sequence would require roughly 296GB of KV cache.

Conclusion: Periscope shows that for many long-context decision tasks, one does not need to process the entire text in a single quadratic forward pass. By factorizing reading into a small number of structured probes that produce an evidence map, frozen LLMs can scale to multi-million-token contexts with significantly reduced memory and compute, while matching or surpassing the accuracy of traditional long-context baselines. This shifts the bottleneck from fitting the text into GPU memory to merely fitting the model itself, enabling practical long-context use of large models without architectural changes or additional training.

Abstract: A language model reads long text in one quadratic forward pass, stops at the context window, and loses accuracy with length before reaching it. We ask whether the read can be factorized when deciding over a finite set: which document is relevant, which option is supported, which passage is the evidence. Periscope, a training-free inference method, arranges the $N$ chunks of a text on a $K{\times}K$ grid with $K{=}\lceil\sqrt{N}\rceil$ and asks a frozen model the same question about $K$ local spans of consecutive chunks and $K$ strided spans that sample the whole text, reading the log-odds of every answer at one token. Each answer takes its best local and strided score, and scoring every chunk by its two spans gives an evidence map at no further cost, whose peak is the chunk behind the answer. Every probe is about $\sqrt{sc}$ tokens for a text of $s$ tokens and chunk size $c$, so a window of $W$ tokens reaches $W^{2}/c$ tokens at $s^{1.5}$ cost. The map replaces the long read. On LongBench v2, reading only the $K$ chunks the map ranks highest, 9k tokens, matches the same model's best window read across windows from 32k to 1M tokens, and on InfiniteBench, where the median context is 150k tokens, it leads the best window read by 5 points. The same map ranks BRIGHT's long-document corpora with the best NDCG@10 of six methods. Each call caches only one probe, so a 27B model reads 4.5M-token contexts on one 80GB GPU, where a single pass would need 296GB of cache. A long read then needs a GPU that holds the model, not one that holds the text.

</details>


### [12] [IdeaScientist: Orchestrating Agents for Grounded Scientific Ideation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04074)
*Jiarui Liu,Renjie Tao,Yiwei Liao,Chuanyang Jin,Kai Sun,Xiao Yang,Xinyuan Zhang,Xilun Chen,Zhuangqun Huang,Lechen Zhang,Yongjin Yang,Yinghui He,Weihao Xuan,Rakesh Wanga,Anuj Kumar,Mona T. Diab,Wen-tau Yih,Xin Luna Dong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces IdeaScientist, a reinforcement-learning-based system that decomposes scientific ideation into roles (gap finding, innovation, report writing) and uses a large corpus of structured ideas to generate novel, well-grounded research proposals that match or exceed human-explored directions and strong LLM baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Even with automation in scientific workflows, generating high-quality, promising research ideas is difficult. The authors argue that ideation deserves focused study and that many scientific problems can be solved by transferring mechanisms that addressed analogous problems in other domains. They want a systematic, automated way to discover such cross-domain analogies and generate research directions that resemble those humans later pursue.

Method: They define research ideation as three sequential roles: (1) gap finding (identifying limitations and gaps in related work), (2) innovation (drawing solution intuitions from analogous domains), and (3) report writing (turning intuitions into full proposals). Each role is trained with reinforcement learning on a backbone model (Qwen3.6-27B). They build the Svalbard Idea Vault, a 2.77M-item corpus of decomposed research ideas, and use it for retrieval, RL training, and temporally controlled evaluation. Evaluation is done by cutting off literature after a date, having the system propose ideas, and then comparing these ideas to the directions in 15K later human-written papers.

Result: On the Qwen3.6-27B backbone, IdeaScientist outperforms the strongest open-source autoresearch baseline by 14.0%, primarily via higher novelty of generated ideas. It also surpasses proprietary SDK-based baselines (Claude Code SDK with Claude-4.8-Opus and Codex SDK with GPT-5.4) by up to 5.9%, under the same evaluation setting that measures alignment with later human research directions.

Conclusion: Decomposing ideation into RL-trained roles and leveraging a large cross-domain idea corpus leads to more novel and human-aligned research proposals than prior autoresearch systems and even strong proprietary LLM setups. This suggests that structured, analogy-driven ideation and temporally controlled evaluation are effective strategies for automating early-stage scientific creativity.

Abstract: Despite rapid progress in automating scientific research, generating promising and well grounded research solutions remains a central challenge. We isolate research ideation as a standalone task and build our solution on the intuition that a challenge in one field can often be addressed by a mechanism that solved an analogous challenge in another. Accordingly, we introduce IdeaScientist, which decomposes ideation into gap finding, innovation, and report writing, and trains each role with reinforcement learning. These roles identify limitations in related work, draw solution intuitions from analogous problem settings, and develop those intuitions into complete research proposals. To facilitate discovery of insights across domains, we construct the Svalbard Idea Vault, a corpus of 2.77M decomposed research ideas for retrieval, training, and temporally controlled evaluation. Our evaluation restricts access to literature available before a cutoff date and assesses how closely proposed directions align with those later explored in 15K papers authored by human researchers. On Qwen3.6-27B, IdeaScientist outperforms the strongest open-source autoresearch baseline by 14.0%, driven mainly by gains in novelty. On this 27B open backbone, IdeaScientist even outperforms Claude Code SDK with Claude-4.8-Opus and Codex SDK with GPT-5.4, by up to 5.9%.

</details>


### [13] [Representation-Aligned Auxiliary Supervision for Language Model Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04098)
*Kyuyoung Kim,Peiyao Sheng,Ashwin Hebbar,Peiyang Xu,Yunfei Xie,Kevin Wang,Rui Xin,Chen Wei,Zhangyang Wang,Jinwoo Shin,Pramod Viswanath,Sewoong Oh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how different state representations affect language models’ ability to learn and generalize in a structured domain (chess), and shows that adding auxiliary tasks in representation-compatible formats significantly improves adaptation and transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although language models can reason well, adapting them to structured, formal domains (like games or other environments) is difficult and unstable. The authors suspect that a key bottleneck is how compatible the task’s representation (input format) is with the model’s internal processing. Chess offers a clean setting with exact rules, optimal actions, and multiple equivalent representations, allowing precise study of how representation choice impacts learning and generalization.

Method: Use chess as a controlled environment with well-defined semantics and optimal-move labels. Compare language models trained on different but semantically equivalent board representations: a symbolic string format (FEN) and a spatial ASCII-based layout. Measure how models trained on these representations perform on: (1) predicting optimal moves and (2) open-ended commentary. Introduce representation-aligned auxiliary supervision: extra training tasks built from the environment (e.g., tasks that reveal dynamics rather than just static or surface features) and expressed in the representation the model handles best. Evaluate how these auxiliary tasks affect performance under a fixed amount of target-task data, and test cross-representation transfer (ASCII→FEN vs FEN→ASCII).

Result: 1) Models process semantically equivalent chess states (FEN vs ASCII) very differently, with significant differences in learning speed and generalization. 2) Adding auxiliary supervision in compatible representations consistently improves optimal-move prediction over training only on the target task with the same target data size. 3) Auxiliary tasks that encode or expose environment dynamics yield the largest and most reliable gains compared with static or surface-level auxiliary tasks. 4) These representation-aligned auxiliary tasks can rival the benefits of substantially increasing target-task data. 5) Models trained on ASCII transfer better to FEN evaluation than the reverse, and can even outperform a baseline trained only on FEN for FEN evaluation. 6) Improvements carry over from pure move prediction to more open-ended, factually grounded commentary generation.

Conclusion: Representation compatibility is crucial for adapting language models to structured domains. Seemingly equivalent input encodings can lead to markedly different behavior, learning, and generalization. By adding auxiliary supervision tasks expressed in representations that the model can process more effectively—especially tasks that reflect environment dynamics—one can significantly improve adaptation, cross-representation transfer, and downstream capabilities without needing large extra amounts of target data. This suggests a general strategy for structured-domain adaptation: design and train on model-compatible, environment-derived auxiliary tasks rather than relying solely on target-task data in a single representation.

Abstract: Language models exhibit strong reasoning capabilities, yet adapting them to structured domains remains challenging and can yield inconsistent outcomes. We identify representation compatibility, the extent to which a model effectively processes a representation for a structured task, as a key factor in adaptation. We study this in chess, which provides a controlled testbed with precise semantics, computable optimal actions, and multiple state representations, including a symbolic encoding (FEN) and a spatial format (ASCII). We find that models often process semantically equivalent inputs substantially differently, affecting both learning and generalization. Building on this observation, we propose representation-aligned auxiliary supervision, which uses environment-derived tasks expressed in compatible representations to improve adaptation to structured domains. Across models and representations, auxiliary supervision consistently improves optimal-move prediction relative to target-only training under identical target data. Tasks that expose environment dynamics provide larger and most consistent gains than surface-level or static supervision, while remaining competitive with substantially increasing the amount of target-task data. Moreover, ASCII-trained models transfer more effectively to FEN than FEN-trained models do to ASCII, even surpassing the FEN target-only baseline on FEN evaluation. The gains also extend beyond optimal-move prediction to open-ended, factually grounded commentary generation. Overall, our results show that auxiliary supervision in model-compatible representations can enable effective adaptation in structured domains.

</details>


### [14] [LongSocialBench: Do Long-Context LLMs Understand Online Discussion Threads?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04118)
*Xinyi Liu,Rinat Khaziev,Dilek Hakkani-Tür,Tarek F. Abdelzaher*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces LongSocialBench, a benchmark to evaluate long-context LLMs on structured social reasoning over entire online discussion threads, revealing a large gap between current models and humans.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While long-context LLMs can read entire discussion threads, genuine social discourse understanding requires tracking the reply tree structure, participant dynamics, and scoped evidence within these long interactions. Existing evaluations mostly test generic long-document comprehension, not fine-grained social reasoning over structured conversations. The authors aim to create a benchmark that specifically probes structure-aware social understanding in long, real-world online discussions.

Method: The authors construct LongSocialBench from 94 complete discussion "episodes" (threads) taken from Hacker News, Stack Exchange, and Reddit r/ChangeMyView, each serialized with its full reply structure and often reaching tens of thousands of tokens (median ~73K). They design 1,462 four-option multiple-choice questions that require recovering structured social evidence, such as parent–reply relations, turning points, scoped subthreads, cross-branch contrasts, and participant trajectories. Items are verified for answerability, unique correct options, and explicit grounding in the thread. They then evaluate 18 LLMs under 29 different prompting and context workflows, including full-context baselines and settings that additionally provide the gold evidence scope.

Result: Humans achieve 72.4% accuracy on the benchmark when reading independently. Across 18 LLMs, the average accuracy with a full-context baseline is 43.9%. The best-performing model, Claude-Opus-4.7 with an option-elimination prompting strategy, attains 63.0% accuracy, still notably below human performance. When models are given the gold evidence scope (the exact relevant part of the thread), mean performance rises from 43.9% to 55.0%, indicating that even when context localization is solved, models still struggle with the underlying structured social reasoning.

Conclusion: LongSocialBench demonstrates that simply providing large context windows and better prompting is insufficient for robust social understanding of long online discussions. The main missing capability is reasoning over the structured reply tree—tracking relationships, contrasts, and conversational dynamics—not just accessing or retrieving relevant context. The benchmark provides a challenging, human-verified testbed to drive progress on structure-aware social discourse understanding in long-context LLMs.

Abstract: Long-context LLMs can now ingest entire online discussion threads, but understanding their social discourse requires more than reading a long document: models must track parent-reply relations, turning points, scoped subtrees, cross-branch contrasts, and participant trajectories. To test this structure-aware social reasoning, we introduce LongSocialBench, a benchmark of 1,462 verified human-authored multiple-choice items drawn from 94 complete Hacker News, Stack Exchange, and Reddit r/ChangeMyView episodes, with a median length of approximately 73K tokens. Each item pairs a complete serialized discussion and reply structure with a four-option question, requiring models to recover structured social evidence. Released items are verified for answerability, option uniqueness, and evidence grounding. Across 18 models and 29 evaluation settings, current long-context workflows remain far below human performance. The best individual result comes from Claude-Opus-4.7, which reaches 63.0% when prompted to eliminate incorrect options before answering, compared with 72.4% for independent human readers. Averaged across all 18 models, the full-context Baseline scores 43.9%. Supplying the gold evidence scope raises this to 55.0%, showing that substantial errors remain even after the relevant thread region is identified. LongSocialBench shows that the missing capability is not context access or prompting alone, but social understanding over structured reply trees.

</details>


### [15] [Copying Before Suppression: What Drives a Below-Chance Dip During Language Model Training?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04119)
*Tejas Dahiya,Cole Blondin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how the internal mechanisms of language models change during training, showing that models can temporarily rely on the wrong computation before converging to the right one.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most mechanistic interpretability work analyzes fully trained models, implicitly assuming that the mechanisms that implement behaviors are stable by the end of training. However, the internal computations responsible for a behavior can be quite different earlier in training. Understanding these transient mechanisms is important both for safety and for a full theory of how circuits form.

Method: The authors focus on the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task in Pythia and other models, where the model must choose between a name mentioned once vs. a repeated name. They track model behavior across training checkpoints and identify a training window where the model systematically prefers the repeated name, even while its overall language modeling loss continues to improve. They then use causal interventions on attention heads: selecting heads that write the repeated name on held-out prompts, replacing those heads’ outputs with averaged outputs from non-repeated-name prompts, and measuring the effect on the correct-minus-repeated logit difference. They also transplant mature head parameters into early checkpoints to quantify their contribution to behavioral recovery.

Result: They find an early training window where models prefer the repeated name, reducing IOI accuracy below chance while general LM loss still improves. This corresponds to a temporary dominance of a “repetition-favoring” computation. By ablating selected attention heads through output replacement, they partially fix the bias toward the repeated name in multiple Pythia sizes. In 160M models, the head that later suppresses the repeated name is largely inactive and causally ineffective early on; its attention to the repeated mention and its negative contribution to that logit both grow over training. Transplanting mature versions of this head into early checkpoints recovers 35–68% of the eventual improvement in the correct-minus-repeated logit gap across 160M, 410M, and 1B Pythia models. Similar early-to-late reversals appear across additional scales and in independently trained GPT-2 models and OLMo.

Conclusion: The mechanisms implementing a behavior in mature language models can be very different from those active earlier in training. In particular, a mature circuit can hide a transient causal configuration that once strongly shaped behavior, implying that static, end-of-training interpretability can miss critical developmental dynamics. Studying how circuits form and change during training is therefore essential for understanding and potentially steering model behavior.

Abstract: Mechanistic interpretability usually studies fully trained models, yet the computations that drive a behaviour can change while the model is still learning the task. On the Indirect Object Identification task, a model should continue with the name mentioned once rather than the name mentioned twice. Pythia models pass through an early training window in which they prefer the repeated name, so accuracy in a choice between the two names falls below one half while language-model loss on a fixed text sample keeps decreasing across the same window. The window reflects a temporary imbalance between two computations. We identify one cause of the wrong preference by selecting a set of attention heads that write the repeated name, on prompts separate from those used for causal evaluation, keeping that selection fixed, and then replacing each head's final-token output with its average output on a separate set of non-repeated-name prompts. This improves the correct-minus-repeated logit difference in a separately trained 160M model and in the official 160M, 410M, and 1B models. At 160M, the head that lowers the repeated name in the mature model shows little of its mature behaviour at this point. It directs less than one percent of its attention to the repeated mention, and its output makes almost no direct contribution to lowering that name's logit. Both properties grow over the interval in which behaviour recovers. Across the 160M, 410M, and 1B models, transplanting the corresponding head's mature parameters into the early checkpoint recovers 35 to 68 percent of the total improvement in the correct-minus-repeated logit difference seen by the end of training. Related early-to-late reversals appear at further Pythia scales, in two independently trained GPT-2 models, and in OLMo. A mature circuit can therefore conceal a transient causal configuration that shaped behaviour earlier in training.

</details>


### [16] [Representational Control over Self-Report & Behavior Coherence in LLM Risk-Taking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04125)
*Rafal Kocielnik,Peiyang Song,Pengrui Han,Myrl G. Marmarelis,Ramit Debnath,Dean Mobbs,R. Michael Alvarez*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how large language models’ (LLMs’) self-reported traits (here, risk-taking) relate to their actual decision behavior, using activation steering to probe internal representations rather than just prompts and outputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work observes that what LLMs say about themselves (self-report) often mismatches how they behave in tasks, but these findings rely on black-box prompting and cannot tell whether the mismatch comes from prompt artifacts or from distinct internal representations of traits vs. behavior. Understanding this distinction is important for evaluating LLM safety, alignment, and psychological profiling, especially for agentic properties like risk-taking.

Method: The authors focus on risk-taking as a test case. They apply activation steering: constructing and injecting steering vectors into model activations to systematically push internal representations in riskier or more cautious directions. They compare nine different ways to extract such vectors: from task-specific directives, from the model’s own choices in risk-related tasks, and from dispositional (trait) descriptions at two levels of granularity. They test these on four open-weight LLMs, evaluating effects on two behavioral decision-making tasks and two psychometric-style self-report instruments, while also diagnosing and debiasing for surface confounds. They also compose multiple steering directions (e.g., behavior-moving plus self-report-moving) and manipulate their signs to study interactions.

Result: (1) A single internal intervention does not generally align self-report and behavior. Vectors derived from trait-like descriptions strongly change self-report but leave behavior near chance, whereas vectors derived from the model’s own task choices shift behavior but not self-report; task-specific directive-based vectors affect both but only weakly. (2) Once surface confounds are removed, the apparent exception for directive-based vectors largely disappears, and they retain only about 32% of their behavioral effect. Overall, self-report and behavior are controlled by nearly orthogonal directions in representation space, and each can be influenced via multiple independent constructions. (3) When a behavior-moving vector is combined with a self-report-moving vector, both channels can be moved together; flipping the sign of one vector sets self-report and behavior in opposition, with 69–89% of such flipped interventions causing reported and enacted risk to diverge across models.

Conclusion: Self-report and behavioral dispositions in LLMs are implemented in largely distinct, nearly orthogonal internal representations that can be independently steered. The partial alignments seen in black-box prompting often stem from surface confounds rather than shared internal structure. By making the self-report–behavior relationship explicitly representational and manipulable via activation steering, the work shows that evaluations of LLMs’ agentic traits should incorporate representational diagnostics alongside behavioral tests, and that self-report cannot be assumed to faithfully track behavioral propensities.

Abstract: Self-report is an appealing low-cost probe of an LLM's dispositions, but recent work finds only selective agreement between what models report and how they behave. Prior accounts establish these patterns by prompting black-box LLMs, leaving open whether the gap is a prompting artefact or a fact about how the underlying constructs are represented internally. We investigate risk-taking, a consequential dimension of agentic decision-making, using activation steering to measure self-report and behavior under the same internal intervention. We survey nine steering-vector extraction methods spanning task-specific directives, the model's own task behavior, and dispositional descriptions at two granularities, evaluated on two behavioral tasks and two psychometric instruments across four open-weight LLMs. We find that (1) a shared internal intervention does not ensure shared responsiveness: directions built from trait descriptions move self-report but leave behavior at chance, directions built from the model's own task choices do the reverse, and only task-specific directives reach both, weakly. (2) Diagnosis dissolves that exception: removing surface confounders leaves the directives only 32% of their behavioral effect. The two channels are otherwise steered by near-orthogonal directions, each channel reachable by several independent constructions. (3) An intervention composing one behavior-moving and one self-report-moving direction moves both together; flipping one sign sets them in opposition, with reported and enacted risk pointing in opposite directions on 69-89% of flipped compositions in all models. These findings move the self-report-behavior relationship from a black-box observation to a representational one that can be inspected and controlled, motivating representational checks alongside behavioral evaluation.

</details>


### [17] [PB-GRPO: Learning Socially Adaptive LLM Agents from Persona-Driven Simulation with Preference-Batched GRPO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04132)
*Jingquan Wang,Jun Yin,Xu Han,Yongsheng Mei,Jie Hao,Bin Guo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose PB-GRPO, a reinforcement learning post-training method that uses preference-batched normalization to train LLMs for socially adaptive, multi-turn behavior using conversation-level feedback in a simulated persona-based environment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs need to be not just factually correct but also socially competent: inferring unstated goals, respecting user preferences, and adapting over multi-turn conversations. Such social behaviors are hard to optimize because real multi-turn interaction data is scarce and user preferences are latent, so better learning frameworks are needed to leverage limited, noisy social feedback.

Method: They use a persona-driven social simulation environment with a persona library, LLM-based user simulators, and a [0,1] user-satisfaction score to generate conversation-level feedback. On top of this, they introduce preference-batched GRPO (PB-GRPO), a post-training reinforcement learning algorithm where advantages are normalized within batches (buckets) of users who share similar preferences, rather than globally as in vanilla GRPO, to stabilize learning across diverse social types.

Result: In the simulated environment, models trained with PB-GRPO show improved social behavior relative to strong RL baselines, including vanilla GRPO, as measured by the user-satisfaction scoring system and multi-turn conversational performance.

Conclusion: Preference-batched GRPO is an effective way to train LLMs to be more socially adaptive by leveraging persona-based simulations and conversation-level feedback, and its preference-aware normalization leads to more stable and better social behavior learning than standard GRPO in diverse user populations.

Abstract: Building LLMs that behave well socially, not merely correctly, requires Building LLMs that behave well socially, not merely correctly, requires more than producing locally helpful responses. A socially competent agent must infer users' unstated goals, respect their preferences, and adapt as the conversation unfolds. These behaviors are inherently multi-turn and social, making them hard to optimize: real interaction data is scarce, and user preferences are typically latent rather than directly observable. To address these challenges, we build on a persona-driven social simulation environment (consisting of a persona library, LLM-based user simulators, and a user-satisfaction scoring system ranging from [0, 1]), to introduce preference-batched GRPO (PB-GRPO), a post-training algorithm that learns socially adaptive policies from conversation-level feedback. Compared to vanilla GRPO, PB-GRPO computes advantages using a normalization estimated across a bucket of users with similar preferences, stabilizing training across a diverse social population.
