Empirical evidence shows that PB-GRPO improves models' social behavior over strong reinforcement learning baselines in our simulated environment.

</details>


### [18] [Trajectory-Derived Confidence for Reliable, Resource-Aware Clinical Text-to-SQL Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04156)
*Mincheol Daniel Song,Joshua Ward,Jake Jung,Guang Cheng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Sentinel, a confidence and stopping mechanism for LLM-based clinical text-to-SQL agents that improves reliability, safety, and efficiency by learning when to abstain or stop early.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents used for clinical text-to-SQL tasks must be highly reliable because errors in healthcare settings are costly and unsafe. Current agents autonomously perform multi-step reasoning but lack the ability to judge whether their reasoning processes or outputs are trustworthy. This leads to two major problems: (1) safety and reliability risks, since untrustworthy answers may be delivered in high-stakes domains; and (2) resource waste, because computational budget is spent on trajectories that turn out to be incorrect and must be discarded. The authors aim to provide a principled way to monitor and control these agents so that they only answer when sufficiently reliable and avoid wasting computation on doomed reasoning paths.

Method: The authors propose Sentinel, a trajectory-derived, classifier-based confidence layer that sits on top of LLM agents for text-to-SQL. Sentinel monitors multiple information sources—agent reasoning traces, code, and database outputs—and makes three types of stop/abstain decisions: (1) pre-run refusal of unanswerable questions, (2) mid-run halting of trajectories that appear doomed to fail, and (3) post-run withholding of answers deemed untrustworthy. They formulate the decision-making problem using Chow’s rule to optimally trade off coverage and accuracy under a utility-based Reliability Score, which reflects the EHRSQL shared task’s evaluation scheme. Sentinel is trained and evaluated on the EHRSQL benchmark, using agent trajectories and outcomes as supervision for the confidence classifier.

Result: On the EHRSQL benchmark, Sentinel significantly improves reliability and efficiency. Under a low-penalty (low utility) setting for mistakes, the Reliability Score increases from +0.08 for the base agent to +0.24 with Sentinel, outperforming a naive strategy of refusing all questions, which yields +0.03. With Sentinel, the accuracy of delivered answers rises from 54% to 69%, while coverage decreases from 84% to 55%, indicating more selective but higher-quality responses. In high-stakes settings where incorrect answers are heavily penalized, the underlying agents almost never meet the reliability threshold, and Sentinel learns to abstain, achieving the baseline refusal score of +0.03, whereas the unmonitored agent performs very poorly with a score of -3.02. Additionally, Sentinel’s stopping decisions reduce computational cost by eliminating 13–28% of agent steps in low-stakes conditions, with minimal or no degradation in reliability.

Conclusion: Sentinel provides an effective confidence and stopping mechanism for LLM-based clinical text-to-SQL systems, improving both safety and computational efficiency. By learning when to refuse, halt, or withhold answers based on trajectory-derived signals and optimizing decisions under a utility-weighted Reliability Score, Sentinel yields more accurate delivered answers at controlled coverage, detects when agents are not reliable enough to respond in high-stakes scenarios, and saves computational resources by cutting unproductive reasoning steps. This framework demonstrates that integrating principled abstention and early stopping into LLM agents can substantially enhance their viability for safety-critical applications like healthcare.

Abstract: LLM agents for clinical text-to-SQL applications reason autonomously over multiple steps but cannot assess whether their own reasoning or outputs can be trusted. In high leverage applications such as healthcare, this presents a critical risk where system mistakes can be costly. These reliability failures are also resource failures: an incorrect reasoning trajectory spends computation budget on outputs that must be discarded. We introduce Sentinel, a trajectory-derived, classifier-based confidence layer that analyzes an agent's reasoning, code and database outputs to decide at three points whether to stop: refusing unanswerable questions before the agent runs, halting doomed trajectories mid-run, and withholding untrustworthy answers at delivery. Here, utilizing Chow's rule, we optimize decisions under the EHRSQL shared task's Reliability Score, which penalizes incorrect answers given a utility weighting, and find on the benchmark EHRSQL that Sentinel raises this score from +0.08 to +0.24 when mistakes have a low utility weighting, well above the +0.03 earned by refusing every question, with delivered-answer accuracy rising from 54% to 69% as coverage falls from 84% to 55%. At higher stakes the agents we test rarely answer reliably enough to deliver, and Sentinel detects this on its own, abstaining to that same +0.03 where the unmonitored agent scores -3.02. The same stopping decisions cut computation: at low stakes, where the system still answers, Sentinel eliminates 13-28% of agent steps at little or no reliability cost.

</details>


### [19] [Can LLMs Separate Pasted Artifacts from User Speech? Absorption at Unmarked Prompt Seams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04210)
*Sugam Panthi,Muhaiminul Yeamin,Rabab Abdelfattah*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how large language models mistakenly absorb trailing user comments into pasted text during editing, introduces a benchmark (SEAM) to test this, and shows that explicit boundaries help but do not fully prevent the issue.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Users often paste text and then add comments or instructions below, but LLMs receive all of this as a single plain-text sequence. This can cause the model to treat user comments as part of the pasted content, especially in editing tasks, leading to unwanted changes and reliability issues. Existing benchmarks assume the model is told exactly which parts are instructions and which are data, so they fail to capture this realistic but subtle failure mode. The authors want to systematically measure and understand this absorption behavior to improve model safety and usability.

Method: The authors build SEAM, a controlled benchmark of 300 text-editing examples. For each example, they create six matched prompt variants that differ only in how the boundary between pasted text and later user speech is indicated (e.g., just a newline, a blank line, explicit boundary markers, etc.). They then evaluate 20 different LLMs, measuring how often the model’s edited output incorrectly includes the user’s trailing comment as if it were part of the pasted text. They also manipulate whether the trailing comment stylistically “fits” the pasted content (e.g., a code comment after code) to test how semantic similarity affects absorption rates.

Result: Across 20 evaluated LLMs, the rate at which trailing user comments are absorbed into the edited text when separated only by a newline ranges from 7.7% to 66.7%, showing the problem is both common and model-dependent. Simply adding a blank line between pasted text and the user comment does not significantly reduce absorption for any model. In contrast, using explicit boundary markers (e.g., textual delimiters) reduces absorption in 19 of 20 models, though it does not eliminate it. When comments are semantically aligned with the pasted material—such as a natural-looking code comment following code—the absorption rate increases significantly for 17 of 20 models.

Conclusion: LLMs frequently fail to distinguish between pasted material and subsequent user speech in realistic editing scenarios, leading to unintended inclusion of user comments in the text being edited. This absorption effect persists even with simple formatting cues like newlines or blank lines, and while explicit boundary markers substantially mitigate the issue, they do not fully solve it. The findings imply that current instruction/data separation capabilities are brittle in naturalistic settings and that both prompt design and model training need to better handle unmarked or weakly marked boundaries between user-provided content and instructions.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) receive each user message as plain text, even when it combines text from different sources. For example, a user may paste text into a prompt and keep typing a comment directly below it. We study absorption: a phenomenon where the model treats a trailing user comment as part of the pasted text, returning it inside the edited text. This happens even though the user did not intend the comment to become part of that text. Existing instruction-data separation benchmarks tell the model which text is instruction and which is data, then test whether it obeys that separation. They do not test harmless user speech following an unmarked paste. We introduce SEAM, a controlled benchmark of 300 editing examples. Each example is tested under six matched conditions that vary how the boundary between pasted text and later user speech is expressed. Across 20 models, absorption at a bare newline ranges from 7.7% to 66.7%. Adding a blank line does not significantly reduce absorption in any model, while boundary markers reduce it in 19 of 20 models. Comments that fit the pasted text, such as a code comment typed after code, are absorbed significantly more often in 17 of 20 models. Models often fail to separate pasted material from later user speech, and explicit boundaries reduce but do not remove this failure.

</details>


### [20] [Conformal Prediction with Paraphrase-Aware Scoring for LLM Uncertainty Quantification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04239)
*Jiayi Xin,Evan Qiang,Zihan Zhu,Xiang Li,Weijie J. Su,Qi Long*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces a paraphrase-aware uncertainty quantification framework for LLMs that remains robust when inputs are reworded, yielding compact, well-calibrated prediction sets across multiple QA benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing uncertainty quantification methods for LLMs, including conformal prediction, produce unstable confidence estimates when inputs are paraphrased but semantically equivalent. This instability undermines reliability, especially in safety-critical or user-facing applications where small wording changes are common. The authors aim to develop an uncertainty quantification method that is robust to such semantic rewordings while preserving formal coverage guarantees.

Method: The authors propose a paraphrase-aware UQ framework that leverages LLM hidden states. They train a lightweight proxy model on these hidden states to predict label-wise scores, then aggregate the proxy’s predictions across multiple paraphrases of each input. These aggregated outputs define label-wise nonconformity scores used in a conformal prediction procedure. They analyze conditions—score exchangeability and a distributional alignment condition for test-only rewording—under which conformal calibration retains marginal coverage. The method is evaluated under three regimes: no rewording, full rewording of both calibration and test sets, and semi-rewording where only the test set is paraphrased.

Result: Across seven multiple-choice QA benchmarks and multiple LLM families, the proposed method yields prediction sets that are both compact (small set sizes) and have empirical coverage close to the target nominal level. This performance holds even in the challenging semi-reworded setting where only test data are paraphrased. Ablation studies indicate that the learned proxy model is primarily responsible for the reduction in prediction set size, while paraphrase-augmented training and inference-time paraphrase aggregation contribute to improved robustness and stability under rewording.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that paraphrase-aware UQ can substantially improve the robustness and efficiency of conformal prediction for LLMs under semantic rewordings. By combining a hidden-state-based proxy model with paraphrase aggregation, the framework maintains near-nominal coverage with smaller prediction sets, even when test inputs are rephrased. This demonstrates a practical path toward more reliable confidence estimates for LLMs in realistic, paraphrase-rich usage scenarios.

Abstract: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) for large language models (LLMs) aims to provide reliable measures of predictive confidence, yet current methods are often unstable under meaning-preserving perturbations. Semantically equivalent paraphrases can induce substantial variability in predictive confidence, even for methods with formal guarantees, such as conformal prediction. To address this issue, we propose a paraphrase-aware UQ framework robust to semantic rewordings. Our approach trains a lightweight proxy model on LLM hidden states and aggregates its predictions across paraphrases to construct label-wise nonconformity scores. Under score exchangeability, conformal calibration retains marginal coverage. This guarantee can also hold under test-only rewording, provided that the paraphrase pipeline satisfies an additional distributional alignment condition. We evaluate three settings (normal, fully reworded, and semi-reworded) which apply rewording to neither dataset, both calibration and test datasets, or only the test dataset, respectively. Across seven multiple-choice QA benchmarks and multiple model families, our method produces compact prediction sets with empirical coverage generally near the nominal target, even in the semi-reworded setting. Ablation studies show that the learned proxy accounts for most of the reduction in set size, while paraphrase-augmented training and inference-time aggregation improve stability under rewording. Code is available at https://github.com/Raina-Xin/PA_Score.

</details>


### [21] [Playing social deduction games with reinforcement fine-tuned large language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04261)
*Lingzhe Zhang,Yunpeng Zhai,Tong Jia,Kening Zheng,Chiming Duan,Minghua He,Zhaoyang Liu,Bolin Ding,Philip S. Yu,Ying Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how reinforcement fine-tuning changes LLMs’ behavior in social deduction games, finding that simple win/loss optimization is insufficient but carefully designed social feedback can substantially improve social reasoning and influence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs are increasingly deployed in interactive and multi‑agent settings, it is important to understand how reinforcement fine‑tuning shapes their social behaviors, especially in contexts requiring strategic reasoning, perspective‑taking and coordination. Social deduction games provide a controlled yet rich testbed to probe these capabilities and to identify which training signals actually lead to better social intelligence.

Method: The authors use hidden‑role social deduction games as an evaluation and training environment for LLM agents. They compare base models and reinforcement‑fine‑tuned models across tasks that demand hidden‑state inference (social reading) and strategically shaping others’ actions (social influence). They experiment with different reward designs: terminal win–loss rewards, behaviour‑specific rewards reflecting social‑reading or influence performance, and a multi‑agent ‘social‑cognitive’ RFT setup where same‑side agents are jointly trained using both reading and influence signals. Performance is measured on game‑play tasks (e.g., inferring roles, steering votes) and via human judgements of strategic competence, persuasiveness and social utility.

Result: Optimizing only for terminal win–loss leads to weak and unreliable improvements in actual social deduction skill, indicating that such rewards are too sparse and noisy. In contrast, RFT with richer, behaviour‑specific rewards markedly improves social reading: models get better at inferring hidden roles from public discussion, updating beliefs and forecasting others’ actions. Social influence abilities—steering votes, team approvals and group decisions—also improve under RFT but are more sensitive to the exact reward design and interaction structure. The best performance is obtained with multi‑agent social‑cognitive RFT that jointly trains agents on both reading and influence, yielding the strongest gains in gameplay metrics and in human‑rated strategic and social qualities.

Conclusion: Reinforcement fine‑tuning meaningfully alters LLMs’ social behavior, but naive optimization of final game outcomes is insufficient for cultivating robust social deduction skills. Dense, behaviourally targeted social signals and structured multi‑agent training are far more effective, especially when they jointly train social reading and social influence. These findings move toward a behavioral learning theory for machine social intelligence and suggest concrete principles for designing RFT pipelines when deploying LLMs in complex, interactive social environments.

Abstract: Reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) is increasingly used in applications where large language models (LLMs) interact with humans and other agents. Here we use social deduction games to study how RFT changes LLMs' social behaviour. We let fine-tuned and base LLM agents play hidden-role games that require hidden-state inference, social reading and vote steering. Our results show that LLM agents do not reliably acquire social-deduction ability by directly optimizing terminal win--loss outcomes, suggesting that final game results provide a sparse and noisy signal for socially interactive learning. However, RFT is particularly effective at improving social reading, including tasks that require agents to infer hidden roles from public discussion, update beliefs over time and predict other agents' future decisions. We further show that RFT can also improve social influence, including tasks that require agents to steer votes, team approvals and collective decisions, although these gains depend more strongly on behaviourally specific rewards and structured interaction settings. Finally, we show that LLMs' ability to play social deduction games can be further improved through multi-agent social-cognitive reinforcement fine-tuning, which combines social-reading and social-influence signals during same-side multi-agent training. These learned behaviours also receive more favourable human evaluations of strategic competence, persuasiveness and social usefulness. Together, these results enrich our understanding of how RFT changes LLMs' social behaviour and provide a step toward a behavioural learning theory for machine social intelligence.

</details>


### [22] [AI-Enabled Quality Assurance for Multiple-Choice Assessment Items](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04267)
*Steven Moore,Nicholas Diana*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper reviews methods for automatically checking and improving the quality of multiple-choice questions, showing current tools are limited and proposing a more rigorous, stepwise evaluation framework.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multiple-choice questions can now be generated at scale, especially with NLP and generative models, but assessing their quality (e.g., detecting flaws, ensuring fairness and validity) is hard and resource-intensive. There is a need to understand what automated methods exist for detecting item-writing flaws and how effective they are, in order to support scalable, reliable assessment and benchmarking.

Method: The authors conduct a focused narrative review. They search databases, follow citations, and include nominated sources to identify relevant work, ending up with fourteen full-text research reports. They analyze these studies by distinguishing between surface-level checks (e.g., format or grammar) and deeper, content-sensitive judgments (e.g., validity of options). They develop and apply a 19-criterion rubric for item quality, mapping each criterion to detection methods used in the literature and summarizing the reported evidence for those methods.

Result: The review finds that many systems report high overall or label-level accuracy, but often perform poorly at detecting positive cases of flaws (low sensitivity/recall). The definitions used for rubric criteria and the reference standards (gold labels) vary considerably across studies, reducing comparability. Evidence that automated systems can effectively revise or repair items is mixed, and previous reports of associations between quality indicators and outcomes do not demonstrate that fixing identified issues actually improves assessment quality.

Conclusion: Current automated approaches to quality assurance for multiple-choice questions are fragmented and only partially effective, especially for content-sensitive judgments and actual item repair. The authors recommend conceptualizing quality assurance as a sequence of distinct, independently validated decision steps. They call for criterion-specific reporting of performance, careful calibration of human review in the loop, and outcome-based evaluation of whether automated revisions genuinely enhance assessment quality and measurement properties.

Abstract: Generating multiple-choice questions is increasingly scalable, but establishing their assessment quality remains difficult. We present a focused narrative review of automated item-writing flaw detection, revision, psychometric screening, and NLP benchmark auditing. Database searches, citation retrieval, and nominated sources yield fourteen research reports reviewed in full text. We distinguish surface checks from content-sensitive judgments and map a 19-criterion rubric to detection methods and reported evidence. High label-level accuracy often coexists with weak positive case detection, while rubric definitions and reference standards vary. Revision evidence is mixed, and the associations reported in prior work do not establish the effects of repair. We propose evaluating quality assurance as a sequence of independently validated decisions, with criterion-specific reporting, calibrated human review, and outcome-based assessment of revisions.

</details>


### [23] [Evaluating Modeling Approaches for Experience-Level Classification in Job Description](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04304)
*Celia Liang,Eddie Wu,Shiqi Wang,Yonah You*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a structure-aware Section-Aware BERT model to predict required job experience levels from recruitment texts by explicitly modeling different sections (title, responsibilities, requirements) and compares it with rule-based, TF-IDF, and large language model approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recruitment texts have explicit internal structure, and different sections contribute unequally to signaling required experience level, but typical text classification methods ignore this structure. There is also a need to understand the limits of classical models versus large language models on structured recruitment data, particularly for accurately identifying job experience requirements, which is challenging when titles are ambiguous and experience-level boundaries are fuzzy.

Method: The authors design a Section-Aware BERT framework that first segments recruitment postings into key paragraphs (title, responsibilities, requirements) and encodes them separately, then integrates these representations for final experience level prediction. They compare this structure-aware method against rule-based systems, TF-IDF-based baselines, and large language models evaluated in both few-shot prompting and fine-tuning regimes on the same dataset. They also conduct error analysis to understand systematic failure modes, such as confusion between adjacent experience levels.

Result: Experiments show that incorporating explicit structural segmentation of recruitment texts into the BERT model significantly boosts accuracy for predicting experience levels, especially when job titles alone are not clearly indicative. The structured model outperforms rule-based, TF-IDF, and LLM baselines under the evaluated settings, and analysis highlights prevalent misclassification patterns, such as conflating Entry with Senior roles and difficulty distinguishing Mid-level positions.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling the section structure of recruitment postings leads to better prediction of required experience levels compared with traditional flat text classification and current LLM approaches in the tested setups. The work offers both an effective architecture (Section-Aware BERT) and an analytical lens for studying structured recruitment texts, while revealing inherent task challenges like ambiguous titles and fuzzy boundaries between experience levels.

Abstract: This paper investigates the task of predicting job experience levels in recruitment texts, aiming to automatically identify the qualifications required for positions. Unlike traditional text classification, recruitment texts typically possess explicit internal structures, with different paragraphs playing disproportionate roles in conveying experience clues. To address this, we propose a structure-aware Section-Aware BERT approach that segments and encodes key paragraphs (titles, responsibilities, requirements) for integrated modeling, building upon rule-based systems and classical baselines TF-IDF. Simultaneously, we evaluate large language models under both few-shot and fine-tuning settings on the same dataset to compare the capability boundaries of different modeling paradigms. Experimental results demonstrate that explicitly leveraging text structure significantly improves experience level prediction performance, particularly in scenarios with ambiguous job titles. Further error analysis reveals systemic challenges in this task, including confusion between Entry and Senior levels and the blurred boundaries of Mid-level positions. This research provides an effective modeling approach and analytical framework for understanding structured recruitment texts.

</details>


### [24] [Evidence and Intervention: A Coupled Active-Inference Extension of Rational Speech Act Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04347)
*Yonghyeon Gwon,Elliot Murphy,Chun Kee Chung*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose a new active-inference model of dialogue that generalizes RSA, separating different kinds of updates (state inference, partner learning, clarification decisions, and habits), and showing how RSA appears as a special one-shot case.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard one-shot Rational Speech Act (RSA) models treat interpretation as inference over speaker meaning but do not distinguish different causal sources of identical utterances or the different learning consequences of identical interpretations. This makes it hard to capture how people simultaneously infer a partner’s current state, learn longer-term properties of that partner, decide whether to clarify, and develop habits over time in dialogue. The authors aim to build a model that more faithfully reflects the dynamic, interactive, and partner-specific nature of conversation.

Method: They construct a coupled active-inference model of dialogue where the listener’s likelihood for an utterance is given by the policy distribution they attribute to the speaker. Technically, this embeds the speaker’s expected free energy within the listener’s variational free energy. In this framework, each utterance is treated simultaneously as evidence about the partner and as an intervention on them. They analytically identify four distinct update processes—state inference, parameter learning, clarification/repair evaluation, and policy priors shaped by habit and time cost—and examine a restricted one-step, exact-inference case to show that the model reduces to standard RSA. They then work through concrete scenarios to illustrate the model’s behavior.

Result: The model cleanly separates four processes that RSA usually collapses into a single update: (1) inference about the partner’s current pragmatic state, (2) learning of partner-specific parameters, (3) prospective evaluation of clarification or repair moves, and (4) the formation of policy priors reflecting habits and time pressure. Under strong restrictions (single step, exact inference), the model reproduces RSA speaker and listener behavior, establishing RSA as a limiting case. In more general settings, the updates follow different rules and timescales, leading to testable predictions about when adaptations will be transient, partner-specific, or generalizable. Worked examples show phenomena such as audience design reversing after clarification, stable but mistaken mutual understanding (self-confirming misunderstanding), and rationally ending a conversation despite residual uncertainty.

Conclusion: The coupled active-inference framework positions dialogue as mutual, ongoing inference rather than just code-like message passing. It generalizes RSA by embedding speaker and listener as interacting agents whose utterances are both communicative signals and epistemic actions. This allows the model to capture rich phenomena like partner-specific adaptation, clarification strategies, and persistent misunderstandings, while viewing standard RSA as a special, limited case. The authors argue that this supports critiques of equating language with communication and instead emphasizes communication as one application of a more general inferential use of linguistic structure.

Abstract: Identical utterance choices can arise from different communicative causes, and identical interpretations can leave different traces in what a listener learns. Rational Speech Act (RSA) models treat interpretation as inference over speaker meaning, but standard one-shot RSA does not intrinsically distinguish these causal update targets. We develop a coupled active-inference model of dialogue in which a listener's likelihood for an utterance is the policy distribution attributed to the speaker, placing the speaker's expected free energy within the listener's variational free energy. Each utterance is therefore both evidence about and an intervention on a partner. The model separates four updates that RSA approaches typically collapse: inference about the partner's current pragmatic state; learning of partner-specific parameters; prospective evaluation of clarification or repair; and a policy prior shaped by habit and a context-sensitive price of time. Under one-step, exact-inference restrictions, the model recovers the RSA speaker and listener, with RSA as the restricted single-turn limit of the coupled process. Outside these restrictions, the updates obey distinct rules and timescales, predicting which adaptations persist, remain partner-specific, or transfer. Worked examples show audience design reversing after clarification, self-confirming misunderstanding in which both interlocutors have low free energy while disagreeing about reference, and rational closing before uncertainty is resolved. Consistent with critiques of equating natural language with communication, the model treats communication as a downstream use of linguistic structure and recasts production and interpretation as coupled inference: speaking is both an intervention on a partner and an epistemic action that samples evidence for the speaker's model of that partner.

</details>


### [25] [Boundaries Agree, Labels Do Not: Intra-Annotator Dynamics as a Kind of Training Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04370)
*Marharyta Shvets*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a new way to evaluate annotation quality by measuring how consistently the same annotator reproduces their own interpretations of text over time, and uses this to distinguish human-like from model-like annotation patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current work on annotation quality in language model training either aggregates annotators into a pseudo–ground truth and measures agreement, or treats disagreement as a useful signal. Both approaches compare different people at a single point in time, which misses how an individual’s interpretations may vary across time. Since much training data is interpretive and lacks an objective ground truth, there is a need for a measure that captures the temporal stability and structure of a single annotator’s judgments, and that can also detect when purportedly human annotations might actually be model-generated or model-contaminated.

Method: The authors study intra-annotator consistency over time for both a human expert and several LLM families. One expert human and three LLM families each annotated three Sumerian myths. The task had two layers: (1) segment the text into units; (2) label each segment with one of seven causal function states. The same annotators (human or model, with fixed prompts/settings) repeated the task months apart. The authors then compared, for each annotator, how similar the segment boundaries were across runs and how similar the label assignments and function start points were, analyzing alignment and shifts between runs.

Result: The expert human was highly consistent in where they segmented the text but less consistent in the labels they applied to those segments across time, in all three myths. Specifically, the labels changed in a structured way: across runs, the same functional sequence appeared but with the starting point shifted by about one step. In contrast, the LLMs did not show this human-like pattern. For the models, the relationship between boundary stability and label stability varied by myth: sometimes labels were more stable than boundaries, sometimes less, and the magnitude and sign of the gap were inconsistent. Moreover, model runs tended to initiate functional sequences at the same positions rather than showing the shifted-start pattern observed in the human.

Conclusion: The temporal pattern of stability between segmentation and labeling, and how functional sequences line up across repeated annotations, can serve as a measure of data quality and a diagnostic for contamination. Genuine human interpretive annotations are expected to show stable boundaries but more flexible, structured variation in labels, including shifted starting points in functional sequences. Annotations whose labels are as stable as their boundaries and whose functional sequences start in sync across runs resemble model behavior and may indicate that the data is model-generated or model-influenced rather than authentic human annotation.

Abstract: Data quality now matters as much as compute for training language models. Much training data comes from human annotation of text, and interpretive annotation has no ground truth that could settle what is "accurate". Two lines of work respond to this. One combines annotators into a "ground truth" and measures how well they agree with each other; the other treats their disagreement as a signal. Both compare different people at one point in time. We measure something else: how well one reader reproduces their own reading of the same text over time. One expert human reader and three LLM families segmented three Sumerian myths and labelled the causal function of each segment with one of seven states. Across runs months apart, the human cut the text in much the same places but named the segments differently, in every myth. The models show no such consistent pattern: their gap between the two layers is positive in some myths and negative in others, and its size varies. The human's label changes are not random: the runs go through much the same functions but start them one step apart, while model runs start them at the same places. We argue that this pattern is a usable measure of data quality and a contamination check: a "human" annotation whose labels are as stable as its boundaries, and whose functions start in sync, looks like a model's.

</details>


### [26] [GlitchPatch: Repairing Glitch Tokens in Frozen Language Models via Local Retokenization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04399)
*Kunsheng Tang,Peigui Qi,Yide Song,Peijun Huang,Weiming Zhang,Nenghai Yu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces GlitchPatch, a tokenizer-side method to repair glitch tokens in frozen LLMs by locally retokenizing them with behaviorally optimized replacements, greatly reducing glitch-induced failures without changing model parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Glitch tokens cause LLMs to produce outputs that are inconsistent with their inputs, harming reliability. Existing repair approaches require modifying model internals, which is infeasible for frozen or closed-source checkpoints and can be risky to deploy. The authors want a practical, deployable way to fix glitch tokens from the tokenizer side while minimizing collateral damage to normal tokens.

Method: First, the authors empirically analyze a naive repair strategy: deleting BPE merge rules associated with glitch tokens. They study how different decomposition granularities affect fix rates and side effects on normal tokens, finding non-monotonic behavior in fixes and monotonically increasing collateral damage. Based on these insights, they design GlitchPatch, a two-stage framework for frozen LLMs. In an offline stage, they apply Behavioral Path Optimization (BPO) to search for and validate the best replacement token sequences for each glitch token, compiling them into a rule table. In an online stage, incoming text is tokenized as usual, but any token IDs matching glitch tokens are replaced with their optimized token sequences according to the rule table, without modifying model parameters or internal states. They test this across ten models and six tokenizer families.

Result: GlitchPatch achieves an average fix rate of 85.10% across evaluated glitch tokens, which is 14.37 percentage points better than the strongest baseline method. It reduces the overall glitch rate from 14.88% to 2.27%. The method shows 0.00% regression rate (RR) in full-vocabulary evaluation and, by design, leaves inputs unchanged when no rule is applicable. Additional experiments show that the approach has acceptable time cost and does not significantly harm language understanding or model capabilities, supporting its practicality.

Conclusion: Tokenizer-side repair via local retokenization can substantially mitigate glitch token behavior in frozen LLMs without touching the model weights. GlitchPatch, using behaviorally optimized replacement sequences and a rule table applied at inference time, provides a practical and low-risk approach that generalizes across models and tokenizer families, significantly improving tokenizer reliability while avoiding regressions on normal tokens.

Abstract: Glitch tokens are anomalous vocabulary entries that can cause large language models (LLMs) to produce outputs inconsistent with their inputs. Existing repair methods require access to model internals, making them impractical for frozen checkpoints. We investigate whether glitch tokens can be repaired outside the model by optimizing the input tokenization. An empirical study on BPE merge-rule deletion reveals that (1)deleting a glitch token's merge rule can fix a substantial fraction of failures, yet disrupting normal tokens sharing intermediate merge nodes causes the overall glitch rate to rise, and (2)different decomposition granularities yield non-monotonic fix rates while collateral damage on normal tokens grows monotonically. Motivated by these findings, we propose GlitchPatch, a repair framework for frozen language models based on local retokenization, consisting of two stages: the offline stage uses Behavioral Path Optimization (BPO) to find the behaviorally optimal replacement token sequence for each glitch token and compiles validated replacements into a rule table; the online stage substitutes only the IDs of matched glitch tokens in the canonical token sequence, with no modification to model parameters or internal states. Experiments on ten models spanning six tokenizer families show that GlitchPatch achieves an 85.10% mean fix rate, outperforming the strongest baseline by 14.37 percentage points, and reduces the average glitch rate from 14.88% to 2.27%. GlitchPatch achieves a 0.00% RR in full-vocabulary evaluation and leaves rule-unmatched inputs unchanged by design. We further evaluate the practical impact of repair from the perspectives of time cost, language understanding, and capability, supporting its deployment feasibility. We hope this work provides a practical option for improving tokenizer reliability.

</details>


### [27] [XTurnix: Large-Scale Self-Supervised Turn Control through Two-State Binary Decisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04400)
*Zhanxun Liu,Yifan Duan,Hengtao Wu,Chen Yang,Qinyuan Cheng,Kun Wang,Xingyu Zeng,Xipeng Qiu,Chaochao Lu,Xie Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: XTurnix is a compact text-based model for unified turn-taking control in dialogue systems, making binary decisions for starting/stopping listening or speaking based on full dialogue history, and achieving state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing real-time dialogue turn-taking systems rely on heterogeneous, task-specific turn labels, limited annotations, and evaluations on isolated utterances. This makes it hard to deploy a single, causal controller that operates consistently across both listening and speaking states using full conversational context. There is a need for a unified, data-efficient, and context-aware turn control mechanism that can be easily applied across tasks and benchmarks.

Method: The authors design XTurnix, a compact, text-only model that casts turn-taking as two binary decisions conditioned on whether the AI is currently listening or speaking. The model outputs a single control token representing one of four state-action combinations, using the entire dialogue history as input. It is pretrained on 5.5M automatically derived causal action examples from timestamped two-speaker transcripts and then fine-tuned on synthetic multi-turn data that balances the distribution across the four labels. XTurnix is evaluated on four public benchmarks (SemanticVAD, LiveKit, Smart-Turn Bench, Easy-Turn) and a balanced, self-curated benchmark.

Result: On public benchmarks, XTurnix achieves the best performance on all SemanticVAD and LiveKit splits, matches the native Smart-Turn model on Smart-Turn Bench, and attains the highest incomplete-turn accuracy on Easy-Turn. On the self-curated balanced benchmark, XTurnix attains 89.06% accuracy, surpassing the strongest third-party baseline by over 20 percentage points (68.75%), with F1 scores between 84.21% and 90.63% across all four action categories.

Conclusion: XTurnix demonstrates that a single compact, text-based model can serve as a unified controller for turn-taking in dialogue systems across both listening and speaking states, using complete conversational context. Its strong results across multiple benchmarks indicate that such unified, data-driven turn control is feasible and competitive with or superior to task-specific baselines. The authors release code and an interactive demo to facilitate adoption and further research.

Abstract: General turn-taking behavior in real-time dialogue systems requires deciding whether to keep listening or start responding while listening, and whether to continue or stop while speaking. Existing turn detectors use heterogeneous, task-specific label spaces and are often trained on limited annotations or evaluated on isolated utterances, making them difficult to use as a unified causal controller with comprehensive context. We propose XTurnix, a compact text-based model that formulates turn control as two binary decisions conditioned on the AI's current listening or speaking state and predicts a single control token from the complete dialogue history. XTurnix is pretrained on 5.5 million causal action examples automatically derived from timestamped two-speaker transcripts, then fine-tuned on synthetic multi-turn examples with a flatter distribution across the four state-action labels. We evaluate XTurnix on four public benchmarks and a balanced self-curated benchmark. Across the public benchmarks, XTurnix achieves the best results on all SemanticVAD and LiveKit splits, ties the native Smart-Turn model on Smart-Turn Bench, and achieves the highest incomplete-turn accuracy on Easy-Turn. On the self-curated benchmark, it reaches 89.06% accuracy, more than 20 percentage points above the strongest third-party baseline at 68.75%, while maintaining F1 scores between 84.21% and 90.63% across all four categories. These results demonstrate unified listening- and speaking-state turn control in a single compact model. Code is available at https://github.com/xcc-zach/xturnix, with an interactive demo at https://huggingface.co/spaces/xcczach/xturnix-demo.

</details>


### [28] [Ideological Stance Detection in a Low-Resource Language: Polarization in Bangladeshi Public vs Private University Discourse on Social Media](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04401)
*Safaruzzaman Shovo,Monowar Islam,Asif Hossain,Sameya Akhter,Md. Shamsul Islam*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper builds and analyzes a labeled Bengali social media dataset to study polarization between public and private universities and evaluates multiple ML and LLM models for stance classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Debates about public vs. private universities in Bangladesh are intense and polarizing on social media, but Bengali is a low-resource language with little existing data or tools for systematically measuring this polarization. The authors aim to fill this gap by creating a labeled dataset and benchmarking models that can automatically classify user stances, enabling quantitative study of polarization in Bengali.

Method: The authors manually collected 4,060 Bengali social media comments related to public vs. private universities and annotated them into three stance categories: Pro-Public, Pro-Private, and Neutral. Annotation quality was assessed using Fleiss's Kappa, achieving 0.89, indicating high inter-annotator agreement. They trained and evaluated classical machine learning models (SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost), a BiLSTM neural network, and a hybrid BanglaBERT+XGBoost model. They also evaluated several state-of-the-art large language models in zero-shot mode (Claude Sonnet 4, DeepSeek-V3.1, Llama 4 Maverick, Kimi K2 Thinking, Qwen3-235B Thinking) on the same classification task, comparing performance using accuracy and macro F1 scores.

Result: The hybrid BanglaBERT+XGBoost supervised model achieved 91.81% accuracy and a macro F1 score of 91.70%, outperforming all other supervised baselines (classical ML, BiLSTM, and transformer-only models). However, the zero-shot Llama 4 Maverick Thinking model surpassed all supervised approaches, achieving a macro F1 of 0.931 and overall accuracy of 93.31% without any task-specific fine-tuning. The content analysis revealed recognizable patterns of polarization: Pro-Private comments focus on modern facilities and timely graduation, while Pro-Public comments stress affordability and access to government jobs.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates that polarization between public and private universities in Bangladesh can be effectively quantified using a newly constructed, high-quality Bengali social media dataset. Advanced LLMs, particularly Llama 4 Maverick in zero-shot mode, can outperform traditional ML, DL, and transformer-based supervised models on stance classification in a low-resource language setting. The observed thematic differences between Pro-Private and Pro-Public stances highlight distinct priorities and grievances among users. The dataset and benchmarks provide a foundation for future computational studies of social media polarization in Bengali and other low-resource languages.

Abstract: Public vs. private universities is a debatable issue, and it creates polarization on social media in Bangladesh. Debate on quality, jobs, and prestige is passionate among the students, parents, and graduates, the majority of whom speak Bengali, a low-resource language. To measure this polarization, this paper introduces a manually annotated dataset of 4,060 Bengali comments labeled as Pro-Public, Pro-Private, or Neutral. We evaluated the quality of our annotations by Fleiss's Kappa agreement that was 0.89, corresponding to a high agreement among annotators. The classical ML (SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost), BiLSTM network, hybrid BanglaBERT+XGBoost models and the state-of-the-art zero-shot LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4, DeepSeek-V3.1, Llama 4 Maverick, Kimi K2 Thinking, Qwen3-235B Thinking) models are evaluated. The accuracy of BanglaBERT+XGBoost is 91.81% and macro F1 score is 91.70%, which is higher than all the supervised baselines. The zero-shot Llama 4 Maverick Thinking achieves a macro F1 of 0.931 (overall accuracy of 93.31%) without any fine-tuning. All machine learning (ML), deep machine learning (DL) and transformer models were outperformed by the zero-shot Llama 4 Maverick model. Polarization also is evident, in some ways more clearly in the Pro-Private comments, which emphasize modern facilities and timely graduation, versus the Pro-Public comments, which emphasize affordability and government jobs. Our findings open new directions for analyzing social media polarization in low-resource languages.

</details>


### [29] [Saying, Not Knowing: Aggressively GGUF-Quantized Small Language Models Still Write Rare Words They Can No Longer Define](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04403)
*Saurabh Kumar Singh,Yogeshwar Singh Dadwhal,Malhar Vedak*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how aggressive post-training quantization (especially Q2 K-quants in GGUF) affects language models’ ability to understand and define rare words.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although mixed-precision K-quant GGUF quantization is standard for deploying open-weight LLMs on consumer hardware, its impact on fine-grained lexical/semantic competence—particularly for rare words—has not been systematically evaluated.

Method: They examine 27 quantized model artifacts across 13 model families and 4 architecture types (0.35B–14B parameters), stepping down each quantization ladder to Q2_K (~2.6 bits/weight). They test 429 frequency-validated rare English words with two probes: (1) surface inclusion of a prompt-given word and its one-sentence definition, scored by a tiered multi-synonym matcher; (2) correctness of the generated definitions, evaluated via a blind LLM-judge panel with human verification. They add two control experiments: rarity-sensitivity within the rare set and a 100-word common-word set. They correlate degradation with tokenizer vocab size and parameter count, and compare quantization levels (e.g., Q4_K_M) and WikiText-2 perplexity against lexical performance.

Result: At Q2 three regimes appear: (i) some models collapse entirely; (ii) all sub-2B models show severe semantic degradation, especially in definitions; (iii) models above ~3B largely preserve lexical competence. In sub-2B models, definition accuracy drops 20–67% from baseline, usually much more than simple word-inclusion. Within rare words, performance declines with rarity in 6/7 sub-2B models; on the mixed rare/common set, rare words degrade more in all 8 tested models, significantly in 6. Tokenizer vocab size weakly correlates with damage (rho=0.12), while parameter count strongly correlates (rho=0.72), consistent within most same-tokenizer families. Q4_K_M stays lexically accurate for models ≥1B. Lexical damage is frequency-graded, model-provider dependent, and not predicted by WikiText-2 perplexity; e.g., across 9 matched ladders, Q2 penalties are similar while definition retention varies wildly (3.6% vs 43.6% loss).

Conclusion: Aggressive quantization, especially Q2 on small models, can yield systems that produce fluent text but lose genuine semantic knowledge of rare words. The harm is strongly size- and provider-dependent, not well-captured by standard perplexity metrics, and can be severe even when text remains coherent. Safer deployment requires per-artifact validation of semantic competence—particularly for rare, high-stakes vocabulary—rather than relying on generic benchmarks or assuming quantized models preserve meaning.

Abstract: Post-training quantization to the GGUF format's mixed-precision K-quants is commonly how open-weight language models reach consumer hardware, yet its effect on fine-grained lexical competence is uncharacterized. We audit 27 quantized artifacts across 13 families and four architecture backbones, 0.35B-14B parameters, evaluated down their published ladder to Q2_K (about 2.6 bits per weight), on 429 frequency-validated rare English words under two probes: surface inclusion of a prompt-supplied word and its one-sentence definition, scored by a tiered multi-synonym matcher, its error measured by a blind LLM-judge census of every definition, with human verification. Three regimes emerge at Q2: total collapse into unusable builds, severe semantic dissociation in sub-2B models, and mostly robust preservation above about 3B. In every sub-2B artifact, definitions fall 20-67% below the artifact's baseline, typically several times the inclusion loss. Two controls separate rarity from task difficulty: within the rare set, loss rises with rarity in six of seven sub-2B artifacts, and on a 100-word common-word set rare words lose more than common words in all eight, significantly in six. Tokenizer vocabulary size does not predict the damage (Spearman rho=0.12); parameter count dominates (rho=0.72), confirmed within five of six same-tokenizer families. Q4_K_M remains lexically clean at >=1B. The damage is frequency-graded, provider-dependent, and not calibrated by WikiText-2 perplexity: across nine artifact-matched ladders, near-identical Q2 penalties (44.7%/47.6%) separate an artifact keeping its definitions (3.6%) from one losing them (43.6%). Aggressively quantized small models can keep generating fluent text while no longer knowing what it means, risking hardware-constrained deployments in domains where semantics carries consequences. Validation must be per artifact.

</details>


### [30] [Understanding and Mitigating Hallucination Escape in Tool-Using LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04409)
*Peigui Qi,Kunsheng Tang,Yide Song,Weiming Zhang,Nenghai Yu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper identifies and addresses a new failure mode, Hallucination Escape, in LLM tool use, where methods that reduce tool hallucinations on one configuration increase them on others, and proposes EscapeGuard, an inference-time method that robustly reduces tool-selection hallucinations across configurations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used as autonomous agents that call external tools, they suffer from tool hallucinations—choosing incorrect tools or producing invalid calls. Existing mitigation methods claim strong gains but are evaluated only on the tool configurations they are tuned on. The authors notice that these methods can fail when the tool set changes, leading to unrecognized risks for real-world applications where tool configurations vary. This motivates a deeper analysis of how models’ intrinsic tool-use tendencies interact with different tool configurations and the design of methods that remain robust across configurations.

Method: The authors first analyze existing tool-hallucination mitigation methods across multiple tool configurations and identify a failure mode they call Hallucination Escape: hallucinations decrease on the tuned configuration but increase elsewhere. They study how the model’s built-in tendencies to use certain tools can conflict with the currently available tools, and show that current methods inadvertently amplify these tendencies. Based on this, they introduce EscapeGuard, a training-free, inference-time technique. EscapeGuard uses conflict-aware gating to detect when the model’s preferred tool use clashes with the current configuration, and it applies configuration-derived attention enhancement to steer the model’s attention toward tools that fit the active configuration, thereby mitigating hallucinations and preventing escape across different tool setups.

Result: On six benchmarks and multiple models, EscapeGuard reduces tool-selection hallucination by 9.0 percentage points on average. It also significantly suppresses Hallucination Escape, lowering the cross-configuration hallucination mean by 23.7 percentage points and achieving an 89.1% net improvement in paired-query evaluations that compare behavior across tool configurations.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that existing tool-hallucination mitigation methods can be misleadingly optimistic when evaluated on a single tool configuration, since they may induce Hallucination Escape under configuration changes. The proposed EscapeGuard method offers a training-free, general approach that not only reduces hallucinations but also maintains robustness under different tool configurations. The authors advocate for broader, cross-configuration evaluation protocols to build more reliable tool-using LLM agents.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as autonomous agents that invoke external tools. However, this capability introduces tool hallucination, selecting incorrect tools or generating invalid calls. Existing mitigation methods report substantial improvements, yet we identify a previously overlooked failure mode that we term Hallucination Escape. These methods reduce hallucination on the tool configuration they are tuned on but increase it on other configurations, canceling out the gain. We further investigate this phenomenon and find that hallucination rises sharply when a model's intrinsic tool-use tendencies conflict with the current tool configuration, and that existing methods reinforce rather than suppress these tendencies, which in turn contributes to hallucination escape. Building on these findings, we propose EscapeGuard, a training-free inference-time method that combines conflict-aware gating with configuration-derived attention enhancement to mitigate tool hallucination while preventing hallucination escape. Across six benchmarks on various models, EscapeGuard reduces tool-selection hallucination by 9.0 pp and suppresses hallucination escape, lowering the cross-configuration mean by 23.7 pp and achieving an 89.1% net improvement in paired-query evaluation. We hope this work can encourage evaluation beyond a single tool configuration and pave the way for more reliable tool-using LLM agents.

</details>


### [31] [DV-Lens: Revealing the Functional Organization of Language Model Parameters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04489)
*Chenhang Cui,Jian Yu,Shuyi Miao,Xiaohao Liu,Rui Huang,Fei Shen,An Zhang,Tat-Seng Chua*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose DV-Lens, a parameter-level interpretability method that maps individual weight columns in LLMs to their average effects on vocabulary logits, and use this to relate weight structure to model behavior and capability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: We know LLMs work well but don’t yet understand how individual parameters and modules contribute to outputs or overall capability, and how functional organization of weights relates to model performance. Existing interpretability mainly focuses on activations or specific circuits rather than systematically connecting native parameters across modules to concrete, testable output effects and global capability metrics.

Method: 1) For many prompts, estimate module-specific downstream Jacobians that map changes in each module’s outputs (Q/K/V/O and FFNs) to changes in final vocabulary logits. 2) Use these Jacobians to project each native parameter column into the vocabulary space, producing a signed “readout vector” describing that column’s average influence on token logits. 3) Cluster/group parameter columns by these vocabulary readouts and define DV-Complexity as the normalized reconstruction residual when approximating original weights from these groups, capturing within-group structural variation. 4) Validate at parameter level via randomized baselines, finite-difference checks, and interventions (ablation, steering, swapping) guided by readouts. 5) Aggregate DV-Complexity across parameters into a joint-parameter score and correlate this with external benchmark-based capability rankings over many models.

Result: 1) DV-Lens readouts exhibit structured, non-random vocabulary preferences and predict local logit changes with 98% coordinate-orientation agreement across 720 parameter-level tests on nine models. 2) Using these readouts to design targeted parameter interventions (ablation/steering/swapping) in 21 models reliably shifts token probabilities in the directions predicted by DV-Lens. 3) The aggregated DV-Complexity score strongly correlates (Spearman 0.904) with independent benchmark-based capability rankings across 48 language models, indicating a robust link between internal parameter organization and external performance.

Conclusion: DV-Lens provides an empirically validated way to interpret LLM parameters by mapping them to downstream vocabulary effects, and DV-Complexity offers a scalar measure of weight organization that aligns closely with model capability. This establishes an intervention-backed bridge between parameter-level structure and observable behavior, suggesting that analyzing vocabulary-aligned parameter complexity can serve as a useful proxy for, and possibly a driver of, overall LLM capability.

Abstract: Understanding parameter functions helps elucidate the internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs). However, how to connect parameters from different modules to verifiable output effects and further characterize the relationship between their functional organization and model capability remains to be explored. To this end, we introduce the downstream vocabulary lens (DV-Lens), a parameter-level interpretability framework that links native parameter directions to their downstream vocabulary responses. Specifically, we first estimate module-specific downstream Jacobians over a reference prompt set for attention query, key, value, and output (Q/K/V/O) projections and feed-forward networks (FFNs). Second, we use these mappings to project native parameter columns into the final vocabulary space, obtaining signed readouts that characterize their average local output responses. Third, we group parameter columns by their vocabulary readouts and introduce downstream vocabulary complexity (DV-Complexity), which quantifies within-group structural variation using normalized reconstruction residuals of the original weights. At the parameter level, randomized controls and finite-difference tests show that DV-Lens readouts capture non-random vocabulary structure and predict local logit changes with 98.0% coordinate-orientation agreement across 720 cases from nine models. These readouts further guide parameter ablation, steering, and swapping across 21 models, shifting target-token probabilities in the predicted directions under controlled conditions. At the model level, the joint-parameter score of DV-Complexity achieves a Spearman correlation of 0.904 with benchmark-based capability rankings across 48 language models. Together, these results provide intervention-based evidence for DV-Lens interpretations and reveal an association between DV-Complexity and model capability.

</details>


### [32] [Emoji-Emotion Ranking System Using Twitter Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04495)
*Danila Khlebokazov,Nurkhan Tashimov,Pakizar Shamoi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper builds an emoji-aware emotion analysis framework that models each emoji as a probabilistic distribution over multiple emotions rather than a fixed sentiment label, using 100k Twitter replies and projection into valence-arousal space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing computational approaches generally treat emojis as static sentiment indicators (e.g., positive/negative), which oversimplifies their nuanced and context-dependent emotional meanings. There is a need for a more fine-grained, probabilistic characterization of emojis that captures their distribution over multiple emotions and supports continuous affective analysis.

Method: Collect 100,000 emoji-containing Twitter (X) replies from 2020–2025. Preprocess and clean the text, then apply a text-to-emotion classifier that assigns scores for five primary emotions (Happy, Angry, Sad, Fear, Surprise) to each message. Aggregate the emotion scores across all contexts in which a specific emoji appears to estimate the emoji’s emotion distribution. From these distributions, construct (1) an emoji-emotion ranking system indicating dominant emotions per emoji and (2) project emojis into the Russell valence-arousal space for continuous affect representation.

Result: The framework yields probabilistic emotion distributions for each emoji, a ranking of emojis by their dominant emotions, and positions of emojis in valence-arousal space. The empirical findings show that emojis are better described by context-sensitive emotional profiles spanning multiple emotions rather than by single, fixed sentiment polarities.

Conclusion: Emojis encode rich, context-dependent emotional information that cannot be captured by simple positive/negative sentiment labels. Modeling emojis as probabilistic distributions over discrete emotions and embedding them in valence-arousal space provides a more realistic and flexible basis for emoji-aware emotion analysis, which can improve downstream affective computing and social media analysis tasks.

Abstract: Nowadays, emojis are often replacing words. Yet computational systems still oversimplify them. Most existing approaches treat emojis as static sentiment indicators and overlook their emotional distributions. In this study, we propose an emoji-aware emotion analysis framework based on a Twitter (X) dataset of 100,000 emoji-containing replies collected between 2020-2025. After preprocessing and text cleaning, we applied text-to-emotion classification to detect five primary emotions (Happy, Angry, Sad, Fear, and Surprise) for each message. By aggregating emotion scores across contexts in which each emoji appears, we estimate emoji-emotion association distributions and construct an emoji-emotion ranking system reflecting relative emotional dominance. Furthermore, we project emojis into the Russell valence-arousal space to enable continuous affective interpretation. Our results demonstrate that emojis exhibit probabilistic, context-sensitive emotional profiles rather than fixed sentiment polarities.

</details>


### [33] [Correctness Is a Direction: Geometric Answer Selection in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04512)
*Marcus Armstrong,Navid Ayoobi,Pradham Mummaleti,Alexander Chulzhanov,Arjun Mukherjee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper discovers that whether an answer is correct corresponds to a consistent geometric direction in LLM hidden states, which can be estimated from a small labeled set and then used to score answers more accurately than standard log-probabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard LLM scoring via log-probabilities often misranks correct vs. incorrect answers, leading to factual errors and hallucinations. The authors want to understand whether internal representations contain a clearer correctness signal than is visible in the output, and whether this signal has a simple geometric structure that can be exploited without any parameter updates.

Method: 1) Collect small labeled sets of (question, correct answer, incorrect answer) examples. 2) Run the model and extract hidden states around 70% depth for each answer. 3) Compute the mean displacement vector from incorrect to correct answer representations; this is the "correctness direction." 4) At test time, for each candidate answer, compute its hidden state at the same layer and take the dot product with this direction to obtain a correctness score—no generation or fine-tuning is used. 5) Compare performance of this geometric scoring to standard log-probability scoring on benchmarks and as a hallucination detector. 6) Analyze the geometry of directions trained on different task types (factual reasoning, domain knowledge, truthfulness) by examining angles/orthogonality between them.

Result: The learned correctness direction, derived from about 50 labeled examples and no parameter updates, significantly outperforms zero-shot log-probability scoring: up to +32 points on ARC-Challenge and MMLU, and +38.1–51.8 points on TruthfulQA across multiple models (1B–8B, Llama/Qwen/Gemma). As a hallucination detector on single QA pairs, it achieves AUROC 0.693 vs. 0.578 for log-probability. Geometric analysis shows that correctness directions for different task types are nearly orthogonal, meaning the model uses separate representational subspaces for factual correctness, domain knowledge, and calibrated truthfulness, with variation across architectures.

Conclusion: Correctness is linearly decodable as a stable direction in the hidden-state geometry of LLMs, even from few-shot supervision and without modifying model weights. This direction yields better answer scoring and hallucination detection than log-probabilities, and reveals that different notions of correctness live in distinct, near-orthogonal subspaces. These findings imply that LLMs internally encode richer correctness information than their outputs reflect, pointing to calibration as a routing/decoding problem rather than purely a knowledge or capacity limitation.

Abstract: Answer correctness is encoded as a recoverable geometric direction in the hidden states of language models. We show that the mean displacement from incorrect to correct answer representations, computed at approximately 70\% of model depth from fifty labeled examples with no parameter updates, yields a scoring direction that outperforms zero-shot log-probability scoring by up to +32.0 percentage points on factual benchmarks (ARC-Challenge and MMLU) and by +38.1 to +51.8 percentage points on TruthfulQA, across five models spanning 1B to 8B parameters in three architecture families (Llama, Qwen, Gemma). The method requires one forward pass and one dot product per candidate; no generation is performed at inference. Applied as a hallucination detector on individual (question, answer) pairs, the recovered direction achieves 0.693~AUROC versus 0.578 for log-probability scoring. We additionally find that correctness directions for factual reasoning, domain knowledge, and calibrated truthfulness are near-orthogonal in representation space, revealing that language models allocate geometrically independent subspaces to qualitatively distinct notions of correct answer, with architecture-dependent variation in the degree of separation. This structure explains the observed transfer pattern---the direction calibrated on factual questions transfers within task type but not across it---and suggests that LLM calibration failures may reflect a routing problem: the model's internal representation contains more correctness signal than its output behaviour exploits.

</details>


### [34] [From Probe Scores to Alarm Policies: Operational Validity of Activation Monitors for Language-Model Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04575)
*Xueping Gao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Paper examines how to evaluate and deploy activation-based safety monitors for language-model agents, showing that typical AUROC metrics are insufficient for operational alarm policies under false-alarm constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although activation probes for language models often show high AUROC for detecting unsafe behavior, deployed monitors need to make hard thresholded decisions with strict limits on false alarms and must work at the level of semantic tasks or trajectories. Current evaluation practices don't fully capture this operational setting, raising concerns about whether high AUROC really translates to reliable safety in deployment.

Method: The authors define an Operational Validity Contract specifying precise monitoring targets and constraints (target, observability, identity, timing, intervention unit, comparator, calibration, and cost). They formalize risk at the semantic request/trajectory level and analyze how repeated alarm opportunities within a task affect any-alarm risk. They study requirements for confidence-certified thresholds, including enough independent negative units, tie-breaking rules, and distributional transport to deployment. Empirically, they test activation-based monitors on multiple safety/agent benchmarks (Models Under Pressure, LASR refusal prediction, immutable AgentDojo, and a protocol-frozen ST-WebAgentBench replication), locking monitor thresholds to 5% and 10% false-alarm operating points and examining realized detection rates and calibration properties.

Result: Across benchmarks, activation-based monitors achieve high AUROC (e.g., 0.957 and 0.935 on Models Under Pressure and LASR), but their locked 5%/10% detection rates are substantially lower (e.g., ~0.64–0.78) than AUROC might suggest. On AgentDojo, a mean-activation rollout monitor achieves AUROC 0.922 but fails to detect any of 38 positive semantic cases at the 5% operating point, and thresholds intended for 10% false alarms actually yield 18.7–20.0% FPR. For ST-WebAgentBench, activation monitoring attains AUROC 0.874, but the calibration set has only 23 independent negatives, making it impossible to confidently identify a 10% controller; the system abstains instead of claiming a misleadingly perfect FPR. Some counterexamples show that optimizing AUROC can even reduce realized utility at a fixed false-alarm rate. Overall, none of the evaluated settings satisfy the criteria for an alarm-policy valid monitor under the proposed contract, due to limits in predictive value, representation access, and data support.

Conclusion: High AUROC for activation probes does not guarantee that monitors will perform acceptably as operational safety alarms under realistic false-alarm constraints and semantic-unit risk definitions. Robust deployment requires a more stringent Operational Validity Contract, attention to semantic-unit any-alarm risk, adequate calibration data, and careful threshold selection and transport. Under these criteria, current activation-based monitors fall short of alarm-policy validity on the tested benchmarks, implying that safety evaluations must move beyond AUROC and address the full operational monitoring context.

Abstract: Activation probes can predict safety-relevant properties of language models with high area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUROC), but deployed agent monitors make thresholded alarm decisions under tight false-alarm budgets. These are different estimands. We introduce an Operational Validity Contract that fixes a monitor's target, observability, identity, timing, intervention unit, comparator, calibration, and cost. We formalize risk at the semantic request or trajectory level: when one task contains repeated alarm opportunities, row-level AUROC and false positive rate do not identify semantic-unit any-alarm risk. A confidence-certified threshold also requires enough independent negative units, a tie-safe rule, and transport to deployment. Across Models Under Pressure, LASR refusal prediction, immutable AgentDojo, and a prospectively protocol-frozen ST-WebAgentBench replication, joint activation-observable monitors reach AUROC 0.957 and 0.935 on the first two benchmarks, yet their locked 5%/10% detection rates are only .642/.742 and .719/.782, respectively. On AgentDojo, the secondary mean-activation rollout monitor reaches AUROC 0.922 but detects none of 38 positive semantic cases at the locked 5% operating point; thresholds intended for 10% false alarms realize 18.7-20.0% on test. Because the test misses its prospectively frozen 40-positive support gate, we label it support-insufficient. On ST-WebAgentBench, activation reaches AUROC .874, but 23 independent calibration negatives cannot identify even a 10% controller; the locked policy abstains rather than reporting its mechanical zero FPR as a success. An exploratory counterexample also lowers full AUROC while improving realized 10% utility. The fail-closed compiler caps MUP and LASR at restricted predictive value and AgentDojo and ST-Web at representation accessibility; no setting reaches alarm-policy validity.

</details>


### [35] [SIFT: Robust Meta-Faithfulness Verification of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Under Distribution Shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04594)
*Noor Islam S. Mohammad,Md. Basim Al Zabir Shammo,Hasan Siddiki,Mahmudul Hasan,Md. Faisal Sheikh,Jakaria Habib*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether chain-of-thought faithfulness detectors themselves remain reliable under distribution shift, formalizes an invariance-based notion of “meta-faithfulness,” shows strong limitations for existing detector designs, and proposes a new detector and evaluation protocol revealing that variance (especially sampling stochasticity) is a bigger problem than shift itself.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Chain-of-Thought faithfulness detectors are widely used to judge whether reasoning traces generated by models truly reflect their internal decision process. These detectors are often treated as if their outputs were stable and trustworthy across settings, but there has been little work examining whether the detectors themselves remain faithful under distribution shifts or other perturbations that should not affect ground-truth faithfulness. The authors are motivated to provide a principled way to evaluate and stress-test such detectors, clarify fundamental limitations of current approaches, and understand what actually drives detector unreliability in practice.

Method: The paper formalizes “meta-faithfulness” as an invariance principle: a valid detector must give the same verdict on traces that differ only by transformations that preserve ground-truth faithfulness. Theoretically, it proves three results: (i) detectors relying solely on intervention-response profiles cannot distinguish truly faithful mechanisms from epiphenomenal ones with matching signatures; (ii) detectors that use shift-sensitive features are guaranteed to violate invariance at a rate unrelated to their in-distribution accuracy; and (iii) an asymptotic certified selective-risk framework can guarantee safe abstention. Empirically, the authors implement FaithShift, a stress-test protocol covering ten types of distribution shift, and develop SIFT, a detector based on hidden-state trajectory analysis, trained with cross-environment invariance objectives and equipped with certified abstention. They evaluate across 14,996 traces, four domains, and eight models, and also explore ensemble methods and multi-model training for robustness and transfer.
