Result: FaithShift evaluations show that all existing chain-of-thought faithfulness detectors suffer substantial transfer collapse, with AUROC drops of at least 0.15 under shift. However, detailed analysis reveals that over 80% of the detectors’ instability is due to sampling stochasticity (e.g., random seeds) rather than the induced distribution shifts, contradicting the authors’ preregistered expectation that shift-driven violations would dominate (>0.25). The new SIFT detector reduces invariance violations by 64% relative to the strongest single-seed baseline, but its advantage mostly disappears when using a four-seed ensemble of any detector: the performance gap shrinks to about 0.01 AUROC and is statistically indistinguishable at matched coverage (p=0.21). SIFT also requires a high abstention rate (51%) to achieve its guarantees. Furthermore, cross-model transfer performance worsens progressively when moving from within-family to cross-family to open-weight-to-API settings, though multi-model training partly mitigates this degradation.

Conclusion: The study concludes that current CoT faithfulness detectors are fragile under transfer, but that the main source of unreliability is variance—particularly sampling stochasticity—rather than distribution shift per se. While invariance-based training and abstention (as in SIFT) can substantially cut invariance violations, simple multi-seed ensembling can close most of the remaining gap, raising questions about the cost–benefit tradeoffs of more complex detector designs. The authors propose their invariance-based formalism, FaithShift protocol, and empirical findings as a general framework for “auditing the auditors,” emphasizing that future work on detector robustness must directly confront detector variance and the limits of what can be inferred from intervention-response signatures alone.

Abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) faithfulness detectors are widely used to audit reasoning models, yet a detector is itself a predictor whose verdicts are treated as stable properties. We ask whether a detector is faithful to itself under distribution shift. We formalize meta-faithfulness as an invariance principle: a valid detector must return identical verdicts on traces that differ only by transformations preserving ground-truth faithfulness. We prove three results: (i) no detector using only intervention-response profiles can separate faithful from epiphenomenal mechanisms with identical signatures; (ii) any detector relying on shift-sensitive features violates invariance at a rate independent of its in-distribution accuracy; (iii) an asymptotic certified selective-risk guarantee enables confident abstention. We operationalize the principle in FaithShift, a stress-test protocol spanning ten shift axes, and propose SIFT, a hidden-state trajectory detector trained with cross-environment invariance objectives and certified abstention. Across 14,996 traces, four domains, and eight models, three findings emerge. First, transfer collapse is real: all existing detectors show gaps $\geq 0.15$ AUROC. Second, the dominant bottleneck is sampling stochasticity, not shift: over 80% of detector instability stems from random seed variation, falsifying our preregistered prediction that shift-attributable violations exceed 0.25. Third, SIFT cuts invariance violations by 64% over the best single-seed baseline, but a four-seed ensemble of any detector narrows the margin to 0.01 (indistinguishable at matched coverage, $p=0.21$), and SIFT needs a 51% abstention rate. Cross-model transfer degrades from within-family to cross-family to open-weight-to-API, partly closed by multi-model training. We offer a framework for auditing auditors: the real barrier is detector variance, not distribution shift.

</details>


### [36] [Stance Drift: How AI-mediated Communication Distorts Our Message](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04620)
*Lingchong Liu,Yanfei Zhou,Jacob Bien,Y. X. Rachel Wang,Lucy Xia,Xin Tong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper examines how reliably large language models preserve a speaker’s original stance when they are used to generate and then interpret arguments, revealing substantial stance drift even in advanced models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used to draft, transform, and summarize opinionated content, it is critical to know whether they faithfully preserve a person’s stated stance. Misrepresentation or distortion of stance in AI-mediated communication can have serious consequences in domains like journalism, policy debates, and scientific discourse. Yet, there has been little systematic, quantitative evaluation of this fidelity. The paper aims to fill this gap by rigorously modeling and measuring stance drift across multiple models and prompts.

Method: The authors formalize AI-mediated communication as a two-step pipeline: an LLM first generates an argument given a specified stance on a debate proposition; a second LLM then extracts the stance from the produced argument. They discretize stance into five Likert-type categories and model the full process as a probabilistic state transition matrix between initial and extracted stances. From this, they define the stance preservation rate (SPR) as the average probability that the extracted stance matches the original stance. They evaluate nine LLMs over 112 debate propositions and analyze drift patterns such as polarization, movement away from neutrality, and stance flipping. They also test several mitigation strategies (e.g., in-context learning, multiple extraction with shuffled options, assertion, reflection, and different reasoning-effort prompts) and conduct a limited comparison to human extraction on one proposition to determine where in the pipeline drift arises.

Result: Across 112 propositions and nine LLMs, none surpassed an SPR of 0.7 under standard settings, indicating substantial stance drift. The majority of drift followed three patterns: increased extremity of positions (polarization), systematic movement away from neutral stances, and complete flipping from one side to the opposite. Among multiple attempted mitigations, only adding medium reasoning effort to a reflection-style prompt for GPT-5.4 produced a notable improvement, raising the SPR to about 0.775; even then, polarization remained the dominant drift pattern, accounting for roughly 0.119 of the transition probability mass. The exploratory human comparison on one proposition showed that both the generation and extraction steps contribute to drift, suggesting that the issue is not confined to a single stage of the pipeline.

Conclusion: The study identifies a clear fidelity gap in how LLMs preserve user stances during AI-mediated communication. Even advanced models frequently alter, polarize, or flip stances as they move from generation to subsequent interpretation, and common prompting or aggregation techniques provide only limited relief. Since such stance drift can subtly misrepresent people’s views, the findings raise concerns for any domain where opinionated content passes through LLMs, including journalism, public policy discussions, and scientific communication. The work underscores the need for better methods, interfaces, or model designs that more reliably maintain stance fidelity across complex language-model pipelines.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate human communication, from drafting emails to summarizing scientific reports, yet whether they faithfully preserve a speaker's position remains largely untested. We model AI-mediated communication as a two-step generation-extraction pipeline: one LLM produces an argument from a specified stance, and a second LLM extracts the stance from that argument. We represent the pipeline as a probabilistic state transition over five Likert-type stance categories and define the stance preservation rate (SPR) as the average probability that the extracted stance matches the initial stance. Across 112 debate propositions, none of the nine LLMs tested exceeded an SPR of 0.7 under the default configuration. Three drift patterns accounted for most of the drift: polarization, deviation from neutrality, and flipping. Among the mitigation strategies tested, including in-context learning, multiple extraction with shuffled options, assertion, and reflection, only adding medium reasoning effort to a reflection prompt for GPT-5.4 substantially improved the SPR, to 0.775, yet polarization remained the largest pattern, with 0.119 of the transition mass. An exploratory comparison with human extraction on a single proposition suggests that drift arises at both the generation and the extraction stage. These results point to a fidelity gap in AI-mediated communication, with implications for journalism, policy deliberation, scientific communication, and other domains where opinion-laden messages pass through language models.

</details>


### [37] [Does Neural Complexity Improve Health Misinformation Detection? A Leakage-Controlled Cross-Corpus Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04636)
*Mkululi SIKOSANA*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper benchmarks multiple compact neural and classical models for health misinformation detection under tightly controlled, leakage-aware conditions, showing that added model complexity does not consistently outperform simpler linear methods and that dataset design strongly shapes results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on health misinformation detection often reports improvements from more complex neural architectures, but these gains are hard to interpret because different studies use different datasets, preprocessing steps, data splits, and data leakage controls. This makes architecture comparisons unreliable and can mislead practitioners choosing models for real-world deployment. The paper aims to provide a fair, controlled comparison of several commonly used neural architectures against classical baselines on multiple corpora, clarifying whether complexity truly yields robust benefits.

Method: The authors conduct a controlled cross-corpus benchmark on two health misinformation datasets, COVID19-FNIR and CONSTRAINT. They evaluate five compact neural architectures (1D-CNN, LSTM, BiLSTM, CNN-LSTM, CNN-BiLSTM), a soft-voting ensemble of these neural models, and three classical machine-learning baselines including a linear SVM. To ensure fairness, they (1) remove exact-text duplicates before modeling to mitigate leakage, (2) apply a shared preprocessing pipeline and optimization protocol across neural models, and (3) repeat neural experiments over three random seeds to obtain stable performance estimates. They then compare macro-F1 and ROC-AUC scores and analyze how architecture rankings vary across the two corpora.

Result: On the COVID19-FNIR dataset, the neural ensemble achieves very high performance with a mean macro-F1 of 0.9963 and ROC-AUC of 0.9994, and individual neural models also perform strongly, with macro-F1 between 0.9945 and 0.9957. On the CONSTRAINT dataset, however, the ensemble attains a lower macro-F1 of 0.9272 and ROC-AUC of 0.9811, and is outperformed by a classical linear SVM, which reaches a macro-F1 of 0.9574 and ROC-AUC of 0.9931. The relative ranking of neural architectures differs between the two datasets, and simple sparse linear models remain highly competitive overall.

Conclusion: Model complexity does not guarantee a consistent performance advantage across different health misinformation datasets, and architecture rankings are unstable across corpora. Well-designed benchmarks, including strict deduplication and standardized preprocessing and optimization, can have more impact on measured performance than incremental architectural sophistication. The paper offers a reproducible, leakage-controlled evaluation framework that supports evidence-based model selection for health misinformation classification rather than defaulting to more complex neural solutions.

Abstract: Increasing architectural complexity is often assumed to improve health misinformation detection, yet reported gains are difficult to interpret when studies use different corpora, preprocessing pipelines, data splits, and leakage controls. This study provides a controlled cross-corpus benchmark of five compact neural architectures (1D-CNN, LSTM, BiLSTM, CNN-LSTM, and CNN-BiLSTM), a soft-voting neural ensemble, and three classical machine-learning baselines using COVID19-FNIR and CONSTRAINT. Exact-text duplicate controls were applied before modelling; all neural systems used a common preprocessing and optimisation protocol, and neural results were repeated across three random seeds. On COVID19-FNIR, the deep ensemble achieved a mean macro-F1 of 0.9963 and ROC-AUC of 0.9994, while individual neural models ranged from 0.9945 to 0.9957 macro-F1. On CONSTRAINT, the ensemble achieved macro-F1 of 0.9272 and ROC-AUC of 0.9811, whereas a linear SVM achieved macro-F1 of 0.9574 and ROC-AUC of 0.9931. Architecture rankings changed across corpora, and simple sparse linear models remained highly competitive. The findings show that model complexity does not provide a stable performance advantage and that benchmark construction can dominate architecture choice. The study contributes a reproducible, leakage-controlled basis for evidence-driven model selection in health misinformation classification

</details>


### [38] [Grounding Probes: Generator-Independent Hallucination Detection from Observer Model Hidden States](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04642)
*Michael Rathmayr,Ádám Kovács,Gábor Recski*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A new detector called Grounding Probe uses an external observer model’s hidden states to identify ungrounded (hallucinated) responses in retrieval-augmented generation efficiently and robustly across different generators.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods to detect ungrounded or fabricated content in retrieval-augmented generation either rely on shallow surface checks, which are fast but miss paraphrased hallucinations, or sampling-based approaches, which are accurate but slow because they require extra generations. Hidden-state probes provide a middle ground but depend on the generating model’s internal activations, making them unusable when the generator changes or is closed-source. The paper aims to decouple grounding detection from the specific generator while keeping high accuracy and efficiency.

Method: The authors introduce the Grounding Probe, a logistic regression classifier built over mean-pooled hidden states from a middle layer of an independent observer language model. The observer reads the context, question, and response jointly in a single forward pass but does not generate text. The probe pools activations over response tokens only, uses a carefully chosen middle layer, and is capacity-controlled to avoid overfitting, which significantly narrows the train-test AUROC gap. The model is trained on 15,090 annotated RAG responses, and evaluated with different observer models and generators. The probe is also combined with a supervised span-level detector by averaging scores.

Result: The Grounding Probe substantially outperforms simple methods that query the observer model directly about grounding, with at least +0.166 AUROC gain across four observer models. Trained on 15,090 labeled examples, it achieves 0.879–0.894 AUROC on the RAGTruth benchmark across four observers. When its scores are averaged with those from a supervised span detector, the combined system attains 0.924 AUROC and 0.820 F1 at a 0.5 threshold, which is 0.060 AUROC better than the span detector alone. A single trained probe generalizes across six different generators, and hold-out control experiments suggest that removing dependence on the generator incurs only about a 0.02 AUROC cost. The approach also nearly closes the train-test AUROC gap compared to previous probes.

Conclusion: A simple, generator-agnostic probing method over an external observer model’s middle-layer hidden states can detect ungrounded content in RAG responses with high accuracy, low computational cost, and good generalization across generators. Careful design choices—pooling over response tokens, using a middle layer, and limiting probe capacity—are key to closing generalization gaps. The technique outperforms direct querying of the observer and improves over existing supervised detectors when combined, offering a practical and reusable component for monitoring hallucinations in RAG systems. The authors provide open-source code, trained probes, and prediction outputs to facilitate adoption and further research.

Abstract: Detecting responses that retrieval-augmented generation does not ground in its context trades speed against accuracy: surface checks miss paraphrased fabrication, sampling-based methods cost extra generations. Hidden-state probes sit between the two, but every existing one reads the generating model's own activations, so a change of generator invalidates the detector and a closed-weight generator is out of reach. This paper removes that coupling. The Grounding Probe is logistic regression over the mean-pooled middle-layer hidden states of an observer language model that reads the context, question, and response in one forward pass and generates nothing, with the recipe it needs: pool over response tokens, read a middle layer, and control capacity, which closes the train-test AUROC gap from 0.087-0.202 to 0.009-0.013. Asking the observer outright, rather than reading its hidden state, costs at least +0.166 AUROC in every one of four models. Fitted on 15,090 annotated responses it reaches 0.879-0.894 AUROC on RAGTruth test across four observers, and 0.924 AUROC with 0.820 F1@0.5 averaged with a supervised span detector, 0.060 above that detector alone. One probe holds across six generators, and hold-out controls, including one in which no evaluation prompt appears in training, bound the cost of removing a generator at about 0.02 AUROC. Code, probes, and predictions are released.

</details>


### [39] [Extracting Persona Subspaces Through Iterative Nullspace Projection For Modulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04676)
*Ananya Malik,Mai ElSherief*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes PaSS, a method to control and modulate LLM personas by modeling them as multi-dimensional subspaces in latent space, enabling fine-grained, interpretable control without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing persona control techniques for LLMs largely treat a persona as a single dominant direction, which fails to capture nested or finer-grained traits and struggles when persona signals are already embedded in the content. There is a need for precise, safe, and reliable persona modulation that can amplify or suppress existing traits instead of injecting them from scratch, all without extensive supervision or retraining.

Method: The authors introduce PaSS, an inference-time control paradigm that represents personas as multi-dimensional subspaces in a model's latent space. They extract these persona subspaces using Iterative Nullspace Projections (INLP), performing iterative concept erasure to isolate multiple persona-specific directions. These subspaces are then used to modulate LLM generation—amplifying or suppressing persona traits—without requiring supervised contrastive examples or retraining the base model. They also analyze individual “peeled” directions in the subspace to understand their behavioral role.

Result: Across six personas and multiple benchmarks (MATH-500, TinyAlpaca, GSM8K, IFEval), the method achieves stronger and more extensive persona modulation than single-direction additive approaches while preserving the underlying task content. The extracted subspaces capture multiple, diverse behavioral traits associated with each persona, and empirical evaluations suggest a causal effect on model behavior. Analysis of separate directions within each subspace reveals that they correspond to distinct aspects of persona expression.

Conclusion: Persona subspaces, as instantiated in PaSS, provide a controllable, interpretable, and generalizable framework for modulating persona behavior in LLMs at inference time. Multi-dimensional, iteratively extracted persona directions enable finer-grained and stronger control than single-vector methods, without degrading task performance or requiring model retraining.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can adopt distinct personas to tune their semantics, expertise, and perspective to different users and tasks. Precise control over these traits is critical to ensure safety and reliability in model behavior. Existing methods like activation steering and prompt-based persona induction reduce a persona to a single dominant direction, missing the finer, nested traits that emerge only once that dominant signal is factored out. We introduce modulation as a setting where the persona context is already embedded in the content being manipulated, requiring control methods to amplify or suppress a trait already present rather than inject it from scratch. PaSS is an inference-time control paradigm that models personas as multi-dimensional subspaces in a model's latent space without supervised contrastive examples. The persona subspaces are extracted via iterative concept erasure and applied to modulate persona-guided generation without retraining. To extract this subspace, we use Iterative Nullspace Projections (INLP) to linearly and iteratively isolate persona-specific directions. We causally evaluate six personas against diverse tasks like MATH-500, TinyAlpaca, GSM8K, and IFEval, showing that discriminative, iterative subspace extraction captures diverse traits underlying a given persona, enabling stronger and larger modulation than single-direction additive methods, while maintaining content fidelity. We further study individual peeled directions within each subspace to uncover the distinct aspects of persona behavior they encode. Overall, we show that persona subspaces offer a controllable, interpretable, and generalizable framework for modulating LLM behavior without sacrificing task performance.

</details>


### [40] [Steering Speech-Language Models: Training-Free Task Specialization via Contrastive Activation Addition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04683)
*Séverin Baroudi,Yanis Labrak,Pierfrancesco Melucci,Sergio Burdisso,Petr Motlicek,Hervé Bredin,Mirco Ravanelli,Ricard Marxer*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces a training-free method, Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), to steer SpeechLLMs toward specific speech tasks at inference time using steering vectors derived from a few labeled examples.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While activation steering is effective for controlling text-only LLMs at inference time, its application to multimodal SpeechLLMs is still new and underexplored, especially in a training-free setting. There is a need for simple, data-efficient methods to better control SpeechLLMs for tasks like ASR and emotion recognition without retraining or fine-tuning.

Method: The authors propose Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), a protocol that computes steering vectors for SpeechLLMs from a small set of labeled speech utterances. These vectors capture directions in the model’s internal representation space that correspond to desired behaviors (e.g., accurate transcription, specific emotion categories, or target scripts). At inference time, the method adds these steering vectors to the model’s activations, optionally in combination with task-specific prompts, to bias the model toward the targeted speech task or script normalization behavior.

Result: CAA improves performance on common SpeechLLM tasks such as Automatic Speech Recognition and Emotion Recognition compared to using prompting alone. The improvements hold across most evaluated tasks and also generalize to out-of-domain data. The authors also find that specific script-normalization directions effectively enforce a target writing script for a given language.

Conclusion: Training-free Contrastive Activation Addition is an effective and data-efficient way to steer SpeechLLMs at inference time. It enhances task performance, works well with prompting, generalizes to new domains, and can control output script, suggesting that activation-based steering is a powerful tool for controlling SpeechLLM behavior without additional training.

Abstract: Activation steering has proven effective for controlling the behavior of Large Language Models (LLMs) at inference time, but its application to SpeechLLMs remains new, and training-free steering approaches for such models are still largely unexplored. We propose a training-free Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) protocol that derives steering vectors for common speech tasks (e.g. transcription) in SpeechLLMs from a small number of labeled utterances. We showcase that adding these vectors in the representation space, at inference time, enforces better the targeted speech task. We further show that, when combined with prompting, these vectors yield to consistent improvement over prompting alone on most evaluated tasks such as Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) or Emotion Recognition (ER), and transfer to out-of-domain data. We additionally demonstrate the usefulness of script-normalization directions to enforce the target script of a specific language.

</details>


### [41] [Understanding Errors in LLM-Based Question Answering over Imperfect Tables](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04687)
*Baowen Zhang,Wei Fan,Ruman Wang,Hangting Ye*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how large language models discover and handle errors in tables for question answering, and introduces a workflow (GBDI) that improves error detection and handling to boost QA accuracy on imperfect tables.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In realistic settings, tables often contain errors that can change the answers to questions posed over them. Existing QA systems over tables typically assume clean data or do not carefully separate the challenges of detecting errors from handling them once found. The authors want to understand how robust current LLM-based table QA systems are to such imperfections, how factors like row order and error layout affect error discovery, and whether simply marking error locations suffices for accurate QA. They also aim to design a practical method to improve performance on noisy, real-world tables.

Method: The authors conduct controlled experiments on the RADAR-T dataset using three large language models. They systematically vary row order (front vs back placements; compact vs widely spaced error layouts) while keeping table content and gold answers fixed, and compare performance across three table variants: original, error-marked, and repaired (with human-reviewed corrections). They measure how these manipulations affect error discovery and QA accuracy. Based on insights from these experiments, they propose GBDI, a simple workflow that aggregates error discovery across multiple shuffled table views and adds explicit instructions for verifying and handling detected errors, then evaluate GBDI against a code-agent baseline across five systems on RADAR-T.

Result: Reordering table rows significantly affects LLMs’ ability to discover errors, even when the underlying data and correct answers are unchanged. Errors placed later in the table (back placements) are more fully discovered than those at the front, and compact error layouts yield better discovery than widely spaced ones across mean positions. Merely providing verified error locations does not close the performance gap: substantial QA accuracy differences remain between error-marked and fully repaired tables. When given already repaired tables, code-assisted QA accuracy improves by 39.0–59.1 percentage points over error-marked tables across the three systems. The proposed GBDI workflow further improves observed QA accuracy by 3.8–18.5 percentage points over a code-agent baseline on RADAR-T across five systems.

Conclusion: Error discovery in table QA with LLMs is sensitive to presentational factors like row order and error layout, indicating that current models have unstable and incomplete error detection capabilities. Moreover, knowing where errors are is not enough; effective mechanisms for verifying and repairing erroneous entries are crucial for accurate QA. The GBDI workflow operationalizes these insights by combining diverse table views with explicit error handling guidance, yielding consistent accuracy gains. The work underscores that robust QA over imperfect tables requires both reliable error discovery and strong downstream error handling, not just annotations of error locations.

Abstract: We investigate error discovery and handling in question answering over imperfect tables through controlled studies across three large language models (LLMs) on human-reviewed RADAR-T examples. Answering questions over these tables requires handling errors that can affect the answer. We vary row order and compare original, error-marked, and repaired tables to test whether discovery depends on where errors appear and whether providing their locations is sufficient for accurate question answering. First, reordering rows changes error discovery even when the table contents and gold answer remain unchanged. Complete discovery is higher for back than front placements and, averaged over the tested mean positions, for compact than widely spaced layouts. Second, providing verified error locations alone is insufficient for accurate QA, leaving a substantial accuracy gap between error-marked and repaired tables. Providing tables with human-reviewed repairs already applied raises code-assisted QA accuracy by 39.0-59.1 percentage points over the error-marked tables across the three systems. GBDI, a simple workflow, puts these findings into practice by combining error discovery across shuffled table views with explicit guidance for verifying and handling the reported errors. On RADAR-T, GBDI raises observed QA accuracy by 3.8-18.5 percentage points over a code-agent baseline across five systems. These results highlight the importance of both reliable error discovery and effective error handling in question answering over imperfect tables. Our anonymous repository is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/GBDI-ICLR-2027-85BD/

</details>


### [42] [WNet: Discrete Wavelets Transform for Efficient Token Mixing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04720)
*Rana Aref Salama,Abdou Youssef,Mona Diab*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Proposes WNet, a Transformer encoder that replaces self-attention with wavelet-based token mixing to reduce the cost of long-sequence encoding while maintaining strong contextual modeling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Self-attention gives powerful contextual modeling in Transformers but has quadratic cost in sequence length due to all-pairs token comparisons, making it expensive for long sequences. The paper seeks an alternative token mixing mechanism that is more efficient yet expressive enough for language modeling tasks.

Method: Replace self-attention with token mixers derived from the discrete wavelet transform (DWT). Construct several attention-free mixers that recombine multi-scale wavelet coefficients: (1) linear fusion, (2) learned gating over scales, and (3) per-token selection of relevant scales. Also design a hybrid model that adds a self-attention layer only at the top. Analyze the effective receptive field of wavelet mixers, comparing short two-tap filters (e.g., Haar) versus longer learned filters, and implement models pretrained with masked language modeling on a fixed-token subset of C4 and fine-tuned on GLUE, alongside BERT, FNet, and a no-mixing control.

Result: Wavelet mixers with two-tap filters are shown theoretically to never connect tokens outside fixed blocks regardless of network depth, while longer filters can cover the entire sequence in just two layers. Empirically, on MLM pretraining and GLUE fine-tuning, WNet variants—especially the token-gated mixer—match competitive baselines while being substantially faster: the token-gated mixer trains at comparable speed to self-attention on 256-token sequences and is 2.7× faster on 4,096-token sequences.

Conclusion: Wavelet-based token mixing is a viable, attention-free alternative for Transformer encoders in long-sequence regimes. With appropriately long filters and gating over scales, WNet can achieve full-sequence context and strong performance while significantly improving training efficiency compared to standard self-attention, particularly for long inputs.

Abstract: In a Transformer, token mixing is the step that lets each token draw information from other tokens, and it dominates the cost of encoding long sequences. Self-attention does this mixing very well: every token weighs every other token by content, which gives strong contextual modeling. That all-pairs comparison is also why its cost grows quadratically with sequence length. We introduce WNet, a Transformer encoder that replaces self-attention with token mixing based on the discrete wavelet transform (DWT). Three attention-free mixers recombine the scales: by linear fusion, by learned gating, or by letting each token choose its scales. A hybrid adds self-attention in the last layer only. A receptive-field analysis shows that wavelet mixers built from two-tap filters, such as Haar, never relate tokens outside fixed blocks, however deep the network, even when the filters are learned. Longer filters reach the whole sequence within two layers. We pre-train every model with masked language modeling on a fixed-token subset of C4 and fine-tune on GLUE, using one controlled setup with size-matched BERT and FNet baselines and a control that cannot mix tokens. The token-gated mixer trains as fast as attention at 256 tokens and 2.7 times faster at 4,096.

</details>


### [43] [Verb-ICL: Rethinking In-Context Learning for Structured Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04725)
*Fan Bai,Hengshuo Miao,Sanjit S Batra,Hamid Reza Hassanzadeh,Ardavan Saeedi,Mark Dredze*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Verb-ICL is a selective annotation framework that improves in-context learning for structured prediction by choosing token-level representative examples and adding targeted error-feedback-based guidelines into prompts, yielding better performance than strong baselines across multiple datasets and budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In-context learning with large language models struggles on structured prediction tasks (like information extraction and semantic parsing) because these tasks require fine-grained, token-level structure and follow human-designed labeling conventions that are not naturally acquired during pretraining. Existing sentence-level selection and naive prompting fail to capture these properties, leading to suboptimal performance, especially in low-resource settings. There is a need for a method that both captures local semantic/token patterns and explicitly injects task-specific annotation guidelines into the ICL setup.

Method: The authors introduce Verb-ICL, a two-stage selective annotation framework for structured prediction with ICL. First, it selects representative training examples using a token-level coverage strategy that focuses on capturing diverse local semantic patterns relevant for structured outputs. Second, it automatically generates actionable error feedback based on model mistakes, transforming these into explicit task-specific annotation guidelines. These guidelines are then incorporated back into the ICL demonstrations (prompts) so that the model can learn from both examples and the codified feedback. The framework is evaluated on six datasets covering information extraction and semantic parsing using recent LLMs, under different annotation budgets and selection strategies.

Result: Across six structured prediction datasets, Verb-ICL consistently outperforms strong selective annotation baselines under low-resource settings (small annotation budgets) and continues to deliver performance gains as the annotation budget increases. Analyses show that the generated feedback is mostly useful according to a four-category quality taxonomy, acts as general task-level guidance rather than merely instance-specific corrections, and improves model performance regardless of the particular underlying data selection strategy used.

Conclusion: Verb-ICL effectively adapts in-context learning for structured prediction by combining token-level coverage-based example selection with explicit, error-driven feedback that encodes annotation guidelines. This leads to robust improvements over existing selective annotation methods across tasks, data budgets, and selection strategies. The work suggests that incorporating structured, task-specific feedback into ICL prompts is a promising direction for enhancing LLM performance on complex structured prediction problems.

Abstract: Structured prediction tasks pose unique challenges for in-context learning (ICL): their compositional outputs require modeling fine-grained, token-level patterns that sentence-level approaches fail to capture, and their task-specific annotation conventions are human-defined artifacts that cannot be acquired through pretraining alone. We propose Verb-ICL, a selective annotation framework for ICL-based structured prediction that addresses both challenges. Verb-ICL first selects representative examples using a token-level coverage strategy that captures local semantic patterns critical for structured prediction, then generates actionable error feedback that codifies task-specific annotation guidelines and incorporates this feedback into ICL demonstrations. We evaluate Verb-ICL on six structured prediction datasets spanning information extraction and semantic parsing. Experiments with recent LLMs show that Verb-ICL consistently outperforms strong selective annotation baselines under low-resource settings and continues to provide gains as the annotation budget increases. Extended analyses demonstrate that the generated feedback is predominantly useful across a four-category quality taxonomy, generalizes as task-level guidance beyond instance-specific corrections, and improves performance regardless of the underlying selection strategy.

</details>


### [44] [More Value per Key: Asymmetric Sparse Attention for Faster LLM Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04753)
*Noam Elata,Itay Lamprecht,Mikey Shechter,Daniel Ohayon,Itay Hubara,Daniel Soudry*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes SAGA, an attention mechanism that uses fewer key heads and more value heads, combined with a new sparse attention scheme (Atop-N), to significantly speed up LLM decoding while preserving model quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoregressive LLMs are slowed down by the quadratic cost of attention, especially at long context lengths. Existing sparse attention approaches reduce the cost of computing attention scores but, in practice, make the value-weighted sum relatively cheap while leaving the query-key multiplication as the new bottleneck. There is a need to redesign attention so that models are faster at inference time without significantly hurting generation quality, and ideally in a way that can be applied to existing pretrained models.

Method: The authors analyze the compute distribution in sparse attention and note that query-key products dominate runtime when sparsity is high. They propose Sparse Asymmetric Group-Query Attention (SAGA), which decouples the number of key heads from the number of value heads, using fewer key heads (to reduce query-key cost) while maintaining or increasing value heads (to preserve representational capacity with minor extra cost). They pair this with Atop-N, an approximate top-N sparse attention scheme that selects the most relevant keys per query efficiently. They provide theoretical analysis of the computational benefits of head-count asymmetry, implement SAGA+Atop-N in LLMs up to 1.5B parameters, and design a fine-tuning procedure to convert existing GQA-style models into SAGA without full retraining.

Result: Empirical results show that SAGA combined with Atop-N yields more than 2× end-to-end decoding speedup at long context lengths compared to a full-attention Grouped Query Attention (GQA) baseline, while maintaining similar performance on standard quality benchmarks. Latency measurements confirm that reducing key heads substantially lowers the query-key bottleneck, and experiments on models up to 1.5B parameters validate that quality degradation is small when trained from scratch or converted via fine-tuning.

Conclusion: By making key and value head counts asymmetric and integrating a simple approximate sparse attention mechanism, the paper demonstrates that LLM inference can be significantly accelerated with minimal loss in quality. SAGA offers a practical way to exploit sparsity-induced compute patterns and can be retrofitted onto existing pretrained models via efficient fine-tuning, making it a suitable technique for faster deployment of long-context LLMs.

Abstract: utoregressive generation in Large Language Models (LLMs) is constrained by the memory and computational demands of attention mechanisms. Sparse attention methods mitigate this cost by selecting only high-probability entries of the attention matrix. We observe that in many such methods, this renders the probability-value multiplication negligible, shifting the bottleneck to the query-key step. Key heads can therefore be reduced to accelerate inference, while retaining more value heads preserves capacity with limited additional decoding cost. We introduce Sparse Asymmetric Group-Query Attention (SAGA), which decouples key and value head counts to exploit this principle, and pair it with approximate top-N (Atop-N) attention, a simple sparse attention method designed to study the interaction between sparsity and head-count asymmetry. We formalize the benefits of this asymmetry theoretically and validate them empirically through latency measurements and quality evaluations on models up to 1.5B parameters. Together, SAGA and Atop-N achieve end-to-end decoding speedups exceeding $2\times$ over our full-attention GQA baseline at long contexts. Models trained from scratch with SAGA nearly match the quality of comparable GQA variants on the evaluated benchmarks. To facilitate adoption, we introduce an efficient fine-tuning method that converts pretrained models to the SAGA architecture, enabling practitioners to benefit from our approach without costly retraining.

</details>


### [45] [How Do People Challenge Racial Stereotypes Online? Counter-Story Detection Across Reddit Communities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04803)
*Uma Sushmitha Gunturi,Jimin Mun,Maarten Sap,Maria Antoniak*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes the first computational framework to detect and analyze counter-storytelling against racial stereotypes in Reddit data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Counter-storytelling is an important way marginalized people challenge dominant, stereotype-based narratives, but it has been largely ignored in computational social science, especially compared to other forms of counterspeech. Because counter-stories are relational to stereotypes and structurally diverse, they are difficult to automatically identify, motivating a dedicated framework for their large-scale detection and analysis.

Method: The authors build a three-dimensional taxonomy of counter-stories grounded in narratology and Critical Race Theory, and design a multi-stage pipeline to find stereotype–counter-story pairs in noisy Reddit discussions. They then apply this pipeline to annotate 25,549 Reddit posts from 615 communities and identify instances of counter-storytelling.

Result: From the annotated Reddit corpus, the authors identify 1,312 counter-stories and find systematic patterns in how they are told, such as in-group authors more often using first-person testimony and positioning themselves as reflective insiders. They show that both speaker identity and conversational context influence the narrative form of counter-stories.

Conclusion: The framework successfully scales qualitative approaches to the computational detection and characterization of counter-storytelling as a contextual narrative practice. This has implications for improving content moderation tools, enriching narratological theory with large-scale evidence, and deepening empirical analyses of racial discourse online.

Abstract: Counter-storytelling is a powerful mechanism people use to challenge dominant narratives. Unlike other forms of counterspeech that have been widely studied in computational social science, counter-storytelling has largely been overlooked. Counter-stories are difficult to detect automatically; they are relational (defined with respect to expressions of racial stereotypes) and structurally diverse (drawing on stories that describe lived experiences, witnessed events, exemplars, and hypotheticals). We introduce a first framework for detecting and characterizing counter-storytelling against racial stereotypes at scale. This includes (1) a three-dimensional taxonomy grounded in narratology and Critical Race Theory and (2) a multi-stage pipeline that identifies relational pairs of stereotypes and counter-stories in noisy Reddit discourse. Using this pipeline, we annotate 25,549 Reddit posts across 615 communities and identify 1,312 counter-stories. Our analysis shows that speaker identity and post context shape how counter-stories are told. For example, in-group writers favor first-person testimony, often adopting the role of self-reflective insiders. Our work shows how computational methods can scale qualitative approaches to identify and characterize counter-storytelling as a contextual narrative practice, with implications for content moderation, narratology, and racial discourse analysis.

</details>


### [46] [Viva La Vida: Verification and Accumulation Failures in Multi-Agent Proof Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04829)
*Benji Xu,Ken Zheng,Noah Han*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper empirically studies an agentic theorem-proving system working on open problems and identifies systemic verification and supervision failures that corrupt the system’s internal knowledge base.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how autonomous, language-model-based theorem provers behave when no external proof assistant is available, and to identify where trust and reliability break down in such closed AI ecosystems.

Method: The authors instrument an end-to-end agentic prover whose verifier and lemma library are themselves language-model-based. They run it on an open problem three full times, recording 51,754 traced events over 186 hours and $5,694 in API costs, and then analyze verification outcomes, verifier disagreements, parsing/API failures, and how lemmas are extracted from both accepted proofs and reviewer refutations.

Result: They uncover three linked failure modes: (1) a three-model unanimity-based verifier treats parse/API failures as non-approvals, so in 10 of 12 key verification events at least one verifier failed to return parseable output, making acceptance impossible; (2) when the ensemble does work, individual verifiers sometimes approve incorrect purported solutions that the ensemble majority (or GPT) rejects, so a single-verifier design would have falsely declared the open problem solved three times; (3) because essentially nothing can be approved, all reviews are negative, yet the lemma extractor pulls lemmas from both proofs and reviews, so 24 of 93 lemmas (26%) originate from rejected arguments, stripped of their refutational context and thus misrepresented as trustworthy facts.

Conclusion: In closed, LLM-only reasoning systems, supervision and verification become a central trust boundary. Systems must cleanly separate abstention from rejection, maintain and expose useful disagreements rather than collapsing them, and track the provenance and polarity (supporting vs refuting) of information before adding it to contextual memory, or else they risk compounding errors and encoding refuted claims as reusable knowledge.

Abstract: When an agentic prover works on an open problem, there is no proof assistant to fall back on: its verifier and lemma library are ultimately language models judging model outputs. We instrumented such a system end to end and analyzed $51{,}754$ traced observations across three full runs ($186$ hours, \$$5{,}694$). We find three connected failure modes. First, the three-model verifier requires unanimity and treats parse or API failure as non-approval; in $10$ of $12$ verification events, one member returned no parseable output or an API error, making acceptance arithmetically impossible without surfacing an error. Second, when the ensemble did function, one verifier approved $3$ attempts that GPT rejected, each claiming to resolve the open problem; a single-verifier design would therefore have announced a solution three times. Third, because nothing could be approved, every review was a refutation, yet the lemma extractor mines reviews as well as proofs: $24$ of $93$ lemmas ($26\%$) were extracted from rejected arguments with their refutational context removed. Taken together, these findings show that without external verification, supervision is itself a critical trust boundary: systems must distinguish abstention from rejection, preserve useful disagreement, and preserve the provenance and polarity of information before it becomes future context.

</details>


### [47] [Cluster Validation Indices as Self-Supervised Objectives for Text Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04830)
*Kishor Kumar Bhaumik,Nicolas Roque dos Santos,Neil Shah,Jia Chen,Evangelos E. Papalexakis*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SilK is a self-supervised fine-tuning method for language encoders that optimizes a clustering quality metric without labels, avoiding contrastive negatives, augmentations, or auxiliary graphs, while being faster and more memory-efficient than baselines and maintaining competitive downstream performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing self-supervised fine-tuning methods for pretrained language encoders are computationally heavy because contrastive approaches require multiple views, in-batch negatives, or auxiliary graph structures. The authors want a simpler, more efficient method that can still improve embeddings without labels, negatives, or graph data.

Method: SilK (Silhouette-guided K-means) first clusters the corpus with k-means using the encoder embeddings. It then defines a simplified, label-free silhouette-based Cluster Validation Index as an internal measure of cluster quality. The encoder is fine-tuned by regressing each document’s silhouette score toward a target value, comparing each document only to k cluster centroids (not to other documents). This eliminates the need for data augmentation, negative pairs, or multiple views per document.

Result: On BERT-base, SilK achieves a 1.46x faster training speed per epoch than the fastest evaluated baseline and reduces peak GPU memory usage by 45.4% compared to the leanest baseline. Despite the efficiency gains, SilK remains competitive with state-of-the-art baselines under frozen-encoder linear probing on three downstream tasks.

Conclusion: Self-supervised fine-tuning of language encoders can be effectively performed without contrastive negatives, multiple views, or auxiliary graph structures by directly optimizing an internal cluster quality index. SilK offers a more computationally efficient alternative that preserves competitive downstream performance, demonstrating that cluster-validation-based objectives are a viable direction for representation refinement.

Abstract: Self-supervised fine-tuning refines the embedding space of a pretrained language encoder without labels. However, the commonly used approaches are computationally expensive. Specifically, contrastive learning-based methods need multiview data and in-batch negative examples, while negative-free approaches require auxiliary graphs/networks. An interesting question arises: can self-supervised fine-tuning be done without relying on either additional negatives or graph data? To answer this question, we introduce SilK (Silhouette-guided K-means), which trains on a Cluster Validation Index, an internal measure of cluster quality without using labels. SilK clusters the corpus and then regresses a simplified silhouette toward a target value. Each document is compared only against the k cluster centroids, never against other documents, so the method needs no augmentation, no negative pairs and one view per document. On BERT-base, SilK trains 1.46x faster per epoch than the fastest baseline we evaluate and uses 45.4% less peak GPU memory than the leanest one. Under frozen-encoder linear probing, SilK stays competitive with the best baselines on three downstream tasks.

</details>


### [48] [No Hindsight for LLM Fact-Checkers: Measuring Leakage Channels in Misinformation Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04888)
*Kuan-Hua Wu Lu,Yohanes Andre Setiawan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that current automated fact-checking benchmarks overestimate LLM performance because they let models use information that was not available when a claim was originally made.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM-based fact-checking is deployed on social media, their scores can appear unrealistically strong. A key problem is that benchmarks typically let models access information that became available only after the claim date, either through pretraining memorization of future outcomes or retrieval of later-published evidence. This conflates true reasoning over contemporaneous evidence with hindsight and leads to misleading evaluations of real-world fact-checking ability.

Method: The authors analyze two misinformation/fact-checking benchmarks, AVeriTeC and QuanTemp++, and explicitly reconstruct what evidence was available at the time each claim was made. They then separate two information channels: (1) parametric knowledge in the LLM (future outcomes memorized during pretraining) and (2) retrieved documents that may have been published after the claim. They probe model representations to detect outcome information (parametric leakage) and compare mitigation strategies, including a simple representation bottleneck versus a mutual-information-based training penalty. They also run experiments with and without access to post-claim evidence to quantify its impact on zero-shot accuracy.

Result: They find substantial parametric leakage: LLM internal representations often encode future outcomes that should not be knowable at claim time, and aggregate accuracy hides this issue. A simple representation bottleneck is more effective at reducing future leakage than a more complex mutual-information-based penalty. Allowing retrieval of post-claim evidence boosts zero-shot fact-checking accuracy on AVeriTeC by 6.3 percentage points but has negligible effect on QuanTemp++, where little evidence is available after the claim date. This demonstrates that benchmark scores can be artificially inflated when temporal evidence constraints are ignored.

Conclusion: Benchmarks for automated fact-checking can systematically overstate LLM performance because they fail to respect what information was actually available when claims were made. Both parametric memorization of future outcomes and retrieval of post-claim evidence distort evaluation. Separating these channels and enforcing point-in-time evidence conditions is crucial for building reliable, temporally faithful fact-checking systems and for reporting realistic performance numbers.

Abstract: As automated fact-checking scales on social media, large language model (LLM) verdict scores can look stronger than warranted. One reason is that evaluations mix in information that was not knowable at claim time. Two channels are easy to conflate: outcomes memorized in pre-training and retrieved evidence published after the claim. Yet standard benchmarks rarely separate the two. In this study we measure both channels on AVeriTeC and QuanTemp++ by reconstructing point-in-time evidence conditions and probing for outcome information encoded in model representations. We find substantial evidence of parametric leakage, that can be hidden by the aggregate accuracy, while a simple representation bottleneck reduces this future leakage more efficiently than a mutual-information-based training penalty. We also find that allowing post-claim evidence inflates zero-shot accuracy by 6.3 points in AVeriTeC while the effect is negligible in QuanTemp++, where retrieval provides little post-claim evidence. These results show that misinformation benchmarks can overstate fact-checking performance when they do not account for what information was actually available at claim time.

</details>


### [49] [A Systematic Analysis of the Predictive Power of LM Surprisal in Reading Chinese](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04898)
*Hongao Zhu,Muxiaoqiao Xu,Yikang Liu,Siyuan Song,Yuxia Wang,Byung-Doh Oh,Hai Hu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies whether surprisal from Chinese language models predicts Mandarin reading times and how this relationship scales with model size across different corpora.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work in psycholinguistics has found mixed or null results for surprisal predicting Mandarin Chinese reading times, unlike in alphabetic languages. A possible issue is the mismatch between eye-tracking corpora’s word segmentation and LMs’ subword tokenization. The authors want to resolve this alignment problem and reassess whether and how surprisal predicts Chinese reading behavior, especially as model size and training scale up.

Method: They introduce the Shortest Matching Sequence (SMS), a new alignment method that maps eye-tracking word-level units to LM subword tokens when tokenizations disagree. They compute token-level surprisal using a family of Chinese-Pythia transformer LMs ranging from 14M to 1.4B parameters trained from scratch on 30B tokens. Using these surprisal values, they model first fixation duration, gaze duration, and total reading time across three paragraph-level Mandarin eye-tracking corpora (GECO-CN, HKP, MECO). They then analyze how predictive power changes with model size and how closeness to n-gram surprisal statistics relates to prediction quality, especially where inverse scaling appears.

Result: Surprisal from Chinese LMs significantly predicts Mandarin reading times, overturning previous null results. However, scaling behavior is corpus-dependent: larger models yield better predictive power in GECO-CN, while inverse scaling (smaller or earlier models predicting better) appears in HKP and, for the largest models, in MECO. For HKP, they find that model checkpoints whose surprisal distributions more closely resemble n-gram statistics are better predictors of reading behavior.

Conclusion: Surprisal is a meaningful predictor of Mandarin reading times, but its predictive power and its scaling with model size are strongly corpus-specific. The dependence on corpus and on how “LM-like” vs. “n-gram-like” the surprisal is suggests that researchers should be cautious in generalizing scaling results from a single dataset and should pay close attention to tokenization alignment when relating LMs to human reading behavior.

Abstract: This study analyzes the predictive power of LM-derived, token-level surprisal on Mandarin Chinese reading times. We first propose the Shortest Matching Sequence (SMS), an alignment scheme that maps between the word segmentation assumed by eye-tracking corpora and the LMs' subword tokenization, as the two tokenizations often disagree in the context of Mandarin Chinese. Then, using a suite of Chinese-Pythia models (14M-1.4B) trained on scratch with 30B tokens, we examine how well surprisal predicts first fixation duration, gaze duration, and total reading time in three paragraph-level eye-tracking corpora of Mandarin Chinese (GECO-CN, HKP, and MECO). Contrary to previous null findings, our results show that surprisal is predictive of Chinese reading times. However, whether predictive power scales with model size and the amount of training is corpus-specific: bigger models predict better in GECO-CN, whereas inverse scaling emerges in HKP and, at the largest sizes, in MECO. Subsequently, we tested one possible explanation for the inverse scaling in HKP and found that checkpoints whose surprisal remains closer to $n$-gram statistics are better predictors of reading. All in all, the predictive power of surprisal on Chinese reading time measurements is corpus-specific, which cautions against drawing scaling conclusions from a single corpus.

</details>


### [50] [Rewrite What Matters: Adaptive Multilingual Query Rewriting for Reasoning via Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04899)
*Rui Qi,Yufeng Chen,Yunlong Liang,Chuan Meng,Sijin Lu,Ge Shi,Jinan Xu,Fandong Meng,Kaiyu Huang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper introduces mRewriter-R1, a reinforcement-learning-based, multilingual query rewriting framework that treats rewriting as a multi-turn decision process to reduce reasoning performance gaps across languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multilingual settings, semantically equivalent queries in different languages can push large reasoning models into different reasoning paths, causing uneven performance. Existing approaches typically use a single, fixed rewriting strategy (e.g., direct translation) that ignores task-specific and query-specific needs for more nuanced semantic transformation. The paper aims to close this multilingual performance gap by learning adaptive rewriting behaviors that better align queries—across languages and tasks—with the strengths of downstream reasoning models.

Method: The authors propose mRewriter-R1, an agentic multilingual query rewriting framework optimized via reinforcement learning. Instead of rewriting a query once, mRewriter-R1 models rewriting as a multi-turn, sequential decision-making process. At each turn, an agent selects from a set of rewriting operators (e.g., translation, paraphrasing, simplification, or other semantic transformations) and applies them to the query. A learned policy, trained with RL signals from downstream reasoning performance, adaptively chooses operators and stops when a satisfactory rewritten query is obtained. This yields multi-aspect optimization of the query form tailored to the task, language, and backbone reasoning model.

Result: Experiments show that mRewriter-R1 consistently outperforms strong multilingual rewriting baselines, including standard translation-based methods, across multiple large reasoning backbones. The improvements hold over diverse reasoning tasks, indicating that the learned multi-turn rewriting strategy yields better alignment of multilingual queries with the capabilities of various LLM reasoners.

Conclusion: The study concludes that treating multilingual query rewriting as an RL-driven, multi-turn decision process enables more effective and flexible semantic transformations than one-shot, one-size-fits-all rewriting. The learned policy can adapt its choice of operators to query characteristics, generalizes across reasoning tasks and languages, and integrates in a plug-and-play manner with different reasoning language models, substantially narrowing multilingual performance disparities.

Abstract: In multilingual scenarios, queries with equivalent semantics but in different languages could guide the model into different reasoning trajectories, leading to performance disparities. To mitigate this gap, previous studies typically apply a one-size-fits-all query rewriting strategy, such as translation, which overlooks the fact that different scenarios require diverse types of semantic transformations. In this paper, we propose mRewriter-R1, an agentic multilingual query rewriting framework with reinforcement learning. Unlike single-turn rewriting, mRewriter-R1 formulates multilingual query rewriting as a multi-turn sequential decision-making process, where the model dynamically performs multi-aspect optimization through adaptive operator selection. Experimental results demonstrate that mRewriter-R1 outperforms all strong multilingual rewriting baselines on different large reasoning backbones. Further analyses show that the learned policy can adaptively decide on rewriting operators according to query characteristics, exhibiting strong generalization ability across diverse reasoning tasks, and plug-and-play compatibility with heterogeneous reasoning language models.

</details>


### [51] [Scaling Verifiable Environments for Long-horizon Work Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04906)
*Jiazheng Zhang,Long Ma,Yunxian Yang,Zhiheng Xi,Zhikai Lei,Yajie Yang,Chenyang Liao,Enyu Zhou,Yang Nan,Yuchen Tian,Senjie Jin,Yibo Wang,Wei He,Boyang Liu,Jixuan Huang,Xin Guo,Zhezheng Hao,Xinbing Liang,Zhihao Zhang,Changzhi Zhou,Wiggin Zhou,Tao Gui,Qi Zhang,Xuanjing Huang,Clarenceai,Aiden Adams*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduces WorkForge, a scalable framework that automatically builds realistic, verifiable work-agent training environments from real-world resources, significantly boosting work-agent performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing training environments for work agents either require costly, hand-crafted engineering to achieve realism and verifiability or use synthetic setups that lack complexity, realism, or grounded verification. There is a need for scalable, realistic, and verifiable environments built from real-world artifacts to train and evaluate work agents on long-horizon, knowledge-intensive tasks.

Method: WorkForge starts from expert workflows and decomposes them into required resources, decisions, and deliverables. It then (1) retrieves relevant real-world files and assembles them into a workspace, (2) inspects these files to extract concrete, checkable factual anchors, and (3) uses these anchors to define which task types the workspace supports and how outputs can be verified. From these anchors, WorkForge automatically derives task instructions, solution plans, and both programmatic and semantic verifiers whose checks are traceable to evidence in the workspace. The authors instantiate this pipeline to synthesize thousands of environments across many domains.

Result: Using WorkForge, the authors construct 16.7K verifiable environments spanning 40 professional domains and 60 file types. Training Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base on these environments substantially improves evaluation metrics: GDPVal increases from 45.5 to 73.6 and APEX Score from 5.0 to 21.3. WorkForge-trained data also allows Qwen3.5-27B to attain highly competitive performance and surpass strong baselines.

Conclusion: WorkForge enables scalable construction of realistic, verifiable work-agent environments directly from real-world resources, overcoming the limitations of hand-crafted and naive synthetic setups. The framework delivers large, diverse benchmarks and demonstrably improves model performance, with analyses indicating robust scaling with both more data and longer interaction horizons.

Abstract: Work agents operate over digital artifacts to execute professional knowledge-intensive work, requiring training environments that support long-horizon interaction and trustworthy verification. However, hand-crafted environments incur prohibitive engineering overhead that prevents environment scaling, whereas synthesis methods sacrifice workspace complexity, realism, or grounded verifiability. To bridge this gap, we introduce WorkForge, a scalable synthesis framework for constructing verifiable work-agent environments from real-world resources. Starting from expert workflows, WorkForge first identifies the resources, decisions, and deliverables required by each workflow. It then retrieves relevant real-world files and organizes them into a workspace. WorkForge inspects the workspace to extract concrete, checkable facts about its content. These factual anchors fix which task types the workspace can support and how their outcomes can be verified. Therefore, WorkForge derives each task's instructions, solution plan, and complementary programmatic and semantic verifiers directly from these factual anchors, keeping verification traceable to observable workspace evidence. Furthermore, we construct 16.7K verifiable environments across 40 professional domains, with workspaces collectively covering 60 file types. Post-training Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base improves GDPVal from 45.5 to 73.6 and APEX Score from 5.0 to 21.3, while enabling Qwen3.5-27B to achieve highly competitive performance and outperform strong competitors. Our analyses confirm the efficacy of the proposed method and reveal consistent scaling behaviors across both data volume and interaction horizons.

</details>


### [52] [From Overloaded to Guaranteed: High-Throughput Multi-SLO Enforcement for LoRA-Assisted On-Premise LLM Deployment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04956)
*Zeshen Zhang,Han Zhao,Weihao Cui,Quan Chen,Yu Liu,Yongjun Deng,Jing Yang,Jiuchen Shi,Chen Chen,Youmin Chen,Yu Feng,Minyi Guo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Proposes HALO, a scheduling technique for LoRA-based, on-premise LLM serving that reduces SLO violations and improves throughput via spatial GPU multiplexing and SLO-aware request scheduling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-premise LLM servers in privacy-sensitive environments (e.g., hospitals, governments) must meet strict and heterogeneous SLOs under limited computational resources. When these servers host multiple LoRA-adapted services, existing serving frameworks suffer from high SLO violation rates due to the added computation of LoRA layers and inflexible batching mechanisms, making them unsuitable for such constrained, multi-tenant scenarios.

Method: Design HALO, a specialized scheduling scheme for LoRA-enabled on-premise LLMs, with two main components: (1) a spatial multiplexing strategy that partitions GPU Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) to overlap base model and LoRA-specific computations, thereby reducing contention and better utilizing GPU resources; and (2) an SLO-aware scheduler that introduces the notion of per-request "request-level slack" to decouple and prioritize requests based on urgency, using available slack to shape traffic and schedule less urgent work without harming SLOs.

Result: Experimental evaluation (details not in abstract but implied on realistic multi-service workloads) shows that HALO substantially reduces SLO violations and simultaneously improves throughput compared with state-of-the-art LLM serving baselines that lack such LoRA- and SLO-aware scheduling mechanisms.

Conclusion: HALO is an effective approach for deploying multiple LoRA-adapted LLM services on resource-constrained, on-premise servers, as its combination of spatial GPU multiplexing and request-slack-based scheduling significantly mitigates resource contention, lowers SLO violation rates, and improves overall system throughput relative to existing frameworks.

Abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become essential in privacy-sensitive sectors like hospitals and government agencies, the on-premise LLM servers offer a cost-effective and secure alternative to public cloud services. However, these resource-constrained servers struggle to guarantee heterogeneous Service Level Objectives (SLOs) when serving multiple LoRA-adapted services simultaneously. Existing serving frameworks suffer from severe SLO violations due to the computational overhead of LoRA layers and the rigid nature of batch scheduling. To address this, we propose HALO, a scheduling method tailored for LoRA-assisted on-premise LLM deployment. HALO introduces two key innovations: a spatial multiplexing strategy that overlaps Base and LoRA computations by partitioning GPU Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs), and an SLO-aware scheduler that decouples request execution based on "request-level slack." By prioritizing urgent tasks and utilizing idle budget for traffic shaping, HALO significantly mitigates resource contention. Our evaluation demonstrates that HALO minimizes SLO violations while improving throughput compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

</details>


### [53] [Building LLM Agent Systems the Deep Learning Way: From Modular Design to Architecture Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04961)
*Tao Feng,Pengrui Han,Zhongjie Dai,Jiaxuan You*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a deep-learning-style recipe for automatically constructing and optimizing modular LLM agent systems, achieving notable performance gains via structured architectures, automatic prompt "backpropagation," and architecture search.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM agent systems are largely hand-engineered using heuristics or insights from other domains, which is labor-intensive and often suboptimal for downstream tasks. The authors are motivated to bring the systematic, trainable, and automatable design principles of deep learning (e.g., modular composition, backpropagation, and neural architecture search) into the construction of LLM agent systems to reduce manual effort and improve performance.

Method: They conceptualize components of LLM agents (retrieval, memory, prompting strategies) as analogues of deep learning modules (MLPs, attention, RNNs). Based on this analogy, they (1) organize LLM modules into layered, deep-learning-like architectures; (2) treat prompts as tunable weights and design a feedback-driven prompt optimization method analogous to backpropagation, using task-specific signals to iteratively refine prompts; and (3) apply a search procedure similar to neural architecture search to automatically discover effective LLM agent architectures over this modular design space.

Result: Experiments show: (1) Structuring LLM modules into deep-learning-inspired architectures yields clear performance improvements over ad-hoc designs; (2) the feedback-based prompt optimization mechanism brings at least 5% performance gains by efficiently utilizing task feedback; and (3) the NAS-like search over agent architectures further improves performance, achieving around 11% gain compared to randomly assembled architectures.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that transferring core deep learning ideas—modular composition, gradient-like feedback optimization, and architecture search—to the design of LLM agent systems leads to substantial empirical benefits. This suggests that LLM agents can be systematically engineered and optimized using a "deep learning recipe" rather than relying on manual, heuristic-based system design.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized AI research and enabled exciting agent systems. To build a complex LLM agent system, most existing research relies on insights from other domains or heuristics to manually build the agent system. However, this approach often requires heavy hand-engineering and fails to fully optimize for the downstream task of interest. Inspired by the tremendous success of deep learning, we propose to construct LLM agent systems in a modular manner, similar to building a deep neural network. Our key insight is to make analogies between LLM building blocks, such as retrievals, memories, and prompting strategies, and the successful deep learning modules, such as MLPs, attention, and recurrent modules. We further design forward inference and feedback mechanisms for LLMs, where prompts in LLMs are considered as the weights in deep models, and the prompt optimization from feedback is analogous to the back-propagation algorithm. We additionally leverage a search algorithm to search for the best configuration of LLM agent systems, similar to the neural architecture search (NAS) in deep learning research. Comprehensive experimental results demonstrate that the proposed deep learning recipe for LLM agent systems is highly effective, in particular: (1) Organizing LLM modules into deep-learning-style architectures yields noticeable performance gain; (2) Automatic prompt optimization, equivalent to backpropagation, is efficient in incorporating feedback from the task of interest and achieves at least 5% performance improvement; (3) NAS equivalent algorithm works well for further optimizing the LLM agent system architecture with 11% performance gain compared with randomly designed architectures. Overall, our research demonstrates the exciting opportunity of transferring the success of deep learning to building LLM agent systems.

</details>


### [54] [TrajLong: Co-Designing Agentic and Long-Context Supervision for Mid-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04973)
*Miao Peng,Qintong Zhang,Nuo Chen,Yuhan Li,Guochen Yan,Xinran Gu,Hongqiu Wu,Hai Wang,Lydell Huang,Wentao Zhang,Jia Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TrajLong is a training framework that turns agent interaction trajectories into long-context tasks with dense labels to improve both long-context reasoning and core agent skills in LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents for coding, search, and office workflows increasingly need to work over long interaction histories, but current training underuses the rich structure in agent trajectories. Prior work includes trajectories in mid-training, yet it is unclear how to best organize and supervise the information in these long logs so that models actually acquire the atomic skills needed for effective agents.

Method: The authors propose TrajLong, which systematically compiles agent trajectories into synthetic long-context training tasks that provide dense supervision. These tasks explicitly target three atomic capabilities important for agents: (1) evidence grounding—linking answers to specific pieces of context; (2) cross-evidence aggregation—combining multiple pieces of information; and (3) temporal state maintenance—tracking evolving states over time. They mid-train base Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-30B models on this TrajLong-compiled data, then apply a standard supervised fine-tuning stage. They also construct baselines using raw and masked trajectories to isolate the effect of TrajLong’s structured compilation.

Result: On a suite of 6 long-context benchmarks and 12 agent benchmarks, models mid-trained with TrajLong consistently outperform those trained on raw or masked trajectories. Ablation experiments isolate the contribution of TrajLong’s structured supervision, showing that the gains are not simply from more data or longer contexts but from how trajectories are transformed into capability-targeted tasks. Capability-level diagnostics show that different downstream tasks rely on different mixtures of the three targeted atomic capabilities.

Conclusion: Structuring agent trajectories into long-context, densely supervised tasks around core atomic skills yields broad improvements in both long-context reasoning and agent performance.
