Conclusion: Instruction-following benchmarks that rely on a single canonical phrasing of each constraint can be highly unstable: rewording alone can materially change measured compliance and model rankings, even when humans agree on the intended requirement. WISE is proposed as a supplement to conventional evaluation, adding metrics such as mean and worst-form compliance, wording gaps, failure profiles, and ranking stability under paraphrase. This supports the view that robust assessment of instruction following should account for wording sensitivity rather than relying on one fixed template per constraint.

Abstract: Verifiable instruction-following benchmarks often express each constraint through one fixed template. We test whether scores remain stable when the operational requirement is unchanged but its wording varies. We introduce WISE, a matched evaluation suite and reporting protocol instantiated on exact word count, keyword inclusion exactly once, and an inclusive 8--12 word range. Across 100 matched tasks, up to thirteen models from seven providers, and repeated generations scored over the complete visible output, wording alone produces substantial compliance shifts. In an avoidance-family panel, five avoidance and exclusion forms fall below the positive baseline, while constructional controls also shift compliance substantially: in the nine-model control panel, compliance is 54.9% for the original positive form, 48.2% for a longer positive form, 36.7% when the target appears later, and 33.8% for AVOID1. A strict JSON-structure probe shows wording sensitivity beyond counting, with a different direction of effect. Effect sizes, failure directions, weakest forms, and model rankings vary across realizations. Under the most disruptive exclusion form, the top-ranked model changes and 24.1% of strictly ordered model pairs reverse. Human validation further shows that unanimous agreement on an exact-count interpretation can coexist with substantially different model behavior. WISE supplements conventional scores with mean and worst-form compliance, wording gaps, failure profiles, and ranking stability.

</details>


### [72] [Red-TTT: Test-Time Training for Automated Jailbreaking Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05282)
*Tongyan Hu,Hao Li,Xiaogeng Liu,Ruida Wang,Zhengyu Liu,Shuyao Xu,Ning Zhang,Ziyang Li,Yinzhi Cao,Bryan Hooi,Chaowei Xiao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Red-TTT is an online, gradient-updated jailbreaking attacker that adapts its prompts during each attack, significantly improving automated red-teaming success over static sampling methods under the same query budget.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing automated red-teaming methods for large language models either do search/rewriting/tree expansion at test time or pretrain a powerful attacker offline. In both cases, once an attack on a particular target behavior starts, the attack model’s parameters are frozen. Any information the attacker learns about the victim model and the specific behavior lives only in the transient context and is discarded after the attack, making the attack’s success mostly a function of how many samples can be drawn. Under realistic query budgets, many unsafe behaviors remain undiscovered. There is a need for an attacker that can update itself online during an attack, using feedback from the victim to adapt its proposal distribution in real time and better exploit limited sampling budgets.

Method: The authors introduce Red-TTT, an online red-teaming framework that performs parameter updates during each attack episode. For a fixed target behavior and victim model, Red-TTT operates in rounds. In each round, the attacker policy produces a batch of candidate prompts, queries the victim with these candidates, and scores them based on how successful they are at eliciting the target unsafe behavior. Using these scores, Red-TTT applies a policy-gradient update (a form of reinforcement learning) to the attacker’s parameters before sampling the next batch. This consolidates information about the victim’s vulnerabilities into the model’s weights instead of just accumulating in the context. Additionally, the objective is tailored to red-teaming: it optimizes for success defined by the single best candidate in a batch rather than the average performance, aligning the learning signal with the “best-of-N” evaluation used in jailbreak attacks. The approach only assumes sampling access to the victim and can be plugged into existing automated attack pipelines without architectural changes.

Result: In experiments comparing against a Best-of-N baseline across multiple configurations and a fixed query budget of 120 samples per target behavior, Red-TTT consistently outperforms the baseline. Average attack success rate increases from 55.9% with Best-of-N to 72.4% with Red-TTT. The method improves results in every tested configuration and is able to compromise (“crack”) many target behaviors that previous automated methods fail to break under the same sampling budget, demonstrating better exploitation of limited queries via online adaptation.

Conclusion: Red-TTT shows that making the attacker adaptive at test time—updating its parameters online with policy-gradient steps informed by the victim’s responses—substantially increases automated red-teaming effectiveness under realistic query budgets. By aligning the training objective with best-of-N style success criteria and requiring only black-box sampling access, Red-TTT can be integrated into existing red-teaming pipelines to discover jailbreaks that static or offline-trained attackers miss. This suggests that future safety evaluations of large language models should consider such online, learning-in-the-loop attackers as a stronger and more realistic threat model.

Abstract: Large language models remain vulnerable to jailbreaks, and automated red teaming is the standard way to find jailbreaks in large language models at scale. Current methods either draw more samples at test time through search, rewriting, and tree expansion, or train a stronger attacker offline with reinforcement learning. Both share a limitation: once an attack on a specific target behavior begins, the attacker's weights are frozen. Any signal it gathers about the behavior stays in its context window and is discarded afterward. The attacker never adapts its proposal distribution mid-attack, so success depends almost entirely on the sampling budget, and under a budget affordable at scale, many behaviors remain unbroken. We propose Red-TTT, which updates the attacker's parameters during the attack on each behavior. At each round, the attacker samples a group of candidates, scores them against the victim's replies, and takes a policy-gradient step before drawing the next group, so what it discovers about the current victim is consolidated into weights rather than accumulated as context. We also adapt the training objective to red teaming, where success is judged by the single best sample rather than the average. Red-TTT requires only sampling access to the victim and integrates into existing attack pipelines with no other changes. Against the Best-of-N baseline, Red-TTT raises attack success rate from 55.9\% to 72.4\% on average at a budget of 120 samples, improving over the baseline in every configuration and cracking many behaviors previous method cannot. The code is available at https://github.com/SaFo-Lab/Red-TTT

</details>


### [73] [RubricArmor: Adversarial Evolution Improves LLM-Based Rubric Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05308)
*Haocheng Yang,Yuchao Zhang,Licheng Pan,Jiajun Fan,Maolin Wang,Kangning Zhang,Shuai Shao,Shijian Wang,Yuan Lu,Chunyuan Zheng,Hao Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RubricArmor is an adversarial rubric-generation framework that makes LLM-based rubrics more robust against reward hacking in rubric-based reinforcement learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rubric-based RL aligns LLMs using interpretable, query-specific criteria, but rubrics directly generated by LLMs often miss or underspecify key criteria. These gaps let a learned policy "hack" the reward by producing responses that satisfy the rubric text while still being low quality or failing the task. Existing methods mainly focus on increasing rubric detail and coverage, not on systematically stress-testing rubrics for vulnerabilities to reward hacking before RL training. There is a need for a principled way to expose and fix these vulnerabilities at the rubric design stage.

Method: RubricArmor introduces an adversarial evolution loop over rubrics. Starting from an initial rubric, it alternates two steps: (1) an attack step, which simulates reward hacking by generating adversarial responses that score well under the current rubric yet do not truly solve the task; and (2) a repair step, which analyzes the discovered defects and revises the rubric to explicitly capture and penalize those failure modes while preserving correct criteria. This iterative process continues for multiple rounds, progressively hardening the rubric against exploitative responses.

Result: In experiments, rubrics produced by RubricArmor are more robust against adversarial or low-quality responses that attempt to exploit rubric loopholes, compared with rubrics generated by strong baseline methods. When used as reward models in downstream rubric-based RL, these improved rubrics lead to better-aligned and higher-quality LLM policies, showing consistent performance gains across evaluation benchmarks.

Conclusion: Adversarially stress-testing and refining rubrics during generation substantially reduces reward hacking in rubric-based RL for LLMs. RubricArmor’s attack–repair evolution produces more comprehensive and reliable rubrics than prior LLM-based methods, and these stronger rubrics translate into better downstream RL outcomes. The work suggests that proactive, adversarial rubric design is an effective strategy for robust LLM alignment.

Abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) provides interpretable rewards for aligning large language models (LLMs) by evaluating responses against query-specific evaluation criteria. To construct rubrics at scale, a straightforward approach to LLM-based rubric generation is to prompt an LLM to generate a rubric directly from the query. However, rubrics directly generated by LLMs are vulnerable to reward hacking, since omitted or underspecified criteria allow the policy to obtain high rubric rewards with low-quality responses. Existing LLM-based rubric generation methods improve the granularity and coverage of the generated criteria but do not proactively guard against reward hacking. To address this limitation, we propose RubricArmor, an adversarial framework that exposes and mitigates potential reward hacking at the rubric generation stage before it occurs in subsequent RL. Specifically, RubricArmor performs adversarial evolution, in which an attack step and a repair step alternate over multiple rounds. The attack step simulates the reward hacking of the policy by constructing adversarial responses that satisfy the current rubric but fail to properly complete the task. The repair step then revises the rubric to detect the response defects exposed by the attack step while preserving other valid criteria. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RubricArmor outperforms competitive rubric generation baselines and translates into more effective downstream rubric-based RL.

</details>


### [74] [MemStrata: 95% and 90.91% Source-Aware Accuracy on LongMemEval-500 and LoCoMo-1540 with a Local Qwen 3.8 27B Q4_K_M Reader](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05343)
*Neeraj Yadav*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates MemStrata CL1, a memory/retrieval scheme for long conversational histories, using source-aware grading and finds it substantially improves measured answer adequacy over reference-only grading and over several baselines, though with notable limitations and no strong leaderboard claim.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Benchmarks that grade conversational QA only against short or imperfect references can misjudge answer adequacy, especially for long histories. The authors want a more faithful evaluation of long-context systems that accounts for the full conversation history and tests whether a structured retrieval method (MemStrata CL1) can efficiently capture relevant context while remaining practical and robust across models and benchmarks.

Method: They introduce source-aware grading, where a judge model (GPT-5.5) first compares the benchmark reference to the full underlying source and then evaluates blinded system answers, contrasting this with traditional reference-only grading. Using a local Qwen 3.8 27B reader and a 24k-token evidence budget, they test the MemStrata CL1 retrieval/memory scheme on LongMemEval-S, LongMemEval-M, LoCoMo, and BEAM-1M, and compare against baselines: full-history reading, keyword-only selection, dense retrieval, a Letta-style system, and alternative judge/reader models (GLM 5.3 flash, Muse Spark 1.3). They perform registered interventions and replay experiments to study label stability and feasibility, and analyze where performance degrades (e.g., multi-session and temporal questions).

Result: Under source-aware grading, MemStrata CL1 attains 95.0% on LongMemEval-S and 90.91% on LoCoMo categories 1–4, higher than when the same answers are scored reference-only (92.6% and 78.25%), showing that richer grading recognizes more answers as adequate. It matches or slightly exceeds a full-history control despite using about 4.7× less evidence, and clearly beats keyword-only and Letta-style baselines at the same budget. On LongMemEval-M, where only ~1.6% of each history is available, it drops to 427/500, with deficits in multi-session and temporal queries. On BEAM-1M it outperforms dense retrieval (0.738 vs 0.706, Wilcoxon p=0.011). Label replays show 1.5–2.3% variability. GLM 5.3 flash performs within 3 points of Qwen on identical packets, while Muse Spark 1.3 fails non-inferiority on 269 questions. None of the four preregistered interventions meets its full advancement/feasibility targets.

Conclusion: MemStrata CL1 is an efficient and competitive memory/retrieval strategy for long conversational histories that can rival or beat full-history reading and several baselines under more faithful, source-aware grading, particularly on single-session and non-temporal questions. However, its advantages are sensitive to evaluation protocol, it struggles with multi-session and temporal reasoning at low coverage, and the overall study cannot support strong leaderboard or replicability claims due to judge dependence, lack of held-out data, and possible development bias. Source-aware grading appears promising but its superiority over careful human adjudication is not yet demonstrated.

Abstract: An adequate conversational answer may differ from a short or incomplete benchmark reference. To measure adequacy against the recorded history we prefer source-aware grading, in which the judge checks the reference against the full source before assessing system-blinded answers; original reference-only grading is reported alongside. With a local Qwen 3.8 27B Q4_K_M reader and a 24,000-token evidence ceiling, MemStrata CL1 scores 475/500 (95.0%) on LongMemEval-S and 1,400/1,540 (90.91%) on LoCoMo categories 1-4 under source-aware GPT-5.5 adjudication, against 463/500 (92.6%) and 1,205/1,540 (78.25%) under reference-only grading of the same answers. It preserves a retrieval backbone and adds nonduplicated, dated, speaker-attributed source spans. A same-reader full-history control with about 4.7 times the evidence scores 464/500 reference-only and 470/500 (94.0%) source-aware; neither difference is decisive. Keyword-only selection at the same budget scores 425, and a matched-reader Letta arm 438. On LongMemEval-M, where the packet holds about 1.6% of each history, MemStrata CL1 scores 427/500, with losses concentrated in multi-session and temporal questions. On 300 BEAM-1M questions it outscores dense retrieval, 0.738 to 0.706 (Wilcoxon p = 0.011). A same-seed replay of unchanged requests changed 1.5-2.3% of labels. On identical packets GLM 5.3 flash is non-inferior within 3 points (462 versus 463); Muse Spark 1.3 did not show non-inferiority on 269 questions. None of four pre-registered interventions met all of its registered advancement or feasibility criteria. Signed read-side artifacts support inspection but do not regenerate the private retrieval pipeline. The superiority of source-aware grading to human adjudication is not established, and development exposure, automated-judge dependence and the absence of held-out data preclude an independent-replication or leaderboard claim.

</details>


### [75] [The ÌròyìnSpeech Text Corpus: 24,905 Curated Yorùbá Sentences for Speech and Language Technology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05366)
*Kola Tubosun,Aanuoluwapo Aremu,Tolulope Ogunremi,Iroro Orife,David Ifeoluwa Adelani*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper releases and describes the text component of ÌròyìnSpeech, a hand-verified, tone-marked Yorùbá sentence corpus supporting speech and language technology.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Yorùbá corpora are dominated by religious translations and often lack tone marks, limiting their usefulness for speech technologies and linguistic research. There is a need for a large, carefully curated, tone-accurate, and domain-diverse Yorùbá text resource aligned with read speech data.

Method: The authors curated 24,905 Yorùbá sentences (around 276k tokens) as prompts for a 42-hour, 80-speaker read-speech corpus. About 11k sentences were adapted from openly licensed news sources, while the rest were original in-house creations to diversify domains. All sentences were manually verified for correct tone marking, edited for clarity and neutral register, localised for Yorùbá-appropriate forms of names, and checked for Unicode normalisation issues, which were then systematically documented and corrected.

Result: They produced a high-quality, tone-marked Yorùbá text corpus with 24,905 unique sentences, 275,897 tokens and 15,687 types, all cleaned, normalised, and suitable as validated prompts. They also identified and fixed widespread Unicode normalisation problems affecting over 60% of lines, ensuring consistent encoding of diacritics.

Conclusion: The released corpus provides a reliable resource for diacritic restoration, grapheme-to-phoneme conversion, TTS front-end development, and orthographic research, and it can be reused as a validated prompt set for new Yorùbá speech recordings, addressing gaps in existing Yorùbá language resources.

Abstract: ÌròyìnSpeech is a 42-hour, 80-speaker Yorùbá read-speech corpus whose audio has been distributed by ELRA since 2024. This paper describes the release of its text component: 24,905 unique, hand-verified, tone-marked Yorùbá sentences (275,897 tokens; 15,687 types), curated in 2022 as recording prompts. Roughly 11,000 sentences were adapted from openly licensed news material; the remainder were written in-house to broaden coverage beyond the religious translation that dominates existing Yorùbá corpora. Every sentence was checked by hand for tone-mark accuracy, edited for read-aloud clarity and a neutral register, and localised so that non-Yorùbá personal and place names appear in Yorùbá form. Preparing the text for release surfaced systematic Unicode normalisation failures affecting more than 60% of lines (with precomposed and decomposed forms of the same letter co-occurring within single sentences) which we document and correct. The corpus supports diacritic restoration, grapheme-to-phoneme conversion, TTS front-end development and orthographic research, and serves as a validated prompt set for new recording.

</details>


### [76] [Towards Unbiased On-Policy Distillation for Block Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05373)
*Zaiquan Yang,Fei Wei,Yong Wang,Yudong Han,Yiyu Li,Zhuofan Zong,Gerhard Petrus Hancke,Xiangxiang Chu,Rynson WH Lau*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper identifies key optimization biases that destabilize on-policy distillation for block diffusion language models with large blocks and proposes Un-OPD, a method that filters misaligned steps and rebalances confidence updates, stabilizing training and improving performance and efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-policy distillation has shown promise as a post-training method for language models, and has recently been extended to block diffusion language models. However, prior work mainly handles small block sizes; when scaling to larger blocks, training becomes unstable. The authors aim to understand why this instability arises and how to enable robust distillation into large-block student BDLMs, which are attractive for efficiency and performance.

Method: The authors analyze on-policy distillation dynamics for BDLMs with larger blocks and identify two main optimization biases: context misalignment caused by mismatched block boundaries between teacher and student, and an intrinsic bias favoring rapid learning from high-support tokens that leads to premature overconfidence. To address these, they propose Un-OPD, which (1) applies boundary-aware step filtering to discard decoding steps where teacher and student contexts are misaligned, and (2) introduces a support-rebalanced confidence calibration that reduces optimization intensity on high-support positions to prevent overconfidence collapse. They also add a rollout reuse mechanism to amortize the cost of generating on-policy rollouts.

Result: Experiments on math reasoning and code generation benchmarks show that Un-OPD significantly stabilizes BDLM on-policy distillation for large blocks, avoiding catastrophic training collapse. It consistently outperforms baseline OPD approaches in accuracy and reasoning quality while roughly halving wall-clock training time, thanks in part to rollout reuse.

Conclusion: Instabilities in on-policy distillation for large-block BDLMs stem from context misalignment and an intrinsic optimization bias toward high-support tokens that induces overconfidence. By filtering out misaligned steps and rebalancing confidence updates, Un-OPD provides an unbiased and stable distillation framework that improves both performance and efficiency. This suggests that carefully handling context alignment and optimization bias is crucial for scalable, reliable OPD of block diffusion language models.

Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as an effective post-training paradigm for language models, with recent efforts extending it to block diffusion language models (BDLMs). However, existing studies focus almost exclusively on small block sizes, leaving distillation into student models with larger blocks underexplored. In this work, we investigate this regime and reveal two critical optimization biases that induce severe training instability. First, mismatched block boundaries between teacher and student cause \textbf{\textit{context misalignment}}, providing distorted supervisory signals that misguide student decoding. Second, even under aligned contexts, an \textbf{\textit{intrinsic optimization bias}} in OPD, where the student tends to rapidly absorb high-support signals while lagging on low-support updates, drives a premature confidence surge that traps weaker students in catastrophic overconfidence collapse. To resolve these, we propose \mbox{\textbf{Un-OPD}}, an unbiased on-policy distillation framework with two novelties for stabilizing BDLM training. First, Un-OPD introduces a boundary-aware step filtering strategy that eliminates context-misaligned decoding steps. Second, Un-OPD proposes moderating optimization intensity at high-support positions via a support-rebalanced confidence calibration, thereby bypassing overconfidence collapse. Beyond stability, we also introduce a rollout reuse mechanism to reduce rollout generation overhead. Extensive experiments on math reasoning and code generation benchmarks show that Un-OPD consistently stabilizes training and delivers superior performance while reducing wall-clock training time by approximately half.

</details>


### [77] [Harness-Search: Guiding Long-Horizon Search through Multi-Agent Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05382)
*Shanyong Wang,Zhenwen Ji,Lei Jin,Yining Zhao,Yicheng Qian,Chengqiang Lu,Yi Wu,Yao Hu,Lizhen Cui,Yanyu Xu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduces Harness-Search, a multi-agent search framework that improves long-horizon information retrieval and answer generation by splitting responsibilities across specialized agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-agent search harnesses for long-horizon tasks often fail as histories grow: the agent may lose track of unresolved questions, miss important evidence, or stop too early. Local decision errors in exploration, state updating, and termination can propagate and degrade performance.

Method: Propose a multi-agent search harness called Harness-Search that decomposes long-horizon search into three roles: (1) a Retrieval Policy that proposes search actions, (2) a Memory Operator that validates and commits updates to a persistent memory state, and (3) a Summary Auditor that decides whether to terminate based on evidence sufficiency. These components interact in a Propose-Commit-Audit loop to manage exploration, evidence curation, and stopping decisions with permission-bounded authority.

Result: On seven long-horizon search benchmarks, Harness-Search, using the same policy backbone as baselines, improves retrieval Recall by 4.60–27.92 points and Final-Answer Recall by 12.34–30.13 points over the strongest harness-based baseline in each benchmark. Trajectory analysis indicates that it accumulates more useful, less redundant evidence and maintains or expands coverage as search histories become longer.

Conclusion: Decoupling retrieval, memory updating, and stopping decisions into a structured multi-agent harness reduces error propagation in long-horizon search. This Propose-Commit-Audit framework leads to better evidence collection and answer quality, particularly as interaction histories grow, demonstrating a more reliable approach to long-running search processes.

Abstract: Long-horizon search requires agents to gather evidence across multiple steps and synthesize it into well-supported answers. The recent agent harnesses provide a natural and promising framework to support such long-running search processes. As interaction histories grow, one single agent in harnesses might get stuck and cause the policy to lose track of unresolved questions, overlook useful evidence, or terminate before sufficient support has been collected. One of promising way is to decouple three distinct responsibilities of proposing retrieval actions, updating persistent state, and deciding when to stop rather than concentrating them within a single policy. Targeted at it, we introduce Harness-Search, a multi-agent search harness to reduce the local errors propagating across subsequent exploration, evidence curation, and termination decisions. In particular, Harness-Search assigns these responsibilities to three permission-bounded authorities: a Retrieval Policy that proposes search operations, a Memory Operator that validates and commits persistent-state updates, and a Summary Auditor that accepts or rejects termination based on the sufficiency of the curated evidence. Together, these roles form a Propose-Commit-Audit loop in which actions are proposed, persistent evidence is selectively committed, and stopping decisions are subjected to an explicit sufficiency check. Across seven long-horizon search benchmarks, Harness-Search improves both retrieval and answer generation under the same policy backbone, increasing Recall by 4.60-27.92 points and Final-Answer Recall by 12.34-30.13 points over the strongest harness-based baseline on each evidence-retrieval benchmark. Moreover, trajectory-level analyses show that Harness-Search continues to accumulate useful evidence and expand evidence coverage with less redundant retrieval as the search history grows.

</details>


### [78] [The Hidden States Cookbook: A Large-Scale Ablation Study for Noise-Robust Conversational Intent Classification in Industry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05394)
*Bogdan Bogachov,Nikita Letov,Yaoyao Fiona Zhao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates which embedding pooling strategy best preserves intent classification accuracy for conversational database interfaces under realistic noisy user input.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conversational database interfaces must classify user intent from queries that naturally include greetings, politeness, and off-topic chatter. This conversational noise harms classification accuracy and wastes computation, yet practitioners lack clear, empirical guidance on which pooling strategies make classifier embeddings most robust to such noise.

Method: The authors run 360 controlled experiments using Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct as the encoder on two intent-classification benchmarks (BANKING77 and CLINC150). They compare four main pooling strategies—mean, max, last-token, and attention pooling—plus FFT-augmented variants, under both clean and noise-augmented query conditions, and average results across ten random seeds.

Result: Attention pooling yields the best performance under noisy conditions, improving F1 by about 2.6–2.8 points over the default configuration, while mean pooling can reduce F1 by up to about 5 points. Last-token pooling works well for clean queries but is less robust to noise. FFT-based frequency-domain filtering does not consistently improve accuracy and behaves more as a structural modification than a beneficial component.

Conclusion: For building noise-robust conversational intent classifiers, attention pooling is the preferred strategy; mean pooling should be avoided due to its noise sensitivity, and last-token pooling is a good option when inputs are relatively clean. Frequency-domain enhancements offer no reliable accuracy gains. These findings provide practical, evidence-backed design guidance for real-world conversational database interfaces.

Abstract: Conversational database interfaces face a critical challenge: users naturally embed queries in conversational noise (greetings, politeness, off-topic remarks), which degrades intent classification accuracy and wastes computational resources. Despite advances in orchestration and retrieval strategies, a fundamental question remains unanswered: which pooling strategy maximizes intent classification accuracy under realistic conversational noise in production language models? This work addresses this gap through 360 controlled experiments spanning four pooling configurations (mean, max, last-token, attention, and FFT-augmented variants) using Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct on BANKING77 and CLINC150 datasets under clean/noisy conditions with ten random seeds. Key findings reveal that attention pooling consistently outperforms alternative strategies under noisy conditions (~+2.6-2.8 F1 over the default), while mean pooling degrades performance by up to ~5 F1 points. Frequency-domain filtering does not produce consistent accuracy improvements and functions primarily as a structural variation rather than an accuracy-enhancing component. These results provide concrete, evidence-based guidance for building noise-robust conversational classifiers: attention pooling is recommended for noisy interfaces, mean pooling should be avoided, and last-token pooling is appropriate for clean-query scenarios.

</details>


### [79] [Writing as a Self-Organized Critical Process](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05466)
*Nikolay Mikhaylovskiy*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies why autocorrelation in texts follows power laws and explains it via self-organized criticality using keystroke-level writing data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autocorrelation power laws are widely observed in texts, but it is unclear what underlying cognitive or dynamical process in human writing produces them. The authors want to move from static, final-text analysis to a dynamic, process-level explanation.

Method: They use the KLiCKe keystroke dataset, which records full writing and revision histories, to analyze (1) autocorrelation patterns in completed texts and (2) how revisions over time move the text's autocorrelation toward or away from a characteristic manifold. They examine scaling behavior and revision-size-dependent dynamics consistent with self-organized criticality and finite-size scaling.

Result: They find that autocorrelations of final texts lie on a manifold following a power law with finite-size scaling, and that the sequence of revisions exhibits “restoring dynamics”: larger or smaller revisions push the text's correlation structure back toward this manifold in a size-dependent way.

Conclusion: Human writing behaves like a self-organized critical system in which semantic correlations are dynamically regulated toward a critical state, explaining the pervasive power-law autocorrelation in texts.

Abstract: We explain autocorrelation decay power laws omnipresent in texts by self-organized criticality. Specifically, we analyze the recently released KLiCKe keystroke dataset and show that not only the final texts' autocorrelations form a manifold that adheres to a power law with a finite-size scaling, but also the text revisions generate revision-size-dependent restoring dynamics toward that manifold. Thus, human writing appears to dynamically regulate semantic correlations in a text toward a critical state.

</details>


### [80] [Dataset Signatures in Human-LLM Interactions and User Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05534)
*Joseph Suh,Serina Chang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper analyzes how different human–LLM interaction datasets are from each other and how these differences impact user modeling and LLM evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human–LLM interaction datasets are widely used to study AI usage patterns and to train and evaluate user models. Many new datasets claim to reflect ‘real-world’ interactions, but it is unclear how similar or different these datasets actually are, and what that implies for any research or systems built on top of them.

Method: The authors examine seven human–LLM conversation datasets, including in-the-wild chat logs and human preference data. They repeat the dataset classification experiment of Torralba & Efros: training neural network classifiers to predict which dataset a given conversation comes from, using only user messages. They compare this separability with traditional, human-designed taxonomies of conversation properties, and then study how dataset-specific signatures propagate into user models trained on each dataset. They analyze how dataset choice affects user model quality evaluations, evaluations of LLM assistants paired with these user models, and explore using dataset classifiers to guide data selection for training user models.

Result: Neural classifiers can reliably identify the source dataset of a conversation from user messages alone, significantly above chance, showing that each dataset has a distinctive ‘signature’. This separability remains even when datasets are matched on high-level taxonomy dimensions, which means these taxonomies miss important, subtler differences. These dataset signatures influence user models trained on them, leading to variations in downstream evaluations of user models and LLM assistants. Dataset classifiers can also be used to select or mix data more deliberately for training user models.

Conclusion: Human–LLM interaction datasets, though all intended to represent ‘real-world’ behavior, differ in systematic and detectable ways. These differences materially affect user modeling and the evaluation of LLM assistants. Researchers should treat dataset choice as a crucial design decision, not a neutral one, and can use dataset classification tools to better understand, diagnose, and curate training data for user models and downstream systems.

Abstract: Human--LLM interaction datasets shape our understanding of AI use and provide a foundation for downstream research, including training and evaluation of user models. In recent years, a growing number of datasets have sought to capture a representative picture of human--LLM interactions. But how different are the pictures these datasets provide, and what do those differences mean for research built on them? We study these questions across seven conversation datasets, spanning in-the-wild chat logs and human preference data. We begin by revisiting the dataset classification experiment of Torralba & Efros and find that neural network classifiers identify the source of a conversation from user messages alone well above chance, indicating distinctive dataset signatures. This separability persists after matching datasets on the dimensions of human-designed taxonomies, implying subtle differences that these taxonomies do not capture. We then examine the implications for user modeling: how dataset signatures propagate to the outputs of user models trained on these datasets; how dataset choice influences evaluations of user model quality and subsequent evaluations of LLM assistants paired with these user models; and how dataset classifiers can guide data selection for training user models. While each dataset is meant to capture a slice of 'real-world' interactions, our findings reveal the extent to which these slices diverge, and the consequences of those differences for research built on these foundations.

</details>


### [81] [Lend Me Your Eyes: Instruction-Aware Text Embeddings via Attention Relay](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05564)
*Yiyuan Luo,Vaggos Chatziafratis*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They show that you can make existing embedding models follow natural-language instructions without retraining, simply by reusing attention weights from an instruction-tuned LLM.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard contrastively trained embedding models become instruction-following only if they are explicitly trained on instruction–text pairs. Yet modern instruction-tuned LLMs already know how to follow diverse task instructions. The authors aim to exploit this existing capability to upgrade many different embedders into instruction-aware models without costly retraining or architecture-specific modifications, and to better understand how and where in an LLM the instruction-following behavior is encoded.

Method: They introduce Attention Relay: given an instruction and text, an instruction-tuned LLM is run and its internal attention weights are extracted. These attention patterns, especially from later layers, are then injected into or shared with the self-attention mechanism of a separate Transformer-based embedding model, effectively steering the embedder’s attention using the LLM’s instruction-aware focus. They systematically apply this to combinations of six instruction-tuned LLMs (Qwen3, Llama 3.1, OLMo 3) and ten diverse embedding models (varying in tokenizer, size, pooling) and perform ablations to see which layers and training aspects matter.

Result: For almost every LLM–embedder pair they test, relaying the LLM’s attention makes the embedding model instruction-aware, improving its ability to focus on the instruction-relevant parts of the text. Analysis shows that the LLM’s later-layer attention heads strongly track the instruction, and that this behavior is largely due to instruction tuning rather than base pretraining. Experiments further show that using these relayed weights shifts the embedding to emphasize the text aspects requested by the instruction, or recovers those aspects when naive averaging would otherwise wash them out.

Conclusion: Instruction-following behavior can be transferred from instruction-tuned LLMs to diverse embedding models without additional training by reusing attention weights. Later-layer attention in instruction-tuned LLMs encodes instruction tracking, and injecting this signal into embedders effectively tells them which parts of the input text matter for a given task. This offers a simple, general mechanism to create instruction-aware embedding models and provides insight into how instruction tuning shapes LLM attention.

Abstract: Text embedding models trained with contrastive learning learn to follow task instructions from instruction-paired data, while instruction-tuned LLMs already know how to follow them. We show that this instruction-following ability can carry over from an LLM to a Transformer-based embedder without any training. We propose Attention Relay, which passes the attention weights an LLM produces to the embedder's own attention. Across six instruction-tuned LLMs from the Qwen3, Llama 3.1 and OLMo 3 families and ten widely used embedding models that differ in tokenizer, size and pooling type, Attention Relay makes nearly every combination instruction-aware. Experiments that break the method down into its parts show that the LLM's attention weights track the instruction in its later layers and come largely from instruction tuning. They also show that relaying these weights selects which content in the text matters: it makes the aspect of the text that the instruction asks about dominant in the embedding, or restores that aspect where averaging had diluted it.

</details>


### [82] [Can Prosodic Style Be Inferred from Text Alone? Evidence from Unsupervised Acoustic Clusters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05575)
*Abdul Rehman,Jian-Jun Zhang,Xiaosong Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper tests whether text alone carries enough information to select expressive speech styles, finding that text predicts acoustic style clusters only modestly and mostly through word choice rather than deeper sentence semantics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Expressive TTS systems typically assume that written text contains sufficient cues to determine an appropriate prosodic style, but this assumption has not been directly tested. Existing work evaluates style models and appropriateness within context, yet does not measure how much of acoustic style variation is actually recoverable from text alone. The authors aim to rigorously test this core assumption as a falsifiable hypothesis.

Method: Using a 1,200-hour multi-speaker conversational speech corpus, the authors derive style labels by clustering utterances in the latent spaces of five different speech models, including a prosody-only control model. For each of six speakers, they: (1) cluster utterances based purely on acoustic model embeddings; (2) hold out some utterances; (3) attempt to predict each held-out utterance’s acoustic-cluster label using twelve different text embedding models. They incorporate three controls: (a) removing utterance length information from speech embeddings to avoid trivial correlations; (b) computing accuracy relative to a majority-class baseline instead of uniform chance to handle unbalanced cluster sizes; and (c) using a bag-of-words baseline to quantify the contribution of raw word identity. They then compare top-3 prediction accuracy across embedding types, inspect how sentence encoders trained for semantics behave (including tree-based probing), and test whether acoustic clusters are compact in text-embedding space across 360 text–speech model configurations, including a prosody-only acoustic space.

Result: For all six speakers, text-based models predict the acoustic cluster labels better than the majority-class baseline, with an average gain of +0.111 in top-3 accuracy. However, a simple bag-of-words representation achieves about 75% of this improvement, indicating that most predictive power comes from word identity. Sentence-level embeddings add only a small further gain (+0.026 on average), and this gain is largest for encoders not specifically trained for sentence semantics. For sentence encoders trained on semantic tasks, tree-based probing shows that the added benefit is actually reversed, suggesting that semantic abstraction may wash out style-relevant signals. Across 360 combinations of text and acoustic representations, acoustic style clusters do not form compact or separable regions in text-embedding space. When clustering is performed in a prosody-only acoustic space, the text–cluster association becomes weaker for five of the six speakers, though one speaker still shows a relatively strong association.

Conclusion: The mapping from text to acoustic style clusters is real but limited: text predicts delivery style only modestly above a majority-class baseline, and most of this signal is attributable to specific word choices rather than richer sentence-level semantics. Acoustic style clusters are not well reflected as compact regions in text-embedding space, and focusing on prosody-only acoustic features generally weakens the text–style relationship. Consequently, the common assumption in expressive TTS that written text alone provides sufficient information for reference-free style selection is not supported by these results. At best, text offers coarse cues, mainly via word choice that may correlate with prosody, topic, or recording conditions, and style control systems should not rely solely on textual input for expressive appropriateness.

Abstract: Much of expressive text-to-speech research rests on an untested assumption that written text carries enough information to select an appropriate prosodic style for its delivery. Text-predicted style models improve listener preference, and expressive-appropriateness evaluation presupposes that context constrains style, yet neither measures the assumption itself. This paper tests it as a falsifiable hypothesis against style labels derived from acoustics alone. For each of six speakers in a 1,200-hour conversational corpus, utterances are clustered in the spaces of five speech models, including a prosody-only control, and the cluster of held-out utterances is predicted from twelve text embedding models. Three controls are applied: utterance length is erased from the speech embeddings; accuracy is scored against the majority-class floor of unbalanced clusters rather than uniform chance; and a bag-of-words baseline measures word identity alone. Text predicts the cluster above that floor for all six speakers (+0.111 top-3 accuracy), but bag-of-words achieves three quarters of this. Sentence embeddings add only +0.026, largest for encoders not trained for sentence semantics and reversed by tree-based probes for all others. Acoustic clusters are not compact in text embedding space in any of 360 configurations. The prosody-only space weakens the association for five speakers, but not for the speaker showing it most strongly. Text thus informs these delivery clusters mainly through word choice, whether as a cue to prosody or as a marker of topic and recording situation, and reference-free style selection cannot assume more.

</details>


### [83] [What Is a Repeated Token Worth? The Scaling Geometry of Multi-Epoch Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05591)
*Yekun Chai,Haoyi Xiong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper empirically characterizes how much value you get from repeating pretraining data vs using fresh data, and provides a simple scaling rule for how many epochs to run as a function of model size and data availability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern LLM pretraining increasingly reuses the same corpus because high-quality, diverse text is limited. Practitioners lack clear guidance on how many epochs of repeated data are optimal, how this choice should scale with model size, and whether repetition strategy (ordering, concentration, source entropy, tokenization) affects final loss. The paper aims to provide principled, empirical answers for data-limited (rather than compute-limited) regimes.

Method: Define a notion of the “price” of a repeated token by comparing it to (1) a token in a first epoch over the same data and (2) a fresh token trained with equal compute. Run controlled pretraining experiments across multiple model sizes and data sizes, varying epoch counts, data replay patterns (consecutive vs interleaved shards, concentration of repeats on subsets of data), data entropy, and tokenization strategies. Measure bits-per-byte loss to quantify how the marginal value of repeated tokens decays with repetition and how this decay scales with tokens-per-parameter and training budget per parameter.

Result: 1) The cost of repetition relative to fresh data collapses to a single scaling variable: extra epochs divided by unique tokens per parameter. 2) A second epoch is nearly as valuable as an additional epoch on fresh data. 3) After a critical number of epochs—growing mainly with training budget per parameter, weakly with model size—the value of repeated tokens drops to about half that of fresh ones. 4) With fixed unique data, the compute-optimal strategy is to scale model size and number of epochs together up to roughly this critical epoch. 5) Larger models can sustain fewer epochs on a fixed corpus (e.g., ~15 at 127M vs ~4 at 2B parameters), but this restriction relaxes when the unique data size also grows. 6) Data counts alone do not determine performance: (a) replaying the same shards consecutively worsens loss by up to 0.46 bits/byte; (b) concentrating repeats on fewer samples hurts; (c) lower-entropy data degrades faster under repetition; (d) re-tokenizing helps only under heavy repetition.

Conclusion: In data-limited pretraining, the optimal amount and strategy of data repetition can be predicted by a simple scaling rule based on extra epochs per unique token per parameter. Practitioners should increase model size and epochs together until marginal loss improvements stall near a critical epoch count, avoid pathological replay patterns (like consecutive shard replays and over-concentrating repeats), and recognize that data entropy and repetition strategy materially affect returns to repeated tokens. The work provides an empirical recipe for choosing epochs and repetition schemes when unique high-quality data—not compute—is the main bottleneck.

Abstract: As pretraining increasingly repeats data, every run faces three questions: how many epochs to take, how that number should change with model size, and whether anything besides the epoch count matters. We answer them by pricing a repeated token against two references: one epoch on the same data, which gives its value, and fresh data at equal compute, which gives its cost. Against fresh data, the cost of repetition follows a single variable, the number of extra epochs divided by the unique tokens per parameter. Against the same data, a second epoch is worth nearly as much as a fresh one, and repeated tokens fall to half the value of fresh ones after a critical epoch count that grows with the training budget per parameter but hardly with model size. With unique data fixed, the predicted compute-optimal run grows model size and epochs together until loss stops improving, near the critical epoch count. The same variable accounts for the direction of size trends that appear to conflict: larger models tolerate fewer epochs when the corpus is fixed, from about 15 at 127M to 4 at 2B parameters, but not when unique data grow with the model. Counts alone do not determine loss: at identical counts, replaying shards consecutively raises loss by up to 0.46~bits per byte, concentrating repeats on fewer samples also raises it, lower-entropy sources degrade faster with repetition, and re-tokenizing repeats helps only under heavy repetition. These results offer an empirical guide to pretraining when unique data, rather than compute, are the binding constraint.

</details>


### [84] [More Than Words: Compositional Tokenization for Efficient Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05597)
*Yuval Reif,Guy Kaplan,Roy Schwartz*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose a new tokenizer, CoBPE, that composes words and their surrounding function words/punctuation into single structured tokens, reducing sequence length and improving model performance at the same compute.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard BPE tokenization makes models predict many small tokens like prepositions, articles, and punctuation separately, which increases sequence length and inference cost. The authors want a more token-efficient representation that still captures surface variation but uses fewer positions, potentially improving both efficiency and downstream task performance.

Method: They design CoBPE, a compositional tokenization scheme where common content words (e.g., nouns) act as lexical base tokens and frequent nearby items like prepositions, articles, and punctuation are encoded as reusable surface modifiers. These modifiers are composed with base tokens in embedding space at input time and predicted jointly at output time, letting phrases such as "On the table." be treated as a single structured token instead of four separate tokens. They pretrain language models from scratch with CoBPE and with standard BPE at 780M and 1.3B parameter scales, carefully matching training compute to compare efficiency and performance.

Result: Using CoBPE reduces sequence lengths by about 30% compared to standard BPE while, under matched training compute, yielding an average improvement of 1.2 points on downstream benchmarks for models with 780M and 1.3B parameters.

Conclusion: A significant portion of what current LMs represent via long token sequences can instead be encoded as structured, compositional tokens that bundle content words with surface modifiers. This structured tokenization both shortens sequences and improves task performance at fixed compute, highlighting a broad and promising design space for token-efficient, more capable language models.

Abstract: Language models process and generate text sequentially in token units, and the tokenizer determines how much text each inference step covers. Under standard tokenization, a short English phrase such as "On the table." is usually produced as four separate predictions for the preposition (On), article (the), noun (table), and punctuation (.), where each consumes a sequence position and adds inference cost. We introduce CoBPE, a compositional tokenization approach that represents such phrases as a lexical base token (table) attached with a small set of reusable surface modifiers, composed in embedding space at input and predicted jointly at output. In controlled pretraining from scratch at 780M and 1.3B scales, CoBPE shortens sequences by 30% and improves average downstream performance by 1.2 points relative to standard BPE under matched training compute. Our results suggest that part of what is now expressed through token sequences can instead be modeled through structured representations, opening a broad design space for more token-efficient and capable language models.

</details>


### [85] [Atomic Visual Entailment: Enhancing Zero-Shot Vision-Language Reasoning through Atomic Fact Decomposition and Learned Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05630)
*Nallathambi Vethiappan,Derya Soydaner,Gijs Wijnholds*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Atomic Visual Entailment (AVE), a method that decomposes textual hypotheses into atomic facts and combines predictions from full and decomposed forms using frozen vision-language models and a small classifier, achieving strong performance in visual entailment without fine-tuning large models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Visual entailment tasks require determining whether an image supports, contradicts, or is neutral towards a textual hypothesis. Existing strong methods depend on fine-tuning large vision-language models, which is costly in labelled data and compute, while zero-shot and hybrid methods lag far behind. Moreover, VE hypotheses often contain multiple visual claims, but current zero-shot approaches treat the hypothesis as a monolithic unit, missing opportunities for more granular reasoning. There is a need for a more data- and compute-efficient approach that leverages large frozen models while better aligning with the compositional structure of hypotheses.

Method: The authors propose Atomic Visual Entailment (AVE). First, they decompose each VE hypothesis into atomic visual facts. Then, using frozen (non–fine-tuned) vision-language models, they generate candidate predictions (entailment/contradiction/neutral) from both the original full hypothesis and each atomic fact, evaluated in the image context. These multiple candidate predictions are then fed into a lightweight classifier that is trained only on how these candidates behave, rather than on the raw image-text pairs, to output the final VE label. They also explore variants where atomic facts are judged in isolation versus with preserved hypothesis context, and analyze error complementarity between full-hypothesis and atomic predictions. The system additionally identifies visual regions corresponding to the evidence for its decisions, without explicit region-level supervision.

Result: Experiments on the SNLI-VE dataset show that simple decomposition of hypotheses into atomic facts does not always help: evaluating facts in isolation can perform worse than not decomposing. However, when atomic facts are evaluated while preserving hypothesis context, the combined approach significantly improves performance. Full-hypothesis and atomic predictions make complementary errors; by training a small classifier to learn which source to trust for each example, the method recovers much more of this complementarity than naïve majority voting. The approach achieves a test accuracy of 0.803 on SNLI-VE without any fine-tuning of the underlying vision-language models. The method also successfully localizes the visual evidence behind its predictions in the image, despite not using any region-level annotations during training.

Conclusion: AVE demonstrates that decomposing hypotheses into atomic facts and learning to selectively trust candidate predictions from both full and decomposed formulations can close a substantial part of the performance gap between zero-shot/hybrid methods and fully fine-tuned vision-language systems. This offers a practical alternative when labelled data or compute are insufficient for end-to-end fine-tuning. The findings highlight the importance of maintaining hypothesis context when decomposing, show that complementary error patterns can be effectively exploited with a lightweight classifier, and indicate that useful evidence localization can be obtained without explicit region-level supervision.

Abstract: Visual entailment (VE) asks whether an image supports, contradicts, or leaves undecided a textual hypothesis. Strong results come from fine-tuning large vision-language models on labelled data, while zero-shot and hybrid approaches remain far behind. A VE hypothesis often bundles several visual claims, yet existing zero-shot methods reason over it as a single unit. We propose Atomic Visual Entailment (AVE), which decomposes the hypothesis into atomic facts, produces candidate predictions from both the full hypothesis and its facts using frozen vision-language models, and predicts the final label with a lightweight classifier trained only on how those candidates behave. We find that decomposition helps only when the hypothesis context is preserved: judging facts in isolation is worse than not decomposing at all. Full-hypothesis and atomic prediction make complementary errors, and learning which to trust recovers far more of that complementarity than majority voting, reaching 0.803 test accuracy on SNLI-VE without fine-tuning any vision-language model. AVE also localises the visual evidence behind its prediction without region-level supervision. These results suggest that learning which candidate prediction to trust can close much of the gap to fine-tuned systems, offering a practical alternative where fine-tuning a vision-language model directly would need more labelled data or compute than is available.

</details>


### [86] [Automatic Speech Recognition for Low-Resource Sinhala: A Critical Review of Methods, Challenges, and Future Directions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05681)
*Chanuka Dinuwan,Sanath Jayasena,Buddhika Karunarathne*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper is a survey and gap analysis of automatic speech recognition (ASR) for Sinhala, reviewing past and current systems and outlining a research roadmap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ASR for Sinhala is difficult due to its complex morphology, large phoneme inventory, SOV syntax, and lack of annotated speech data. Existing systems perform poorly, are hard to compare, and lack standardized resources, so a systematic review is needed to clarify the current state and guide future work.

Method: The authors conduct a critical literature review of Sinhala ASR from early HMM-based systems to modern deep learning and self-supervised models (e.g., wav2vec 2.0, XLS-R, Whisper, MMS). They compare architectures, training data, WER, and robustness; contrast Sinhala work with related low-resource languages; analyze the comparability of reported results; and synthesize findings into identified research gaps and a proposed research agenda.

Result: They find that most reported Sinhala WERs are not directly comparable due to inconsistent corpora, data splits, and scoring methods. A single controlled comparison shows that cleaning and correcting the training corpus alone yields an 18.1% relative WER reduction. They also observe limited use of contextual (phonological, syntactic, semantic) information and a lack of work on code-switching and parameter-efficient adaptation of large pre-trained models.

Conclusion: Sinhala ASR research is fragmented, with serious data, benchmarking, and modeling limitations. The field needs large, diverse annotated corpora, stronger morphosyntactic context modeling, robust real-world evaluation, standardized benchmarks, studies on parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large self-supervised models, and resources for Sinhala-English code-switching. Addressing these six gaps can benefit Sinhala and other morphologically rich, low-resource languages.

Abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) for low-resource languages remains a major challenge. Sinhala, the primary language of Sri Lanka with about 16 million speakers, illustrates the difficulty: agglutinative morphology, a 54-phoneme inventory, subject-object-verb (SOV) syntax and scarce annotated speech data limit both conventional and modern ASR systems. This paper presents the first critical review of Sinhala ASR research, tracing its development from Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) through deep neural networks to self-supervised pre-trained models such as wav2vec 2.0, XLS-R, Whisper and Massively Multilingual Speech (MMS). We compare existing Sinhala systems with related low-resource ASR work on Tamil, Malayalam and Hindi in terms of architecture, training data, word error rate (WER) and robustness to real-world acoustic conditions, and we assess self-supervised and transfer learning as responses to scarce labeled data. We show that most reported WERs are not directly comparable because they differ in corpus, data split and scoring, and that the only controlled comparison in the literature attributes an 18.1% relative WER reduction to corpus correction alone. We also discuss context-aware ASR that draws on phonological, syntactic and semantic knowledge. We identify six research gaps: (1) the lack of large annotated corpora covering multiple dialects and acoustic conditions; (2) weak contextual modeling of Sinhala morphosyntax; (3) high WER in real-world conditions; (4) the absence of standardized benchmarks; (5) the lack of parameter-efficient fine-tuning studies; and (6) the absence of annotated code-switched Sinhala-English speech resources. We outline a research agenda to address these gaps, intended as a roadmap for researchers working on Sinhala and other morphologically rich languages.

</details>


### [87] [Knowing the Rules, Applying the Rules: Evaluating Language Models on Traditional Chinese Bazi](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05682)
*Jiulin Li,Ping Huang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper builds a benchmark in traditional Chinese Bazi to show that systems can know the rules but still struggle to apply them to real cases, with large accuracy gaps between theory-type and case-type questions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To examine whether AI systems that perform well on knowledge questions in a cultural domain (here, traditional Chinese Bazi) can also correctly apply that knowledge to concrete cases, and to show that aggregate knowledge scores may hide important weaknesses in case-based reasoning.

Method: The authors construct a 3,000-item multiple-choice benchmark in Bazi, split into 14 theory categories and 11 case categories. They evaluate six endpoint systems, focus on a 2,492-item refined subset, and analyze accuracies by category (e.g., Twelve Stages, Nayin, Shensha Basics, Luck Pillars, Career, Family Relations). They also compare paired configurations of a specific provider (DeepSeek native vs disabled) to see how provider-level settings correlate with performance differences in theory vs case items, while stressing that these are associations, not clean causal tests.

Result: All evaluated systems perform better on Theory than on Case questions, with persistent gaps of about 17–30 percentage points even after removing invalid responses. Some theory categories achieve high accuracies (around 89% for Twelve Stages and 88.6% for Nayin) while others are lower (about 76% for Shensha Basics). Within Case questions, some categories like Luck Pillars do reasonably well (~84.6%), but others such as Career and Family Relations perform poorly (roughly 37–38%). Overall performance rankings obscure these category-specific strengths and weaknesses. In paired DeepSeek experiments on the original 3,000 items, native configurations are associated with substantial gains on Theory (+6.53 and +12.20 points for Flash and Pro) but mixed changes on Case (-3.67 and +1.27 points).

Conclusion: Knowledge of domain rules, as captured by theory questions, does not reliably translate into correct case-based application in Bazi for current systems. Aggregate or overall knowledge scores can mask substantial deficits and heterogeneity across subdomains and task types. The benchmark is limited because it measures agreement with model-generated, model-verified answers rather than real-world outcomes, and the final results are descriptive post-selection findings with incomplete expert validation and provenance, so conclusions must be interpreted cautiously. The work underscores the need for task-specific, culturally grounded evaluations rather than relying solely on global knowledge metrics.

Abstract: Knowing domain rules does not guarantee applying them to a case. We study this distinction in traditional Chinese Bazi through 3,000 Chinese multiple-choice questions spanning 14 Theory and 11 Case categories. Six endpoint systems are evaluated, with primary results reported on a 2,492-item model-informed refinement. Theory accuracy exceeds Case accuracy for every system, and gaps of 16.60-29.56 percentage points remain when invalid responses are excluded. The contrast is more specific than a general case-reasoning deficit. Across six systems, Twelve Stages and Nayin reach mean accuracies of 89.10% and 88.62%, while Shensha Basics reaches 75.96%. Within Case, Luck Pillars averages 84.62%, but Career and Family Relations average only 36.98% and 38.19%. Overall rankings also conceal different category strengths. On the original 3,000 items, paired DeepSeek native/disabled comparisons associate native configurations with Theory gains of 6.53 and 12.20 points for Flash and Pro, respectively; Case changes are -3.67 and +1.27 points. These are provider-configuration associations, not isolated causal effects of reasoning. The results motivate task-specific evaluation of cultural-domain applications rather than reliance on aggregate knowledge scores. The benchmark measures agreement with a model-generated, model-verified answer key, not real-world predictive validity. Final-set results are post-selection descriptions, and incomplete provenance and expert validation constrain their interpretation.

</details>


### [88] [Spend Bytes on Breadth: Precision-Count Trade-offs for Decode-Time KV Compression in Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05685)
*Runguo Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how to best use a fixed KV-cache memory budget for long reasoning chains by trading off token count versus precision, proposing BreadthKV, which stores more tokens at lower precision and beats pure eviction strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reasoning models with long chains of thought quickly fill the KV cache, forcing online compression under a fixed memory budget. Existing decode-time methods mainly choose which tokens to evict, ignoring how many bits are used per token. The authors want to understand how to optimally allocate a fixed byte budget between caching more tokens at lower precision versus fewer tokens at higher precision, to preserve reasoning quality under tight memory constraints.

Method: They introduce BreadthKV, which combines quantization with eviction to allocate KV-cache memory. BreadthKV spends the memory budget on caching more tokens but at reduced precision. It selects the bit-width for each model and memory budget via a small, 60-problem end-to-end calibration procedure because offline attention-error metrics do not reliably predict performance. They compare BreadthKV against pure eviction baselines, ThinKV, and a theoretically motivated joint rate–distortion allocator (RDKV) that uses more KV memory-time, across three reasoning models and four math/science benchmarks.

Result: Across three reasoning models and four math/science benchmarks, BreadthKV outperforms eviction-only methods in 17 of 18 experimental settings and yields shorter model outputs. Eviction-only strategies frequently cause derailed reasoning runs that hit the maximum length cap without reaching an answer. For example, on Qwen3-8B under the tightest memory budget, eviction causes 91% of AIME samples to hit the length cap, whereas BreadthKV reduces this to 40%. Under the same evaluation protocol, BreadthKV’s performance is statistically indistinguishable from RDKV, despite RDKV using 27% more KV memory-time, and BreadthKV also outperforms their reimplementation of ThinKV.

Conclusion: Allocating KV-cache budget towards storing more tokens at lower precision (via quantization plus eviction) is more effective for long-chain reasoning than simply evicting tokens at full precision. A small end-to-end calibration is sufficient to choose good quantization bit-widths, since proxy metrics like offline attention error are unreliable. BreadthKV nearly matches a more complex rate–distortion optimizer while using less effective memory-time, and improves both answer rates and output length behavior over existing KV eviction methods.

Abstract: Reasoning models write most of their KV cache while decoding long chains of thought (CoT), so the cache has to be compressed online under a fixed memory budget. Decode-time methods mostly decide which tokens to evict. We ask how a fixed byte budget should be split between the number of cached tokens and their precision. BreadthKV spends the bytes on more tokens at low precision, combining quantization with eviction, and picks the bit-width for each model and budget with a 60-problem end-to-end calibration, since offline attention error does not predict it reliably. On three reasoning models and four math and science benchmarks, it scores above eviction alone in 17 of 18 settings and produces shorter outputs. Much of what eviction loses comes from derailed runs, which keep reasoning until the length cap without reaching an answer. On Qwen3-8B at our tightest budget, eviction sends 91% of AIME samples to the cap and BreadthKV 40%. Under the same protocol, BreadthKV is statistically indistinguishable from a joint rate-distortion allocator (RDKV) that uses 27% more KV memory-time, and it outperforms our re-implementation of ThinKV.

</details>


### [89] [MedicalHarness: A Controlled Evaluation of LLMs and Agent Harnesses on Medical Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05778)
*Ziqing Wang,Lili Zhao,Kaize Ding*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces MedicalHarness, a framework and benchmark to systematically study how different agent harness designs affect LLM performance on medical tasks, showing that the harness–model interaction explains a significant portion of outcome variance and that no single harness is universally optimal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of medical LLM agents report scores as if they were a property of the model alone, but in practice these scores depend strongly on the agent harness—the control system that manages the model’s interaction loop with its environment (context management, tools, planning, etc.). For medical applications, where reliability is critical, it is important to know how much performance depends on the harness, which aspects of harness design matter, and whether some harnesses are consistently better across models and task types. Prior work rarely isolates the harness effect or its individual mechanisms, creating a gap in understanding and in fair, reproducible evaluation of medical LLM agents.

Method: The authors introduce MedicalHarness, composed of two main components. (1) MedicalHarnessBench: a benchmark of 107 medical tasks spanning four domains, each crafted to stress different agent harness capabilities (such as context handling, planning, and tool use). They evaluate five open‑weight LLMs under five distinct agent harnesses, carefully controlling experiments so that within each comparison only the harness changes; they then analyze both performance metrics and execution traces. (2) MH‑Lab: a controlled, modular harness that allows ablating individual mechanisms within a shared execution loop. Specifically, they selectively switch off context management, planning, or tool exposure one at a time while holding other aspects constant, to measure each mechanism’s causal contribution to performance. This design allows both whole‑harness comparisons and fine‑grained mechanism‑level analysis.

Result: Across 107 tasks, the experiments show that the choice of agent harness and its interaction with a given model account for roughly one quarter of the variance in medical task outcomes. Performance differences between harnesses are substantial, and the best-performing harness depends on both the underlying model and the task domain; no single harness dominates across all settings. The MH‑Lab ablation studies further reveal that individual mechanisms such as context management, planning, and tool exposure can significantly affect performance, but their impact is heterogeneous: a mechanism that helps one model or task type may have neutral or even negative effects in other settings.

Conclusion: Medical LLM performance cannot be treated as a property of the model alone; it is a property of the model–harness pair. The agent harness design, including specific mechanisms like context management, planning, and tool use, explains a sizable share of outcome variance, and there is no universally optimal harness across models and medical task types. Consequently, evaluations and deployments of medical LLM agents should report and scrutinize harness details, and developers should co-design models and harnesses rather than optimizing them in isolation. MedicalHarness and its open-source benchmark and code provide a standardized way to study and compare harness designs going forward.

Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly built for medical work and scored on clinical benchmarks. Each such score, however, comes from a model running inside an agent harness, the system that controls the loop between the model and its environment. An agent's score is therefore a property of a model--harness pair. For medical agents, how much outcomes change with the harness has rarely been measured. Measuring this change, and explaining it, raises two challenges. First, a harness comparison must change nothing but the harness and be repeated across models and kinds of task. Second, comparing whole harnesses leaves their mechanisms bundled together, so it cannot show when an individual mechanism helps. To address these challenges, we present MedicalHarness, a controlled study of models and agent harnesses on medical tasks. We first build MedicalHarnessBench to evaluate agents on $107$ tasks across four domains that each test a different harness capability. Using this benchmark, we run five open-weight models under five agent harnesses, changing only the harness within a comparison, and analyze both outcomes and execution traces. To study individual mechanisms, we build MH-Lab, a controlled harness that switches off context management, planning or tool exposure one at a time within a shared execution loop. We find that the harness and its interaction with the model account for about a quarter of the outcome variance, and that no single harness is best across models and tasks. Code and data are available at https://github.com/REAL-Lab-NU/MedicalHarness.

</details>


### [90] [CLARA: Can AI Assess Developmental Appropriateness in Children's Stories?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05783)
*Sijing Yin,Zirui Wang,Qian Liu,Jiamou Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces CLARA, a cognitively grounded framework and bilingual benchmark to automatically assess the developmental suitability of children’s stories, showing it aligns better with human judgments than traditional readability or direct prompting approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluating whether children’s stories are developmentally appropriate is crucial for education and literacy research, but current assessments depend on subjective, labor-intensive human judgments that are hard to scale. The authors want to know if AI can approximate these human developmental judgments in a reliable, interpretable way.

Method: They design CLARA, a structured annotation framework that breaks developmental narrative understanding into three dimensions: cognitive (COG), language (LAN), and social-emotional (SEL). They construct a bilingual Chinese–English benchmark of 1107 children’s stories, each with normalized silver developmental level references and fine-grained annotations along these dimensions. They then evaluate CLARA via benchmark comparisons with readability metrics and direct prompting baselines, component-wise analyses, cross-lingual (translated) consistency checks, and blinded human evaluation by educators.
