Method: They propose list-powered BISG (ℓBISG), which uses group-specific name lists instead of full frequency tables. Names are embedded into a vector space, and membership in these group-specific lists is treated as a proxy prediction task. Using proximal inference, they correct for biases in these lists to obtain calibrated estimates of group membership probabilities. Name lists can be created by experts or generated synthetically by large language models.

Result: On U.S. voter files with self-reported race, the 1900 full-count U.S. Census, and the Lebanese voter registry, ℓBISG with LLM-generated name lists yields accurate, well-calibrated group probability estimates and precise disparity estimates comparable to methods that rely on full name–race data.

Conclusion: ℓBISG extends probabilistic race/ethnicity prediction to settings without name–race frequency tables by leveraging possibly biased group-specific name lists and correcting them via proximal inference, showing that even LLM-generated lists can provide reliable estimates for disparity analysis.

Abstract: Statistically valid estimation of racial and ethnic disparities often requires inferring the probability that an individual belongs to a particular racial or ethnic group given only their name and geographic location. The standard approach, Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding (BISG), relies on group population frequencies for each name. Although the U.S. Census Bureau provides such information for common names and a limited set of racial categories, comparable data do not exist for many racial and ethnic groups and are rarely available outside the U.S. We propose the list-powered BISG ($\ell$BISG) method, which can be used to derive calibrated group probabilities from group-specific name lists. These lists may be compiled based on expert knowledge or generated synthetically using large language models (LLMs), and thus may be subject to unknown biases. Representing names as embeddings, we treat list membership as a proxy prediction task and apply a correction based on proximal inference to recover the target group probabilities. We validate the method on U.S. voter files with self-reported race, on the full-count 1900 U.S. Census, and on the Lebanese voter registry. We find that LLM-generated name lists yield accurate and well-calibrated probabilities as well as precise disparity estimates comparable to those obtained using methods that require name-race data. Thus, $\ell$BISG substantially broadens the applicability of probabilistic race and ethnicity prediction to settings where name-race data are unavailable.

</details>


### [110] [DeferKV: Rethinking Eviction Timing for One-Shot KV Cache Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06286)
*Zhe Wang,Jiakai Li,Yujia Sun,Rongzheng Wang,Shuang Liang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes DeferKV, a method that delays KV cache eviction from the end of prefill to the first decoding step, using early decode attention to better estimate token importance, thus improving long-context LLM performance under KV compression.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-context LLMs require storing large KV caches, which leads to high memory use and inference overhead. Existing KV compression methods typically evict tokens right after prefill without seeing any real generation behavior, which can discard tokens later needed for decoding. The authors want a simple, training-free way to compress KV caches that is better aligned with the actual attention patterns during generation.

Method: The authors first conduct a quantitative analysis of attention patterns, showing that early decode queries, especially at the prefill-decode boundary, are more predictive of later decode attention than prefill-only signals. Based on this, they propose DeferKV: instead of deciding which KV entries to evict at the end of prefill, the model waits until the first real decoding step, uses both prompt-side and the first decode-side attention/importance signals, and then performs KV eviction. The method does not require retraining, auxiliary draft models, or predictive modules; it purely changes when and how KV importance is estimated for compression.

Result: On benchmarks for long-context understanding—LongBench, RULER, and Needle-in-a-Haystack—DeferKV improves task performance under the same KV cache compression ratios compared to prior one-shot compression/eviction baselines, while preserving low inference latency. Quantitatively, it yields consistent accuracy/quality gains without introducing substantial computational overhead.

Conclusion: Deferring KV cache eviction decisions from the end of prefill to the first decoding step, and combining prompt and early decode attention signals, yields more accurate KV importance estimates and thus better KV compression. DeferKV offers a simple, training-free, and deployment-friendly mechanism that improves long-context LLM performance under memory-constrained settings while keeping inference efficient.

Abstract: Long-context large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities across a wide range of tasks, but the growing KV cache introduces substantial memory and inference overhead. Existing one-shot KV cache compression methods typically commit to irreversible eviction immediately after prefill, before any signal from actual generation becomes available. Our quantitative analysis shows that early queries from the actual generation stage provide attention signals that are more consistent with subsequent decode attention, with the largest single-step gain occurring at the prefill-decode boundary. Based on this observation, we propose DeferKV, which moves the eviction decision from the end of prefill to the first real decoding step and temporally combines prompt-side and decode-side observations, thereby better aligning KV importance estimation with subsequent generation requirements. DeferKV requires no additional training, draft model, or future-query prediction module, making it simple and easy to deploy. Experiments on LongBench, RULER, and Needle-in-a-Haystack demonstrate that DeferKV consistently improves model performance under KV cache compression while maintaining low inference latency.

</details>


### [111] [From Abusive Language Classification to Sequence Labeling Identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06287)
*Nicolas Zampieri,Ignacio Lopez,Manon Girard,Jeremy Auguste*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes treating abusive language identification as a sequence-labeling task that jointly marks abusive spans and their targets, showing it can match standard sentence-level classifiers while giving more actionable, localized information for content moderation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing abusive language detection systems usually perform sentence-level classification, which flags entire messages as abusive or not. This limits their usefulness for moderation workflows because they do not localize which parts of the text are abusive nor specify who is being targeted. Industrial moderation systems must also work across domains, under latency constraints, and cope with implicit abuse. The authors aim to explore whether a more structured formulation—jointly detecting abusive spans and targets—can provide richer, more precise signals for moderators without sacrificing performance.

Method: The authors define Abusive Language Identification (ALI) as a sequence-labeling problem that jointly extracts abusive language (AL) spans and their corresponding target mentions. They build models for ALI and compare them against conventional Abusive Language Classification (ALC) models on a pilot corpus drawn from a production moderation pipeline. They evaluate both approaches on cross-domain generalization and detection of implicit abuse, and for ALI they additionally assess the accuracy of predicted abusive spans and target spans. A qualitative analysis further examines model outputs and informs discussion on more complete target–span linking and future benchmark design.

Result: ALI-based models perform competitively with traditional sentence-level ALC models on the core abusive language detection task while providing localized, token-level outputs that can directly support moderation decisions. ALI shows a modest, configuration-dependent advantage in handling implicit abuse. However, achieving exact boundaries for abusive spans and accurately identifying target mentions remains challenging, with errors and ambiguity in span recovery.

Conclusion: Formulating abusive language detection as a sequence-labeling task (ALI) is viable for industrial content moderation, delivering competitive performance with added benefits of localized abusive-span and target information. While current models struggle with precise span and target boundary detection, the framework offers promising directions for richer moderation tools. The authors highlight the need for improved methods for complete target–span linking and call for structured benchmarks specifically designed for ALI to advance research in this area.

Abstract: Industrial content moderation must process massive message streams under tight latency constraints, yet most abusive language (AL) detection systems rely on sentence-level classification (ALC), which neither localizes abusive spans nor identifies who is targeted. We define Abusive Language Identification (ALI) as a sequence-labeling task that jointly extracts AL spans and target mentions, and assess whether this approach can be used for text moderation. On a pilot corpus drawn from a production moderation pipeline, we compare ALI with ALC on cross-domain generalization and implicit abuse, and we also evaluate AL and target span detection. ALI remains competitive with ALC while providing localized outputs for moderators, with a modest and configuration-sensitive advantage on implicit abuse. Exact AL boundaries and target spans remain difficult to recover. We complement this comparison with a qualitative analysis and discuss perspectives on complete target--span linking and on structured benchmarks for ALI.

</details>


### [112] [DialectSentEval 2026: Arabic Dialect Sentiment Analysis and Swapping Shared Task](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06298)
*Saad Ezzini,Shadi Abudalfa,Maram Alharbi,Salmane Chafik,Hind Alatawi,Mo El-Haj,Ahmed Abdelali,Osamah Alnahari,Salima Lamsiyah*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents DialectSentEval, a shared task for sentiment analysis and sentiment swapping in Arabic dialects, detailing subtasks, data, and participating systems’ findings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Arabic sentiment analysis is difficult due to the prevalence and variability of dialectal Arabic, for which existing resources and benchmarks are limited. The authors aim to advance research by providing a common evaluation framework and dataset that specifically targets multiple dialects and a more complex generative sentiment manipulation task.

Method: They organize a shared task (DialectSentEval) at ArabicNLP 2026 with two subtasks. Subtask 1 is a supervised multi-class, multi-dialect sentiment classification benchmark. Subtask 2 is a generative sentiment-swapping task where systems must invert sentiment polarity while preserving the main meaning. The paper describes how they design the tasks, build the dataset, and evaluate submitted systems.

Result: The paper reports and compares the performance of participating models on both subtasks, highlighting which approaches work best for multi-dialect classification and for generative sentiment swapping. It also provides observations on model strengths and weaknesses across dialects and task types.

Conclusion: DialectSentEval establishes a new benchmark for Arabic dialect sentiment analysis and controlled sentiment generation. The shared task reveals current capabilities and limitations of state-of-the-art models, and the authors suggest that the released datasets and results will guide future research on robust, dialect-aware sentiment systems and controllable text generation in Arabic.

Abstract: Sentiment analysis is a fundamental problem in Natural Language Processing (NLP). Standard sentiment classification for the Arabic language remains challenging due to the high volume of dialectal Arabic. To advance research in this area, this paper proposes the Shared Task on Sentiment Analysis and Swapping in Arabic Dialects (DialectSentEval), hosted with the Arabic Natural Language Processing Conference (ArabicNLP 2026). This shared task consists of two subtasks: Subtask 1 focuses on multi-class and multi-dialect sentiment analysis, requiring models to identify sentiment polarity across various Arabic dialects. Subtask 2 introduces a generative task for Arabic sentiment swap, challenging models to invert sentiment polarity while preserving core semantics. In this overview paper, we present the motivation, dataset creation, and summarize the main findings from participating models.

</details>


### [113] [Agentic schema-guided extraction of materials process knowledge from scientific literature](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06322)
*Sameer Sadruddin,Jennifer D'Souza*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SciKGExtract is a schema-guided, LLM-based framework that normalizes and refines experimental information from materials papers into a structured knowledge graph, using chemical canonicalization and agentic verification to improve extraction quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Experimental procedures and measurements in materials science papers are rich but hard to reuse because they are written in heterogeneous, context-dependent ways, making it difficult to aggregate and computationally analyze them. The authors want a robust way to transform this unstructured literature into a consistent, machine-actionable knowledge representation.

Method: The authors design SciKGExtract, a multi-stage pipeline: (1) large-language-model-based information extraction guided by a detailed experimental schema; (2) chemical entity normalization using PubChem to canonicalize chemical information; (3) agent-based evaluation and refinement loops that check, correct, and improve the extractions; and (4) integration of the refined data into a knowledge graph. They benchmark the framework on 176 atomic-layer-deposition (ALD) papers on ZnO and IGZO, using an expert-annotated subset for full-schema evaluation across 65 experimental properties and 155 quantitative measurement nodes.

Result: PubChem-based chemical normalization improves exact-match F1 scores for all tested LLMs. For ZnO ALD papers, F1 increases from 0.591 with direct normalized extraction to 0.805 when agentic refinement is applied, demonstrating substantial gains from the refinement stage. For IGZO, the best F1 reaches only 0.344, indicating that more complex multicomponent supercycle processes remain challenging. Detailed evaluation against the nested schema uncovers systematic errors in segmenting processes and assigning numerical values.

Conclusion: SciKGExtract successfully converts complex, heterogeneous experimental descriptions in materials papers into structured, machine-actionable knowledge by combining schema-guided LLM extraction, chemical canonicalization, and agent-based verification. Chemical normalization and agentic refinement act as complementary control mechanisms that significantly improve extraction quality, though complex multicomponent systems like IGZO still pose challenges that highlight areas for further method development.

Abstract: Materials literature contains detailed experimental knowledge, but procedures, chemical entities and measurements remain difficult to aggregate because they are reported in heterogeneous forms and depend on process-specific context. We present SciKGExtract, a schema-guided framework that combines large-language-model extraction with chemical normalization and agent-based evaluation and refinement before knowledge-graph integration. We evaluate the framework on 176 atomic-layer-deposition papers describing zinc oxide (ZnO) and indium--gallium--zinc oxide (IGZO), together with an expert-annotated full-schema subset. PubChem normalization improves exact-match extraction F1 for every tested model. For ZnO, the best F1 increases from 0.591 for direct normalized extraction to 0.805 with agentic refinement, whereas the best IGZO result is 0.344, revealing the greater difficulty of multicomponent supercycle processes. Evaluation against a deeply nested schema containing 65 experimental properties and 155 quantitative measurement nodes further exposes errors in process segmentation and numerical assignment. These results show that chemical canonicalization and targeted agentic verification provide complementary controls for converting complex materials literature into reusable, machine-actionable experimental knowledge.

</details>


### [114] [Breaking Bureaucracy: Evaluating open-source LLMs for legal document review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06345)
*Farrukh Baratov,Niki van Stein,Suzan Verberne*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates open-source generative LLMs in zero-shot settings for legal NLI tasks and compares them with a supervised baseline, finding that some large open models approach or sometimes match supervised performance, making them viable when labeled data is unavailable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Legal inspection tasks are domain-specific, often involve confidential data, and may lack labeled datasets, making it difficult or undesirable to use cloud-based or heavily supervised models. The authors want to know whether local, open-source, generative LLMs used in a zero-shot way can handle legal NLI tasks well enough to be practical in such constraints.

Method: They reproduce the Span NLI BERT supervised baseline on the ContractNLI benchmark and evaluate several open-source generative LLMs in zero-shot mode on ContractNLI and two NLI4Wills datasets. They compare accuracy and other metrics, examine invalid output rates, and study stability across temperature settings and domains.

Result: Gemma-4 26B achieves the best performance among the generative models with up to 81.2% accuracy and even surpasses the supervised baseline on one metric, though supervised remains superior on overall accuracy. Qwen-3.6 35B also performs strongly and transfers well across both ContractNLI and wills datasets. The models exhibit varying invalid rates and stability profiles across temperatures and domains.

Conclusion: Zero-shot, open-source, generative LLMs can provide competitive performance on legal NLI tasks without any supervised training data, making them a practical alternative for real-world legal applications where labeled data is scarce and confidentiality constraints demand local deployment, though supervised models still have an accuracy edge when available.

Abstract: In this paper, we evaluate open-source generative LLMs on legal Natural Language Inference (NLI). Legal inspectorial processes take place in specific domains and often deal with confidential data. This creates a need for working with local models that do not require labeled training data. We evaluate our models on the ContractNLI benchmark and two NLI4Wills datasets. We successfully reproduce the baseline for the task (Span NLI BERT) and we evaluate multiple open-source LLMs on the same task. We analyze the invalid rate of the models, and their stability across temperature settings and domains. Among the generative models, Gemma-4 26B performs the best, reaching an accuracy of 81.2%, even outperforming the supervised model on one metric. On accuracy, it is not possible to beat the supervised model with zero-shot approaches. Qwen-3.6 35B performs well on both ContractNLI and additional datasets in the legal wills domain. Our findings indicate that zero-shot, open-source, generative LLMs are a viable alternative for real-world legal NLI when no supervised data is available. Our code is available at https://github.com/fbaratov/contractnli-llms.

</details>


### [115] [Ontology Concept Overlap as a Training Signal: Knowledge-Grounded Reinforcement Learning for Clinical Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06360)
*Aditya Tanna,Abhishek Jindal*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces a new reinforcement learning–based post-training approach for clinical question answering LLMs that uses a soft ontology-based verifier combined with an LLM judge and a consistency term, achieving substantial gains over supervised fine-tuning on MedQA and PubMedQA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL post-training methods for language models mainly rely on human preference data (e.g., RLHF, DPO) or binary verifiers (RLVR). Clinical QA does not fit well into either framework because clinically near-correct answers can differ only by a small entity change, and there is no simple executable program that can definitively verify correctness. Exact match metrics also fail to credit partially correct clinical responses. The authors are motivated to design a more graded, domain-aware reward signal that captures clinical entity correctness without requiring model-in-the-loop verifiers or extensive human labeling.

Method: They build a soft, automatic verifier using the UMLS controlled vocabulary. Clinical entities in model answers and references are mapped to UMLS Concept Unique Identifiers using scispaCy, and a set-level F1 over these CUIs is used as a graded reward signal. This ontology-derived reward is combined within GRPO with: (1) an entropy-normalised LLM judge that scores safety and evidence quality aspects not visible to ontology overlap, and (2) a small consistency penalty that discourages padding and repetition, keeping generated samples scorable early in training. This yields a three-term composite reward used for RL post-training on base models (Phi-3-mini and Llama-3.2-3B). They also perform a reward ablation by varying the contributions of the ontology and judge components and run negative experiments with DPO under random negatives, PPO with sparse neural reward, and GRPO with KL regularisation at larger scale.

Result: On MedQA, their method improves Phi-3-mini from 0.680 to 0.700 EM (+2.9% relative) and from 0.145 to 0.202 Token-F1 (+39% relative). For Llama-3.2-3B, they see a 14% relative EM gain and 35% relative Token-F1 gain over SFT. Token-F1 is adopted as the primary metric to better reflect partial clinical correctness in open-ended generation, and results averaged over three seeds show low variance (std < 0.005). The same composite reward, trained only on the PubMedQA train set and without additional tuning, improves Token-F1 over SFT by 22% for Phi-3-mini and 17% for Llama-3.2-3B, indicating transfer across datasets. Reward ablation on Phi-3 attributes about 3 EM points specifically to the ontology-based term, showing it catches entity substitution errors missed by the judge. They also find that DPO with random negatives can underperform SFT for stronger prior models, PPO with a sparse neural reward can diverge, and GRPO with an explicit KL term in the loss collapses at 7B scale.

Conclusion: A composite reward that blends an ontology-based soft verifier, an LLM judge, and a simple consistency penalty enables effective RL post-training for clinical QA models without handcrafted binary verifiers or heavy human preference data. The approach yields consistent improvements over SFT on MedQA and PubMedQA, better captures partial clinical correctness through a Token-F1 metric, and isolates the unique value of ontology-aware rewards for catching subtle entity errors. Their negative findings on DPO, PPO, and large-scale GRPO with KL suggest design constraints and pitfalls for RL-based post-training in this domain.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning post-training for language models relies on two reward designs: human preferences (RLHF, DPO) and binary verifiers (RLVR). Clinical question answering fits neither. Near-correct answers differ by a single substituted entity, and no executable check decides clinical correctness. We instantiate a soft verifier from a maintained controlled vocabulary: UMLS Concept Unique Identifier overlap (via scispaCy, set-level F1) gives a graded, externally specified reward computed without a model in the loop. We combine it inside GRPO with an entropy-normalised LLM judge, which covers the safety and evidence axes overlap cannot see, and a small consistency penalty on padding and repetition that keeps early-training samples scorable. This three-term composite improves over SFT on Phi-3-mini (3.8B) over MedQA by 2.9% on EM (0.700 vs 0.680) and 39% on Token-F1 (0.202 vs 0.145); on Llama-3.2-3B the corresponding gains are 14% on EM and 35% on Token-F1. We report Token-F1 as the primary metric because it credits partially-correct clinical content that EM discards at this open-generation scale. Main-table results are means over 3 seeds with standard deviations below 0.005. The method transfers to PubMedQA, where training on the PubMedQA train set with the same composite reward improves Token-F1 over SFT by 22% on Phi-3-mini and 17% on Llama-3.2-3B without retuning. A reward ablation on Phi-3, varying the judge-ontology split at a fixed consistency weight, attributes 3 EM points to the ontology term, the contribution that catches entity substitutions the judge cannot. Three negative findings constrain the design: DPO under random negatives underperforms SFT for strong-prior models but helps the weakest-prior one; PPO under a sparse neural reward diverges; GRPO with KL-in-loss collapses at 7B.

</details>


### [116] [Do Speech Representations Preserve Regional Accent Across Read and Spontaneous Speech?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06430)
*Paula A. Perez-Toro,Tomas Arias-Vergara,Annette Schwarz,Abner Hernandez,Andreas Horr,Cornelia Kristen,Andreas Maier*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates how well different speech representations encode regional accent information in German, and whether this information transfers from read to spontaneous speech; high in-domain accuracy does not translate into robustness across speaking styles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Regional accents are increasingly used in speech technology for tasks like dialect recognition and geolocation, often evaluated only under matched conditions (same speaking style, such as read-read). It is unknown whether strong performance in such settings reflects true, stable regional information or just style-specific cues that fail when moving to spontaneous speech, which is more realistic. The paper aims to quantify this gap and understand which types of representations best preserve regional accent cues across styles.

Method: Using the RVG1 corpus of 500 German speakers from nine regions, the authors compare ten different speech representations, including Whisper, self-supervised models, and speaker embeddings. They evaluate two tasks: (1) nine-way regional classification (reporting unweighted average recall, UAR) and (2) continuous geolocation (measuring median geographic error in kilometers). They test both matched-style scenarios (train and test on the same style: read-read or spontaneous-spontaneous) and speaker-independent cross-style transfer (train on read, test on spontaneous and vice versa). They analyze robustness via performance drops, relate it to style-invariance (measured with cross-style speaker retrieval as a proxy), and control for potential confounds such as age, sex, sentence overlap, duration, and channel characteristics.

Result: Under matched conditions, Whisper achieves the best performance at 0.489 UAR for nine-way regional classification and 148 km median geolocation error. However, its performance collapses in cross-style transfer, with UAR dropping to 0.11/0.18 (depending on transfer direction) and median geolocation error worsening to 363 km. Self-supervised models show similar degradation. In contrast, speaker embeddings, though weaker in-domain, degrade less when transferring between read and spontaneous speech. This robustness pattern is consistent for both classification and geolocation tasks. Across all representations, better robustness correlates with greater style-invariance (smaller shifts between read and spontaneous styles), which is captured by stronger cross-style speaker retrieval. Confound analyses indicate that age, sex, sentence overlap, and duration do not explain the performance gap, while channel characteristics have some effect.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that high performance on regional accent recognition and geolocation under matched conditions does not imply that a representation carries robust, transferable regional information. Many strong models, including Whisper and self-supervised representations, rely on style-dependent cues that fail when moving between read and spontaneous speech. Representations that are more style-invariant—approximated by cross-style speaker retrieval—are more robust across conditions, even if they are less discriminative in-domain. Future evaluation and model development for regional speech tasks should therefore explicitly consider cross-style robustness and style-invariance rather than relying solely on matched-condition benchmarks.

Abstract: Regional accent cues can be captured under matched conditions, but it remains unclear whether they persist between read and spontaneous speech. We study RVG1, with 500 German speakers from nine regions, comparing ten speech representations on regional classification and continuous geolocation under matched conditions and speaker-independent read--spontaneous transfer. Whisper performs best under matched conditions, reaching 0.489 nine-way UAR and 148 km median geolocation error, but drops to 0.11/0.18 UAR across transfer directions and 363 km geolocation error. Self-supervised models show a similar degradation, whereas speaker embeddings are less discriminative in-domain but more robust under transfer. This contrast is consistent across classification and geolocation. Across representations, robustness is associated with how little a representation shifts between styles (style-invariance), for which crossstyle speaker retrieval is an interpretable proxy. Age, sex, sentence-overlap, and duration controls do not account for the gap, although channel characteristics contribute. These results show that strong matched-condition performance does not indicate robust regional information.

</details>


### [117] [The Assistance Dilemma: Learning to Teach via Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06446)
*Jakub Macina,Manu Kapur,Mrinmaya Sachan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They design a new reinforcement-learning training setup for LLM tutors that rewards actual student learning on new, unseen but related problems, not just solving the current problem, and show it produces smaller models that tutor as well as frontier models with far fewer tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Question-answer-trained LLMs often "tell" answers instead of teaching. Prior RL-based tutors rewarded success on the same problem while the tutor’s text stayed visible, so the easiest way to get high reward was to simply give away solutions, requiring hand-tuned penalties. The authors want a more principled, learning-science-inspired reward that promotes real student understanding, supports transfer to new problems, and reduces cognitive offloading and solution handover.

Method: They introduce a masked near-transfer post-test: after a tutoring dialog on one problem, a simulated student must solve a new but closely related problem with the tutor’s prior utterances masked. Reward is based on the student’s performance on this post-test and is gated by two binary checks: (1) the tutor’s response is factually correct and (2) the tutor has not directly handed over the full solution. This removes the need for a continuous handover penalty. Using this reward, they implement Eduardo, a multi-turn RL training recipe for LLM tutors, and train 4B, 9B, 14B and 27B models from two different base LLM architectures on an 8,671-problem near-transfer dataset, with ablations (e.g., removing gates or the near-transfer test) to study each component’s impact.

Result: Ablation experiments show that the learning-gain reward alone does not sufficiently discourage telling; the binary reward gates reduce solution handover, while the masked near-transfer post-test improves out-of-domain transfer. The best model, Eduardo-27B, achieves performance comparable to frontier systems (Gemini-3.1-Pro on MathTutorBench and Claude Opus 4.8 on TutorMoments) while using 2.4–6.2x fewer thinking tokens in tutoring interactions. Behavior analysis reveals a substantial, emergent increase in pedagogically desirable moves like "push-for-justification" without directly rewarding them, whereas behaviors whose benefits extend beyond a single problem, such as fading support and assigning independent work, are diminished by the current episodic setup.

Conclusion: Rewarding actual learning via a masked near-transfer post-test, together with simple binary correctness and no-handover gates, yields RL-trained LLM tutors that teach rather than tell, transfer better, and operate efficiently in terms of tokens. The Eduardo recipe demonstrates that mid-sized models can reach frontier-level tutoring quality under this scheme. However, the episodic reward structure disincentivizes some long-horizon teaching strategies (like support fading), suggesting future work should incorporate longer-term or curriculum-level objectives. The authors release their environment, dataset, and models to enable further research on principled, learning-science-grounded RL for AI tutors.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) trained to answer questions are natively poor at teaching. Reinforcement Learning (RL) against a simulated student is a promising approach to improve their pedagogy, but existing RL-trained tutors reward the student's success on the tutored problem with the tutor's words still in context. The reward is then easiest to raise by telling the student the answer, and a tuned penalty is needed to reduce telling. Drawing on learning sciences, we introduce a masked near-transfer post-test: the student is tested on an unseen variant of the tutored problem with the tutor's utterances masked, so the reward can rise only through what the student wrote in its own turns. This discourages cognitive offloading by the student and allows the continuous penalty to be replaced by two binary reward gates (factual correctness of tutor response, no solution handover). A leave-one-out ablation shows that the learning-gain reward on its own does not separate teaching from telling: the gates reduce solution handover while the near-transfer post-test improves out-of-domain transfer. Using these reward designs we develop Eduardo, a multi-turn RL recipe for training LLM tutors, and use it to train 4B, 9B, 14B and 27B models from two distinct LLM architectures. Our post-trained Eduardo-27B model matches Gemini-3.1-Pro on MathTutorBench and Claude Opus 4.8 on TutorMoments at 2.4-6.2x fewer thinking tokens than frontier models, which matters for interactive tutoring. Without being named in the reward, the model more than doubles its use of the push-for-justification teacher move while support fading (e.g., assigning independent work), whose payoff lies beyond a single-problem dialog episode, is trained out. We open-source our training environment, an 8,671-problem near-transfer dataset, and trained models for further development.

</details>


### [118] [Behavior-Preserving KV Cache Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06479)
*Doo Hwan Hwang,Junyoung Jang,Junho Na,Hosung Lim,Kee-Eung Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a new training-free method to compress KV caches in large language models by explicitly preserving the model’s output behavior, leading to better quality under aggressive compression than attention-based heuristics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: KV cache size is a major bottleneck for long-context inference and long-form generation, both in memory and speed. Existing cache eviction or compression strategies mainly use simple proxy signals like attention mass, which often fail to preserve the model’s actual predictive behavior and can degrade performance, especially under strong compression. There is a need for a better, still training-free, policy that directly focuses on preserving what the model would predict if it had the full cache available.

Method: They introduce Behavior-Preserving KV Cache Compression, a framework that, for each candidate cache entry to evict, estimates the logits the model would produce if that entry were removed, then measures how much the resulting next-token distribution diverges from the full-cache distribution using KL divergence. This KL score is used as an importance metric: entries whose removal causes minimal KL change are evicted. To keep computation practical, they reuse pre-eviction forward statistics to approximate the masked logits instead of running a separate masked forward pass per candidate. The method is training-free and can operate both during prefill and during generation.

Result: Across multiple LLM architectures and for both prefill-time and generation-time compression, the proposed method consistently outperforms lightweight attention-based heuristics at the same retained-KV budget. The advantage is most pronounced under aggressive compression, where heuristic policies suffer larger quality drops. Although the method adds some computation at compression time, overall it still yields an end-to-end speedup versus full-cache inference in the evaluated scenarios.

Conclusion: Directly preserving the model’s predictive behavior via KL-based scoring is a more effective principle for KV cache compression than relying on proxy importance metrics like attention mass. A practical, training-free approximation of behavior-preserving eviction can significantly improve downstream task quality under KV budget constraints while maintaining net inference speedups, making it a promising approach for long-context and long-form LLM applications.

Abstract: KV caches are a major bottleneck in long-context inference and long-form generation with large language models. Existing training-free eviction policies largely rely on proxy importance signals, such as attention mass, to decide which past tokens to retain. We argue that cache compression should instead preserve the predictive behavior of the full-cache model, retaining entries whose removal would substantially change the model's output distribution. We propose Behavior-Preserving KV Cache Compression, a training-free framework that scores candidate evictions by estimating the compressed-cache logits induced by their removal and evaluating the resulting KL to the full-cache next-token distribution. Using pre-eviction forward statistics, the method avoids running separate masked forward passes for each candidate. Across diverse architectures and both prefill-time and generation-time compression, our method delivers substantial gains in downstream task quality over lightweight attention-based heuristics at matched retained-KV budgets, with the largest gains under aggressive compression. It achieves these gains with additional compression-time computation while retaining an end-to-end speedup over full-cache inference in our evaluated settings.

</details>


### [119] [AECP: Artifact-Exclusive Communication Protocol for Multi-Agent Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06481)
*Jiaqi Xue,Yanjun Wang,Xiangci Li,Lingbo Mo,Aritra Sengupta,Shweta Garg,Murali Krishna Ramanathan,Myeongsoo Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes Artifact-Exclusive Communication Protocol (AECP), where multi-agent coding systems communicate only via structured artifacts managed by an execution harness, yielding higher reliability, speed, and safety than free-form messaging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-agent AI systems for repository-level coding currently coordinate via free-form messages whose contents serve only as loose context. This makes shared findings easy to ignore, interface contracts easy to violate without detection, and collaboration less reliable and efficient. It also allows malicious instructions to spread between agents. The authors aim to make coordination more systematic, enforceable, and secure.

Method: They introduce AECP, a protocol that constrains agents to communicate solely through structured artifacts, with explicit semantics enforced by an execution harness. The harness: (1) injects relevant recorded findings when agents access associated code; (2) checks implementations against previously committed interfaces and flags mismatches; and (3) forces agents to revisit work when interface agreements change. The authors implement AECP in multi-agent coding setups and compare it to a baseline using free-form inter-agent messaging, evaluating both closed- and open-source models on Doc2Repo, NL2Repo, and CodeProjectEval benchmarks. They also test how well AECP prevents propagation of malicious instructions across agents.

Result: On repository-level coding benchmarks (Doc2Repo, NL2Repo, CodeProjectEval) with models like Opus-4.8 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, AECP increases average test pass rate by 28.2% and reduces wall-clock time by 16.5% compared to a free-form messaging baseline. In security tests, artifact-exclusive communication prevents malicious instructions from being relayed between agents (reduction from 95% to 0%) and from influencing their behavior (reduction from 40% to 0%).

Conclusion: Structuring all inter-agent communication as artifacts and letting the execution harness manage and enforce their use yields more reliable, efficient, and secure collaboration in multi-agent coding systems than free-form messaging. Coordination responsibilities that used to rely on agents reading and acting on prior messages can instead be built directly into the harness, improving both performance and safety.

Abstract: As AI agents increasingly tackle complex repository-level coding tasks, distributing work across multiple agents is a natural way to scale beyond the capabilities of a single agent. To coordinate their interdependent work, these agents share findings and agree on interfaces between modules. However, exchanged information often serves only as context, leaving individual agents to interpret it and incorporate it into subsequent work. Consequently, shared findings may go unused and deviations from interface agreements may go undetected, undermining the reliability and efficiency of collaboration. This motivates moving part of the coordination responsibility from individual agents to the execution harness. To make shared information actionable during execution, we introduce the Artifact-Exclusive Communication Protocol (AECP). AECP requires agents to communicate exclusively through structured artifacts and specifies how the harness processes them. The harness supplies findings when agents access relevant code, screens implementations for mismatches with recorded interface commitments, and requires affected agents to revisit revised agreements. These coordination steps become part of harness execution rather than actions that agents must initiate from prior messages. Across Doc2Repo, NL2Repo, and CodeProjectEval, using closed- and open-source models including Opus-4.8 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, AECP improves average test pass rate by 28.2% and reduces average wall time by 16.5% relative to an agent team using free-form inter-agent messages. Artifact-exclusive communication also blocks the relay of malicious instructions between agents, reducing how often they reach other agents from 95% to 0% and how often those agents act on them from 40% to 0%.

</details>


### [120] [SOL: Measuring Gaps between Text Distributions by Double Sliced Wasserstein Metrics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06513)
*Gregor Kornhardt,Moritz Piening,Jannis Chemseddine,Gabriele Steidl*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces SOL, a new metric for comparing text distributions across generative language models, particularly non-autoregressive ones like diffusion and flow models, providing a principled distance based on hidden-state Wasserstein geometry instead of likelihood or ad‑hoc sample scores.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluation for autoregressive language models relies on perplexity, which directly reflects how well the model distribution matches the data distribution. For diffusion and flow-based language models, only a likelihood bound is available, and its tightness varies between architectures, making cross-model comparison unreliable. Sample-based alternatives, such as generative perplexity with entropy terms, overlook how closely the overall distribution of generated text matches real data and can fail to detect distributional mismatches. There is therefore a gap in robust, comparable metrics to evaluate non-autoregressive text generators by their distributional fit.

Method: They define SOL as a distance between text distributions using a fixed transformer’s hidden representations as an embedding space. For any text sequence, they compute the empirical measure of its hidden states (e.g., token-level embeddings from a frozen transformer). To compare two text distributions (e.g., data vs. model samples), they compare the corresponding distributions of these empirical measures using the double sliced Wasserstein distance, a variant of optimal transport that is computationally tractable in high dimensions. Theoretical analysis shows SOL is a proper metric when the transformer mapping from text to hidden states is injective. They then empirically evaluate SOL across various generative model families trained on OpenWebText, comparing its behavior to standard metrics and assessing stability and sensitivity to distributional pathologies.

Result: Theoretical results prove that under an injective transformer encoder, SOL satisfies the properties of a metric on text distributions (non-negativity, symmetry, identity of indiscernibles, triangle inequality). Empirically, SOL identifies distributional failures of generative models that are not captured reliably by likelihood bounds or sample-based perplexity proxies. It recovers expected trends in model quality across architectures and scales, meaning models believed to be better by other strong indicators also show better (lower) SOL distance to the data. The metric yields stable estimates from finite samples, indicating practicality for evaluation without requiring enormous sample sizes.

Conclusion: SOL offers a principled, sample-based way to compare how well different language models, including non-autoregressive ones like diffusion and flow models, match the real data distribution. By leveraging hidden representations from a fixed transformer and double sliced Wasserstein distance, it provides a true metric under mild conditions and empirically aligns with qualitative expectations about model quality while revealing distributional issues. The authors propose SOL as a missing component in current evaluation protocols and demonstrate its use by re-assessing a range of models trained on OpenWebText.

Abstract: Evaluating text generation requires measuring how well the generated distribution matches the data distribution. For autoregressive models, this is done by the perplexity. Diffusion and flow-based language models can only provide a likelihood bound, whose tightness differs between model families. Sample-based substitutes such as generative perplexity with entropy do not consider the distribution fit. We propose SOL,
  a distance between text distributions. Each sequence is represented by the empirical measure of its hidden states under a fixed transformer and the distributions of these measures are compared by the double sliced Wasserstein distance. We prove that SOL is a metric if the transformer is injective. Experiments show that SOL detects distributional failures, recovers expected model trends, and provides stable sample-based estimates. We put forward SOL to fill the gap in the current evaluation protocol used for non auto-regressive models. As a first step we use SOL to re-evaluate a variety of models trained on OpenWebText.

</details>


### [121] [Test-Time Adaptation of Reasoning Strategies with Bayesian Nonparametric Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06516)
*Keshav Ramji,Tahira Naseem,Ramón Fernandez Astudillo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a Bayesian ‘cheatsheet’ memory module for LLMs that clusters and retrieves reusable reasoning behaviors to improve accuracy and efficiency at test time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs that use chain-of-thought often follow long, suboptimal reasoning paths, increasing inference cost. Additionally, when LLMs discover useful reasoning strategies (e.g., via self-reflection), there is no principled, structured way to store, organize, and reuse these across future queries and domains. The authors aim to build a memory mechanism that can capture, structure, and adaptively reuse such behaviors for better test-time reasoning and adaptation.

Method: They represent reasoning behaviors as embeddings and model them with a Hierarchical Dirichlet Process Gaussian Mixture Model (HDP-GMM). This nonparametric Bayesian model clusters behaviors into shared components across domains while allowing domain-specific mixture weights. At inference (test-time training), the system uses the posterior predictive distribution to retrieve relevant behaviors for a query, updates sufficient statistics online after each sample, and can instantiate new mixture components when behaviors are novel. The module can also reassign behaviors to components using a single step of collapsed Gibbs sampling, enabling adaptive reorganization of the memory.

Result: On reasoning benchmarks including AIME’25, Omni-MATH, and PhysReason, the Bayesian Cheatsheet memory yields clear performance improvements over prior memory modules, even when starting from cold (i.e., with little or no prior stored behaviors). It effectively retrieves and updates strategies online, showing advantages in both accuracy and adaptation ability.

Conclusion: Structured, Bayesian memory modules that organize reasoning behaviors into shared, adaptable clusters can significantly improve LLM test-time adaptation and reasoning performance. The Bayesian Cheatsheet provides a principled way to store, retrieve, and reorganize metacognitive behaviors, underscoring the importance of Bayesian structure in building more adaptive and efficient reasoning systems.

Abstract: While modern large language models (LLMs) have been trained to reason through verbalized chains-of-thought, the generation cost grows substantially due to suboptimal paths to reach the final answer. Furthermore, as new insights are discovered while observing various input queries (e.g. through self-reflection), limited mechanisms exist for carrying forward these findings to be applied to subsequent problems. One can view the list of such strategies or behaviors as a growing cheatsheet, with elements retrieved from this memory module at inference-time. In this work, we consider structured cheatsheets, with learned clusters of behaviors. We introduce a Hierarchical Dirichlet Process Gaussian Mixture Model (HDP-GMM) over behavior embeddings, which shares components across domains while allowing domain-specific mixing weights, and uses the posterior predictive to retrieve relevant behaviors for a query; we call this a $\textit{Bayesian Cheatsheet}$. This mechanism allows for cheap adaptation in an online test-time training (TTT) setting, softly updating the mixture's sufficient statistics following each sample and enabling the creation of new components when the synthesized behaviors are sufficiently novel. We demonstrate that Bayesian Cheatsheet achieves clear performance gains relative to existing memory modules across reasoning benchmarks such as AIME'25, Omni-MATH, and PhysReason, even in the cold-start setting. We show that the Bayesian Cheatsheet is an adaptively reorganizing memory module, as behaviors can be re-assigned to components through a single step of collapsed Gibbs sampling. Our findings highlight the value of Bayesian-inspired memory modules for effective test-time adaptation and the role of structure in metacognitive reasoning.

</details>


### [122] [Anatomy of LLM Sycophancy: What a Flip Rate Hides](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06522)
*Haonan Huang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how language models change their answers when users push back, showing that measured “sycophancy” heavily depends on the kind of pressure and evaluation setup used.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Flip rate—how often a model changes its answer after user pushback—is widely used as a proxy for sycophancy, but it conflates genuine self-correction with capitulation and is highly sensitive to prompt and evaluation design. Current measurements risk mischaracterizing model behavior and making cross-model comparisons unreliable, so a more systematic, controlled way to study pushback effects is needed.

Method: The authors introduce SycoLens, a modular, stateless replay protocol: each measurement replays a prior item and committed answer, then applies a single scripted user pushback line, comparing outcomes to a matched control without that line. They systematically vary factors such as pushback wording, the original committed text, answer format, distance to the model’s decision boundary, and ground-truth status. Using several instruments (protocol variants), they run around 760,000 controlled replays across eleven frontier models from three providers, including arithmetic tasks where correctness is known and conditions with planted derivations versus bare answers, and they also compare full-answer and yes/no readouts.

Result: The same model’s apparent sycophancy varies strongly with the form of user pushback: prompts that assert the opposite verdict and prompts that merely challenge the answer induce largely uncorrelated model rankings. Flip rates grow several-fold near model decision boundaries, but even items that are answered identically across screenings still account for about half of the flips in the most-affected settings. In arithmetic tasks, one model tends to recompute and correct under pressure, while another abandons correct answers without showing work. A planted derivation suppresses release of its argued-for answer, regardless of truth, while a bare numerical value does not; incorrect answers are corrected far more often than correct ones are abandoned. Under a yes/no readout, model rankings converge somewhat but become entangled with a pushback-driven shift toward answering “no.” Thus a single flip-rate score per model actually aggregates divergent behaviors across models and benchmarks.

Conclusion: Flip rate is not a simple, model-intrinsic measure of sycophancy: it depends heavily on how users push back, where the question lies relative to the model’s decision boundary, the answer format, and whether reasoning is shown. Because different pushback designs can invert or decorrelate model rankings, single-number sycophancy scores are misleading and can conflate productive self-correction with harmful capitulation. The authors propose a richer reporting profile, built from their SycoLens protocol and released instruments/data, as a more faithful way to characterize model behavior under user pressure and to enable more interpretable cross-model comparisons.

Abstract: A model under pushback can correct itself, capitulate, or hold, and one flip rate counts a correction and a capitulation alike. Using SycoLens, a modular replay protocol, we test how user pressure and evaluation settings shape measured flip rates. Each measurement is one stateless replay of an item, a committed answer, and one scripted user line in a fixed form. Every effect is read against a matched control with the line deleted. Pushback wording, committed text, answer format, boundary distance, and ground truth become factors of one instrument; earlier instruments vary one to three of them. Across eleven frontier models from three providers and about 760,000 controlled replays, which models look sycophantic depends on how the user pushes back. Lines that assert the opposite verdict and lines that challenge the answer without asserting one rank the models almost unrelatedly. Flip effects grow several-fold near a model's boundary, yet items answered identically in every screening draw still carry about half of the most-affected totals. On arithmetic tasks where the truth is known, one model re-derives and corrects itself under pressure while another abandons correct answers without written work. On the model tested, a planted derivation lowers release of the answer it argues for, true or wrong, where a bare stated value does not; the wrong answer is corrected much more often than the true one is abandoned. Under a yes/no readout the rankings come closer, entangled with a pressure-induced shift toward "no". One score per model therefore compares different behaviours across models and benchmarks. We condense these dependencies into a reporting profile; the instrument, records, and analyses will be released upon publication.

</details>


### [123] [Before Agent Tells The Lie: Has Deception Already Been Represented?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06576)
*Xinling Li,Dadi Guo,Qingyu Liu,Qinghua Mao,Yi R. Fung,Na Zou,Xia Hu,Dongrui Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that LLM agents’ deceptive behavior can be predicted and reduced using internal model representations before deception appears in outputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agents can behave deceptively (e.g., hiding failures, fabricating results), and current monitoring only reacts after deception appears in external actions, which is often too late. The authors want to know whether deception leaves detectable traces inside the model early enough to enable proactive monitoring and mitigation.

Method: They treat deception monitoring as a trajectory-level representation analysis problem. Agent trajectories are aligned around key decision points, and hidden states from earlier model calls are extracted and analyzed. Classifiers are trained to distinguish trajectories that will later be honest vs. deceptive. They study how the predictive signal evolves over time and perform activation steering: intervening along discovered representation directions during inference to see if behavior changes.

Result: Internal hidden-state features can reliably predict whether an agent will later act deceptively, even several model calls before the final decision. Deception-related signals are weak at the start but grow stronger over the trajectory; some transferable structure appears before the strongest, decision-adjacent signals. Activation steering along the honest–deceptive directions reduces downstream deceptive behavior, indicating causal influence of these representations on decisions.

Conclusion: Deception in LLM agents is not just a last-moment choice but an evolving internal process that leaves increasingly strong traces in the model’s hidden states. These traces can be detected ahead of time and causally manipulated, suggesting that proactive monitoring and mitigation of deceptive behavior via representation-level tools is feasible.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents can exhibit deceptive behavior during task execution, including hiding failures, fabricating results, or falsely signaling task completion. Existing monitoring approaches mainly detect deception after it appears in observable actions or outputs. In this paper, we investigate whether deceptive behavior can be predicted from an agent's internal representations before it becomes externally visible. We frame deception monitoring as a trajectory-level representation analysis problem and align agent trajectories around key decision points. Using hidden states extracted before these points, we show that future honest and deceptive outcomes can be reliably distinguished, with predictive signals remaining detectable several model calls before the final decision. We further characterize the temporal evolution of these signals: deception-related representations are weak early in execution but become increasingly identifiable as trajectories progress, while transferable structure can emerge before the strongest decision-adjacent signals appear. Finally, we intervene on the identified honest-deceptive representation directions during inference and find that activation steering reduces downstream deceptive behavior, suggesting that these representations influence agent decisions. Our findings indicate that agent deception is an evolving internal process that can be detected and potentially mitigated before it is expressed externally.

</details>


### [124] [Molecules of a Story: Community Detection in PMI-weighted Narrative Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06600)
*Kasper Fyhn,Rebekah Baglini*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose a simple PMI-weighted narrative network method to surface peripheral narrative structures—rare, minor-entity configurations—and show, on The Lord of the Rings, that these form distinct types of episodic, long-distance, and recurring narrative threads.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing automatically extracted narrative networks focus on central, high-frequency entities and their relations, which reveal macro-level narrative structures but miss small, fine-grained sub-plots and minor-character configurations in the long tail of rare entities. The authors want a way to systematically detect and analyze these peripheral narrative structures that are overshadowed by dominant entities and thus invisible in traditional centrality-focused views.

Method: They build narrative networks where nodes are entities and edges capture their relations, but they weight edges using pointwise mutual information (PMI). Because PMI tends to inflate scores for rare co-occurrences, this re-weights the network to foreground rare entity configurations rather than dominant ones. They then perform community detection on this PMI-weighted network; the resulting communities are interpreted as structural traces of underlying narrative elements. For each community, they analyze how its activations (occurrences of the entities or their co-occurrences) are distributed across the text—whether they are temporally concentrated or dispersed—to derive a typology of peripheral structures.

Result: Applied to The Lord of the Rings, the PMI-weighted narrative network yields communities composed largely of rare, peripheral entities and their relations. Analysis of where and how these communities appear in the text shows that they do not all behave the same: some are tightly localized in short passages (episodic), others connect distant parts of the text (echoing long-distance connections), and others recur intermittently across the narrative (recurring threads). This demonstrates that the method can systematically surface fine-grained, peripheral narrative details that standard centrality-based methods overlook.

Conclusion: The PMI-weighted narrative network combined with community detection is a conceptually simple tool for exploring peripheral narrative structures composed of rare entities. It successfully brings to light episodic, long-distance, and recurring peripheral configurations that are usually lost amid abundant central entities. However, because it intentionally amplifies weak, rare-event signals, the method is sensitive and should be treated as an exploratory lens rather than a robust, fully reliable extraction pipeline.

Abstract: Automatically extracted narrative networks -- graphs with entities as nodes and their relations as edges -- have proven useful for revealing central narrative structures through salient entities and their connections (Tangherlini et al. 2020; Labatut and Bost 2019). But a narrative is more than those central structures that everything else revolves around. This work is concerned with the everything else: brief sub-plots, small clusters of descriptions, or associations between minor characters that go under the radar at the macro-level. We present an approach to unearth such peripheral structures. They involve rare entities with limited textual presence, overshadowed by dominant entities and lost among each other in the long tail of many but rare entities (Baayen 2001). We leverage the known tendency of pointwise mutual information (PMI, Church and Hanks 1990) to inflate for rare events, turning its weakness into a strength by weighting edges with PMI to foreground peripheral entity configurations. Communities extracted from the resulting network are structural traces of underlying narrative elements. We demonstrate the approach on The Lord of the Rings. From measures of how concentrated or dispersed a community's activations are across the text, a typology emerges that reveals that peripheral structures form more than a single class: episodic passages, echoing long-distance connections, and recurring threads each surface as distinct configurations. The approach is conceptually simple and surfaces fine-grained narrative details that are lost in abundance, though its deliberate amplification of weak signals comes with inherent sensitivity -- best understood as a lens for exploration rather than a robust extraction pipeline.

</details>


### [125] [Word-Level Text Unmixing via Evidence-Preserving Ownership Routing with Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06603)
*Jinglin He,Siyang Jiang,Lixing He,Guoliang Xing,Hongkai Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Evidence-Preserving Ownership Routing (EPOR), a method for word-level text unmixing that separates source-ownership prediction from text reconstruction, achieving more accurate separation of interleaved text streams without altering the observed words.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When texts from multiple sources get interleaved and their attribution metadata is lost (e.g., overlapping speech, complex document layouts, or multiple agents writing concurrently), we need to recover the original per-source sequences exactly, without losing, duplicating, or fabricating words. Existing LLM-based approaches that directly regenerate separated texts often violate this exactness requirement by omitting, duplicating, or hallucinating tokens. There is a need for a method that can respect the integrity of the observed lexical evidence while disentangling mixed streams into their original sources.

Method: The authors formalize the problem as Word-Level Text Unmixing: given a mixed lexical sequence and a known number of sources K, recover K sequences that together contain every observed word exactly once in the correct within-source order. They propose Evidence-Preserving Ownership Routing (EPOR), which adapts a causal LLM to predict, for each token in the mixed stream, a canonical ownership route (i.e., which source it belongs to) conditioned on both the input and previous routing decisions. Reconstruction is then performed deterministically by routing tokens into their assigned source streams via completion-safe constrained decoding, ensuring no token is dropped or duplicated. This decouples the classification of ownership from the generative reconstruction. They also build UNMIXBENCH, a benchmark suite spanning synthetic mixtures, speech-derived mixtures (AMI, ICSI), document-layout mixtures (ReadingBank), and simulated concurrent digital outputs, for systematic evaluation.

Result: On UNMIXBENCH’s five evaluation tracks, a 4-billion-parameter EPOR model achieves the lowest mean minimum-permutation word error rate compared to finetuned baselines, improving the five-track mean by 22.3% over a compact source-array generation baseline. EPOR also stays competitive with much larger zero-shot frontier LLMs, while guaranteeing structurally valid K-way partitions that preserve all observed words exactly once.

Conclusion: Decoupling ownership inference from text regeneration enables accurate, evidence-preserving separation of interleaved text streams. EPOR demonstrates that when all lexical evidence is observed, predicting token-to-source assignments and then deterministically reconstructing per-source sequences is a robust alternative to directly having LLMs generate separated texts, yielding lower word error rates and eliminating omissions, duplications, and hallucinations in the reconstruction.

Abstract: Text from multiple sources can become interleaved into a single sequence when attribution metadata is lost, such as overlapping speech transcripts, document reading flows, or concurrent agent streams. We formalize this challenge as Word-Level Text Unmixing: given an interleaved lexical stream and source count K, recover the original source sequences while preserving every word occurrence and its within-source order exactly. Directly generating separated texts with LLMs can omit, duplicate, or hallucinate words, violating this exact-reconstruction objective. We therefore propose Evidence-Preserving Ownership Routing (EPOR), which decouples source-ownership prediction from reconstruction. EPOR adapts a causal LLM to predict canonical ownership routes conditioned on the mixed stream and prior routing decisions. At inference, completion-safe constrained decoding is combined with deterministic indexed reconstruction, yielding structurally valid K-source partitions that preserve every observed occurrence exactly once. We also introduce UNMIXBENCH, covering controlled synthetic mixtures, timestamp-derived speech from AMI and ICSI, layout-derived document streams from ReadingBank, and simulated concurrent digital outputs. Across five evaluation tracks, a 4B EPOR model achieves the lowest mean minimum-permutation word error rate among finetuned baselines, reducing the five-track mean by 22.3% relative to compact source-array generation and remaining competitive with zero-shot frontier LLMs. These results show that when lexical evidence is fully observed, separating ownership inference from lexical regeneration provides a reliable alternative to direct generation.

</details>


### [126] [JEV versus LLMs: Accuracy, Cost and Calibration on Seven Political Science Replications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06625)
*Matthew DiGiuseppe,Steven Denney*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates a new "System One" decision-focused model (JEV) against large language models and humans for social science text annotation, finding comparable accuracy but no clear cost advantage and only modest calibration benefits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Social scientists increasingly use LLMs to annotate or scale large political text corpora, but these models are token-generating, expensive, and provide opaque or poorly calibrated uncertainty estimates. A new commercial model class ("System One" models like JEV) promises cheaper, faster, and better-calibrated decision outputs over fixed answer sets, but these claims and their suitability for social science tasks have not been independently validated.

Method: The authors benchmark JEV against several baselines: (1) human coders and LLMs reported in previous published studies; (2) a contemporary mid-tier commercial LLM (GPT-6 Luna); and (3) an open-weight LLM (Qwen3.8-27B). They evaluate performance across multiple social-science-relevant text classification and scaling tasks, comparing accuracy, cost, inference speed, and probability calibration of outputs (i.e., how well predicted probabilities correspond to empirical frequencies).

Result: JEV performs on par with, or close to, both commercial and open-weight LLMs in task accuracy across a range of social science text applications. However, the empirical analysis does not substantiate the claimed cost advantage over GPT-6 Luna when using OpenAI’s batch pricing. In terms of uncertainty estimates, JEV’s output probabilities are better calibrated than GPT-6 Luna’s token probabilities under a single-query regime, but JEV does not consistently outperform the open-weight Qwen3.8-27B in calibration.

Conclusion: JEV is technically capable and competitive with established LLMs for social science text annotation in terms of accuracy, but it lacks a demonstrated cost edge relative to a mid-tier commercial LLM. Its primary distinctive benefit lies in providing directly interpretable choice probabilities that are reasonably well calibrated, especially relative to some token-based systems. Consequently, the authors argue that JEV is mainly attractive in scenarios where researchers either prioritize ease of parsing probability outputs or have strong speed requirements; otherwise, standard LLMs remain similarly effective without clear disadvantages.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) annotate and scale political text or constructs by generating text tokens. A new class of models, which TypeSafe markets as "System One" models, instead returns decisions and probability distributions across a user-supplied fixed answer set. A commercial model, JEV, is advertised as having a dramatic cost and speed advantage over traditional LLMs along with better calibrated decisions. As such, it might be useful for social scientists looking to quickly and cost-effectively annotate or scale large corpora of text and have a reliable indicator of a classifier's uncertainty. Yet, the accuracy of these claims and the broader model accuracy in social science text-based tasks are not yet established. In this paper, we do just that and hope to establish the suitability of JEV for social science tasks. We compare JEV with LLMs and human coders from published research, and with a current mid-tier commercial LLM (GPT-6 Luna) and an open-weight alternative (Qwen3.8-27B). We find that JEV matches, or comes close to, the capabilities of both LLMs in a variety of tasks. However, we find no cost advantage over GPT-6 Luna at OpenAI's batch prices. Further, we find that, when each question is asked once, JEV's probabilities are better calibrated than GPT-6 Luna's token probabilities, but not consistently better than Qwen3.8-27B's. We conclude that unless researchers have a need for speed, JEV's only obvious advantage is ease of parsing the underlying choice probabilities.

</details>


### [127] [Long-Horizon Textual World Modeling through Structured Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06637)
*Fangxin Wang,Xiang Gao,Yuguang Yao,Kaiwen Dong,Nikash Walia,Kamalika Das*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose a new way to train multi-step world models by representing intermediate states as explicit text and supervising them via predictive-gain rewards, improving long-horizon prediction and counterfactual sensitivity in text-based environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard world models for long-horizon prediction either roll out a one-step model (which accumulates error) or use direct multi-step prediction (which is hard to learn over long horizons due to state-tracking difficulty, weak credit assignment, and information loss in intermediate steps). The authors aim to build world models that can accurately reason about long sequences of actions and their consequences, and that are sensitive to counterfactual actions, without succumbing to compounding errors or learning instability.

Method: They recast multi-step transitions as structured reasoning over textual world states. The model maintains explicit textual representations of the world at intermediate steps and reasons over sparse state changes instead of full states. Training uses a predictive-gain objective: the learned intermediate states are rewarded when they help predict the future better than a matched baseline predictor that conditions only on raw history. Intermediate predictive rewards supervise every intermediate textual state, providing stronger credit assignment and encouraging states that preserve information helpful for later predictions. Because the states are text, they can be inspected, scored, and corrected during training.

Result: On three text-based benchmarks—ScienceWorld, Jericho, and CEO-Bench—the method achieves the best average long-horizon performance compared with both recursive (rolled-out one-step) and non-recursive baselines that operate directly on raw history. The performance gains are larger at longer prediction horizons. In a controlled counterfactual experiment, their model is uniquely found to have statistically significant sensitivity to variations in future actions, unlike the baselines.

Conclusion: Explicit textual intermediate world states, combined with a predictive-gain training objective and intermediate predictive supervision, enable more reliable long-horizon world models that better track sparse but important state changes and meaningfully respond to counterfactual actions. This structured reasoning approach outperforms traditional transition modeling techniques, particularly over long horizons, and produces interpretable internal states that can be evaluated and refined during training.

Abstract: World models must predict how an environment evolves under sequences of actions, enabling agents to compare possible futures and reason about counterfactual actions before acting. Long-horizon prediction is commonly obtained by recursively applying a one-step transition model, but intermediate errors can compound over time. Multi-step dynamics models instead condition on a sequence of future actions and predict their consequences directly, but become harder to learn as horizon grows: the model must track interacting state changes across the trajectory, endpoint supervision provides weak credit assignment, and intermediate predictions can remain plausible while losing information needed for later states. We show that these challenges can be addressed by casting the internal evolution of a multi-step transition as structured reasoning over textual world states: reasoning over sparse state changes reduces the burden of state tracking, a predictive-gain objective rewards the learned state for improving over a matched predictor that conditions on raw history instead, and intermediate predictive rewards supervise each state along the trajectory. Because these intermediate states are explicit textual representations of the world, they provide semantically meaningful targets that can be inspected, scored, and corrected during training. Across ScienceWorld, Jericho, and CEO-Bench, our approach achieves the strongest average long-horizon performance against recursive and non-recursive baselines that condition directly on raw history, with gains increasing at longer horizons. In a controlled counterfactual study, our model is also the only one with statistically significant sensitivity to future actions.

</details>


### [128] [LoGRA: Scaling LLM Reinforcement Learning with Low-Rank Gradient Sketches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06647)
*Shaokun Zhang,Yifan Zhang,Jian Hu,Yueying Li,Hao Zhang,Binfeng Xu,Jan Kautz,Yi Dong*

Main category: cs.CL
