TL;DR: LoGRA is a memory-efficient reinforcement learning post-training method for large language models that uses low-rank gradient sketches and KL-based step control to match standard performance while cutting training memory by up to ~46%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reinforcement learning significantly improves large language models, but standard optimizers like dense Adam require large amounts of memory, which limits model size, training length, and accessibility to users with modest hardware. There is a need for RL training methods that maintain performance while reducing memory overhead so that large models can be post-trained on fewer GPUs and longer horizons.

Method: LoGRA stores gradients in compact low-rank sketches instead of full dense tensors, using these sketches both to update model parameters and to synchronize policies across devices. To keep compressed updates from destabilizing learning, it predicts the KL divergence between the current and updated policies before applying each step and rescales the update if the predicted change is too large, effectively combining gradient compression with KL-based step-size control.

Result: On a range of reasoning benchmarks, LoGRA achieves performance comparable to standard RL training while reducing average training memory usage by up to 45.7%. It further demonstrates the ability to train a 27B-parameter language model with RL for more than 1,100 steps on a single 8-GPU node, a setting where conventional dense Adam optimization runs out of memory.

Conclusion: LoGRA makes RL post-training for large language models significantly more memory-efficient without degrading performance. By using low-rank gradient sketches and predicted-KL step control, it enables stable training of large-scale models in hardware-constrained environments, effectively turning previously infeasible RL runs into practical ones and offering a scalable path for broader adoption of RL post-training.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has greatly advanced the capabilities of large language models (LLMs), but its memory demands remain a barrier to broader adoption. We introduce LoGRA, an approach to RL post-training that reduces memory by retaining useful learning signals in low-rank gradient sketches. These compact representations support both model updates and efficient policy synchronization. To prevent overly large updates from disrupting learning, we complement gradient compression with predicted-KL step control, which estimates policy changes before applying each update and adjusts its magnitude accordingly. Across reasoning tasks, LoGRA reduces average training memory by up to 45.7\% without sacrificing performance. It also enables stable training of a 27B-parameter model for over 1,100 steps on a single eight-GPU node, where dense Adam runs out of memory, making previously memory-infeasible RL training practical. Code is available in the \href{https://github.com/skzhang1/labs-molt/tree/logra/examples/scripts/logra}{Molt library}.

</details>


### [129] [Representation-Space MMD for Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06648)
*Ilya Drobyshevskiy,Ilia Sudakov,Maksim Semenov,Denis Kuznedelev,Maksim Ignatov,Pavel Temirchev,Nikita Balagansky,Viacheslav Meshchaninov,Nikita Gushchin,Dmitry Baranchuk*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Post-training method for diffusion language models using MMD minimization in feature space to improve generation quality and decoding parallelism.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Improve diffusion language models’ sample quality and efficiency without expensive retraining, auxiliary models, or full sampling trajectories, and enable higher-parallelism decoding while maintaining accuracy.

Method: Use a frozen pretrained diffusion language model as a feature extractor and minimize Maximum Mean Discrepancy between generated and reference text distributions in its feature space. Retain contextual token-level features to get multiple observations per sequence. Optimize this objective via policy gradients for discrete models and by differentiating through latents for continuous models, computing the loss directly on features to allow efficient post-training.

Result: Experiments on OpenWebText show reduced generative perplexity at similar entropy; on GSM8K the method yields better accuracy-compute trade-offs. On 16B DMax-LLaDA2.0 models with hybrid masked-uniform diffusion, the approach enables more parallel decoding steps while achieving similar or higher accuracy on math and code benchmarks.

Conclusion: MMD-based feature-space post-training for diffusion language models can efficiently improve generation quality and enable more parallel decoding, offering a practical way to enhance large DLMs without full retraining or additional auxiliary models.

Abstract: We introduce a post-training method for diffusion language models (DLMs) that minimizes Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) between generated and reference distributions in the feature space of a frozen pretrained DLM. To estimate MMD, we retain contextual features at individual token positions, obtaining multiple observations per sequence from a single extractor pass. We optimize this objective using policy gradients for discrete models and direct differentiation through generated latents for continuous models. In both cases, computing the loss directly from these features enables efficient post-training without full sampling trajectories or jointly trained auxiliary models. Experiments show lower generative perplexity at comparable entropy on OpenWebText and better accuracy-computation trade-offs on GSM8K. On 16B DMax-LLaDA2.0 models with hybrid masked-uniform diffusion, we increase decoding parallelism with similar or higher accuracy on math and code benchmarks.

</details>


### [130] [Wikidata Search Traces: A Dataset for Training Knowledge Graph Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06650)
*Mohamed Chenene,Carlos Rosas-Hinostroza,Pierre-Carl Langlais,Anastasia Stasenko*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces a recursive language-model-based agent that answers complex Wikidata questions by actively exploring the graph instead of relying on memorized knowledge, and shows this improves accuracy, including for open-weight models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Complex queries over Wikidata still require precise SPARQL, while language models tend to hallucinate or fail on less prominent entities when answering from memory. Existing graph-exploring agents are limited by a lack of supervised traces of good search behavior and by interfaces that dump large graph results directly into the model context, hurting long-horizon reasoning. The authors want to systematically study what makes graph search hard, how evidence management vs. model capability contributes to errors, and whether open models can rival closed ones when given better tooling.

Method: They design a controlled benchmark of complex, multi-hop Wikidata questions by starting from entity-centric queries and replacing entities with nested conditions, ensuring at each step that there is still a unique answer and that each added condition is necessary. They then build and use a recursive language model (RLM) harness: the model issues batched graph calls, stores the graph results in persistent Python state instead of the prompt, and selectively retrieves and interprets evidence via sub-calls. Using this setup, they collect and release 10,235 detailed solving traces for both single-entity and multi-hop questions, and compare different LMs and tool interfaces on a 100-question subset.

Result: On the 100-question evaluation, the RLM harness significantly improves performance relative to a baseline of direct tool calls over the same graph functions. For gpt-6-luna, accuracy increases from 49 to 61 questions correct, with multi-hop accuracy approximately doubling. For Qwen3.8-27B, an open-weight model running on a single GPU, accuracy rises from 60 to 74. These results support the hypotheses that question structure can control graph-search difficulty, that better evidence management reduces long-horizon failures, and that open models can match or outperform closed models in an appropriate environment.

Conclusion: Carefully structured multi-hop questions over a fixed Wikidata snapshot, combined with a recursive LM harness that manages graph calls and evidence outside the prompt, enable more reliable complex question answering via graph exploration. The released dataset of solving traces and the RLM framework demonstrate that much of the difficulty in long-horizon graph reasoning comes from interface and evidence-handling issues rather than inherent model limits, and that open-weight models can be competitive with closed models under these improved conditions.

Abstract: Wikidata is one of the largest open knowledge bases, yet answering a complex question over it still requires a SPARQL query that names the right entities and properties and chains their relations. Language models offer a natural-language alternative but answer largely from memory, which is least reliable for less prominent entities. We study agents that instead answer by exploring the graph, and argue that two obstacles limit them: the lack of training data recording how a solver explores, and interfaces that add large graph results directly to the model's context. We test three hypotheses: that the difficulty of graph search can be controlled through the structure of a question rather than only through obscure entities or wording; that much of the failure on long-horizon search comes from how retrieved evidence is managed rather than from the model itself; and that, in a suitable environment, open-weight models can match commercial closed ones. We construct multi-hop questions on a frozen Wikidata snapshot by replacing named entities with nested conditions, checking after each expansion that the target remains unique and that every new condition is necessary. We release 10,235 solving traces over single-entity and multi-hop questions, together with the recursive language model (RLM) harness that produced them, in which models batch graph calls, keep results in persistent Python state and interpret selected evidence through sub-calls. On 100 questions, the harness improves both models we ran under both interfaces compared with direct tool calling over the same functions: gpt-6-luna rises from 49 to 61 correct answers, doubling its multi-hop accuracy, and Qwen3.8-27B, an open-weight model served on a single GPU, from 60 to 74.

</details>


### [131] [Reward Stealing Attack on Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06670)
*Jiaming Qian,Pengyang Zhou,Jiahe Xu,Chaochao Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Reward Stealing Attack (ReSA), a transferable, efficient adversarial attack on aligned LLMs that works by reconstructing and then reversing their latent safety reward function.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing adversarial attacks on LLMs are either computationally expensive or tightly coupled to specific model pairs, which limits their scalability and cross-model transfer. The authors want an attack that is both efficient and broadly transferable by going after the shared alignment signals rather than model-specific quirks.

Method: They model LLM safety alignment as a latent reward function over outputs and use maximum entropy inverse reinforcement learning to infer a proxy of this reward purely from the observable behavior of an aligned target LLM. At inference time, they flip this learned reward to favor low-safety, high-violation outputs and integrate it into a reward-guided decoding scheme to generate adversarial prompts or continuations.

Result: The learned reward function, once reversed, enables the generation of harmful or policy-violating content across a wide range of prompts and across different LLMs. Experiments show that ReSA achieves higher attack success rates and better transfer to unseen models than prior attack techniques, while being more computationally efficient.

Conclusion: Alignment leaves a recoverable safety reward signal that can be extracted and inverted to systematically bypass safety defenses in multiple LLMs. This exposes a fundamental vulnerability of current alignment paradigms and suggests that robust defenses must assume adversaries can approximate and exploit the latent reward structure itself.

Abstract: Adversarial attacks on Large Language Models (LLMs) aim to induce harmful content. However, existing methods suffer from high computational costs or strict model-pairing dependencies, limiting their scalability and transferability. We propose Reward Stealing Attack (ReSA), an adversarial attack framework that targets the latent safety reward underlying LLM alignment. ReSA employs maximum entropy inverse reinforcement learning to recover a proxy reward model solely from the aligned model's behavior. The extracted reward is then reversed at inference time to derive an adversarial policy, efficiently implemented via a reward-guided decoding mechanism. Experiments demonstrate that a single recovered reward generalizes across prompts and diverse models to reveal a fundamental alignment vulnerability, enabling ReSA to significantly outperform existing attacks in effectiveness and transferability. The code is available at https://github.com/GarminQ/ReSA.

</details>


### [132] [Programmatic Search Agents: Extending Agentic Search Beyond Query Reformulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06689)
*Jiaming Qian,Huiyan Yang,Mandi Liu,Jie Liu,Wenkai Shen,Pengyang Zhou,Jing Jin,Jin Ma,Dezhi Ye,Chaochao Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Programmatic Search Agent (PSA), a new search-agent interface where each search step is an executable program cell operating on retrieved candidates, enabling better control over evidence processing and presentation and yielding higher task success and fewer tokens than query-centered baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing search agents can reformulate queries but have little control over how retrieved documents are processed and what evidence is shown to them. Analyses show that useful supporting passages are often retrieved but never exposed to the agent, and that simply changing which evidence is presented can reduce the need for further search. This motivates an interface that gives agents more direct control over candidate processing and evidence selection, beyond just query generation.

Method: The authors design Programmatic Search Agent (PSA), where the core action is an executable program cell applied to a persistent candidate workspace. Each cell specifies operations over candidates (e.g., scoring, filtering, combining) with explicit data dependencies; the runtime resolves these dependencies and executes the cell, and the agent then inspects selected outputs and decides the next cell. PSA offers flexible composition of primitive operations, re-use of previously retrieved candidates, and selective evidence presentation. They compare PSA against a Query-based Agent (standard query-only interface) and a Tool-based Agent (which shares PSA’s primitives and persistent workspace but not its program-cell interface) on two benchmarks, InfoSeek-Eval and BrowseComp-Plus, using five different backbone policies, all without task-specific training.

Result: Under a shared search substrate across all interfaces, PSA achieves higher macro-averaged task success than the Query-based Agent by 4.00 percentage points on InfoSeek-Eval and 7.56 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus. PSA also substantially reduces the number of final-step tokens used, with average within-backbone reductions of 28.3% and 33.9% on the two benchmarks. The Tool-based Agent, which controls similar primitives but without PSA’s structured program-cell interface, serves as an additional comparison point to isolate the effect of PSA’s design.

Conclusion: The experiments indicate that giving agents programmatic control over the processing and presentation of retrieved evidence—rather than limiting them to query reformulation—yields both higher task success and greater efficiency. PSA’s notion of executable program cells over a persistent candidate workspace is a promising abstraction for search agents, suggesting future systems should integrate evidence handling and interface design, not only retrieval quality. The authors plan to release their code, pending approval, to facilitate further research on programmatic search interfaces.

Abstract: Search agents adapt their queries, yet fixed search interfaces leave candidate processing and evidence presentation outside the agent's direct control. Our trajectory analysis shows that supporting passages can be retrieved yet never delivered to the agent; a same-page oracle intervention shows that changing the returned evidence can reduce subsequent search. We introduce Programmatic Search Agent (PSA), which makes a local executable computation over candidates the unit of a search action. PSA unifies a persistent candidate workspace, flexible primitive composition, and selective evidence presentation. It incrementally generates program cells that reuse candidates, execute dependent operations, and select what the agent inspects next. The runtime resolves specified data dependencies within each cell, while the agent adapts its search strategy across cells as new evidence arrives. We compare PSA with the Query-based Agent and Tool-based Agent on InfoSeek-Eval and BrowseComp-Plus using five policy backbones without task-specific training. All three interfaces share the search substrate, and the Tool-based Agent also shares PSA's primitives and persistent workspace. Relative to the Query-based Agent, PSA improves macro-averaged task success by 4.00 and 7.56 percentage points on the two benchmarks, respectively; within-backbone reductions in final-step tokens average 28.3% and 33.9%. These results support extending agent control beyond query reformulation to the processing and presentation of retrieved evidence. Code will be released subject to approval.

</details>


### [133] [MedPrune: Topology-Efficient Multimodal Multi-Agent Communication Evolution for Medical VQA Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06695)
*Jiuheng Wan,Runze Li,Chen Chen,Tingyuan Hu,Daiyang Yu,Yimin Jing,Taolin Zhang,Richang Hong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MedPrune is a medical multimodal multi-agent framework that prunes unnecessary specialist agents and their connections to improve medical VQA accuracy, robustness, and token efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Med-MLLM multi-agent systems model clinical workflows with many interacting specialist agents, but they suffer from redundant communication patterns, high computational and token costs, and suboptimal reasoning due to noisy or irrelevant interactions. There is a need for a principled way to reduce this redundancy while preserving or enhancing diagnostic performance.

Method: The authors model the diagnostic process as a heterogeneous communication graph, where nodes are specialist agents (from different medical departments) and edges are intra- and inter-departmental communication channels. On this graph, they apply two adaptive sparsification mechanisms: (1) Heterogeneous Node Sparsification uses reinforcement learning-based topological optimization to remove specialist agents that are irrelevant to the current multimodal query; (2) Heterogeneous Edge Sparsification learns to keep only the most diagnostically informative connections by jointly optimizing downstream task performance and a penalty on topological complexity. This yields a dynamically pruned communication structure per query.

Result: In extensive experiments on medical visual question answering under both full-data and few-shot training regimes, MedPrune outperforms prior multi-agent frameworks in accuracy while also reducing token usage. It also demonstrates strong robustness under adversarial settings, indicating that the pruned, sparser communication topology leads to more reliable reasoning.

Conclusion: Dynamic pruning of agents and their communication links in a Med-MLLM multi-agent framework—via heterogeneous node and edge sparsification—can simultaneously increase diagnostic reasoning quality, improve token and computational efficiency, and enhance robustness. Modeling clinical workflows as a learnable, sparsifiable communication graph is an effective strategy for building more efficient and capable multi-agent medical VQA systems.

Abstract: While medical multimodal large language models (Med-MLLMs) advance medical visual question answering (VQA), existing clinical workflow-inspired multi-agent frameworks suffer from interaction patterns and excessive computational overhead caused by redundant communication topologies. In this paper, we propose MedPrune, an efficient medical multimodal multi-agent collaboration framework that dynamically prunes both nodes and edges from the communication topology to enhance reasoning ability and token efficiency. Specifically, we first formulate the diagnostic process as a heterogeneous communication graph, where nodes represent specialist agents from various departments and edges capture intra- and inter-departmental interactions. Building on this graph, we introduce two sparsification mechanisms to enable adaptive collaborative evolution: (1) Heterogeneous Node Sparsification, which eliminates task-irrelevant specialist agents irrelevant to the current multimodal question via reinforcement learning-driven topological optimization, and (2) Heterogeneous Edge Sparsification, which selectively retains only the most diagnostically salient intra- and inter-departmental connections by jointly optimizing task performance and topological complexity. Extensive medical VQA experiments under full-set and few-shot training settings prove MedPrune surpasses multi-agent baselines and boosts token efficiency with strong adversarial robustness.

</details>


### [134] [SAFE-MR: Evidence Sufficiency Learning for Selective Multimodal Rumor Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06708)
*Shiwen Ni*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SAFE-MR is a multimodal rumor verification framework that explicitly separates whether a claim is true from whether the available evidence is sufficient, leading to more reliable, selective predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal rumor detectors rely heavily on retrieved evidence, but they often equate having some relevant evidence with having enough evidence. Problems like missing provenance, duplicated reports, and unresolved contradictions can cause overconfident predictions that are not properly supported, harming reliability in real-world verification settings where evidence quality and completeness are variable.

Method: SAFE-MR decomposes each image-text post into multiple fine-grained verifiable claims, then builds a relation-aware graph connecting claims and evidence items. It aggregates evidence by modeling provenance and contextual compatibility instead of treating all evidence equally. The architecture has separate prediction heads for claim veracity and for evidence sufficiency, enabling the model to decide not only whether a claim is true/false but also whether it has enough support to be confident. Additionally, the training includes evidence-intervention strategies: the model is trained to remain stable when irrelevant evidence is added and to be sensitive when supporting evidence is removed, encouraging robust sufficiency-aware behavior.

Result: On three benchmark datasets—NewsCLIPpings, VERITE, and XFacta—SAFE-MR attains macro-F1 scores of 91.2%, 75.8%, and 85.2%, respectively, outperforming a matched backbone model that uses evidence by 2.2, 4.9, and 4.8 macro-F1 points. In selective prediction evaluation on a diagnostic selection set, it improves uncertainty-based rejection performance, reducing AURC from 0.105 to 0.075 and lowering error at 80% prediction coverage from 13.8% to 8.5%. Evidence perturbation and ablation analyses further show that explicitly learning sufficiency and using intervention-based training are key contributors to these gains.

Conclusion: SAFE-MR shows that explicitly disentangling claim veracity from evidence sufficiency in multimodal rumor verification leads to more accurate and better-calibrated systems. By modeling claim–evidence relationships, provenance, and contextual compatibility, and by training with evidence interventions, the framework improves both overall verification performance and the reliability of selective predictions, making it better suited for real-world rumor and misinformation detection tasks where evidence may be incomplete or noisy.

Abstract: Multimodal rumor detectors increasingly rely on retrieved evidence, yet relevant evidence is not necessarily sufficient for verification. Missing provenance, duplicated reports, and unresolved contradictions can produce confident predictions without adequate support. We introduce SAFE-MR, a framework that separates claim veracity from evidence sufficiency. The method decomposes image-text posts into verifiable claims, constructs a relation-aware claim-evidence graph, and aggregates evidence using provenance and contextual compatibility. Separate veracity and sufficiency heads support selective prediction, while evidence interventions encourage stability under irrelevant additions and sensitivity to evidence removal. On NewsCLIPpings, VERITE, and XFacta, SAFE-MR achieves macro-F1 scores of 91.2%, 75.8%, and 85.2%, respectively. Against the matched backbone with evidence, its macro-F1 gains are 2.2, 4.9, and 4.8 percentage points. On the diagnostic selection set, SAFE-MR reduces AURC from 0.105 for maximum-probability rejection to 0.075 and lowers error at 80% coverage from 13.8% to 8.5%. Evidence-perturbation and ablation results support the role of sufficiency learning and intervention training in improving selective verification.

</details>


### [135] [Domain adaptation of Russian ModernBERT for long legal documents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06715)
*I. Litvak,D. Gvozdetsky,F. Lashkin,V. Kirova,S. Lagutin,V. Volf,T. Maksiyan,A. Kostin,R. Leva,I. Kiselev*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper tests if continued pretraining of Russian ModernBERT on a large corpus of Russian legislative documents improves its performance on legal text, finding modest gains in masked-token prediction but almost no demonstrated improvement in legal-entity extraction or evidence of broader legal utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: General-purpose language models often perform suboptimally on specialized domains such as legal text. The authors want to know whether continued pretraining (domain adaptation) on a large corpus of Russian legislative documents will meaningfully improve a Russian ModernBERT encoder for legal tasks, and to what extent any gains can be quantified and interpreted rigorously.

Method: They take an existing Russian ModernBERT encoder and continue pretraining it on a corpus of 304,382 Russian legislative documents (about 194 million corpus tokens) using a masked language modeling objective. They then compare the original and adapted encoders (RuModernBERT-ruLaw) on (1) masked-token prediction over a fixed set of 1,031 court-decision segments, using five masking realizations and multiple maximum input lengths (512, 2,048, 8,192 tokens), and (2) a legal-entity extraction task, measuring entity-level F1. The evaluation carefully controls hidden positions, uses overlapping windows, and defines precise averaging and boundary-scoring rules, illustrated with editable diagrams and examples. They also distinguish corpus token counts from tokenizer positions and provide 95% intervals for sensitivity to masking, noting that these intervals do not capture variation across document collections.

Result: On the masked-token prediction task, continued pretraining yields lower mean cross-entropy loss: reductions of 0.10942, 0.07052, and 0.06604 natural-log units for maximum input lengths of 512, 2,048, and 8,192 tokens, respectively. This indicates improved masked-token prediction on the evaluated court-decision segments. On legal-entity extraction, however, the original and adapted models achieve nearly identical performance, with entity-level F1 scores of 0.99852 and 0.99820, respectively. Moreover, 99.95% of test entity spans are already seen (same normalized surface form and class) in training, showing that the task is almost entirely memorization-like and offers little evidence about generalization to unseen entities or forms.

Conclusion: Continued pretraining of Russian ModernBERT on Russian legislative documents (RuModernBERT-ruLaw) reduces masked-token prediction loss on a fixed set of court decisions, demonstrating improved modeling of this specific legal text collection. However, the legal-entity extraction results are effectively saturated and provide little insight into improved generalization, because the test entities almost all appear in the training data. The study therefore supports a narrow claim: the adapted model has lower masked-token loss on this dataset and setup. It does not clarify the contribution of very long context, nor does it establish that the adapted model has better practical utility for real-world legal applications or unseen legal language.

Abstract: We investigate whether continued pretraining on Russian legislative documents improves a Russian ModernBERT encoder on legal text. The adapted model, RuModernBERT-ruLaw, was trained on a corpus reported to contain 304,382 legislative documents and 194,425,905 corpus tokens. Corpus token counts are distinguished from positions produced by the model tokenizer. We compare the original and adapted encoders on a fixed external collection of 1,031 court-decision segments. Both models receive the same hidden positions in each of five masking realizations. At maximum input lengths of 512, 2,048, and 8,192 tokens, mean masked-token cross-entropy decreases by 0.10942, 0.07052, and 0.06604 natural-log units, respectively. The reported 95% intervals summarize sensitivity to masking on this fixed collection; they do not quantify uncertainty across document collections. A second evaluation addresses legal-entity extraction. The original and adapted models achieve entity-level F1 scores of 0.99852 and 0.99820. However, 99.95% of test spans have the same normalized surface form and class in the training split. This evaluation therefore provides limited evidence about transfer to previously unseen forms. The paper explains the masking objective, overlapping windows, averaging rules, and exact entity-boundary scoring using editable diagrams and clearly marked illustrative examples. The comparison supports lower masked-token prediction loss for the studied pair of models and collection. It does not isolate the contribution of distant context or establish practical legal utility.

</details>


### [136] [Improving Diversity in LLM Short Story Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06729)
*Zahra Solati Dehkordi,Vasileios Lampos*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A post-training framework (DivLM) for large language models that increases diversity in creative short story generation while preserving quality and instruction following.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs tend to produce accurate but stylistically similar and bland outputs, especially for creative writing tasks. There is a need to systematically increase diversity in generated stories—across genre, tone, style, and named entities—without sacrificing coherence, quality, or adherence to user instructions.

Method: The authors propose DivLM, a two-phase post-training framework. In phase one, they continue pre-training the base LLM on a creative writing corpus and then restore its instruction-following abilities using weight residuals. In phase two, they perform reinforcement learning with a custom composite reward function designed to explicitly promote diversity in genre, tone, style, and named entities while also preserving general response quality.

Result: Across two different LLM families, DivLM improves diversity metrics by over 9% on average compared to competing methods. At the same time, it maintains instruction-following behavior, overall generation quality, and similarity to human-written stories.

Conclusion: Targeted post-training with continued pre-training plus diversity-aware reinforcement learning can significantly enhance the narrative diversity of LLM-generated stories without degrading quality or instruction adherence, offering a practical way to make creative text generation more varied and human-like.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate accurate responses, but these are void of diversity. We attempt to address this for the task of creative short story generation. Drawing on established writing conventions and known LLM limitations, we target variation in genre, tone, style, and named entities. To promote diversity across these dimensions, we introduce DivLM, an LLM post-training framework consisting of two phases. First, we perform continued pre-training on a creative writing corpus and restore instruction-following capabilities using weight residuals. We then apply reinforcement learning with a custom, composite reward function that jointly maximizes diversity across the targeted narrative dimensions while maintaining response quality. Our empirical results on two LLM families show that DivLM increases diversity metrics by more than 9% on average compared to alternative approaches, while preserving instruction following, overall response quality, and similarity to human outputs.

</details>


### [137] [ufakzeka-karar: An Open Turkish Typed-Decision Model with Order-Invariant Option Scoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06744)
*Sait Furkan Teke*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduces ufakzeka-karar, a 182M-parameter Turkish decision model that outputs calibrated option probabilities and uncertainty without text generation, with order-invariant scoring and released Apache-2.0 weights/code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many practical NLP tasks in Turkish (e.g., guardrails, moderation, support) require choosing among predefined options with good calibration and efficiency, rather than generating free text. Existing models are often sensitive to option order, may be poorly calibrated, and can be expensive to run. The authors aim to build an open, efficient Turkish decision model that produces reliable probabilities and a "not sure" signal while avoiding option-order artifacts, and to evaluate it transparently on a public benchmark (HakemBench).

Method: They build ufakzeka-karar on top of ufakzeka-1-base by adding a decision head that scores each option independently at shared input positions, so scores are invariant to option order. The model takes Turkish text plus a question with fixed answer type (choice, ordered scale, yes/no), and in a single CPU forward pass outputs temperature-scaled probabilities for up to ten options and an expected error estimate. They compare this order-invariant head to a sequential head trained with shuffled options, and also compare REINFORCE vs cross-entropy training for decision quality. They evaluate multiple runs on HakemBench v1.0 across seven tracks, track calibration with smooth ECE, and carefully document how later training runs are influenced by reading test results, marking affected numbers as "shaped by reading the test results."

Result: The order-invariant head matches the sequential head in accuracy while eliminating dependence on option order: the sequential head changes 2.3–2.8% of answers when options are permuted. REINFORCE training underperforms cross-entropy by 10.2 macro-F1 points. On the full HakemBench v1.0 (7 tracks, 4,275 questions), the released ufakzeka-karar model achieves a composite score of 0.660 (95% CI 0.642–0.677), ranking 7th of 16 rows; when restricted to the four non-guardrail/moderation/support tracks it scores 0.678, ranking 6th of 16. Temperature scaling improves calibration (smooth ECE) on the development set but slightly worsens it on held-out support questions, e.g., from 0.027 to 0.045 for the first scored run; for the released model, ECE moves from 0.036 to 0.064, though this is not an unseen-question setting because it was later trained on them. Weights and code are released under Apache-2.0.

Conclusion: ufakzeka-karar is an efficient, open Turkish decision model that provides calibrated probabilities and an explicit uncertainty signal without option-order artifacts. Its order-invariant head maintains accuracy while improving robustness over a sequential head, and cross-entropy proves superior to REINFORCE for training. On HakemBench it performs competitively (mid-pack among 16), and the authors emphasize transparent reporting of how test-set feedback shaped later training. The released Apache-2.0 weights and code make this decision-focused architecture available for broader use in guardrails, moderation, and customer support tasks.

Abstract: ufakzeka-karar is an open Turkish decision model with 182,494,466 parameters. Given a Turkish text and questions of a fixed answer type (a choice, a level on an ordered scale, or yes or no), it returns a temperature-scaled probability for every option and an expected error that serves as a "not sure" signal, without generating text and in one CPU forward pass for up to ten options. Built on the lab's ufakzeka-1-base, its head scores each option blind to the others at shared positions, so the answer does not depend on option order. A sequential head trained with shuffled options was about as accurate but changed 2.3 to 2.8 percent of its answers when only the option order changed; REINFORCE lost 10.2 points (0.102) of macro F1 to cross-entropy. On the open set of HakemBench v1.0 (4,275 questions, 7 tracks) the released model ranks 7th of 16 rows with a composite of 0.660 (95% interval 0.642 to 0.677). Temperature scaling lowers calibration error (smooth ECE) on the development set but raises it on held-out support questions, from 0.027 to 0.045 for the first scored run, which never trained on them; the released model later trained on them, so its 0.036 to 0.064 is not an unseen-question test. The released model is the last of three runs scored on HakemBench, and its numbers are not blind. The second run's new training data was aimed at the first run's errors on the full test set in guardrails, moderation and customer support, and the released run was trained after the second run's guardrail results on the full test set were read, under a protocol fixed in writing before any of its data, code or runs. All its numbers come after these readings; its guardrail, moderation and customer support numbers carry the flag "shaped by reading the test results". With every model scored on the other four tracks only, its composite is 0.678, 6th of 16. Weights and code are under Apache-2.0.

</details>


### [138] [Balancing Memory Pathways: Analyzing and Improving Memory Utilization in Hybrid LMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06750)
*Hyunji Lee,Joykirat Singh,Zaid Khan,Justin Chih-Yao Chen,Elias Stengel-Eskin,Alessandro Sordoni,Arman Cohan,Mohit Bansal*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how hybrid language models that mix attention and recurrence actually use their two memory pathways, finds they over-rely on attention, and proposes an auxiliary loss to better balance and coordinate them, improving long-context and aggregation tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hybrid models mixing attention and recurrent layers are thought to combine the strengths of both: attention for precise long-range recall and recurrence for gradual integration of information across long contexts. However, it is unclear whether these models truly exploit both memory pathways in practice or merely default to one, which matters for efficiency, robustness on long contexts, and the design of future architectures. The authors aim to diagnose how these pathways are used and to improve their coordination if it is suboptimal.

Method: The authors empirically analyze recurrent-attention hybrid language models by measuring the relative contribution and utilization of attention-based and recurrent-state-based information when processing sequences. They examine how standard supervised fine-tuning affects this balance. Observing an over-reliance on attention, they introduce an auxiliary training objective that constrains attention’s access to earlier tokens while letting the recurrent state propagate over the entire sequence. This forces the model to retain and use information through the recurrent pathway. They evaluate this modified training procedure on multiple hybrid and attention-based models, across question-answering, agentic tasks, and long-context or information-aggregation benchmarks.

Result: The analysis shows that hybrid language models, even though they include both attention and recurrent layers, predominantly depend on attention and make limited use of recurrent state for memory. Supervised fine-tuning further amplifies this dependence on attention without improving coordination with recurrence. With the proposed auxiliary loss that limits attention’s early context access, models learn to rely more on the recurrent pathway. This leads to improved overall performance, with particularly pronounced gains on tasks that require processing very long contexts or aggregating dispersed information. The pattern holds across different hybrid LMs and even extends to attention-only models that use multiple memory mechanisms.

Conclusion: Merely endowing language models with multiple memory pathways—attention and recurrence or multiple attention-based memories—does not guarantee that they will be used effectively or in a complementary fashion. In practice, models tend to overuse attention and underuse recurrent memory. Targeted supervision, such as the proposed auxiliary loss that selectively restricts attention while leaving recurrence unconstrained, is necessary to encourage better coordination between memory pathways. This coordinated use enhances performance, especially on long-context and information-aggregation tasks, and informs how future multi-memory architectures should be trained.

Abstract: Recurrent-attention hybrid language models (LMs), which interleave attention and recurrent layers, are increasingly used to combine the efficiency of the recurrent layers with the strong performance of attention layers. Prior work suggests that attention and recurrent layers offer complementary pathways to use past information: attention supports precise memory recall from earlier tokens, while recurrent layers support consolidation of disparate information over long contexts. However, we observe that simply having access to both pathways does not mean that hybrid LMs are effectively using them. We find that they rely substantially more on attention than on the recurrent state. Standard supervised fine-tuning improves overall performance but does not improve how the two memory pathways are coordinated: the model becomes more reliant on information propagated by attention layers, while its use of information propagated by recurrent layers remains limited. To encourage better coordination between the two memory pathways, we add an auxiliary loss that limits attention's access to earlier context while the recurrent state propagates through the full sequence. This objective encourages the model to retain and use information through the recurrent pathway alongside attention. It improves overall performance, with particularly strong gains on tasks involving longer contexts or requiring information aggregation, consistent with the strengths of recurrent layers observed in analysis. Crucially, this imbalance and the benefit of our auxiliary loss generalize: they apply to multiple recurrent-attention LMs in question-answering and agentic tasks, as well as to attention-based LMs that combine different forms of memory. Together, our findings show that simply providing multiple memory pathways does not ensure their effective use, and that targeted supervision is needed to better coordinate them.

</details>


### [139] [IdeaLens: Detecting AI Ideas in Long-form Writing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06778)
*Rishanth Rajendhran,Minjoon Choi,Jenna Russell,Ramya Namuduri,Deniz Bölöni-Turgut,Marzena Karpinska,John Wieting,Mohit Iyyer*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents IdeaLens, a detector that determines whether the underlying ideas in a document originate from a human or an AI, independent of who wrote the actual words.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI detectors mainly focus on surface text to infer authorship, which fails when humans rewrite AI content or when AI elaborates on human ideas. Policy and academic concerns are increasingly about the origin of ideas, not just the wording, so there is a need for a tool that can trace idea provenance instead of prose provenance.

Method: The authors represent documents as outlines consisting of discourse-role-labeled, paraphrased content snippets that strip away most surface-level text information. They generate silver labels for idea provenance from Pangram, an existing prose provenance detector, over 1M FineWeb documents. IdeaLens is then trained on these outline representations so that it must learn from the underlying ideas rather than lexical overlap. They evaluate IdeaLens in controlled setups where models write from either human- or AI-derived plans, and across 19 standard detection benchmarks, plus a new dataset of human stories written from AI-generated plans. They also analyze 90K predictions to study patterns distinguishing human and AI ideation.

Result: IdeaLens’s AI-flag rate is highly sensitive to whether the plan originates from humans or AIs: when models expand detailed human plans, the AI flag rate falls dramatically (95%→7%), while a prose-based detector (Pangram 4) keeps flagging most texts as AI (~92%). For AI-derived plans, IdeaLens maintains a high AI flag rate (>96%). On 50 stories written by humans from AI plans, IdeaLens flags 68% as AI versus only 8% for Pangram 4. Across 19 benchmarks, IdeaLens achieves strong detection with low false positives, robust across domains, formats, and languages.

Conclusion: Idea-level information provides a powerful, generalizable signal for distinguishing human- from AI-generated content. By abstracting documents into outline representations and training on large-scale silver-labeled data, IdeaLens can infer the provenance of ideas even when the surface text is heavily edited or written by a different agent. The tool outperforms standard prose-based detectors, especially in scenarios with mixed human–AI collaboration, and the released models and datasets enable further research into idea provenance and systematic differences between human and AI ideation.

Abstract: While modern AI detectors identify who wrote the words, emerging policies on AI use increasingly hinge on a different question: who came up with the ideas? We introduce IdeaLens, a detector that identifies whether a document's ideas came from a human or AI (idea provenance), regardless of who wrote its words. To focus IdeaLens on ideas rather than prose, we represent documents as outlines: lists of items that each pair a discourse role with a brief, paraphrased description of the content, minimizing word-level overlap with the raw text. We train IdeaLens on 1M FineWeb documents with silver labels from Pangram, a prose provenance detector. Since the outlines are largely stripped of surface-level information, the labels must be fit mainly through the ideas. In a controlled study, IdeaLens's AI flag rate drops from 95% to 7% as models write from increasingly detailed human plans, while Pangram 4 still flags 92%; from AI-derived plans, IdeaLens stays above 96%. Conversely, on a new dataset of 50 stories that human authors wrote from AI-generated plans, IdeaLens flags 68% of the stories as AI, compared to 8% for Pangram 4. On a comprehensive suite of 19 existing detection benchmarks, we show that IdeaLens maintains strong detection rates at low false positive rates, suggesting that ideas themselves provide a powerful discriminative signal, and its performance holds across domains, formats, and languages. Finally, we examine 90K predictions from IdeaLens to characterize systematic differences between human and AI ideation. We release our models and labeled datasets to facilitate future research on idea provenance detection.

</details>


### [140] [T-Search: An Open Agentic Retriever and Playground for Hard Multi-Step Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06782)
*Olga Tsymboi,Ramil Latypov,Aleksandr Medvedev,Danil Taranets,Dmitrii Stoianov,Nikita Gulyakov,Gleb Alektorov,Anatolii Potapov*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: T-Search is an open-weight retrieval agent that performs multi-step search to find and rank supporting evidence chunks, independent of the answer-generation model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hard multi-step information retrieval over fixed corpora is challenging for standard retrievers, and current systems often entangle retrieval with answer generation, limiting modularity and reuse.

Method: They build an agentic retriever on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, training it on adversarially filtered synthetic multi-step search tasks. Training uses round-sliced supervised fine-tuning to teach stepwise search behavior, followed by GSPO optimization on a recall-based reward. At inference, the agent runs a bounded multi-round search via a search tool, then outputs ranked evidence chunks with short justifications.

Result: Across seven English and Russian benchmarks with gold evidence annotations, T-Search achieves 56.0 Recall@10 with a single rollout (14.4 points higher than its base model) and 61.3 Recall@10 with three fused rollouts, outperforming larger open models.

Conclusion: An agentic, tool-using retriever trained with synthetic tasks and recall-optimized policy learning can substantially improve hard multi-step search performance while remaining modular with respect to downstream answer generators; the authors also contribute open models, infrastructure, and new benchmarks including a challenging Russian dataset (TRuST).

Abstract: We present T-Search, an open-weight agentic retriever for hard multi-step search. Given a question and a search tool over a fixed corpus, it runs a bounded multi-round search and returns a ranked list of evidence chunks with short justifications, leaving answer generation to a downstream model, so backend and generator can be swapped without retraining. T-Search is built on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and trained on adversarially filtered synthetic search tasks with round-sliced supervised fine-tuning followed by GSPO on a recall reward. Averaged over seven English and Russian benchmarks with gold evidence annotations, it reaches 56.0 Recall@10 with one rollout, 14.4 points above its base, and 61.3 with three fused rollouts, outperforming larger open models. We release the model, harness, live demo, and three benchmarks, including TRuST, the first native-Russian hard-search benchmark.

</details>


### [141] [PlotGround: Grounding Plot Digitization in Real Scientific Figures and Their Source Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06825)
*Yaohui Zhang,Binxu Li,Haoyi Duan,Jiacheng Miao,Yixin Wang,Xinran Du,Chenyue Li,Shilong Liu,Kevin Wu,James Zou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents PlotGround, an automated pipeline and benchmark using real scientific figures and corresponding source data to evaluate how accurately models can digitize plots and recover quantitative values.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scientific plots encode key quantitative results, but these values are often inaccessible in machine-readable form. Existing digitization benchmarks mostly use synthetic data or narrow chart types, so we lack a realistic measure of how well current models can recover numbers from actual research figures.

Method: The authors build PlotGround, which automatically links real figures from bioRxiv preprints to their author-released source tables, detects which figure panels are reconstructable, and generates quantitative question–answer pairs grounded in the source data. They then curate PlotGround-1k, a human-verified subset with 1,119 questions from 1,066 papers, and evaluate 16 multimodal models on it under different relative error tolerances. They also compare performance when models are given figures versus original source tables, using a coding agent to query tables.

Result: On PlotGround-1k, the best multimodal model achieves 87.5% accuracy at a ±5% relative error tolerance. Reducing the tolerance to ±2% drops every model’s accuracy by 11–24 percentage points, exposing limitations in precise value extraction. When the same values are queried from source tables instead of figures, a coding agent’s accuracy increases from 90.0% to 97.4%, with a 72% reduction in cost.

Conclusion: PlotGround provides a realistic, scalable benchmark for assessing plot digitization from real scientific figures, revealing that current multimodal models are reasonably good at approximate visual reading but still struggle with precise quantitative recovery. Access to underlying source tables substantially improves accuracy and efficiency, underscoring the value of sharing machine-readable data alongside figures.

Abstract: Scientific figures often encode quantitative results that are not readily available in machine-readable form, making accurate plot digitization important for verifying and reusing published findings. Yet it remains unclear how accurately current models recover plotted values from real scientific figures, as existing benchmarks rely largely on synthetic charts or cover only a limited range of chart types. We introduce PlotGround, an automated pipeline for building plot digitization benchmarks from real scientific figures and their author-released source data. PlotGround maps figures to source tables, identifies reconstructable panels, and generates quantitative questions with source-grounded reference values. We use PlotGround to construct PlotGround-1k, a human-verified benchmark of 1,119 questions from 1,066 bioRxiv preprints. Across sixteen multimodal models, the best reaches 87.5% accuracy at a $\pm 5\%$ relative-error tolerance. Tightening the tolerance to $\pm 2\%$ lowers every model's accuracy by 11-24 percentage points, revealing a gap between approximate visual reading and precise quantitative recovery. PlotGround's paired figure-source structure lets us compare how accurately the same values are recovered from figures and from source tables. Providing source tables instead of figures raises a coding agent's accuracy from 90.0% to 97.4% while cutting cost by 72%.

</details>


### [142] [CLIFT: Conformal Self-Verification for Web Agent Training and Test-Time Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06829)
*Yifan Zhang,Yutong Dai,Viraj Prabhu,Zhiyuan Hu,Ran Xu,Zeyuan Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CLIFT is a conformal self-verification framework that converts expensive judge feedback into reusable supervision and test-time guidance for web agents, improving state-of-the-art performance on several web benchmarks without relying on external judges at deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing reinforcement learning for open-source web agents relies on weak or impractical supervision: sparse binary success rewards make credit assignment hard, and calling powerful LLM judges at each step is too costly and cannot be assumed available at test time. The authors want a scalable way to extract richer, fine-grained supervision from limited judge calls during training and then deploy agents that do not depend on external judges.

Method: The authors propose CLIFT, which uses conformal self-verification both during training and testing. During training, the agent generates natural-language answers to verification questions about its own trajectories. A Compositional Conformal Certifier compares these answers with a training-time judge conditioned on URLs, filters to those with agreement, and assigns signed trust weights via polarity-aware lift. These verifier-derived scores are blended into per-step rewards without reducing the original judge-based reward. At test time, the same certified question-answer bank is frozen and used for Conformal Trajectory Selection (CTS): the agent generates a greedy rollout plus diverse retries, the self-verifier summarizes each URL-specific trace, and a conservative majority-vote rule decides whether to replace the current best trajectory, all without external judges.

Result: On WebArena Infinity, CLIFT attains state-of-the-art performance among open-source web agents. On VisualWebArena, a verifier bank trained using an open model successfully transfers to guide GPT-5.5 at test time and achieves state-of-the-art results under the standard benchmark harness. On Online Mind2Web, the certified question bank, translated for the setting, improves a live-web agent in zero-shot mode, without any benchmark-specific agent training.

Conclusion: Conformal self-verification via CLIFT provides a practical mechanism to distill limited, costly judge feedback into both dense training signals and effective, judge-free test-time selection. This approach scales web agent performance, yields state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks, and demonstrates that reusable, certified self-verification can reduce reliance on frontier LLM judges during deployment.

Abstract: Open-source web agents are now strong enough to execute realistic browser tasks, but training them with reinforcement learning still depends on weak supervision: binary task success is too sparse for credit assignment, while frontier-language-model judges are too expensive to call at every step and cannot be assumed available at deployment. We introduce CLIFT, a training and test-time scaling method built around conformal self-verification. During training, the agent answers natural-language verification questions about its own rollouts; a Compositional Conformal Certifier keeps only question signals whose URL-conditional evidence agrees with a training-time judge, assigns signed trust weights through polarity-aware lift, and blends the resulting verifier score into per-step rewards in a way that never subtracts from the judge baseline. At test time, the same certified bank is frozen and reused as structured evidence for Conformal Trajectory Selection (CTS): the agent samples a greedy rollout and one or more diverse retries, the self-verifier summarises each URL trace, and a conservative majority-vote rule chooses whether to swap away from the current incumbent without calling any external judge. This single mechanism supports three settings. On WebArena Infinity, CLIFT achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source web agents. On VisualWebArena, a bank trained with the open model transfers to GPT-5.5 at test time and reaches state-of-the-art performance under the canonical harness. On Online Mind2Web, without training an agent on the benchmark, translating the certified question bank improves a live-web agent in zero-shot evaluation. Together these results position conformal self-verification as a way to turn costly judge feedback into a reusable training signal and a judge-free test-time scaling signal.

</details>


### [143] [MemPilot: Orchestrating On-Demand Multimodal Memory Curation for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06830)
*Haozhen Zhang,Haodong Yue,Quanyu Long,Jianzhu Bao,Qingyuan Liu,Tao Feng,Bohan Liu,Weida Liang,Wenya Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MemPilot is a flexible RL-trained framework that dynamically decides how to build and use memory for multimodal LLM agents, optimizing the trade-off between task performance, computation cost, and latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agent memory systems usually build and preprocess memory in a query-agnostic way, which can waste computation and lose details that may become important later. Recent adaptive methods move some work to runtime but are rigid, specialized for particular operations, and do not give fine-grained control over performance–cost–latency trade-offs. There is a need for a general mechanism that can flexibly orchestrate what memory to construct and how much computation to spend, conditioned on the current query and user preferences over multiple competing objectives.

Method: The authors propose MemPilot, a framework that uses a multi-step LLM policy trained via reinforcement learning to orchestrate on-demand memory curation. At each step, the policy can choose between (1) using existing query-agnostic memory or (2) triggering query-specific curation of raw multimodal interaction history using heterogeneous LLMs and vision-language models (VLMs). The policy jointly decides the amount of evidence to gather, the curation instructions to issue, which models to use, and whether to access visual information, thus allocating runtime computation at a fine grain. To train this policy under multiple competing objectives (performance, cost, latency), they adapt objective-wise advantage decoupling: they estimate the advantage for each objective separately and then aggregate. They also introduce prefix-based marginal utility estimation to assign credit at a finer granularity across the steps in a rollout, measuring how much each prefix of actions contributes to the final outcomes.

Result: On five multimodal agent-memory benchmarks, MemPilot achieves better trade-offs between performance, cost, and latency than baselines that are aware of such trade-offs but less flexible. When sweeping over different optimization preferences (e.g., emphasizing accuracy vs. cost vs. latency), MemPilot traces out broader Pareto frontiers, demonstrating its ability to adaptively manage memory and computation under diverse constraints.

Conclusion: MemPilot provides a general, RL-based orchestration layer for LLM agent memory that adaptively curates query-specific information from multimodal histories, instead of relying solely on static, query-agnostic memory. By jointly deciding retrieval, curation, model choice, and visual access and by training with decoupled multi-objective advantages plus fine-grained credit assignment, it achieves superior performance–cost–latency trade-offs on multimodal benchmarks. This suggests that dynamically controlled, preference-aware memory management is a promising direction for scaling practical LLM agents under resource constraints.

Abstract: Memory has become integral to the LLM agent ecosystem, supporting information retention and reuse across interactions. However, most existing agent memory systems construct memory in a query-agnostic manner, which can incur unnecessary preprocessing cost and discard details that later prove essential. Recent studies have begun shifting memory processing toward runtime adaptation, but typically specialize in particular operations or fixed processing schemes, leaving flexible control over performance, cost, and latency largely underexplored. To address this challenge, we present \textbf{MemPilot}, a flexible framework that orchestrates on-demand memory curation under different performance--cost--latency preferences. Specifically, we optimize a multi-step LLM policy via reinforcement learning to iteratively choose between retrieving from query-agnostic memory and delegating query-specific curation of raw multimodal history to heterogeneous LLMs and VLMs. The policy jointly controls evidence amount, curation instructions, model selection, and visual access, enabling fine-grained allocation of runtime computation. To optimize this policy under competing objectives, we adapt objective-wise advantage decoupling by separately estimating each objective's advantage before aggregation. Moreover, we introduce prefix-based marginal utility estimation for fine-grained credit assignment across multi-step rollouts. Experiments on five multimodal agent-memory benchmarks demonstrate favorable performance--cost--latency trade-offs across optimization preferences, with preference sweeps yielding broader frontiers than existing trade-off-aware baselines.

</details>


<div id='cs.AI'></div>

# cs.AI [[Back]](#toc)

### [144] [Training Numerical Intelligence via Auto-Diagnosis and Skill Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03872)
*Peter Chen,Wotao Yin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes ADSD, a framework that automatically diagnoses why numerical solvers perform poorly and then discovers and packages appropriate numerical methods into reusable skills, consistently boosting solver performance across multiple challenging domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI agents can generate scientific code, but they struggle to truly improve the underlying numerical algorithms. Execution feedback (like runtime, convergence, or error) shows that a solver is underperforming, but not why or how to fix it. Numerical algorithm design and debugging is still largely manual, trial-and-error, and domain-specific, limiting scalability and reuse. The authors want a principled way to connect performance failures to interpretable numerical diagnoses and then to systematic solver improvements that can generalize across tasks and domains.

Method: The authors introduce Auto-Diagnosis and Skill Discovery (ADSD), a diagnosis-first framework for solver self-improvement. ADSD first analyzes solver performance to identify specific numerical issues (e.g., stiffness, bad conditioning, inappropriate step sizes) and formulates them as explicit diagnoses. Guided by these diagnoses, it then searches for and selects suitable numerical techniques (methods, preconditioners, control strategies, etc.) and packages the resulting improvements as reusable solver skills. These skills can then be reapplied or composed in future problems, turning solver development into a repeatable loop of diagnosis, discovery, and implementation rather than ad hoc editing.

Result: Across four numerical problem classes—power flow equations, AC optimal power flow control, stiff ODEs, and heterogeneous diffusion PDEs—ADSD produces solvers with higher accuracy, robustness, and efficiency compared to their initial baselines. In particular, on the challenging GOC-500 power flow benchmark, ADSD achieves a roughly 71× reduction in mean solver error, and the discovered skills transfer well to new, unseen grid topologies and operating conditions, indicating strong generalization of the learned solver improvements.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that ADSD effectively bridges raw execution feedback and principled numerical algorithm design, enabling AI-driven solvers to self-diagnose and systematically improve. By packaging numerical insights as reusable skills, ADSD turns solver enhancement into a structured, reusable process rather than isolated trial-and-error, and demonstrates substantial, transferable gains across diverse numerical domains.

Abstract: AI agents are becoming increasingly capable of generating scientific code, but generating code is not the same as improving the algorithms behind it. For numerical solvers, execution feedback can expose poor performance, but rarely reveals its underlying cause and how to address it. We introduce Auto-Diagnosis and Skill Discovery (ADSD), a framework that links numerical diagnosis to reusable solver self-improvement. ADSD follows a diagnosis-first paradigm that first explains why a solver performs poorly, then uses this diagnosis to guide the discovery of appropriate numerical methods. The resulting knowledge is packaged into reusable solver skills, turning solver improvement from trial-and-error editing into a structured process of diagnosis, discovery, and implementation. Across four challenging numerical domains--power flow equation, AC optimal power flow control, stiff ordinary differential equations, and heterogeneous diffusion PDEs--ADSD consistently improves solver accuracy, robustness, and efficiency. On GOC-500 power flow, for example, ADSD reduces mean solver error by nearly $71\times$, with improvements further transferring to unseen grid topologies and operating regimes.

</details>


### [145] [REACT: Physically and Chemically Consistent Reconstruction of Marine Active Tracers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03888)
*Wenbin Dai,Hao Zheng,Shiyu Liang,Chaofan Sun,Xueying Zhang,Hanbo Huang,Xuan Gong,Yiran Zhang,Enhui Liao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes REACT, a physics-guided AI framework that reconstructs global sea surface pH more accurately and consistently by modeling conserved carbon inventories first, then decoding to pH under carbonate chemistry constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods to reconstruct global sea surface pH are either physically based but computationally expensive, or AI-based but designed mainly for passive tracers. pH is an active tracer linked to carbonate chemistry where dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) is the conserved quantity. Current AI reconstructions can achieve low pH errors while breaking key physical and chemical constraints like carbonate closure and conservation of total carbon. This limits their reliability for ocean acidification monitoring and carbon-cycle studies, motivating a new framework that remains efficient yet enforces carbon and carbonate consistency.

Method: The authors introduce REACT, a carbon-first reconstruction framework that separates (1) transport, (2) active correction, and (3) chemical decoding. First, a latent carbonate state—representing the conserved carbon inventory—is transported using a conservative advection–diffusion solver to respect physical conservation. Second, a source module accounts for non-conservative variations in the carbon cycle (e.g., biogeochemical sources and sinks) and corrects the transported latent state. Third, a chemical decoder maps the corrected carbonate state to sea surface pH while enforcing carbonate equilibrium constraints to maintain chemical consistency. This design treats pH as the prediction target but enforces consistency on the underlying DIC-based carbonate system.

Result: On simulation datasets, REACT outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, reducing normalized root mean square error (NRMSE) in reconstructed pH by 14.7% and lowering chemical consistency errors by 24.0%. Cross-temporal-scale experiments demonstrate that REACT is robust to error accumulation when moving from coarse to fine temporal resolutions. Ablation studies confirm that each architectural component—the conservative transport, source module, and chemical decoding with equilibrium constraints—contributes significantly to overall accuracy and consistency.

Conclusion: REACT effectively bridges the gap between efficient AI-based reconstruction and physically consistent carbon-cycle modeling for sea surface pH. By modeling the conserved carbonate inventory and applying chemically constrained decoding, it delivers more accurate and chemically consistent pH fields than existing methods. The framework appears robust across temporal scales and modular, suggesting potential extensibility to other active tracers and Earth system reconstruction tasks where underlying inventories differ from the target variable.

Abstract: Reconstructing global sea surface pH from sparse observations is critical for monitoring ocean acidification and understanding marine carbon cycling. Traditional assimilation and inverse models are physically grounded but costly for large-scale reconstruction. Recent black-box and physics-guided AI models improve efficiency, but are mainly designed for passive tracers, where the reconstructed variable is also the transported inventory. In contrast, pH is an active carbonate tracer: it is the prediction target, while dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) is the conserved carbon inventory. This mismatch can produce low pH error while violating carbonate closure and source-free carbon conservation. To address this, we introduce \textbf{REACT}, a carbon-first reconstruction framework that decouples transport, active correction, and chemical decoding. REACT transports a latent carbonate state with a conservative advection--diffusion solver, captures non-conservative carbon-cycle variations with a source module, decodes the corrected state into pH, and constrains the output through carbonate equilibrium. This design keeps pH as the target while enforcing consistency on the underlying carbon state. On simulation data, REACT reduces pH NRMSE by (14.7%) and chemical consistency error by (24.0%) over the best baseline. Cross-temporal-scale evaluations show robustness against error accumulation from coarse to fine temporal scales, and ablation studies validate the effectiveness of each component.

</details>


### [146] [Proxy Confidence: Auditing Black-Box LLM Agents with a Surrogate's Log-Probabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03894)
*Yikai Zhao,Saurabh Pandey,Pradeep Kumar Misra*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They use a cheaper open-weight model, run in parallel with a deployed LLM agent, to score the agent’s tool calls and detect likely errors in real time, enabling gating and feedback that significantly improve reliability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deployed LLM agents often make silent mistakes in tool calls and code: errors only appear after actions run. Existing APIs don’t expose token probabilities, self-reported confidence is weak, and resampling fails because frontier models respond almost deterministically. There is a need for a reliable, low-cost way to estimate call correctness without modifying the production model or its API.

Method: Run an open-weight surrogate model in parallel with the main LLM agent. Give it the same context, tool schema, and proposed tool call, then compute several log-probability-based ‘readouts’ over the call: (1) teacher-forcing likelihood of each argument value; (2) request-PMI style scores to normalize for base frequency; (3) a discriminative verdict that classifies the whole call as correct vs incorrect; and (4) competition among alternative tools to see if another tool would have been more likely. Use a principle for combining readouts: generative likelihood is used to pinpoint wrong arguments; the discriminative verdict flags holistically wrong calls; when the error type is unknown, use an ensemble of readouts as the default decision signal. This is all done without extra training or access to the frontier model’s internals and requires only one surrogate prefill per tool call.

Result: On challenging coding tasks, their surrogate-based confidence achieves AUROC 0.825 in detecting bad tool calls, whereas the main actor’s self-reported confidence is barely above chance at 0.598. Generative readouts improve AUROC by +0.07 to +0.28 over three different actor models. Compared to self-consistency (resampling), their method gains +0.14 to +0.19 AUROC for near-deterministic actors at a fraction (1/K) of the compute cost. Using the signal for deployment, a real-time gate that escalates the least trustworthy calls for review raises accepted-action accuracy by +0.05 to +0.30 at 50% coverage. When used as feedback to the agent (returning the tool result plus a confidence score), it significantly boosts end-to-end task success on live-execution benchmarks (+0.119 and +0.137, p ≤ 1e-4) and outperforms a random-value feedback control by +0.078 (p = 0.003).

Conclusion: A parallel open-weight surrogate model can recover strong uncertainty signals for LLM tool calls using only log-probability-based readouts, without any access to proprietary model internals or extra training. This signal is substantially better than the actor’s own confidence and than self-consistency, and it can be practically deployed to gate risky actions and provide adaptive feedback that improves downstream task success and reliability of LLM agents.

Abstract: A deployed LLM agent emits tool calls, queries, and code that can be silently wrong -- by the time the error surfaces, the action has run. Frontier chat APIs hide the model's token probabilities; the agent's stated confidence barely beats chance on the mistakes that matter; and resampling does not help, since frontier models are highly repetitive, reproducing the same call across samples.
  We recover the missing signal from a low-cost open-weight surrogate run in parallel. It reads the same context, schema, and proposed action as the agent, then scores the call from its own log-probabilities through a family of complementary readouts: teacher forcing and request-PMI weigh the likelihood of each argument value, a discriminative verdict judges the call as a whole, and tool-choice competition tests the function against its siblings. One principle says which to trust: a generative likelihood localizes wrong argument values, while the verdict catches holistically wrong calls. When the error type is unknown, an ensemble is the low-regret default. The readout is training-free, needs no access to the agent's internals, and costs one prefill pass alongside the tool call.
  On difficult coding tasks it reaches AUROC 0.825 where the actor's stated confidence is near chance (0.598), and the generative readouts beat it by +0.07 to +0.28 across three further actors. Against self-consistency it gains +0.14 to +0.19 on near-deterministic actors, at 1/K the cost. The signal drives two deployment modes: a real-time gate escalating the least-trustworthy calls for review (+0.05 to +0.30 accepted-action accuracy at 50% coverage), and confidence feedback, returning the tool result with the score so the agent adapts its next step -- lifting task success on live-execution benchmarks (+0.119 and +0.137, p <= 1e-4) and beating a random-value control where step errors are silent (+0.078, p = 0.003).

</details>


### [147] [SGAnalog: An End-to-End Circuit Benchmark from Open-Source Silicon Tapeouts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03934)
*Yueting Li,Weihang Ding*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They build a rigorous, open, process-tied benchmark from Tiny Tapeout analog IC designs to test whether ML models can (1) transcribe schematics to SPICE netlists and (2) size devices correctly, showing current models are far from reliable and that different tasks expose different abilities and policy limits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current analog IC benchmarks can’t clearly tell if models are (a) truly learning transferable circuit skills vs. memorizing examples, or (b) producing designs that actually work under specific manufacturing processes and test setups. The authors want a benchmark grounded in real, human-designed circuits, with clear provenance, process context, and simulation conditions, so they can study model generalization, training-cutoff effects, and realistic design performance.

Method: They collect 273 top-level analog designs from open-source Tiny Tapeout shuttles, freezing each at the exact commit used for fabrication.
