TL;DR: They introduce Spatial-SAE, a sparse autoencoder that explicitly models spatial dependencies between image patches, leading to better concept recovery and interpretability than standard SAEs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard sparse autoencoders used in mechanistic interpretability assume independence across spatial patches in vision models, which contradicts the strong spatial correlations present in natural images and their neural activations. This mismatch may limit how well learned dictionary atoms correspond to true, human-meaningful concepts. The authors want a framework that respects both the linear representation view of features and the spatial structure specific to vision.

Method: They refine the Linear Representation Hypothesis into the Markov-Field Linear Representation Hypothesis (MFLRH), which augments the usual linear feature assumptions with Markov/random-field style spatial dependencies between patches. Under this new prior, they derive Spatial-SAE as an amortized maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimator: a sparse autoencoder architecture and objective that incorporate the MFLRH spatial prior. They implement several Spatial-SAE variants and compare them to standard SAEs on both synthetic data with ground-truth concepts and real vision model activations (DINOv2).

Result: On synthetic benchmarks designed to test concept recovery, the four Spatial-SAE variants achieve an average 96% win rate over standard SAEs, meaning they more accurately recover the underlying ground-truth concepts. On real DINOv2 activations, Spatial-SAE yields dictionary atoms that are judged more interpretable, while the additional reconstruction error relative to standard SAEs is mainly confined to high spatial frequency components (fine details).

Conclusion: Incorporating spatial dependencies into the sparse autoencoder framework via the MFLRH leads to better alignment between learned features and human-interpretable visual concepts. Spatial-SAE demonstrates that respecting the spatial structure of vision data improves both synthetic concept recovery and practical interpretability of features in vision models, with only a limited reconstruction trade-off focused on high-frequency details.

Abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) decompose model activations into sparse combinations of interpretable dictionary atoms. Although SAEs are grounded in the Linear Representation Hypothesis (LRH), their objective smuggles in an additional prior: concepts across patches are treated as independent, an assumption clearly violated by natural images and by the activations they induce. We therefore specialize LRH to vision through the Markov-Field Linear Representation Hypothesis (MFLRH), which adds the missing spatial dependencies to the LRH assumptions. We thus propose Spatial-SAE as an amortized MAP estimator under the MFLRH. Spatial-SAE consistently outperforms standard SAEs in concept recovery and interpretability. Across four variants, it achieves a 96% average win rate on synthetic concept recovery and improves interpretability on DINOv2 activations, at a reconstruction cost concentrated in high spatial frequencies.

</details>


### [166] [CUAWright: A Minimal Unified Interface for Digital Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04116)
*Yadong Lu,Theodore Lee,Yifei Li,Lawrence Keunho Jang,Tianci Xue,Yu Su,Huan Sun,Ahmed Hassan Awadallah*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes CUAWright, a minimal terminal-based harness for computer-use agents that uses only bash commands and the filesystem, and shows it significantly outperforms GUI and hybrid interfaces on diverse digital and CAD benchmarks in both effectiveness and cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing computer-use agents rely on GUI- or desktop-based harnesses with fixed, human-engineered tools. As models’ coding and tool-building abilities improve, these static, GUI-native setups limit agents: they can’t directly programmatically manipulate system state or flexibly create and evolve tools. The authors want to test whether a minimal, fully programmable interface can unlock better performance and efficiency across a wide range of digital tasks.

Method: The authors design CUAWright, a lightweight (~3K LOC) terminal harness where the only action interface is bash commands and the main workspace is a filesystem. This lets agents script behavior, generate and execute code, create and manage tools as files, and structure their own context. They then evaluate CUAWright against GUI-native and hybrid CLI harnesses using powerful LLMs (e.g., GPT-5.5) on multiple benchmarks: OSWorld 2.0 (digital OS tasks), Online-Mind2Web (web tasks), Odysseys (long-horizon tasks), and CADGenBench/BenchCAD (CAD tasks that mix visual understanding with CLI operations). Metrics include success rate, partial reward, and estimated cost.

Result: On OSWorld 2.0, CUAWright achieves a 33.2% relative improvement in partial reward and a 37.5% reduction in estimated cost compared with the GPT-5.5 baseline using a published harness. On Online-Mind2Web, it improves success rate by 4.7% over a GUI-native harness, and by 44.0% on the long-horizon Odysseys benchmark. On CADGenBench and BenchCAD, CUAWright consistently beats other CLI-based harnesses using GPT-5.5 with relative gains of 8.1%–41.6% in performance metrics.

Conclusion: A minimal, terminal-centric harness that exposes a programmable bash interface and an evolvable filesystem workspace enables LLM agents to construct tools and operate on system state more effectively than GUI-native or hybrid interfaces. The experimental results across OS, web, long-horizon, and CAD benchmarks indicate that digital environments are much more programmable than conventional GUIs suggest, and that focusing on a simple terminal interface can yield substantial gains in both task performance and computational cost.

Abstract: The prevailing approach to computer-use agents couples a model with a domain-specific harness: a browser or desktop environment equipped with human engineered tools that are fixed before task execution. As models' coding capabilities improve, the GUI native and static harness prevents them from direct programmatic operation on system state, as well as flexible construction of tools. To this end, we introduce CUAWright, a minimal terminal harness of roughly 3K lines of code that uses bash commands as its sole action interface, and a file system as its evolvable space for dynamically creating tools and managing the context. We conduct comprehensive experiments across a wide range of digital tasks, and demonstrate that by giving the agent a minimal, programmable interface, it achieves substantially stronger results compared to their GUI or hybrid CLI interface across a wide range of tasks. On OSWorld 2.0, CUAWright delivers a 33.2% relative improvement in partial reward while reducing estimated cost by 37.5% compared with the published GPT-5.5 baseline. On Online-Mind2Web and the long horizon Odysseys benchmark, CUAWright substantially outperforms GUI native harness by 4.7% and 44.0% in success rate, respectively. Furthermore, we found the gains extend to CAD applications that require accurate visual understanding and CLI interaction: on CADGenBench and BenchCAD, our unified harness yields 8.1%-41.6% relative improvements over other CLI based harnesses with GPT-5.5. Together, these results suggest digital environments are far more programmable than their GUI interfaces imply, and a minimal terminal-focused harness is the key for better performance and efficiency.

</details>


### [167] [InvestigationWorlds: An Agentic Environment for Legal Investigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04129)
*Albert Yu Sun,Andrew Benard,Sil Hamilton,Anna Teresita A. Marcelo,Yong Jae Kim,Carl-Leander Henneking,Rundong Hu,Yuhong Wang,David Mimno,Bishan Yang,Igor Labutov*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An agent-based benchmark for legal reasoning where AI agents investigate real U.S. federal cases via summary judgment records and must recover the court’s adopted factual hypothesis among plausible alternatives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Legal reasoning systems are evaluated mostly on small, synthetic, or question-answer style datasets that do not reflect how lawyers actually reason with evidence and competing factual stories. Summary judgment motions in U.S. civil litigation create rich, evidence-backed records and a court-adopted factual hypothesis, but they have been underused in AI benchmarks. The authors want a realistic environment to test whether agentic systems can navigate large legal records, construct and revise hypotheses, and converge on the same factual conclusions as courts when multiple plausible narratives exist.

Method: The authors construct InvestigationWorlds, an agentic environment from real U.S. federal civil cases. For each case, they start from the summary judgment record obtained from PACER. They then run an attorney-validated generation pipeline that synthesizes additional, role-tagged documents (e.g., from different parties or witnesses) around the original record, increasing narrative richness while preserving legal fidelity. Each environment encodes several coherent factual hypotheses about what happened, but exactly one corresponds to the court-adopted hypothesis underlying the summary judgment ruling. AI agents operate in this environment by retrieving and reading evidence, forming and updating hypotheses, and ultimately committing to one factual explanation. Performance is measured by whether the agent’s final hypothesis matches the court’s adopted one and by analysis of its evidence retrieval behavior.

Result: On a benchmark of 100 InvestigationWorlds built from real cases, evaluated agents frequently choose incorrect factual hypotheses even when they successfully retrieve evidence that would support the correct one. This shows a disconnect between evidence access and correct hypothesis selection. Agents struggle most with discriminating the subtle evidentiary differences that separate the court-adopted hypothesis from alternative, still-coherent narratives.

Conclusion: InvestigationWorlds exposes significant weaknesses in current agentic legal reasoning systems: they can gather relevant documents but often fail at fine-grained evidentiary reasoning and hypothesis discrimination in realistic legal settings. The benchmark demonstrates that simply improving retrieval is not enough; methods must better model how courts weigh evidence to prefer one coherent factual story over others. This environment can serve as a challenging, legally grounded testbed for developing more reliable investigative and reasoning agents in law and other domains involving complex evidence and competing narratives.

Abstract: We introduce InvestigationWorlds, an agentic environment for legal investigation. We build on an underused artifact of U.S. civil litigation: the summary judgment motion. This motion relies upon a record composed of real evidence exhibits, and results in a court-adopted hypothesis that is treated as ground truth for the purposes of deciding the motion. Each environment is built from a real U.S. Federal Court case retrieved from Public Access to Court Electronic Records (PACER) and augmented by an attorney-validated generation pipeline that synthesizes role-tagged documents around the original record. The resulting corpus admits multiple coherent factual readings, only one of which matches the court-adopted hypothesis. Evaluating on 100 cases, we find agents often commit to incorrect hypotheses despite retrieving relevant evidence, struggling to distinguish the court-adopted hypothesis from alternative hypotheses.

</details>


### [168] [Auditing Pairwise Equivalence Judgments: Self-Critique Effects and Diversity Measurement in Multi-Agent Hypothesis Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04133)
*Ji Young Byun,Anthony Hu,Jesse Rogers,Roujia Wang,Manasa Kesapragada,Falgun Shah*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper evaluates how self-critique and different “equivalence” rules affect the measured diversity of LLM-generated scientific hypotheses, showing that diversity estimates are highly sensitive to how we define when two hypotheses describe the same mechanism.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems are used to generate scientific hypotheses, but we lack ground truth during generation. Researchers typically estimate both refinement effects and diversity by judging whether hypotheses are pairwise equivalent (i.e., same underlying mechanism). However, it is unclear (1) how much iterative self-critique actually changes mechanisms beyond normal randomness, and (2) how much the specific criterion for mechanism equivalence biases measurements of hypothesis diversity.

Method: Using four proprietary multi-agent LLM instances, the authors (a) fix initial hypotheses and rerun downstream workflows with different numbers of critique rounds (0, 1, 5), then compare resulting hypotheses using an LLM-as-a-judge to measure additional mechanism-level divergence beyond baseline run-to-run variability; and (b) compare three equivalence rules—TF–IDF similarity, dense embeddings, and an LLM-as-a-judge—on controlled hypothesis pairs that either preserve the underlying causal mechanism via wording/terminology changes or alter one causal component while holding the rest constant. They then quantify how each rule classifies pairs as same or different mechanisms under these controlled edits.

Result: (1) Adding one round of critique substantially changes mechanisms beyond run-to-run variability: moving from 0 to 1 critique round yields 34.5 percentage points extra mechanism-level divergence, while 1 to 5 rounds adds only 1.3 pp more, indicating sharply diminishing returns. (2) All three equivalence rules correctly treat meaning-preserving edits as the same mechanism. But when the initiating causal event is swapped, the LLM-judge identifies 83% of such pairs as different mechanisms, compared with 0% for TF–IDF and 8% for embeddings. Depending on how “same mechanism” is defined, the estimated proportion of different mechanisms in their setup ranges from 38% to 96%.

Conclusion: Pairwise mechanism-equivalence judgments are a methodological choice that substantially shapes evaluation outcomes in LLM-based hypothesis generation. Both the apparent impact of self-critique and the measured diversity of hypotheses depend heavily on how “same mechanism” is operationalized. LLM-based judges are far more sensitive to mechanistic changes than surface-text methods like TF–IDF or embeddings, implying that evaluations based solely on text similarity can severely under- or over-estimate diversity and refinement effects.

Abstract: Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to scientific discovery and hypothesis generation. Both the effect of refinement and the diversity of the delivered set are hard to interpret before experimental ground truth exists, and both are typically reported by deciding whether pairs of generated hypotheses describe the same underlying mechanism. We study two evaluation questions that rest on this pairwise equivalence judgment: (1) how much self-critique changes delivered hypotheses beyond run-to-run variability, and (2) how the equivalence rule used to group hypotheses affects measured diversity. Across four proprietary instances, we hold opening hypotheses fixed, rerun the downstream workflow with 0, 1, and 5 critique rounds, and score matched hypothesis pairs with an LLM-as-a-judge. Relative to matched same-depth reruns, moving from 0 to 1 round produces 34.5 percentage points (pp) of additional mechanism-level divergence, whereas 1 to 5 rounds adds 1.3 pp. We then compare three equivalence rules: term frequency--inverse document frequency (TF--IDF) similarity, dense embeddings, and the same LLM-as-a-judge. We construct controlled hypothesis pairs that either preserve the causal explanation through wording or biological-terminology changes, or replace one component of the causal chain while holding the rest fixed. All three rules are invariant to meaning-preserving edits, but when the initiating event is replaced, the LLM-as-a-judge identifies 83% of valid pairs as different mechanisms, versus 0% for TF--IDF and 8% for embeddings; varying only the rubric that defines same mechanism moves this figure from 38% to 96%. Together, these results show that pairwise equivalence judgments are a measurement choice: how mechanism equivalence is defined affects both the estimated effect of self-critique and the measured diversity of generated hypotheses.

</details>


### [169] [Agentic Cognitive Depth: Operational Criteria for Evaluating LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04168)
*Nijesh Upreti,Chris Sypherd,Vaishak Belle*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Defines a framework to evaluate agentic LLM systems via a multi-criteria cognitive depth profile, beyond simple task success.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agentic LLM work focuses on building systems with planning, memory, tools, and control flow, but evaluation typically stops at binary or scalar task success. There is no standardized way to analyze how and why an agent succeeds or fails along interpretable cognitive dimensions, nor to compare different architectures beyond end-to-end performance.

Method: The paper conceptualizes agentic LLM systems as LLM-in-the-loop architectures with planning, memory, tools, and control flow, and introduces the notion of agentic cognitive depth. It specifies five operational criteria—context sensitivity (C), temporal continuity (T), multimodal coordination (M), adaptive interaction (A), and metacognitive monitoring (Mc)—and for each provides operational proxies and trajectory perturbation procedures to test that capacity. It then connects these criteria to aspects of the agent’s world model and outlines how to extend existing benchmarks (GAIA, SWE-bench, WebArena, TRIP-Bench) with per-criterion diagnostics. It also discusses concrete mechanisms—symbolic verifiers, structured memories, planner coupling, and tool constraints—to engineer and probe these capabilities.

Result: The work delivers a formalized five-dimensional profile for characterizing the cognitive depth of agentic LLM runs, along with suggested measurable proxies and perturbation-based tests for each dimension. It shows, at least conceptually, how popular agent benchmarks can be augmented to report not only success/failure but also criterion-specific diagnostics, and it identifies practical architectural components that can improve and expose these abilities.

Conclusion: Agentic LLM systems should be evaluated using a richer, trajectory-level profile rather than only end-to-end task success. The proposed agentic cognitive depth framework—with criteria C, T, M, A, and Mc, plus associated diagnostics—offers a practical path to more interpretable and fine-grained assessments of agent capabilities and their underlying world models, and can be integrated into existing benchmarks and system designs.

Abstract: Agentic large language model (LLM) systems are commonly implemented as an LLM in a loop with Planning, Memory, Tools, and Control Flow. This application-focused view connects agentic LLM research with deployable systems and leaves open how such systems should be evaluated beyond end-to-end task success. Building on this view, we define agentic cognitive depth as a trajectory-level profile across five operational criteria. The profile contains context sensitivity ($C$), temporal continuity ($T$), multimodal coordination ($M$), adaptive interaction ($A$), and metacognitive monitoring ($Mc$). The first four criteria measure how well Control Flow, Memory, Tools, and Planning are used across a trajectory. The fifth measures whether the system monitors and regulates the full run. For each criterion, we give operational proxies and a perturbation procedure, then connect the profile to the agent's world model. We provide the structure needed to extend benchmarks such as GAIA, SWE-bench, WebArena, and TRIP-Bench with per-criterion diagnostics. Symbolic verifiers, structured memory, planner coupling, and tool constraints provide practical ways to build and test these capacities.

</details>


### [170] [SHarP: Saliency-based Pruning of Agent Harnesses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04178)
*Xinyi Gao,Qiucheng Wu,Kaizhi Qian,Handong Zhao,Shiyu Chang,Yang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces SHarP, a saliency-based pruning method to remove redundant modules in agent harnesses while preserving task performance and reducing token cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent harnesses for coordinating LLM tools and workflows become increasingly complex as they are iteratively patched and extended. This growing complexity likely introduces redundant modules that add token overhead without improving task performance. However, the extent of this redundancy and how to systematically simplify harnesses without degrading performance is unclear. The paper aims to better balance performance and efficiency by identifying and removing such redundancies.

Method: The authors conceptualize harness components—such as tools, instructions, and supporting mechanisms—as individually switchable modules. They propose SHarP (Saliency-based Harness Pruning), which estimates each module’s saliency by ablating it: they disable one module at a time and measure the change in task performance and token cost relative to the full system and to other single-module ablations. Modules that contribute the least to performance or incur disproportionate computational/token cost are marked as low-saliency and are pruned, yielding a simplified harness.

Result: Across multiple existing agent harnesses evaluated on held-out validation sets, SHarP reveals that many harnesses are highly redundant. A substantial fraction of modules can be removed while maintaining comparable task performance and efficiency. This demonstrates that harness complexity is often overgrown relative to its actual utility and that principled pruning can retain capabilities with fewer tokens and simpler configurations.

Conclusion: Harnesses used to orchestrate LLM agents often contain redundant modules that offer little marginal benefit but add token and computational overhead. By quantifying module saliency through ablation-based evaluation, SHarP can prune these low-value components and produce leaner harnesses with similar performance. The study suggests that systematic pruning should be part of the design and maintenance of agent harnesses, offering a new lens on how to optimize and streamline complex LLM-based systems.

Abstract: Agent harnesses are systems that coordinate model calls, tool use, and task execution to help large language models complete complex tasks. To meet task requirements and address failures, these systems are often iteratively refined by amending and patching their instructions, tools, and workflows, continuously increasing harness complexity. It is therefore unclear whether some resulting harness modules are redundant, introducing substantial token overhead with little, if any, performance gain. Inspired by neural network pruning, in this paper, we study harness pruning as a means of striking a better balance between task performance and token cost. We propose SHarP (Saliency-based Harness Pruning), a simple yet effective pruning strategy based on the saliency of each harness module with respect to performance and efficiency. Specifically, we first identify tools, instructions, and supporting mechanisms as components that can be individually disabled. We then estimate the saliency of each module by ablating it and assessing its task performance and token cost relative to the full set of single-module ablations. Modules with the smallest contribution to performance or largest computational overhead are subsequently pruned. Our evaluation across various harnesses on held-out validation sets reveals a surprising finding: most harnesses that we studied are highly redundant and can maintain comparable performance and efficiency even after a substantial portion of their modules are pruned. Our pruning approach and empirical findings provide new perspectives on agent harness design and optimization.

</details>


### [171] [Language Model Activations Inhabit Privileged Error-Correcting Basins](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04183)
*Matthew Finlayson,Francisco Pernice,Eric Todd,Amir Zur,Daniel Wurgaft,Fenil R. Doshi,Vasudev Shyam,Matt Feiszli,Satchel Grant,Lucius Bushnaq,Tal Haklay,Usha Bhalla,Matthew Kowal,Thomas Fel,Jack Merullo,Atticus Geiger,Xiang Ren,Owen Lewis,Ekdeep Singh Lubana*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies why language models remain coherent under activation perturbations, revealing that their activations lie in structured "attracting basins" in activation space, which can be exploited to better control model behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language models are surprisingly robust to interventions such as linear steering, continuing to generate coherent text even when internal activations are perturbed. The mechanisms behind this robustness and error-correction are not well understood. The authors want to understand the geometry of activation space and to see whether there are passive, structural dynamics in the forward pass that constrain activations to regions that support coherent behavior, and whether this structure can be used to interpret and more effectively steer language models.

Method: The authors probe the geometry of activation space by tracking how model layers act on low-dimensional curves embedded in activation space. They analyze the resulting trajectories to identify geometric structures such as attracting regions or basins. They compare natural model activations with distributionally similar synthetic activations to see how they differ geometrically. They then apply this geometric lens to language model steering: they examine steering along semantic directions, identify feature-specific basins along these directions, and experimentally test steering procedures that adaptively adjust steering strength to move activations across basin boundaries, especially for inter-language steering tasks.

Result: They find that language model activations cluster into distinct attracting basins in activation space, and that these basins separate natural activations from synthetic activations despite similar distributions. Along semantic steering directions, they observe feature-specific basins, with steering trajectories moving activations between basins. Using this understanding, they design an adaptive steering scheme that modulates the intervention strength to transport activations across basins. This adaptive scheme improves inter-language steering, significantly increasing the probability that the model generates tokens from the target language compared with fixed-strength steering methods.

Conclusion: Language models appear to have intrinsic geometric structure in their activation spaces, organized into attracting basins that support robust and coherent behavior. This structure underlies the models' robustness to activation perturbations and can be explicitly leveraged to design better steering interventions. Analyzing activation space geometry is thus a promising direction for both interpreting internal neural computations and improving fine-grained control over language model outputs.

Abstract: Language models exhibit remarkable robustness, continuing to produce coherent text even when their activations are perturbed by interventions like linear steering. We hypothesize that this robustness is a result of passive dynamics, i.e., constraining mechanisms in the forward pass that funnel activations toward "good" regions that produce coherent outputs. To investigate these hypothesized error-correcting mechanisms, we probe the geometry of language model activation space by observing the action of model layers on low-dimensional curves. In doing so, we discover that model activations occur within a cluster of distinct attracting basins, which differentiate natural activations geometrically from distributionally similar synthetic activations. Applying this lens to language model steering, we observe feature-specific basins along semantic steering directions, and find that steering moves activations between these basins. To demonstrate the active role of this geometry in neural computation, we show that adaptively modulating steering strength to transport activations across basins improves inter-language steering, significantly increasing the probability of sampling tokens from the target language compared to fixed-strength steering. Our findings establish analysis of activation space geometry as a promising approach to interpreting and controlling language models.

</details>


### [172] [EvalResearchBench: Can AI Agents Design Their Own Evaluations?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04184)
*Yaolun Zhang,Tianyi Xu,Yujie Zhao,Jishen Zhao,Qingyun Wu,Huazheng Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces EvalResearchBench (ERB), a benchmark to test whether AI agents can autonomously design effective evaluation suites for other AI systems under resource constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recursive self-improvement in AI needs frequent evaluation to guide progress, but running large, complex benchmark suites is expensive and slows iteration. Humans mitigate this by manually curating smaller, representative subsets, but this is labor-intensive and not scalable. The authors want to know if AI agents themselves can take over this evaluation-design role, automatically creating efficient yet reliable evaluators that approximate the behavior of established benchmarks while respecting practical time and budget limits.

Method: The authors create EvalResearchBench (ERB), a meta-benchmark where an AI agent (the “researcher”) receives: (1) target materials (benchmarks to approximate), (2) development references, (3) candidate APIs, and (4) fixed time and API budgets. Within these constraints, the agent must (a) select or synthesize tasks, (b) implement automatic graders, and (c) iteratively refine them using pilot runs, then finally “freeze” an executable evaluator. They instantiate and compare 9 different researcher setups and 13 candidate model backends. The frozen evaluators are then assessed by comparing their system rankings and pairwise model orderings against 14 established target benchmarks. Metrics include score correlations, pairwise agreement rates, and execution cost. They also compare against a human-designed sample of public tasks as a baseline and analyze qualitative behavior such as task/grade repairs and common failure modes.

Result: The best AI-designed evaluators achieve around 75% pairwise agreement with the target benchmarks’ model orderings, but this remains significantly below the 91% upper bound determined by disagreements among the targets themselves. No single researcher configuration dominates across all metrics: the evaluator that performs best on development benchmarks is not the best on held-out, sealed targets. A relatively simple, human-curated sample of public tasks remains a very competitive baseline. Interestingly, the evaluator with the lowest execution cost obtains the highest pairwise agreement, indicating that more expensive evaluation is not necessarily better. The agents do manage to repair some tasks and graders using feedback from pilot tests, yet important problems remain, such as truncated model responses, budget exhaustion, and high sensitivity of domain scores to a small number of questions.

Conclusion: AI agents can partially automate the design of evaluation suites for other AI models, constructing compact evaluators that approximate the behavior of large benchmark collections with moderate fidelity. However, current agents do not consistently outperform strong human-designed baselines, and there is no universally best researcher configuration across all metrics or target sets. The work demonstrates both the promise and limitations of automated evaluation research, highlighting that cost-efficient evaluators can be surprisingly strong while also suffering from brittleness, budget mismanagement, and sensitivity to individual items. EvalResearchBench is proposed as a platform to systematically study and improve autonomous evaluation-design agents, with the broader goal of supporting more scalable recursive self-improvement in AI systems.

Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) relies on evaluation feedback to assess progress and guide further research, yet repeatedly running complex benchmarks is costly and slows iteration. Human experts reduce this cost by selecting benchmark subsets or designing compact suites. We ask whether AI agents can automate this design process and introduce EvalResearchBench (ERB), a benchmark for autonomous evaluation research. Given target materials, development references, candidate APIs, and fixed time and API budgets, an agent called the researcher selects or synthesizes tasks, implements graders, and revises them in pilot tests before freezing an executable evaluator for coding, co-work, and reasoning. We study 9 researchers and 13 candidate models and compare each frozen evaluator with 14 target benchmarks on score concordance and pairwise agreement. The best evaluators order about 75\% of candidate pairs as the targets do, below the 91\% ceiling set by disagreements among the targets. No researcher leads on every metric, and the best evaluator on development targets is not the best on sealed targets hidden from the researcher. A human-designed sample of public tasks remains a strong baseline, and the evaluator with the lowest recorded execution cost attains the highest pairwise agreement. Agents repair tasks and graders through pilot feedback, yet their evaluators can still truncate answers, exhaust the evaluation budget, or let a few questions dominate a domain score.

</details>


### [173] [Agentic AI with Structured CoT for Enhancing AI's Spatial Intelligence: Visualization and Reasoning of Rotation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04188)
*Uttamasha Monjoree,Wei Yan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper evaluates how different Chain-of-Thought prompting strategies affect a generative vision-language model’s ability to reason about 3D object rotations, finding that structured CoT with contextual cues substantially boosts performance, while CoT alone has limited impact.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although modern vision-language AI systems are powerful, they still struggle with spatial reasoning, particularly 3D rotations. The authors aim to rigorously measure and improve this capability, because spatial reasoning is crucial for many real-world tasks but is underexplored compared to language-centric benchmarks.

Method: They adapt the Revised Purdue Spatial Visualization Test: Visualization of Rotations (PSVT:R) to create two datasets: the original and a version enriched with coordinate systems and contextual cues. Using these rotation diagrams, they evaluate an agentic generative model (GPT-5.6 VLM) under three prompting strategies: (1) Structured Chain-of-Thought (CoT), (2) few-shot Structured CoT, and (3) Structured CoT with a self-optimized prompt. Performance across conditions—with and without contextual information—is quantitatively compared.

Result: All three CoT prompting variants improve the model’s ability to solve 3D rotation problems relative to the base model, and they perform similarly to one another (no statistically significant differences). The largest gains occur when structured CoT is combined with added contextual/graphical information (e.g., coordinate systems). When those contextual aids are removed, CoT by itself yields only modest improvements, and substantial failure modes in spatial transformation understanding remain.

Conclusion: Structured reasoning alone is insufficient for strong spatial intelligence in current VLMs; substantial benefits arise when Chain-of-Thought prompting is integrated with carefully designed visual and textual context. Future agentic AI systems targeting spatial reasoning should tightly couple visual inputs, explicit contextual cues (like coordinate frames), and step-by-step reasoning mechanisms to achieve robust 3D spatial understanding.

Abstract: Recent studies show that artificial intelligence (AI) with language and vision capabilities still experiences limitations in spatial reasoning. In this paper, we have studied the spatial capabilities of advanced generative AI to understand the rotations of objects in 3D space, utilizing AI's image processing and language processing features. We trained and examined the spatial intelligence of a generative Agentic AI model (GPT-5.6) to understand the spatial rotation process with rotation diagrams based on the revised Purdue Spatial Visualization Test: Visualization of Rotations (Revised PSVT:R). We improvised the Revised PSVT:R by superimposing additional graphical and contextual features to evaluate how different Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning strategies influence model performance. The results indicate that structured CoT reasoning improves the spatial reasoning performance of the base GPT-5.6 model in both datasets (PSVT:R and PSVT:R with coordinate system). We used three CoT approaches - (1) Structured CoT, (2) few-shot Structured CoT, and Structured CoT with Self-optimized Prompt. The three CoT approaches evaluated in this study showed no significant performance difference. Results showed that combining structured CoT reasoning with relevant contextual information leads to considerable improvements in VLM performance on 3D rotation tasks, demonstrating the potential of agentic AI for more effective spatial reasoning. However, when contextual information is removed, structured CoT reasoning alone provides limited improvement, and the models continue to exhibit notable difficulties in understanding spatial transformations. These findings suggest that effective spatial reasoning in VLMs relies on the integration of visual, textual, and reasoning-based information in future agentic AI systems for spatial intelligence.

</details>


### [174] [MemLeak: Cross-User Semantic Leakage in Multi-Tenant AI Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04195)
*Priyanka Mudgal,Kai Zhao,Guilin Zhang,Andy Olsen,Ezekiel Miller,Xu Chu,Aletta Johanna Blanken*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper shows that sharing a vector store across multiple enterprise users causes serious cross-user memory leakage, and that only strict post-retrieval ownership checks reliably fix it with minimal latency cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise deployments often let many users’ personal AI agents share a common vector store for long-term memory to save cost and complexity. However, using a shared embedding space means that semantic similarity search may return another user’s data, even without any attack, creating a privacy and safety risk that is not well formalized or measured in current practice.

Method: The authors formalize cross-user admissibility failure—when retrieval returns memories not owned by the querying user—and run six experiments plus ablations on both sparse (TF-IDF) and dense (MiniLM-L6-v2, production-like) retrieval. They measure incidental leakage in pooled team settings, test adversarially crafted memories designed to be retrieved by others, and evaluate end-to-end response contamination through full LLM pipelines, comparing different architectural mitigations, including post-retrieval ownership gating.

Result: They find high rates of memory leakage: incidental non-adversarial leakage reaches 70–100% in pooled same-team retrieval; adversarial memories achieve 90–100% top-k ranking and large score lifts (+0.416 to +0.511) under dense retrieval. End-to-end, contaminated responses can reach perfect contamination scores (5.00/5) on a production retrieval stack and 4.67/5 with Claude Sonnet 4.5. Contaminated responses are often rated as equally or more helpful than clean ones, a result corroborated by human evaluations. Among tested mitigations, only strict hard post-retrieval ownership gating fully restores clean-baseline behavior (1.00/5 contamination) across two generation models, adding about 1.4 ms latency per query.

Conclusion: Shared vector stores in multi-tenant enterprise AI create a strong and often invisible privacy and safety vulnerability via cross-user memory leakage. Both incidental and adversarial leakage are frequent and impactful, and standard architectural choices do not reliably prevent it. The practical fix is to enforce strict post-retrieval ownership gating, which effectively eliminates leakage with negligible latency overhead, implying that multi-tenant systems should be redesigned to treat user ownership as a hard constraint on retrieval results.

Abstract: Personal AI agents in enterprise multi-tenant deployments share a common vector store for long-term memory. Shared embedding spaces create a surface for cross-user memory leakage: a user's query can retrieve semantically adjacent memories belonging to another user through ordinary cosine-similarity retrieval, without any exploit. We formalize this as cross-user admissibility failure and evaluate it across six experiments, plus follow-up ablations, under both sparse (TF-IDF) and production-faithful (MiniLM-L6-v2) retrieval. Non-adversarial, incidental leakage reaches 70--100\% under pooled {same-team} retrieval; adversarially crafted memories achieve 90--100\% top-$k$ placement, exceeding weaker keyword-based attacker baselines, with score lifts of $+0.416$ to $+0.511$ under production-faithful dense retrieval (Config B); and end-to-end response contamination reaches 5.00/5 under a production retrieval path and 4.67/5 with Claude Sonnet~4.5, with contaminated responses often scoring as helpful or more helpful than clean ones, a gap validated against human judgment. Among three architectural mitigations, only hard post-retrieval ownership gating consistently restores the clean baseline (1.00/5) across {two generation models, at a measured latency overhead of roughly 1.4~ms per query.

</details>


### [175] [Asynchronous Is Nearly Free for Evolution Strategies on Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04196)
*William Hoy,Jingxuan Fan,Nurcin Celik,Xu Pan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a bounded-staleness asynchronous evolution strategies (ES) method for long-horizon LLM agent post-training and shows it maintains performance close to synchronous ES despite delayed, stale trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM long-horizon agentic post-training is slowed by synchronous rollout generation where long, variable-length trajectories cause idle time and compute inefficiency. Asynchronous RL alleviates this but incurs policy lag and off-policy complications. ES is an appealing alternative because it avoids backpropagation and some RL complexities, but current ES-based post-training is typically synchronous and requires many rollouts. The authors want to enable efficient, asynchronous ES for LLM agents while understanding how much policy staleness ES can tolerate without major performance loss.

Method: They design a bounded-staleness asynchronous ES scheme where rollout workers generate trajectories under slightly outdated (stale) policies, and updates proceed without waiting for all workers, subject to a cap on how stale a trajectory can be. They compare a natural "Async-1" configuration against fully synchronous ES and also test controlled schedules where 10% of trajectories in each update cohort are delayed by four or eight policy updates, inducing controlled staleness. The approach is evaluated on the multi-turn Endless Terminals agentic coding benchmark using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and they compare against a GRPO-based RL baseline.

Result: On Endless Terminals, natural Async-1 achieves 25.9% held-out success, comparable to 25.4% for synchronous ES across three random seeds. When artificially inducing staleness—delaying 10% of trajectories by four or eight policy updates—held-out success drops only modestly by about 1.6 and 3.1 percentage points, respectively. GRPO outperforms ES overall, reaching 29.0% held-out success, but ES performance remains competitive and robust to moderate policy staleness, even without any explicit off-policy correction.

Conclusion: Asynchronous ES with bounded policy staleness can be effectively applied to long-horizon LLM agent post-training. ES tolerates moderate lag in policy updates with only limited performance degradation, suggesting it is a viable, scalable alternative to backpropagation-based RL methods for multi-turn agentic tasks. The work provides, to the authors’ knowledge, the first demonstration of both synchronous and asynchronous ES on a multi-turn terminal-based coding benchmark, and opens up avenues for more efficient ES-based asynchronous post-training algorithms for LLM agents.

Abstract: LLM-based long-horizon agentic post-training is often bottlenecked by rollout generation: trajectories span many interaction turns, completion times vary substantially, and synchronous update barriers leave faster workers waiting for stragglers. Asynchronous reinforcement learning which has been adopted in LLM post-training addresses this inefficiency by consuming trajectories as they arrive, but introduces policy lag and off-policy optimization. Evolution strategies (ES) offer a backpropagation-free alternative for LLM post-training, yet it relies on a larger number of rollouts and existing practices have remained largely synchronous. In this short-form paper, we introduce bounded-staleness asynchronous ES and demonstrate it on Endless Terminals benchmark using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Across three evaluation seeds, natural Async-1 matches synchronous ES, achieving 25.9\% versus 25.4\% held-out success. Controlled schedules that delay 10\% of each update cohort by four or eight policy updates reduce success by only 1.6 and 3.1 percentage points, respectively, without explicit off-policy correction. GRPO performs better overall, reaching 29.0\% held-out success, but importantly our results show that ES tolerates moderate policy staleness with limited degradation, opening possibilities for future improvement of ES-based post-training with asynchronous algorithms. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to demonstrate the effectiveness of sync and async ES on a multi-turn terminal style agentic coding task.

</details>


### [176] [ALoDLM: Adaptively Looped Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04198)
*Liancheng Fang,Zhuowei Li,Youngeun Kim,Tianchen Zhao,Rajat Koner,Jiaye Wu,Linghan Xu,Xuanbai Chen,Xiang Xu,Zheng Zhang,Jakub Zablocki,Nishant Sankaran,Yifan Xing*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes ALoDLM, a diffusion language model that adaptively allocates computation per token to close the quality gap with autoregressive models while preserving fast parallel decoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion language models can generate multiple tokens in parallel and thus are fast, but they underperform similarly sized autoregressive models in generation quality. The authors hypothesize this is due to using the same computation depth for all tokens, even though some tokens are easy and others are hard to predict within a partially observed sequence. They aim to address this computation-difficulty mismatch to improve quality without sacrificing efficiency.

Method: They introduce ALoDLM, which incorporates token-adaptive latent recurrence into diffusion language models. At each denoising step, the model iteratively refines latent token representations and dynamically decides per token how much further computation is needed. Tokens that are confidently predicted are "committed" and fed back as discrete context, while more uncertain tokens keep latent representations that are further refined via additional recurrent passes. The token-wise computation schedules are treated as latent variables, and training is based on a conditional negative evidence lower bound (NELBO) that jointly learns both prediction and computation allocation.

Result: ALoDLM is instantiated at 1.7B and 8B parameters and evaluated on eleven benchmarks. At both scales, it outperforms all other evaluated diffusion language models and also surpasses autoregressive baselines of comparable size in average benchmark score. It maintains fast, parallel decoding and performs well under optimized inference engines, demonstrating an improved quality-efficiency trade-off compared with both diffusion and autoregressive models.

Conclusion: Adaptive, token-level allocation of computation within diffusion language models can close and even reverse the quality gap with similarly sized autoregressive models while preserving the key advantage of fast parallel decoding. Modeling computation schedules as latent variables and training with a conditional NELBO enables effective joint learning of token prediction and compute allocation, yielding state-of-the-art quality-efficiency trade-offs among evaluated models.

Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable fast generation by predicting multiple tokens in parallel, but their practical adoption remains limited by a persistent quality gap relative to comparably sized autoregressive (AR) models. We attribute this gap to a computation-difficulty mismatch: within a partially observed sequence, some unknown tokens are easy to predict, while others require substantially more computation. Existing DLMs nevertheless apply uniform computational depth to all unknown positions at each denoising step. We introduce ALoDLM, which replaces uniform computation with token-adaptive latent recurrence. At each denoising step, ALoDLM iteratively refines latent representations and allocates computation according to token difficulty. Tokens ready to commit are fed back as discrete context, while unresolved tokens retain and further refine their latent states through additional recurrent passes. To learn token prediction and computation allocation jointly, we formulate token-wise computation schedules as latent variables and derive a conditional negative evidence lower bound (NELBO). We train ALoDLM at 1.7B and 8B parameter scales. Across eleven benchmarks, ALoDLM outperforms all evaluated DLMs and the corresponding AR baselines in average benchmark score at both scales. ALoDLM also retains fast parallel decoding, yielding a strong quality-efficiency trade-off among evaluated autoregressive and diffusion models under optimized inference engines.

</details>


### [177] [Fine-Tuning VLM for Enhancing AI's Spatial Intelligence: Understanding 3D and 2D Rotations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04206)
*Uttamasha Monjoree,Wei Yan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how well Vision-Language Models handle spatial rotation tasks and shows that fine-tuned Gemma-4 MoE models achieve better 2D and 3D rotation detection than generalist versions, especially in estimating rotation angles without explicit coordinates, with linear-featured objects helping more than identifiable ones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Spatial intelligence is crucial across STEM, medicine, architecture, and construction, but current Vision-Language Models still struggle with spatial reasoning. This gap limits AI’s ability to perform practical spatial tasks involving object rotations, so the authors aim to evaluate and improve VLM performance on such tasks.

Method: The authors use multiple object-rotation datasets designed for both training and evaluation. They fine-tune two variants of Google DeepMind’s Gemma-4 models—mixture-of-experts (MoE) models and generalist models—on tasks involving detecting 2D and 3D rotations. They then compare performance on predicting rotations specified by axes and angles, and analyze how object characteristics (identifiability and presence of linear features) affect angle estimation accuracy, including in 2D without explicit coordinate systems.

Result: Fine-tuned Gemma-4 MoE models outperform fine-tuned Gemma-4 generalist models at predicting rotations defined by axes and angles in both 2D and 3D. Fine-tuning substantially improves 2D angle estimation even without explicit coordinate systems. The experiments also show that using easily identifiable objects does not improve angle-detection accuracy, whereas objects with strong linear features yield better performance.

Conclusion: Targeted fine-tuning on rotation datasets can significantly enhance VLM spatial reasoning, particularly when using MoE architectures such as Gemma-4 MoE. Accurate 2D angle estimation is achievable without explicit coordinate systems, and object design matters: linear features are more beneficial than semantic identifiability for rotation detection. These findings point toward architectural and data-design strategies for building AI systems with stronger spatial intelligence.

Abstract: Spatial intelligence is a fundamental skill in multiple domains, such as Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM), Medicine, Architecture, and Construction. Recent studies indicate that Vision-Language Models (VLMs) still face limitations in spatial reasoning, which inhibits artificial intelligence (AI) from performing practical spatial tasks. Using multiple object-rotation datasets developed for training and evaluation, our experiments demonstrated promising improvements in both 2D and 3D rotation detection. Fine-tuned Google DeepMind-built Gemma-4 mixture-of-experts (MoE) models significantly outperformed fine-tuned Gemma-4 generalist models in predicting rotations defined by both their axes and angles. Fine-tuning also substantially improved angle estimation for 2D representation without requiring an explicit coordinate system. Furthermore, identifiable objects did not improve angle-detection accuracy; instead, objects with prominent linear features showed improved performance.

</details>


### [178] [TCMClinicalReason-Bench: Can Language Models Reason from Pathogenesis to Prescription over Real-World Clinical Cases?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04215)
*Jirui Dai,Chenkai Zhang,Yan Jia,Yukai Wang,Ruiyang He,Changyong Luo,Zhi Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces TCMClinicalReason-Bench, a benchmark to test whether LLM-generated traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) clinical reasoning is truly grounded in patient data rather than just fluent, and shows that while models output complete-looking answers, their evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic quality is only moderate, especially for prescriptions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs often produce plausible but insufficiently evidence-grounded clinical narratives, which is especially risky in traditional Chinese medicine where reasoning errors can cascade from etiology to prescriptions. Existing evaluations focus on fluency or final task accuracy and ignore whether each step and cross-step relation is supported by the case data. The authors aim to create a benchmark that can distinguish well-grounded, case-based TCM reasoning from unsupported yet fluent outputs, and to pinpoint where models fail so human clinicians know where oversight is most needed.

Method: The authors build TCMClinicalReason-Bench using 2,000 multicenter EHR TCM cases, defining an evidence-constrained rubric that evaluates seven within-block diagnostic and therapeutic components and three cross-block logical relations (e.g., between syndrome diagnosis and treatment principles). They allow multiple case-supported alternatives instead of single gold answers. Five general-purpose LLMs and two smaller TCM-specialized LLMs are evaluated in zero-shot mode. An automated judge based on Qwen3.7-Plus with TCM retrieval scores outputs, and its ratings are compared with blinded ratings from five senior TCM clinicians on a 600-case subset. Additional stress tests on 100 cases with deliberate perturbations assess how well the judge detects contradictions and omissions in cross-block relations.

Result: All models produced nearly fully structured outputs (99.3–100% structural completeness), but normalized content quality was modest, from 40.7% to 54.1%. General-purpose LLMs averaged about 50% content scores, outperforming the two smaller TCM-specific models at 41.3%. Cross-block logical consistency scores ranged 60.8–66.8% and showed moderate correlation with content quality (Pearson r = 0.515–0.656). The weakest areas were prescription generation, prescription analysis, and symptom-guided prescription modifications. In stress testing of the automated judge on 100 independent cases, detection of injected perturbations in the three cross-block relations was only partial (57%, 56%, and 31%), with contradictions recognized more reliably than omissions.

Conclusion: The benchmark reveals that LLMs can easily produce complete-looking TCM clinical reasoning chains that are only partially grounded in patient evidence, with especially poor reliability in the prescription-related steps. By separately scoring component-level quality and cross-block consistency, TCMClinicalReason-Bench can localize reasoning failures that standard endpoint or completeness metrics overlook and clarifies where clinician oversight remains essential. The automated judge is promising but still imperfect, particularly for detecting omissions, indicating a need for more robust evaluation tools alongside model improvements.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate clinical narratives that are insufficiently grounded in patient-specific evidence. In traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), errors can propagate from etiology and pathogenesis through syndrome diagnosis and treatment principles to prescription generation. We developed TCMClinicalReason-Bench using 2,000 multicenter electronic health record cases to distinguish case-grounded responses from fluent but unsupported diagnostic and therapeutic conclusions. Five general-purpose and two TCM-specific LLMs were evaluated in zero-shot settings. An evidence-constrained rubric assessed seven diagnostic and therapeutic components and three cross-block relations, allowing case-supported alternatives. Qwen3.7-Plus with TCM retrieval served as the automated judge, alongside parallel blinded ratings by five senior TCM clinicians on a 600-case subset. Structural completeness was nearly saturated (99.3-100.0%), but normalized content scores ranged from 40.7% to 54.1%. The five general-purpose models averaged 50.0%, versus 41.3% for the two smaller TCM-specific models. Cross-block logic consistency ranged from 60.8% to 66.8% and correlated moderately with content across cases (Pearson's r = 0.515-0.656). Deficits were greatest in prescription generation, prescription analysis, and symptom-guided modification. In judge stress testing on 100 independent cases, perturbation detection rates across the three relations were 57%, 56%, and 31%, with contradictions detected more reliably than omissions. Separating component quality from cross-block consistency localizes failures missed by endpoint and completeness metrics and identifies where clinician oversight remains necessary.

</details>


### [179] [On the Steering Dimensionality of Refusal in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04245)
*Han Wang,Erik Miehling,Dennis Wei,Karthikeyan Natesan Ramamurthy,Huan Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper examines how many activation directions (dimensions) are needed to reliably control different types of refusal behaviors in language models and shows that some refusals are simple (1D) to steer while others are much higher-dimensional.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most activation steering work assumes a high‑level behavior (like refusal) can be controlled via a single linear direction in activation space, with adding that vector inducing the behavior and ablating it suppressing the behavior. However, real model behaviors may occupy richer, multi‑directional geometries, and similar behaviors may correspond to distinct directions. The authors want to understand the true geometric complexity of refusal behaviors and how many directions are actually needed for reliable control.

Method: They generalize from single steering vectors to steering subspaces and define “steering dimensionality” as the minimum subspace dimension required for reliable behavior control. They construct and evaluate steering subspaces for two refusal types—alignment‑triggered refusal and general‑context refusal—measuring how performance improves as the dimension increases, and identifying when performance saturates to infer sufficient dimensionality.

Result: For refusals specifically triggered by safety alignment, they find that the behavior is effectively one‑dimensional: a 1D steering direction suffices to control it, though multiple distinct single directions can work similarly well. For refusals in broader, general contexts, the activation geometry is much richer: even 5‑dimensional steering subspaces do not reliably capture or control the full variation of this behavior, indicating a substantially higher intrinsic steering dimensionality.

Conclusion: Refusal behavior in language models is not uniformly captured by a single linear direction; its activation geometry is highly context‑dependent. Safety‑alignment‑triggered refusals are simple and approximately 1D steerable, but general‑context refusals are complex and high‑dimensional. This challenges the common assumption that high‑level behaviors can be steered via a single vector and suggests future steering methods should explicitly model multi‑dimensional subspaces for robust control.

Abstract: Existing activation steering methods often assume that a high-level concept can be mediated by a single steering direction. To support this, two complementary interventions should be achieved: additive steering should induce the target behavior, while directional ablation should suppress it. Yet behaviors may occupy richer activation geometries beyond a single direction, and semantically similar behaviors may be represented by distinct directions. In this work, we study how many directions can reliably control two different types of refusal behaviors: refusal triggered by the safety alignment and refusal in general contexts. Given the limited expressive capability of a single steering vector, we study the general setting of steering subspaces and introduce the notion of steering dimensionality as the minimum subspace dimensionality required to reliably control a behavior. We characterize sufficient steering subspaces that cover the full extent of the target behavior through both the (monotonic) improvement before the sufficient dimensionality, and the saturation beyond it. Empirically, we find that refusal triggered by safety alignment is 1-dim steerable, while multiple distinct steering directions can achieve comparable control. In contrast, refusal in general contexts exhibits substantially richer activation geometry where even 5-dim steering subspaces fail to reliably capture its full steerable variation. Our results reveal that the activation geometry underlying refusal is highly context-dependent and can be substantially more complex than a single linear steering direction.

</details>


### [180] [Spec2Game: Can LLMs Generate Complete Playable Games from Detailed Specifications?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04253)
*Yixue Cai,Yuzhe Zhao,Hanxiang Chao,Qingsen Ma,Ziheng Xiong,Jinhu Qi,Irwin King*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Spec2Game is a benchmark to test how well large language models can turn detailed natural-language game specs into fully working Pygame programs, showing that running code often still fails to follow the specified rules and goals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although LLMs can generate executable code, it often only superficially matches the intended behavior in the natural-language specification. Existing benchmarks typically use small functions or partial programs and do not fully test whether models can realize complex, interactive software with detailed rules and goals. The authors want a rigorous way to measure how well LLMs implement complete applications that must respect intricate specifications, here instantiated as video games.

Method: The authors build Spec2Game, a benchmark where models must generate full Pygame projects from natural-language specifications of games. The benchmark covers 15 game families and 150 tasks, with each family having one canonical game and nine systematic rule variants at three complexity levels. They generate code with 14 LLMs, yielding 3,330 projects, and evaluate them using multiple types of evidence (source code inspection, runtime behavior, visual output). The evaluation spans four dimensions: whether the code runs (Executability), how well it matches the specification (Specification Realization), software engineering aspects (Code Quality), and the end-user experience (User-Facing Quality). They also perform component-level analysis on different aspects of game implementation: game elements, rules and mechanisms, and goals/termination.

Result: Across all models and thousands of generated projects, many programs execute successfully but still fail to implement the specified behavior. Models are relatively strong at modeling game elements (objects, entities, basic interactions) but substantially weaker at implementing detailed rules and mechanisms or correctly handling win/lose conditions and termination logic. This shows a clear gap between syntactic correctness/executability and true adherence to natural-language specs.

Conclusion: Spec2Game exposes that current LLMs, while capable of producing runnable game code, struggle to faithfully realize detailed natural-language specifications, especially around rules and termination. Executability alone is an insufficient measure of success. The benchmark provides a structured way to diagnose where implementations break down and highlights the need for improved methods and evaluations focused on specification-faithful program synthesis.

Abstract: Generating an executable program does not necessarily mean that it correctly implements the behavioral requirements specified in natural language. To evaluate large language models' ability to realize detailed specifications as complete interactive programs, we introduce Spec2Game, a benchmark that requires models to generate complete Pygame projects from detailed natural-language game specifications. Spec2Game comprises 15 game families and 150 task instances, with one canonical task and nine controlled rule variants per family, spanning three levels of implementation complexity. Using source-code, runtime, and visual evidence, we evaluate generated projects along four dimensions---Executability, Specification Realization, Code Quality, and User-Facing Quality. Across 14 LLMs and 3,330 generated projects, we find that high executability does not imply faithful specification realization. Component-level analysis further shows that models perform substantially better on Game Element Modeling than on Rule and Mechanism Modeling or Goal and Termination Modeling, indicating that faithfully implementing game rules and termination logic remains a major challenge.

</details>


### [181] [CADForge: Agentic Single-View CAD Reconstruction with Explicit Geometry Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04262)
*Keyang Lu,Zhifei Yang,Tianao Dong,Mingzhe Xing,Zhen Xiao,Yikai Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes CADForge, an agent-based system that reconstructs editable parametric CAD models from a single image by generating CadQuery code with iterative refinement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-view images are cheap and common, but reconstructing full, editable parametric CAD models from them is hard due to missing 3D information and complex relationships between parts. Existing methods struggle to produce accurate, editable CAD suitable for manufacturing. The paper aims to bridge this gap.

Method: Introduce CADForge, an agentic framework that decomposes the object into CAD-meaningful components, explicitly reasons about each component’s geometry and constraints, converts these constraints into precise numerical parameters using mathematical code, and synthesizes corresponding CadQuery programs. A review agent evaluates the generated geometry, provides feedback, and iteratively refines the programs. The framework also has a failure-guided toolkit construction to turn recurring reasoning patterns into reusable tools, and maintains a compact parametric CAD memory to retrieve past modeling context.

Result: On various single-part and multi-part objects, CADForge shows higher reconstruction fidelity and better perceptual quality compared with previous baselines for single-view CAD reconstruction.

Conclusion: Agentic, component-wise reasoning combined with code-based parametric modeling, feedback-driven refinement, and experience distillation into tools and memory yields a more accurate and robust approach to reconstructing editable CAD models from a single image.

Abstract: Reconstructing editable parametric CAD models from a single-view image is of great practical value for modern manufacturing, yet remains challenging due to incomplete geometric observations and complex inter-part relationships. To address it, we propose CADForge, an agentic framework that progressively converts a single image into CadQuery programs. CADForge decomposes an object into CAD-meaningful components and performs explicit geometric reasoning for each component, a process that first identifies CAD-relevant constraints and then translates them into precise modeling parameters through mathematical code. The inferred parameters then drive component-wise synthesis of executable CadQuery programs, with a review agent evaluating the resulting geometry and providing targeted feedback for iterative refinement. To further improve robustness and efficiency, CADForge incorporates a failure-guided toolkit construction mechanism to distill accumulated experience into tools, and maintains a compact parametric CAD memory for retrieving modeling context on demand. Experiments on diverse single- and multi-part objects show that CADForge consistently outperforms existing baselines in reconstruction fidelity and perceptual quality, demonstrating an effective approach to accurate single-view CAD reconstruction.

</details>


### [182] [Dense Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning in a Unified Geometry State](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04280)
*Ruoran Xu,Wending Gao,Haoyu Cheng,Xiaoqiang Kang,Qiufeng Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents a neural-symbolic framework for stateful geometry reasoning that tightly couples neural guidance with symbolic execution, achieving strong performance across multiple geometry benchmarks and IMO problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Geometry problem solving involves iterative interaction between proposing constructions/theorems and performing exact symbolic deductions, which standard purely neural or purely symbolic systems struggle to model effectively and efficiently. The authors aim to create a unified, general-purpose geometric theorem prover/solver that can handle diverse geometry domains (plane, analytic, and solid) while leveraging large language models for guidance without sacrificing formal exactness.

Method: They introduce a densely coupled neural-symbolic architecture where a shared typed state is updated by both neural and symbolic components at each search step. Neural models propose executable actions—such as theorem instantiations, new constructions, and algebraic links—while a symbolic runtime executes these actions, propagates exact constraints, and tracks provenance. A nested controller allocates computation between neural and symbolic proposal sources and then selects among candidate actions. This framework is instantiated as OmniGeo, a single solver covering multiple geometric settings, powered by the Claude Sonnet 4.6 model for neural guidance.

Result: OmniGeo, using Claude Sonnet 4.6, achieves 94.2% accuracy on the FormalGeo7K plane geometry benchmark, 88.5% on the Conic10K analytic geometry benchmark, and 89.8% on the SolidFGeo solid geometry benchmark, yielding a 90.8% macro-average performance. Additionally, it solves 21 out of 30 challenging competition-style problems from the IMO-AG-30 set, demonstrating strong generalization and problem-solving capability.

Conclusion: Densely coupling neural guidance with symbolic geometric reasoning via a shared typed state and executable actions enables a single system to perform state-of-the-art, exact geometry reasoning across multiple domains. The OmniGeo instantiation shows that LLM-guided theorem proving can be made both powerful and general-purpose when integrated tightly with a symbolic engine, suggesting a promising direction for broader neural-symbolic reasoning systems.

Abstract: Geometry reasoning is naturally stateful: solving a problem repeatedly alternates between structural proposals and exact deductions. We formulate this process as dense neural-symbolic coupling, in which neural guidance and symbolic execution share a typed state and communicate through executable actions at every search step. Neural proposals contribute theorem instances, constructions, and algebraic bridges; the symbolic runtime applies registered rules, propagates exact constraints, and records provenance. A nested controller allocates computation first between neural and symbolic proposal sources and then among admitted actions. We instantiate the framework in OmniGeo, a single solver for plane, analytic, and solid geometry. With Claude Sonnet 4.6, OmniGeo reaches 94.2%, 88.5%, and 89.8% on FormalGeo7K, Conic10K, and SolidFGeo, respectively (90.8% macro average), and solves 21/30 IMO-AG-30 problems.

</details>


### [183] [VIGIL: Verifier-Informed Gated Improvement Loop for Spreadsheet Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04287)
*Kang Li,Lu He,Sandarsita Guntupalli*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes VIGIL, a method for safely and incrementally improving spreadsheet QA agents from delayed feedback without retraining the backbone model, and shows it yields consistent accuracy gains with bounded, auditable changes but also exposes limits of replay-based safety gates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise agents that answer questions over spreadsheets need to learn from user feedback over time, but letting every correction update the system risks destabilizing behavior or overfitting. The authors aim to design a continual-learning framework where an agent can improve using delayed labels while keeping core components fixed, changes auditable, and regressions minimized, especially for corpus-level spreadsheet question answering using SQL over workbooks.

Method: They build on FiCo, a static find-then-compute pipeline that retrieves tables and executes SQL. On top of that, they introduce VIGIL (Verifier-Informed Gated Improvement Loop). Within a single question, VIGIL generates diverse SQL candidates via prompting, then uses a verifier to check and repair these candidates. Across episodes (over time), when gold labels become available, only a contract calibrator and a query/result-column selector are updated; the base LLM, prompts, retriever, and the stored pool of candidate queries remain fixed. They test several variants: ungated, single-gated (accuracy-only), dual-gated (e.g., accuracy + stability/other criteria), and replay-based protocols that use a buffer to decide whether to promote an updated harness or retain the incumbent based on non-regression tests over past data and restricted training splits.

Result: On a main benchmark with access to the gold workbook and expected output type over 79 documents, the best full-replay variants achieve 82.4% (ungated) and 82.0% (dual-gated) forward accuracy, improving over a 75.8% static FiCo baseline. Retrospective gains are 2.3 points for the ungated and 2.7 points for the dual-gated variant, while the dual gate achieves a 6.3-point forward gain with a 95% t-interval of 5.6–6.9, indicating robust improvement. On a stricter split that withholds 16 documents and 380 questions from both fitting and online promotion decisions, an accuracy-only gate boosts mean held-out accuracy across ten final harnesses from 80.3% to 86.7%. Adapting only the calibrator yields a 5.9-point gain, close to the 6.4-point gain from using both calibrator and gate. However, 3 out of 26 gate-approved updates still reduce held-out accuracy compared to the previous version, showing that non-regression on the replay buffer does not guarantee non-regression on unseen data. Additional case studies on MiMoTable and other external tasks demonstrate effective within-task verification and reuse of the promote-or-retain discipline.

Conclusion: VIGIL enables enterprise spreadsheet QA agents to improve over time from delayed supervision while freezing core model components, providing bounded and auditable adaptation via calibrated scoring and promotion gates. The method yields substantial, statistically supported accuracy gains both in-distribution and under stricter held-out conditions, and highlights that finite replay buffers and non-regression gates, while helpful, are not sufficient to fully prevent regressions on unseen data. This underscores the need for careful design of continual learning harnesses and evaluation protocols when deploying such agents in real-world settings.

Abstract: Enterprise agents should improve from delayed feedback without allowing every correction to rewrite system behavior. We study continual harness learning for corpus-level spreadsheet question answering. Building on FiCo (Find-then-Compute), a static retrieval-and-execution backbone, we introduce VIGIL (Verifier-Informed Gated Improvement Loop). Within a question, VIGIL verifies and repairs diversely prompted Structured Query Language (SQL) candidates. Across episodes, delayed labels update only a contract calibrator and query/result-column selector. The base model, prompts, retriever, and recorded candidate pool remain fixed in the continual-learning protocol. With the gold workbook and expected type supplied, the ungated and dual-gated full-replay variants reach 82.4% and 82.0% forward accuracy over 79 documents, from a 75.8% static baseline. The dual gate has the larger retrospective gain (2.7 versus 2.3 points), and its 6.3-point forward gain has a 95% t-interval of 5.6-6.9. In a separate stricter split that excludes 16 documents and 380 questions from fitting and online promotion, the accuracy-only gate raises mean held-out accuracy across ten final harnesses from 80.3% to 86.7%. Calibrator-only adaptation gains 5.9 points, close to the combined 6.4-point gain. Yet three of 26 gate-approved updates reduce held-out accuracy relative to their incumbents, so replay-buffer non-regression does not imply held-out non-regression. MiMoTable and external-task case studies test within-task verification and reuse the same promote-or-retain discipline.
