Overall, the results support bounded, auditable harness adaptation while revealing where finite replay gates fail to generalize beyond their promotion buffers.

</details>


### [184] [LMBuild: Evaluating LLM Agents for Generating Buildable and Functional Structures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04292)
*Jiateng Liu,Rushi Wang,Cheng Qian,Xuejun Zhang,Sun Li,Jiayu Liu,Yifan Shen,Xu Cao,Jiarui Yao,Bingxuan Li,Ruhi Sarikaya,Heng Ji*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents LMBuild, a benchmark and interactive framework to evaluate LLM-based agents on generating 3D structures that are not only geometrically plausible but also physically buildable and functional.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLM-based agents can now generate complex 3D geometries, most evaluations focus on visual or geometric quality and ignore whether designs are structurally sound, buildable, and functionally operable in the real world. There is a need for a benchmark that explicitly measures physical realizability and functional affordance to guide progress toward practical design agents.

Method: The authors construct LMBuild, which: (1) represents generated objects as assembled structures with explicit parts, joints, materials, and assembly sequences; (2) provides an interactive environment where agents use tools to retrieve, create, and place components; (3) repurposes existing CAD datasets and enriches them with Wikipedia-derived knowledge; and (4) defines an evaluation protocol that scores structural soundness, functional affordance, design quality, and physical realizability. They test 30 different LLM-based systems within this unified setup.

Result: Across 30 systems, they find: (a) frontier closed-source models are generally sound and instruction-aligned, but still struggle with functional affordances and physical operability; (b) stronger models are better at inventing new components rather than just retrieving existing ones, a strategy more common in weaker models; and (c) providing explicit functional specifications significantly improves part completeness, kinematic correctness, and physical operability of designs.

Conclusion: LMBuild demonstrates that success in geometric generation does not guarantee real-world buildability or functional performance. The benchmark highlights remaining gaps in reasoning about mechanics, functional affordances, and novel component design, and is proposed as a standardized foundation to measure and accelerate progress toward agents capable of generating truly buildable, functional real-world structures.

Abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly capable of generating complex 3D structures, with the potential to reshape how objects are designed and realized in the physical world. Yet, producing elegant geometry is fundamentally different from producing objects that can be built and perform their intended functions. Existing evaluations largely focus on geometric quality while overlooking physical realizability. We introduce LMBuild, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on generating buildable and functional structures. LMBuild represents generated objects as assembled structures comprising part decompositions, joints, materials, and sequences. To support reproducible evaluation, we provide a unified framework consisting of: (1) an interactive environment in which agents can use tools to retrieve, create, and place components to construct objects; (2) a curated benchmark that repurposes established CAD datasets and augments them with knowledge from Wikipedia; and (3) a evaluation framework covering structural soundness, functional affordance, design quality, and physical realization. Evaluations across 30 systems reveal several intriguing findings: (a) Soundness and alignment are no longer the primary bottlenecks for frontier closed-source models, while functional affordance and physical operability remain substantially more challenging; (b) stronger models more effectively create new components, whereas weaker models tend to rely on retrieval; and (c) providing functional specifications substantially improves part completeness, kinematics, and physical operability. These results show that generating real-world structures requires deeper reasoning about functional affordances, mechanics, and designing and creating novel components. We expect LMBuild to provide a foundation for measuring progress and incentivizing research toward agents that generate buildable and functional structures.

</details>


### [185] [Language-Conditioned Token and Reasoning Efficiency in Large Language Models: A Paired Cross-Lingual Study Protocol](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04295)
*Genliang Zhu,Chu Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Prospective, highly controlled study design to disentangle language effects on LLM tokenization, trace cost, and answer realization, with no confirmatory results yet.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Comparisons of LLM behavior across languages often mix up three things: the language of the input, the language used for the model’s step-by-step reasoning trace, and the language used for the final answer. This conflation makes it difficult to understand where performance or cost differences between languages actually come from. The authors are motivated to design a rigorous, preregistered experimental protocol that cleanly separates these factors, enabling precise measurement of how language choice affects representation cost, inference cost, and answer quality without overinterpreting model traces or noisy energy proxies.

Method: They specify a prospective paired experimental protocol using 240 exactly scorable items generated from templates, rendered into English plus seven other languages. They test three open-weight LLM checkpoints from distinct model lineages, three different trace-token budgets, and 22 combinations of input-language and trace-language conditions, all while holding the underlying semantic task, model checkpoint, and answer oracle fixed. This yields 47,520 core runs before any sample-size adaptation. Research questions RQ1–RQ3 focus on estimating the effects of input and trace languages via intention-to-treat analysis with inclusive accounting of failures. For answer realization, they clone a sealed prefix and the model’s runtime KV state into eight branched continuations, allowing a controlled comparison of how answers are realized under different conditions. They enforce rigorous controls—independent language review, ASCII-only selectors, and consistency checks between code, surface instructions, and solver behavior—to reduce realization-test confounds. Hypotheses H1–H5 are tested within one Holm-corrected family plus a global simultaneous confidence band. A secondary randomized experiment compares two answer-generation policies—one long attempt vs. multiple short attempts (K-short)—given equal trace budgets, under frozen seeds and blinded aggregation, recognizing this as a full-policy contrast since answer capacity differs. They measure token spans, correctness, latency, runtime-reported memory, and constrained OS-reported energy usage on predefined hardware, while explicitly treating these as observable proxies rather than direct cognition or physical energy measurements.

Result: The abstract explicitly states that no confirmatory model outcomes are reported yet. All result fields are disabled until an evidence ledger, presumably containing raw and processed data and analysis code, passes independent verification. Thus, the current contribution is the detailed experimental protocol and analysis plan, not empirical findings.

Conclusion: The paper’s main contribution is a carefully specified, preregistered protocol for disentangling three cost components in multilingual LLM evaluation: tokenizer expansion cost (representation), observable trace-token cost (inference), and answer-realization cost. The design emphasizes strict separation of visible traces from assumptions about internal cognition and treats OS-level energy estimates as limited, system-specific proxies rather than physical cross-device energy measures. By doing so, the protocol aims to enable cleaner causal and statistical claims about how language choice affects LLM behavior and cost, while deferring any substantive conclusions about model performance until independently verified results become available.

Abstract: Large language models incur language-dependent representation and inference costs, but existing comparisons often conflate input language, assigned observable-trace language, and answer realization. We specify a prospective paired study that separates these interfaces while holding the semantic item, checkpoint, and answer oracle fixed. The initial design instantiates 240 exactly scored items rendered from templates in English and seven non-English languages, three distinct-lineage open-weight checkpoints, three trace-token budgets, 22 input- and trace-language conditions, a fixed answer reserve, and a separately counted delimiter: 47,520 initial core runs before prospective sample-size selection. RQ1-RQ3 estimate input and trace effects by intention-to-treat with failure-inclusive terminal accounting and test answer realization by cloning a sealed prefix and runtime-native KV state into eight crossed branches. Pre-freeze independent language review, fixed-form ASCII selectors, and code/surface/solver agreement constrain the realization test. H1-H5 share one Holm family and a global simultaneous component band. A secondary randomized experiment compares one-long-attempt and complete K-short-attempt policies at equal trace allowance under frozen seeds and oracle-blind aggregation; it is a full-policy contrast because answer capacity differs. Outcomes include exact token spans, correctness, latency, runtime-exposed memory, and qualified same-host operating-system-reported energy over prespecified hardware rails. The protocol separates tokenizer expansion, observable-trace cost, and answer-realization cost without treating visible traces as internal cognition or operating-system estimates as physical cross-device energy. No confirmatory model outcome is reported; result fields remain disabled until the frozen evidence ledger passes independent verification.

</details>


### [186] [EnvDreamer: Large-Scale Multimodal-to-Environment Generation for Embodied AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04301)
*Kabir Swain,Sijie Han,Antonio Torralba*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EnvDreamer is a framework that uses large language and vision-language models to generate rich Unreal Engine 5 environments for training and evaluating embodied AI and robots, releasing a 20k-environment dataset and showing competitive performance on multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite major advances in vision and language from large models and datasets, progress in embodied AI and robotics is limited by the difficulty of creating large, diverse, interactive environments with annotations and tasks at scale. There is a need for an automated, scalable way to generate realistic training environments and benchmarks for navigation, manipulation, and world modeling, as opposed to manually designed or small fixed simulators.

Method: The authors propose EnvDreamer, a system that leverages large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) to programmatically generate Unreal Engine 5 environments. The pipeline samples diverse, customizable scenes along with task programs, scene graphs, trajectories, and metadata, and uses validators to ensure environments meet specified constraints. EnvDreamer can also reconstruct simulation environments from images for real-to-sim transfer. They train simple baseline policies directly on these generated environments, without explicit mapping modules or hand-designed task supervision, and then evaluate on standard embodied AI benchmarks.

Result: EnvDreamer can automatically generate a large set of diverse, interactive, and validated Unreal Engine 5 environments, culminating in the EnvDreamer-20k dataset of 20,000 such environments with rich annotations. Policies trained purely on EnvDreamer-generated data obtain competitive performance on multiple embodied AI benchmarks covering navigation, rearrangement, and manipulation tasks, even without explicit mapping or human task supervision. The framework also demonstrates the ability to build simulation counterparts from real-world images for real-to-sim experiments.

Conclusion: Automated, LLM- and VLM-driven generation of rich 3D environments is a viable way to scale up data for embodied AI and robot learning. EnvDreamer offers a reusable platform and a large open dataset (EnvDreamer-20k) that enable more scalable training and more reproducible benchmarking across a range of embodied tasks, suggesting a path toward gains in embodied learning similar to those seen in vision and language.

Abstract: Large datasets and high capacity models have accelerated progress in vision and language. This work introduces a platform aimed at bringing comparable gains to embodied learning, world models, and robotics. We present EnvDreamer, a framework that uses large language and vision language models to generate Unreal Engine 5 environments for embodied AI and robot training. EnvDreamer enables sampling of large, diverse, interactive, customizable, and validator passed virtual environments for training and evaluation across navigation, interaction, and manipulation. We illustrate the platform with a large set of generated scenes and simple baselines. Policies trained on EnvDreamer generated environments, without explicit mapping or human task supervision, achieve competitive results on multiple embodied benchmarks spanning navigation, rearrangement, and manipulation. EnvDreamer also supports image-conditioned reconstruction for real-to-sim studies. Finally, we release EnvDreamer-20k, a dataset of 20,000 validator passed environments with task programs, scene graphs, trajectories, and metadata to support reproducible benchmarking.

</details>


### [187] [MOIRA: Mass-Oriented Indexing with Ragged Attention for Long-Context Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04313)
*Dich Nhat Minh Nguyen,Tran Dang Duong Nguyen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MOIRA is a training-free, adaptive sparse decoding method that adjusts KV cache page budgets per head and layer and uses a new self-planning attention kernel to keep execution inside CUDA graphs, achieving large speedups with near-dense accuracy on long contexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-context decoding in LLMs is bottlenecked by memory bandwidth because each generated token reads the full KV cache across all layers and heads. Existing sparse decoding either uses fixed budgets that are wasteful and workload-specific, or adaptive methods that incur extra selection overhead or require retraining. Kernel-level implementations like FlashAttention-3 and FlashInfer assume similar sequence lengths across rows, which clashes with per-head, per-layer sparsity patterns and leads to padding, load imbalance, or costly host-side planning that breaks CUDA graph execution. There is a need for a sparse decoding approach that is both highly adaptive and efficiently implementable on GPUs without retraining.

Method: The authors introduce MOIRA, a training-free sparse decoding path integrated into vLLM. For each request, layer, KV head, and decoding step, MOIRA applies a coverage rule to select the smallest set of KV cache pages whose estimated attention mass reaches a target fraction γ, effectively setting an adaptive per-head, per-layer page budget. They design a new GPU kernel called self-planning attention, where each thread block autonomously determines its work based on the length of its page list, avoiding padding and load imbalance. This design allows the entire sparse decoding process to run inside a CUDA graph, eliminating the need for host-side planning and preserving high GPU utilization.

Result: On an NVIDIA H200 GPU with the RULER benchmark at 128k context length, MOIRA with γ=0.99 achieves accuracy comparable to dense decoding while reading only about 30% of KV cache pages. This configuration reduces time per output token (TPOT) by 2.2–2.5× compared to dense FlashAttention-3. With γ=0.98, MOIRA attains a 2.7× TPOT reduction while the accuracy remains within measurement noise relative to dense decoding. Under high serving load, MOIRA improves throughput by up to 51%, demonstrating substantial practical gains in deployment scenarios.

Conclusion: Adaptive, per-head and per-layer KV cache budgeting, when coupled with a self-planning attention kernel that keeps execution inside CUDA graphs, can make sparse decoding both highly flexible and efficient. MOIRA delivers large speedups and throughput gains on long-context workloads while maintaining accuracy essentially on par with dense attention, and it does so without any model retraining.

Abstract: Long-context decoding is limited by memory bandwidth, because every output token reads the KV cache of every layer. Sparse decoding reduces this cost by reading only part of the KV cache. We observe that the number of pages a query needs varies widely across KV heads, layers and steps. Fixed budgets are simple, but they are sized for demanding cases and tuned per workload; adaptive budgets follow this variation more flexibly, but existing designs pay for it with extra selection cost or training. At the kernel level, FlashAttention-3 (FA3) and FlashInfer are designed for rows of similar length: with page lists whose length differs per KV head, they either pad the lists (forfeiting much of the sparse saving), leave thread blocks unbalanced, or rely on a host-side plan that runs outside the CUDA graph. We propose MOIRA, a training-free sparse decode path in vLLM whose budget adapts per KV head and per layer. For every request, layer, KV head and step, a coverage rule keeps the smallest set of pages whose estimated attention mass reaches a fraction $γ$. A new kernel, self-planning attention, lets each thread block derive its own share of the work from the list lengths, so the whole decode step stays inside the CUDA graph. On an H200, at RULER's 128k context, MOIRA with $γ=0.99$ matches dense accuracy while reading about 30% of the pages and reduces the time per output token (TPOT) by 2.2-2.5$\times$ relative to dense FA3; with $γ=0.98$ it reduces TPOT by 2.7$\times$ and stays within the noise of dense. Under high serving load it raises throughput by up to 51%. These results suggest that a budget adapted per head and layer, paired with a kernel that keeps such budgets inside the CUDA graph, makes sparse decoding both flexible and fast.

</details>


### [188] [From Latent Space to Jacobian Space: Measuring, Evading, and Training Against Safety-Content Accessibility](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04316)
*Mohammad Mosafer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how to monitor and understand the safety-relevant internal states of language models using Jacobian-based readouts, and shows that models can appear safe at the output level while remaining vulnerable internally.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing safety monitoring tools mostly look only at model outputs, even though the model has already formed an internal answer before emitting it. Prior work on Jacobian-space readouts suggested we can read safety-relevant signals in internal activations, but it was unclear how these relate to latent safety directions from representation engineering or how safety training modifies this relationship. The authors want quantitative tools to connect latent-space safety geometry with behaviorally observable internal content and to test whether current training and monitoring really secure what is internally accessible, not just visible in outputs.

Method: The authors use Jacobian-space (J-space) readouts that linearly map hidden states to the output vocabulary via the input-output Jacobian, then build two main tools: (i) a transport-amplification profile A_l that measures how strongly a given latent safety direction is transported toward the output space by each layer’s Jacobian; and (ii) a paired base-vs-tuned protocol to attribute which safety-relevant signals in J-space are due to the base model versus the safety-tuning. They run experiments on four small model pairs (135M–1.5B, multiple lens-fitting seeds), perform DPO-style safety fine-tuning, and analyze layer-wise recognition and refusal behavior. They then perform deployment-style red-teaming with monitor-aware GCG suffixes, re-attacks on monitors, training-time defense re-attacks, steering interventions guided by the amplification profile, and both continuous-prefix optimization and discrete search for adversarial prompts.

Result: They find that safety recognition measured in J-space tends to concentrate in upper-middle layers of tuned models. At the 0.5B scale, DPO training makes the model refuse unsafe outputs while J-space danger recognition drops to chance, demonstrating that training can increase the gap between internal accessibility and observable behavior exactly where apparent safety is strongest. In deployment audits, monitor-aware GCG-style suffixes can disable prompt-side monitors without degrading benign behavior across all scales, and only a learned monitor rung remains somewhat robust to its own adaptive re-attacks. Training-time defenses systematically fail under re-attack regardless of penalty weight. Steering experiments show that the transport-amplification profile describes where safety signals emerge but does not causally guarantee control, and continuous-prefix optimization fails to find some attacks that discrete search can uncover.

Conclusion: Output-only safety monitoring is insufficient because it can miss critical internal accessibility of unsafe content, which can be widened by safety training itself. J-space readouts and the proposed amplification profile and base-vs-tuned protocol reveal how safety directions move (or fail to move) toward the output space and how training can obscure rather than eliminate unsafe capabilities. Robust safety monitoring, training, and evaluation must explicitly target and measure accessibility in internal representations, not just final outputs, and defenses should be validated against adaptive, monitor-aware attacks that operate at the representation level.

Abstract: Output-only safety monitoring sees only the end of a model's computation, yet the model computes its answer before emitting it: what it is internally poised to say is safety-critical. Jacobian-space (J-space) readouts, linear maps from hidden states to the output vocabulary via the model's input-output Jacobian, have been proposed as a window on behaviorally accessible internal content, and a first safety protocol (JADR) showed that danger recognition is readable there. What remains unknown is how this accessible content relates to the latent-space safety geometry studied by representation engineering, and how safety training shapes it. We introduce two quantitative bridges: (i) a transport-amplification profile $A_\ell$, measuring how strongly a latent safety direction is carried toward output space by each layer's Jacobian, and (ii) a paired base-vs-tuned protocol that attributes accessibility to training provenance. Across four small model pairs (135M to 1.5B, three lens-fit seeds), tuned checkpoints concentrate recognition in upper-middle layers, and at 0.5B DPO installs refusal while J-space recognition drops to chance: training can widen the accessibility gap exactly where behavioral safety looks best. A deployment audit closes the loop: monitor-aware GCG-style suffixes suppress the prompt-side monitor at zero behavioral cost at every scale; only a learned monitor rung resists its own adaptive re-attack; the training-time defense fails its re-attack at every penalty weight; steering shows the amplification profile is descriptive, not causal; and continuous-prefix optimization fails where discrete search succeeds. Safety monitoring, training, and evaluation must operate on accessibility itself, not on outputs alone.

</details>


### [189] [Bidirectional Preference Synthesis: Learning Prompt-Conditioned Preferences from Boundary Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04328)
*Junbo Wang,Lidong Lu,Zhuoqun Li,Guiping Jiang,Xiangyu Wu,Tinghai Zhang,Tong Lu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Bidirectional Preference Synthesis (BPS), a data construction method that augments Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) with bidirectional preference pairs so that the same response is penalized where it violates the prompt and rewarded where it correctly fulfills a nearby intent, improving preference alignment on boundary failures without changing the DPO objective or requiring online sampling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing offline preference-learning pipelines, particularly correction-based ones for DPO, treat model failures only as rejected responses under the original prompt. This is insufficient for boundary failures, where a response is wrong for the given instruction but still coherently satisfies a related or nearby intent. Such cases lose valuable signal about what the model did correctly, and standard DPO data does not make prompt dependence explicit. The authors aim to better use these boundary failures to teach models when a response is appropriate by connecting them to alternative prompts that they actually satisfy.

Method: The authors introduce Bidirectional Preference Synthesis (BPS), a data construction method for standard DPO. For each validated boundary failure (a response that violates the original instruction yet achieves some nearby intent), they keep the conventional forward preference pair under the original prompt: (chosen = correct response, rejected = boundary-failure response). They then synthesize an “achieved prompt” that the boundary-failure response does satisfy, and construct a reverse pair under this new prompt where the boundary-failure response becomes the chosen output and some contrasting response becomes the rejected one. Thus, the same response appears as rejected under the original prompt and chosen under the achieved prompt. This is all done offline, without altering the DPO objective, training an explicit reward model, or using online sampling. They test BPS on Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and probe it using cross-teacher evaluations (e.g., Kimi-K2.6).

Result: On Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, BPS maintains pairwise ranking performance on the original prompts while dramatically improving accuracy on the achieved-prompt side: achieved-side ranking accuracy on held-out crossed anchors increases from 6.8% to 62.3%. A cross-teacher probe using Kimi-K2.6 shows a similar improvement trend, indicating robustness. A blind human audit confirms that the synthesized reverse preferences align with human judgments about when the boundary-failure responses are actually preferable. Downstream tasks show that, compared with standard Forward-DPO, BPS yields clearer gains on multilingual, multi-turn instruction following, while largely retaining capabilities on agentic behavior, tool use, and coding benchmarks.

Conclusion: BPS offers a practical way to exploit boundary failures by turning them into informative bidirectional preference pairs, explicitly tying responses to the prompts they genuinely satisfy. This improves preference alignment on nuanced instruction-following cases without modifying the standard DPO training objective, requiring a reward model, or relying on online data collection. The method scales to real models like Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and shows consistent benefits in both automatic and human evaluations, particularly for complex multilingual multi-turn interactions, while preserving broader capabilities.

Abstract: Correction-based offline preference pipelines commonly treat model failures only as rejected responses under the original prompt. This supervision is incomplete for boundary failures: responses that violate the given instruction yet coherently satisfy a nearby intent or constraint setting. We introduce Bidirectional Preference Synthesis (BPS), a data-construction method for standard Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) that makes this missing prompt dependence explicit. For each validated boundary failure, BPS keeps the conventional forward pair under the original prompt and adds a reverse pair under a synthesized achieved prompt, so the same response is rejected where it is wrong and chosen where it is right, without changing the DPO objective, training a reward model, or requiring online sampling. On Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, BPS preserves original-side pairwise ranking while raising achieved-side ranking accuracy from 6.8% to 62.3% on held-out crossed anchors, with a similar shift under a Kimi-K2.6 cross-teacher probe. A blind human audit supports the intended reverse preference direction, and downstream evaluations show the clearest separation from Forward-DPO in multilingual multi-turn instruction following, with consistent capability-retention patterns on agentic, tool-use, and code checks.

</details>


### [190] [Suppressing Pressure, Amplifying Evidence: Self-Guided Attention Steering to Mitigate Sycophancy and Stubbornness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04329)
*Yinghao He,Mengyu Xu,Haixiang Sun,Donghan Li,Yibo Wang,Lixu Wang,Kezhen Chen,Chi Li,Chunwei Liu,Bharat Bhargava,Chongyang Gao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces CoPE-Bench to jointly measure language-model sycophancy and contextual stubbornness, and proposes SPAE, an attention-steering method that reduces following unsupported user pressure while improving evidence-based updating.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations often test only one failure mode at a time: either sycophancy (overly agreeing with user pressure) or contextual stubbornness (ignoring new relevant evidence). This separation hides the trade-offs between resisting user pressure and updating on contextual information, and it is unclear whether improving one behavior worsens the other. The authors want a principled way to quantify both behaviors together and to design interventions that balance them without retraining models.

Method: The authors create CoPE-Bench, a benchmark where each question appears in six experimental conditions: (1) neutral baseline with no extra influence, (2) correct user pressure, (3) incorrect user pressure, (4) contextual information that supports the neutral answer, (5) contextual information that contradicts the neutral answer, and (6) a joint condition combining incorrect user claims with contextual information that conflicts with the neutral answer. They then propose SPAE (Suppressing Pressure, Amplifying Evidence), a training-free framework that uses the model’s internal judgments to identify which tokens correspond to user pressure and which to contextual evidence. SPAE modifies token-level attention weights—downweighting pressure tokens and upweighting evidence tokens—to steer the model’s reasoning at inference time without changing the underlying parameters. They evaluate SPAE on five different model backbones, in both single-turn and two-turn dialogue settings, and compare against prompting and other steering baselines.

Result: Across five backbone models, SPAE reduces the rate at which models follow user pressure by 18.8 percentage points and improves updating in the joint condition by 5.5 percentage points relative to the strongest baseline in the main comparison. In two-turn dialogues, SPAE further increases joint-condition updating by 13.2 percentage points over the strongest prompting baseline. These gains demonstrate that SPAE can simultaneously decrease sycophancy and improve evidence-based updating without retraining the model.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that it is possible to mitigate sycophancy and contextual stubbornness jointly rather than treating them in isolation. CoPE-Bench provides a structured way to expose the trade-off between resisting user pressure and responding to contextual evidence. SPAE, as a training-free attention-steering framework, effectively balances these objectives, improving robustness to misleading user pressure while enhancing responsiveness to relevant context. The authors release data and code to facilitate further research on aligned and context-sensitive language-model behavior.

Abstract: Reliable language models should resist unsupported user pressure while effectively using objective contextual information. However, models may exhibit sycophancy by yielding to unsupported user pressure or contextual stubbornness by failing to update their answers when relevant contextual information warrants revision. Evaluating interventions for these failures separately can obscure whether mitigating one failure exacerbates the other. To assess this trade-off, we introduce CoPE-Bench with six conditions per question: a neutral baseline, correct or incorrect user pressure, contextual information consistent with or conflicting with the neutral answer, and a joint condition combining incorrect claims with conflicting contextual information. To regulate the influence of user pressure and contextual information, we propose SPAE (Suppressing Pressure, Amplifying Evidence), a training-free framework that uses the model's own judgments to identify relevant tokens, suppressing user pressure and amplifying contextual information through token-level attention steering. On average across five backbones, SPAE reduces pressure following by 18.8 percentage points and increases joint-condition updating by 5.5 percentage points relative to the strongest baseline in the main comparison. In two-turn dialogue, it improves joint-condition updating by an average of 13.2 percentage points over the strongest prompting baseline. The source data and codes can be found at https://github.com/03Grant/sycophancy-and-stubbornness.

</details>


### [191] [ShadowMiner v1 - An Experience Report on Implementing and Measuring a Problem-and-Hypothesis Discovery Engine](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04339)
*Jinhyuk Choi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ShadowMiner v1 is a nine-stage system that builds a knowledge graph from AI papers, detects missing connections as potential research gaps, uses LLMs to generate hypotheses about those gaps, and then automatically checks that the hypotheses are novel, high quality, and factually grounded.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manually finding good, novel research problems in the rapidly growing AI literature is difficult and time-consuming. Prior work has suggested using knowledge graphs and LLMs to help, but it is unclear how well these ideas work in practice and which components actually add value. The paper is motivated by the need for a practical, end-to-end system that can systematically mine research gaps and hypotheses from existing AI papers and by the desire to empirically validate previously proposed techniques in a realistic pipeline.

Method: The authors implement ShadowMiner v1 as a nine-stage pipeline. First, it parses AI research papers and structures their contents into a knowledge graph. Second, it analyzes this graph to identify "graph gaps"—structural blind spots that correspond to missing connections or underexplored areas. Third, these gaps are encoded into prompts for a large language model, which generates candidate research hypotheses aimed at filling them. Fourth, the system performs automated verification on each hypothesis along three axes: (1) novelty checking, by searching whether similar ideas already exist in the literature; (2) quality scoring, to assess promise or usefulness; and (3) factual grounding checks, ensuring that the claims in the hypotheses are correctly derived from the underlying sources. The work focuses on implementing and integrating ideas from previous research into one pipeline and instrumenting it so that the contribution of each stage to overall performance can be measured.

Result: The system successfully runs end-to-end: it can build a knowledge graph from AI papers, detect graph gaps, generate hypotheses with an LLM conditioned on these gaps, and automatically filter and assess the generated hypotheses for novelty, quality, and factual correctness. The study yields empirical observations about which stages and design choices meaningfully improve the usefulness and reliability of the generated hypotheses, as opposed to those that contribute little. However, the report does not introduce new algorithms; its main results are implementation experience and measurements of component-wise contributions when applying existing methods in practice.

Conclusion: ShadowMiner v1 demonstrates that an end-to-end, automated pipeline for mining research problems and generating hypotheses from AI literature is feasible using existing techniques. By representing papers as a knowledge graph and targeting structural gaps within that graph, the system can focus LLM generation on potentially underexplored areas and then use automated checks to filter out non-novel, low-quality, or poorly grounded suggestions. The contribution lies in the practical implementation and systematic evaluation of previously proposed ideas, clarifying which components are effective in a realistic setting rather than in proposing new generation or evaluation methods.

Abstract: ShadowMiner v1 is a system that automatically discovers research problems and generates hypotheses from AI papers. It is a nine-stage pipeline. It structures documents into a knowledge graph and finds graph gaps in it - structural blind spots in research. These graph gaps are included in the LLM generation prompt. Each generated hypothesis is then verified by checking whether it is already covered by existing research, scoring its quality, and checking that the facts it relies on are accurately drawn from its sources. This report does not propose a new generation or evaluation technique. It describes our experience of implementing and applying ideas from prior work, and measuring whether each one actually contributed.

</details>


### [192] [Functionally Equivalent or Not? Graph-Grounded Differential Surrogate Execution for Code Equivalence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04371)
*Amit Kachroo,Like Hui,Haitao Mao,Yuhao Zhang,Nguyen Vo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents FEAgent, an auditable agent system for assessing functional equivalence between programs when direct execution is hard or impossible.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for checking program equivalence—tests, textual similarity, and unconstrained LLM judgments—are unreliable or non-auditable, especially when code depends on obsolete, unavailable, or unsafe environments. There is a need for a middle ground between lightweight testing and heavyweight formal verification that provides clearer evidence and acknowledges uncertainty.

Method: FEAgent operates as a selective equivalence assessor. It (1) aligns public interfaces and key behavioral graph anchors of the source and target programs; (2) issues bounded structural queries over program graphs (call-flow, control-flow, data-flow, type, import, and side-effect relations); (3) uses a branch-aware generator agent to propose inputs likely to distinguish behaviors; (4) employs two blinded LLM surrogate executors to independently predict observables for source and target on those inputs; (5) logs all claims and divergences in an evidence ledger; and (6) uses a deterministic reconciler that, based on the collected evidence, returns one of three labels: EQUIVALENT, INEQUIVALENT, or UNCLEAR, explicitly avoiding overconfident claims when evidence is insufficient or conflicting.

Result: Applied to function-level equivalence (EquiBench) and repository-level bug patches (SWE-bench Verified), FEAgent frequently disagrees with existing oracles (benchmark labels or passing test suites). When these disagreements are checked via direct execution, many turn out to be correct: on EquiBench, 216 of 1,200 pairs (18.0%) have mis-labeled equivalence; on SWE-bench Verified, 94 of 331 test-passing patches (28.4%) actually diverge from the reference patch’s behavior.

Conclusion: FEAgent provides an auditable, uncertainty-aware mechanism for assessing program functional equivalence that sits between traditional testing and full formal verification. It uncovers substantial errors in existing benchmarks and test-based evaluations, demonstrating that relying solely on tests or labels can mischaracterize equivalence. While it does not prove equivalence, it makes its reasoning and limitations explicit, offering a practical audit layer for modernization, patch validation, refactoring, and code-generation evaluation.

Abstract: Determining whether two programs are functionally equivalent is central to code modernization, patch validation, refactoring, and code-generation evaluation. Yet the usual signals are incomplete: tests cover only finite inputs, textual similarity confuses implementation with behavior, and unconstrained LLM judgments are difficult to audit. Direct execution is often impossible when a program depends on an obsolete, licensed, unavailable, or unsafe environment. We introduce FEAgent, a selective equivalence assessor agent that combines typed program-graph evidence with differential surrogate execution. FEAgent first aligns public interfaces and behaviorally relevant graph anchors, then issues bounded queries over call-flow, control-flow, data-flow, type, import, and effect relations. Next, a branch-aware generator agent proposes discriminating inputs, and two blinded LLM surrogates independently predict source and target observables. Every claim and predicted divergence is recorded in an evidence ledger. A deterministic reconciler then returns EQUIVALENT, INEQUIVALENT, or UNCLEAR rather than forcing a verdict when paths are uncovered or evidence conflicts. We evaluate FEAgent on function-level equivalence and repository-level bug patches, where the existing oracle is a benchmark label or a passing test suite. Every disagreement with that oracle is adjudicated by direct execution, revealing errors in benchmark labels and behavioral divergences missed by unit-test-only scoring. On EquiBench, execution confirms FEAgent's disagreements with published labels on 216 of 1,200 evaluated pairs (18.0%); on SWE-bench Verified, 94 of 331 test-passing agent patches (28.4%) diverge from the reference patch. FEAgent thus serves as an audit layer between testing and formal verification, keeping its evidence reviewable and its uncertainty explicit without claiming a proof of equivalence.

</details>


### [193] [Do Tool Calls Execute as Intended? Measuring and Repairing Intent-Execution Correspondence in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04375)
*Boyang Yang,Zhenhao Li,Ziyao Yang,Kanghui Jia,Xin Yin,Mingmou Liu,Haoye Tian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how intermediate components (“hops”) in LLM agent tool pipelines silently change tool calls, causing hidden bugs and mis-attributed failures, and proposes a protocol (IntAct) and benchmark (IEC-Bench) to detect, measure, and mitigate these issues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents rely heavily on tool calls (e.g., shell, code execution), which often pass through multiple middleware layers, harnesses, and wrappers. Any intermediate hop can silently transform the call in ways that break the tool’s contract (e.g., escaping, truncation, string mangling). Current benchmarks and failure analyses typically only compare the LLM’s emitted call with the final tool result, so they miss where and how the call was altered, falsely attributing many failures to the LLM itself. This undermines reliability, obscures real failure modes, wastes user resources (retries, extra tokens), and makes harness design and debugging difficult. The paper is motivated by the need to define and enforce a precise notion of correspondence between the LLM’s intended action and the actually executed tool call, and to empirically quantify the impact of path-induced call changes in real production settings.

Method: 1) Formalization: Introduce the concept of intent-execution correspondence (IEC), which requires that the executed action match the semantic intent of the tool call as emitted by the LLM, under a known tool contract.
2) Instrumentation protocol (IntAct): Develop a protocol that intercepts each hop in the tool-call path, records exactly what each hop receives (without executing the tool), parses calls with the receiver’s own parser, and identifies the first hop that changes the call relative to the original. It then either delivers the call in a representation that this hop cannot alter or refuses the call when safe delivery is not possible.
3) Benchmark construction (IEC-Bench): Build a benchmark from call transformations observed in real-world production usage. This benchmark includes realistic, chained, and dependent calls (e.g., shell commands) and runs them across execution paths using 4 widely-used harnesses.
4) Empirical evaluation: Analyze 47,828 shell calls from production sessions (including Claude Code’s Bash tool) and evaluate 10 different harnesses to measure rates and types of call changes, failure patterns, attribution errors, and cost inflation due to path issues. Evaluate IntAct’s effectiveness at recovering failures with altered calls in a commercial deployment.

Result: Key empirical findings: (1) In 47,828 real production shell calls, Claude Code’s Bash tool modifies 12.0% of calls that contain code, escape sequences, or long text, often via escaping or text rewriting. (2) For 80.7% of calls whose backslashes are altered, the wrong command executes successfully from the system’s perspective, so no explicit error is surfaced despite incorrect behavior. (3) All 10 evaluated harnesses modify at least some calls, indicating this is a systemic issue across tooling ecosystems. (4) Trajectory-based evaluation techniques, which look only at the LLM’s call and the final outcome, attribute 95.1% of observed production failures to the LLM, even though over half are actually induced by path or harness transformations. (5) On IEC-Bench, path-induced changes increase the token cost per successfully completed task by a factor of 2.4 on average, and up to 12.3x in the worst case. (6) Because a hop that changes a call also masks subsequent changes, 55.1% of failures on a path become visible only after the first problematic hop is repaired. (7) Deploying IntAct in a commercial product allows recovery of 79.2% of failures involving changed calls, demonstrating that enforcing IEC can substantially improve reliability and efficiency.

Conclusion: Tool-call paths for LLM agents are a major, under-recognized source of failures and inefficiencies: intermediate harnesses frequently and silently modify calls, breaking the intended semantics without surfacing errors and leading to widespread misattribution of failures to the LLM. The paper argues that correctness must be defined and enforced at the level of intent-execution correspondence, not just end-to-end success. IntAct shows that instrumenting and constraining each hop, and either delivering an unaltered, contract-respecting call or refusing it, can recover the majority of such failures in practice. As a result, agent and harness designers should adopt hop-by-hop design, testing, and benchmarking (e.g., using IEC-Bench) to ensure that once an LLM generates a correct call under the tool contract, the execution pipeline either carries it out faithfully or explicitly rejects it, rather than silently mutating it.

Abstract: Agents built on large language models (LLMs) build and run software through tool calls. A call reaches its program through several hops, and any hop can change the call without notice. When the changed call fails, the agent retries a correct call, which costs users time and money. Benchmarks and failure analyses do not see the change, because they read the call and its result but not what a hop received. We define intent-execution correspondence (IEC) as the property that the executed action matches the action the emitted call denotes under the tool contract. Our protocol observes what each hop received without executing the call, and names the first hop that changed it by the receiver's own parser. IntAct then delivers the call in a form that this hop cannot alter, or refuses the call. We build IEC-Bench from the changes observed in real-world use, with chains of dependent calls under the execution paths of 4 widely-used harnesses.
  In 47,828 shell calls within production sessions, Claude Code's Bash tool changes 12.0% of the calls that carry code, escape sequences, or long text. For 80.7% of the calls whose backslashes are changed, the wrong action runs without any reported error. All 10 measured harnesses change a call. Trajectory-based judgment attributes 95.1% of the production failures to the LLM, although the path caused more than half of them. On IEC-Bench, the path raises the token cost per passed task 2.4 times (up to 12.3 times). A hop that changes a call also hides the changes after it, so 55.1% of the failures on one path appear only after its first hop is repaired. IntAct, deployed in a commercial product, recovers 79.2% of the failures with a changed call. Harnesses should therefore be designed and tested hop-by-hop to ensure a correct call executes as intended or is refused.

</details>


### [194] [AgentPersonaBench: Benchmarking Persona-Driven User Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04379)
*Jintao Huang,Yifan Wang,Hongyu Shen,Yi Daniel Lu,Shirley Huang,Minsik Oh,Yewen Wang,Muhammad Ahmed Mohsin,Zhen Xu,Yilan Fan,Zichen Yuan,Ahsan Bilal,Zibu Wei,Sankalp Jajee,Henry Gagnier,Saksham Kapoor,Jicheng Wang,Qianfeng Wen,Yixuan He,Steven Dillmann,Jiashu He,Yucheng Lu,Linqiang Guo,Danyang Zhang,Shi Bo,Raunak Mondal,Haixiang Tang,Weihang Xiao,Allen Nie,Jing Tang,Yueying Li,Yifan Simon Liu,Jianheng Hou,Dianzhuo Wang,Qianyu Zhu,Zhixu Silvia Tao,Zhejian Peng,Zihan Wang,Ishan Gupta,Jinxuan Fan,Wanting Jiang,Shushu Liang,Chenxi Qiu,Yijun Wang,Xiaomin Li,Yuexing Hao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents AgentPersonaBench (APB), a benchmark to test whether persona conditioning reliably shapes agent behavior, focusing on observable actions rather than self-reports or style.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing persona benchmarks mainly evaluate how models describe themselves or adjust stylistic cues, not whether they actually behave in line with a persona across realistic tasks and environments. As language models are increasingly used as user simulators and agents, there is a need to rigorously measure true behavioral adherence to personas, especially at the trait level and across diverse interaction modalities.

Method: The authors design APB to test one latent trait at a time, embedding that trait into a full synthetic persona profile without explicitly naming it or revealing that it is under test. They then evaluate adherence based solely on observable actions over four increasingly realistic interaction surfaces: survey questions, chat interactions, interactive web environments, and desktop app environments. The benchmark contains 2,460 tasks covering 867 traits, and they validate ground-truth adherence with automated audits plus expert review. They then run a systematic evaluation of 20 frontier model variants under unprompted persona-conditioning conditions.

Result: Leading language models can achieve up to 84.7% full-pass adherence to the target persona trait when evaluated under unprompted conditions on APB. However, adherence rates drop when models must maintain behavior across multiple interaction modalities, with only 37.9–64.3% of cases passing on all four surfaces. Multi-attribute persona specifications further reduce behavioral retention, and different model families show notable divergence in how consistently they follow personas behaviorally.

Conclusion: Persona conditioning can already yield relatively high-fidelity behavioral control for single traits in certain settings, indicating strong potential for realistic user simulation with current LMs. Nonetheless, APB reveals limitations: behavioral adherence is fragile across modalities, becomes harder when multiple persona attributes must be maintained, and varies across model families. APB thus serves both as evidence of current capabilities and as a diagnostic tool to guide the development of more robust, behaviorally faithful persona-conditioned agents.

Abstract: We introduce AgentPersonaBench (APB), a benchmark evaluating whether persona conditioning faithfully steers downstream agent behavior. While language models are increasingly deployed for persona-driven user simulation, existing benchmarks primarily evaluate conversational styling or self-reports rather than authentic behavioral fidelity. APB evaluates latent persona adherence one trait at a time, embedding each target trait within a complete synthetic profile without explicitly naming the trait or disclosing the test. Ground-truth adherence is verified strictly from observable actions across four interaction surfaces of increasing realism: survey, chat, web (interactive web environments), and app (desktop software environments). APB comprises 2,460 tasks spanning 867 traits, verified through automated audits and expert review. Our evaluation of 20 frontier model arms demonstrates that high-fidelity user simulation is already attainable: leading models achieve up to 84.7% full-pass adherence under unprompted conditions. At the same time, APB identifies clear behavioral boundaries: adherence drops across interaction modalities (only 37.9-64.3% pass all four surfaces), multi-attribute demands degrade retention, and competing model families exhibit pronounced behavioral divergence.

</details>


### [195] [TrustMed-RL: Long-Horizon Reinforcement Learning for Evidence-Grounded Clinical Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04387)
*Wenxin Zhan,Yizheng Jiao,Haifeng Song,Shuai Xu,Chencheng Pan,Jiayi Feng,Anjie Xie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes TrustMed-RL, a vision-language medical diagnosis agent trained with reinforcement learning to be both accurate and evidence-grounded over long diagnostic trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing medical language models may output correct diagnoses but often rely on incomplete investigations and unsupported or hallucinated reasoning, making them unreliable for clinical decision-making. There is a need for systems that can perform long-horizon diagnostic reasoning, gather appropriate evidence (tests, imaging, consultations), and ground their conclusions in actual medical data, especially for complex and rare diseases.

Method: Construct a dataset from PubMed rare-disease case reports and over 24,000 manually annotated medical image panels. Formulate diagnosis as a sequential decision-making process that integrates patient interviews, physical examinations, diagnostic tests, specialist consultations, and literature searches via state-dependent actions. Train an 8B-parameter vision–language policy model with a clinically adapted GiGPO reinforcement learning algorithm and coverage-adjusted diagnostic reward signals to encourage both correct diagnoses and sufficient supporting evidence collection.

Result: On 2,500 evaluation cases, TrustMed-RL attains 37.1% diagnostic accuracy, beating all evaluated open-weight baselines and outperforming supervised fine-tuning by 12.4 percentage points. Under a stricter criterion requiring at least 50% of supporting test evidence to be obtained, it still achieves 32.5% accuracy, which is 6.8 percentage points higher than GPT-4o. It also outperforms all compared methods on MTMedDialog and surpasses multiple larger 27–32B models on the AgentClinic benchmark.

Conclusion: TrustMed-RL improves both diagnostic accuracy and evidential grounding compared to strong baselines, including larger and proprietary models. Physician review shows that most successful diagnostic trajectories receive high evidential-grounding scores (4–5/5), indicating alignment with human diagnostic reasoning and suggesting that the system’s diagnostic processes are comparatively trustworthy and clinically meaningful.

Abstract: Medical language models can produce correct diagnoses despite incomplete investigations and unsupported reasoning. To support long-horizon, evidence-grounded diagnosis, we introduce \textbf{TrustMed-RL}. Built from PubMed rare-disease cases and over 24,000 manually annotated image panels, it integrates interviews, examinations, testing, specialist consultation, and literature search through state-dependent actions. Our 8B vision--language policy, trained with clinically adapted GiGPO and coverage-adjusted diagnostic rewards, achieves 37.1\% diagnostic accuracy on 2,500 evaluation cases, outperforming all evaluated open-weight baselines and improving over supervised fine-tuning by 12.4 percentage points.. When success additionally requires acquiring at least 50\% of supporting test evidence, TrustMed-RL achieves 32.5\%, exceeding GPT-4o by 6.8 percentage points. Furthermore, it surpasses all evaluated baselines on MTMedDialog and multiple larger 27--32B models on AgentClinic. In physician review of 200 diagnostically accepted test-set trajectories, 83.0\% receive evidential-grounding scores of 4--5 out of 5. Physicians' assessments suggest that these diagnostic trajectories are trustworthy and aligned with human diagnostic reasoning.

</details>


### [196] [TimeNet: An Extensible Unified Data Infrastructure for Next-Generation Temporal Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04407)
*Martin Maritsch,Timo Stoffregen,Thomas Kaar,Behsad Riemer,Maxwell A. Xu,Max Rosenblattl,Juncheng Liu,Nicolas Zumarraga,Yu Yvonne Wu,Denys Herasymuk,Sparsh Rastogi,Hyungjun Yoon,Bosong Huang,Arvind Pillai,Dmytro Lopushanskyy,Tony Chen,Robin Deuber,Yichen Liu,Shvat Messica,Dan Li,Jian Lou,Yuwei Zhang,Jaeho Kim,Renée Rosillo Garcia,Fan Wu,Robert Müller,Elgar Fleisch,Flora D. Salim,Dimitris Spathis,Yuzhe Yang,Aaqib Saeed,Daniel McDuff,Ming Jin,Markus Kreft,Kevin O'Sullivan,Robert Jakob,Azul Garza,Paul Schmiedmayer,Patrick Langer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TimeNet is an open, unified data standard and infrastructure for temporal data that lets many different time-series datasets and tasks be represented and trained together for Temporal Foundation Models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Temporal Foundation Models currently suffer from fragmented, task-specific data formats, annotations, and pipelines that prevent easy combination of datasets and hinder generalization across domains and tasks. A common, scalable representation for temporal data and tasks is missing.

Method: The authors design TimeNet, an open-source data standard and infrastructure that decouples temporal signals from task definitions via a shared, extensible data model. TimeNet can represent multimodal signals with different types of time axes (regular, irregular, ordinal) and express diverse temporal task families (classification, forecasting, localization, QA, generation, editing) as reusable views over the same recordings. They transcode many existing datasets into TimeNet, measure I/O performance against native formats, and plug TimeNet into an existing TFM training pipeline to enable joint training over heterogeneous datasets through configuration alone.

Result: Using TimeNet, the authors convert datasets comprising 1.5M task instances from varied domains, modalities, temporal scales, and supervision types while maintaining practical I/O performance comparable to original data formats. They show that an existing TFM pipeline can now jointly train on multiple heterogeneous datasets simply by changing configuration, and that such joint training yields a 14% F1 improvement over training separate models on individual datasets.

Conclusion: TimeNet successfully provides a unified data and systems layer for temporal data, enabling scalable, cross-dataset, and cross-task training of Temporal Foundation Models. This shared temporal data model facilitates learning across heterogeneous domains and supervision types and represents a key step toward more general, broadly applicable temporal foundation models.

Abstract: Temporal Foundation Models (TFMs) aim to generalize across domains, datasets, and tasks. Yet, their development remains constrained by fragmented, task-specific data formats, annotations, and processing pipelines. We introduce TimeNet, an open-source data standard and scalable infrastructure that decouples temporal data from task definitions and represents signals, metadata, annotations, and supervision in a shared, extensible data model. TimeNet supports multimodal signals with regular, irregular, or ordinal time axes and expresses different task families (including classification, forecasting, temporal localization, question answering, generation, and editing) as reusable views over the same recordings. This shared representation enables heterogeneous time-series datasets to be combined for large-scale model training across domains, modalities, and tasks. We demonstrate TimeNet by transcoding datasets with 1.5M task instances spanning diverse domains, modalities, temporal scales, and forms of supervision, while retaining practical I/O performance relative to native formats. TimeNet enables an existing TFN training pipeline to support joint training on a configurable number of heterogeneous datasets through configuration changes alone. We show this capability by training TFM across multiple datasets and tasks, obtaining a 14% F1 score improvement compared with models trained on individual datasets. These results show that TimeNet provides the data and systems foundation needed to move beyond task- and dataset-specific TFMs toward models that can learn jointly across heterogeneous domains, modalities, temporal scales, and forms of supervision from a common data model.

</details>


### [197] [CORE-RL: Confidence-Oriented Reliability Evaluation of Black-Box Reinforcement Learning Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04418)
*Santhosh GS,Ananya Ravi,Devika Jay,Abhishek Sarkar,Perepu Satheesh Kumar,Saurav Prakash,Kaushik Dey,Balaraman Ravindran*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes CORE-RL, a pipeline to quantitatively evaluate the safety, reliability, and robustness of black-box RL policies under noise and environment changes using statistical confidence bounds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In safety-critical applications, RL agents must be checked for alignment with complex, multi-objective safety and performance requirements and robustness to real-world changes. Many deployed RL policies are available only as black-box executables or APIs, so existing evaluation methods that rely on access to policy internals cannot be used. There is a need for a principled, statistically grounded framework to evaluate and certify such black-box RL solutions under realistic disturbances.

Method: The paper introduces CORE-RL, a confidence-oriented evaluation pipeline for black-box RL policies. It defines a Unified Reliability Metric that jointly accounts for early episode termination and violations of safety constraints so that unsafe policies cannot appear successful by ending episodes prematurely. The framework then exposes the policy to a “noise certification envelope” including perceptual noise, actuation noise, and variations in environment dynamics. From rollouts under these perturbations, CORE-RL computes finite-sample Clopper–Pearson confidence intervals for the unified reliability metric and Hoeffding-based lower bounds for expected reward and safety cost. Based on these bounds, it identifies and reports a high-confidence safe Operational Design Domain (ODD) where the policy satisfies required safety and performance levels.

Result: On continuous control benchmarks, the CORE-RL pipeline automatically rejects policies that fail to meet safety and performance requirements and, for safety-aware policies, delineates the regions of the disturbance space (ODD) where they operate safely and reliably. This demonstrates that the method can effectively stress-test black-box RL agents and distinguish compliant from non-compliant ones.

Conclusion: CORE-RL offers a quantitative, transparent, and reproducible framework for evaluating black-box RL policies in terms of safety, reliability, and robustness. By integrating safety violations and early termination into a unified metric, subjecting agents to structured perturbations, and using statistically rigorous confidence bounds, it supports high-confidence certification of an RL agent’s safe operational domain and facilitates safer deployment and comparison of RL solutions in critical settings.

Abstract: The deployment of Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents in critical domains must be preceded with a pipeline to evaluate the alignment of the RL agent with complex multi-objective specifications and robustness under real-world environmental drift. However, to protect intellectual property, the RL agent may be delivered for evaluation as opaque executable or remote API, which makes traditional evaluation techniques based on the internals of the policies infeasible. To address this gap, CORE-RL: Confidence-Oriented Reliability Evaluation of black box RL policy is proposed in this paper. The CORE-RL pipeline introduces a Unified Reliability Metric that formally integrates early task termination and safety constraint violations, preventing unsafe policies from masking failures through premature episode halts. By subjecting the policy to a noise certification envelope of perceptual noise, actuation noise and change in environment dynamics, the pipeline computes the finite-sample Clopper-Pearson bounds on unified reliability metric and Hoeffdings' lower bound on reward and safety cost. The pipeline then defines safe operational design domain to report high-confidence certificates for safety and expected performance. Experiments on continuous control tasks demonstrate the CORE-RL pipeline's ability to automatically reject non-compliant policies and map the safe Operational Design Domain (ODD) of safety-aware policies. Thus CORE-RL provides an evaluation framework towards a quantitative, transparent and reproducible, statistical rationale necessary to safely evaluate, compare, and deploy black box RL solutions.

</details>


### [198] [Asking Earns Nothing: Scoring the Decision to Act in BFCL Multi-Turn](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04429)
*Yangze Liu,Zhongyi Han*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper shows that a popular multi‑turn agent benchmark (BFCL) structurally fails to reward agents for asking necessary questions, and instead rewards reckless action, so its leaderboard rankings misrepresent agents’ decision quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi‑turn agent benchmarks and leaderboards are supposed to evaluate whether an agent knows when to ask for missing information versus when to act. However, in BFCL multi‑turn, the scoring design for two of its four categories ignores the crucial "should ask" decision turn. As a result, agents can improve scores by acting without asking, contrary to the benchmark’s own task definitions. This misalignment between intended behavior and actual scoring can mis-rank models and incentivize unsafe or irrational behaviors in agents, so the authors aim to measure and expose this flaw and provide better diagnostics.

Method: The authors analyze the BFCL multi‑turn benchmark design, focusing on the two "should-ask" categories. They identify that on the key decision turn, the gold trajectory is empty, the checker ignores that turn, and the user simulator cannot answer, so asking yields no reward and guessing carries no direct penalty. They then construct a control condition already implicit in the benchmark: for each "should-ask" item, there exists a corresponding "base" item where the same request at the same turn index includes the missing information, so the agent should act instead of ask. Each such pair defines a clear decision: on that turn, should the model attempt a world‑changing call or hold back? They create a simple turn‑level scorer, independent of any LLM judge, that inspects stored trajectories and scores only whether the model attempted the world‑changing call at the decision turn across both members of the pair. They evaluate seven models, including gpt‑5.4 and gemma‑4‑31B‑it, on 223 such pairs. They also run prompt interventions: adding a line that discourages asking (for gpt‑5.4) or encourages asking first (for gemma‑4‑31B‑it) and measure both decision accuracy and the official BFCL scores under these variants. They manually verify and release a set of 31 flawed benchmark items, along with their pair list and the new scorer.

Result: For the 223 item pairs, gpt‑5.4 attempts the world‑changing call on 83.4% of the complete (base) turns and correctly refrains from acting, i.e., "holds back," on 78.0% of the incomplete (should‑ask) ones, yielding an 80.7% decision accuracy—the highest among seven evaluated models. Yet, on the same items, the official BFCL scoring ranks gpt‑5.4 only sixth, while the top‑ranked model performs substantially worse on this should‑ask/should‑act decision. Modifying gpt‑5.4’s prompt by adding a single line telling it not to ask shifts its behavior toward acting on both complete and incomplete turns; this leaves its pair‑wise decision accuracy essentially unchanged but increases its official BFCL score by 13.5–23.5 points in the two should‑ask categories and their base twins. Conversely, adding an opposite instruction to gemma‑4‑31B‑it—telling it to ask first—improves its decision accuracy by 4.5 points but does not raise its official BFCL score. In all cases, changes that push models toward more aggressive action are rewarded by the benchmark’s official score, while improvements in the core decision of when to ask versus act are not reflected in the leaderboard.

Conclusion: The BFCL multi‑turn benchmark, as currently scored, is mis‑aligned with its own task definitions for two categories that are supposed to test whether agents know when to ask for missing information. Because the critical decision turn is unscored and asking is unrewarded (or even harmful if repeated), the benchmark systematically incentivizes models to act without asking and can elevate models that make poorer ask‑vs‑act decisions. Leaderboard positions therefore do not reliably reflect decision quality or safety-relevant behavior. The authors argue that multi‑turn agent benchmarks must score the critical decision of whether to act or seek information, and they provide practical tools to do so: a publicly released set of item pairs, a turn‑level scorer that runs on any BFCL output folder without API access, and a list of 31 manually verified problematic items. They recommend revising BFCL and similar leaderboards so that agents are evaluated on aligned, decision‑sensitive metrics rather than on action‑biased scores.

Abstract: An agent that lacks the information it needs should ask rather than act, and the task definitions of agent leaderboards say so. BFCL multi-turn builds two of its four categories around a turn on which the model is supposed to ask, and its scorer never looks at that turn: the gold trajectory there is empty, the checker skips it, and the scripted user cannot answer, so asking earns nothing, guessing costs nothing on that turn, and asking twice loses the item. The benchmark also contains the control experiment for that decision. A should-ask item is a base item with one piece of information removed from one turn, so the same request appears twice at the same turn index, once complete and once not: on the first the model should make the call that changes the world, on the second it should ask. We score one decision per pair, whether the model attempted a world-changing call on that turn, read off the stored trajectories with no LLM judge; acting always and asking always both score 50. On the 223 pairs that pose this decision, gpt-5.4 attempts the call on 83.4% of the complete turns and holds back on 78.0% of the incomplete ones, the best decision accuracy of seven models at 80.7%; on the same items the official score ranks it sixth and puts first a model that lands in the middle here. One added line telling gpt-5.4 not to ask pushes it toward acting on both sides of the pair, so its decision accuracy shows no detectable change, while its official score rises by 13.5 to 23.5 points on the two should-ask categories and on the base twins; the opposite line, telling gemma-4-31B-it to ask first, improves its decision by 4.5 points and gains no official score. The score moves with the push toward action, not with the decision. We release the pairs, a turn-level scorer that runs on any BFCL output directory without an API key, and 31 manually verified bad items.

</details>


### [199] [MERCI Cards: An LLM Evaluation and Deployment Framework for High-Stakes Domains](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04430)
*Aparna Komarla,Annalisa Szymanski*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a formal, iterative framework (using weighted multi-objective optimization) to evaluate, choose, and repeatedly improve LLM-based systems in high-stakes applications, illustrated in criminal justice via MERCI Cards for guiding updates and user attention.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are moving into high-stakes, professional, and resource-constrained environments where ad-hoc, one-off benchmarks are insufficient. Engineers and researchers need structured, repeatable methods to track performance over time, compare models, align them with complex objectives (accuracy, fairness, cost, safety, etc.), and ensure each deployment cycle improves the system in a controlled way.

Method: The authors introduce a mathematical framework that models LLM deployment as an iterative, weighted multi-objective optimization problem spanning model selection, evaluation rubric design, evaluation execution, and deployment policies. They operationalize this via MERCI Cards, which seem to be structured artifacts or scorecards that encode objectives, metrics, weights, and evaluation results to steer both engineering decisions and user practices across deployment iterations.

Result: Applying this framework to AI systems in criminal justice, the authors show that MERCI Cards help: (1) identify and prioritize underperforming aspects of the system; (2) guide developers on where to focus improvements in subsequent deployment cycles; and (3) influence end-users to pay more attention to validating and correcting LLM outputs in areas of higher risk or uncertainty.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that iterative, formalized evaluation using a multi-objective optimization framework—instantiated via MERCI Cards—provides a principled way to integrate LLMs into high-stakes, high-risk, and resource-limited domains. This approach can make deployments more accountable and improvable over time by structuring how trade-offs are managed and how both developers and users adapt their behavior based on systematic evaluation feedback.

Abstract: As LLMs are increasingly deployed in high-stakes professional workflows, engineers and researchers require principled protocols to systematically track, monitor, and improve model performance across deployment cycles. We present a mathematical framework for iterative LLM evaluation and deployment, and demonstrate its application to AI systems used in criminal justice. Our framework formalizes LLM integration in high-stakes, high-risk, and resource-constrained domains across model selection, rubric design, evaluations and deployment via a weighted multi-objective optimization. We demonstrate that MERCI Cards can guide improvements of the system across deployment iterations, direct developer attention toward under-performing areas, and focus user attention on validation and error-correction in the LLM's outputs.

</details>


### [200] [What Does a Harness Buy? Tokens, Mostly](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04433)
*Yangze Liu,Zhongyi Han*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how much the “harness” (system prompt, tools, context management) affects coding benchmark scores and cost when the underlying model is fixed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many coding agents claim improvements from better harnesses, but benchmarks and leaderboards often mix different harnesses without quantifying how much the harness alone changes performance. This raises questions about the validity of reported gains and comparisons.

Method: The authors evaluate five language models with three production coding harnesses (Claude Code, mini-SWE-agent, OpenCode) on SWE-bench Verified. They run multiple trials to separate true harness effects from run-to-run variance, including a 447-task main set and a 45-task hard subset. They analyze success rates, task-level flips, and detailed cost breakdowns (prompt preambles, number of steps, tool calls, caching effects).

Result: On the large 447-task set, the best and worst of Claude Code and mini-SWE-agent are within about 5 percentage points, indicating small practical differences. On the 45-task hard subset with five models, changing the harness flips task outcomes about as often as simply rerunning the same harness (13%), and which tasks are won is unstable across runs. OpenCode consistently underperforms the other harnesses by up to 9 points, partly because an output cap truncates some runs. Cost per task, however, varies by up to 3× between harnesses, mainly due to large, repeated system/tool preambles and number of steps; caching prices scale overall cost but do not change the relative ranking.

Conclusion: For current coding agents on SWE-bench Verified, most harnesses do not reliably change success rates beyond run-to-run noise, except when they introduce clear limitations (like output caps). However, harness design strongly affects cost, often far more than it affects accuracy. Reliable harness comparisons require large task sets: around 45 tasks give weak power to detect a 13-point gap, and 447 tasks are needed to resolve about a 5-point difference. Many reported harness improvements on small benchmarks are therefore likely overstated or statistically underpowered.

Abstract: A coding agent is a language model wrapped in a harness: the system prompt, the tool set, and the context management that turn a chat model into something that can work inside a repository. Production harnesses ship releases daily, vendors advertise pass-rate gains from harness changes, and leaderboards mix harnesses freely. What is rarely measured is how much the harness itself moves the score when the model is held fixed. We run five models through three production harnesses, Claude Code, mini-SWE-agent, and OpenCode, on SWE-bench Verified, and rerun the same configurations to calibrate how much a score moves when nothing changes but the run. On 447 tasks and the two models we ran there, Claude Code and mini-SWE-agent, the heaviest and the lightest harness, are equivalent within five points.
