On a 45-task hard subset and five models, swapping the harness flips as many tasks as rerunning the same harness, 13% in both cases, and the tasks a harness wins in one run are not the tasks it wins in the next. The one harness effect that clears the noise is a loss, not a gain: OpenCode trails by up to 9 points on the large pool, and on one model half of that gap sits in runs its output cap cut short. What the harness does decide is the bill. With the same model, the same tasks, and one price list, cost per task differs by up to 3x across harnesses. The gap is set at the first call, by the preamble of system prompt and tool schemas each harness sends with every step, and scaled by the number of steps; per-step growth and per-call tool output differ far less. The provider's price for cached input scales the bill and does not reorder it. The rerun data also give the resolution a harness comparison needs: at the discordance we observe, 45 tasks catch a 13-point gap only half the time and no gap with 80% power, and 447 tasks resolve 5 points, still coarser than the gains many harness changes claim.

</details>


### [201] [CRAFT: An Agentic Spreadsheet Form Filling System with Template Awareness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04437)
*Leyao Gu,Yingjie Xiong,Zirui Tang,Jiangtao Zhou,Yeye He,Chunwei Liu,Xuanhe Zhou,Fan Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces CRAFT, a template-aware agent framework for robust spreadsheet form filling, and FormFillBench, a benchmark to evaluate it. CRAFT significantly improves accuracy over strong baselines by using reflective validation, structure-aware grounding, and constrained local repair of spreadsheet edits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Spreadsheet-based forms are widely used, but automated agents filling them must consolidate external evidence, align values to the correct cells, and respect irregular template structures. Early mistakes (like overwriting labels or misaligning fields) can cascade and corrupt the form, and existing reflection approaches often regenerate entire workbooks in a free-form way, which is unsafe for structured templates. There is a need for a framework that can detect and localize errors, repair corrupted template structure, and safely continue editing while respecting protected and writable regions. A standardized benchmark for this task has also been missing.

Method: The authors propose CRAFT, a template-aware agent framework that connects reflective validation with constrained local repair. The system first detects errors and grounds them to specific spreadsheet regions instead of regenerating the whole workbook. When template corruption is detected, it restores the template state and re-identifies (re-grounds) plausible writable slots before any further edits. A key component is the Rectangle-Aware Slot Grounder (RASG), which proposes candidate writable cells based on spreadsheet regions. Label-slot hints and protected regions are then used to constrain all subsequent edits so that only appropriate cells are modified. The framework is evaluated on a new benchmark, FormFillBench, and ablation (component-removal) experiments are conducted to test the contribution of structural adjudication and slot re-grounding. The authors also test CRAFT with a second model backbone to verify robustness of the relative gains.

Result: On FormFillBench, which contains 327 forms divided into Instruction-Only and Multi-File tracks, CRAFT substantially outperforms the strongest baseline systems. It improves pair accuracy by 8.51 percentage points on the Instruction-Only track and by 23.38 percentage points on the Multi-File track. Ablation experiments show that removing structural adjudication and slot re-grounding components degrades performance, supporting their importance. When evaluated with a second backbone model, CRAFT maintains its relative advantage over alternative methods, indicating that the framework’s benefits are not tied to a specific backbone.

Conclusion: CRAFT provides a robust, template-aware approach to spreadsheet form filling by tightly coupling error reflection with localized, structure-respecting repairs and slot re-grounding. Its design avoids unsafe full-workbook regeneration and effectively preserves complex template layouts while improving accuracy. The newly introduced FormFillBench benchmark facilitates standardized evaluation of form-filling agents. Overall, the results demonstrate that leveraging structural signals, explicit writable-slot grounding, and constrained editing leads to large and backbone-agnostic performance gains in automated spreadsheet form filling.

Abstract: Spreadsheet form filling requires agents to consolidate external evidence, ground values to precise cells, and preserve irregular template structure. Errors in early edits can overwrite labels or misalign fields, undermining later decisions. We propose CRAFT, a template-aware agent framework that connects reflective validation to constrained local repair. Instead of treating reflection as a free-form request to regenerate the workbook, CRAFT grounds detected errors to spreadsheet regions, restores corrupted template state when necessary, and re-grounds plausible writable slots before subsequent edits. A Rectangle-Aware Slot Grounder (RASG) proposes writable cells, while label-slot hints and protected regions constrain subsequent edits. We introduce FormFillBench, with 327 forms across Instruction-Only and Multi-File tracks. Compared with the strongest baselines, CRAFT improves pair accuracy by 8.51 and 23.38 percentage points on these tracks, respectively. Component-removal experiments support structural adjudication and slot re-grounding within the pipeline, and the framework retains its relative advantage among the methods evaluated with a second backbone. The code and benchmark FormFillBench are available at https://github.com/Glllllly/CRAFT.

</details>


### [202] [RAGrasp: Geometry-Semantic Template Retrieval and Grasp Transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04438)
*Shenzhe Zhu,Chengxiao He,Jan Harder*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RAGrasp is a retrieval-augmented pipeline that transfers grasps from locally collected RGB-D templates, avoiding end-to-end retraining while achieving high grasp success on seen and unseen objects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing grasping methods often rely on large public or synthetic datasets and need task-specific retraining for new deployments, which may not match local sensing, embodiment, or environmental conditions. There is a need for a grasping system that can adapt to a specific deployment with only a small set of locally collected examples, while remaining robust to viewpoint and illumination changes.

Method: RAGrasp builds a memory of grasp-annotated RGB-D templates collected in the target workspace with the actual deployment hardware. For a query scene, it uses self-supervised DINOv2 visual features plus appearance and depth cues to prompt SAM2 to segment the target object. It then performs a two-stage geometry-semantic retrieval to select the most relevant template. A confidence gate chooses between two alternative grasp-transfer estimators. The transferred grasp is refined by enforcing mask-support and silhouette-contact constraints, followed by calibrated 2D-to-3D conversion to obtain an executable grasp for planar parallel-jaw grippers.

Result: In real-world experiments, RAGrasp attained 20/20 successful grasps on objects seen in the template set and 19/20 on previously unseen objects, under varying viewpoints and lighting conditions, using only a compact set of local annotations without retraining a large model end-to-end.

Conclusion: RAGrasp shows that retrieval-augmented grasp transfer from a small, locally collected template set can provide deployment-specific adaptation and robust performance, reducing or eliminating the need for extensive retraining on large generic datasets while remaining effective on both seen and unseen objects in the evaluated setting.

Abstract: We present RAGrasp, a retrieval-augmented pipeline for planar parallel-jaw grasping from a compact set of locally collected, grasp-annotated RGB-D (color and depth) templates. Unlike task-specific predictors trained primarily on large public or synthetic grasp datasets, RAGrasp requires no end-to-end retraining for a new deployment.Its template memory is constructed from observations collected with the deployment camera, robot, and gripper in the target workspace, thereby aligning stored examples with the local sensing and embodiment conditions. The system uses self-supervised DINOv2 visual fea- tures together with appearance and depth cues to prompt the Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2), which isolates the query object. A two-stage geometry-semantic retrieval cascade then selects a template, and a confidence gate chooses one of two grasp- transfer estimators. The transferred grasp is refined using mask- support and silhouette-contact constraints before calibrated 2D- to-3D conversion. In real-world trials, RAGrasp achieves 20/20 successful grasps on seen objects and 19/20 on unseen objects. Within the evaluated setting, the results demonstrate deployment- specific grasp adaptation from limited local annotation and tolerance to the tested viewpoint and illumination changes.

</details>


### [203] [Causally Fair Generation with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04444)
*Patrik Okanovic,Torsten Hoefler,Drago Plecko*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a causal-inference-based framework (CFG) to measure and selectively remove unfair demographic disparities in LLM outputs while preserving necessary utility-related effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are used in high-stakes decisions, and their outputs can differ across demographic groups, potentially creating or amplifying unfair disparities. Existing fairness approaches are often purely statistical and cannot attribute disparities to underlying causal mechanisms, especially in complex LLM generation where multiple interdependent variables are produced and prompts do not follow simple causal or temporal order. There is a need for a principled, causal method to diagnose and correct unfairness in LLM generations, while allowing justified, utility-related differences to remain.

Method: The authors introduce Causally Fair Generation (CFG), a pipeline that (1) extracts task-relevant concepts from prompts and outputs, (2) anchors generation to a reference population and an explicit causal diagram, and (3) surgically removes user-specified causal effects that correspond to unfair or discriminatory pathways. CFG also supports preserving selected pathways that correspond to legally or practically justified differences, referred to as business necessity. They formalize the procedure with causal assumptions and derive guarantees about fairness when discriminatory causal effects are fully removed in the adapted population model. The framework is implemented on top of existing LLMs.

Result: CFG is applied to four different LLMs across three real-world applications derived from population data, as well as a synthetic dataset with known causal structure. Across these settings, CFG successfully adjusts generations to eliminate or reduce targeted unfair causal effects while preserving specified justifiable pathways. In the synthetic setting, results match the known causal ground truth, validating the method’s correctness under its assumptions. Empirical evaluations show that CFG can modify LLM outputs in ways consistent with formal causal fairness objectives.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates that causal inference can be effectively integrated with LLM generation to obtain finer-grained and principled control over fairness. CFG provides a way to interpret disparities in LLM outputs in terms of causal pathways, remove those deemed discriminatory, and retain those necessary for utility or legal compliance. Under suitable causal assumptions, CFG offers formal guarantees of eliminating discriminatory effects, suggesting a practical route for deploying LLMs in consequential domains with explicit fairness controls.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate, complete, and transform information in settings where their outputs can shape consequential decisions, raising concerns about their impact on demographic disparities. In this context, causal inference provides a principled basis for assessing fairness, because it attributes observed disparities to the mechanisms that generated them, which a purely statistical approach cannot do even with infinite data. In LLM generation, a query may request several causally related variables, each of which is both an outcome of interest and a possible cause of other outputs, and the information supplied in the prompt need not follow a topological or a temporal order. This calls for methods that can analyze and selectively remove disparities from such a flexible generation process. In this paper we introduce Causally Fair Generation with LLMs (CFG, for short). CFG extracts relevant concepts, grounds generation in a reference population and causal diagram, and removes user-selected causal effects. CFG also allows pathways deemed justifiable for the task's utility to be retained, which is known in legal literature as business necessity. Further, we provide formal guarantees for our method when eliminating all discriminatory causal effects in the adapted population model, under appropriate causal assumptions. We evaluate CFG with four LLMs in three real-world settings based on population data and on a synthetic dataset with a known causal ground truth.

</details>


### [204] [Understanding Generative AI Use in Programming MOOCs: The Role of Course Context and Learner Characteristics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04447)
*Marina Lepp*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Study of how learners use GenAI tools in two Estonian programming MOOCs of different length and intensity, finding widespread adoption, higher and more varied use in the longer course, and limited links to learning outcomes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: With GenAI tools like ChatGPT and code assistants rapidly entering educational practice, especially in open online courses with diverse learners, educators lack empirical evidence on who uses these tools, how often, and for what purposes, as well as whether learner background or course design matters more. This study aims to fill that gap in the context of programming MOOCs.

Method: The authors surveyed participants in two Estonian-language programming MOOCs that differed in duration, workload, topic complexity, and assignment volume. Post-course questionnaires captured self-reported GenAI adoption, usage frequency, and purposes of use. Non-parametric statistical analyses compared patterns of use across the two courses and across learner characteristics such as gender, age, education level, and prior programming experience. Exploratory analyses examined associations between GenAI use and learning-related outcomes.

Result: GenAI tools were widely adopted in both MOOCs, and adoption did not significantly differ by gender, age, education, or prior programming experience. Learners in the longer, more intensive course reported significantly higher frequency of GenAI use overall and were more likely to use GenAI for debugging and idea generation; they also reported higher frequencies of using GenAI for code explanation and debugging. Relationships between GenAI use and learning outcomes were weak and limited in the exploratory analyses.

Conclusion: Course context—such as length, workload, and complexity—appears to be more influential than learner demographic or background characteristics in shaping how GenAI tools are used in programming MOOCs. While GenAI adoption is broadly widespread, its specific uses (e.g., debugging, idea generation, explanation) scale with course demands rather than who the learners are. These findings point to the need for course-level instructional design and explicit guidance on productive GenAI use in programming education, rather than targeting particular learner subgroups.

Abstract: The increasing availability of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools, such as ChatGPT and code-completion assistants, raises questions about how learners integrate these tools into learning activities, particularly in MOOCs that attract diverse participant populations. This study examines the use of GenAI in two programming MOOCs taught in Estonian that differ in duration, workload, topic complexity, and assignment volume: About Programming (4 weeks, 26 expected hours, n = 187) and Introduction to Programming (8 weeks, 78 expected hours, n = 182). Post-course questionnaire data were analyzed using non-parametric statistical methods to examine self-reported adoption, usage frequency, and purposes of GenAI use across courses and learner backgrounds. The results show that GenAI adoption was widespread in both MOOCs, with no statistically significant differences by gender, age, education level, or prior programming experience. However, participants in the longer, more extensive MOOC reported significantly higher usage frequency and were more likely to use GenAI for debugging and idea generation. Reported usage frequency for code explanation and debugging was also higher in the longer course. Exploratory analyses found limited relationships between GenAI use and learning-related outcomes. The findings suggest that course context may play a greater role than learner characteristics in shaping how GenAI tools are used. These results provide implications for instructional design and guidance in programming education.

</details>


### [205] [Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Models with a Self-Verifier](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04469)
*Youngwan Lee,Yong-Ju Lee,Sung Ju Hwang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Trinity is a self-evolving vision-language framework where one VLM acts as Questioner, Solver, and EMA-based Verifier to generate and filter its own training data from unlabeled images, significantly improving visual math and biology reasoning without labeled supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Self-evolving VLMs aim to expand reasoning using unlabeled images to avoid expensive human annotations. Existing self-play methods reward agreement between a Questioner and Solver, but mere answer agreement is a poor proxy for truth: it cannot guarantee that questions are grounded in the image, that reference answers are correct, or that a confident majority is not consistently wrong. This limits the reliability and usefulness of self-generated training data and caps the potential of unsupervised self-improvement.

Method: The authors propose Trinity, where a single VLM assumes three roles: Questioner, Solver, and Verifier. The Verifier is implemented as an exponential moving average (EMA) of the main policy, eliminating the need for labels or external judges. During self-play on unlabeled images, the Questioner generates image-related questions and reference answers, the Solver attempts to answer them, and the Verifier (EMA model) evaluates: (1) whether questions are properly grounded in the image, (2) whether reference and Solver answers are correct, and (3) how well the Solver’s reasoning is aligned with the image. The Verifier filters out low-quality questions, scores reasoning, and resolves conflicts: if a strong Solver consensus contradicts the reference answer and is judged correct, the reference answer is corrected and the Questioner is penalized. These verified interactions are then used as training supervision for further self-improvement of the VLM.

Result: Using only unlabeled images for training, Trinity improves a base Qwen3-VL-8B model on benchmarks requiring visual scientific and mathematical reasoning. Notably, it yields +8.6 accuracy points on the biology split of the SciVQR benchmark and +12.8 points on MathVerse, compared to the base model. Additionally, the reward dynamics observed during training follow a stable and meaningful self-play curriculum, suggesting that the system learns progressively more challenging and instructive tasks rather than collapsing or overfitting to spurious patterns.

Conclusion: Trinity demonstrates that a VLM can reliably self-verify and self-improve its scientific reasoning capabilities using only unlabeled images, thanks to an EMA-based Verifier that ensures image grounding and answer correctness for self-generated training data. This tri-role, self-play framework overcomes the weaknesses of agreement-only rewards in prior work and indicates that self-evolving multimodal agents can become stronger scientific reasoners without external labels or judges.

Abstract: Self-evolving vision-language models (VLMs), a form of self-improvement in which a model generates its own training data from unlabeled images, are a promising route toward agents that expand their reasoning capability in an unsupervised manner, without relying on ever-larger annotation budgets. Existing methods pair a Questioner that proposes problems with a Solver that answers them, but reward both roles mainly by agreement among sampled answers. Agreement is a weak proxy for truth: it cannot tell whether a question is grounded in the image, whether the proposed reference answer is right, or whether a confident majority is wrong in the same way. We present Trinity, in which one VLM plays three roles, Questioner, Solver, and Verifier, and the Verifier is a self-verifier: an exponential moving average (EMA) of the policy itself, requiring neither labels nor an external judge. The Verifier screens every generated question for image grounding and answer correctness before it becomes supervision, scores Solver reasoning against the image, and adjudicates disputes between the reference answer and a strong Solver consensus, correcting the reference and penalizing the Questioner when the consensus is right. Trained on images alone, Trinity improves Qwen3-VL-8B on mathematical visual reasoning and on science benchmarks with biology content, for example, +8.6 points on the biology split of SciVQR and +12.8 on MathVerse, and its reward dynamics behave as a healthy self-play curriculum should. These results suggest that a self-evolving multimodal agent can strengthen its scientific reasoning from unlabeled scientific images alone, with the model itself serving as the verifier.

</details>


### [206] [Reactivating Alignment: Defending LLMs from Jailbreaks via Intention-Aware Input-Output Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04470)
*Luoyu Chen,Weiqi Wang,Chenhan Zhang,Zhiyi Tian,Shui Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces SENTINEL, a plug-and-play defense that detects jailbreak attacks by extracting and judging the true intent from the model’s own generated text, substantially reducing successful jailbreaks with minimal over-refusal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are easily jailbroken by prompts that hide harmful intent in complex ways. Existing defenses perturb inputs or suppress harmful outputs without explicitly identifying where the malicious intent lies, which makes them brittle and prone to over-refusal. The motivation is to build a defense that directly targets and reveals the attacker's true intent even under sophisticated jailbreak strategies.

Method: The authors propose SENTINEL, a generation-time defense that treats jailbreak mitigation as intent extraction. It leverages the observation that LLM outputs tend to semantically align with the attacker’s true intent. SENTINEL finds semantically aligned regions between the input prompt and the generated output, extracts subsequences that reveal intent, projects them onto a refusal direction to score harmfulness, and can interrupt generation if the score exceeds a threshold. This is designed as a plug-and-play mechanism that works across models.

Result: On HarmBench and multiple LLM backbones, SENTINEL reduces jailbreak success rates to around 5% while keeping over-refusal low. The framework also shows robustness against adaptive attacks that attempt to circumvent the defense.

Conclusion: Reframing jailbreak defense as intent extraction and using input–output semantic consistency enables a more robust, low-overhead, and general defense. SENTINEL effectively shifts jailbreak features from alignment blind spots into regions where alignment mechanisms can act, thereby improving safety against sophisticated attacks while preserving helpfulness.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that conceal harmful intent within complex adversarial prompts. Existing defenses primarily rely on input perturbation or harmful-output suppression, but they rarely model where malicious intent resides, resulting in brittle protection and excessive over-refusal.
  We propose SENTINEL, a plug-and-play, generation-time jailbreak defense that reframes mitigation as an intent extraction problem. Our key insight is that instruction-tuned LLMs exhibit strong input--output semantic consistency: regardless of jailbreak complexity, generated outputs tend to align with the attacker's true intent. SENTINEL exploits this property by matching semantically aligned input--output regions to extract intention-revealing subsequences, scores these subsequences using refusal-direction projections to estimate harmfulness, and halts generation when necessary. Experiments on HarmBench across multiple LLMs show that SENTINEL reduces jailbreak success rates to close to 5\% while maintaining low over-refusal. We further demonstrate robustness to adaptive attacks and provide a mechanistic interpretation: SENTINEL re-distributes jailbreak features from alignment blind spots to aligned regions.

</details>


### [207] [Semantic Causal-Factor Inference from Aviation Incident Narratives Using A Variational Autoencoder with Cosine-Similarity-Based Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04472)
*AZIIDA NANYONGA1,HASSAN WASSWA,UGUR TURHAN,KEITH FRANCIS JOINER,GRAHAM WILD*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They build a VAE-based NLP framework that maps long aviation accident narratives into a probabilistic latent space to infer semantic representations of expert-assessed causal factors, achieving high similarity to official probable-cause statements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Aviation investigation reports contain rich, unstructured text describing evidence and reasoning about accident causes, but this text is long, complex, and difficult to process automatically. Safety analysts and AI systems need ways to extract causal factors from these narratives at scale without replacing expert judgment. Existing NLP approaches struggle when causal evidence is distributed across long reports, and there is a need for models that can capture latent causal semantics linking narratives to expert-reported probable causes.

Method: They propose a semantic causal-factor inference framework using natural language processing plus a variational autoencoder (VAE). First, investigation narratives and their associated probable-cause texts are converted into numerical (vector) representations. The encoder maps narrative vectors into a probabilistic latent space. The decoder then estimates the representation of the corresponding probable causes from these latent variables. Training uses a VAE-style objective that combines a Kullback-Leibler divergence term (regularizing the latent space) with a cosine-similarity-based reconstruction loss that encourages the decoded vectors to be semantically close to the expert-reported probable-cause vectors. After training, the model can infer probable-cause representations for new narratives and extract interpretable terms associated with causal information.

Result: Using 20,919 NTSB aviation investigation reports (2005–2020), the framework was evaluated on a held-out test set. The cosine similarity between predicted probable-cause representations and the actual expert-reported probable-cause representations averaged 0.786 with a standard deviation of 0.120. The predicted representations also produced interpretable terms that correspond to causal content in the reports, indicating that the model captures meaningful causal semantics rather than just superficial text similarity.

Conclusion: Probabilistic latent representation learning via a VAE can effectively link complex aviation safety narratives to their expert-labeled causal factors. The approach achieves strong semantic alignment with official probable-cause statements and yields interpretable causal terms, suggesting it is useful for AI-assisted extraction and exploration of causal information in investigation reports. Importantly, the method is framed as supporting, not replacing, formal expert-led causal determination.

Abstract: Aviation accident and incident investigations generate extensive unstructured textual information containing evidence relevant to the causes and contributing factors of safety occurrences. Automatically extracting such information is challenging because causal evidence may be distributed across long and complex investigation narratives. This study proposes a semantic causal-factor inference framework combining natural language processing with a variational autoencoder (VAE) to learn the relationship between aviation investigation narratives and expert-reported probable causes. Investigation narratives and their corresponding probable causes are transformed into numerical representations, after which the encoder maps narrative representations to a probabilistic latent space. The decoder estimates representations of the corresponding probable causes and is trained using an objective that combines Kullback-Leibler divergence with cosine-similarity-based semantic reconstruction. The framework was evaluated using 20,919 finalized U.S. National Transportation Safety Board investigation reports from 2005 to 2020. On the held-out test set, the predicted and expert-reported probable-cause representations achieved a mean cosine similarity of 0.786 (SD = 0.120). The predicted representations also yielded interpretable terms associated with causal information in the reports. The results demonstrate the potential of probabilistic latent representation learning for AI-assisted extraction of causal information from aviation safety narratives while retaining expert investigation as the basis for formal causal determination.

</details>


### [208] [InferOpt: Constrained Multi-Objective Search for LLM Inference Configurations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04473)
*Qi Chen,Yingying Cheng,Zhaoyi Sun,Li Zhou,Fan Zhang,Jie Sun*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose InferOpt, a general search framework that automatically tunes many inference-time knobs for LLM serving (e.g., KV cache pruning and MoE expert counts) as a constrained multi-objective black-box optimization, achieving better latency/memory–quality trade-offs than existing heuristics and baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Serving large language models efficiently requires choosing many inference-time configuration parameters (like per-layer KV cache retention and number of experts in MoE layers). Current practice uses hand-designed, mechanism-specific heuristics that give a single operating point and do not scale to large, layer-wise configuration spaces or multiple objectives (e.g., resource use vs. quality). There is a need for a principled, reusable method that can automatically search these high-dimensional configuration spaces under resource constraints while preserving model quality.

Method: They formulate inference configuration as a constrained multi-objective black-box optimization problem where objectives include resource cost (e.g., KV cache size, routed token–expert pairs) and quality metrics, under a budget constraint. They propose InferOpt, a general-purpose search framework that requires only: (1) bounds on each configuration variable, (2) a deterministic resource-cost function, and (3) an evaluation hook for quality on a proxy dataset. The pipeline: (i) search over the configuration space using a frozen sampled proxy set; (ii) reject configurations that exceed resource budget before model evaluation; (iii) adaptively tighten the budget during search; and (iv) re-validate Pareto-optimal candidate configurations on the full-scale dataset. They demonstrate InferOpt on two high-dimensional spaces: a 28D continuous KV cache pruning configuration for Qwen2.5-7B and a 26D discrete MoE top-k expert schedule for DeepSeek-V2-Lite, and compare against standard multi-objective optimizers like Random Search, NSGA-II, and MOTPE.

Result: On the KV pruning task for Qwen2.5-7B, InferOpt discovers post-prefill pruning configurations that reduce a 16K token KV cache by 64.4% and reduce TPOT (tokens processed over time) by 22.9–48.5%. The InferOpt-found layer-wise budget outperforms a matched uniform KV budget by 7.3% and 14.0% when normalized to Full KV reference points, meaning better quality for the same memory or vice versa. On the MoE expert scheduling task for DeepSeek-V2-Lite, InferOpt finds a layer-wise top-k schedule that removes 43.0% of routed token–expert pairs yet stays within 0.59 evaluation points of the default configuration, while also outperforming matched-budget baselines in closeness to the uncompressed reference. Compared against Random Search, NSGA-II, and MOTPE across both the KV and MoE spaces, InferOpt achieves the highest proxy hypervolume (best Pareto front approximation), the lowest KV retention for given quality, and the smallest quality drop at the lowest expert counts, indicating more efficient trade-offs between resource cost and model performance.

Conclusion: Inference-time configuration for LLM serving can be effectively treated as a constrained multi-objective black-box optimization problem. InferOpt provides a reusable, mechanism-agnostic framework that takes minimal problem-specific inputs and can handle large, heterogeneous configuration spaces. By searching on a proxy set with budget-aware rejection and adaptive tightening, then re-validating on full data, InferOpt achieves better resource–quality trade-offs than hand-tuned heuristics and standard multi-objective optimizers on both KV cache pruning and MoE expert selection. This suggests that automated, budget-aware multi-objective search is a practical and superior alternative to current ad hoc inference configuration practices, and it should generalize to other LLM serving knobs beyond the two case studies.

Abstract: Serving an LLM means setting dozens of inference-time knobs, from per-layer KV retention to per-layer expert counts. Practice sets them with mechanism-specific heuristics that return a single operating point and do not scale to layer-wise search spaces. We recast inference configuration as constrained multi-objective black-box optimization and build InferOpt, a reusable search framework that requires only variable bounds, a deterministic resource cost, and an evaluation hook. InferOpt searches on a frozen sampled proxy set, rejects over-budget candidates before any model call, tightens the budget adaptively, and re-validates Pareto representatives on full-scale dataset. One pipeline covers a 28-dimensional continuous KV space (Qwen2.5-7B) and a 26-dimensional discrete MoE space (DeepSeek-V2-Lite). On KV, post-prefill pruning cuts the 16K cache by 64.4% and TPOT by 22.9--48.5%, and the searched layer-wise budget by InferOpt beats a matched uniform budget by 7.3% and 14.0% of the Full KV reference points. On MoE, a searched top-k schedule by InferOpt removes 43.0% of routed token--expert pairs while staying within 0.59 points of the default, closer than the matched-budget baselines. Against Random Search, NSGA-II, and MOTPE, InferOpt leads on both spaces, taking the best proxy hypervolume and the lowest retention on KV and staying closest to the uncompressed reference at the lowest experts on MoE.

</details>


### [209] [VCLMU: Mechanism-Centric Virtual Cell World Modeling for Perturbation Response](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04475)
*Yuwei Miao,Azim Dehghani Amirabad,Scott Oloff,Junzhou Huang,Tianyu Cui,Rui Liao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes VCLMU, a mechanism-centric virtual cell model that uses latent mechanism units to predict cellular transcriptional responses to genetic perturbations, achieving better perturbation-specific prediction and interpretable biological programs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurately predicting how cells respond to genetic perturbations is crucial for building virtual cells and designing biological interventions. Existing models typically map from unperturbed profiles and perturbations directly to outcomes, without explicitly modeling the latent cellular state transitions caused by interventions, which limits interpretability and potentially performance. The authors aim to build a model that captures these mechanism-level transitions in a structured and biologically grounded way.

Method: The authors design VCLMU, a world-model-like framework where cellular state is represented as a set of Latent Mechanism Units (LMUs). Each LMU has a reusable identity, grounded in multimodal biological evidence, and an observation-specific state. Genetic perturbations are treated as actions that stochastically update LMU states, and the resulting latent configuration is decoded to predict transcriptional responses. Training is done in two pretraining stages: first on about 200K pseudo-bulk perturbation profiles, then fine-tuned on gene-aligned single-cell perturbation data.

Result: Across six benchmarks where the tested perturbations are disjoint from those seen in training, VCLMU improves perturbation-specific response prediction compared with strong baseline models while maintaining competitive overall response accuracy. The learned LMUs are analyzed via enrichment of their gene sets with perturbation responses, revealing that they correspond to structured biological response programs.

Conclusion: Mechanism-level latent state transitions, instantiated as LMUs acted on by perturbations, provide a valuable formulation for virtual cell models. VCLMU not only enhances prediction of cellular responses to unseen genetic interventions but also yields interpretable modules that reflect underlying biological mechanisms, supporting its use for both prediction and interpretation in computational cell modeling.

Abstract: Predicting cellular responses to genetic perturbations is a central capability for virtual cells and a key step toward computational modeling of biological interventions. Most existing models directly map an unperturbed molecular profile and perturba- tion to the resulting observation without explicitly representing the latent cellular transition induced by the intervention. We introduce a mechanism-centric virtual cell world model that represents cellular state as a set of Latent Mechanism Units (LMUs) and treats genetic perturbations as actions on these latent states. Each LMU combines a reusable identity grounded in multimodal biological evidence with an observation-specific state, allowing a perturbation to induce mechanism- specific stochastic transitions before decoding the resulting transcriptional response. We train VCLMU through two-stage pretraining, first on around 200K pseudo-bulk perturbation profiles and then on gene-aligned single-cell perturbation data. Across six perturbation-disjoint benchmarks, VCLMU consistently improves perturbation- specific response recovery over strong baselines while maintaining competitive global response accuracy. We further analyze learned LMUs through enrichment between perturbation responses and LMU gene sets and show that they capture structured biological response programs. These results support mechanism-level latent state transition as a useful formulation for virtual cell models that aim to predict and interpret cellular responses to biological interventions.

</details>


### [210] [ManifoldCache: Training-Free Diffusion Acceleration via Constraint Manifold Caching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04510)
*Prashant Pandey,Devineni Sri Venkatraya Chowdary,Brejesh Lall*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces ManifoldCache, a training- and data-free accelerator for diffusion models constrained to geometric manifolds, achieving faster sampling without violating hard physical or geometric constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Structured scientific generative tasks—such as medical imaging, molecular conformations, protein and crystal design, and 3D scenes—require outputs that strictly obey geometric or physical constraints. Diffusion models can handle these tasks but are extremely slow at inference, and existing acceleration methods either break constraint satisfaction, are memory-prohibitive, or cause mode confusion. There is a need for a principled acceleration method tailored specifically to constraint-manifold diffusion models (CMDMs) that maintains fidelity to constraints while reducing computational cost.

Method: The authors formalize eight different structured generative settings under a common framework called Constraint-Manifold Diffusion Models (CMDMs), where the target distribution lies on a manifold defined by external constraints. They analyze the conditional score function and show it decomposes into orthogonal normal (constraint-enforcing) and tangential (within-manifold) components. Based on this, they design ManifoldCache, a training-free, data-free caching strategy that uses the diffusion noise schedule to determine a sharp boundary—the noise-schedule midpoint—before which network features can be safely cached. They provide theoretical guarantees that caching before this boundary leads to bounded error and characterize how deeper network blocks admit larger safe caching strides via Jacobian-based analysis of the score decomposition.

Result: They theoretically prove that (1) the score splits into normal and tangential components aligned with constraint geometry; (2) the noise-schedule midpoint is a sharp phase boundary separating a safe caching regime from a regime where a positive fraction of trajectories inevitably suffer mode confusion; and (3) deeper blocks allow provably larger cache strides within the safe regime. The resulting ManifoldCache schedule needs no calibration data or retraining and accelerates inference for a wide range of CMDMs without sacrificing constraint satisfaction, unlike existing acceleration approaches.

Conclusion: The work establishes a unified CMDM framework for many scientific diffusion models and introduces ManifoldCache, a principled, training-free accelerator that respects geometric constraints. By exploiting the geometric decomposition of the score and identifying a theoretically sharp safe-caching phase, it enables faster sampling with bounded error and avoids the failures of prior acceleration techniques on constraint-manifold problems.

Abstract: Diffusion models for structured scientific generation must produce samples satisfying hard geometric constraints imposed by physics, chemistry, or biology, yet inference in these settings is prohibitively slow, demanding hundreds to thousands of neural-function evaluations per sample. We unify eight state-of-the-art models spanning medical volumetrics, molecular conformations, protein backbone design, crystal structure prediction, and multi-view 3D scenes under a single abstraction, Constraint-Manifold Diffusion Models (CMDMs), in which the target distribution is supported on a manifold defined by an externally specified constraint map. All existing acceleration families fail on this class: quantization exhausts memory on high-dimensional volumetric operators; pruning breaks constraint fidelity; fast ODE solvers allow trajectories to drift off the constraint manifold; and feature-caching heuristics are blind to constraint geometry, inducing mode confusion in the high-noise regime. We introduce ManifoldCache, the first training-free, data-free accelerator designed from first principles for CMDMs. The key insight is that the conditional score decomposes orthogonally into a normal component, which enforces constraint satisfaction, and a tangential component, which navigates within the manifold. Exploiting this structure, we prove that the noise-schedule midpoint is a sharp safe-caching boundary: caching before it incurs provably bounded error, while caching after it guarantees a strictly positive fraction of trajectories suffer mode confusion, a gap that persists up to the boundary. We further prove that deeper network blocks admit provably larger certified cache strides within the safe phase, as a consequence of the score decomposition propagating through block Jacobians. The resulting schedule requires no calibration data, along with zero training overhead.

</details>


### [211] [Towards Credible Agent-Based Policy Simulations: Disentangling Opportunities and Preferences in a Financial Inclusion Case Study of Egypt](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04515)
*Alba Aguilera,Georgina Curto,Nardine Osman,Ahmed Al-Awah*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Presents and applies a general, data‑driven agent‑based modelling framework (grounded in the Capability Approach) to build credible policy simulations, demonstrated on financial inclusion in Egypt.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Policy-oriented agent-based models are often questioned for their credibility and empirical grounding. Policymakers need to trust that model assumptions, parameters, and outputs closely reflect reality and are accurate enough for decision support. There is a need for a systematic framework that links theory (here, the Capability Approach), empirical data, and expert knowledge to construct and validate simulations that can meaningfully inform policies, such as those addressing financial inclusion gaps.

Method: The paper proposes a general modelling framework aligned with the Capability Approach for constructing credible, data-informed policy simulations. It implements this framework via an agent-based model of financial inclusion in Egypt. The model represents heterogeneous individuals and firms whose behaviour is driven by their financial states, barriers, opportunities, and preferences. The empirical grounding is done in two stages: (1) initialisation, where representative synthetic populations are built from real data; and (2) calibration, where behavioural (preference) parameters are estimated to fit observed outcomes. Feasibility parameters (opportunities) are fixed while preference parameters are calibrated across population groups to disentangle structural and motivational factors.

Result: The agent-based model successfully fits real-world data on financial inclusion in Egypt while maintaining a clear distinction between feasibility (opportunity-related) parameters and preference parameters. By holding opportunity parameters fixed and varying preferences by population group, the model can separate the effects of institutional and social barriers from those of agents’ motivations and priorities. The calibration produces transparent, group-specific hypotheses about what drives observed financial inclusion gaps.

Conclusion: The proposed Capability Approach–aligned modelling framework, combined with a structured two-stage data-fitting process (initialisation and calibration), improves the credibility and interpretability of agent-based policy simulations. Applied to financial inclusion in Egypt, it reveals how gaps can be understood as mismatches between agents’ opportunities and realised outcomes, providing actionable insights for policymakers. The work demonstrates how tighter links between model structure, empirical data, and stakeholder concerns can make simulation models more trustworthy and useful for policy analysis and design.

Abstract: Credibility is a central topic for agent-based models intended to support policy-making. Simulations must not only represent the target scenarios and their core dynamics but also demonstrate that their assumptions, parameters, and outputs are empirically grounded and sufficiently accurate for their intended use. This paper addresses this challenge by presenting a general modelling framework, aligned with the Capability Approach, for building credible policy simulations that rely on data and domain-expert knowledge. It then demonstrates how it can be contextualised and implemented to study the social challenge of financial inclusion in Egypt, building on an agent-based model that represents heterogeneous individuals and firms behaving according to their financial states, barriers, opportunities, and preferences. The model is fitted to real-world data in two stages, initialisation and calibration, which respectively build representative synthetic populations and estimate behavioural parameters. By fixing the feasibility parameters, which determine agents' opportunities, and calibrating preference parameters across different population groups, we are able to distinguish and analyse the role of institutional and social barriers in the system, as well as the role of agents' motivations and priorities. This calibration stage provides transparent and group-specific hypotheses about the drivers of observed financial-inclusion gaps, which can further be analysed as gaps between agents' opportunities and realised outcomes, a very relevant insight for policy-making. This paper is thus a step towards improving the credibility and usefulness of policy simulations, strengthening the relationship between the model, the real target system, and the stakeholders who will use it. The code is available at: \url{https://www.comses.net/codebase-release/df8383cb-f49b-4f09-8cce-73603b59adcc/}.

</details>


### [212] [EvoCast: Reliable Autonomous Research Agents for Iterative Forecasting Architecture Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04517)
*Kaipeng Xu,Xianli Yan,Yan Wang,Xiang Liu,Shan Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EvoCast is an autonomous research-agent system that iteratively evolves deep time-series forecasting architectures for specific tasks, outperforming strong baselines with lower agent cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Adapting deep time-series forecasting models to specific tasks is labor-intensive, requiring expert-driven choices in model selection, diagnosis, architecture design, implementation, and evaluation. Existing AutoML tools are limited by fixed search spaces, and generic LLM research agents cannot reliably manage rigorous experimental protocols or decide when to promote models. There is a need for an autonomous system that can both innovate architectures and rigorously control the experimentation lifecycle.

Method: EvoCast is an autonomous research-agent framework that iteratively refines forecasting architectures. It first builds and diagnoses a task-specific baseline using mechanism ablations. It then proposes new research directions based on dataset properties, diagnostic outcomes, history of prior iterations, and failure logs. The framework enforces a cognition-authority separation: LLM agents handle open-ended hypothesis generation and code writing, while deterministic program components strictly control code modification boundaries, standardized evaluation, and decisions about promoting new models. Experimental results are logged and used as evidence to inform subsequent rounds of evolution.

Result: EvoCast successfully carries out complex architecture modifications with higher implementation success rates and reduced token and time consumption on the LLM side. In three real-world forecasting applications, it produces task-specialized architectures that surpass handpicked baselines, strong existing forecasting models, and baseline LLM research-agent systems.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates that EvoCast can autonomously and reliably evolve deep forecasting architectures for specific tasks, combining LLM-driven creativity with deterministic experimental control. This approach mitigates expert effort, overcomes constraints of fixed AutoML search spaces, and improves performance and efficiency over strong baselines in real-world time-series forecasting scenarios.

Abstract: Deep time-series forecasting models have rapidly diversified, yet adapting them to a specific task still requires extensive expert effort in model selection, mechanism diagnosis, architecture design, implementation, and evaluation. Existing AutoML methods are constrained by predefined search spaces, while general-purpose LLM research agents lack reliable control over experimental protocols and model promotion. We introduce EvoCast, a fully autonomous research-agent system for iterative forecasting architecture evolution. EvoCast first establishes and diagnoses a task-specific baseline through executed mechanism ablations, then generates evidence-grounded research directions from dataset characteristics, diagnostic results, prior rounds, and failure records. Its central design, cognition-authority separation, assigns open-ended hypothesis generation and code implementation to LLM agents, while deterministic program authorities control source-edit boundaries, canonical evaluation, and promotion decisions. Experimental outcomes are accumulated as evidence to guide subsequent rounds. Results show that EvoCast completes complex architecture modifications with higher implementation success and lower agent-side token/time cost, and develops task-specific architectures that outperform selected baselines, strong forecasting models, and agent baselines in three real-world forecasting cases. The code is available at https://github.com/18e0-x/EvoCast.

</details>


### [213] [Action-Consequence Alignment for Reliable Planning and Self-Improving in Latent World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04539)
*Jinping Wang1,Zhiqiang Gao,Xiantong Zhen,Ling Shao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper shows that standard latent world models can prefer actions with lower prediction error but worse real-world outcomes, and proposes Action Consequence Alignment (ACA) to align prediction-based learning with accurate goal-directed planning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: World models are used for planning by predicting future states and rewards, but simply minimizing prediction error does not ensure that the model’s preferred actions actually lead to the most accurate achievement of goals in the real environment. Neuroscience findings on self-produced sensations suggest that the correspondence between actions and their sensory consequences is crucial; disrupting this correspondence leads to prediction mismatches. The paper is motivated by the possibility that learned world models may similarly fail to preserve a faithful correspondence between actions and their consequences for planning purposes, creating a gap between predictive accuracy and planning reliability.

Method: The authors empirically examine whether latent world models preserve action–consequence correspondence by comparing the model’s prediction errors for factual action sequences versus nearby alternative actions. They show that alternatives can have lower prediction error while leading to physically worse outcomes relative to the target. To address this, they introduce Action Consequence Alignment (ACA), a training objective added on top of standard forward-prediction loss. ACA penalizes cases where locally searched alternative actions obtain lower prediction error than the factual (recorded) actions, thus encouraging the model to maintain that factual actions are locally optimal in prediction space. ACA requires no extra model components or additional environment interaction during training. They also propose using the same ACA principle to guide targeted data collection by selecting new trajectories where this alignment is poor.

Result: Experiments across varied environments and evaluation regimes show that ACA-trained world models yield better planning performance than baselines trained only with prediction loss. Specifically, when used for planning, ACA reduces the real goal error—i.e., the discrepancy between desired targets and actual environment outcomes. Moreover, when using ACA to guide exploration and data collection, the resulting datasets improve performance more than datasets obtained via random local action sampling. These results empirically confirm the presence of prediction–planning mismatch in standard training and demonstrate that ACA can effectively reduce this gap.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that low prediction error in latent world models is not sufficient to guarantee good planning performance, because models can assign lower predictive cost to actions that in reality achieve goals less accurately. By explicitly aligning actions with their predicted consequences through ACA, world models can be trained to better preserve local optimality of factual actions, leading to more reliable planning. ACA is presented as a simple, practical principle—requiring no extra components or training interaction—that both improves goal-directed performance and enables more informative data collection, thereby helping to bridge the gap between predictive learning and effective decision making.

Abstract: Latent world models learn to predict observed transitions, yet low prediction error alone does not guarantee reliable planning. Inspired by self tickling experiments in neuroscience showing that disrupting motor sensory correspondence increases prediction mismatch, we examine whether learned world models preserve an analogous action consequence correspondence.The results show nearby alternatives can receive lower prediction errors despite producing physical outcomes farther from the recorded target. With that future treated as a goal, this reveals a concrete prediction planning mismatch: the model assigns a lower cost to an action that achieves the target less accurately. To mitigate this gap, we introduce Action Consequence Alignment (ACA), a training objective that complements forward prediction by penalizing the prediction error advantage of locally searched alternatives over factual actions without additional model components or environment interactions during training. The same principle can also guide additional data collection for self improvement. We demonstrate that across diverse environments and evaluation settings, ACA improves planning performance and reduces real goal error, while ACA guided data collection outperforms random local sampling. These results support action consequence alignment as a practical principle for bridging predictive learning and reliable planning.

</details>


### [214] [Autonomous Structuring of Radiology Reports Across Modalities at Archive Scale Using an Open-Weight Large Language Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04541)
*Friedrich Puttkammer,Fabian Drexel,Marlene Fritzsche,Era Stambollxhiu,Miriam Kumpf,Lena Schmitzer,Lea Schumann,Lina Xu,Johannes Moll,Jannik Lübberstedt,Zeineb Ben Chaaben,Anirudh Narayanan,Hartmut Häntze,Renato Cuocolo,Antonios Billis,Alexander Löser,Jawed Nawabi,Marcus R. Makowski,Cosmin I. Bercea,Shahrooz Faghihroohi,Lisa C. Adams,Keno K. Bressem*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They built and tested an open-weight LLM pipeline that automatically converts a whole archive of free‑text radiology reports into structured reports, achieving high accuracy and scalability, with most remaining errors in multi‑region studies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Radiology still relies heavily on unstructured free‑text reports, which are hard to search, analyze, and reuse for research, quality assurance, and clinical decision support. Manual structured reporting is time‑consuming, unpopular among radiologists, and not feasible to retroactively apply to large historical archives. The authors aim to enable large‑scale, automated, and fully local conversion of existing multimodality radiology report archives into structured form without requiring human-in-the-loop oversight or reliance on closed, proprietary LLMs.

Method: They designed a hierarchical template-based pipeline powered by an open-weight 120B-parameter LLM (gpt-oss-120B) that runs on a single local GPU. The pipeline uses 150 hierarchically organized report templates. In three constrained-decoding stages, the model (1) selects the most suitable template family, (2) refines to a specific template variant, and (3) populates the template fields from the free‑text report. They developed the templates at one institution and externally tested the pipeline at another on radiology reports (2010–2025) across modalities. Performance was evaluated by: (a) comparing model template selection against expert labels for 914 sampled reports, (b) assessing structuring quality on 920 radiography and CT reports where five residents corrected each field, and (c) then running the pipeline on the entire archive of the second center. They reported proportions with Wilson 95% CIs, macro semantic textual similarity between model output and corrected reference, the proportion of fields left unchanged, the frequency of unsupported content flags, and throughput in reports per hour on one GPU.

Result: The LLM pipeline chose the optimal template in 74.4% of reports and at least an appropriate template in 82.3% overall, with better performance on single-region (87.7%) than multi-region (54.1%) reports. For radiography and CT, semantic similarity between model outputs and resident‑corrected references was very high (0.95 and 0.97). Residents left 88.7% of 24,638 fields unchanged, implying relatively few corrections were required. Unsupported or hallucinated content was flagged in only 1.0–1.5% of reports. When applied to the full institutional archive of 2,186,982 reports, 96.5% successfully yielded structured outputs (2,401,544 structured reports in total, indicating some reports mapped to multiple structures), at a processing speed of 1,258 reports per hour on a single GPU.

Conclusion: An open-weight, locally deployable LLM pipeline can automatically convert an entire multimodality radiology report archive from free text to structured format with high fidelity and scalability, without human oversight. The main residual weakness lies in handling complex multi-region reports, which are still a significant source of template selection errors. This demonstrates the feasibility of large-scale, privacy-preserving retrospective structuring of radiology data using open LLMs, while highlighting the need for improved modeling or template design for multi-region examinations.

Abstract: Purpose: To develop and evaluate an open-weight large language model (LLM) pipeline that converts an entire archive of free-text radiology reports into structured reports without human oversight. Materials and Methods: In this retrospective study, a pipeline with 150 hierarchically organized templates was developed at one center and tested at a second center on reports from 2010 to 2025. The open-weight model gpt-oss-120B selects the template in three constrained-decoding steps and fills it on one local graphics processing unit. Template selection was scored against expert labels on 914 randomly sampled reports of five modalities, structuring quality on 920 radiography and CT reports corrected field by field by five residents. The pipeline then processed the complete archive of the second center. Proportions are reported with Wilson 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results: An optimal template set was selected for 74.4% of reports (680 of 914; 95% CI: 71.5%, 77.1%) and an appropriate set for 82.3% (752 of 914; 95% CI: 79.7%, 84.6%), 87.7% for single-region and 54.1% for multi-region reports. Macro semantic textual similarity between output and corrected reference was 0.95 for radiography and 0.97 for CT, residents left 88.7% of 24,638 fields unchanged, and unsupported content was flagged in 1.0% and 1.5% of reports. Of 2,186,982 archive reports, 96.5% received structured output, 2,401,544 structured reports, at 1,258 reports per hour on one graphics processing unit. Conclusion: An open-weight LLM pipeline structured a complete multimodality report archive without human oversight with high content fidelity. Multi-region reports remained the main source of template errors.

</details>


### [215] [Decide, Ask, or Defer: Clinical LLMs under Incomplete Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04542)
*Mingzhan Yang,Weili Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose and evaluate a new three-way decision framework (DECIDE/ASK/DEFER) for clinical language models, showing it reveals important tradeoffs between autonomy, safety, and information acquisition that binary DECIDE/ABSTAIN schemes obscure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing clinical LLM setups force models into a binary choice: either make a diagnosis or abstain. This lumps together several qualitatively different behaviors (e.g., needing more data vs. deferring to a clinician) and ignores how models should choose to gather additional information. The authors want a framework that distinguishes between deciding, asking for more information, and deferring to humans, to better understand and manage clinical AI autonomy and safety.

Method: They design a DECIDE/ASK/DEFER action space for clinical LLMs and a blinded experimental protocol so models cannot exploit metadata about evidence completeness. Using 200 carefully matched clinical evidence states derived from the DDXPlus dataset, they test three LLM families (Qwen, Gemini, GPT). They compare how often each model chooses to decide, ask for more information, or defer under identical evidence; they analyze disagreements across models; and, for Qwen, they compare performance under targeted versus random information acquisition. They also create a matched DECIDE/ABSTAIN baseline to quantify tradeoffs introduced by the three-way policy.

Result: Across the 200 matched clinical scenarios, the three models often choose different actions despite seeing the same evidence, disagreeing in 137 cases. For Qwen, the pattern of which additional information is requested has a clearer effect on whether the model later decides autonomously than on whether that decision is correct. Compared to a binary DECIDE/ABSTAIN setup, the three-way DECIDE/ASK/DEFER policy reduces some unsafe autonomous decisions but also eliminates some correct ones, revealing a tradeoff between safety and autonomy rather than a monotonic improvement.

Conclusion: A three-way DECIDE/ASK/DEFER formulation, together with blinded evidence protocols, provides a more expressive and informative way to analyze clinical LLM behavior than binary DECIDE/ABSTAIN. It uncovers heterogeneity in action selection across models and a nuanced autonomy–safety tradeoff. However, it does not automatically yield a better decision policy overall, underscoring the need for careful design and evaluation of information acquisition and deferral strategies in clinical AI systems.

Abstract: Clinical LLMs must decide not only what diagnosis to produce, but also whether the available evidence is sufficient for autonomous decision making. Binary DECIDE/ABSTAIN formulations merge distinct non decision states and do not explicitly evaluate information acquisition. We introduce a DECIDE/ASK/DEFER formulation together with a blinded protocol that prevents models from using evidence completeness metadata. We evaluate Qwen, Gemini, and GPT on 200 matched clinical evidence states constructed from DDXPlus. The models show substantial differences in action selection under identical evidence, with disagreement in 137 of 200 states. For Qwen, a matched targeted versus random analysis shows that selected information changes the likelihood of a subsequent autonomous decision more clearly than diagnostic correctness. Its matched DECIDE/ABSTAIN baseline further reveals a safety autonomy tradeoff: the three action policy rescues some erroneous autonomous decisions but also removes some correct autonomous deci sions. These results show that separating information acquisition from clinician deferral exposes behavior that binary abstention hides, without yielding a uniformly improved decision policy.

</details>


### [216] [Label Agreement Does Not Measure Authorization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04544)
*Amir Sabbaghziarani,Bradley Thomas Baker,Theodore J. LaGrow,Sergey Plis*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper shows that standard label agreement metrics miss critical failure modes in LLM-based labeling/ontology pipelines and proposes a richer evaluation and gating scheme to expose these failures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic LLM pipelines are increasingly used to harmonize labels and metadata across datasets, often evaluated only by label agreement with reference labels. The authors observed that their pipeline looked good by aggregate agreement scores but still failed in practically important ways. They aim to understand and expose these hidden failure modes because traditional agreement metrics do not capture authorization to act, output completeness, or responsiveness to changing evidence—properties that matter for safe deployment in neuroimaging cohorts.

Method: They construct and audit an agentic LLM pipeline used for label ontology and metadata harmonization on two neuroimaging cohorts (COBRE and FBIRN). Instead of only computing label agreement with rule-derived reference labels, they separately measure: (1) authorization/choice of action—whether the agent was entitled to propose a label or operation; (2) completeness/structural correctness—whether outputs are sufficiently complete and correctly formatted (e.g., JSON with all required fields) to be operational; and (3) stability with respect to evidence—whether labels change appropriately when underlying evidence changes. They compare conditions with and without exposing the agent to upstream proposals and test adversarial setups like an agent that simply replays its first answer. They also inspect downstream effects such as row-order errors that standard metrics ignore. They then design a scheme that measures these properties separately, includes appropriate controls, and gates commitment (automation) based on those metrics, escalating problematic cases to humans.

Result: They find that these different properties diverge sharply from each other and from standard label agreement. Providing an upstream proposal has almost no effect on label agreement (0.857 to 0.870) but dramatically improves agreement on the chosen action (from 0.409 to 0.830), showing that agreement scores understate practical improvements. Despite syntactically valid JSON outputs, one model omits a required field in 10% of cases, another in 33%, revealing structural reliability problems invisible to agreement metrics. An agent that simply replays its first answer can achieve perfect scores on original cases yet fails completely when evidence is changed, exposing a lack of evidence-responsiveness. A downstream row-order bug erases most diagnostic signal without affecting any of the standard metrics. Their multi-metric, gated evaluation surfaces such issues and routes suspect cases to humans.

Conclusion: Label agreement alone is an inadequate metric for evaluating LLM-driven labeling and ontology harmonization systems: it does not test whether the model is authorized to act, whether its outputs are complete and structurally usable, or whether its decisions track changes in evidence. These dimensions can diverge, and naïvely good agreement scores can coexist with serious practical failures and even catastrophic downstream errors. The authors advocate evaluating these properties separately, pairing each with explicit controls, and gating automated commitments on these richer checks so that failures become visible and can be handled by humans. However, even this framework does not guarantee correctness, since the reference labels are rule-derived and thus measure internal consistency rather than ground truth. The work is made reproducible via released code.

Abstract: Many groups now delegate label ontology and metadata harmonization to agentic LLM pipelines. We built one and audited it. Our aggregate scores looked healthy, but the pipeline kept failing in ways they did not show, so we set out to find what they hid. Label agreement asks whether a proposed label matches a reference. It does not ask whether the agent was entitled to propose it, whether the output was complete enough to act on, or whether the label moved when the evidence moved. We measured those three separately on COBRE and FBIRN, two schizophrenia and control neuroimaging cohorts from different consortia, and they come apart, from label agreement and from each other. Showing the agent an upstream proposal barely moves label agreement, 0.857 to 0.870, while agreement on the chosen action doubles, 0.409 to 0.830. Output that parses as JSON still drops a required field on 10% of one model's cases and 33% of the other's. And an agent that replays its first answer scores perfectly on original cases and zero once we change the evidence that decides them. Downstream, a row-order error that none of these metrics reports erases most of the diagnostic signal. So we measure these properties apart, pair each with a control, and gate commitment on the result, which makes failures visible and easy to route to a person. None of this prevents failure. Our reference labels are rule-derived, so agreement with them means consistency, not correctness. Code is available at https://github.com/amir-sbg/Label-Agreement-Does-Not-Measure-Authorization.

</details>


### [217] [$\mathrm{TRIZ}^{a}$: Guiding Agent Evolution from Pattern Recognition to Solution Invention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04555)
*Wenyin Liu,Yiheng Huang,Kai Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces TRIZ^a, an automated R&D paradigm that merges TRIZ inventive theory with LLM-based agents for theory-guided search and validates it on cybersecurity benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To move from random or unstructured mutation in automated R&D toward a structured, explainable, and theory-driven search process that can handle rapidly evolving, adversarial domains like cybersecurity.

Method: Combine TRIZ’s 40 inventive principles and contradiction matrix with an LLM-driven agent evolutionary search; use Functional Information under a frozen reference contract plus TRIZ Ideality to quantify useful vs. harmful function on a common information scale; enforce hard promotion gates; validate on multiple cybersecurity datasets (PowerDuck GOOSE, CICIoT2023, CIC-DDoS2019) with paired reruns, protocol fingerprinting, and hard-gate validation.

Result: Across three legacy cybersecurity experiments, TRIZ^a yields absolute F1 improvements of +2.88, +4.23, and +0.15 points. A larger 45-activity campaign on CICIoT2023 raises macro-F1 from 0.8325 to 0.8483 but fails its pre-defined promotion gate. All results are recorded with full traceability from problem contradictions and TRIZ principles through code changes and evaluation outcomes.

Conclusion: TRIZ^a demonstrates that TRIZ-guided, agent-based evolutionary search can produce measurable performance gains in cybersecurity tasks while maintaining strong explainability and traceability, though strict promotion gates may prevent deployment despite metric improvements.

Abstract: We propose $\mathrm{TRIZ}^{a}$ (TRIZ exponentiated by an agent), a general R\&D automation paradigm that combines TRIZ inventive theory with LLM-driven agent evolutionary search. TRIZ's 40 inventive principles and contradiction matrix provide structured, explainable directions for solution generation, replacing random or untyped mutation with theory-guided ideation. Functional information (FI), operationalized under a frozen reference contract, is combined with TRIZ Ideality to measure useful and harmful function on a commensurable information scale, while hard gates keep promotion distinct from metric improvement. We validate $\mathrm{TRIZ}^{a}$ in cybersecurity--an adversarial and rapidly evolving domain--on PowerDuck GOOSE, CICIoT2023, and CIC-DDoS2019. Under paired-rerun protocols with protocol fingerprinting and hard-gate validation, the legacy experiments yield absolute F1 improvements of $+2.88$, $+4.23$, and $+0.15$ percentage points, respectively. A completed 45-activity CICIoT2023 campaign further increases macro-F1 from $0.8325$ to $0.8483$, but does not pass its frozen promotion gate. Every result remains traceable from contradiction identification and TRIZ principle selection to code transformation, evaluation metrics, and promotion decision.

</details>


### [218] [Recursive Improvement of a Differentiable Scientific Software Ecosystem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04561)
*Pengcheng Hou,Xiaojun Tan,Sihan Hu,Ruisi Wang,Shuo Chen,Lei Wang,Youjin Deng,Kun Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces an AI-agent-driven environment to systematically add and validate differentiable programming capabilities across many existing scientific software packages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Differentiable programming enables gradient-based inference, learning, and design, but extending it to the diverse, existing ecosystem of scientific software is difficult. Each package often requires bespoke derivative implementations, interface integration, and quality checks. With the emergence of AI coding agents, there is an opportunity to automate and accelerate this process, but it requires a structured way to identify research needs and to verify that agent-produced differentiable code is correct, efficient, and reusable.

Method: The authors design an environment that links three stages: (1) identifying research tasks that need gradients; (2) developing differentiable extensions, aided by AI coding agents; and (3) rigorously evaluating the resulting implementations. A unified differentiation interface exposes reusable derivative rules alongside existing numerical routines, allowing multiple workflows to share them. Implementations are validated using independent derivative checks (e.g., comparisons against finite differences or other references), workflow-level tests, and performance benchmarks. Validated code, tests, and research workflows are stored as reusable building blocks for future projects.

Result: Using this environment, the authors build and validate automatic differentiation extensions for 20 existing scientific software packages across physics, chemistry, and biology. They demonstrate that these shared derivatives can be reused across different research workflows. Benchmarks show that gradient computations via automatic differentiation are cheaper and more scalable than finite-difference methods, both for single gradient evaluations and full parameter-estimation tasks. The framework also uncovers and fixes previously unsupported workflows, derivative errors in scientific observables, and redundant computations.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates a practical, research-driven pipeline for propagating differentiable programming capabilities through established scientific software, using AI agents to iteratively improve a shared ecosystem of codes, derivatives, and tests.
