This approach both improves scientific design tasks—such as quantum control and thermal design—and serves as a model for organizing AI coding agents around continual refinement of complex computational infrastructures.

Abstract: Differentiable programming connects scientific computation with gradient-based inference, learning and design. Extending these capabilities across a heterogeneous software ecosystem requires specialized effort to implement derivatives, integrate interfaces and evaluate quality. AI coding agents can accelerate this transformation, but translating their capabilities into useful scientific software requires identifying research needs and evaluating how well implementations meet them. We present an environment for agent-driven evolution of differentiable scientific software that connects demand identification, development and quality evaluation. A unified differentiation interface exposes reusable derivative rules alongside existing numerical routines, allowing research tasks to share these capabilities. Research requirements guide development, with implementations assessed through independent derivative checks, workflow tests and performance evaluation. Validated software, research programs and tests become shared resources for subsequent studies. We construct and validate automatic differentiation extensions across 20 packages spanning physical, chemical and biological modeling, with research workflows demonstrating reuse across tasks. Benchmarks demonstrate computational savings over finite differences in gradient evaluation and complete parameter estimation. Research-driven revisions make previously unsupported workflows differentiable, correct derivatives of scientific observables and eliminate redundant computation. Quantum-control and thermal-design studies revise objectives in response to physical evaluation, improving designs while reusing existing derivatives. This work provides a practical approach to expanding differentiable programming across established scientific software and organizing AI agents around the recursive improvement of a shared computational ecosystem.

</details>


### [219] [Strong Helps Weak: Directional Cross-Modal Alignment Transfer in Multi-modal LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04580)
*Hoigi Seo,Byung Hyun Lee,Minjun Kim,Dohyun Mah,Jongho Lee,Se Young Chun*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes DCAT, a framework that merges multimodal LLMs by transferring cross-modal alignment from a strong, data-rich modality model to a weaker, data-scarce modality model, improving performance without additional fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training multimodal large language models for each modality (vision, audio, video, etc.) usually requires expensive, large-scale, modality-specific datasets. Existing model merging techniques often assume multiple strong models in the same modality, which is unrealistic for data-scarce or domain-specific modalities. The authors are motivated to find a way to leverage a well-aligned, data-rich source modality model to improve a weaker target modality model efficiently, without collecting more data or performing costly retraining.

Method: The authors study an asymmetric merging setup: a strong, well-aligned source-modality MLLM (donor) and a weaker, data-scarce target-modality MLLM (recipient). They provide theoretical and empirical analysis showing that merging can enhance alignment between modality-specific tokens and textual tokens, which correlates with downstream performance. They derive a mutual-information lower bound that is monotonic in alignment-related quantities and use it as a guiding principle. Based on this, they propose Directional Cross-modal Alignment Transfer (DCAT), which transfers textual alignment from the donor modality to the recipient in a directional way, via a closed-form weight-space update. The update is computed using only a small calibration set, avoiding additional fine-tuning.

Result: DCAT significantly improves the target-modality model’s performance on its own benchmarks, despite using only small calibration data and no further fine-tuning. The method outperforms existing model-merging baselines and demonstrates that alignment transfer from a strong donor modality can effectively boost a weaker modality’s understanding capabilities. The mutual-information-based alignment measure shows strong correlation with performance in experiments, validating the theoretical insight.

Conclusion: The work shows that cross-modal, directional merging of MLLMs—specifically transferring alignment from a strong, data-rich modality to a weaker, data-scarce modality—is an effective way to enhance modality understanding without costly retraining. The proposed DCAT framework provides a closed-form, calibration-based weight-space solution that improves alignment and downstream performance, outperforming existing model-merging techniques and offering a practical approach for expanding MLLM capabilities across modalities.

Abstract: Multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) achieve strong modality understanding by pairing a large language model (LLM) with an encoder for a target modality such as vision, video, or audio. However, improving an MLLM's capability for a given modality typically requires additional training on large modality-specific datasets, incurring substantial data collection and compute costs. Model merging offers an alternative, but it is often infeasible for data-scarce, large per-sample size, or domain-specific modalities (\textit{e.g.}, audio and video), where same-modality model variants are rarely available. In this work, we characterize an intriguing asymmetric phenomenon: merging a well-aligned, data-rich source-modality MLLM into a data-scarce target-modality MLLM substantially improves the target on its own benchmarks. Our theoretical and empirical analyses show that this gain stems from enhanced alignment between modality-specific and textual tokens, induced by the stronger donor modality. Specifically, we derive a mutual-information lower bound that is monotonic in alignment-related quantities and strongly correlated with downstream MLLM performance. Building on this principle, we propose Directional Cross-modal Alignment Transfer (DCAT), a novel framework that transfers textual alignment from a strong, well-aligned source (donor) modality to a weak target (recipient) modality, boosting target-modality performance without further fine-tuning. We further show that the alignment-enhancing objective admits a closed-form weight-space solution computed from only a small calibration set. DCAT outperforms existing model-merging methods, offering an efficient path toward cross-modal alignment transfer. Project page with code is available at \url{https://seohoiki3215.github.io/DCAT_project_page}

</details>


### [220] [Bounds, Decompositions and Null Behaviour of KRATOS: A Mathematical Specification of a Recognition-Comparability Diagnostic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04592)
*Maria Dolores Gonzalez,Alberto Barbado*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Defines and analyzes KRATOS, a group-structured bibliometric diagnostic comparing document participation with citation-based recognition across groups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bibliometrics often needs to compare how much different groups contribute to a corpus (number of documents) versus how much they are recognized (citations). Existing indicators may conflate structure and value judgments or behave unpredictably with small groups or skewed citations. The paper aims to give a precise mathematical specification of KRATOS and to understand how it behaves, so that users can interpret group differences and composite scores rigorously without importing normative claims about fairness or epistemic justice.

Method: Formally define KRATOS as a diagnostic over a fixed set of analytical groups, based on distributions of participation (share of documents) and recognition (share of citation weight). Derive theoretical properties of its components: dependence of recognition-alignment on ratios of group mean citation rates to the overall mean; bounds and equality conditions; characterization of the maximum feasible composite score (composition ceiling) as an affine function of total variation distance to a uniform reference; Fréchet-type bounds relating the composite factor to this ceiling and to a participation-weighted recognition score. Provide an exact logarithmic decomposition of the composite index, prove ordering relations between primary and reciprocal-symmetric recognition scores, show invariance properties, and derive closed-form expressions for first and second moments of recognition ratios under permutation-based null models (global and stratified). Validate all results through numerical checks implemented in an accompanying script.

Result: The paper shows that the recognition-alignment score depends only on relative mean citation rates of groups, not on absolute citation levels. It derives explicit bounds and equality conditions for each component of KRATOS, and proves that the composition ceiling is an affine function of the total variation distance between the actual participation distribution and a uniform reference. It establishes Fréchet-type bounds that constrain the participation–recognition factor using this ceiling and a participation-weighted recognition score. The authors obtain an exact logarithmic decomposition of the composite index, prove that the primary recognition score consistently orders groups relative to a reciprocal-symmetric variant, and demonstrate several invariance properties. They also provide closed-form formulas for the first and second moments of recognition ratios under both global and stratified permutation null models, and numerically verify all analytical results.

Conclusion: KRATOS is given a complete mathematical foundation as a purely measurement-structural diagnostic comparing group participation and citation-based recognition. Its behavior is shown to depend on relative mean citation rates and structural features such as total variation distance from uniform group composition. The index is bounded and decomposable, but composite rankings can be sensitive to small group sizes, heavy-tailed citation distributions, and reassignment of metadata. The framework itself is explicitly non-normative: it does not by itself measure epistemic change, justice, or fairness, but rather supplies a transparent, rigorously analyzed measurement structure that others may use, with appropriate caution, in substantive evaluations of group recognition in bibliometric data.

Abstract: KRATOS is a group-structured bibliometric diagnostic that compares the distribution of documents (participation) with the distribution of citation weight (recognition) over a fixed, finite universe of analytical groups. This note gives its complete mathematical specification and derives the properties that govern its interpretation. Beyond bounds and equality conditions for each component, we show that the recognition-alignment score depends on citation data only through ratios of group mean citation rates to the corpus mean; that the composition ceiling of the participation--recognition factor is an affine function of the total variation distance to the uniform reference; and that the factor itself satisfies Fréchet-type bounds in terms of this ceiling and a participation-weighted recognition score. We establish an exact logarithmic decomposition of the composite index, an ordering between the primary and a reciprocal-symmetric recognition score, invariance properties, and closed-form first and second moments of the recognition ratios under global and stratified permutation nulls. These results explain why composite orderings can be sensitive to small groups, heavy-tailed citation distributions and metadata reassignment. All results are verified numerically with an accompanying script. The specification concerns measurement structure only; it does not define a measure of epistemic change or justice.

</details>


### [221] [LatentIndex: Cross-Layer Sharing with Layer-Specific Selection for Sparse Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04635)
*Zhaohui Wang,Zhixin Pan,Fanxu Meng,Muhan Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LatentIndex shares a continuous latent cache across multiple attention layers to reduce sparse-attention indexing cost and memory while keeping layer-specific token selection quality and speed close to dense/sparse baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sparse attention reduces computation but existing indexers still repeatedly compute token selection and store separate key caches per layer, causing memory and speed overhead. Reusing indices across layers saves cost but forces all those layers to attend to the same tokens, hurting flexibility and potentially accuracy. The authors want a way to efficiently reuse information across layers without tying them to identical token subsets, improving long-context efficiency for modern LLMs.

Method: They introduce LatentIndex, which applies latent-sharing across indexer layers: (1) group several layers and build a shared latent cache once from the first (anchor) layer's hidden states; (2) let each layer in the group compute its own scores over this shared latent cache using layer-specific scoring so that token subsets can still differ; (3) absorb key decoders into the queries so historical per-layer keys need not be reconstructed; (4) design a training-free calibration scheme so LatentIndex can be plugged into existing models and also explore a training-aware version; and (5) propose a hierarchical selection (HS) variant where the anchor proposes a candidate token set and follower layers refine it independently for a better trade-off between computation and quality.

Result: On DeepSeek-V3.2, LatentIndex with four-layer sharing cuts logical indexer-cache storage by 61.1%. On DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5, the training-free LatentIndex improves head-wise attention-mass recall by up to 3.28 percentage points over IndexCache, while keeping RULER and LongBench scores close to native dynamic sparse attention (DSA). The HS variant yields 2.30–2.72× decode indexer speedups over DSA for 8K–128K token contexts, preserving most of LatentIndex’s recall benefits.

Conclusion: Sharing continuous latent representations for cross-layer indexing allows efficient reuse of computation and cache storage while preserving layer-specific token selection, outperforming prior index-caching methods in recall and speed, and staying close to original sparse-attention quality on standard long-context benchmarks.

Abstract: Sparse attention reduces core-attention computation, but its indexers still incur repeated selection work and per-layer key-cache storage. Reusing selected indices across layers reduces this overhead but constrains multiple layers to the same token set. We introduce LatentIndex, which extends the latent-sharing principle of Multi-head Latent Attention across indexer layers. Each layer group constructs a shared latent cache from its first layer's hidden states, while layer-specific scoring enables independent token selection. Absorbing key decoders into queries enables direct scoring of the shared cache without reconstructing historical per-layer keys. We develop training-free calibration and investigate a training-aware instantiation of this principle. To balance quality and computation, a hierarchical selection (HS) variant lets followers independently refine a shared candidate set proposed by the anchor. With four-layer sharing, LatentIndex reduces logical indexer-cache storage by 61.1% on DeepSeek-V3.2. Across DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5, training-free LatentIndex improves head-wise attention-mass recall over IndexCache by up to 3.28 percentage points while maintaining RULER and LongBench performance close to native DSA. HS further achieves 2.30-2.72 times decode indexer speedups over DSA across 8K-128K contexts, retaining most of LatentIndex's recall. LatentIndex offers a new perspective on cross-layer indexing: sharing continuous representations rather than discrete selections enables efficient reuse while preserving layer-specific token selection.

</details>


### [222] [SEIS: Self-Evolving Inference Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04646)
*Zhen Xu,Jingyu Liu,Zongze Li,Tahseen Rabbani,Ce Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents SEIS, a self-evolving inference system that autonomously optimizes an LLM inference engine end-to-end, achieving over 3× throughput gains versus the baseline and outperforming existing SOTA systems on single-request workloads.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM inference is expensive and latency-sensitive, and existing optimization work tends to focus on isolated components like kernels or memory rather than the full inference stack. The authors aim to explore whether an autonomous agentic system can holistically redesign and optimize an entire inference engine without human intervention, potentially uncovering non-obvious system-level improvements and reducing manual engineering effort.

Method: They build SEIS (Self-Evolving Inference Systems), an agentic framework that iteratively optimizes the mini-sglang inference engine. SEIS runs multiple optimization sessions where agents propose code changes, test them, inherit experiences from previous sessions, and refine the design end-to-end. The resulting system-level changes are evaluated for correctness (numerical differences and downstream task accuracy) and performance (throughput). They compare SEIS-optimized mini-sglang against the original engine and state-of-the-art inference systems such as vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and SGLang.

Result: On an H100 serving Qwen3-0.6B, the SEIS-optimized engine achieves 3.27× throughput over the original mini-sglang implementation and outperforms vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and SGLang in single-request workloads. Analysis of the code and optimization histories shows that the performance gains stem from substantial redesigns of the entire engine and that cumulative, experience-informed sessions outperform independent optimization attempts.

Conclusion: Agentic self-evolution can successfully optimize a complex LLM inference system end-to-end, delivering substantial performance gains beyond manual per-component tuning. The findings indicate that such agents can autonomously discover system-level design improvements and that iterative, experience-carrying optimization sessions are especially effective. The authors argue that evaluation methodologies must co-evolve with the optimized systems and suggest that allowing agents to also autonomously evolve the evaluation process is a promising next step.

Abstract: Inference systems determine how fast and how cheaply language models can be served, so making them faster has direct practical value. However, prior work focuses mostly on optimizing certain parts such as kernels or memory within the large system. In this work, we take a holistic approach and apply agentic self-evolution to optimize the whole system end-to-end. Our SEIS (Self-Evolving Inference Systems) autonomously optimizes the entire mini-sglang engine without human intervention through iterative sessions with inherited experiences and code changes. Serving Qwen3-0.6B on H100, the resulting engine reaches 3.27X the throughput of the original mini-sglang implementation and beats SOTA engines like vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and SGLang in the single-request workload. The correctness of the optimized inference engine by SEIS is tested in terms of numerical difference and downstream accuracy on math and long-context retrieval tasks. The code and session histories show that the speedup comes from redesigning the whole engine and that building on earlier sessions beats independent attempts. These results suggest that agentic self-evolution can optimize a complex system end-to-end. The evaluation also has to evolve with the engine, and letting agents evolve it is a natural next step.

</details>


### [223] [PermVLA: Factorization Order as a Regularizer for VLA Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04659)
*Yanqiao Chen,Yuhan Rui,Dongsheng Hou,Zijie Nie,Yutong Wan,Qi Hao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a new training regularizer for vision-language-action policies that leverages multiple factorizations (reveal orders) of the same expert action chunk to improve policy robustness and performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing VLA policies usually learn from expert trajectories using a fixed left-to-right (chronological) factorization of action sequences during training. However, the same trajectory admits many valid chain-rule factorizations, and over-reliance on a single factorization (standard teacher forcing) can harm generalization and robustness. The authors aim to treat factorization order as an explicit regularization choice and exploit alternative reveal orders to better use the same demonstration data without collecting more examples.

Method: They introduce causally anchored permutation (CAP), which defines a family of action reveal orders for each expert action chunk, anchored by a tunable chronological prefix and followed by a permutation of the remaining actions. During training, they sample different reveal orders and use an auxiliary objective where a single shared policy predicts each action given different known subsets of the same chunk (conditional-set augmentation). At deployment, the policy still operates with standard left-to-right control. They also propose a diagnostic that measures the expected squared difference in joint log-likelihood of a chunk under two different reveal orders to test consistency across factorizations, and they outline how the same idea can regularize diffusion-based action generators.

Result: In controlled experiments on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus benchmarks, CAP-trained policies consistently outperform standard left-to-right training given the same demonstration data. Similar benefits are observed in cross-dataset evaluations on CALVIN, suggesting improved generalization. The diagnostic shows that policies trained with CAP have reduced disagreement in joint log likelihood across different reveal orders, indicating the model has internalized factorization-invariant structure.

Conclusion: Factorization order is an important and previously underused regularization dimension for VLA policy training. Sampling causally anchored permutations and training with subset-conditioned auxiliary objectives (conditional-set augmentation) improves robustness and performance without requiring additional demonstrations. This approach offers a general recipe for building regularizers for sequence-based VLA models and can extend beyond autoregressive policies to settings like diffusion-based action generation.

Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies commonly learn action chunks through a fixed left-to-right (LTR) factorization, although the same expert trajectory distribution admits many valid chain-rule factorizations. We identify factorization order as an overlooked regularization choice and introduce causally anchored permutation (CAP), which samples action reveal orders with a tunable chronological prefix. Its auxiliary objective trains one shared policy to predict actions from different known subsets of the same expert chunk, while deployment retains deterministic LTR control. We call this conditional-set augmentation: it creates multiple conditional prediction problems from one expert chunk without adding demonstrations. This discourages reliance on the single chronological prefix used by ordinary teacher forcing. Controlled experiments show that CAP consistently outperforms standard LTR training on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, with the same advantage appearing in cross-dataset CALVIN evaluation. A diagnostic that measures the expected squared difference between a chunk's joint log likelihood under two reveal orders verifies that CAP training internalizes agreement across reveal orders. These findings position sampled subset-conditioned auxiliary objectives as a general recipe for constructing VLA regularizers, illustrated by an extension to diffusion action generators.

</details>


### [224] [Efficient Neural Surrogates for Linear Radiation Transport on the Lattice and Hohlraum benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04665)
*Carmelo Gonzales,Steffen Schotthöfer,Cory D. Hauck*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper benchmarks two neural surrogate architectures for solving 2D linear radiation transport equations and shows that inductive-bias choices must be tuned per architecture and quantity of interest.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-fidelity solvers for linear radiation transport equations are too computationally expensive for outer-loop tasks like optimization and uncertainty quantification, so fast and accurate neural surrogates are needed. However, architectural and inductive-bias choices that work on one transport problem do not easily generalize across model families, motivating a systematic comparison.

Method: The authors construct and compare two parameter-matched neural surrogate architectures: Transolver, which uses physics-attention mechanisms, and BSMS-MGN, a multi-scale graph neural network. Both are trained as end-to-end predictors of final-time particle concentration for 2D linear RTEs on standard Lattice and Hohlraum benchmarks. They run ablation studies on the use of Fourier features and region-weighted training losses to probe architecture-dependent inductive biases and evaluate performance per quantity of interest.

Result: Both architectures can approximate the final-time particle concentration, but their performance and sensitivity to inductive-bias choices (like Fourier features and region-weighted loss) differ significantly. The study finds that architectural details strongly affect which biases are beneficial and that a single global field-level error metric is not sufficient to judge downstream usefulness; instead, performance must be assessed per quantity of interest.

Conclusion: Neural surrogate design for radiation transport must be tailored per architecture and per quantity of interest; generic best practices do not reliably transfer across model families. The authors provide an open-source training and evaluation pipeline, enabling reproduction and extension to related transport problems and integration of these surrogates as amortized forward models in larger simulation workflows.

Abstract: Linear radiation transport equations (RTEs) form the simulation foundations underpinning design and analysis tasks in nuclear engineering, inertial confinement fusion, medical imaging, and astrophysics, but resolving the high-dimensional phase space at engineering fidelity remains expensive enough that outer-loop workflows, such as design optimization, uncertainty quantification, and parameter sweeps, are routinely budget-bound on traditional solvers. Neural surrogates promise to relax this bottleneck by amortizing simulation cost across thousands of downstream queries, but the architectural choices and engineered inductive biases that make a surrogate accurate on one transport problem do not transfer straightforwardly across model families. We benchmark two parameter-matched neural surrogate architectures, the physics-attention Transolver and the multi-scale graph network Bi-Stride Multi-Scale MeshGraphNet (BSMS-MGN), as end-to-end approximations of the final-time particle concentration for the two-dimensional linear RTE on the canonical Lattice and Hohlraum benchmarks. An ablation across Fourier features and region-weighted training loss exposes strongly architecture-dependent inductive-bias preferences, indicating that design choices common to physics-informed surrogate workflows must be revisited per architecture rather than imported across model families, and that downstream utility depends on per-QoI sensitivity rather than a single field-level score. The model training recipe, training data, and evaluation pipeline are released alongside this paper to support reproduction, transfer to related transport problems, and evaluation as amortized forward-model components in larger outer-loop simulation workflows.

</details>


### [225] [A Tropical Geometry View of Forgetting: A Per-Unit Projector for Knowledge-Preserving Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04670)
*Yuyang Zhang,Xiaoyin Chen,Chunlin Ren,Qihuang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose a new, gate-aware per-unit projection method to reduce catastrophic forgetting when fine-tuning language models, using tropical geometry of ReLU layers to derive it, and show it outperforms existing replay-free projectors under the same constraint budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fine-tuning large language models on new data often degrades their performance on previous capabilities (catastrophic forgetting). Existing replay-free protection methods (like Adam-NSCL and GPM) use a single shared protected subspace per layer, which is theoretically coarse and empirically suboptimal. The authors want a more precise way to protect prior knowledge while still allowing effective learning, guided by the true geometry of ReLU activations and gating patterns.

Method: They analyze the tropical geometry of ReLU layers: in data space, ReLU unit boundaries form tropical hypersurfaces whose cells relate to zonotopes; in weight space, each past token defines a constraining hyperplane, and all tokens define a polyhedron of weights that preserve their activation signs. They derive an exact identity decomposing the squared output change under weight updates into three terms: in-cell, open-to-closed, and closed-to-open, with the first two depending only on tokens that actually activate a unit. This yields a gate-aware, per-unit projection rule and a budget-separation theorem quantifying how many constrained directions are needed for exact protection, showing per-unit gating is more parameter-efficient than a shared subspace constraint. They implement this projector for transformer LMs (OPT-1.3b and OPT-6.7b) and compare against Adam-NSCL and GPM at matched constraint budgets, also studying pruning repair with different local error models and penalties.

Result: On OPT-1.3b, where most (token, unit) pairs are inactive (closed), the proposed projector consistently forgets less than Adam-NSCL for all matched budgets of 9–60 constrained directions per row, with relative forgetting reductions from 1.1x up to 4.3x; at a fraction (1/5.5) of the constrained directions, it achieves half the forgetting of Adam-NSCL at GPM’s energy threshold. On OPT-6.7b it achieves similar forgetting as Adam-NSCL at the same budget but allows more learning on new data. Experiments show that choosing constraint tokens based on whether units are open (activated) is crucial: open-token sets beat random, sign-blind, and anti-gate token selections in 18/18 seed pairs. For pruning repair, they show that gradient-based local models of the output error at dense weights are blind to sign changes (open/closed transitions), causing unconstrained minimizers to leave the safe polyhedron; a standard closed-form solution performs 1.94 nats worse than no repair on OPT-1.3b, while introducing a convex one-sided penalty can bound such escapes.

Conclusion: A gate-aware, per-unit projection scheme derived from the tropical geometry of ReLU layers provides a more efficient and effective way to protect prior knowledge during fine-tuning than existing shared-subspace replay-free methods. The key is to respect the open/closed gating structure of tokens at each unit, yielding better forgetting–learning trade-offs for a given constraint budget and clarifying why sign-blind local error models fail in pruning repair. The open/closed partition emerges as the main operative variable for both theory and practice, and convex one-sided penalties can enforce staying within the safe activation polyhedron when repairing pruned models.

Abstract: Fine-tuning a language model on new text degrades what it already does. Replay-free projectors such as Adam-NSCL and GPM forbid one shared subspace of a layer's inputs in every row of the update. The tropical geometry of a ReLU layer shows why this is too coarse. In data space, the units' walls are tropical hypersurfaces whose cells are dual to the upper vertices of a zonotope; in weight space, each old token is a hyperplane, and the tokens cut out a polyhedron, the closure of the weights that keep every token on its side. An exact identity joins the two pictures: the squared change of the layer's output under any weight change splits into in-cell, open-to-closed and closed-to-open terms, and the first two live on the tokens each unit fires on. The identity names a gate-aware per-unit projector, and a budget-separation theorem prices exact protection: it costs a unit the rank of its own open tokens, while a shared subspace pays at least the rank of their union in every row. On OPT-1.3b, where 96% of (token, unit) pairs are closed, the projector forgets less than Adam-NSCL at all six matched budgets from 9 to 60 constrained directions per row, the gap widening from $1.1\times$ to $4.3\times$; with 1/5.5 of the directions it halves the forgetting of Adam-NSCL at GPM's energy threshold. On OPT-6.7b, it matches Adam-NSCL's forgetting at matched budget while learning more. As the theory predicts, the open/closed partition is the operative variable: open tokens beat random, sign-blind and anti-gate token sets on 18 of 18 seed-pairs. In pruning repair, every derivative-based local model of the output error at the dense weights is blind to pairs that open: the minimisers of the gate-weighted objective can leave the polyhedron, the objective's closed-form solution is 1.94 nats worse than no repair on OPT-1.3b, and a convex one-sided penalty bounds the escape.

</details>


### [226] [MASBench: Benchmarking LLM-based Multi-Agent Collaboration under Partial Observability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04672)
*Qizhi Chu,Zekai Yu,Sijie Wen,Yang Liu,Chen Qian,Cheng Yang,Chuan Shi,Zhiyuan Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces MASBench, a benchmark to evaluate LLM-based multi-agent collaboration under partial observability, with structured tasks and deterministic metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based multi-agent systems often assume full/global observability and lack systematic ways to evaluate collaboration mechanisms, despite real-world settings being partially observable and dependent on good coordination designs.

Method: The authors design MASBench, a benchmark of multi-agent tasks built with partial observability constraints. It contains three progressive categories of tasks—Reasoning, Scheduling, and Game—each aimed at stressing different collaboration aspects. They test three representative collaboration mechanisms (Protocol, Memory, Routing) across various LLM backbones, and define deterministic evaluation metrics such as performance score, communication cost, and cost-effectiveness.

Result: MASBench reveals how different collaboration mechanisms and LLM backbones perform under partial observability, quantifying both task success and communication overhead. The experiments provide comparative data and empirical patterns of which designs work better under which conditions.

Conclusion: MASBench offers a structured, partially observable benchmark and clear metrics for evaluating and comparing LLM-based multi-agent collaboration mechanisms, giving practitioners guidance for designing more effective multi-agent systems.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have progressively evolved into the core of autonomous agents. Building on this progress, LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) coordinate multiple agents into a synergistic team to accomplish complex tasks that exceed the capabilities of individual agents. The effectiveness of such systems depends not only on the agents themselves, but also on how collaboration mechanisms are designed and organized. Note that real-world collaboration is typically partially observable, where each agent can only access partial information about the environment due to physical or privacy-related constraints. However, many existing multi-agent benchmarks assume global observability, and leave limited support for systematically evaluating collaboration mechanisms. To bridge this gap, we introduce MASBench, a multi-agent collaboration benchmark designed under partially observable constraints. It is organized into three progressive task categories: Reasoning, Scheduling, and Game. Through this structure, we progressively evaluate three representative collaboration mechanisms: Protocol, Memory, and Routing. MASBench further provides deterministic evaluation metrics, including performance score, communication cost, and cost effectiveness, to characterize both collaboration outcomes and communication overhead. Experiments across diverse LLM backbones and mechanism configurations offer empirical guidance for effective MAS design. Code is available at: https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/MASBench

</details>


### [227] [When Debate Helps: Proposal Supply and Verification-Aware Readout in Multi-Agent Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04686)
*Zihao Zhao,Tunyu Zhang,Haizhou Shi,Yusong Zhao,Xinxi Zhang,Hao Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies why multi-agent debate doesn’t reliably outperform simple majority voting and identifies two key ingredients: having a diverse set of correct proposals and a mechanism that can detect and select the correct one. It introduces a formal metric and a latent verification model, and shows how to build agent societies that improve both proposal coverage and truth-sensitive evidence use, leading to higher reasoning accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although multi-agent debate is widely used to improve reasoning in language models, it often fails to beat naïve majority voting over model outputs. This raises a puzzle: when and why does debate help? The authors want to understand the conditions under which debate yields genuine gains, diagnose failure modes, and move beyond opaque empirical comparisons toward a principled account of what debate must provide over simple voting.

Method: 1) They formalize the notion of “recoverable headroom”: cases where at least one agent proposes a correct answer but the majority is still wrong. This quantifies the potential benefit of better readout beyond voting. 2) They introduce Latent Verification Debate (LVD), an abstract accounting model where each candidate answer gets its own verification evidence before the final choice is generated. Using controlled interventions with a fixed set of proposals, they manipulate only the verification evidence to measure its effect on answer probabilities and decisions, expressed in peer-support units. 3) To improve the supply of correct proposals, they construct multi-agent “societies” from neural-thicket agents and select them using coverage-based objectives, both with and without labels, to maximize complementary (diverse and correct) proposals. 4) They run matched-budget reasoning benchmarks across two backbone models, using repeated stochastic evaluations and round-level controls to isolate the effects of proposal coverage and interaction.

Result: Empirically, they find: (a) the fixed-proposal LVD interventions show that truth-aligned verification evidence significantly shifts answer probabilities and final decisions, independent of proposal supply; (b) coverage-based selection of neural-thicket agent societies increases complementary proposal coverage—more questions have at least one correct but non-majority proposal; (c) these coverage-selected societies achieve higher aggregate accuracy than baselines on reasoning benchmarks under the same compute budget; and (d) round-level controls indicate that the interactive debate process itself contributes gains beyond just applying a strong finalizer model to the initial, non-interacting proposals.

Conclusion: Debate helps over majority voting only when two complementary conditions are met: (1) proposal coverage is high enough that correct answers are present among agents’ suggestions, and (2) the system uses verification-style evidence in a truth-sensitive way to preferentially select those correct proposals. Their formal recoverable headroom metric and the Latent Verification Debate model disentangle proposal supply from readout quality, and their society-construction experiments show that improving both aspects leads to consistent gains in reasoning accuracy. This framework clarifies when multi-agent debate is beneficial and guides the design of more effective debating systems.

Abstract: Multi-agent debate can improve reasoning, yet often fails to beat simple majority voting. We argue that successful debate requires two distinct mechanisms: proposal supply must surface a correct answer, and readout must identify that answer when voting misses it. We formalize the first requirement through recoverable headroom, which measures cases where a correct proposal is available but the majority answer is wrong. For the second, we develop Latent Verification Debate (LVD), an accounting model in which candidate proposals receive answer-specific verification evidence before final generation. Controlled fixed-proposal interventions estimate this latent effect in equivalent peer-support units and show that correct evidence changes answer probabilities and generated decisions while proposal supply remains fixed. To improve proposal supply, we construct societies from neural-thicket agents using labeled and label-free coverage objectives. Across two backbones and matched-budget reasoning benchmarks, coverage-selected societies increase complementary proposal supply and improve aggregate accuracy in repeated stochastic evaluations. Round-level controls further show that interaction provides gains beyond applying the same finalizer directly to the initial proposals. These results identify proposal coverage and truth-sensitive evidence use as complementary conditions for debate to outperform voting. Code is available at https://github.com/Wang-ML-Lab/when-debate-helps.

</details>


### [228] [RAGStress: A controlled benchmark for evaluating retrieval-augmented generation under knowledge-base degradation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04691)
*Shiqi Yang,Jiekai Ma,Gaoyuan Du*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce RAGStress, a benchmark to systematically stress-test Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models when the knowledge base is corrupted, showing current evaluations on clean data hide major robustness issues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most RAG evaluations assume a clean, perfectly reliable knowledge base, which is unrealistic in real-world deployments where documents can contain errors, contradictions, or irrelevant content. The authors want to understand how robust RAG systems are when the underlying knowledge base is systematically degraded, and to provide a controlled way to study different types and severities of corruption.

Method: They build RAGStress, a benchmark that systematically corrupts a single MMLU-based knowledge base using four realistic corruption types—factual corruption, numeric typos, relevance poisoning (irrelevant but plausible content), and explicit contradiction injection—each applied at three severity levels: subtle, moderate, and obvious. The KB is metadata-filtered and constructed from 57 MMLU subjects and 182,546 documents. They run 52,500 evaluations across combinations of models, questions, and corruption conditions to analyze performance trends and robustness properties. They also release scripts, prompts, schemas, and evaluation code as an artifact bundle.

Result: Empirical results show: (1) Evaluations on clean retrieval hide important robustness differences between RAG systems; (2) Corruptions that change semantic meaning (e.g., factual changes, contradictions) are much more damaging than ones that primarily affect surface form or utility (e.g., numeric typos); (3) A model’s accuracy without retrieval does not reliably predict how robust it is when retrieval is corrupted; and (4) Measuring accuracy on a mixture of clean and corrupted KBs does not give a reliable worst-case robustness estimate.

Conclusion: RAGStress provides a controlled stress-testing framework for analyzing how RAG systems behave under different types and severities of knowledge base corruption. The authors argue it should be used as a robustness diagnostic tool and stress test for RAG under KB degradation, rather than as a general-purpose leaderboard, and they clarify the supported claims, intended usage, and limitations of the benchmark.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is typically evaluated under the implicit assumption that the underlying knowledge base (KB) is clean, leaving the behaviour of RAG systems under realistic KB degradation poorly characterised. We introduce RAGStress, a controlled evaluation benchmark for stress-testing RAG systems under systematic KB corruption. The benchmark pairs four naturalistic corruption types (factual corruption, numeric typo, relevance poisoning, and contradiction injection) with three severity levels (subtle, moderate, and obvious) over a single-KB, metadata-filtered experimental design built from 57 MMLU subjects and 182,546 documents. Across 52,500 model-question-condition evaluations, RAGStress reveals that clean retrieval can mask robustness differences, semantic-fidelity corruptions are substantially more harmful than signal-utility perturbations, no-retrieval accuracy does not predict corrupted-retrieval robustness, and mixed-KB accuracy should not be treated as worst-case robustness. We document the benchmark's intended use, supported claims, and limitations, and provide an artifact bundle including generation scripts, corruption prompts, metadata schema, and evaluation code. RAGStress is intended as a controlled stress test for RAG robustness under KB corruption, not as a general model leaderboard.

</details>


### [229] [Penumbra: Sample-Efficient Adversarial Search for Regulatory Obligations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04693)
*Anthony Rhodes*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Penumbra, an adaptive adversarial search method to efficiently find minimally-different pairs of compliant and non-compliant LLM responses for regulatory obligations, enabling sample-efficient red-teaming of high-stakes agent behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agents are being deployed in high-stakes domains like finance, healthcare, and law, where regulatory obligations often hinge on subtle omissions or wording. Violations may leave no obvious textual signature, and whether a response is compliant depends critically on what is *not* said. Regulators and red-teamers need to find responses that lie just on either side of compliance boundaries, but searching for such minimally different pairs is expensive: each probe requires generating a response and having it adjudicated, often by multiple evaluators. Thus, the key bottleneck is not how much text can be generated, but how efficiently probes can discover the boundary between compliant and non-compliant behaviors. Existing naive or uniform search methods are sample-inefficient and do not target the most informative parts of the obligation–defeat space.

Method: The authors propose Penumbra, an adversarial search procedure that starts from a verified compliant (or non-compliant) anchor response and then iteratively explores edits under an expanding edit budget. The search walks through the space of minimally edited variants until a committee of two evaluators flips its verdict from compliant to non-compliant (or vice versa). When such a flip is detected, Penumbra outputs the two adjacent responses that lie on opposite sides of the compliance boundary. The algorithm allocates its search adaptively across obligations and defeat modes, with an explicit objective of maximizing coverage of the "defeat surface"—the set of distinct (obligation × defeat mode) combinations for which it has identified a boundary-straddling pair. Penumbra is compared to baselines such as uniform allocation and naive enumeration under matched generation and adjudication budgets.

Result: Under equal budget conditions, Penumbra's adaptive allocation achieves the same coverage as uniform allocation using only 59% of the budget for 59% of candidates, demonstrating substantially higher sample efficiency. When constrained by the number of adjudicated records, Penumbra covers 1.43× as many distinct defeat modes as naive enumeration, with improvements localized to the targeted axis of exploration. Applied to a financial advisory constitution with 60 obligations, Penumbra finds 144 minimally-different pairs of responses (one compliant, one violating) that a two-evaluator committee labels differently, with the pairs differing only by a few words. Directly prompting a model to generate both compliant and non-compliant outputs for the same obligation tends to produce responses that are lexically dissimilar and thus less informative for boundary analysis. A second experiment on a clinical triage constitution with 18 obligations yields 49 such pairs, showing consistent behavior and identifying similar obligations as hardest to defeat.

Conclusion: Penumbra offers an efficient, targeted way to discover minimally-different compliant/violating response pairs that lie on the boundary of regulatory obligations. These pairs reveal where the text of the obligation itself stops resolving compliance, highlighting subtle defeat modes that deployed agents must be robust against. The method scales its cost with the complexity of the compliance boundary rather than the length or number of obligations, making it suitable for systematic regulatory red-teaming in high-stakes domains such as finance and healthcare.

Abstract: Agents are entering finance, healthcare and law, sectors where a violation leaves no lexical signature and carries real penalties. Whether an omission is material, or a disclosure sufficient, depends on what the response left out. Probing such an obligation means finding responses one minimal edit from flipping compliance, and every probe costs a generation and two adjudications, so the binding constraint on regulatory red-teaming is sample efficiency, not volume. We introduce Penumbra, an adversarial search that walks from a verified anchor under an expanding edit budget until a two-evaluator committee changes its verdict, and emits the two adjacent responses that straddle the change. Allocation is adaptive, and the objective is coverage of the defeat surface: distinct (obligation x defeat mode) cells resolved per candidate. At matched budget, adaptive allocation reaches uniform allocation's full-budget coverage on 59% of the candidates; at equal records it covers 1.43x the defeat modes of naive enumeration, and the gain is confined to the axis it targets. On 60 screened obligations of a financial advisory constitution, Penumbra returns 144 pairs, each a compliant and a violating response that the committee places on opposite sides of the boundary, differing by a handful of words where a model asked for both directly produces texts sharing almost nothing. A second constitution, for clinical triage, reproduces this on 18 obligations: 49 pairs at the same tightness, with the same modes hardest. Pairs like these show where an obligation's own terms stop deciding, which is what an agent deployed under it must be tested against, and the search finds them at a cost that scales with the boundary, not the text.

</details>


### [230] [Not Self-Decidable: LLMs Cannot Draw the Boundary of What an Agent Verifier Can Check](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04699)
*Anthony Rhodes*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how to reliably decide which rules an automated agent can check mechanically and which require human judgment, shows that models are unreliable at making this distinction, and proposes a more conservative verification framework (CoVer) to construct this boundary.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automated agents in regulated domains must enforce external rules (e.g., finance, healthcare, law). Each rule’s predicates may or may not be decidable by fixed, auditable checks. Existing practice assumes models can self-decide this split (what can be automated vs. escalated), but this assumption is untested and risky because errors can silently bypass escalation and evade audit, especially on complex regulatory text.

Method: The authors evaluate self-decidability by collecting around 22,000 labels across six corpora, including regulatory texts (EU AI Act, FINRA guidance) and the rule-set of a deployed credit agent. Four different language models from three labs label whether individual rule predicates are amenable to fixed checks or require a judge. They compare model agreement patterns, error directions, and calibration. They then propose CoVer (corroborate-then-verify), which (1) uses model unanimity only as an initial nomination that a predicate is decidable, and (2) accepts it only if a synthesized check passes robustness tests—reading fields the agent cannot write and remaining valid under deterministic rewordings. They empirically measure how this gate affects precision and coverage relative to naive model-based schemes and agreement-with-judge baselines.

Result: Models agree almost perfectly on trivial cases but fail badly and inconsistently on regulatory text; their errors are anti-correlated, so no single model is safely conservative. On a real credit agent’s own rule-set, multiple models make the same systematic error: over-asserting that rules can be handled by fixed checks, in the very direction that suppresses escalation. CoVer’s unanimity-plus-intervention gate filters out most false positives that naive corroboration would admit, improving trustworthiness at a reported cost in coverage. By contrast, using agreement with a human reference judge as a criterion is misleading: reported accuracy rises from 30% to 77% across calibration bands even though the true fraction of genuinely decidable predicates remains flat, indicating that both models and judges share the same blind spots.

Conclusion: The work argues that “self-decidability” — letting models decide which rules can be automated — is fundamentally unsafe as a standalone capability. Simple escalation or corroboration schemes cannot guarantee conservative behavior, because models share and amplify blind spots with human judges. Instead, verifiers must construct an explicit boundary using stricter mechanisms like CoVer: treating multi-model unanimity as a tentative signal, but only certifying predicates as decidable if synthesized checks survive targeted robustness and information-access tests. Reliable governance for regulated AI agents thus requires externally built verification boundaries, not trust in a model’s own judgments about when it can be trusted.

Abstract: A verifier for an agent faces rules of two kinds: the ones a fixed check can settle and the ones that require a judge. A team that derives its own checks fixes that split up front. Where the requirements come from outside, as in finance, healthcare and law, the agent enforces rules it did not write, so the split falls to runtime, recurring for every predicate of every rule on every action at a rate no reviewer can audit. Every escalation scheme assumes a model can make that decision itself, that it is self-decidable. Across six corpora, including the EU AI Act, FINRA guidance and a deployed credit agent, we collect roughly 22,000 labels from four models built by three labs. They agree almost perfectly where the answer is obvious and collapse on regulatory text; their errors run in opposite directions, so no model can be trusted as the conservative choice; and on the deployed agent's own rule-set they err together, over-claiming that a fixed check will do, the direction that never gets escalated. We introduce CoVer (corroborate-then-verify), which treats unanimity as a nomination, admitting a predicate only when the check synthesized for it survives intervention, reading fields the agent cannot write and holding under deterministic rewording. That gate rejects most of what corroboration wrongly admits, at a cost in coverage we report rather than tune away. The obvious alternative, agreement with a reference judge, certifies nothing: it climbs from 30% to 77% across calibration bands while the genuinely decidable share does not move, because a judge drawn from the population under indictment ratifies the blind spot it shares. Self-decidability is not a capability to elicit from a model but a boundary the verifier must construct.

</details>


### [231] [Learning to Clarify Underspecified Intents Under Limited Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04719)
*Pranav M R,Manuel Cherep,Pattie Maes,Nikhil Singh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper frames question-asking by AI assistants as a value-of-information problem and uses reinforcement learning with simulated multi-turn users to train assistants that ask the most informative clarifying questions, improving users’ task outcomes with fewer interactions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI assistants often act on incomplete requests and must decide whether and what to ask to clarify user intent. Naively asking many questions burdens users, while guessing can lead to poor outcomes. There is a need for a principled way to decide which missing information is worth querying, given limited interaction budget and uncertain user preferences.

Method: The authors model clarification as a value-of-information decision problem: the assistant should acquire information whose absence would cause the largest avoidable loss in user utility. They instantiate this in an image generation setting, constructing multi-turn simulated users and designing a reinforcement learning framework where the assistant learns policies over when and what to ask to maximize expected utility recovery under uncertainty about user goals. Policies are trained and then evaluated with real users.

Result: In a preregistered human study with 76 participants and 456 interactive sessions, assistants trained with the proposed RL value-of-information framework enabled users to match reference images more accurately while asking significantly fewer questions, reducing total interaction time and lowering cost relative to baselines.

Conclusion: Modeling question-asking as a value-of-information optimization and training via RL on simulated multi-turn interactions yields assistants that disambiguate user intent more efficiently. This provides a simple, scalable framework for training language model assistants to ask more informative clarifying questions, improving user utility while reducing interaction burden.

Abstract: AI assistants receive requests that leave out information needed for a good outcome, for example about users' preferences or goals. They must then either speculate or ask for more information before proceeding. We reconceptualize this as a value-of-information problem: the assistant should acquire information whose absence causes the greatest avoidable loss in user utility. This is rarely known ex ante; rather, assistants must predict it in order to optimally allocate limited user interactions. We instantiate this problem in image generation and derive a reinforcement learning framework using multi-turn simulated users to maximize utility recovery under uncertainty. In a preregistered study with 456 interactive sessions across 76 human participants, this helped users significantly better match reference images with significantly fewer questions, less total interaction time, and lower cost. This points toward a simple and scalable framework for training language model assistants to better disambiguate user intent by asking more informative questions.

</details>


### [232] [PyINE: A Framework for Scalable Elicitation and Oversight via Code Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04737)
*Pierre-Luc St-Charles,Alessandro Palmas,Damiano Fornasiere,Storm Lei,Mirko Bronzi,Jean-Pierre Falet,Iulian Serban,Yoshua Bengio*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They build a large, program-based benchmark (PyINE) to study when and how overseers can detect shortcut-driven reasoning failures in LLMs, showing that many oversight methods miss rare but important errors, and providing a reusable framework to evaluate better oversight approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reasoning models often exploit cheap shortcuts, giving plausible-looking but wrong answers. Human or automated overseers must decide when to trust such outputs, yet it is hard to know whether the shown reasoning is genuinely reliable or hides shortcut-driven failures, especially rare ones. Existing datasets and evaluations are limited by static human annotations and are not tailored to verifiable, fine-grained oversight of model reasoning. The authors aim to create a scalable, rigorous testbed to study oversight quality and failure coverage under realistic shortcut behaviors.

Method: They introduce PyINE, a framework in which tasks are defined as instrumented Python programs. These programs generate deterministic execution traces that serve as ground truth for outcomes and intermediate facts. The framework allows mechanical generation of many task variants and matched LLM-generated code variants for counterfactual evaluation. Using PyINE-v1 (≈1M execution traces and >500k code variants), they train a shortcut-following model with reinforcement learning, using verifiable rewards from the program outcomes on cue-varied tasks. The model becomes good at predicting execution results yet still relies on misleading human-facing cues. They then test several oversight methods—activation probes, text classifiers, prompted model judges, and a lightweight debate protocol—on their ability to detect shortcut-induced errors and to make reliable thresholded trust decisions.

Result: The RL-trained model attains strong average performance on predicting program execution outcomes but continues to make systematic mistakes when surface cues conflict with the underlying program behavior, demonstrating persistent shortcut reliance. Evaluated overseers show that dataset-level metrics can obscure poor coverage of critical failure modes: simple, cheap learned overseers miss many rare shortcut-driven errors, while more powerful, model-based oversight methods provide more balanced detection but at higher computational cost and with difficulty in defining robust decision thresholds. PyINE-v1 successfully exposes these gaps in oversight performance and supports detailed analysis of when oversight fails.

Conclusion: PyINE-v1 provides a scalable, verifiable environment for studying oversight of reasoning models, particularly their shortcut-driven failures. The work shows that naive or cheap oversight approaches cannot reliably catch rare but consequential errors, even when overall metrics look good, while stronger methods are costly and hard to operationalize. By framing oversight as a failure-mode coverage and cost-sensitivity problem grounded in executable programs and traces, PyINE-v1 offers a reusable experimental setting to design, compare, and improve oversight techniques that are more robust, verifiable, and aware of shortcut behaviors.

Abstract: Reasoning models can remain capable of solving a task while still defaulting to cheaper but misleading shortcuts. This creates a central oversight problem: when a model gives an answer with plausible but incomplete reasoning, can an overseer determine whether that output should be trusted? To study this problem, we introduce PyINE, a framework for scalable elicitation and oversight using instrumented Python programs as a verifiable execution substrate. In PyINE, programs define task environments, execution traces provide authoritative labels for outcomes and intermediate facts, and task variants can be generated mechanically rather than through static human annotation. We instantiate the framework in PyINE-v1, a first release built from nearly one million deterministic execution traces and over 500,000 matched LLM-generated code variants used for counterfactual evaluation. Using standard RL with verifiable rewards on cue-varied tasks, we train a shortcut-following model that improves substantially at predicting execution outcomes while still making systematic errors when misleading human-facing cues conflict with the program's realized behavior. We then evaluate activation probes, trained text classifiers, prompted judges, and a lightweight debate protocol as overseers of this model. We find that performance pooled at the dataset level can hide weak coverage of the failures that matter most: cheap learned overseers often miss rare shortcut-driven errors, while stronger model-based checks are more balanced but substantially costlier and harder to turn into reliable thresholded decisions. PyINE-v1 turns this failure-mode coverage problem into a reusable experimental setting for developing oversight methods that are verifiable, failure-mode-aware, and cost-sensitive.

</details>


### [233] [Toward a Locally Deployable Agentic Co-Scientist: Small-Model Planning for Early-Stage Drug Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04740)
*Tian Liang,Jiayu Chang,Alejandro F. Frangi,Mobarak I. Hoque,Richard A. Bryce*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper builds a lightweight framework where small, locally run language models plan multi-step computational drug discovery workflows by calling modular tools via a unified molecular schema, and evaluates their accuracy and generalization in tool planning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Early-stage computational drug discovery requires chaining many heterogeneous tools over multiple steps, but existing solutions often rely on large cloud-based models and ad-hoc integrations. There is a need for a lightweight, locally deployable system that can reliably plan and coordinate tool calls, while being modular and extensible, and that addresses how well compact models can generalize to new workflows.

Method: The authors design a tool-augmented framework where a compact local language model plans calls to 18 modular drug discovery tools coordinated by a Unified Molecular Schema, with a plug-in interface for swapping/extending tools. They build a dataset of 1,263 manually refined query-plan pairs using workflow-graph path coverage, then apply LoRA fine-tuning to three small LLM families. They evaluate under two data splits: a query-level split (standard i.i.d.-like) and a stricter workflow-grouped split that prevents identical ordered tool sequences from appearing in both train and test, and they measure metrics like tool-selection F1, sequence exact match, and argument F1.

Result: On 47 held-out cross-group queries in the query-level split, all fine-tuned compact models generate fully parseable, schema-compliant plans. The best model, Llama 3.2-3B, achieves high performance: tool-selection F1 of 0.998, sequence exact match of 0.979, and argument F1 of 0.960. Under the workflow-grouped split that enforces unseen tool-order compositions at test time, sequence exact match drops to 0.452–0.548, indicating difficulty in composing entirely new workflow paths, even though tool calls remain mostly valid and schema-compliant.

Conclusion: Compact, locally deployable language models can effectively plan multi-step computational drug discovery workflows when supported by a unified schema and modular tool interface, achieving near-perfect tool selection and high plan accuracy on familiar workflow patterns. However, performance degrades substantially on unseen tool-order compositions, underscoring that compositional generalization in workflow planning remains a key open challenge and a priority for future work.

Abstract: Early-stage computational drug discovery requires coordinating heterogeneous scientific tools across multi-step workflows. We present a lightweight, tool-augmented framework in which a locally deployable compact language model plans calls to 18 modular tools. A Unified Molecular Schema maintains shared molecular records, while a plug-in interface supports tool replacement and extension. We construct 1,263 manually refined query-plan pairs through workflow-graph path coverage and apply LoRA fine-tuning to three compact model families. Under the query-level split, all fine-tuned models generate fully parseable and schema-compliant plans on 47 held-out cross-group queries. Llama 3.2-3B achieves a tool-selection F1 of 0.998, sequence exact match of 0.979, and argument F1 of 0.960. Under the stricter workflow-grouped split, which excludes identical ordered tool sequences across partitions, sequence exact match reaches 0.452 to 0.548, highlighting the remaining difficulty for compact models in generating complete workflow paths unseen during training. These results demonstrate the feasibility of compact, locally deployable planning while identifying compositional generalization as an important direction for further improvement.

</details>


### [234] [Formalizing the Moral Evaluation of Speech Acts: Truthfulness, Lies and Ethical Dilemmas](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04747)
*Benjamin Icard,Gauvain Bourgne,Jeanne Bonnaventure,Jean-Gabriel Ganascia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper builds a logical, ASP-implemented framework for evaluating the morality of speech acts (like lying vs truth-telling) under different ethical theories, especially in high-stakes cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a classic moral tension, going back to Kant and Constant and revisited in literature like Sartre's The Wall, about whether it is ever morally right to lie in life-or-death situations, given that benevolent lies can also lead to severe unintended consequences. Existing discussions are largely philosophical and lack a precise, formal tool for systematically comparing what different moral theories imply about specific speech acts in concrete scenarios.

Method: The authors design a formal logical framework that represents agents, their beliefs, possible utterances, and resulting outcomes. They then encode this framework in Answer Set Programming (ASP) to automatically evaluate the moral status of different speech acts (e.g., lies, truths, silence) under three ethical viewpoints: deontology, consequentialism, and principlism. They demonstrate the framework using the narrative scenario from Sartre's The Wall, and show how the framework can be adapted to other moral situations via parameter changes rather than changes to the core rules.

Result: The implemented ASP framework can, given a modeled scenario and agents' beliefs, output moral evaluations of alternative speech acts under each of the three ethical theories. Applying it to Sartre's The Wall shows that the same lie can be classified as morally right or wrong depending on how outcomes unfold and which moral theory is applied. The authors also show that the core logical structure is robust and that modeling new scenarios only requires changing parameters such as beliefs or payoffs, not the underlying ethical rules.

Conclusion: A general, flexible logical framework can capture and compare deontological, consequentialist, and principlist evaluations of speech acts in high-stakes moral contexts. By formalizing scenarios like Sartre's The Wall and earlier Kant-Constant debates, the framework clarifies when and why a benevolent lie may be judged permissible or impermissible by different theories. Its parameter-based extensibility suggests it can be used as a reusable tool for analyzing speech-act ethics across diverse situations.

Abstract: In life-or-death situations, a benevolent lie may appear more moral than telling the truth. Yet such lies can backfire, producing unintended and sometimes fatal consequences. This tension, famously disputed by Kant and Constant in 1797, applies not only to lying but to assertive speech acts in general, raising the question of which utterance should be chosen when moral stakes are high. We present a logical framework for the ethical evaluation of speech-act utterances based on agents' beliefs. Implemented in Answer Set Programming (ASP), the framework assesses utterances under deontologism, consequentialism, and principialism, and is illustrated on Sartre's The Wall (1939), a reworking of that controversy in which lying leads alternately to rescue and to death. Our setting is general by design: as two variants show, accommodating a new moral situation amounts to adjusting parameters, not rules.

</details>


### [235] [Agentic discovery of blood biomarker from distilled private health records](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04749)
*Seffi Cohen,Liat Antwarg Friedman,Amir Anisman,Ruth Johnson,Michelle M. Li,Ayush Noori,Ben Reis,Ran Balicer,Noa Dagan,Marinka Zitnik*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They built and released a privacy-preserving scoring model, trained on 5.4M patients’ CBC data, that lets AI agents evaluate and refine candidate blood-based biomarkers for 13 immune diseases without ever accessing raw patient data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Complete blood counts are widely available and cheap, so new biomarkers derived from them could greatly improve disease detection. However, rigorously evaluating many candidate CBC-derived biomarkers requires access to large, sensitive patient datasets that cannot be shared with powerful language model agents that are otherwise well-suited for hypothesis generation. The authors want a way to let such agents benefit from real-world clinical signal while preserving patient privacy and data governance.

Method: Using the Clalit Health Services dataset of 5.4 million patients, the authors trained a separate graph attention network for each of 13 immune-mediated diseases. Each network was trained to predict the case-control AUC that a given candidate expression of CBC features would achieve. Only the resulting model weights (the scoring tools), not any raw or intermediate patient data, were released. These scorers can be queried by external agents in a propose-score-refine loop to evaluate and iteratively improve CBC-based biomarker expressions. They then performed external validation: agents started from literature-based expressions, optimized them using the scorer, and they also re-ranked outputs from three existing frontier research tools across three independent cohorts.

Result: Agent-discovered CBC expressions, optimized using the released scorers, improved their AUC performance over starting literature-derived expressions by a median of 4.18 percentage points. When they used their scorer to re-rank candidate biomarkers proposed by three separate frontier tools, the re-ranked choices outperformed the tools’ original top picks in most head-to-head comparisons, though the size of the gain depended on the validation cohort. These results held across three independent external datasets.

Conclusion: The authors demonstrate that it is possible to distill the predictive signal of a massive private clinical dataset into a released scoring tool that supports biomarker discovery without exposing any patient-level data. Their graph attention network–based scorers enable privacy-preserving, data-grounded hypothesis generation for CBC-derived biomarkers across multiple immune-mediated diseases and improve upon both literature baselines and existing automated research tools.

Abstract: Routine complete blood counts (CBCs) could yield new biomarkers, but the private records needed to evaluate candidates cannot be shared with frontier language model agents that excel at discovery. We distilled the evidence held in the Clalit Health Services panel of over 5.4 million patients into a released scoring tool: for each of 13 immune-mediated diseases, a graph attention network was trained inside the data boundary to predict the case-control AUC of candidate CBC expressions, and only the trained weights were released. The tool grounds an agent's propose-score-refine loop in real-world data without exposing any patient data. In external validation, agent-discovered expressions improved on their literature-seeded starting points by a median of 4.18 AUC percentage points, and across three independent cohorts, reranking the candidates of three frontier research tools improved on their first choices in most comparisons, with gains that varied by cohort. The released scorer supports privacy-preserving biomarker hypothesis generation.

</details>


### [236] [Dynamic Routing as a New Dimension for Test-time Versatility of LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04751)
*Michal Štefánik,Marek Kadlčík,Josef Kuchař,Michal Spiegel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies whether dynamic routing in LLMs—selectively executing or iterating layers at test time—can be quickly adapted to new tasks using only a few in-context examples, without gradient updates, and shows that such routing complements chain-of-thought prompting and improves performance, especially out-of-distribution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs currently adapt at test time mainly by spending more tokens on chain-of-thought reasoning, which has limits and costs. Prior work on dynamic routing (executing subsets of layers) showed gains but typically required task-specific training and focused on similar tasks. There is a need to understand if routing programs can be rapidly discovered and used for new, possibly out-of-distribution tasks, with minimal supervision and no training, to expand LLM plasticity beyond just longer CoT.

Method: The authors consider dynamic routing programs that either skip certain layers or iterate them. They propose confidence-based selection strategies that, given a small number (3 or 10) of labeled demonstrations, evaluate different routing programs by the probabilities they assign to the correct labels, adjusted by the model’s own confidence. These strategies are applied in a training-free, transfer setting across multiple post-trained LLMs and tasks. They test performance on 49 MMLU tasks and out-of-distribution benchmarks such as ARC-AGI, compare routing vs. CoT, and analyze where confidence-based selection fails, including examining behavior early in pretraining and the distribution shift in the residual stream caused by unsuccessful routes.

Result: Confidence-based routing program selection provides consistent accuracy gains on average across the 49 MMLU tasks and yields substantial improvements for four of seven evaluated models. On challenging out-of-distribution tasks like ARC-AGI, the chosen routing programs can double the accuracy of a 7B model whose chain-of-thought prompting is ineffective. Routing and CoT succeed on different subsets of questions so that combining them outperforms CoT alone.
