Abstract: AI agents can now carry out data-driven scientific analyses end to end, and benchmarks assess them by giving an agent a question and a dataset and scoring its final answer against a fixed key. These benchmarks assume that a correct answer was derived from the supplied data, a property we call evidence grounding. However, an agent can also reach the key from prior knowledge or by ruling out the other options, and a score based on a single run cannot tell these cases apart. We show how to test this assumption and find that it often fails. For each question, we build versions of its data files in which the evidence for the answer is left intact, withdrawn or reversed, check each edit with a pre-registered reference statistic, and run the same agent on every version. We then measure evidence-grounded accuracy, which credits a correct answer only if the agent also responds when the evidence is withdrawn and follows it when it is reversed. We evaluate three agent scaffolds and five models on 18 single-cell questions from BAISBench and four synthetic problems from GeneBench-Pro. On the single-cell questions, the Claude agents are 95% accurate and answer 83% correctly without any data, but their evidence-grounded accuracy is only 41%. Hiding gene names raises the share of runs that follow reversed evidence from 58% to 93% on ten gene tasks, suggesting that prior knowledge competes with the supplied data. The benchmark score and LLM judges can also reward answers that ignore the changed evidence. Measuring scientific intelligence rather than recall therefore requires checking whether answers follow the evidence and whether scores reward them for it.

</details>


### [254] [Zero-Shot Time-Series Question Answering via Decoupled Perception and Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04942)
*Jing Xie,Haochen Yuan,Yunbo Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces TSHarness, an agent-based, zero-shot framework for time-series question answering that separates numerical perception from semantic reasoning to improve cross-dataset generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing time-series question answering models tend to overfit to specific datasets and cannot robustly handle simultaneous shifts in time-series inputs, question wording, and answer formats. There is a need for a generalizable, zero-shot approach that can work across datasets without retraining or answer feedback, while handling complex numerical observations and varied question types.

Method: The authors design TSHarness, an agentic framework that decomposes TSQA into two main components connected by a Time-Series Perception State (TPS). A learned Tool Selector consults a reusable memory of analytical knowledge and adaptively calls numerical tools to compute salient statistical and temporal features from the raw series, populating the TPS. An answering agent then conducts semantic reasoning over the TPS to generate answers, and if it judges the evidence as insufficient, it triggers iterative re-perception by re-invoking tools via a feedback loop. This workflow is fully decoupled from any dataset-specific answer supervision.

Result: TSHarness reportedly supports cross-dataset zero-shot TSQA without requiring task-specific training or answer-side supervision. By focusing on reusable numerical perception and decoupled reasoning, it better handles variations in input series, questions, and answer formats compared to prior overfitted approaches. (Exact quantitative improvements are not provided in the abstract.)

Conclusion: Separating numerical feature extraction from question-specific reasoning through the TPS and agentic tool use yields a more general, cost-efficient foundation for zero-shot time-series question answering. This decoupled, feedback-driven framework improves robustness and transfer across datasets by avoiding target-side training and explicit answer feedback.

Abstract: Time-series question answering (TSQA) requires grounding linguistic queries and diverse answer formats in complex numerical observations. However, existing methods heavily overfit to specific datasets and struggle to generalize when input series, question contexts, and answer requirements shift simultaneously. To address this challenge, we propose TSHarness, an agentic framework that establishes a decoupled workflow for cross-dataset zero-shot TSQA. At its core, TSHarness divides and conquers numerical perception and contextual reasoning via a structured Time-Series Perception State (TPS). Guided by a reusable memory of analytical knowledge, a learned Tool Selector adaptively invokes numerical tools to extract salient statistical and temporal features into the TPS. The answering agent then performs semantic reasoning over the TPS to generate target outputs, triggering iterative re-perception through the feedback loop when evidence is deemed insufficient. By separating numerical feature extraction from question-specific reasoning, TSHarness eliminates the need for target-side training or answer feedback, providing a generalizable, cost-efficient foundation for zero-shot TSQA.

</details>


### [255] [BACAM: Behavior-Aware Continual Agent Merging for Multi-Turn Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04966)
*Shuaitong Li,Baochen Xiong,Xiaoshan Yang,Xizhe Zheng,Yifan Xu,Jianhao Huang,Changsheng Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes BACAM, a method for continually merging specialized interactive agents so that a single model can sequentially acquire experts’ behaviors without needing past experts at merge time, achieving significantly higher success rates across multiple interactive tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing model/agent merging approaches assume all specialized experts are available simultaneously and typically operate only in parameter or feature space. These methods do not guarantee that the merged model reproduces the experts’ actual interactive behaviors on trajectories, and updates toward new experts can overwrite or interfere with previously merged skills. There is a need for a behavior-aware, continual merging framework that (1) does not require storing all experts, (2) explicitly aligns behavior on trajectories, and (3) balances stability (preserving old capabilities) with plasticity (acquiring new ones) in interactive tasks.

Method: The authors introduce Behavior-Aware Continual Agent Merging (BACAM). BACAM sequentially integrates new experts by learning parameter-wise merging gates, supervised by expert behavior on candidate-generated trajectories. Using expert-guided behavioral supervision, these gates control how much of each parameter is updated toward the incoming expert. The framework incorporates task-level stability-plasticity control to regulate how strongly the model should change for new tasks and tensor-level conflict-aware update budgets to cap parameter changes in regions that would interfere with existing capabilities. After training, the learned gates are folded into the base model’s weights so that no extra parameters are needed at inference.

Result: On four interactive tasks—web shopping, tool use, information retrieval, and embodied interaction—BACAM yields an average success rate of 62.82%, outperforming the best evaluated merging baseline by 21.69 percentage points. This demonstrates that BACAM more effectively preserves previously acquired behaviors while successfully integrating new expert capabilities in a continual setting.

Conclusion: BACAM provides an effective behavior-aware framework for continual agent merging, enabling a single model to sequentially absorb interactive behaviors from multiple experts without retaining past experts. By learning parameter-wise gates under behavioral supervision and constraining updates with stability-plasticity and conflict-aware budgets, BACAM mitigates interference between old and new capabilities. The strong empirical gains across diverse interactive tasks suggest that behavior-aligned continual merging is a promising direction for building versatile, continually improving agents.

Abstract: Model merging offers a way to integrate the capabilities of specialized experts, but existing agent merging methods typically require all of them to be available at once. We study continual agent merging, which integrates incoming experts sequentially without retaining previously merged experts. Yet merging in parameter space or feature subspaces does not ensure that the merged model acquires an incoming expert's behavior on interaction trajectories. Moreover, updates toward a new expert can disrupt the merged model's previously integrated interactive behavior. Therefore, we propose Behavior-Aware Continual Agent Merging (BACAM), which learns parameter-wise merging gates from candidate-generated trajectories using expert-guided behavioral supervision. Task-level stability-plasticity control and tensor-level conflict-aware update budgets limit interference with existing capabilities while allowing new ones to be acquired. The learned gates are folded into the model weights without additional inference-time parameters. Across four interactive tasks - web shopping, tool use, information retrieval, and embodied interaction - BACAM achieves an average success rate of 62.82%, exceeding the strongest evaluated merging baseline by 21.69 percentage points. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/shuaitongli/BACAM.

</details>


### [256] [Runtime Authorization of Self-Generated Subgoals in Long-Horizon Tool-Using AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04975)
*Genliang Zhu,Chu Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They design and test a formal authorization mechanism that keeps long-horizon, tool-using AI agents from gaining new authority via self-generated subgoals, while still allowing flexible replanning, and they show it is both sound and decidable in a finite domain.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon AI agents that use tools can create, revise, and delegate subgoals, which makes traditional per-tool permission checks insufficient; as agents replan and generate new goal structures, it becomes hard to guarantee that all actions stay within what the human principal originally authorized. The paper aims to close this authorization gap so that self-generated subgoals and complex goal graphs cannot become a source of new, unintended authority.

Method: The authors work in a finite, structured domain with a single principal and a single authorization root. They introduce a contract-based mechanism where each mutation to the agent’s goal graph must carry a version-bounded witness showing that its continuations, resource uses, obligations, invariants, and termination condition are refinements of the active root contract. Protected effects are revalidated at atomic commit boundaries, and free-form goal text is treated as non-authoritative. They formalize the system and prove properties such as trace-policy preservation and forbidden-state preservation under specific assumptions (explicit mediation, abstraction, freshness, atomicity). They also analyze decidability and monotonicity of safety under abstraction refinement. The mechanism is implemented as an executable model and evaluated via exhaustive exploration and structured case studies, including runtime paths, synthetic cells, and a history-aware continuation comparator.

Result: The formal model explores 340 states and 419 transitions. Across 96 matched cases spanning 25 structural schemas, the mechanism never commits a forbidden state in any of the 48 “drifted” (unsafe) cases and successfully completes all 48 benign counterparts. Two public upstream runtime paths covering 32 cases show 258 native dispatches, with every decision and receipt chain exactly matching the model. In a frozen host-local study of 129 synthetic one-factor-at-a-time cells, all outcomes align with fixed decisions and rationales. A history-aware continuation comparator successfully blocks all modeled bad trace prefixes, while still committing all operations in 11 cases where violations exist only in aspects (typed resources, freshness, explicit-join evidence) not included in its trace projection.

Conclusion: Within the considered structured domains, the proposed runtime authorization mechanism soundly enforces that self-generated subgoals do not extend an AI agent’s authority beyond what the principal originally granted. It preserves the agent’s ability to replan and manage complex goal graphs while provably preventing entry into forbidden states, with safety guarantees that are decidable and robust under suitable abstraction refinements.

Abstract: Long-horizon tool-using AI agents create subgoals, replan, delegate work, and compose sibling results. Per-tool permission checks cannot establish that a changing goal graph remains within the principal-approved task. We address this authorization gap in a finite structured domain with one principal and one authorization root. Each proposed goal-graph mutation carries a version-bound witness that its continuation traces, resources, obligations, invariants, and closing condition refine the active root contract; every protected effect is rechecked at an atomic commit boundary. Free-form goal text supplies no authority.
  We prove trace-policy and modeled forbidden-state preservation under explicit mediation, abstraction, freshness, and atomicity assumptions, plus conditional root-success preservation, a separation result for memoryless allowlists, exact finite-domain decidability, and universal-safety monotonicity under sound abstraction refinement. An executable model explores 340 states and 419 transitions. Across 96 matched cases covering 25 structural schemas, the complete mechanism commits zero forbidden states in 48 drifted cases and completes all 48 benign counterparts. Two public upstream runtime paths execute 258 native dispatches across 32 cases, with every case-level decision and receipt chain matching. A frozen host-local study covers 129 synthetic one-factor-at-a-time cells, all matching fixed decisions and reasons. A history-aware continuation comparator blocks every modeled bad trace prefix but commits all operations in 11 cases whose violations lie in typed resources, freshness, or explicit-join evidence outside its trace projection. Within the registered structured domains, runtime authorization preserves useful replanning while preventing self-generated subgoals from becoming a source of new authority.

</details>


### [257] [Do LLMs Understand Sequential Structure? A Controlled Study of Inference and Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04977)
*Jerry Wang,Zhengxiang Wang,Ting Yu Liu,Hsin-Ling Hsu,Yi-Cheng Lai,Tengfei Ma*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper evaluates whether LLMs can infer and follow latent sequential strategies, not just match action frequencies, using Rock–Paper–Scissors and stochastic n-gram tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although LLMs appear to simulate human-like behavior, it's unclear if they truly capture underlying sequential decision rules that depend on context, which is essential for valid behavioral simulation and modeling.

Method: The authors design controlled experiments: (1) two-player Rock–Paper–Scissors interactions with latent strategies, and (2) a one-player stochastic n-gram continuation task. They then measure LLMs’ ability to identify hidden strategies, follow Markovian rules, and maintain higher-order conditional dependencies, while distinguishing between mere distribution matching and true conditional rule following.

Result: They find that increasing context length does not necessarily improve the model’s ability to identify latent strategies; even when an LLM correctly recognizes a rule, it does not reliably simulate behavior consistent with it; and performance drops sharply as the order of conditional dependencies increases.

Conclusion: LLMs can produce behavior that looks realistic at the distribution level, but often fail to implement the correct underlying generative mechanisms, especially for higher-order sequential dependencies. This means that apparent behavioral fidelity in LLM simulations may be misleading and should be interpreted with caution.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as interactive agents and simulators, yet it remains unclear whether they can recover latent sequential structure beyond surface action frequencies. This distinction is critical for behavioral simulation, where actions are often shaped by prior context rather than marginal frequencies alone. We study this question using controlled two-player Rock--Paper--Scissors interactions and a one-player stochastic n-gram continuation task. Across these experiments, we test whether LLMs can identify latent strategies, follow simple Markov rules, and sustain higher-order conditional dependencies. Our framework separates distribution matching from conditional rule following. Results show that longer context does not improve identification, correct recognition does not ensure faithful simulation, and higher-order dependencies substantially degrade rule recovery. Apparent behavioral fidelity can therefore mask incorrect generative mechanisms.

</details>


### [258] [CIPO: Counterfactual Imagination Policy Optimization for Adaptive Tool Granularity Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04991)
*Yu Li,Yunlu Wan,Zijian Zhu,Han Luo,Chao Ren,Long-Fei Li,Lei Feng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes CIPO, a framework that teaches LLM agents when to use low-level tools vs. higher-level composite skills, improving success rates and efficiency in tool-using tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents solve complex tasks by calling tools over many steps, but these sequences often repeat. Manually or naively using composite skills can either over-abstract (losing fine control) or under-abstract (wasting steps). There is no principled way for an agent to decide, at each state, whether to invoke a single atomic tool or a multi-step skill. The authors aim to formalize and optimize this "tool granularity" choice to make tool-using agents more efficient and reliable.

Method: They reinterpret skill use as an adaptive tool-granularity selection problem: at each state, the agent chooses among atomic tools and composite skills. They introduce CIPO (Counterfactual Imagination Policy Optimization), which has two core components: (1) Mining composite skills by extracting frequently recurring, high-utility tool subsequences from successful trajectories under a budget constraint; (2) Training a policy over tool granularity using counterfactual branch rollouts. During training, for each base rollout, they identify the first decision where multiple granularities are available (atomic vs. skill). They then create counterfactual branches where the original choice is replaced by feasible alternatives and execute these branches. The differences in resulting outcomes (success, reward, efficiency) between actual and counterfactual branches provide a paired, localized learning signal that serves as an auxiliary reward to optimize the policy for choosing appropriate granularity.

Result: Across several benchmarks and different LLM backbones, CIPO-trained agents outperform baselines in both task success rate and decision efficiency (e.g., fewer tool calls or steps). Ablation and diagnostic studies show that the performance gains are not just from using skills more often, but from better context-dependent selection between atomic tools and composite skills.

Conclusion: Skill use in tool-using LLM agents should be treated as an adaptive tool-granularity decision problem. By mining executable composite skills and using counterfactual rollouts to directly compare atomic vs. skill choices at the same state, CIPO provides targeted learning signals that teach agents when and how to use skills. This leads to more successful and efficient tool use, demonstrating the importance of explicit granularity selection rather than naive or uniformly higher-level abstraction.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents solve complex tasks through multi-step interactions with external tools. These interactions often contain recurring local tool sequences. Treating such sequences as composite "Skills" can shorten tool-use trajectories and reduce repeated low-level decisions. However, when atomic tools and composite skills coexist, skill use becomes a policy problem: the agent must decide whether the current state requires atomic fine control or skill-level abstraction. In this paper, we argue that effective skill use should be studied as adaptive tool granularity selection. The most direct training signal for this problem is to compare the consequences of atomic and skill choices available from the same state. Based on this view, we propose CIPO, a Counterfactual Imagination Policy Optimization framework for adaptive tool granularity. CIPO constructs executable skills through budget-constrained mining of successful tool-use trajectories and trains granularity decisions with counterfactual branch rollouts. For each base rollout, CIPO branches at the first eligible granularity decision and replaces the chosen action with a feasible atomic or skill alternative. The paired outcome difference serves as a supplementary reward for policy optimization. Experiments across multiple benchmarks and model backbones show that CIPO improves task success and decision efficiency over baselines. Further analyses show that CIPO learns effective skill use by improving the choice between atomic tools and composite skills based on the current state, without simply increasing skill frequency.

</details>


### [259] [EmoRSS: Mitigating Emotion-Induced Over-Refusal in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04998)
*Shuyi Miao,Yaojin Ma,Chenhang Cui,Xiaohao Liu,Dang Jisheng,Shengda Zhuo,Fei Shen,Tat-Seng Chua*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Emotional wording in user prompts can make LLMs refuse safe queries too often. This paper identifies and counteracts the internal activation pattern that causes emotion-induced over-refusal, improving the balance between safety and helpfulness without retraining the model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety alignment work has shown that adversarial emotional prompts can help bypass safety, so models have been tuned to be more cautious. However, this can backfire: when users express strong emotions in otherwise harmless requests, LLMs may over-refuse, reducing usefulness and accessibility, especially for emotional users. There is a lack of mechanistic understanding and targeted methods for correcting this emotion-induced over-refusal while maintaining robust refusal on genuinely harmful requests.

Method: The authors propose EmoRSS, an activation-steering method. (1) They locate a refusal-sensitive layer by training layer-wise linear probes that predict refusal vs. compliance from activations. (2) At that layer, they build a low-dimensional “refusal subspace” using sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that align with the probe’s refusal direction. (3) They construct paired prompts—neutral vs. emotionally expressed but semantically equivalent—and measure the mean shift in the SAE features within the refusal subspace due to emotional expression. (4) They decode this mean shift into an activation intervention vector and, at inference time, subtract (apply in the reverse direction of) this vector for emotional prompts, without changing model weights. This is intended to remove the emotion-specific over-activation of the refusal subspace while leaving baseline safety intact.

Result: On two LLMs, EmoRSS reduces unnecessary refusals on benign but emotional queries compared with existing over-refusal mitigation baselines. It preserves or improves the rate of correct refusals on harmful requests and maintains general task performance on standard benchmarks. Quantitatively, it yields a better trade-off curve between safety (refusing harmful inputs) and helpfulness (answering benign inputs) under emotional expression than prior methods, suggesting that the targeted activation steering effectively counteracts emotion-induced bias rather than globally lowering refusal tendencies.

Conclusion: Emotional language in prompts systematically pushes LLM internal representations toward refusal, even for safe requests. By identifying and steering a refusal-related activation subspace, EmoRSS can selectively cancel the extra refusal pressure introduced by emotional expression. This yields safer and more helpful behavior under emotional user inputs, without retraining or degrading general capabilities. The work illustrates how mechanistic interpretability tools (probes, SAEs, subspace steering) can produce fine-grained safety interventions that are more precise than coarse alignment or debiasing techniques.

Abstract: Emotional expression can influence the safety decisions of large language models (LLMs), offering a potential avenue for improving safety alignment. Existing studies have mainly focused on how emotional expressions facilitate attacks under harmful requests, while overlooking their effects on benign requests. We find that emotional expression can also systematically increase refusal tendencies on benign requests, leading to unnecessary over-refusal. Based on this observation, we propose emotion-guided refusal subspace steering (EmoRSS), an activation-steering method that mitigates emotion-induced over-refusal while preserving refusal behaviour on harmful requests. Specifically, we first identify a refusal-sensitive layer using layer-wise linear probes and construct a refusal subspace from sparse autoencoder (SAE) features aligned with the probe direction. Next, we use paired regular and emotional requests with the same queries to estimate the mean activation shift in the features defining the refusal subspace. Finally, we decode this shift into an activation intervention vector and apply it in the reverse refusal direction during inference, without updating the backbone parameters. Experiments on two LLMs show that, when requests contain emotional expressions, our method achieves a more favourable trade-off between refusing harmful requests and answering benign ones than prior over-refusal mitigation baselines, while better preserving general task performance.

</details>


### [260] [How corner is a corner case? Percentile control for highway scenario generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05003)
*Jiaxi Liu,Hang Zhou,Hangyu Li,Yifan Wang,Keke Long,Chengyuan Ma,Bin Ran,Xiaopeng Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a way to generate and precisely control the extremeness (“cornerness”) of risky traffic scenarios for testing autonomous vehicles, by tying each generated scenario to a calibrated risk percentile conditioned on the observed driving history.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous vehicles must be tested on rare but critical “corner-case” scenarios in simulation before real-world deployment. Existing scenario generators can create risky or constrained situations but lack a calibrated control of *how* extreme or rare a scenario is relative to typical futures in the same traffic context. This makes it hard to systematically probe different risk levels, compare methods on a common scale, or ensure that generated scenarios correspond to realistic but high-risk situations. The paper aims to provide a principled way to define, request, generate, and evaluate scenario adversity on a shared, context-relative risk scale.

Method: The authors represent adversity as a percentile in the conditional distribution of future risk given an observed traffic history. They (1) define history-conditioned risk-percentile requests (e.g., “generate a 99th-percentile risk future for this scene”), (2) learn a reference risk distribution that maps requested percentiles to concrete physical risk targets, and (3) use a percentile-conditioned joint diffusion model with sampling-time risk guidance to generate multi-agent futures that aim to match those targets. They also design a reference-based evaluation criterion to check how well the generated scenarios realize the requested percentile using a common risk scale. The risk surrogate used in experiments is the minimum post-encroachment time (PET) between the ego vehicle and surrounding vehicles.

Result: On the highD dataset, using minimum PET as the risk surrogate, the method achieves very accurate control over requested risk percentiles. On the primary evaluation set, it satisfies 1,422 out of 1,440 risk-percentile requests within a 0.05 percentile tolerance (98.75% success), with a mean percentile error of 0.00673 and mean PET-target error of 0.00991 seconds. This demonstrates that the approach can finely tune and reliably realize the desired adversity level of generated scenarios.

Conclusion: The paper introduces a calibrated, percentile-based framework for generating context-relative risky scenarios for AV testing. By mapping requested risk percentiles to physical risk targets and generating futures with a diffusion model guided to those targets, it enables precise control and evaluation of scenario “cornerness” on a unified risk scale. This creates a practical interface between specification (desired risk percentile), physical realization (generated trajectories with specific PETs), and evaluation (checking percentile realization), potentially improving systematic safety assessment of autonomous driving systems.

Abstract: Generating corner-case scenarios with appropriate adversity in a simulation environment is critical for testing an autonomous vehicle (AV) software stack's safety performance before deployment. Existing autonomous-driving scenario generators can enforce specific behavior, adversity, or feasibility conditions, but they provide limited control over how extreme a generated scenario is relative to plausible futures in the same traffic context. This study represents the adversity of a generated scenario as its percentile in the conditional distribution of future risk given the observed history. This view supports calibrated answers to two questions: how "corner" a generated corner-case scenario is and how its "cornerness" can be fine-tuned.
  To this end, we formulate history-conditioned risk-percentile requests and learn a reference risk distribution that maps each requested percentile to a physical risk target. We then use a percentile-conditioned joint diffusion model with sampling-time risk guidance to generate multi-agent futures, together with a reference-based criterion for evaluating percentile realization.
  Experiments use the minimum post-encroachment time (PET) between the ego and its surrounding vehicles as the risk surrogate on highD. On the primary evaluation set, our method realizes 1,422 of 1,440 requests within a 0.05 percentile tolerance (98.75%), with mean percentile error 0.00673 and PET-target error 0.00991 seconds. The resulting interface connects context-relative risk specification, physical realization, and evaluation through a common risk scale. Project website and videos of generated scenarios are available at https://hhj233.github.io/CornerPercentile/.

</details>


### [261] [EVISKILL: Grounding Skill Evolution in Replayable Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05030)
*Yan Zhou,Yili Wang,Yiwei Dai,Qinggang Zhang,Xin Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EVISKILL is a framework for continual skill evolution in LLM agents that maintains explicit, replayable evidence for experience-based edits, verifies them via targeted re-execution, and gradually consolidates supported changes into persistent skills.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Continual skill evolution aims to let LLM agents improve over time from interaction without changing model parameters, by accumulating procedural knowledge. Current experience-driven approaches struggle because they often lose the contextual behavioral evidence that justified specific edits, and rely on coarse global validation: if a composite revision fails, all its local changes may be discarded, even if some are valid. Conversely, some potential improvements may need more experience before being reliably integrated. The authors want a way to (1) preserve fine-grained evidence, (2) explicitly connect edits to their supporting context, and (3) validate and refine edits over time rather than in a single global step.

Method: The authors propose EVISKILL, an evidence-driven framework where execution traces from interactions are organized into Replayable Evidence Cards that capture the relevant context and behavioral observations. From these, the system synthesizes candidate procedural edits, each explicitly linked to its supporting evidence. EVISKILL then performs targeted replay: re-executing specific scenarios using the candidate edits to verify their effectiveness and gather corrective feedback. Across learning epochs, evidence is preserved, and edits that are locally supported are provisionally retained and further refined, while an overarching global validation mechanism decides when these edits should be consolidated into the agent’s final persistent skill set.

Result: On three interactive benchmarks and across six different LLM backbones, EVISKILL shows improved performance compared to prior experience-driven skill evolution baselines. The experiments demonstrate that explicitly preserving evidence, replaying targeted contexts, and incrementally validating edits yield more reliable and effective skill updates for LLM agents.

Conclusion: EVISKILL provides a structured, evidence-centered approach to continual skill evolution for LLM agents. By encoding experience into replayable evidence cards, tightly coupling edits with their justifying contexts, and using targeted replay plus staged validation, it mitigates the loss of behavioral evidence and the crudeness of global-only validation. The framework enables agents to accumulate, refine, and ultimately consolidate more robust procedural skills from interaction without modifying underlying model parameters.

Abstract: Continual skill evolution enables LLM agents to accumulate and refine reusable procedural knowledge from interaction experience without updating model parameters. Its effectiveness depends on determining not only what to change, but also why a change is justified and when it should become persistent guidance. However, existing experience-driven methods can lose the behavioral evidence and task contexts supporting edits. Moreover, a global validation outcome provides an incomplete judgment of its constituent changes: locally supported corrections may be discarded with a rejected revision, while evidence may require further experience to inform useful updates. To this end, we introduce EVISKILL, an evidence-driven framework that organizes execution observations into Replayable Evidence Cards and synthesizes edits with explicit links to their supporting contexts. Targeted replay verifies these edits through re-execution and provides feedback for correction. Across epochs, EVISKILL preserves evidence and provisionally retains supported edits for further refinement, while global validation governs their incorporation into the final skill. Experiments on three interactive benchmarks across six LLM backbones demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach.

</details>


### [262] [CI-JEPA: A Counterfactual Analysis of Latent Representations in Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures for Self-Supervised Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05043)
*Mintu Dutta,Ritesh Vyas,Mohendra Roy **

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper extends I-JEPA with a counterfactual, intervention-aware objective that predicts representation changes between original and modified images, and uses controlled image edits to probe semantic selectivity and robustness of learned visual representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing self-supervised vision models like I-JEPA learn useful features but their training objectives do not explicitly account for how representations should change under specified visual interventions, especially distinguishing task-relevant semantic changes from nuisance variations. There is a need for a framework to systematically probe and quantify how joint-embedding predictive architectures respond to controlled, interpretable image modifications.

Method: The authors propose CI-JEPA, which augments I-JEPA with a counterfactual intervention-aware objective. Instead of only predicting latent representations of masked regions, CI-JEPA learns to predict the change in representation ΔZ = Z_CF − Z between an original image and its modified counterpart. They design controlled interventions on Flowers102: flower-center occlusion as a semantic change and background blur/tint as nuisance changes. Using frozen-encoder linear probing, they evaluate classification accuracy and measure mean L2 distances between representations before and after interventions to characterize selective sensitivity.

Result: On Flowers102, CI-JEPA reaches 78.14% validation accuracy with a frozen encoder and linear probe, slightly outperforming both pretrained ViT-B/16 and I-JEPA baselines at 77.55% (a 0.59 percentage point gain). Mean L2 representation shifts under interventions are 4.42 for center occlusion, 3.48 for background tint, and 2.83 for background blur, indicating the strongest response to the semantically important occlusion and weaker responses to background changes.

Conclusion: CI-JEPA can encode some degree of selective sensitivity, reacting more strongly to task-relevant semantic interventions than to nuisance changes, consistent with relative semantic selectivity rather than strict invariance. However, the modest accuracy gains and limited intervention set mean the work does not demonstrate broad robustness, causal feature discovery, or invariance to all visual changes. Instead, the proposed controlled interventions and ΔZ-prediction objective offer a useful framework for systematically analyzing how JEPA representations change under specific visual manipulations.

Abstract: Self-supervised visual representation learning learns useful features without manual annotations during representation training. The image-based joint-embedding predictive architecture (I-JEPA) predicts latent representations of masked image regions, but its objective does not explicitly model responses to specified visual interventions. We introduce CI-JEPA, a counterfactual intervention-aware extension that learns to predict the representation change $ΔZ = Z_{\mathrm{CF}} - Z$ between an original image and a modified counterpart. We assess representation robustness through selective sensitivity: stronger responses to task-relevant semantic changes than to nuisance changes. Experiments on Flowers102 use flower-center occlusion as a candidate semantic intervention and background blur and tint as candidate nuisance interventions. With frozen-encoder linear probing, CI-JEPA achieves a best validation accuracy of 78.14\%, compared with 77.55\% for both the pretrained ViT-B/16 and the I-JEPA baseline, a gain of 0.59 percentage points. The reported mean $L_2$ representation changes are 4.42 for center occlusion, 3.48 for background tint, and 2.83 for background blur. This ordering is consistent with relative semantic selectivity for the evaluated interventions, rather than complete nuisance invariance. The accuracy comparison is complementary and does not establish improved robustness over the baselines. These controlled image modifications provide a framework for studying intervention-induced changes in JEPA representations; they do not establish causal feature discovery or robustness to all visual changes.

</details>


### [263] [Why, Where, How: Taxonomy-guided Error Grounding for Code Repair in NL2SQL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05060)
*Suchan Lee,Woomin Song,Hwanjo Yu,Sangwoo Mo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A taxonomy-guided framework (TEG) improves automatic correction of NL2SQL queries by converting error diagnoses into targeted edit instructions and iteratively refining queries using execution feedback.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs can generate SQL that executes but yields wrong answers; simply executing the query does not show how to fix it, and existing error taxonomies describe why a query is wrong but not how to localize and correct errors. Current correction approaches either expose the full query without focusing edits, or provide feedback that is not tightly structured around specific error types. There is a need for a systematic way to ground high-level error diagnoses into concrete, localized edits that LLMs can use to reliably repair faulty NL2SQL queries.

Method: The paper proposes TEG (Taxonomy-guided Error Grounding), which converts an externally supplied error-type diagnosis into a structured correction input for an LLM-based NL2SQL repair system. For each error type in a taxonomy, TEG defines type-specific rules that identify which SQL construct classes (e.g., SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY) should be reconsidered and which edit operation (e.g., add, remove, modify) to request. TEG then prepares a modified query where the targeted constructs are masked when appropriate and attaches a natural-language edit instruction that encodes the desired operation. The LLM generates candidate corrections following this guidance; TEG evaluates these candidates via query execution feedback, selects promising ones, and iteratively applies this process error-by-error for multi-error queries.

Result: On the NL2SQL-BUGs benchmark, using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, TEG achieves 47.3% execution accuracy on single-error queries and 37.0% overall. Across various model sizes and “thinking” modes, TEG consistently outperforms baseline methods on single-error queries, including methods given the same error-type annotations. Even when the error types are predicted (rather than gold), TEG remains better than direct LLM correction and ErrorLLM on single-error cases.

Conclusion: Structuring error-type information into targeted, taxonomy-guided edit instructions and masking relevant SQL constructs enables LLMs to more effectively correct faulty NL2SQL queries. TEG demonstrates that grounding error diagnoses into localized, rule-driven query modifications, combined with execution-based feedback and iterative repair, yields superior correction performance compared to existing approaches, and remains robust even when error-type predictions are noisy.

Abstract: SQL queries that large language models write from natural language questions can execute successfully yet produce incorrect results, so execution alone does not reveal what to fix. An error taxonomy says why the query is wrong, but not where to look or how to change it. Existing methods can guide SQL correction through feedback, error reports, or generated plans alongside an unmasked query. We introduce TEG(Taxonomy-guided Error Grounding), which turns a supplied diagnosis into a structured correction input for natural language-to-SQL (NL2SQL) correction. Type-specific rules map each error type to construct classes to reconsider and an edit operation to request. TEG masks the selected constructs in the query when applicable and states that operation in an edit instruction. TEG generates candidate corrections from this input, uses execution feedback to guide candidate selection, and repeats the process one annotation at a time for queries with several errors. On NL2SQL-BUGs, TEG reaches 47.3 single-error execution accuracy and 37.0 overall with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Across the model sizes and thinking modes evaluated in the main comparison, TEG outperforms all evaluated baselines on single-error queries, even when the baselines receive the same error-type annotations. With predicted types, TEG stays above direct LLM correction and ErrorLLM on single-error queries.

</details>


### [264] [SharpDraft: Accelerating Long-Context Speculative Decoding with Cardinality-Aware Query Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05106)
*Jeonghoon Park,Seongwoon Jo,Jongwon Lee,Taesik Gong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Paper proposes SharpDraft, a training-free method to speed up speculative decoding for long-context reasoning by correcting attention mass dilution via query scaling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speculative decoding speeds up long-form reasoning by validating multiple draft tokens at once, but its gains shrink for long contexts because softmax attention spreads probability mass over many keys, reducing draft token acceptance. The authors aim to preserve speedups at long context lengths without costly online adaptation or retraining.

Method: They analyze attention-mass dilution in transformers and, under explicit assumptions, derive an exact correction for the top-k attention mass as context grows. Based on this, they design SharpDraft, a cardinality-aware query scaling scheme that sharpens attention scores according to the number of visible keys, implemented as a closed-form fixed-slope approximation that is training-free and avoids online adaptation overhead. SharpDraft is plugged into existing speculative decoding algorithms such as DFlash, PARD, and EAGLE 3.1.

Result: On benchmarks focused on long-form reasoning and long-context generation—AIME-26, GPQA-Diamond, and LongGenBench Diary—SharpDraft combined with DFlash, PARD, or EAGLE 3.1 yields 2.59–3.19× geometric-mean end-to-end speedups compared with standard autoregressive decoding. With DFlash in particular, SharpDraft both accelerates decoding and surpasses full-parameter and LoRA-based online adaptation in end-to-end speedup, without increasing peak allocated GPU memory beyond that of the original drafter.

Conclusion: SharpDraft effectively mitigates attention-mass dilution in long-context speculative decoding via a simple, training-free query scaling mechanism. It preserves and even enhances speedups of existing speculative decoding methods at long sequence lengths while keeping memory usage unchanged and avoiding the complexity of online adaptation, offering a practical drop-in improvement for long-form reasoning workloads.

Abstract: Long-form reasoning makes inference expensive, and speculative decoding mitigates this cost by verifying multiple draft tokens in parallel. Its speedup, however, can fade as context grows and draft acceptance declines. We focus on attention-mass dilution: as softmax normalizes over more visible Keys, the mass concentrated on the highest-scoring Keys can decrease. We introduce SharpDraft, a training-free method that counteracts this effect through cardinality-aware Query scaling, without the computational overhead of online adaptation. Under explicit assumptions, we derive an exact top-$k$ mass correction and deploy a closed-form fixed-slope approximation. Across AIME-26, GPQA-Diamond, and LongGenBench Diary, SharpDraft achieves $2.59$-$3.19\times$ geometric-mean end-to-end speedups over target-only autoregressive decoding when applied to DFlash, PARD, and EAGLE 3.1. With DFlash, it improves decoding speed and outperforms full-parameter and LoRA-based online adaptation in end-to-end speedup, while matching the unmodified drafter's reported peak allocated GPU memory.

</details>


### [265] [LexiHorizon: Stabilizing Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Deep Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05119)
*Zhiqing Nong,Liang Wen,Chao-Hsuan Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LexiHorizon is a training framework that makes deep search agents better at long-horizon, multi-step web search when retrieval is brittle and sensitive to query wording.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep search agents must solve complex knowledge tasks via iterative retrieval and reasoning, but real-world retrieval is often brittle: small changes in query wording or entity names can hide crucial evidence. Existing agents assume short interaction horizons and relatively stable retrieval, so they struggle to recover when early queries miss key documents and the trajectory becomes long and cluttered with partial results. There is a need for training methods that let agents explore many query reformulations over long horizons while coping with growing amounts of retrieved content.

Method: LexiHorizon introduces a training framework for long-horizon search agents with three main components: (1) an expanded trajectory context budget that allows the agent to operate over longer sequences of tool calls and observations; (2) a context-management scheme that keeps a window of recent retrieval observations for grounding, while explicitly preserving the reasoning history so prior thought processes are not lost; and (3) an outcome-gated search-effort reward that grants a bounded positive bonus for using search tools, but only on trajectories that eventually obtain a nonzero answer reward, thereby encouraging sufficient search effort without rewarding fruitless tool usage. The framework is used to train a 9B-parameter model as the search agent policy and evaluated on several benchmarks.

Result: On three benchmarks—XBench, WebWalkerQA, and BrowseComp-ZH—the 9B model trained with LexiHorizon consistently surpasses both its underlying base model and the MiroThinker-1.7-mini baseline. The paper reports maximum absolute improvements of 8.7 percentage points over its own base model and 23.8 percentage points over MiroThinker-1.7-mini, indicating substantial gains in performance on complex, long-horizon search tasks.

Conclusion: Extending the effective context horizon, managing retrieval observations with a recency window while preserving reasoning traces, and using an outcome-gated search-effort reward together make deep search agents more effective in brittle, long-horizon retrieval settings. The experiments suggest that reasoning-preserving context management, combined with a larger trajectory budget, is a practical way to improve multi-step, tool-using search agents on challenging web-style benchmarks.

Abstract: Deep search agents tackle complex knowledge tasks through iterative retrieval, multi-hop reasoning, and evidence synthesis across multiple sources. Existing approaches typically assume relatively stable retrieval systems and operate over short-horizon tool interaction. However, when retrieval is sensitive to query formulation, even a semantically appropriate query may fail to surface critical evidence because of mismatched entity names, aliases, or keyword combinations. Recovering from such failures requires repeated query reformulation and longer interaction trajectories. This setting poses a distinct training challenge, as the policy must sustain long-horizon query exploration while managing an expanding volume of retrieved content. We propose LexiHorizon, a framework for training search agents over long horizons that expands the trajectory context budget, manages accumulated retrieval content using a window over recent tool observations while preserving the reasoning history, and introduces an outcome-gated search-effort reward that provides a bounded bonus for tool invocations to trajectories with nonzero answer reward. Experiments on XBench, WebWalkerQA, and BrowseComp-ZH show that the resulting 9B model consistently outperforms both its base model and MiroThinker-1.7-mini, with maximum absolute gains of 8.7 and 23.8 percentage points, respectively. These results suggest that combining an extended context budget with reasoning-preserving context management benefits long-horizon deep search agents.

</details>


### [266] [Memory Canonicalization: A Framework and Benchmark for Cross-Model Drift in Persistent LLM Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05124)
*Amit Vadnere,Aishwarya Lonarkar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a write-time memory canonicalization pipeline for LLM external memories and introduces a benchmark (CMSC-E) to measure cross-model semantic drift and emotional consistency. A small pilot suggests possible gains in emotional consistency but no statistically robust effects after multiple-comparison correction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents increasingly rely on persistent, external memory stores (e.g., MemGPT/Letta, Mem0, Zep) accessed via standards like MCP. However, the same stored memory item can be interpreted differently by different LLMs, both factually and emotionally, leading to cross-model semantic drift and inconsistent emotional reasoning. The authors aim to standardize how memories are stored so multiple models can interpret them consistently.

Method: They design a write-time canonicalization pipeline that processes raw memory objects, detects ambiguity, conditional statements, and emotional tone, and rewrites each memory into an explicit, structurally disambiguated canonical form. Emotional content is extracted into a separate structured field rather than left implicit in the text. They formalize this pipeline, define a benchmark called Cross-Model Semantic Drift / Emotional Consistency Score (CMSC-E), and run a three-arm pilot experiment on 176 synthetic memory objects evaluated with three LLM families, comparing raw vs. canonicalized memories on factual and emotional consistency across models.

Result: Canonicalized memories show an uncorrected improvement in cross-model emotional consistency relative to raw memories: +0.050 in CMSC-E with a 95% bootstrap confidence interval [0.013, 0.086] and a paired t-test p = 0.010. However, after correcting for multiple comparisons across six tested contrasts (Bonferroni, Holm, and Benjamini-Hochberg), this emotional-consistency improvement is no longer statistically significant. No comparison for factual drift (CMSD) reaches significance, with or without correction.

Conclusion: Memory canonicalization is a promising but not yet empirically validated technique for reducing cross-model emotional inconsistency in LLM external memories. The pilot results suggest possible benefits but are exploratory and not confirmatory due to limited sample size and multiple-comparison issues. The authors call for larger-scale studies, independent judge models, human validation of canonical forms, and preregistered analyses to rigorously test the effectiveness of canonicalized memory representations.

Abstract: Persistent memory for Large Language Models (LLMs) has matured rapidly: systems such as MemGPT/Letta, Mem0, and Zep now provide agents with tiered, temporally-aware, model-agnostic external storage, while the Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes access to memory servers. A less addressed problem is that an identical stored memory object, retrieved by two different LLMs under otherwise identical conditions, may not be interpreted the same way, factually or emotionally. This paper proposes memory canonicalization: a write-time pipeline that detects ambiguity, conditional structure, and emotional loading in a raw memory object and rewrites it into an explicit, structurally disambiguated canonical form, with emotional valence represented as a separate field rather than inferred from tone. We formalize the pipeline, define a companion Cross-Model Semantic Drift / Emotional Consistency Score benchmark (CMSC-E), and report results from a three-arm pilot using 176 synthetic memory objects and three downstream model families. We find an uncorrected improvement in cross-model emotional consistency for fully canonicalized memory relative to raw memory (+0.050, 95% bootstrap CI [0.013, 0.086], paired t-test p = 0.010), but this result does not survive Bonferroni, Holm, or Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the six comparisons tested. None of the factual-drift (CMSD) comparisons reach significance at any correction level. We report these results as exploratory rather than confirmatory and outline needed follow-up work, including larger samples, independent judge models, human-validated rendering, and preregistration.

</details>


### [267] [AutoSciBench: Autonomous Benchmark Generation for Evaluating Scientific Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05140)
*Dongki Kim,Namkyeong Lee,Surag Nair,Carl Edwards,Xiner Li,Edward De Brouwer,Jenna Lynn Collier,Sung Ju Hwang,Gabriele Scalia,Ehsan Hajiramezanali*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents AutoSciBench, a framework to automatically generate and iteratively refine scientific-agent benchmarks so they stay challenging as agents improve.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing scientific benchmarks quickly become saturated as AI agents improve, and building new, high-quality scientific benchmarks requires substantial expert effort. This creates a misalignment between evaluation difficulty and evolving agent capabilities, especially in complex scientific domains that need domain knowledge, realistic data, and careful ground-truth verification. The authors aim to reduce this human bottleneck and create a way for benchmarks to co-evolve with agent capabilities, preserving their diagnostic power and exposing remaining failure modes.

Method: They propose AutoSciBench, which formalizes each benchmark task using (1) a high-level concept (scientific domain, data modality, and reasoning type) and (2) a low-level recipe (how to construct questions, environments, and verifiable answers). Agents attempt the tasks, producing solution trajectories and judge feedback. AutoSciBench analyzes these to iteratively modify the concept and recipe: closing shortcuts, increasing emphasis on raw data re-analysis, interpretation of intermediate results, and evidence integration. It also distills experience from these refinement trajectories to guide generation of new task concepts, so knowledge from past refinements informs future benchmark construction. They instantiate this starting from existing benchmarks in computational biology, materials science, and clinical imaging.

Result: The automatically generated benchmarks are more difficult: solver accuracy drops by 22.4 and 25.5 percentage points compared with original human-curated benchmarks in computational biology and materials science. Despite higher difficulty, human raters score the generated tasks as higher quality across all three domains (computational biology, materials science, clinical imaging).

Conclusion: Automatically generated and iteratively refined benchmarks, as implemented in AutoSciBench, can remain challenging and informative as agent capabilities grow, reducing reliance on manual expert curation. This suggests that scientific-agent evaluation can dynamically adapt over time while improving task quality and preserving discriminative power.

Abstract: As agents rapidly evolve, existing benchmarks can become saturated, limiting their ability to distinguish capabilities and reveal remaining failure modes. Particularly in scientific domains, constructing and updating benchmarks requires substantial time, labor, and domain expertise, making it difficult to keep evaluation aligned with advances in agent capabilities. We address this challenge by investigating whether scientific-agent benchmarks can be automatically generated and iteratively adapted as agent capabilities evolve. We introduce AutoSciBench, a framework that represents each task as a high-level concept specifying the scientific domain, data modality, and required reasoning approach, together with a low-level recipe specifying how the question, environment, and ground-truth answer are constructed and verified. Agents attempt to solve each task, producing solver trajectories and corresponding judge feedback which AutoSciBench uses to revise the recipe or concept, closing observed shortcuts and shifting tasks toward raw-data re-examination, interpretation of intermediate results, and evidence integration. Experience distilled from completed refinement trajectories further guides new concept generation, allowing lessons from earlier task refinement to inform subsequent benchmark construction. Starting from existing benchmarks, we evaluate AutoSciBench across computational biology, materials science, and clinical imaging. Generated benchmarks reduce average solver accuracy by 22.4 and 25.5 percentage points relative to the human-curated benchmarks in computational biology and materials science, respectively, while generated tasks receive higher average quality ratings across all three domains, suggesting that scientific-agent evaluation can adapt as agent capabilities advance.

</details>


### [268] [R1A-PC: Physics-Guided Electromagnetic Inversion of Three-Dimensional Human Point Clouds in Complex Static Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05144)
*Xudong Yuan,Ruyun Xu,Jingtai Yang,Xianzheng Sun*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: R1A-PC reconstructs detailed 3D human point clouds from complex electromagnetic measurements in cluttered static environments using physics-guided background subtraction and adjoint-based features.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recovering 3D human geometry from electromagnetic measurements in realistic environments is hard because strong multipath reflections from walls, floors, and objects overwhelm the weak perturbations caused by the human target. Existing learning-based methods struggle to generalize across different backgrounds and often ignore explicit physical modeling, leading to poor performance in complex scenes. The paper aims to leverage physical principles and background information to robustly separate target contributions and accurately reconstruct human geometry.

Method: The authors propose R1A-PC, a physics-guided neural reconstruction framework that takes as input paired complex electromagnetic fields measured with and without the human target. They perform complex background subtraction to highlight target-induced amplitude and phase changes while still retaining the background field as a conditioning signal. A frequency-balanced discrete Born adjoint operator is used to compute a 3D spatial “knowledge map” encoding position-dependent physical features. The decoder reconstructs a 2048-point human point cloud through two bounded deformation stages: at each stage, it fuses complex measurement features, background features, and multi-scale adjoint-based physical features queried at the current point coordinates; the second stage re-queries features after the first coordinate update. They also analyze the residual from paired subtraction, the weighted normal-operator form of the raw adjoint, and the geometric constraints defining the feasible set of point clouds.

Result: On a held-out background generated via full-wave simulation with a fixed acquisition geometry, R1A-PC achieves a squared Chamfer distance of 0.001434 m² and an F-score of 0.963080 at a 0.05 m threshold. Relative to TopNet, the Chamfer distance is reduced by 70.28%. Ablation studies show that removing physical guidance or background subtraction severely degrades performance, increasing Chamfer distance by 242.06% and 241.18%, respectively. Additional experiments across multiple background layouts and human poses demonstrate that both paired subtraction and position-dependent adjoint features are crucial and complementary for robust reconstruction.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that integrating physics-guided operators and explicit background-aware processing enables accurate recovery of human 3D geometry from complex electromagnetic measurements, even in heavily cluttered static environments. The combination of complex background subtraction and a frequency-balanced Born adjoint provides informative, position-dependent features that substantially improve reconstruction quality over purely data-driven baselines. The strong performance and ablation results indicate that such hybrid physical–learning approaches are effective for electromagnetic imaging of humans and potentially other targets in realistic scenes.

Abstract: Recovering three-dimensional human geometry from electromagnetic measure?ments in a complex static environment is difficult because strong multipath responses from walls, floors, and other objects obscure the weak target per?turbation. We propose R1A-PC, a physics-guided method that reconstructs a 2048-point human cloud from paired complex fields measured with and without the target. Complex background subtraction emphasizes target-induced ampli?tude and phase changes, while the background field remains available as an environmental condition. A frequency-balanced discrete Born adjoint produces a three-dimensional spatial knowledge map. At each of two bounded deformation stages, the decoder combines complex measurement features, background fea?tures, and multiscale physical features queried at the current point coordinates; the second stage queries again after the first coordinate update. We analyze the residual of paired subtraction, the weighted normal-operator structure of the raw adjoint, and the feasible set of the predicted cloud. In a held-out background generated by full-wave simulation under a fixed acquisition geometry, R1A-PC obtains a squared Chamfer distance of 0.001434 m2 and an F-score of 0.963080 at 0.05 m. Compared with TopNet, the Chamfer distance decreases by 70.28%. Removing physical guidance or background subtraction increases the Chamfer distance by 242.06% or 241.18%, respectively. Experiments across background layouts and poses support the complementary roles of paired subtraction and position-dependent adjoint features.

</details>


### [269] [Beyond Instruction Following: Learning Grounded Skill-Following with Skill Contracts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05161)
*Jianghan Shen,Zhenjie Liu,Yue Li,Jie Huang,Siqi Luo,Yiming Cheng,Yizhi Yao,Kaijie Zhang,Cheng Tang,Minghui Zhang,Ming Hu,Yirong Chen,Ziyan Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes Grounded Skill-Following, a framework for training agents to follow expert-authored procedural skills step-by-step in interactive environments, with verifiable progress and high procedural compliance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing instruction-following mainly checks discrete, final responses and does not ensure that agents execute all intermediate procedural steps required by complex skills. The authors aim to enforce multi-phase, environment-grounded skill execution rather than only optimizing for final task outcome.

Method: The authors formalize each expert skill as a "skill contract" that has visible instructions plus a contract runtime specifying phases, valid actions, transitions, and termination conditions. They introduce Verified Progress Credit, a reward scheme that gives credit when contract milestones are first achieved and sums them to guide reinforcement learning, and Contract-State Feedback, runtime feedback on whether actions are accepted and which next actions are valid. They evaluate by defining a new metric, Protocol Completion Rate (PCR), representing full execution of all required phases, distinct from final task success. They train Qwen3.5-4B with this framework on Math and Search tasks.

Result: When trained with the proposed framework, Qwen3.5-4B achieves very high Protocol Completion Rates—99.27% on Math and 99.96% on Search—while slightly improving final task success compared to baselines (Task Outcome of 82.95% and 46.61%, respectively). Ablation and controlled studies explore the contribution of skill instructions, reward shaping, and contract feedback and test whether behavior depends on observations.

Conclusion: Grounded Skill-Following with skill contracts, Verified Progress Credit, and Contract-State Feedback enables agents to reliably follow expert-authored procedural protocols in interactive environments, achieving near-perfect procedural compliance without sacrificing final task performance. The separation of procedural completion (PCR) from task outcome offers a clearer evaluation of whether agents actually follow specified protocols.

Abstract: Instruction following typically enforces discrete, response-level requirements, whereas an expert-authored skill prescribes procedural requirements spanning multiple phases and environment interactions. Given such a skill, we train the executor to execute all required phases instead of focusing solely on the final answer. We therefore introduce Grounded Skill-Following, which requires an agent to execute a fixed, expert-authored skill across its required phases by grounding decisions in environment observations. To achieve verifiable procedural execution, we formulate each skill as a skill contract combining visible skill instructions with an explicit contract runtime. The runtime specifies required phases, admissible actions, permitted transitions, and accepted termination. This structure provides a dense, verifiable training signal throughout execution. We leverage this by introducing Verified Progress Credit, which assigns rewards upon the initial completion of contract milestones and aggregates them into the trajectory return to guide policy optimization. During rollout, the contract runtime continuously tracks state transitions to provide Contract-State Feedback, which indicates whether the latest action is accepted and guides the agent toward valid next actions. To measure procedural compliance, we introduce the Protocol Completion Rate (PCR), defined as reaching accepted termination through all required phases, and decouple it from the final Task Outcome. Jointly trained with our framework, Qwen3.5-4B achieves Protocol Completion Rates of 99.27% on Math and 99.96% on Search, while slightly outperforming original baselines in Task Outcome (82.95% and 46.61%, respectively). Controlled studies examine how skill instructions, training signals, and contract-state feedback affect both metrics, while withholding interventions evaluate behavioral dependence on observation content.

</details>


### [270] [Memadapter: Counterfactual Adaptation Against Memory-induced Sycophancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05162)
*Ruqing Ning,Haibo Meng,Zhishang Xiang,Zerui Chen,Jinsong Su,Xin Wang,Qinggang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemAdapter is a framework to make LLM agents use long-term memory without becoming sycophantic, by adaptively controlling how retrieved memories influence reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents with long-term memory can personalize and handle long-horizon interactions, but persistent memories may cause sycophancy: the agent aligns too much with a user’s past beliefs, even when those beliefs are wrong, outdated, or inconsistent with evidence. Existing defenses mostly try to detect and filter biased/incorrect memories, assuming that only those are dangerous. In practice, even correct memories can inappropriately bias responses, and the same memory may be safe in one context and harmful in another. This creates a need for a context-sensitive mechanism that evaluates and adjusts the influence of each memory on the fly, rather than a static filter.

Method: The authors propose MemAdapter, an adaptive memory-integration framework with three key components: (1) Counterfactual Induction: the model simulates counterfactual scenarios (e.g., reasoning with vs. without a memory) to estimate how much a retrieved memory could skew or riskily bias the answer. (2) Context-Aware Reflection: for each retrieved memory, the model performs self-reflection conditioned on the current task to calibrate how strongly that memory should affect the reasoning process. (3) Evidence-Based Reasoning: in generating the final response, the model explicitly grounds its reasoning in appropriate evidence (such as external facts or up-to-date context) while still allowing legitimate and beneficial influence from memory, balancing personalization with objectivity.

Result: Across three different benchmarks designed to stress-test memory usage and susceptibility to sycophancy, MemAdapter yields more reliable use of long-term memory compared to baselines. It consistently reduces memory-induced sycophancy and improves objective reasoning performance while retaining useful personalization effects. The reported experiments indicate robustness across diverse scenarios rather than improvements limited to a single dataset or setting.

Conclusion: MemAdapter provides a general, modular approach for mitigating memory-induced sycophancy in LLM-based agents. By adaptively assessing the risk and contextual relevance of each memory and grounding final answers in evidence, it improves the reliability and objectivity of long-term-memory-augmented systems. The work suggests that dynamic, context-aware control of memory influence is more effective than static filtering of “bad” memories, and offers a practical path for safer personalization in LLM agents.

Abstract: Long-term memory enables LLM-based agents to retain and reuse information across tasks and sessions, supporting personalization and long-horizon interactions. However, persistent memories can also induce sycophancy, causing agents to over-align with users' historical beliefs even when they are inaccurate, outdated, or inconsistent with objective evidence. Existing mitigation methods assume that memory-induced sycophancy originates from biased or incorrect memories and attempt to reduce this risk by filtering such memories at different stages of the memory pipeline. However, in the real world, objective and correct memories can still induce sycophancy, and the same memory can warrant different influence across different contexts. To this end, we propose MemAdapter, a novel framework that adaptively integrates retrieved memories to support objective and reliable reasoning. Specifically, MemAdapter consists of three components: (i) Counterfactual Induction, which leverages counterfactual reasoning to uncover the potential risk of retrieved memories; (ii) Context-Aware Reflection, which calibrates the inferential influence of each retrieved memory in light of the current task via self-reflection; and (iii) Evidence-Based Reasoning, which grounds the final response in appropriate evidence while preserving the legitimate influence of memory. Extensive experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate that MemAdapter consistently improves memory reliability across diverse scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/DEEP-JLU/MemAdapter.

</details>


### [271] [A Safe Action Is Not Enough: Feasible-Future Decoding for Vision-Language-Action Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05166)
*Tu Nguyen,Matthieu Zimmer,Vu Anh Vu,Ziyi Wang,Jannik Hammel Nielsen,Xuebing Zhou,Haitham Bou Ammar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies a gap between actions that look safe/likely to a frozen vision-language-action (VLA) policy and actions that actually preserve a path to safe task completion, and proposes a reranking method (VICS-G) that selects actions based on their remaining safe future feasibility without retraining or rollouts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing frozen VLA policies may choose actions that appear safe and likely at the current step but eliminate any policy-supported path to safe completion later, which standard likelihood-based decoding does not capture. There is a need for a principled way to account for the feasibility of safe futures when selecting actions from a pretrained policy, without expensive online search or retraining.

Method: The authors formally derive the next-step marginal distribution over actions induced by the joint policy-environment process, conditioned on eventual safe task completion. This yields, for each candidate action, a feasible-future mass term that reflects how much safe-completion probability remains if that action is chosen. Because exact computation is intractable online, they propose a selective finite-candidate approximation: among a small set of sampled actions, they estimate and use these feasible-future masses to rerank candidates. They provide theoretical conditions ensuring that the best viable candidate among those retained can be recovered, and implement this as an alarm-triggered, training-free reranker on top of a frozen VLA policy.

Result: On the Safety-CHORES benchmark, their method VICS-G reduces mean cumulative safety cost by 1.9% to 57.5% across six experimental settings compared with standard policy sampling, while causing only small degradation in task performance: within 2.5 percentage points in success rate and 0.82 steps in mean episode length.

Conclusion: Explicitly accounting for the feasibility of safe futures, rather than only current-step likelihood, can significantly improve safety outcomes for frozen VLA policies. The proposed VICS-G reranker approximates the ideal safe-completion-conditioned policy target, yields substantial safety gains with minimal performance loss, and does so without retraining the base model or performing expensive online rollouts.

Abstract: A safe action is not necessarily a viable one. Under a frozen vision-language-action (VLA) policy, an action can be likely and locally admissible yet leave no policy-supported route to safe task completion. We call this the feasibility-likelihood gap: likelihood ranks the current action, whereas feasibility depends on the futures that remain after it.
  We derive the exact next-block marginal of the history-conditioned policy-environment trajectory law restricted to safe task completion. The derivation exposes a candidate-dependent feasible-future mass with two roles: its support records whether safe completion remains possible under the frozen continuation process, and its magnitude measures how much weighted safe-completion mass is preserved. Exact evaluation is impractical online, so we develop a selective finite-candidate approximation, derive conditions for recovering the best retained viable candidate, and instantiate it as an alarm-triggered, training-free reranker.
  On Safety-CHORES, VICS-G lowers mean cumulative safety cost by 1.9%-57.5% across six settings while remaining within 2.5 percentage points of policy sampling in success and 0.82 steps in mean episode length. The resulting decoder is tied to an exact policy-relative safe-completion target, yet requires neither retraining of the base policy nor online trajectory rollouts.

</details>


### [272] [CreativeFlow: A One-to-Many Analogical Relation Transfer Method for 3D Asset Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05167)
*Xuechen Li,Shuai Zhang,Nanxuan Zhao,Qing Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces CREATIVEFLOW, an analogical generation framework to reduce creative homogenization in text-to-3D generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current text-to-3D pipelines tend to produce homogenized, less creative outputs; the authors want to better emulate human-like analogical divergent thinking to improve creative novelty and variety in 3D assets.

Method: Design an analogical generation framework called CREATIVEFLOW that explicitly models analogical divergent thinking. It constructs series of source-target 3D asset pairs that are relationally similar but differ in geometric configuration, forming a structured space of analogical variations. The framework is integrated into text-to-3D workflows to guide generation.

Result: Expert evaluations show that CREATIVEFLOW significantly improves the creative novelty and visual appeal (fascination) of the generated 3D assets compared with baseline text-to-3D methods.
