Conclusion: Modeling analogical divergent thinking in text-to-3D generation can effectively counter creative homogenization. The produced workflow and its assets serve as a foundational dataset and benchmark for future relation-aware 3D model training.

Abstract: Inspired by cognitive science, we present CREATIVEFLOW, an analogical generation framework that explicitly models analogical divergent thinking to mitigate creative homogenization in text-to-3D pipelines. Our method derives a series of meaningful yet relationally similar source-target asset pairs, each featuring distinct geometric configurations. Expert evaluations demonstrate that our framework substantially enhances creative novelty and visual fascination. This workflow and its resulting assets establish a foundational dataset and benchmark for future relation-aware 3D model training.

</details>


### [273] [AECG: Asymmetric Experience Consolidation and Governance In Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05176)
*Ao Tian,Jialong Liu,Daqi Zheng,Xin Sun,Mengting Li,Zhizhao Xiao,Zijian Huang,Honglei Wang,Zijian Hei,Yukun Yan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes AECG, a reliability-governance framework for memory in LLM-based multi-agent systems, turning memory from passive storage into an actively managed, auditable process that reduces error propagation and improves benchmark performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems increasingly use memory to accumulate procedural knowledge from past trajectories. However, this memory can become polluted: outdated or spuriously successful strategies are repeatedly retrieved and reused, causing persistent errors. Multi-agent structures add another risk: knowledge effective in a specific coordination scope can leak and be wrongly reused at other decision levels (scope collapse), propagating local mistakes into large cascades of failures. Moreover, overall task failure signals do not clearly indicate which specific recalled memories were responsible, making it hard to correct the right knowledge. The paper aims to address these intertwined problems of memory pollution, scope collapse, and ambiguous supervision in multi-agent systems.

Method: The authors introduce AECG (Asymmetric Experience Consolidation and Governance), a framework that reconceptualizes memory as a dynamic, reliability-governed process instead of static storage. AECG preserves coordination scope when storing and reusing procedural knowledge, attaches multi-scale, confidence-aware reliability estimates to memory items, and continuously monitors them for degradation. When reliability appears to degrade, AECG evaluates both the degradation and the downstream impact of the affected knowledge, prioritizing high-risk items under a limited review budget. It then applies targeted interventions (e.g., revising or constraining specific skills) and only reactivates the updated knowledge after paired replay to validate the revision. The framework is instantiated and evaluated across multiple LLM-based multi-agent setups.

Result: Across three different multi-agent frameworks and four benchmarks, AECG consistently improves system performance. It achieves the best scores in 11 out of 12 framework–benchmark combinations and surpasses the strongest competing memory method by up to 10.23 percentage points. An ablation that removes the scope-preservation mechanism shows substantial accuracy drops, up to 16.89 points, underscoring the importance of maintaining coordination scope in multi-agent memory.

Conclusion: AECG demonstrates that memory in multi-agent LLM systems should be treated as an auditable, actively governed component rather than a passive repository. By preserving scope, tracking reliability over time, prioritizing risky knowledge for review, and validating revisions via replay, AECG reduces memory pollution and scope collapse while substantially improving benchmark performance. This reframes multi-agent memory as a reliability-governance loop and provides a practical framework for safer, more robust multi-agent reasoning, with open-source code available for adoption and extension.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems increasingly rely on memory to transform execution trajectories into reusable procedural knowledge. Yet repeated retrieval also makes memory errors persistent: memory pollution arises when outdated, weakly supported, or spuriously successful procedures become recurring components of future reasoning. Multi-agent execution introduces an additional structural risk. Scope collapse occurs when procedural knowledge escapes the coordination scope in which it was shown effective and is repeatedly reused at incompatible decision levels, allowing local errors to influence cascades of downstream decisions. Meanwhile, task-level failures provide ambiguous supervision because they rarely reveal which recalled knowledge was responsible. We introduce AECG, a framework for asymmetric experience consolidation and governance for multi-agent systems. AECG turns memory from static experience storage into a dynamic reliability-governance loop, preserving coordination scope and using multi-scale, confidence-aware reliability to detect degradation. It then combines degradation with downstream impact to prioritize high-risk knowledge under a bounded review budget, applies targeted interventions, and reactivates revised skills only after paired replay. Across three multi-agent frameworks and four benchmarks, AECG achieves the best score in 11 of 12 framework--benchmark settings and improves over the strongest competing memory method by as much as 10.23 percentage points; removing scope preservation reduces accuracy by up to 16.89 points. AECG thereby reframes multi-agent memory from passive accumulation into auditable reliability governance. Code is available at https://github.com/fenhg297/AECG

</details>


### [274] [From Scientific Observations to Mechanisms: Benchmarking Hypothesis Generation by AI Scientists](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05197)
*Xiaxun Xie,Qingqing Long,Meng Xiao,Wei Ju,Yuanchun Zhou,Xuezhi Wang,Hengshu Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Benchmark to test if AI can turn data into mechanistic hypotheses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is little systematic evaluation of whether AI agents and AI scientists can generate mechanistic hypotheses, not just predictions, from data. Mechanistic hypotheses are central to scientific understanding.

Method: They build MechHypoBench, a benchmark constructed from paper-derived mechanisms across 14 scientific fields, paired with large real-world datasets. Agents see only the data and must generate open-form mechanistic hypotheses. The authors design an evaluation framework that scores these hypotheses via their predictive consequences on withheld conditions, comparing them against the known ground-truth mechanisms.

Result: Running general-purpose agents and specialized AI scientist systems on MechHypoBench shows a large gap between the hypotheses they propose and the true underlying mechanisms encoded from the literature, as measured by performance on withheld conditions.

Conclusion: Current AI agents and AI scientists are far from reliably inferring true mechanistic explanations from observational data. MechHypoBench provides a standardized way to measure and drive progress on this capability across diverse scientific domains.

Abstract: Data-driven mechanistic hypotheses are essential to scientific discovery because they explain how underlying processes produce observed phenomena. AI agents and AI scientists increasingly support scientific data analysis. However, their ability to turn empirical findings into mechanistic hypotheses remains insufficiently examined. To address this gap, we introduce MechHypoBench, the first benchmark for evaluating whether AI agents and AI scientists can generate such hypotheses from empirical data. It combines paper-derived mechanisms from 14 scientific fields with real-world datasets containing 17.98 million records. The construction retains the observational complexity of empirical data while providing a specified underlying mechanism. Agents analyze the observations and propose open-form hypotheses. We develop an evaluation framework that assesses open-form mechanistic hypotheses through their consequences under withheld conditions. Experiments with general agents and AI scientists reveal a substantial gap between generated hypotheses and the underlying mechanisms.

</details>


### [275] [Image Synthesis as an Intermediate for Controllable Time Series Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05211)
*Haochen Yuan,Jing Xie,Yunbo Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VisualBridge is a semantic-driven time-series data augmentation method that uses plots and a multimodal LLM to bridge language-level temporal semantics and numerical sequences for better few-shot forecasting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Few-shot time-series forecasting often suffers from limited data, and directly generating numerical sequences from language descriptions fails to reliably capture complex temporal structures like trend, seasonality, and volatility. There is a need for a controllable augmentation framework that faithfully encodes high-level temporal semantics while producing realistic multivariate sequences that help downstream forecasting models.

Method: VisualBridge first renders time-series as plots and uses a multimodal large language model to extract structured semantic representations of temporal properties (trend, seasonality, volatility, etc.). These semantics are explicitly edited via a learned policy optimized with downstream forecasting rewards, steering the temporal patterns toward those that are beneficial for the target task. Finally, a temporal variational autoencoder models the resulting sequences to generate consistent multivariate augmentations, enabling controllable and semantically grounded data generation.

Result: On standard public time-series forecasting benchmarks, VisualBridge outperforms conventional data augmentation baselines in few-shot settings. Ablation studies show that each component—visual semantic grounding via plots and MLLM, learned semantic editing/control, and temporal VAE-based generation—contributes meaningfully to the performance gains.

Conclusion: VisualBridge demonstrates that using visual intermediates and semantic control can effectively bridge natural-language temporal descriptions and numerical time-series generation. By jointly leveraging MLLM-based semantic extraction, task-rewarded semantic editing, and VAE-based temporal modeling, the method yields better few-shot forecasting performance than traditional augmentation techniques and validates the value of visual semantic grounding for time-series generation.

Abstract: Semantic-driven time-series generation offers a promising way to improve downstream learning in few-shot forecasting, but directly generating numerical sequences from language often fails to preserve the intended temporal structure. We propose VisualBridge, which uses time-series plots as a visual intermediate to bridge high-level temporal semantics and numerical sequences. An MLLM first converts plotted series into structured semantic representations, enabling explicit control over temporal properties such as trend, seasonality, and volatility. We then learn a semantic editing policy with downstream forecasting rewards, allowing the generation process to favor temporal patterns that are beneficial for the target task. The resulting sequences are further modeled by a temporal VAE to produce consistent multivariate augmentations. Experiments on standard public forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that VisualBridge improves few-shot forecasting over conventional augmentation methods, with ablations validating the roles of visual semantic grounding, learned semantic control, and VAE-based generation.

</details>


### [276] [Safe Context Switching for Agents in the Wild: Mitigating Subspace Interference via Orthogonal Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05219)
*Akash Das,Ishan Roy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how training language models for better reasoning can unintentionally hurt their safety, and proposes a geometric regularization method (AURA) to separate reasoning from safety in the model’s representation space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When LLMs are fine-tuned to be better at multi-step reasoning (e.g., math, coding), their internal activations become higher-variance and can interfere with latent safety/alignment features, weakening safety behaviors. Existing adaptation strategies do not explicitly model this interference or ensure that optimization for reasoning is compatible with safety. The authors want to formally characterize this conflict as a geometric phenomenon and design a method that allows improving reasoning while maintaining safety alignment.

Method: The authors define and analyze “Sequential Subspace Interference,” where internal subspaces used for sequential reasoning conflict with those encoding safety constraints. They empirically demonstrate that fine-tuning for logical tasks causes a measurable drop (23.3%) in alignment metrics, calling this “Reasoning Drift,” and argue it arises because reasoning gradients are not orthogonal to safety objectives. To mitigate this, they introduce AURA (Adaptive Unique Residual Allocation), a spectral regularization framework that estimates the alignment manifold and its null space in representation space. Training updates for reasoning tasks are then constrained to the orthogonal complement of the alignment manifold, enforcing “Spectral Independence” between reasoning and safety.

Result: Standard fine-tuning on reasoning tasks significantly degrades safety alignment performance (23.3% interference penalty). Using AURA during training recovers about 23.0% of the lost alignment performance while still improving reasoning. Moreover, the model’s post-training representation remains highly similar to its original aligned state, with cosine similarity greater than 0.98, suggesting that safety priors are largely preserved while reasoning capabilities are enhanced.

Conclusion: Reasoning and safety in LLMs can occupy overlapping subspaces in latent representation space, so naive fine-tuning on reasoning tasks causes geometric interference that weakens alignment. By modeling alignment as a manifold and constraining reasoning-related updates to its orthogonal complement, AURA shows that it is possible to decouple and jointly optimize reasoning and safety. Geometric/spectral regularization is thus a promising approach for scaling LLM reasoning without sacrificing safety alignment.

Abstract: Most Large Language Models exhibit a fundamental tension between two sequential tasks, such as logical reasoning and safety alignment. The high-variance internal states required for sophisticated Chain-of-Thought (CoT) deduction can geometrically interfere with latent representations encoding safety constraints. We identify this phenomenon as Sequential Subspace Interference, showing that standard fine-tuning on logical tasks such as multi-step mathematics and code generation can result in a 23.3% interference penalty on alignment benchmarks, substantially weakening the model's safety priors. This Reasoning Drift is not adequately captured by current adaptation methods because gradients for logical tasks are rarely orthogonal to safety objectives. To address this issue, we propose AURA (Adaptive Unique Residual Allocation), a spectral regularization framework that enforces Spectral Independence between reasoning and safety. By explicitly estimating the null space of the alignment manifold and constraining reasoning updates to its orthogonal complement, AURA enables models to improve logical reasoning without compromising safety. Empirically, AURA recovers 23.0% of the lost performance while preserving greater than 0.98 cosine fidelity to the safe state, demonstrating that reasoning and alignment can be effectively decoupled through geometric regularization.

</details>


### [277] [Look Before You Leap: Thermodynamic Arbitration of Parametric and Non-Parametric Knowledge in LLM Agents via Self-Regulating Memory Architectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05223)
*Akash Das,Ishan Roy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes MARTA, a neuro-symbolic framework that lets LLM agents introspect about their own uncertainty and treat retrieval as an optional, costed action rather than a mandatory step, aiming to better balance internal (parametric) and external (retrieved) knowledge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-based agents show a deep disconnect between their parametric knowledge (what is encoded in weights) and their non-parametric knowledge (retrieval tools, external APIs). The dominant "Retrieve-Always" paradigm forces agents to distrust their internal knowledge, treating each interaction as if they know nothing until they check external sources. This leads to inefficiency, fragility, over-reliance on often-irrelevant context, and a kind of "induced amnesia" of what the model already knows. The authors are motivated to design an architecture that restores a principled balance between using internal knowledge and consulting external tools, inspired by biological cognition’s tendency to "look before you leap."

Method: The authors introduce MARTA (Metacognitive Adaptive Retrieval and Thought Architecture), a neuro-symbolic agent framework that explicitly models retrieval as a costly action. The agent first performs internal reasoning and uses metacognitive signals—such as estimated entropy or uncertainty of its own intermediate thoughts—to decide whether external information is needed. Only when internal confidence is low (or perceived inadequacy is high) does MARTA trigger retrieval or other external tools. This unifies parametric and non-parametric knowledge via an introspective controller that regulates when and how retrieval occurs, instead of hardwiring retrieval into every step.

Result: Within the abstract, the authors claim that MARTA enables "deliberative retrieval" and "uncertainty-aware decision making" by letting agents introspect about their own internal reasoning before querying external resources. While concrete benchmarks are not given in the abstract, the result is positioned as a more efficient and robust balance between internal knowledge and external retrieval, reducing unnecessary tool calls and dependence on noisy or irrelevant context.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that endowing LLM agents with metacognitive capabilities—specifically, the ability to assess their own uncertainty and treat retrieval as an optional, cost-sensitive action—can remedy the current over-reliance on external knowledge. MARTA demonstrates that introspection-based control over retrieval can make agents more efficient, less fragile, and better aligned with how biological systems balance internal cognition with environmental information.

Abstract: The architecture of modern LLMs consists of a profound cognitive polarization. LLMs possess implicit intuition encoded in their parameters, yet rely on a disconnected, explicit mechanism to access the outside world. Agentic frameworks have not bridged this gap; instead, models are often compelled into pathological "induced amnesia." Under the prevailing "Retrieve-Always" paradigm, agents must distrust their internal knowledge, making every user interaction a "tabula rasa" event that must be checked externally. This creates reflexive dependence that can be thermodynamically wasteful, cognitively fragile, and susceptible to irrelevant context. We propose a return to first principles, operationalizing the biological maxim "Look Before You Leap." We introduce MARTA (Metacognitive Adaptive Retrieval and Thought Architecture), a neuro-symbolic framework that bridges parametric and non-parametric knowledge. Rather than treating retrieval as mandatory, MARTA models it as a cost, taking the leap only when perceived internal inadequacy warrants external information. By allowing the agent to gauge the entropy of its own thoughts before acting, MARTA enables deliberative retrieval and uncertainty-aware decision making. Our approach suggests that giving agents the capacity for introspection can restore a more efficient balance between internal knowledge and external information.

</details>


### [278] [GFGE: Unifying Explainable AI Methods through an Interpretation Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05225)
*Jinfeng Zhong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a unified conceptual and operational framework (GFGE) for how XAI methods turn system evidence into explanations tailored to specific audiences and questions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing XAI methods are diverse and fragmented, using different information sources and addressing different explanatory needs. There is no common, rigorous way to describe how they turn model and data evidence into explanations, nor to track assumptions, limitations, and audience needs across methods. This makes it hard to compare, audit, or systematically design explanation workflows.

Method: The authors introduce the Interpret/Explain Schema (IES) that separates three stages: an analyst’s interpretation of system evidence, the communication of an explanatory account, and the recipient’s interpretation of that account. They then operationalise this schema into the General Framework for Generating Explanations (GFGE), which decomposes explanation workflows into five roles: data interpretation, model interpretation, output interpretation, optional post-hoc analysis, and aggregation. They represent concrete XAI methods as role-typed operation graphs that show dependencies among operations, and attach evidence records that document the sources, assumptions, and limitations behind explanatory claims. They instantiate the framework on diverse XAI families (attribution, surrogate models, counterfactuals, concepts/prototypes, intrinsic rules, argumentation, and language-model-based methods) to demonstrate coverage of intrinsic, post-hoc, and hybrid approaches.

Result: GFGE is able to represent a wide spectrum of XAI methods within a single role-based workflow language while making explicit their different evidential requirements and dependencies. The instantiations show that intrinsic, post-hoc, and hybrid explanation pipelines can be mapped to the same set of roles and operation graphs without losing their specific nuances. The evidence records and dependency graphs enable tracing of explanatory claims back to underlying evidence and highlight where assumptions or gaps remain.

Conclusion: The proposed GFGE framework offers a unifying way to analyze, design, and document explanation workflows in XAI. By grounding explanations in an interpretive schema and explicitly modeling roles, operations, and evidence, it supports clearer communication to recipients, better comparison across methods, and more systematic identification of unresolved explanatory dependencies and assumptions.

Abstract: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) encompasses methods that draw on different sources of information and address different explanatory needs. A common framework is needed to describe how this information becomes evidence and is communicated as an explanation for a particular recipient. We propose the General Framework for Generating Explanations (GFGE), grounded in interpretative frameworks and the complementary activities of \emph{sense-reading} and \emph{sense-giving}. Its conceptual foundation is the Interpret/Explain Schema (IES), which connects an analyst's interpretation of system evidence, the communication of a selected account, and the recipient's interpretation of that account. GFGE operationalises this schema through five roles: data interpretation, model interpretation, output interpretation, optional post-hoc analysis, and aggregation. A role-typed operation graph records method-specific dependencies, while evidence records retain the sources, assumptions, and limitations of explanatory claims. The explanatory question, audience, and context guide the procedure. We instantiate GFGE for attribution, surrogate, counterfactual, concept and prototype, intrinsic rule, argumentation, and language-model methods. These instantiations show how intrinsic, post-hoc, and hybrid workflows can be represented through the same roles while preserving their distinct evidential requirements. GFGE provides a common basis for analysing explanation workflows, tracing communicated claims to their evidence, and identifying unresolved explanatory dependencies.

</details>


### [279] [Learning from imperfect teachers for low-resource acoustic generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05256)
*Shuanglin Li,Ruxiao Qian,Jian Liu,Haijun Lin,Wenwu Wang,Siyang Song*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes BA-MPD, a new knowledge distillation method that corrects biased teacher predictions at the decision boundary and partitions probability mass for tailored distillation, improving low-resource acoustic learning, especially with imperfect teachers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In low-resource acoustic learning, knowledge distillation helps small students learn from larger teachers by using soft label distributions. But when teachers are trained with limited or imbalanced labels, their predictive distributions are biased and not uniformly reliable. Directly matching the full distribution transfers these biases, warps the student's decision boundary, and hurts generalization. A method is needed that can exploit useful information in an imperfect teacher while suppressing harmful biases and noisy low-confidence predictions, and that works even when teacher and student are trained with different amounts of labeled data.

Method: The paper introduces Boundary-Anchored Mass-Partitioned Distillation (BA-MPD), a logit-based KD objective combining two key components: (1) Boundary-Anchored Correction (BAC), which examines the teacher's top predicted labels and, if the true label is missing, swaps it with the lowest-ranked entry in this top set. This preserves total probability mass and uncertainty while correcting boundary-level ranking errors around the true class. (2) Mass-Partitioned Distillation (MPD), which partitions the corrected predictive mass into high- and low-confidence groups and applies separate loss terms: one to maintain relational consistency within the top set, another to balance probability mass between high- and low-confidence groups, and a third to appropriately weight dependencies involving lower-confidence predictions. The overall objective distills the corrected distribution at the logit level, emphasizing reliable high-confidence structure and down-weighting noisy low-confidence details.

Result: On two acoustic benchmarks under various label budgets, BA-MPD outperforms standard supervised learning and vanilla KD. It is competitive with strong existing logit-based KD baselines. In cross-budget settings, where teacher and student have different labeled data budgets, BA-MPD continues to yield improvements, indicating robustness to supervision gaps and imperfect teachers.

Conclusion: BA-MPD effectively leverages imperfect teacher models in low-resource acoustic learning by correcting boundary-level label ranking errors and selectively distilling probability mass. The combination of BAC and MPD suppresses harmful biases and noise while preserving useful structural information from the teacher, leading to consistent performance gains over baselines and maintaining competitiveness with advanced KD methods, even when teacher and student label budgets are mismatched.

Abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) improves low-resource acoustic learning by enriching one-hot supervision with the softened predictive distribution of a fixed teacher network. However, a teacher trained with limited or imbalanced annotations may produce a biased distribution whose components are not uniformly reliable. Although this distribution can still encode useful knowledge, direct full-distribution matching may also transfer teacher-induced biases, thereby distorting the student's decision boundary and degrading its generalization performance. To address this limitation, we propose Boundary-Anchored Mass-Partitioned Distillation (BA-MPD), a logit-based distillation objective composed of Boundary-Anchored Correction (BAC) and Mass-Partitioned Distillation (MPD). BAC addresses missing ground-truth labels in the set of the teacher's top predictions by swapping the true label for the lowest-ranked entry of the set, thus keeping the mass and uncertainty of the set unchanged. MPD then distills this corrected distribution through separate losses that enforce relational consistency within the set, balance the mass between high- and low-confidence groups, and weight lower-confidence dependencies. Ultimately, BAC and MPD together suppress harmful ranking errors and noisy low-confidence details, while retaining all useful teacher information. Experiments on two acoustic benchmarks under multiple label budgets show that BA-MPD consistently improves over supervised-learning baselines and vanilla KD while remaining competitive with strong logit-based KD baselines. Cross-budget results further show that BA-MPD remains effective when the teacher and student models use mismatched label budgets, demonstrating its ability to exploit imperfect teachers across supervision gaps. Implementation available at https://github.com/ShuanglinLi/BA-MPD.

</details>


### [280] [When Agent Context Goes Stale: Incoherence in Volatile Agent Context](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05281)
*Yingying Liu,Junzhou Fang,Chenxiong Qian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Concord, a framework to keep LLM agents’ tool-based context consistent with changing underlying data sources, preventing stale observations from causing incorrect reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agents often rely on observations from tools (e.g., file reads) that can become outdated when the underlying data changes. Current agent runtimes lack mechanisms to detect and handle such staleness, leading to agents reusing obsolete information and making wrong claims about the current state of a workspace. There is a need for a general, extensible way to maintain coherence between what’s in the model’s context and the mutable external resources it reflects.

Method: The authors design Concord, a context coherence framework that: (1) links each tool observation in the agent’s context to its originating source; (2) monitors or detects changes to those sources; and (3) applies configurable policies to handle staleness—updating, annotating, or suppressing stale content before the agent reuses it. The framework is built to be runtime- and resource-agnostic, allowing it to be applied across different agent systems and external data sources, and to be extended to new runtime–resource combinations. They also instantiate a concrete application of Concord and create a benchmark (ConcordBench) where file contents previously seen by the agent are later edited, making the earlier observations stale.

Result: In experiments on ConcordBench using three frontier LLMs, Concord consistently produces answers aligned with the true, updated workspace state in all tested constructed scenarios. Under these conditions, it matches an oracle method in terms of ‘recover count’ (the number of cases where the correct, updated state is recovered) while using 46.4% fewer tokens than the strongest non-oracle baseline.

Conclusion: Concord effectively maintains context coherence for tool-using LLM agents by detecting and handling stale observations tied to mutable external sources. It can be integrated with various agent runtimes and resources, and its policies reduce token usage while preserving correctness, achieving oracle-level recovery on the proposed ConcordBench benchmark.

Abstract: Modern agents increasingly ground their reasoning in observations returned by tools, such as file contents read from a workspace. However, the data sources underlying these observations may later be modified by users, other agents, or external tools, while the model retains only the stale content in its context window. Existing agent runtimes provide little support for notifying the model that a previously observed fact has become stale, causing agents to reuse outdated observations and make incorrect claims about the current workspace state. We propose Concord, a context coherence framework that maintains the consistency between tool observation in agent context and the mutable sources from which they were derived. Concord links each observation to its source, detects source changes, and uses configurable handling policies to update, annotate, or suppress stale context before reuse. Concord is applicable across different agent runtimes and external resources, and can be easily extended to new runtime-resource settings. We implement Concord as a general framework, and instantiate a concrete use case to assess its effectiveness. We construct ConcordBench, where previously observed file contents become stale after subsequent edits. Across three evaluated frontier models, Concord produces answers consistent with the restored workspace state in all evaluated cases under these constructed conditions, matching the oracle on recover count for this benchmark, while using 46.4% fewer tokens than the strongest non-oracle baseline.

</details>


### [281] [Fusion is the New Mutation: Bandit-Guided Evolution on Workflow Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05284)
*Zhiwei Shang,Jiahang Sun,Mingrong Gong,Mingze Kong,Zikun Qu,Pingchen Lu,Junhao Dong,Zhipiao Liu,Hongwei Yang,Guoqing Xie,Yao Shu,Zhongxiang Dai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DAGO is a contextual bandit–driven framework for optimizing LLM-based agentic workflows via multi-parent fusion under a limited evaluation budget.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Optimizing automated agentic workflows (e.g., for math reasoning, coding, QA) typically requires many expensive evaluations. Existing multi-parent fusion approaches can reuse prior workflows but do not efficiently decide which combinations of parents to fuse when feedback (evaluations) is scarce. There is a need for a principled, feedback-driven way to allocate a constrained validation budget while exploring and exploiting promising workflow fusions.

Method: The paper proposes DAGO (Directed Acyclic Graph Optimization), which models each candidate combination of parent workflows as an arm in a contextual bandit. Each arm is encoded using pretrained embeddings of its parents’ code and prompts. A diagonal LinUCB policy maintains a shared linear reward model over these embeddings and selects arms by trading off predicted child quality (exploitation) against uncertainty (exploration). When an arm is chosen, an LLM performs summary-guided fusion of the parents to generate a child workflow. The child’s validation score is used as the bandit reward. All workflows and their multi-parent relationships are stored in a directed acyclic graph, which grows over time and provides an expanding pool of candidate parents for new fusions.

Result: On six benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, code generation, and question answering, DAGO attains the best macro-average performance compared with baselines. Under the same validation-evaluation budget, it improves AFlow’s score from 80.3 to 81.7 while cutting total search cost by 11.2%. Ablations indicate that LinUCB-based arm selection yields better performance than both random arm selection and a variant without exploration, demonstrating the importance of feedback-guided choices and exploration–exploitation balancing.

Conclusion: DAGO offers an effective framework for budget-aware optimization of agentic workflows via multi-parent fusion. By using a contextual bandit (diagonal LinUCB) over workflow-combination embeddings and maintaining a DAG of discovered workflows, it can systematically learn which parent sets to fuse, achieving higher quality with lower search cost than prior methods. The results and ablations support the value of bandit-guided selection and explicit exploration in this setting.

Abstract: Automated agentic workflow optimization relies on costly evaluations, making it essential to allocate a limited evaluation budget effectively. Multi-parent fusion can reuse designs from previously discovered workflows, but identifying promising parent combinations requires learning from limited fusion feedback. We introduce DAGO (Directed Acyclic Graph Optimization), a contextual-bandit-guided framework that learns which parent workflows to fuse under a limited evaluation budget. DAGO formulates each candidate parent combination as an arm, represented by pretrained embeddings of its constituent workflows' code and prompts. A diagonal LinUCB policy learns a shared reward model across arms and balances exploitation of arms with high predicted offspring quality against uncertainty-driven exploration. After an arm is selected, an LLM generates a child workflow through summary-guided fusion, and the child's validation score serves as the reward for updating the bandit. A shared directed acyclic graph maintains discovered workflows and their multi-parent lineage, providing an expanding pool of parents for subsequent arm proposals. Across six benchmarks covering mathematical reasoning, code generation, and question answering, DAGO achieves the highest macro-average score among the evaluated baselines. Under matched validation-evaluation budgets, it improves over AFlow from 80.3 to 81.7 while reducing aggregate search expenditure by 11.2%. Ablation studies show that LinUCB-guided arm selection outperforms both random selection and its exploration-free variant, supporting the value of feedback-driven selection and exploration-exploitation balance.

</details>


### [282] [Readable Before Actionable: Causal Tracing of Indirect Prompt Injection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05295)
*Zhe Yu,Wenpeng Xing,Xingxing Yang,Meng Han*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper analyzes how large language model (LLM) agents encode and can be protected against indirect prompt injection, showing that the internal “role” signal is easy to read but hard to use for reliably changing behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection, where malicious instructions are hidden inside external data (e.g., web pages, tools’ outputs). Probing often reveals that models internally distinguish between roles (e.g., who to follow) and content, but it is unclear how this internal representation relates to actual behavior and to possible defenses. The paper aims to characterize the gap between ‘readable’ internal role signals and practically effective interventions that prevent attacks.

Method: The authors use mechanistic interpretability techniques on Qwen and AgentDojo agent trajectories: (1) counterfactual role probes to decode whether the model treats text as instructions vs. data under controlled modifications of content and format; (2) component-wise activation patching to manipulate internal activations along candidate “role directions”; (3) separate interventions at different positions (pre‑action, injected span, random positions) and depths (layers) in the network; (4) comparison of directions learned from hijacked vs. attack-resisting trajectories; (5) experiments on single-token vs. span-wide and repeated edits; (6) analysis of a “learned channel subspace” and how removing it affects role decoding and intervention efficacy.

Result: They find that role decoding is robust: probes can still read out roles despite changes in content and format. In controlled Qwen settings, role effects emerge early and precede strong changes in tool choice caused by activation patches along role directions. On AgentDojo, directions derived from hijacked and resisted trajectories selectively reduce attack success when applied at pre-action and injected-span locations but have little impact when applied at random positions. As trajectories get longer, single-position edits become less effective at later layers, but span-wide and repeated edits reduce attack success on held-out evaluation data. Removing a learned channel subspace does not destroy role decoding, yet intervention directions learned in one channel transfer poorly to other channels.

Conclusion: The paper shows a clear distinction between internal, decodable ‘role’ signals and interventions that reliably alter behavior under indirect prompt injection. Role information is globally readable, but behaviorally effective edits are highly sensitive to layer depth, position in the sequence, and contextual factors. This suggests that simple linear role directions or single-point interventions are insufficient as defenses; robust mitigation likely requires depth-aware, position- and context-dependent mechanisms rather than relying solely on easily probed representations.

Abstract: Indirect prompt injection causes LLM agents to follow commands embedded in external data. A probe may distinguish instructions from data without identifying a state edit that changes the next action. We study this gap through counterfactual role probes, component-wise activation patching, and separate interventions on AgentDojo trajectories. Role decoding survives changes in content and format. In controlled Qwen tests, it precedes strong tool-choice effects from patches along an independently estimated role direction. On AgentDojo, directions estimated from hijacked and resisted training trajectories reduce attack success at pre-action and injected-span positions, but have little effect at random positions. In longer Qwen trajectories, single-position edits become less effective at later layers; span-wide and repeated edits reduce attack success on the same evaluation set. Removing the learned channel subspace preserves role decoding, yet effective intervention directions transfer poorly across the tested channels. These findings distinguish a readable role signal from an effective behavioral intervention: depth matters in controlled tool choice, while position and context also matter in attack trajectories.

</details>


### [283] [MESH-Harness: Self-Improving Agent Harnesses via Bandit-Guided Compositional Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05300)
*Zhiwei Shang,Yu Huo,Mingrong Gong,An Yan,Zikun Qu,Junhao Dong,Bryan Kian Hsiang Low,Chenglin Wu,Zhongxiang Dai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MESH-Harness is a modular, bandit-optimized framework for improving LLM agent harnesses under a limited evaluation budget, achieving better performance and lower cost than a strong baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent performance depends increasingly on the surrounding harness (state management, tools, retrieval) rather than only on model weights, but designing good harnesses is complex and expensive to optimize via brute-force search. There is a need for a systematic, data-efficient way to explore and improve harness designs while keeping model weights fixed and staying within a tight evaluation budget.

Method: The authors decompose an agent harness into functional modules with clearly defined, role-specific interfaces (e.g., retrieval, planning, tool orchestration). For each role they maintain a pool of interchangeable module implementations, represented in a shared feature space. They use a full-covariance LinUCB contextual bandit algorithm to score candidate harness configurations (combinations of modules) based on predicted performance and exploration bonus. A mixed-start coordinate-ascent procedure selects promising complete configurations to actually evaluate, avoiding enumeration of the combinatorial design space. After evaluation, they inspect validation traces to perform targeted local code edits, then add these improved implementations back into fixed-capacity, role-specific module pools for future recombination, enabling iterative, feedback-driven search.

Result: Across several benchmarks—text tasks, retrieval-augmented mathematical reasoning, code generation, and interactive scientific tasks—MESH-Harness consistently outperforms the Meta-Harness baseline by 5.70, 7.01, 2.00, and 5.00 points respectively, under the same number of candidate evaluations. Further, iterating the optimization process improves MESH-Harness by an additional 5.63–7.79 points over its initial round. The optimized configurations also reduce aggregate test-time cost by 44.2% compared to Meta-Harness, and total cost including search by 14.6%.

Conclusion: By treating an agent harness as a recombinable set of modules and applying contextual bandit-guided, compositional search over these modules, it is possible to systematically and efficiently improve agent behavior without changing the underlying model weights. The modular, feedback-driven MESH-Harness approach yields higher task performance and lower computational cost than a strong baseline, demonstrating that structured harness design reuse plus bandit-based exploration is an effective strategy for optimizing LLM-based agents under realistic evaluation budgets.

Abstract: An agent harness is the code that organizes context, maintains state, and coordinates tool calls for a language model. We study how to improve the harness under a limited evaluation budget while keeping model weights fixed. Our method, MESH-Harness, organizes each harness into functional modules with explicit role-specific interfaces, allowing alternative implementations of each module to be substituted and recombined. It uses shared module representations and full-covariance LinUCB to score candidate combinations based on predicted performance and exploration value. Mixed-start coordinate ascent selects complete configurations for evaluation without enumerating the combinatorial space. Validation traces then guide local code edits, and the resulting candidates are incorporated into fixed-capacity role-specific pools for subsequent recombination. On text tasks, retrieval-augmented mathematical reasoning, code generation, and interactive scientific tasks, MESH-Harness outperforms Meta-Harness by 5.70, 7.01, 2.00, and 5.00 points, respectively, under matched candidate-evaluation budgets. Iterative harness optimization improves MESH-Harness by 5.63-7.79 points over its first-round configurations. For the reported configurations, aggregate test-time cost is 44.2% lower than that of Meta-Harness, while total cost including search is 14.6% lower. These results show that combining module-level design reuse with feedback-driven compositional search can systematically improve agent harnesses while keeping overall optimization cost under control.

</details>


### [284] [AgentDiscover: Autonomous Discovery with Minimal Search Scaffolding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05334)
*Mahdi Farahbakhsh,Ilan Sela,Fatemeh Doudi,Vishnu Teja Kunde,Krishna Narayanan,Jean-Francois Chamberland,Dileep Kalathil*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AgentDiscover is a planning-capable LLM-based coding agent that controls its own scientific search using a structured memory/database, outperforming fixed human-designed pipelines in cost-efficiency and benchmark quality across multiple domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most current LLM-based scientific discovery frameworks use a fixed, human-designed search algorithm where the model only proposes candidates and has no global view of the search. As models improve, such hand-designed control may become a bottleneck. Inspired by the Bitter Lesson, the authors want to test whether giving the model control over the search strategy itself, along with suitable memory and tools, can scale better than pre-specified algorithms.

Method: They build AgentDiscover, where an LLM coding agent plans and executes the search loop instead of following a fixed pipeline. The agent uses its context window as working memory, runs experiments, and logs ideas, candidates, and their relations into a structured database that functions as long-term memory. This database is designed so that classical algorithmic selection rules (e.g., MAP-Elites, MCTS) can be executed via single database queries. A separate server maintains and updates the database, and provides steering signals after each agent submission to keep long runs on track. The agent can freely choose, combine, or replace classical strategies through how it queries and updates this database.

Result: Across tasks in kernel engineering, biology, algorithm design, mathematics, and systems optimization, AgentDiscover achieves better results at lower API cost than prior LLM discovery frameworks using the same base model. In particular, its generated programs would have ranked first in seven historical AtCoder heuristic contests, and on eleven mathematical and systems optimization problems it matches or surpasses all baselines with access to the same model.

Conclusion: Allowing an LLM agent to own the search process—using a structured, queryable long-term memory that subsumes classical search algorithms—yields more cost-efficient and higher-performing scientific discovery than fixed human-designed pipelines. This supports the view that less hand-designed structure and more learned/planned search by the model can scale better. The released codebase provides a general framework for future LLM-driven discovery systems.

Abstract: Frameworks that use large language models for scientific discovery typically rely on a fixed, human-designed algorithm that decides what the model sees at each step, leaving the model only the role of proposer. The model knows nothing of the search beyond what it is shown. As models grow more capable, a question arises: does a search strategy chosen by a human before the run scale better than promoting the model from proposer to planner and letting it own the search? The Bitter Lesson suggests that choosing the strategy in advance is the kind of hand-designed structure that general methods eventually outscale. We introduce AgentDiscover, in which a coding agent plans the search using its context as working memory, runs experiments, and records every attempt in a database of ideas, candidates, and their relations. This database serves as the agent's long-term memory and is structured so that the selection rules of classical algorithms such as MAP-Elites and Monte Carlo tree search each reduce to a single query, which the agent is free to use, combine, or replace. A server maintains the database and steers the agent after every submission, keeping it on course over long runs. In our experiments, AgentDiscover is more cost-efficient than existing frameworks, reaching better scores at lower cost. On tasks in kernel engineering, biology, algorithm design, and mathematics, AgentDiscover outperforms prior discovery frameworks. Its programs would have placed first among human competitors in seven past AtCoder heuristic contests, and on eleven mathematical and systems optimization tasks it matches or exceeds every baseline that uses the same model. Our code is available at https://github.com/mhdfb/AgentDiscover.

</details>


### [285] [EnGRICH: Enhancing Generative Reward Modeling with Critiques from Humans](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05370)
*Xuancheng Li,Beining Wang,Haitao Li,Heng Wang,Yujia Zhou,Qingyi Pan,Blaze Chen,Yiqun Liu,Min Zhang,Qingyao Ai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces EnGRICH, a framework that improves generative reward models (GRMs) by training them with a MetaCritic that learns from a small set of human critiques to evaluate and guide the GRM’s own critiques, yielding more reliable and fine-grained training signals than using preference outcomes alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative reward models can give detailed natural-language feedback, but current training mainly optimizes for whether final preference labels are correct. Since preference labels live in a small, constrained space, even poorly reasoned critiques can lead to correct labels and get reinforced. Human-written critiques can offer process supervision, but they are scarce and often reduced to scalar rewards, wasting their fine-grained evaluative content. The authors want a way to learn rich evaluative criteria from limited human critiques and propagate them to large-scale outcome-only preference data, improving critique reliability without needing massive human annotation.

Method: The authors propose EnGRICH, which jointly trains a GRM and a MetaCritic. The MetaCritic is first learned from a small dataset of human critiques and is designed to construct response-specific rubrics capturing criteria such as evidence coverage and factual or logical correctness. During GRM training, for each generated critique, the MetaCritic evaluates it against the rubric, producing structured signals: (1) process rewards for each critique dimension, enabling fine-grained credit assignment, and (2) guidance signals that steer the GRM toward generating more comprehensive and accurate critiques. The MetaCritic itself is further optimized to generalize the human-grounded evaluative criteria to broader outcome-only preference data, so that its feedback remains useful even when no human critique is available. At inference time, only the GRM is used; the MetaCritic is not required.

Result: On seven standard reward-modeling benchmarks, EnGRICH outperforms competitive GRM and scalar reward model baselines. The reported improvements are consistent across datasets, indicating that MetaCritic-based process supervision yields better reward models than outcome-only training. Ablation and diagnostic analyses show that the key components—rubric construction, evidence coverage and correctness evaluation, and the joint optimization of MetaCritic during GRM training—each contribute materially to the performance gains, and that critiques become more reliable and informative.

Conclusion: Learning evaluative criteria from a small set of human critiques and using them via a MetaCritic to supervise generative reward models leads to more reliable and effective GRMs than relying only on final preference outcomes. EnGRICH successfully generalizes human-grounded process supervision to large-scale outcome-only data, enabling the trained GRM to produce both better preference judgments and higher-quality critiques at inference time. The framework demonstrates that structured, critique-level feedback is a powerful complement to traditional scalar reward modeling for LLM optimization.

Abstract: Generative reward models (GRMs) are important for LLM optimization. Unlike scalar reward models, GRMs generate natural-language critiques alongside preference judgments, providing finer-grained evaluation signals. Their effectiveness depends heavily on critique reliability. However, existing GRM training typically uses final preference correctness as outcome supervision. Because the preference outcome space is highly constrained, unreliable critiques can still yield correct outcomes and thus be reinforced. Recent work leverages human critiques for process supervision, but such critiques are scarce and are often reduced to scalar rewards, leaving their fine-grained evaluative information underutilized. We argue that evaluative criteria learned from human critiques can be generalized to broader outcome-only preference data. To this end, we propose \textbf{EnGRICH}, a GRM training framework that pairs the GRM with a training-time MetaCritic learned from a small set of human critiques. MetaCritic constructs response-specific rubrics and uses them to evaluate the evidence coverage and correctness of generated critiques. The resulting signals provide both process rewards for fine-grained credit assignment and structured guidance for exploring better critiques. During GRM training, MetaCritic is further optimized to generalize human-grounded evaluative criteria to outcome-only data. At inference, the trained GRM operates independently. Experiments across seven reward-model benchmarks show that EnGRICH consistently improves over competitive baselines, while further analyses validate the effectiveness of its core mechanisms.

</details>


### [286] [Learning Field Reconstruction from Incomplete Data by Globally Correcting Local Estimates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05375)
*Renhao Zhong,Zihan Zhou,Chiyuan Ma,Tianshu Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose a two-stage, locally trained then globally refined model that reconstructs full physical fields (like ocean variables) from systematically incomplete observations, outperforming prior methods on real ocean datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Physical fields (e.g., ocean temperature, currents) are often only partially observed in space, so models must infer missing regions from fragmented data. Existing context–query approaches can use held-out data for supervision but cannot uniquely identify the full-field distribution when every training example is incomplete. With finite, noisy data and weak evidence of sharp local structures, models tend to produce over-smoothed, averaged fields that miss important localized variations. The authors seek a structural prior that encourages realistic completions based on local spatial relationships learned directly from the available observations.

Method: They introduce a two-stage estimator that combines locally constructed predictions with a globally revisable refinement. First, a shared coordinate-conditioned predictor is trained on incomplete local patches, using relatively well-observed neighborhoods to directly supervise local field structure. This yields overlapping local predictions across the domain, which are reconciled into a single consensus field conditioned on observations. Second, a full-domain estimator is trained to keep the original observations fixed and learn a residual correction with respect to this frozen local consensus field. The global model takes as input both the local estimate and its discrepancies with observed values, and outputs corrections that integrate broader spatial evidence while preserving fidelity to measurements.

Result: On three real-world ocean datasets that contain genuine observation gaps, the proposed estimator achieves the best reconstruction quality among all tested methods. Specifically, on withheld, observation-supported values, it attains the lowest mean squared error (MSE) and highest peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), reducing MSE by 28.9%–34.5% compared to the strongest external baseline method.

Conclusion: Incorporating an explicit local structural prior via patch-based coordinate-conditioned prediction, combined with a subsequent global residual refinement, leads to more accurate and detailed reconstructions of incompletely observed physical fields. By first building a locally consistent consensus estimate and then globally revising it while anchoring to observations, the method mitigates oversmoothing and better captures sharp and localized phenomena, as demonstrated on challenging real-world ocean datasets.

Abstract: Reconstructing physical fields from training samples that are always incomplete requires learning spatial structure from fragmented observations.Existing context--query work establishes how held-out observations provide valid training targets, but this does not make the complete-field distribution identifiable when every training field is incomplete.With finite data, weak evidence of sharp transitions and localized variations can further favor averaged predictions that attenuate local detail.A structural prior is therefore needed to favor plausible completions; local spatial relationships offer one grounded in the observations.We propose a locally constructed, globally revisable estimator that explicitly learns local field estimates and subsequently corrects them using full-domain observations.A shared coordinate-conditioned predictor learns from incomplete patches, allowing relatively well-observed neighborhoods to provide direct supervision of local structure.Its overlapping predictions are reconciled into an observation-conditioned consensus field.A full-domain estimator retains the original observations and learns a residual correction around this frozen field estimate, allowing locally constructed structure to be revised by broader evidence.The local estimate serves as both an explicit input, accompanied by its discrepancies with the observations, and a prediction starting point that the global model can revise.On three real-world ocean datasets with authentic observation gaps, our estimator achieves the lowest MSE and highest PSNR on withheld source-supported values, reducing MSE by 28.9\%--34.5\% against the strongest external baseline.

</details>


### [287] [Sibyl: An Efficient Small-large Model Collaboration Framework for Long-horizon Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05383)
*Zhewei Fang,Yuxin Zhang,Zhenwei Shao,Mengze Li,Zheng Lin,Long Chen,Zhou Yu,Zhe Chen,Zhiwen Chen,Zhaode Wang,chengfei lv*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Sibyl, a training algorithm that lets small language model agents decide when to call a stronger cloud model at each step, achieving high task success with very few cloud calls.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Small language models are fast and resource‑efficient for on-device agents, but they struggle with complex, long-horizon reasoning and planning. Collaborating with larger cloud models can help, yet current approaches lack an effective way to decide, at each step, when cloud help is necessary, especially because the benefit of a cloud call is only observable in the final outcome and there is a trade-off between performance and the cost/latency/privacy of cloud usage.

Method: Sibyl is a three-stage training pipeline for SLM agents. (1) It first learns a strong base policy with self-evolving RL that does not use any cloud consultation, so the SLM can act reasonably well on its own. (2) It then initializes consultation behavior by mining “decisive-disagreement” states—situations where the SLM and the cloud model disagree in ways that strongly affect outcomes—to provide focused supervision on when consultations matter. (3) Finally, it performs consultation-aware RL that jointly learns a policy for when to consult the cloud model and how to internalize (distill) the cloud model’s guidance so that the SLM improves its own future decisions and relies less on the cloud over time.

Result: On ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks, a 0.6B-parameter SLM trained with Sibyl outperforms state-of-the-art agent training and routing baselines by 95.2% and 80.4% relative improvement in success rate, respectively, while using on average only 0.8 and 3.9 cloud calls per trajectory, indicating both strong effectiveness and efficient cloud utilization.

Conclusion: Sibyl enables small, on-device language model agents to achieve competitive performance on long-horizon interactive tasks by learning to selectively and sparingly query a large cloud model and to internalize its knowledge. This approach effectively balances task success with minimal dependence on cloud resources, making SLM-based agents more practical for real-world deployment.

Abstract: Small language models (SLMs) offer a promising foundation for on-device agents through low-latency, resource-efficient inference, yet limited reasoning and planning capabilities constrain their performance on long-horizon tasks requiring multi-step interaction with the environment. Step-level collaboration between SLMs and larger cloud-hosted models can bridge this gap, but identifying states that warrant cloud assistance remains challenging: the contribution of each cloud call is entangled with subsequent actions and can be assessed only from the final task outcome. Compounding this challenge, the SLM must balance two competing objectives: maximizing task success and minimizing cloud calls. To address this, we propose Sibyl, an algorithm that trains SLM agents to selectively consult cloud models at the step level and internalize their guidance for subsequent decisions, achieving strong task performance with minimal cloud reliance. Sibyl follows a three-stage training pipeline that (1) builds a robust base policy through consultation-free self-evolving reinforcement learning (RL); (2) cold-starts consultation behavior via decisive-disagreement state mining; and (3) jointly optimizes consultation decisions and guidance internalization through consultation-aware RL. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate that Sibyl, using only a 0.6B-parameter model, outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, including agent training and routing methods, by 95.2% and 80.4% in success rate while averaging only 0.8 and 3.9 cloud calls per trajectory, respectively.

</details>


### [288] [MMPostTrainBench: Benchmarking Autonomous Research for Multimodal Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05398)
*Yuxin Liu,Yuxuan Wang,Zhenxin Lei,Lingchen Meng,Yuchong Sun,Junming Lin,Hongcheng Liu,Yunfei Chu,Qize Yang,Jin Xu,Lei Zhang,Zhendong Mao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper evaluates how well autonomous LLM-based agents can iteratively improve multimodal models and introduces a new benchmark and framework to address observed failures in sustained improvement and model selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLM agents have shown promise in automating text-only model training and improvement, it is unclear whether they can reliably sustain improvement on harder multimodal tasks involving images, audio, video, and code grounded in media. There is a need to systematically measure these capabilities and understand failure modes such as regressions on non-target abilities and inconsistent gains across research iterations.

Method: The authors build MMPostTrainBench, a benchmark with eight multimodal tasks (image, audio, video, joint audio-video understanding, and image-grounded software repair). Agents start from a common base model, operate under fixed budgets, use development feedback, and then submit models that are independently evaluated. The benchmark measures (1) performance on both target and non-target tasks, (2) changes across research iterations, (3) quality of model selection, and (4) research integrity. Based on the discovered limitations, they propose MMResearch, a multimodal research framework that links media-grounded evidence to hypotheses and interventions, uses hierarchical memory to propagate findings, and retains candidate models via development evaluation. They integrate MMResearch with existing code-agent runtimes.

Result: Across eight tasks, more than half (52.1%) of model–task mean performances fall below the base model, and submissions suffer from non-target task regressions. Model performance does not consistently improve over iterations, and agents often fail to select the best evaluated candidate; final submissions can lag the best candidate by up to 5.38 percentage points. With the proposed MMResearch framework added to code-agent runtimes, submitted-model accuracy improves by up to 7.75 percentage points for Claude Opus 4.8 with Claude Code and 2.33 points for GPT-5.6-sol with Codex.

Conclusion: Autonomous LLM agents currently struggle to sustain and reliably manage multimodal model improvements, showing frequent regressions, poor cross-task preservation, and suboptimal model selection. Extending autonomous research to multimodal domains introduces perception, alignment, and temporal grounding challenges. The proposed MMPostTrainBench exposes these issues and MMResearch partially mitigates them by tying evidence to hypotheses, carrying knowledge across rounds via hierarchical memory, and systematically managing candidate models, leading to measurable gains in final submitted-model accuracy.

Abstract: Autonomous research seeks sustained model improvements through iterative experimentation and feedback. LLM agents show promise in automating machine learning and language-model post-training, but their ability to sustain multimodal improvement remains unclear. We introduce MMPostTrainBench, a benchmark spanning eight tasks in image, audio, video, and joint audio-video understanding and image-grounded software repair. Agents operate from a common base model within fixed budgets, using development feedback before independent evaluation of their submitted models. Evaluation covers target and non-target model outcomes, iterative model improvement and selection, and research integrity. Across all eight tasks, 52.1% of model--task means fall below the base, and evaluated submissions also exhibit non-target regressions. Model performance does not consistently improve across research iterations, and agents do not reliably select the best evaluated candidate for submission; final submissions trail that candidate by up to 5.38 percentage points. Extending autonomous research from text-only to multimodal tasks introduces additional sources of error in perception, cross-modal alignment, and temporal grounding. The observed regressions and selection gaps highlight the need to balance targeted improvements with non-target capability preservation and to retain gains across research iterations. These requirements motivate MMResearch, a multimodal research framework that connects media-grounded evidence to hypotheses and interventions, carries findings across rounds through hierarchical memory, and retains candidates using development evaluation. Added to existing code-agent runtimes, it improves submitted-model accuracy by up to 7.75 percentage points for Claude Opus 4.8 with Claude Code and 2.33 points for GPT-5.6-sol with Codex.

</details>


### [289] [CASE: Cost-Aware Stopping for Efficient Long-Video Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05400)
*Yiming Du,Chenghao Liu,Zhiyuan Liu,Fangxing Zheng,Zhao Wang,Junnan Nie,Songfang Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces CASE, a plug-in framework that teaches long-video question-answering agents when to stop watching and answer, greatly cutting computation while preserving or improving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing long-video reasoning agents can navigate and gather relevant evidence, but they lack an explicit, learned mechanism to decide when they have seen enough video to answer a query. This leads to unnecessary computation and token usage, or premature stopping that harms accuracy. The paper aims to formalize and learn an effective stopping rule that is compatible with existing agents, improves the accuracy-efficiency trade-off, and generalizes across benchmarks.

Method: The authors propose CASE, which treats stopping as a policy-conditioned sequential decision problem. During agent execution over a long video, CASE inserts causal checkpoints where it performs an auxiliary multiple-choice assessment of the evidence gathered so far and inspects the host agent's internal execution state. From complete, full-length trajectories, they construct a cost-aware target that compares the utility of answering immediately versus continuing along the same search path, explicitly trading off answer correctness against the token and computation cost of further reasoning. A simple Ridge regression model is trained to predict this 'decision gap' and then converted into binary STOP/CONTINUE actions during inference. CASE is implemented as a plug-in module on top of three existing vision-language models and evaluated on several long-video benchmarks.

Result: On the Video-MME benchmark, integrating CASE with three vision-language models yields a modest average accuracy gain of +0.67 percentage points while reducing model token usage by 53.63%. When the learned stopping policies are transferred zero-shot (without retraining) to LongVideoBench and MLVU, end-to-end accuracy improves by +3.38 and +4.58 points respectively, while model-token usage is reduced by 58.78% and 51.28%. Across all combinations of agents, models, and benchmarks, CASE achieves the best coverage of the accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier (83.3%) among all compared stopping methods at chosen operating points. In online execution settings, CASE maintains this accuracy-efficiency balance and further lowers measured runtime by 54.1% on average.

Conclusion: CASE is an effective, lightweight, and general plug-in termination framework for long-video reasoning agents. By learning a cost-aware stopping rule from complete trajectories and using a simple regressor to make STOP/CONTINUE decisions at checkpoints, it substantially reduces token consumption and runtime while maintaining or even improving QA accuracy. The approach transfers well across datasets and model backbones, and it outperforms alternative stopping strategies in terms of accuracy-efficiency Pareto coverage, demonstrating that explicit, learned stopping is a key component for scalable long-video reasoning.

Abstract: Long-video agents can actively gather question-relevant evidence, but they typically leave a central decision implicit: when has the agent seen enough to answer? We propose CASE, a plug-in termination framework that frames this decision as policy-conditioned sequential stopping. At each causal checkpoint, CASE combines an auxiliary multiple-choice assessment of accumulated evidence with the host agent's execution state. From complete native trajectories, we construct a cost-aware target that compares answering now with stopping later along the same search path, accounting jointly for answer correctness and the full cost of continued reasoning. A lightweight Ridge regressor learns this decision gap and produces STOP/CONTINUE decisions. We evaluate three vision-language models with VideoSeek and AVP. On Video-MME, end-to-end accuracy changes by +0.67 percentage points on average while CASE reduces model-token use by 53.63%. The same frozen policies then transfer zero-shot to LongVideoBench and MLVU, with end-to-end accuracy changes of +3.38 and +4.58 points while saving 58.78% and 51.28% of model tokens, respectively. Across all agent-model-benchmark combinations, CASE attains the highest accuracy-efficiency Pareto-frontier coverage among the compared stopping methods (83.3%) at the selected operating points. Online execution preserves this favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off and additionally reduces measured runtime by 54.1% on average. CASE provides a plug-in termination framework for long-video reasoning agents, enabling them to decide when further evidence acquisition is no longer worthwhile.

</details>


### [290] [PharmAgent: Constraint-Aware Search with Frozen Language Models for Molecular Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05431)
*Nihui Shao,Guanxing Chen,Jilong Shi,Zhengyang Bai,Haohuai He,Zhenchao Tang,Qiujie Lv,Yu-An Huang,Zhi-An Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PharmAgent is a constraint-aware molecular optimization framework that uses a Lagrangian controller and structure-indexed replay to balance target activity improvement with multiple developability constraints, outperforming existing baselines in both unconstrained and constrained settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Molecular optimization needs to improve biological target activity while also satisfying multiple developability constraints (e.g., properties relevant to drug-likeness) under limited evaluation budgets. Existing classical methods require hand-crafted rules or task-specific training to incorporate chemical instructions and property feedback. Frozen language-model-based approaches can condition edits on such information but lack precise constraint control and often require relevant prior experience. There is thus a need for a general, data-efficient method that can explicitly handle constraints, adapt online, and work effectively with limited evaluations.

Method: The authors propose PharmAgent, a constraint-aware molecular search algorithm that combines a Lagrangian controller with an adaptive external state and structure-indexed replay. The Lagrangian controller converts constraint violations observed in accepted molecules into evolving multipliers ("constraint pressure"), maintaining a separation between the historical record of violations and current property evaluations. A structure-indexed replay buffer stores evaluated molecular transitions and retrieves relevant experiences to guide future molecule proposals. The optimization follows a curriculum that gradually activates constraints; at each step, candidate molecules and the current best (incumbent) are compared under the same active objective set, and the outcome of this comparison determines how the Lagrangian multipliers are updated. The authors derive an exact identity describing how accepted-state violations accumulate into the multipliers, providing theoretical insight into the controller dynamics.

Result: On five molecular optimization tasks with five independent runs each, PharmAgent achieves a summed area under the target-score curves (AUC) of 3.9208 in target-only search, a 37.3% improvement over the prior best baseline MOLLEO. In settings with online constraints, PharmAgent attains a property-adjusted AUC of 0.7076, outperforming the strongest online baseline, ExLLM, by 53.8%. It ranks first among all evaluated methods in both target-only and constraint-aware search across all five baseline frameworks. Ablation studies show that the full PharmAgent system outperforms all its variants in terms of target quality, property-adjusted performance, and Pareto hypervolume. In all five molecular case studies, the method reaches feasible final solutions that demonstrate improved target scores along with explicit trade-offs against constraints.

Conclusion: PharmAgent provides an effective and principled framework for constraint-aware molecular optimization under limited evaluation budgets. By using a Lagrangian controller with external state and structure-indexed replay, it can systematically translate observed constraint violations into adaptive pressure that guides the search towards feasible, high-quality molecules. The method consistently outperforms existing target-only and constraint-aware baselines across multiple tasks, with superior target scores, property-adjusted metrics, and Pareto front quality. The theoretical identity for multiplier accumulation and the empirical demonstrations across five molecular cases indicate that PharmAgent is a strong and general solution for balancing activity improvement with complex developability constraints.

Abstract: Molecular optimization must improve target activity and satisfy developability constraints within limited evaluation budgets. Classical methods require tailored rules or training to incorporate chemical instructions and property feedback. Frozen language models can condition edits on this information, but need explicit constraint control and relevant experience. We therefore present PharmAgent, a constraint-aware molecular search method driven by adaptive external state. Its Lagrangian controller translates violations in accepted states into accumulated constraint pressure, keeping this history separate from current property measurements.
