Structure-indexed replay complements this feedback with relevant evaluated transitions that guide subsequent proposals. As a curriculum progressively activates constraints, candidates and the incumbent are compared under the same current objective, and the accepted state determines the next multiplier update. We derive an exact identity that characterizes how accepted-state violations accumulate in the controller's multipliers. Across five tasks with five independent runs, PharmAgent achieves a summed area under the target-score curves (AUC) of 3.9208 in target-only search, improving over MOLLEO by 37.3%. With online constraints, it achieves a property-adjusted AUC of 0.7076, improving over the strongest online baseline, ExLLM, by 53.8%. These results rank first among all evaluated methods in both target-only and constraint-aware search. The online comparison covers all five baseline frameworks. The full system leads every ablation variant in target quality, property-adjusted performance, and Pareto hypervolume. All five molecular cases reach feasible final states, documenting target gains and trade-offs.

</details>


### [291] [TeleTune: Evolving Agent Skills From Offline Telemetry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05437)
*Justin Chih-Yao Chen,Elias Stengel-Eskin,Yan Chen,Pol Llado,Scott Counts,Mohit Bansal,Benjamin Van Durme,Harsh Jhamtani,Gaurav Verma*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TeleTune learns a reusable textual skill library for computer-use agents from offline user telemetry logs by optimizing skills to better predict user actions, enabling robust workflow retrieval and outperforming prior methods on web task benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Computer-use agents need procedural knowledge of how humans operate software, but existing user telemetry logs lack explicit goals, cannot be replayed for online learning, and often interleave multiple tasks without boundaries. There is a need for a scalable way to learn reusable skills and workflows from such imperfect, offline logs so agents can generalize and perform new tasks more reliably.

Method: TeleTune is a framework that learns a textual skill library from offline, interleaved user action logs without recorded goals. It treats skills as components in a workflow library and uses action-prediction on logged trajectories as an implicit training signal. Candidate edits to the skill library are proposed and only retained if they improve held-out action-prediction accuracy ("skill-guided progress"). The learned workflows are then used at test time to retrieve demonstrations that cover subgoals of new tasks, and the agent is given both the optimized skill library and these retrieved workflows for execution.

Result: On the WorkArena and Online-Mind2Web benchmarks, TeleTune achieves average success rates of 77.1% and 80.6%, respectively, outperforming the strongest baseline in each setting by 6.7% and 7.7%. Under the most heavily perturbed WorkArena training data, TeleTune maintains the highest average success rate of 68.5%, which is 6.3% better than the best baseline. The framework also shows that learning purely from fixed logs can be 5–75 times more token-efficient than validating edits via live episodes, while its skill-guided progress metric closely tracks actual live success rates.

Conclusion: TeleTune effectively turns noisy, offline user telemetry into a reusable textual skill and workflow library for computer-use agents, overcoming goal underspecification, non-replayability, and interleaved trajectories. Its skill-optimization-plus-workflow-retrieval approach is both complementary and more token-efficient than online validation, while reliably improving success rates across benchmarks and remaining robust under data perturbations.

Abstract: Computer-use agents need to capture procedural knowledge of how people use software. User telemetry offers a scalable source of this knowledge. However, learning reusable skills from these logs requires addressing three challenges: (1) Goal Underspecification, since logs do not record the goal behind each action; (2) Non-Replayability, since past activity cannot be replayed to evaluate skill updates; and (3) Interleaved Trajectories, since logs may mix several tasks without marking their boundaries. To address these, we introduce TeleTune, a framework for learning a textual skill library from offline logs without recorded goals, cannot be replayed during optimization, and may interleave tasks. TeleTune uses action-prediction errors on logged trajectories to propose library edits and keep only those that improve held-out action-prediction accuracy, which we call skill-guided progress. The learned workflows also enable retrieval of demonstrations that cover the subgoals of a new task. At test time, the agent is provided with the learned library and the workflow-based retrieved demonstrations. Experiments on WorkArena and Online-Mind2Web show that TeleTune outperforms random retrieval, Agent Workflow Memory (AWM), and their combination. We find that the best baseline varies by setting, whereas TeleTune achieves average success rates of 77.1% and 80.6%, respectively, improving over the strongest baseline on each benchmark by 6.7% and 7.7%. Under the heaviest perturbation of the WorkArena training data,TeleTune keeps the highest average success rate at 68.5%, 6.3% above the strongest baseline. Our analyses show (1) skill optimization and workflow-based retrieval are complementary, (2) optimizing on fixed logs costs 5 to 75 times fewer tokens than validating the same edits with live episodes, (3) skill-guided progress tracks the live success rate.

</details>


### [292] [AI Safety via Debate is Compromised by Cognitive Biases](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05461)
*Gefei Liu,Sonya Rashkovan,Sophia Lloyd George,Isaac Sheidlower,Serena Booth*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper tests whether rhetorical manipulation can undermine the core assumption of AI safety via debate by making human judges prefer misleading arguments over truthful ones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RLHF makes models follow human instructions but also incentivizes being persuasive and flattering instead of accurate. AI safety via debate is proposed to fix this by having models challenge each other so that truth should be easier to defend than lies. The authors want to test if this assumption still holds when arguments deliberately exploit human cognitive biases, because real-world deployment will face such manipulative tactics.

Method: They design 68 dialogues about detective-style mystery cases where the true culprit is known. For each case, two LLM debaters argue for different suspects. They systematically inject four types of rhetorical interventions—anchoring, ignoring logical fallacies, use of technical jargon, and sheer verbosity—into either the ‘true’ side or the ‘false’ side. They then run a user study with 369 human participants who adjudicate which side is more convincing, allowing the authors to separate the effect of correctness from the effect of rhetorical biasing.

Result: Across all four rhetorical bias types, when the manipulation is applied to one side, human judgments systematically shift toward that manipulated side, regardless of whether it is arguing for the true or false culprit. Pooled over conditions, these interventions significantly alter which debater humans perceive as more convincing.

Conclusion: Debate-based supervision is vulnerable because human adjudicators can be swayed by rhetorical manipulation rather than truth. The core assumption that truthful arguments are inherently easier to defend than false ones breaks down when debaters exploit cognitive biases, calling into question the robustness of AI safety via debate as currently envisioned.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has played a central role in making large language models responsive to human instructions. However, human evaluators often favor flattering or persuasive responses over truthful ones, creating incentives for models to appeal to evaluators at the expense of accuracy. AI safety via debate has been proposed as a way to improve the supervision of language models: in this paradigm, two agents argue opposing positions and challenge each other's claims, potentially exposing falsehoods to the adjudicator. A central premise of AI safety via debate is that truthful arguments are easier to defend than false ones under adversarial scrutiny. In this work, we investigate whether this advantage persists when debaters use rhetorical strategies that exploit biases in human judgment. Inspired by competitive debate, we construct 68 LLM-generated dialogues about detective mysteries with known culprits, spanning four interventions: anchoring, fallacy oversight, pro-jargon, and verbosity. We apply each intervention to either the side advocating for the true culprit or the side advocating for an innocent suspect, allowing us to distinguish influence on adjudication from correctness. In a study with 369 participants, we find that, pooled across bias types, these interventions significantly shift judgments toward the manipulated side. These findings expose a vulnerability in debate-based supervision: human adjudication is sensitive to manipulative rhetorical strategies.

</details>


### [293] [Hallucination Across the Reasoning Lifecycle: Interface Visibility, Causal Evidence, and Release Control in Large Reasoning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05472)
*Zhe Yu,Mohan Li,Lei Yu,Ka-Ho Chow,Chengwei Qin,Xingyu Wu,Wenpeng Xing,Shuguang Xiong,Meng Han*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Survey of reasoning hallucinations in text generation and a framework (UIPCA) to categorize and address them.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reasoning errors in language models can spread to future decisions and memory, so it is important to systematically understand, measure, and mitigate them.

Method: Literature and report survey of 312 works, with focused analysis of 58 key sources, organized using the UIPCA scheme: Unsupported premises, Invalid inferences, dependent reuse of errors, answer-trace Consistency, and Action-policy failures.

Result: No reviewed study shows an intervention that improves reasoning quality while simultaneously harming factual reliability under matched conditions; the survey maps existing evidence to different forms of diagnosis and mitigation (verification, repair, selective release, persistent-state control).

Conclusion: Reasoning hallucinations can be systematically categorized with UIPCA, and existing evidence supports integrated approaches to diagnosis and mitigation rather than tradeoffs that boost reasoning at the cost of factual reliability.

Abstract: Reasoning errors can propagate into later decisions and memory. This survey synthesizes 312 papers and first-party reports on text-based reasoning hallucinations around three questions: what evidence is observable, what study designs establish, and which corrective actions the evidence supports. UIPCA records unsupported premises (U), invalid inferences (I), dependent reuse (P), visible answer-trace consistency (C), and action-policy failures (A). Across 58 reviewed sources, no comparison establishes that a specified intervention improves reasoning while reducing factual reliability under matched conditions. The synthesis connects diagnosis to verification, repair, selective release, and persistent-state control across memory, tools, and training feedback.

</details>


### [294] [Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning with Stable Temporal Abstraction for Language Model Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05473)
*Shayan Mohajer Hamidi,Yize Cheng,Yuanda Xu,Zhengze Zhou,Alborz Geramifard*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces STAC, a constrained optimization method that stabilizes when and how hierarchical language agents change or keep subgoals, significantly boosting performance on ALFWorld and WebShop tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hierarchical reinforcement learning and hierarchical language agents use subgoals to handle long-horizon tasks, but in practice the temporal abstraction can be unstable: agents may replan subgoals too frequently (premature replanning) or keep outdated subgoals (stale persistence). This instability undermines the benefits of hierarchy. The paper aims to explicitly model and control this instability so that subgoal changes are neither overly reactive nor too rigid, improving overall task success.

Method: The authors propose Stable Temporal Abstraction via Constrained Optimization (STAC). They define two forms of undesired behavior—premature replanning and stale persistence—as constraint costs on the boundary policy that decides when to change subgoals. Using a constrained optimization / Lagrangian formulation, they penalize only the sampled boundary decisions while leaving the base hierarchical algorithm intact: rewards, critic targets, subgoal advantages, and primitive-action advantages are not modified. STAC is thus a plug-in boundary-policy optimizer layered on top of existing hierarchical language-agent backbones.

Result: On two benchmarks (ALFWorld and WebShop) and with two backbone language models (Qwen3-0.6B and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct), STAC consistently improves success rates over a strong hierarchical baseline. With Qwen3-0.6B, STAC yields gains of 8.1 and 7.9 percentage points on ALFWorld and WebShop respectively; with Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, the gains are larger: 23.5 and 15.8 percentage points on the same benchmarks.

Conclusion: Explicit temporal abstraction in hierarchical language agents is not sufficient; stability of the boundary policy that sets and updates subgoals is crucial. By casting premature replanning and stale persistence as constraints and optimizing the boundary policy via a Lagrangian approach, STAC stabilizes temporal abstraction without altering the underlying RL signals or action policies, leading to substantial performance improvements across tasks and model backbones.

Abstract: Hierarchical reinforcement learning improves long-horizon control by organizing primitive actions around persistent subgoals and assigning credit at multiple temporal scales. Recent hierarchical language agents bring these benefits to interactive tasks by explicitly separating subgoal planning from action execution. We observe, however, that an explicit hierarchy does not by itself determine how stable the resulting temporal abstraction is: the learned boundary policy may replace the subgoal almost every turn, making it effectively transient, or retain a subgoal after it has stopped being appropriate. We call this temporal abstraction instability. We propose Stable Temporal Abstraction via Constrained Optimization (STAC), a constrained boundary-policy optimization method that represents premature replanning and stale persistence as constraint costs. STAC applies the resulting Lagrangian costs only to the sampled boundary decision, leaving the underlying algorithm's rewards, critic targets, subgoal advantages, and primitive-action advantages unchanged. Across two backbones and two benchmarks, STAC improves success over a strong hierarchical baseline by $8.1$ and $7.9$ points on ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen3-0.6B, and by $23.5$ and $15.8$ points with Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct.

</details>


### [295] [CodeForge-MA: Execution-Verified Multi-Agent Learning with Language-Conditioned LoRA for Multilingual Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05481)
*Zhizhou Gu,Xianting Wu,Siyu Gu,Tian Zhang,Kejian Tong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CodeForge-MA is a framework to improve code generation in large language models using multi-agent data creation, execution-verified reinforcement tuning, and language-specific LoRA adapters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLMs for code generation struggle with runtime correctness, multilingual performance, and data contamination, and are often constrained by frozen backbones that limit direct modification of the base model.

Method: They introduce a multi-agent system (Composer, Reviewer, Executor, Curator) to iteratively generate and verify instruction–code pairs; combine masked supervised fine-tuning with a test-based reinforcement signal during training; and apply a language-conditioned mixture of LoRA adapters with sparse expert routing over a frozen backbone.

Result: Experiments show that jointly designing the data pipeline, training objectives, and adapter architecture significantly improves code generation robustness and performance across multiple programming languages.

Conclusion: A coordinated approach—multi-agent data forging, execution-aware reinforcement tuning, and language-aware adapter routing—can substantially enhance code synthesis quality and multilingual generalization without changing the base model at inference.

Abstract: Large language models for code generation often fail on execution, multilingual coverage, and contamination control, especially under frozen backbone constraints. We present CodeForge-MA, a unified framework that improves code synthesis through a multi-agent data forge, execution verified reinforced instruction tuning, and a language conditioned mixture of LoRA adapters. Four specialized agents, Composer, Reviewer, Executor, and Curator, iteratively refine instruction code pairs, validate them with tests, and filter duplicates and benchmark leakage. During training, we combine masked supervised fine tuning with a test driven reinforcement objective to align generations with executable correctness. For the larger model, we use sparse expert routing over low rank adapters to improve cross language transfer while keeping the base model unchanged at inference. Experiments show that joint data, objective, and adapter design yields robust gains across programming languages.

</details>


### [296] [SkillGATE: Gate-Aware Monte Carlo Tree Search for Skill Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05489)
*Rongchen Zhao,Yu Chen,Yanming Yang,Shijia Xu,Juyuan Wang,Jin Xu,Zibin Zheng,Jingping Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces SkillGATE, a graph-guided, MCTS-based hierarchical framework for more accurate and robust skill retrieval from large, diverse skill libraries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As skill libraries grow large and diverse, existing skill retrieval methods struggle. They either rank skills independently, missing structural cues, or rely on fixed graph propagation and hierarchical routing, which are prone to semantic distractors, getting trapped in local regions, and unrecoverable early routing errors. There is a need for a retrieval process that can adaptively explore and exploit the skill space while leveraging graph structure.

Method: The authors reformulate skill retrieval as an adaptive information-foraging process that jointly manages region-level navigation and skill-level selection based on utility and uncertainty during search. They propose SkillGATE, a graph-guided hierarchical retrieval framework that builds a graph-preserving hierarchical index of skills. Retrieval is then framed as Gate-Aware Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), with four standard phases: selection, expansion, simulation, and backpropagation. G-PUCT (a PUCT variant aware of graph gates/structure) guides which actions (regions/skills) to explore during selection; expansion opens up new regions in the hierarchy; simulation evaluates candidate skills’ relevance; and backpropagation updates search statistics to refine future decisions.

Result: On six skill retrieval benchmarks, SkillGATE is tested as a plug-in framework on top of various retrieval and reranking backbones. Across these settings, it consistently boosts retrieval performance, with a reported 16.3% improvement in Recall@1 over the strongest retriever-based baseline, indicating substantially better top-1 skill identification.

Conclusion: Modeling skill retrieval as an adaptive information-foraging process and implementing it via a graph-guided, MCTS-based hierarchical framework (SkillGATE) yields significantly better performance than prior approaches. SkillGATE effectively leverages graph structure and uncertainty-aware search to avoid local traps and routing errors, and can robustly enhance diverse backbone retrievers and rerankers for large-scale skill libraries.

Abstract: Skill Retrieval (SR) aims to identify the most relevant skills from external skill libraries, and becomes increasingly challenging as libraries grow in scale and diversity. Existing methods either rank skills independently or rely on predefined graph propagation and hierarchical routing, making them vulnerable to semantic distractors, local trapping, and early routing errors. We formulate SR as an adaptive information-foraging process that coordinates region-level navigation with skill-level selection according to the utility and uncertainty observed during search. Based on this formulation, we propose SkillGATE, a graph-guided hierarchical retrieval framework with Gate-Aware Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). SkillGATE constructs a graph-preserving hierarchical index and performs adaptive retrieval through selection, expansion, simulation, and backpropagation. G-PUCT guides action selection, expansion explores new regions, simulation evaluates candidate skills, and backpropagation updates search statistics. Experiments on six SR benchmarks show that SkillGATE consistently improves diverse retrieval and reranking backbones, achieving a 16.3\% improvement in overall R@1 over the strongest retriever-based baseline. Our code is available at https://github.com/Edwinbe/SkillGATE-v1/.

</details>


### [297] [The Functional Structure of Post-Compression Recovery in Low-Rank LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05504)
*Zishan Shao,Liang Tian,Georgiy Zemlevskiy,Kangning Cui,Lixun Zhang,Yixiao Wang,Ting Jiang,Jinhee Kim,Yixuan Chen,Rui-Feng Wang,Fan Yang,Hai Li,Yiran Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how different low-rank compression methods for LLMs exhibit distinct and reproducible patterns in how they recover performance after compression, and formalizes this as “recovery pressure,” providing tools to characterize this structure across methods and over training steps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Low-rank compression methods for LLMs can achieve similar final loss but behave differently when fine-tuned or recovered after compression. Empirically, relative performance between methods at the compression point can change—sometimes even reverse—after recovery. This suggests there may be rich, unexplained functional structure in how compressed models recover that is not captured by simple scalar loss curves. The authors aim to understand whether this heterogeneity is systematic and meaningful, and how to measure and track it during recovery.

Method: The authors introduce the concept of “recovery pressure” to formalize compression-induced functional structure that drives recovery behavior. They design a standardized, backbone-specific functional characterization that can be applied consistently across different low-rank compression schemes. They perform two main characterizations: (1) a primary backward characterization that uses loss and gradients to obtain module-wise structure, and (2) a complementary forward-only characterization that infers similar structure without using loss values or backprop. They apply these probes across layers/modules and across different compression methods and recovery trajectories, then track how the induced structure evolves during recovery training and how localized updates propagate through the network.

Result: They find that the heterogeneous recovery behaviors across low-rank compression methods are not random but instead reflect a reproducible functional structure induced by compression, which they term recovery pressure. The backward characterization reveals consistent, module-wise patterns that are reproducible across independent probes. The forward-only characterization recovers related patterns despite not using loss or gradients. Recovery pressure measured at the compression endpoint correlates with how the model will respond to subsequent recovery. During recovery, the module-wise structure of recovery pressure reorganizes in a non-uniform way, and changes applied to specific modules produce distributed effects throughout the network, not just in the directly modified modules.

Conclusion: Compression-induced recovery heterogeneity in LLMs reflects a stable and interpretable functional structure (recovery pressure), rather than just noise in loss curves. This structure can be systematically characterized across different low-rank methods and tracked over time, providing a richer view of recovery than scalar loss alone. Monitoring recovery pressure and its module-wise evolution can therefore inform better understanding, diagnosis, and possibly design of compression and recovery procedures for LLMs.

Abstract: Different low-rank compression methods can produce compressed LLMs that respond differently to the same post-compression recovery procedure, and relative advantages observed between methods at the compression endpoint may shrink, grow, or even reverse after recovery. We ask whether this recovery heterogeneity reflects functional structure beyond scalar loss evolution, and how that structure evolves throughout recovery. Our results establish that this heterogeneity reflects a reproducible compression-induced functional structure, which we formalize as recovery pressure. To characterize this structure consistently throughout recovery, we develop a standardized functional characterization within each backbone that is applicable across heterogeneous low-rank methods. The primary backward characterization reveals reproducible module-wise structure across independent probes, while a complementary forward-only characterization recovers related structure without loss or backpropagation. We further find that recovery pressure measured at the endpoint is associated with subsequent recovery response; during recovery, its module-wise structure is reorganized non-uniformly, and localized updates induce distributed responses beyond directly updated modules. Further evidence indicates that tracking this evolving structure provides a complementary functional view of recovery progress alongside scalar loss.

</details>


### [298] [What Does Fréchet Distance Measure? A Directional Decomposition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05518)
*Yunghee Lee,Jaeyeon Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose a more interpretable variant of Fréchet distance that decomposes it into semantic directions, revealing what aspects of data cause score differences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Fréchet-based metrics like FID (images) and FVD (videos) compress distribution differences into a single scalar. This hides *which* properties differ between generated and real data, and can even yield confusing behavior (e.g., more diffusion steps improving human-aligned ImageReward but worsening FID). The authors want a diagnostic tool that explains why Fréchet scores go up or down and what semantic attributes are responsible.

Method: They define the directional Fréchet distance: the expected squared projection of the optimal transport displacement between generated and reference feature distributions onto a chosen direction in feature space. By examining these projections across directions (e.g., CLIP semantic directions), they can attribute the total Fréchet distance to a small set of interpretable components. They then apply this decomposition in multiple domains (images, video, proteins).

Result: They empirically find that only a small number of meaningful directions explain most of the total Fréchet distance across image, video, and protein benchmarks. Using this, they: (1) explain why FID worsens with more diffusion steps via CLIP-based semantic directions; (2) show that FVD is biased toward per-frame appearance rather than temporal dynamics; and (3) reassess how Protein FID should be interpreted.

Conclusion: Directional Fréchet distance provides an interpretable decomposition of traditional Fréchet-based scores, revealing the semantic or structural directions that dominate distribution discrepancies. This helps diagnose counterintuitive metric behavior, clarifies biases in FID/FVD/Protein FID, and offers a more informative way to evaluate generative models than a single opaque scalar. The authors release code to facilitate adoption.

Abstract: The Fréchet distance is a de facto standard for evaluating generative models across domains, appearing as FID for images and FVD for videos. It summarizes the discrepancy between generated and reference distributions in a single scalar, with lower values typically interpreted as better generation quality. However, this scalar view can obscure what drives the comparison. For example, in COCO dataset, increasing the number of diffusion sampling steps improves ImageReward scores yet worsens (increases) FID. Motivated by this mismatch, we seek to make the Fréchet distance more interpretable by uncovering where the discrepancy lies. To this end, we introduce directional Fréchet distance, the expected squared projection of the optimal transport displacement onto a given direction. Across our image, video, and protein case studies, we find that a small number of interpretable directions account for much of the distance. We use these directions to explain the FID increase in terms of semantic concepts represented by CLIP embeddings, quantify FVD's bias toward per-frame appearance, and revisit the interpretation of Protein FID. We open-source our codebase at https://github.com/yhlee-add/directional-fd.

</details>


### [299] [Have I Scene This Before? Spatially Grounded Conversational Memory for Complex Queries in Egocentric Assistants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05526)
*Jiazhou Liang,Liam Gallagher,Kiko Chen,David Guo,Armin Toroghi,Yifan Simon Liu,Scott Sanner*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces SpaC-MEM, an object-centric 3D spatial memory for egocentric assistants, and Ego-SpaCR, a benchmark for evaluating spatially grounded conversational reasoning; SpaC-MEM improves answer accuracy and efficiency over video-based baselines, especially when 3D spatial information is preserved.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Egocentric AI assistants need to answer user questions that depend on what the user has seen and said over long periods of time and across different scenes. Existing approaches using direct vision-language models are expensive and limited by context length, while keyframe or retrieval-based methods can miss important objects or evidence. The authors want a more compact yet faithful representation that ties conversational facts to persistent objects in the 3D environment, enabling accurate recall and reasoning over long histories.

Method: The authors formalize a new task, Spatially grounded Conversational Reasoning (SpaCR), involving cross-scene, recall-focused, and counterfactual spatial questions that require combining linguistic and geometric evidence. They propose SpaC-MEM, a working memory that builds 3D reconstructions of scenes and segments them into persistent objects, then attaches multimodal and conversational information to these objects. This object-centric memory compresses history while supporting updates through dialogue. They also construct Ego-SpaCR, a benchmark based on 620 ScanNet egocentric video sessions with 95 task-oriented conversations and 3,100 evaluation queries.

Result: On the Ego-SpaCR benchmark, SpaC-MEM attains the highest overall answer accuracy among tested approaches, improves object recall compared to native video-based baselines, and does so while using substantially fewer reference input tokens. Ablation studies show that removing 3D spatial information causes large performance drops, indicating its critical role.

Conclusion: Object-centric 3D spatial memories provide an effective way to support spatially grounded conversational reasoning in egocentric assistants. By grounding dialogue in persistent 3D objects, SpaC-MEM can compress long multimodal histories without sacrificing key spatial and factual information, leading to more accurate and efficient question answering. The Ego-SpaCR benchmark demonstrates the advantages of this approach and highlights the necessity of preserving both spatial and conversational evidence for robust performance.

Abstract: Egocentric assistants must connect what users say with what they see across long interaction histories. We formalize this challenge as Spatially grounded Conversational Reasoning (SpaCR): cross-scene, recall-oriented, and counterfactual spatial queries that combine user-stated facts with geometric evidence. Direct vision-language models incur high inference costs and context limits as histories grow, while keyframe selection and retrieval can omit objects or evidence needed for complete recall. We propose Spatially grounded Conversational Memory (SpaC-MEM), an object-centric working memory that uses 3D reconstruction and segmentation to ground conversational information in persistent physical objects. It compresses multimodal histories while preserving spatial evidence and allowing object-specific facts to be updated through dialogue. We also introduce Ego-SpaCR, a benchmark comprising 620 ScanNet video sessions augmented with 95 task-oriented conversations and 3,100 evaluation queries. SpaC-MEM achieves the highest overall answer accuracy among the evaluated methods and improves object recall while requiring substantially fewer reference input tokens than native-video baselines. Removing 3D spatial information substantially degrades performance, highlighting the importance of preserving spatial and conversational evidence together.

</details>


### [300] [DelegationBench: Measuring When AI Agents Should Ask Before Acting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05532)
*Shiva Pochampally*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces DelegationBench, a benchmark to evaluate when AI agents should act autonomously versus consult users, and shows that standard agreement-based scores are misleading in several systematic ways.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents are increasingly entrusted with real-world actions like sending emails, editing files, and making purchases. A key safety and usability challenge is deciding when agents should act autonomously and when they should defer to users (ask permission, request more info, or refuse). Current evaluations typically measure how often a model’s judgment about a proposed action matches human labels, but it is unclear whether these scalar agreement scores truly capture reliable and nuanced delegation behavior. The authors want to probe whether such standard evaluations are trustworthy and sufficient, and to expose subtle failure modes that might pose safety or user-trust risks.

Method: The authors build DelegationBench, a curated benchmark of 156 scenarios, each requiring one of four responses: act, ask for permission, ask for missing information, or refuse. Most scenarios appear in matched pairs that differ in exactly one salient factor that should affect delegation decisions: whether the user explicitly requested the action, the stakes involved, reversibility (whether the action can be undone), or audience (who will see the outcome). They evaluate ten models from five model families on these scenarios in several ways: (1) standard agreement with human annotator labels; (2) sensitivity to the controlled changes in matched pairs; (3) robustness to semantically equivalent but differently worded prompts; and (4) comparison between the same models acting with tools versus merely judging proposed actions. They also hand-engineer a simple keyword-based decision rule after inspecting the benchmark and compare its performance to the models, and separately test models on explicitly stated rules to assess rule-following capabilities.

Result: The study finds three main issues. First, a simple keyword rule written after seeing the benchmark matches human annotators more often than eight of the ten evaluated models, despite the fact that it changes its decision in only 9 of 48 matched pairs—indicating that high agreement does not imply nuanced, context-sensitive behavior. Second, models are highly sensitive to prompt phrasing: equivalent question formulations can change the frequency of autonomous action by up to 52.5 percentage points, revealing serious brittleness in delegation judgments. Third, all models ask users for input less often when they must actually execute tasks via tools than when they are only asked to judge a proposed action, suggesting they may become more overconfident or less cautious in realistic tool-using settings. At the same time, when delegation rules are stated explicitly, the models follow them almost perfectly, implying that the deficits are not due to a generic inability to follow rules but rather to limitations in inferring and applying implicit norms from context.

Conclusion: Agreement metrics alone are unreliable indicators of whether AI agents will make appropriate delegation decisions in practice. DelegationBench reveals that models can achieve high label agreement while failing to adjust their behavior in important contextual shifts, showing strong prompt sensitivity, and becoming less deferential when directly operating tools. Since the same models can follow clearly specified rules well, the problem lies in how delegation criteria are represented, evaluated, and induced—not in basic rule-following capacity. The authors release DelegationBench and accompanying tools and recommend that future evaluations decompose delegation behavior into multiple reported properties—such as context-sensitivity, phrasing robustness, and behavior with vs. without tools—instead of using a single scalar score.

Abstract: AI agents that send emails, edit files, and make purchases must decide when to act on their own and when to check with the user first. This decision is usually evaluated by showing a model a proposed action, asking whether it should proceed, and scoring agreement with human labels. We introduce DelegationBench to test whether such scores can be trusted. It has 156 scenarios with four possible responses (act, ask for permission, ask for missing information, refuse), and most scenarios come in matched pairs that change a single feature: whether the action was requested, what is at stake, whether it can be undone, or who will see it. Across ten models from five families, agreement scores mislead in three ways. A simple keyword rule, which we wrote after seeing the benchmark, agrees with our annotators more often than eight of the models, yet its decision changes in only 9 of 48 matched pairs. Equivalent ways of asking the same question change how often a model acts by up to 52.5 percentage points. And every model stops to ask the user less often when it must carry out the task with tools than when it judges a proposed action. When rules are stated explicitly, the same models follow them almost perfectly, so the gaps are not explained by a general inability to follow rules. We release the benchmark and evaluation tools and recommend reporting these properties separately rather than as one score.

</details>


### [301] [More Claims, Less Evidence: Bounded Verification of AI-Generated Digital Knowledge Artifacts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05547)
*Feliks Bańka,Jarosław A. Chudziak*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents a Bayesian model explaining how much trust we can place in large, multi-claim AI-generated knowledge objects (like summaries) when we can only verify a small subset of their claims.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As digital libraries and AI systems generate more multi-claim content, humans cannot feasibly check every claim. Reviewers often verify only a few statements but must decide whether to accept the entire artifact. There is a conceptual and quantitative gap between checking some claims and trusting the whole object. The authors want to formally model this gap and understand how verification budget and artifact size affect trustworthiness assessments.

Method: The authors develop a Bayesian model of bounded verification centered on the Predictive Value of Pass (PVP), which quantifies how informative a successful partial check is for judging the whole artifact. They theoretically analyze how PVP changes with artifact size, verification budget, and error sparsity. They then run controlled experiments using FEVER and FEVEROUS datasets, constructing multi-claim artifacts with controlled mixtures of supported and unsupported claims, and simulate partial checking to empirically validate model predictions.

Result: The model predicts and experiments confirm that: (1) As artifacts grow while the number of claims checked stays fixed, the evidentiary value of a pass diminishes. (2) Increasing the verification budget improves PVP. (3) PVP is especially fragile when errors are sparse—adding many true claims around a fixed number of false ones can increase the probability that a random sample passes, while simultaneously making that pass much less informative about overall correctness. The model also yields formulas/estimates for the minimum verification budget needed to hit a target PVP.

Conclusion: Partial verification of AI-generated, multi-claim artifacts can be systematically analyzed with a Bayesian framework. A pass on a small sample of claims is often less informative than it appears, especially for large artifacts with few errors. To maintain a desired reliability (PVP) as artifact size grows, verification budgets must scale appropriately. The framework provides practical guidance for designing AI-assisted quality-assurance workflows for digital libraries and similar systems, by quantifying how many claims must be checked before publication or downstream use.

Abstract: Digital libraries, repositories, and AI-mediated knowledge services increasingly rely on generative systems to produce summaries, descriptions, and other multi-claim knowledge objects. Yet generation can scale far more easily than verification capacity: a reviewer may need to decide whether an object is suitable for publication or downstream use after checking only a small fraction of its claims. This creates a fundamental gap between claim-level verification and confidence in the object as a whole. The central question is therefore what a successful partial check implies about the reliability of the complete artifact when its size grows but the verification budget does not. This paper contributes a Bayesian model of bounded verification centered on the Predictive Value of Pass (PVP). The model predicts that evidentiary value decreases as artifacts grow under fixed verification capacity, improves with larger verification budgets, and is especially fragile when errors are sparse. Controlled experiments on FEVEROUS and FEVER support these predictions and show that adding supported claims around a fixed number of false or unsupported claims can make passing more likely while making a pass less informative. The model further yields the minimum verification budget required to maintain a target PVP, providing a practical component for AI-assisted quality-assurance workflows in which generated knowledge objects must be checked before publication or downstream use.

</details>


### [302] [LifeLong Digital Twin: A Unified Modeling Paradigm and Agent Harness for Event-Driven Lifelong Health State Trajectories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05566)
*Jin Jiang,Sean Yates,Jasper Chong,Raymond Brooks,Alex Lawson,Yuqin Qin,Liangcai Gao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose a LifeLong Digital Twin framework that unifies diverse lifelong health data into an event-driven representation to improve disease prediction and prevention.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Whole-person modeling over the full life course requires integrating heterogeneous, lifelong health information—clinical records, genetics, molecular data, and environmental exposures—but it is difficult to represent and use all this information coherently for prediction and prevention.

Method: They introduce an event-driven representation where individual Life Events are organized into daily Health States and accumulated into a Lifelong Health Context, and pair this with an Agent Harness that lets language models use multimodal evidence beyond text. They test four language models on 25 diseases across tasks: Disease Trajectory Forecasting, Disease Risk Ranking, and Multi-horizon Disease Prediction.

Result: Across 25 disease endpoints, the framework substantially improves performance versus a reference baseline: model-averaged F1 is 22.0% higher for disease identification in trajectory forecasting and 18.3% higher for predicting five-year disease outcomes, with thyroid disease reaching an F1 of 0.669.

Conclusion: This LifeLong Digital Twin and Agent Harness framework provides an effective foundation for whole-person digital twins and supports research on personalized, lifelong disease prevention by better modeling an individual’s cumulative health context.

Abstract: Human health is a continuous, dynamic trajectory shaped by the cumulative interplay of biological processes, clinical events, behaviors and environmental exposures across the life course. Unifying the full breadth of lifelong health information, including longitudinal records, genetic variation, molecular profiles and environmental histories, is essential for whole-person modeling and remains a major challenge. We introduce LifeLong Digital Twin, a unified, event-driven modeling paradigm that organizes Life Events into daily Health States and accumulates them into Lifelong Health Context. An accompanying Agent Harness incorporates multimodal evidence beyond the language model's textual context. We evaluate four language models across 25 disease endpoints on three tasks: Disease Trajectory Forecasting, Disease Risk Ranking and Multi-horizon Disease Prediction. The approach yields marked gains over the reference condition: model-averaged F1 increases by 22.0% for disease identification in trajectory forecasting and 18.3% for five-year disease outcomes; thyroid-disease F1 reaches 0.669. The framework provides a foundation for whole-person digital twins and research on personalized lifelong disease prevention.

</details>


### [303] [Factoriax: A GPU-Accelerated Factorio-Style Simulator for Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05569)
*Mickey Beurskens,Tristan Tomilin,Thiago D. Simão*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Factoriax is a fast GPU-accelerated JAX-based factory-building simulator with an Easy Rocket benchmark; PPO agents learn resource gathering and crafting but fail to build fully functional layouts, leaving the benchmark unsolved.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide a fast, scalable, and challenging benchmark environment for reinforcement learning agents in complex, long-horizon factory-building tasks, enabling large-scale experiments on modern GPUs.

Method: The authors implement Factoriax, a JAX-based simulator for factory-building gameplay, and define the Easy Rocket benchmark where an agent must construct a complex machine (the Rocket) within a fixed number of game ticks. They train PPO agents at massive scale (up to 1 billion steps) using a curriculum reward based on a hand-designed set of achievements, and evaluate learning performance and behaviors.

Result: Factoriax achieves extremely high simulation and training throughput: 1 billion PPO steps (around 500,000 episodes) take about 8 minutes on an NVIDIA A100 and around 84 minutes on a laptop GPU. PPO agents learn to gather resources, craft machines, and place them on the map, following the curriculum rewards, but they fail to arrange machines into a functionally correct spatial configuration needed to fully complete the Easy Rocket benchmark.

Conclusion: Factoriax is a highly efficient RL environment and benchmark for factory-building tasks, making large-scale experiments practical even on modest hardware. While PPO agents can learn many prerequisite skills via curriculum rewards, they struggle with the final, spatially complex objective, so the Easy Rocket benchmark remains unsolved and presents an open challenge for more advanced methods or architectures.

Abstract: We introduce Factoriax, a GPU-accelerated factory-building simulator written in JAX. In Factoriax, an agent must collect resources, build machines using those resources, and then automate the collection and crafting process by arranging machines on the map to build production pipelines. This paper discusses the structure of the Factoriax simulator and an initial benchmark called Easy Rocket in which an agent is tasked with building a resource-intensive machine called the Rocket in a limited number of game ticks to escape the planet. We also publish results from a number of PPO-based training runs on Easy Rocket. Factoriax is built to be fast. A 1-billion-step PPO training run, equivalent to 500,000 episodes, runs on Easy Rocket in about 8 minutes on a single NVIDIA A100. A standard laptop GPU can complete the same run in about 84 minutes. Our trained PPO agent learns to gather resources, craft machines from those resources, and place them on the map through a curriculum reward directly tied to a manually designed set of achievements. After training, the agent does not place machines in a functional spatial configuration, failing to fully complete the benchmark, and leaving the challenge open for future attempts.

</details>


### [304] [Better Retrieval, Limited Clustering Gains: A Controlled Study of Multilingual Company Entity Resolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05573)
*Yijiashun Qi,Yuxuan Li,Hanzhe Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies why better name retrieval does not necessarily improve company clustering, showing that gains are lost at the pair-confirmation (matching) stage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Entity resolution for companies often relies on name retrieval followed by pair classification and clustering. Despite improving name encoders, overall cluster quality may barely change, suggesting that downstream components (pair classifiers and decision thresholds) can bottleneck performance. The authors want to quantify how much retrieval improvement actually translates into better company clusters and identify where gains are lost.

Method: They adapt multilingual E5 text encoders using random-negative and hard-negative training, keeping the positive training schedule, candidate edge budget (72,660 candidates), and downstream decision rules fixed. They evaluate on a GLEIF-derived sample of 3,633 company names, 2,880 underlying identities, and 882 silver-positive name pairs. They also use a multi-view selector for adaptation, then apply an existing primary matcher and clustering pipeline to see how much the improved retrieval affects final clusters. An AI-assisted, single-reviewer audit of 137 pairs qualitatively checks the pattern, though labels are not fully independent gold standard.

Result: Encoder adaptation with a multi-view selector increases direct pair recall from 53.74% to 76.98% at the fixed candidate budget, adding 208 newly retrieved silver-positive pairs. However, the downstream matcher only accepts seven of these and rejects most; 202 of the 208 new positives fall below its decision threshold. As a result, cluster-level improvements are minimal: cluster recall increases slightly from 32.54% to 33.33%, while precision drops from 95.99% to 95.45%. Random-negative and hard-negative training end up producing the same final clustering. The audit of 137 pairs supports that retrieval gains are not being exploited by the matcher, although the evidence is mostly LEI-based and not fully gold standard.

Conclusion: The main source of lost benefit from better name retrieval is the unchanged, conservative downstream pair-confirmation stage, not the encoder. Large improvements in retrieval recall translate into only marginal gains in clustering because the existing matcher and thresholds filter out most of the newly retrieved true pairs. Therefore, evaluation of name encoders for entity resolution must go beyond pair or retrieval metrics and include the quality of final clusters, and improvements to encoders should be coordinated with adjustments to matchers and decision thresholds.

Abstract: Improved name retrieval may have little effect on company clusters when the pair classifier remains unchanged. We examine this dependency by adapting multilingual E5 encoders under fixed candidate budgets and downstream decision rules. Random-negative and hard-negative training use identical positive schedules. Checkpoints are selected before collecting a new GLEIF sample of 3,633 names, 2,880 source identities and 882 silver-positive pairs. At 72,660 candidate edges, adaptation with a multi-view selector increases direct pair recall from 53.74% to 76.98%. The primary matcher adds only seven correct and two incorrect co-cluster pairs: cluster recall rises from 32.54% to 33.33%, while precision falls from 95.99% to 95.45%. Of 208 newly retrieved silver-positive pairs, 202 fall below its decision threshold. Random-negative and hard-negative training produce identical final partitions. An AI-assisted, single-reviewer audit of 137 pairs supports the observed pattern, although its predominantly LEI-derived evidence does not establish independent gold labels. The results locate the immediate loss of retrieval gains at the existing confirmation stage and show why encoder evaluation must also measure final cluster quality.

</details>


### [305] [DREAM: Dynamic Resolution Assignment For Multimodal Multi-agent Debate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05615)
*Khanh-Binh Nguyen,Van Dai Do,Tien Anh Nguyen,Svetha Venkatesh,Hung Le*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DREAM is a multimodal multi-agent debate framework that dynamically selects visual resolutions per agent and uses uncertainty-based rollback to reduce groupthink, improving accuracy vs. token cost over prior MAD methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal multi-agent debate systems give all agents the same fixed visual input resolution, which is suboptimal because different samples and agents benefit from different visual scales. They also suffer from groupthink, where agents follow confident but incorrect peers and discard earlier correct reasoning. There is a need for a general framework that adapts visual resolution per agent and mitigates groupthink without dataset-specific tuning.

Method: DREAM introduces two main components: (1) Dynamic Resolution Assignment: a zero-shot probe round where agents evaluate multiple image resolutions, compute Average Normalized Log-Likelihood (ANLL) as an uncertainty measure for each resolution, and then select an empirically optimal resolution per agent using an adaptive threshold. (2) Uncertainty-Guided Rollback Aggregation: during debate rounds, the system tracks each agent’s uncertainty trajectory and, at aggregation time, can revert to earlier low-uncertainty answers that may have been overridden due to group pressure, thus countering groupthink while still leveraging multi-agent discussion.

Result: On six multimodal benchmarks, DREAM achieves a 1.5–3.2% accuracy improvement over strong multi-agent debate baselines for a comparable or better token budget, and does so without any dataset-specific hyperparameter tuning.

Conclusion: Dynamic, uncertainty-aware control over visual resolution and answer aggregation in multimodal multi-agent debate can reduce groupthink and improve the accuracy-efficiency trade-off. DREAM provides a general, plug-and-play framework that yields consistent performance gains across diverse multimodal tasks without specialized tuning.

Abstract: Multi-agent debate (MAD) has emerged as an effective paradigm to improve the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and is increasingly being extended to multimodal settings. However, existing multimodal MAD frameworks typically expose agents to the same fixed visual input, ignoring substantial variation in the visual scale needed across samples and agents. In addition, these frameworks frequently suffer from groupthink, a phenomenon where agents prematurely abandon correct deductions to conform with confident but hallucinated peer responses. To address these bottlenecks, we introduce DREAM (Dynamic Resolution Assignment For Multimodal Multi-Agent Debate), which operates via two core components: (1) Dynamic Resolution Assignment, a zero-shot probe round where agents test multiple resolutions, quantify uncertainty using Average Normalized Log-Likelihood (ANLL), and use an adaptive threshold to assign each agent to its empirically optimal resolution; (2) Uncertainty-Guided Rollback Aggregation counters groupthink by tracking each agent's uncertainty over rounds and restoring early low-uncertainty answers overridden by group pressure. On six multimodal datasets, DREAM improves the accuracy-token trade-off over multi-agent debate baselines by 1.5-3.2% accuracy without dataset-specific tuning.

</details>


### [306] [A Framework for Automated Multi-Source Satellite Data Analytics and LLM-Based Report Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05625)
*Hind Yousif Alhammadi,Isam Mashhour Al Jawarneh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Automated ArcGIS Pro/ArcPy tool to extract Land Surface Temperature from Landsat 7/8/9, cutting processing time and adding an LLM for result interpretation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual extraction of LST from Landsat data in ArcGIS requires multiple steps—radiometric calibration, emissivity correction, thermal conversion—and manual band selection, which is time‑consuming, error‑prone, and inefficient for batch processing. There is also a lack of integrated tools that both automate these steps and help users interpret statistical results.

Method: Implement an ArcGIS Pro geoprocessing workflow in Python using ArcPy that automates: (1) band identification and selection for Landsat 7, 8, and 9; (2) radiometric calibration; (3) NDVI calculation and NDVI-based emissivity correction; (4) conversion of thermal bands to LST. The tool supports both single-scene and batch processing. An optional Large Language Model module is integrated to read the numerical outputs and produce automated statistical interpretation and reporting.

Result: Processing time for LST extraction decreased from about 11–58 minutes manually to about 4–11 minutes using the automated tool, depending on batch size. When applied to Landsat scenes over Ras Al Khaimah, UAE, the derived LST values ranged from roughly 25°C to 50°C, consistent with local climatic conditions, indicating the method yields realistic temperature maps.

Conclusion: The automated ArcGIS Pro/ArcPy tool streamlines LST extraction from Landsat 7/8/9 by removing repetitive manual steps, reducing human error, and improving accuracy and efficiency for thermal and environmental remote sensing workflows. The integrated LLM-based interface further adds value by automatically interpreting and reporting statistical results, making LST analysis more accessible and user‑friendly.

Abstract: This paper presents the workflow for building an automated ArcGIS Pro tool using ArcPy to extract the Land Surface Temperature (LST) from Landsat 7, 8 and 9 datasets. The tool eliminates the need for manual band selection and repetitive raster computations by automating the multi-step workflow of radiometric calibration, NDVI-based emissivity correction, and thermal conversion. In addition to supporting batch and single-scene processing, the tool has an optional Large Language Model (LLM) for statistical result interpretation and reporting. Depending on batch size, the tool reduced the processing time from around 11-58 minutes when done manually to around 4-11 minutes using the tool. We tested the tool with data from Ras Al Khaimah (RAK) in the UAE, and the LST obtained for Ras Al Khaimah ranged from approximately 25C to 50C, demonstrating an accurate LST mapping compatible with the weather conditions of RAK. In summary, our tool reduces human errors and improves processing accuracy and efficiency for thermal and environmental remote sensing applications, in addition to providing an interactive LLM-based interface for result interpretation.

</details>


### [307] [The GenAI4IDN Benchmark 3.0 - a Public Tool to Assess Generative AI Tools for the Design of Interactive Digital Narratives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05633)
*Hartmut Koenitz,Jonathan Barbara,Mirjam Palosaari Eladhari*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces GENAI4IDN Benchmark 3.0, a blinded, AI-assisted, web-based framework to systematically evaluate generative AI for interactive digital narratives, including complex media, fact-checking, and bias detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior evaluations of generative AI for interactive digital narratives relied heavily on manual testing, had difficulty handling rich multimedia outputs, and lacked systematic mechanisms to detect factual errors and social biases. Community concerns, especially those raised at ICIDS 2025, highlighted the need for scalable, transparent, and fair benchmarking that can capture both creative quality and ethical reliability. This paper aims to provide such a framework and make it accessible for ongoing, community-driven evaluation.

Method: The authors develop GENAI4IDN Benchmark 3.0 as a publicly accessible web application that enables on-demand benchmarking of generative models. The framework uses blinded evaluation to reduce model-brand bias and includes tasks covering complex media types such as music, video, and full interactive digital narratives. Dedicated fact-checking and bias-detection tasks are defined, with rubrics validated by human raters who have lived experience in the relevant contexts. The system allows users to add new models and propose new tasks, supporting iterative community refinement.

Result: Applied to a diverse set of generative models, the benchmark reveals that creative capabilities for producing interactive digital narratives are maturing, but also shows recurring issues like runaway or tangential narrative development and overly aggressive safety filters that limit expressiveness. The fact-checking component successfully identifies nuanced historical inaccuracies, anachronisms, and fabricated information, while the bias-detection component consistently surfaces structural biases, stereotypical tropes, and omissions of marginalized perspectives.

Conclusion: GENAI4IDN Benchmark 3.0 provides a scalable, community-driven, and ethically aware framework for evaluating generative AI in interactive digital narratives. By supporting blinded evaluation, complex media types, and robust fact- and bias-checking procedures validated by affected communities, it advances the state of benchmarking beyond manual, ad hoc assessments. The findings underscore both the growing creative potential of current models and the need to address persistent issues in reasoning, safety filtering, factual reliability, and representational bias.

Abstract: This paper presents GENAI4IDN Benchmark 3.0, the third iteration of an evaluation framework to assess Generative AI tools for creating Interactive Digital Narratives (IDNs). Moving beyond manual testing, this iteration introduces AI-assisted evaluation through a publicly accessible web application (https://genai4idn.com), enabling the community to run benchmarks on demand, add new models, and propose new tasks. The revised evaluation framework is "blinded" to avoid model-bias, and can handle complex media such as music, videos, and full IDNs that previously required human raters. A significant addition - responding to concerns raised during ICIDS 2025 - is the addition of fact-checking and bias detection with dedicated tasks and rubrics, validated by human raters with lived experience in the depicted contexts. Findings from a diverse range of models report on maturing creative capabilities while observing runaway thinking and overzealous safety filters as limitations. Fact-checking reliably caught subtle historical inaccuracies, anachronisms, and fabricated claims while the bias rater consistently exposed structural assumptions, tropes, and marginalized group erasures.

</details>


### [308] [Visual Grounding Safety in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05637)
*Erfan Shayegani,Kundan Krishna,Yue Dong,Nael Abu-Ghazaleh,Leon Gatys,Shruti Palaskar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper analyzes and improves safety alignment of vision-language models when they output structured visual groundings (points/bounding boxes) instead of text.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While vision-language models are often aligned to refuse harmful text responses, their structured outputs like points or boxes can still comply with harmful requests (e.g., identifying sensitive targets). Safety evaluations have focused on text, leaving the grounding channel underexamined. The authors aim to systematically measure and close this safety gap between textual answers and visual groundings across multiple harm domains.

Method: The authors repurpose three existing safety benchmarks—VLSU for direct harm, BBQ-V for social bias, and Asimov-2.0 for situational safety—into 15,401 matched pairs of harmful prompts, each phrased in two ways: (1) as a visual question answering (VQA) request for free-text, and (2) as a request for visual grounding (point or bounding box). They evaluate five vision-language models to compare refusal rates between these channels and test safety system prompts. They then propose a fine-tuning procedure that: (a) explicitly trains models to refuse via grounding (grounding-form refusals), (b) includes capability grounding data to preserve utility, and (c) adds self-distilled benign data to mitigate over-refusal. Finally, they perform representation analysis to study how harmful vs. benign requests move relative to the model’s internal “refusal direction.”

Result: Empirically, models that often refuse harmful questions in text frequently comply when the same request is posed as a grounding task: on average, grounding refusal lags VQA refusal by 31–59 percentage points across domains, and safety prompts alone do not fix this. Their fine-tuning method, applied to Qwen3-VL-8B and VisionReasoner-7B, substantially boosts grounding refusal: +77–95 percentage points on VLSU and BBQ-V, and +64–85 points on the unseen Asimov-2.0 domain. It also improves VQA refusal, maintains grounding performance, and limits over-refusal. Representation analysis shows harmful prompts are shifted toward the model’s refusal direction after fine-tuning—especially for grounding requests—while benign prompts remain close to harmless reference representations.

Conclusion: Safety alignment for visual grounding lags significantly behind text-based alignment in current vision-language models, creating a sizeable vulnerability. A targeted fine-tuning strategy that combines grounding-form refusals, capability-preserving data, and self-distilled benign examples can close most of this safety gap for both seen and unseen domains without sacrificing grounding ability or causing excessive over-refusal. Internally, the method reshapes representations so that harmful requests align more with a refusal direction while benign ones stay near harmless baselines, suggesting a principled way to align structured output channels alongside text.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly trained to generate structured outputs like points and bounding boxes that downstream interfaces, agents, and robots can act on, yet safety alignment of this output channel has not been systematically analyzed. We study visual grounding safety by repurposing three safety benchmarks spanning direct harm (VLSU), social bias (BBQ-V), and situational safety (Asimov-2.0) into 15,401 matched pairs of harmful requests that differ only in the requested output: a free-text answer (VQA) or a grounding (point or bounding box). Across five VLMs, models that refuse a harmful request posed as a question often comply when the same request asks for a grounding: averaged over models, grounding refusal trails VQA refusal by 31-59 percentage points, depending on the domain, and safety system prompts do not close this gap. We propose a fine-tuning approach that combines grounding-form refusals with capability grounding data and self-distilled benign data to counter over-refusal. For Qwen3-VL-8B and VisionReasoner-7B, it improves grounding refusal by 77-95 percentage points on VLSU and BBQ-V and by 64-85 points on the held-out Asimov-2.0 domain, while also improving VQA refusal, preserving grounding capability, and keeping over-refusal limited. Representation analysis shows that fine-tuning moves harmful requests toward each model's refusal direction, most strongly for grounding, while leaving benign requests near the harmless reference.

</details>


### [309] [How Should a Prompt Optimizer Spend a Tight Budget? BudgetAPO with Noise-Adaptive Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05671)
*Haoyue Liu,Zhichao Wang,Huanyu Yan,Xiaoying Tang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes BudgetAPO, a budget-aware automatic prompt optimization method for large language models that achieves strong performance with far fewer API calls than existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing automatic prompt optimization approaches like GEPA and OPRO assume hundreds or thousands of calls to the target model, which is unrealistic for paid, rate-limited APIs. Under tight call budgets, these methods often either waste the budget without improving the prompt (returning the seed prompt unchanged) or evaluate candidate prompts inefficiently using fixed minibatch sizes that ignore task-specific noise levels. There is a need for an APO method that is explicitly designed for low-budget, noisy evaluation settings.

Method: BudgetAPO is a single-stage prompt optimizer tailored to tight query budgets. It introduces three main components: (1) a noise-adaptive evaluation rule that determines the evaluation slice size based on an estimate of task noise obtained from a brief probe; (2) a fixed slice scheme that converts each accept/reject decision into a paired comparison between the current best prompt and a candidate, improving statistical efficiency; and (3) a reflective operator that jointly rewrites both the reasoning strategy and output format of prompts, rather than tweaking them independently. These components are used to iteratively generate, evaluate, and select improved prompts under a strict limit on the number of subject-model calls.

Result: Across seven benchmarks and five different subject models, BudgetAPO consistently achieves the best performance compared to baseline APO methods. It ranks first on every subject model and outperforms all baselines under Holm-corrected paired statistical tests. Under a 250-call budget, BudgetAPO returns the initial seed prompt unchanged in only 13% of runs, compared to 86% for GEPA, indicating more effective use of limited calls. On the GPT-OSS-20B model, GEPA requires 4.5 times more calls than BudgetAPO to reach the performance that BudgetAPO attains with just 100 calls.

Conclusion: BudgetAPO effectively addresses the limitations of existing prompt optimization methods in tight-budget, noisy evaluation settings. By adapting evaluation to task noise, enforcing paired comparisons, and using reflective prompt rewriting, it delivers superior optimization quality with significantly fewer model calls. This makes APO more practical and cost-effective for real-world scenarios where subject-model access is constrained by pricing and rate limits.

Abstract: Automatic prompt optimization (APO) has been widely employed to adapt large language models without updating their weights, yielding promising results. However, existing methods such as GEPA and OPRO assume hundreds to thousands of subject-model calls, far more than is practical behind paid, rate-limited APIs. Under tight budgets they fail in two ways: multi-stage pipelines can exhaust the budget and return the seed prompt unchanged, while single-stage methods compare candidates on fixed-size minibatches, regardless of each task's noise. As a remedy, we introduce BudgetAPO, a single-stage optimizer for the tight-budget regime. BudgetAPO incorporates (1) a noise-adaptive rule that sizes the evaluation slice to each task's noise, measured by a short probe; (2) a fixed slice that turns every accept/reject decision into a paired comparison; and (3) a reflective operator that rewrites reasoning strategy and output format jointly. Extensive results across seven benchmarks and five subject models demonstrate that BudgetAPO ranks first on every subject and beats every baseline under Holm-corrected paired tests, while returning the seed in 13% of runs at 250 calls against 86% for GEPA. On GPT-OSS-20B, GEPA needs 4.5 times as many calls to match BudgetAPO's 100-call score.

</details>


### [310] [Do Time-Series QA Systems Read the Time Series? Evidence Use and Reasoning Reliability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05686)
*Zhuomin Chen,Jingchao Ni,Xu Zheng,Janki Bhimani,Mo Sha,Wei Cheng,Dongsheng Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper evaluates how well time-series question answering (TSQA) systems truly use numerical time-series evidence, beyond just answer accuracy, by benchmarking multiple models under controlled input interventions and auditing their rationales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing TSQA systems report good answer accuracy, but it is unclear whether they genuinely rely on the provided numerical time series, how sensitive they are to changes in that input, and whether their textual rationales are factually grounded and logically valid. Answer correctness alone cannot show grounding in the series or robustness of reasoning, posing risks for applications that depend on trustworthy numerical inference.

Method: The authors systematically evaluate four TSQA systems (TimeOmni-1, ChatTS, TimeOmni-VL, Time-MQA). They first reproduce reported results for three systems and compare each TSQA model to its backbone. They then build a unified benchmark, COMMON-TSQA, by aggregating public evaluation datasets from existing time-series benchmarks and standardizing sample format, task definitions, and answer schemas. Using each model’s native interface, they test performance under the original input and six controlled interventions that modify the numerical series while keeping the question and target answer concept fixed. They also perform a rationale audit, judging rationales for factual grounding in the time series, validity of intermediate inferences, and consistency with the final answer.

Result: Aggregate performance metrics can remain similar even when individual predictions change substantially under input interventions, indicating that models may not be robustly using numerical evidence. Some interventions trigger simple fallback behaviors instead of preserving true task competence. The rationale analysis reveals that models frequently make unsupported numerical claims about the time series; and even when rationales align with final answers, they may contain incorrect numeric descriptions or invalid intermediate reasoning steps.

Conclusion: Evaluating TSQA systems solely via task-level accuracy and final answers is insufficient to assess whether they truly understand and use numerical time-series data. Robust assessment requires intervention-based testing and careful auditing of rationales for factual grounding and reasoning validity. The study highlights current TSQA models’ weaknesses in numerical grounding and inference, and positions COMMON-TSQA as a standardized benchmark for deeper, more reliable evaluation of time-series QA behavior.

Abstract: In recent years, time-series question answering (QA) systems have made significant progress. However, generating a correct answer does not show whether retaining the supplied numerical series improves task performance, nor whether the prediction is sensitive to changes in that input. While some systems provide rationales, answer accuracy also does not show whether their numerical claims are grounded in the supplied series or whether the stated inference is valid. In this work, we focus on evaluating four time-series QA systems: TimeOmni-1, ChatTS, TimeOmni-VL, and Time-MQA. First, for three systems with released evaluation data, we reproduce their reported results and compare the performance of the systems with their backbones. Then, we introduce a benchmark named COMMON-TSQA, which collects public evaluation datasets from existing time-series benchmarks and unifies their sample representation, task definitions, and answer schemas, while evaluating each system through its own interface under common evaluation criteria. The evaluation uses the original condition and six interventions while keeping the question and target fixed. Our analysis shows that aggregate performance alone can obscure how systems use numerical evidence. Similar task-level scores can arise despite substantial changes in individual predictions. Some interventions induce simple fallback behavior rather than preserved task ability. We also evaluate rationales for factual grounding, inference validity, and consistency with the final answer. We find that rationales often contain time-series claims unsupported by the input. Moreover, the rationale audit shows that agreement between a rationale and its final answer can coexist with incorrect numerical descriptions or invalid intermediate inferences.

</details>


### [311] [Toward AI Trustworthiness: Finding Analytically Proven Forward-Invariant Sets for AI-Controlled Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05689)
*Haoyang Song,Xikun Yang,Qixin Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose a method that uses invertible neural networks to find and certify forward-invariant sets for neural-network-controlled systems, enabling formal safety guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural-network controllers are widely used for nonlinear systems, but their complex, opaque behavior makes formal verification and safety certification difficult. A central certification task is computing a forward-invariant set (FIS) that excludes unsafe states, but analytically finding such sets for fixed NN controllers is hard. Existing approaches often fail or do not scale, motivating a new framework that can systematically discover certifiable FISs.

Method: They introduce a framework that learns an invertible neural network (INN) to transform the original state space into a latent space where simple, regular-shaped FIS candidates (e.g., axis-aligned hyper-rectangles) are more likely to be invariant. The INN is trained so that a chosen hyper-rectangular region in the latent space becomes forward invariant for the closed-loop dynamics, and then this candidate region is subjected to formal verification.
