Under a fixed 5% recomputation budget, their document-aligned recomputation policy greatly reduces answer variation across different request orders from 69.0% (with CacheBlend’s token top-k policy) to 26.1%. In scenarios where each prompt is evaluated after a distinct sequence of prior requests, document-aligned recomputation improves fidelity to the full-preload baseline by 34.5–52.5 percentage points over token top-k, while both methods still obtain about a 5.7× median TTFT speedup. Ablations indicate that contiguity of recomputed segments is the dominant factor associated with robust behavior in this rolling-agent setting.

Conclusion: Non-prefix KV-cache reuse with naive token-level selective recomputation can induce substantial history dependence and instability in long-running agent workloads. A document-aligned, contiguous recomputation strategy significantly stabilizes outputs and increases fidelity to a full prefill baseline, without sacrificing large latency gains. The key takeaway is that structuring recomputation around contiguous document segments, rather than scattered high-importance tokens, is crucial for reliable KV-cache reuse in rolling-context agents.

Abstract: Long-running agents repeatedly call an LLM while retaining most of their document window, evicting old documents, and appending new ones. These rolling updates break exact prefix caching and motivate non-prefix KV-cache reuse with selective recomputation. We show that persistent KV-cache reuse with selective recomputation can be history-dependent: in our rolling-agent workload, an unchanged prompt can produce different answers depending on the requests processed before it. At a matched 5% recomputation budget, document-aligned recomputation reduces answer variation across request orders from 69.0% with CacheBlend's token top-$k$ policy to 26.1%. When each prompt is evaluated after a different sequence of preceding requests, document-aligned recomputation improves fidelity to full prefill by 34.5-52.5 percentage points over token top-$k$, while both policies achieve approximately 5.7$\times$ median TTFT speedup. Our ablation study shows that, in our rolling-agent workload, contiguity is the main factor associated with robust selective recomputation.

</details>


### [331] [MiniCorp: The Last Mile of the AI Agent Firm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05912)
*Jingying Zeng,Zhenwei Dai,Jinning Li,Changho Shin,Dylan Zhang,Yuxuan Lu,Qi He,Dakuo Wang,Kai-Wei Chang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MiniCorp is a simulated e‑commerce company environment where multiple AI agents run a virtual firm, interact with a dynamic market, and generate realistic, longitudinal, and counterfactual enterprise data for training and evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise AGI needs agents that can run companies autonomously, but suitable training data is limited: real enterprise logs are scarce, private, expensive, and only show what actually happened, not what could have happened under alternative decisions. Existing archives are incomplete and lack counterfactual trajectories, making it hard to train and evaluate decision-making agents safely and robustly. A controllable, realistic simulation that mimics enterprise dynamics and can generate large-scale, labeled, and counterfactual data is therefore needed.

Method: The authors build MiniCorp, an office simulator centered on an e‑commerce company. It couples two worlds: (1) an external world with simulated customers, competitors, and market mechanisms; and (2) an internal world composed of enterprise agents in different roles who observe events, communicate with each other, deliberate, and make strategic decisions (e.g., pricing, advertising). The simulator logs all communications, observations, decisions, and business outcomes over time. It also supports checkpointing so that identical states can be replayed with different decisions to generate counterfactual trajectories. They evaluate MiniCorp’s fidelity by comparing its emergent market patterns with empirical findings from real markets, to check realism and limit exploitable artifacts.

Result: MiniCorp produces realistic enterprise-like dynamics where agents coordinate across roles, respond to market feedback, and adjust their strategies (e.g., changing decisions as conditions evolve). When agents are given explicit long-term strategic objectives, they maintain exploration in advertising strategies even when early returns are weak, showing the environment can support non-myopic learning and adaptation. The evaluations suggest the simulator gives agents market feedback that aligns with known empirical regularities, decreasing the likelihood that they will exploit simulation bugs or unrealistic loopholes.

Conclusion: MiniCorp serves as a controllable, high-fidelity environment for studying AI systems that collectively operate companies. It addresses data scarcity and lack of counterfactuals by generating scalable longitudinal logs of decisions, communications, and outcomes, plus replayable counterfactual scenarios. This makes it a promising testbed and data source for training, evaluating, and aligning enterprise agents while reducing dependence on sensitive or incomplete real-world enterprise data.

Abstract: The last mile toward enterprise AGI is a company that runs itself. Training and adapting such agents require longitudinal enterprise data, which remain scarce, costly to acquire, and often restricted by privacy constraints. Historical archives are also frequently incomplete and record only what actually happened. They cannot show the outcomes of alternative decisions. We introduce MiniCorp, an office simulator for studying how agents can collectively run a company while generating enterprise data at scale. Using an e-commerce company as a demonstration, MiniCorp connects two interacting worlds. The external world models customers, dynamic competitors, and market mechanisms. The internal world consists of agents that observe events, discuss their options, and make strategic decisions. These decisions have lasting effects on the market, and the resulting feedback informs the firm's later decisions. As the firm and market interact, MiniCorp continuously records the agents' communications and decisions. These records preserve the information available at the time and the business results that followed. Checkpointing allows the same situation to be replayed under different decisions, providing comparisons unavailable in static archives. We evaluate end-to-end fidelity against patterns reported in empirical studies of real markets. These evaluations provide agents with realistic market feedback and reduce the risk that they learn to exploit flaws in the simulator. Our experiments show agents coordinating across roles and adapting their decisions to market feedback. With explicit long-term strategic guidance, they also sustain advertising exploration despite weak early returns. MiniCorp thus provides an environment for studying AI-run companies and a scalable source of longitudinal and counterfactual enterprise data for agent training and evaluation.

</details>


### [332] [VERA: Scaling Verifiable Environments for Agentic co-Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05923)
*Junqi Liu,Yongyang Pan,Zhuosong Jiang,Dongbai Li,Bo Zhang,Xitong Ling,Sheng Wang,Hanrong Ye,Yufan He,Can Zhao,Pengfei Guo,Dong Yang,Andriy Myronenko,Yuyin Zhou,Tianyu Liu,Daguang Xu,Yucheng Tang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces VERA, a system for building and co-evolving long-horizon, verifiable environments and agents, significantly improving performance on complex benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing long-horizon tasks for agents, such as in medical research, require many dependent steps that must be grounded in evidence, but current environments typically only evaluate final outcomes and are not resumable, verifiable sandboxes. This makes stable training and precise attribution of success or failure difficult, limiting the development of competent, reliable agents.

Method: VERA constructs verifiable environments from initial agent trajectories. An agent first generates rubrics and executable checks; a separate judge process verifies each sandbox, and only verified environments are stored in a training bank. Training then alternates between two update types: (1) training the model with rewards derived from rubrics, and (2) editing or improving the environment harness and skills. Additionally, a verifier component gates both new model checkpoints and harness edits based on explicit development-set acceptance criteria, ensuring that changes are reliably beneficial.

Result: Using an open-source collection of over 9,000 long-horizon, verifiable environments, a 9B-parameter model co-evolved with its agent in VERA outperforms the strongest baseline by 10.3 and 13.0 points on two key domains. A larger 27B model further surpasses baselines on AutoCoWorkBench (achieving 71.6) and AutoMedBench (80.7), and demonstrates transfer to previously unseen workflows while retaining general capabilities.

Conclusion: VERA enables scalable construction and co-evolution of verifiable, long-horizon agent environments, improving both training stability and attribution of performance gains. The system yields substantial performance improvements over strong baselines, generalizes to new workflows, and preserves broad capabilities, highlighting the value of environment–agent co-evolution with explicit verification and rubric-based rewards.

Abstract: Competent agents need precise and verifiable environments, such as sandboxes that are resumable at any stage and evolve from observable evidence. However, most long-horizon work exposes how rare these are: for example, an agent in medical research must ground a finding, classify it, and write a report over dozens of dependent steps, yet recent environments score only the outcome. To address the challenges in stable training, we present VERA, which builds such environments at scale and lets agents evolve on them. VERA builds these environments from initial trajectories: an agent writes rubrics, executable checks, a judge verifies each sandbox, and only those that pass enter the training bank. On these environments, VERA alternates between two updates: train the model with rubric rewards, or edit the harness skills. We also create a verifier which gates model checkpoints and harness edits using explicit development-set acceptance criteria. This attribution distinguishes VERA's co-evolution from single-axis baselines: its updates target not only the cause but the outcome. With an open-source corpus of 9,000+ long-horizon verifiable environments, a 9B model paired with its co-evolved agent beats the strongest baseline by 10.3 and 13.0 points in the two domains. At 27B, it surpasses the baseline on AutoCoWorkBench (71.6) and AutoMedBench (80.7), transfers to unseen workflows, and retains general capabilities.

</details>


### [333] [Process Constitutions and Process Stewards: Towards the Next Generation of BPM for Agentic Organizations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05942)
*Amin Jalali,Majid Rafiei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper argues that traditional Business Process Management, which assumes human-driven processes, is becoming obsolete in AI-driven organizations and proposes a new BPM paradigm focused on governing autonomous agents through a "Process Constitution" and a "Process Steward" to ensure organizational legibility and accountability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional BPM was designed for environments where humans are the main actors, and processes are modeled to make work visible, controllable, and optimizable. With the rise of AI agents that autonomously execute, coordinate, and adapt work, these assumptions no longer hold. There is a gap in how to conceptualize, model, and govern processes when the primary actors are autonomous AI systems rather than humans. The authors are motivated to rethink BPM’s foundations to retain governance, accountability, and understandability in AI-agentic organizations.

Method: Conceptual and theoretical work: the authors critically reassess BPM’s underlying assumptions and then introduce two new core concepts tailored to AI-agent ecosystems. They define the idea of a "Process Constitution"—a machine-interpretable, value-laden framework that constrains and guides AI agent behavior—and a "Process Steward"—a dedicated governance agent that interprets, monitors, and enforces this constitution. They then outline a conceptual framework and sketch a research agenda instead of presenting empirical or experimental methods.

Result: The primary result is a reframing of BPM for AI-driven organizations and the introduction of a conceptual architecture for governing autonomous agents. The authors articulate how processes should now be understood less as prescriptive human workflows and more as governed spaces of agent behavior bounded by a Process Constitution and managed by a Process Steward. They clarify that the key benefit of this architecture is organizational legibility—maintaining accountability, contestability, and human intelligibility in complex AI agent ecosystems. They also identify key research directions implied by this shift.

Conclusion: BPM is undergoing a constitutive transformation from describing and optimizing human work to governing autonomous AI agents. To meet this challenge, BPM must adopt new constructs: a Process Constitution to define acceptable agent behavior in a machine-readable, value-laden way, and a Process Steward to enforce and interpret it. Success for next-generation BPM will be measured less by process efficiency and more by organizational legibility—ensuring that AI-driven processes remain accountable, contestable, and understandable to humans. The paper concludes by positioning this as the foundation for a new research agenda in BPM for AI-agentic organizations.

Abstract: Business Process Management (BPM) was built on a foundational assumption that organizations are populated primarily by human actors whose work can be made visible, governable, and improvable through process models. That assumption is depreciating. AI agent ecosystems increasingly execute, coordinate, and adapt organizational work with limited human direction, challenging not only BPM's methods but its core conception of what a process is. We argue that BPM faces a constitutive shift from modeling human work to governing autonomous agents, for which we propose two new concepts: the \emph{Process Constitution}, a machine-interpretable, value-laden framework that defines the space of admissible agent behavior, and the \emph{Process Steward}, a governance agent that interprets and enforces it. The central value proposition of this new generation of BPM is not efficiency but \emph{organizational legibility}: the capacity to keep agentic organizations accountable, contestable, and humanly understandable. We outline what this means and sketch the research agenda it opens.

</details>


### [334] [OntoInk: Interactive Ontology Visualization, Validation, and Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05945)
*Ebrahim Norouzi,Jörg Waitelonis,Harald Sack*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OntoInk is an open-source MkDocs plugin that unifies ontology documentation, visualization, validation, and reasoning in a single documentation-as-code workflow.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current ontology engineering workflows rely on separate tools for documentation, visualization, and validation, leading to fragmented processes, slower development, and harder knowledge transfer. The authors want to streamline ontology work within modern documentation pipelines so that diagrams, validation, and reasoning can be tightly integrated and more accessible.

Method: They implement OntoInk, a plugin for MkDocs that integrates multiple ontology-related capabilities directly into the static documentation generation process. OntoInk parses RDF, dereferences IRIs, overlays SHACL constraints, performs OWL DL reasoning, and enables inline Turtle editing. It generates interactive, editable ontology diagrams embedded in documentation pages and connects these with validation and reasoning services.

Result: The resulting system, OntoInk, allows users to work with interactive ontology diagrams, validate instance data against SHACL shapes, run OWL DL reasoning, and edit Turtle inline, all inside an MkDocs-based documentation workflow. It outperforms generic MkDocs diagram plugins, which lack RDF/SHACL/OWL support, and it offers tighter integration with documentation than standalone ontology visualization tools. A live demo and open-source implementation are made available online.

Conclusion: OntoInk successfully integrates visualization, validation, reasoning, and editing for ontologies into a single documentation-as-code pipeline. This unified approach simplifies ontology development and improves knowledge transfer by embedding rich, interactive ontology tooling directly into documentation pages, surpassing both generic diagram plugins and standalone visualization tools in this use case.

Abstract: Ontology documentation, visualization, and validation are usually carried out with separate tools. This split workflow slows down development and makes knowledge transfer harder. We present OntoInk, an open-source MkDocs plugin that brings these activities together. Within a single documentation-as-code pipeline, OntoInk renders interactive ontology diagrams, validates instance data against SHACL shapes, runs OWL\,DL reasoning, and supports inline Turtle editing. General-purpose diagram plugins for MkDocs cannot parse RDF, dereference IRIs, overlay SHACL constraints, or run OWL reasoning. Compared with standalone ontology visualization tools, OntoInk embeds interactive and editable diagrams directly into documentation pages. A live demo and source code are available at \url{https://ise-fizkarlsruhe.github.io/ontoink/}.

</details>


### [335] [Grounded Joint-Attention Other-Play for Zero-Shot Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06025)
*Giulia Benintendi,Constantin Ruhdorfer,Fabian Kögel,Andreas Bulling*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose MATE, a joint-attention-inspired MARL method that aligns agents’ visual attention on salient objects to enable better zero-shot coordination with unfamiliar partners, outperforming symmetry-breaking baselines across several benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Humans can coordinate with unfamiliar partners via joint attention, but multi-agent RL agents typically rely on partner-specific conventions learned during training, which fail under zero-shot coordination with new partners. Existing symmetry-breaking methods only try to avoid brittle conventions rather than providing a positive, shared basis for coordination. The authors want a general, environment-grounded mechanism that lets independently trained agents coordinate robustly without prior agreement.

Method: They design MATE (Mutual Attention for zero-shot TEaming), a multi-agent RL approach that augments standard training with an auxiliary objective encouraging agents to align their visual attention maps on scene-salient objects. Instead of focusing on arbitrary learned conventions, agents are guided to attend to the same task-relevant entities in the environment during interaction. This attention alignment acts as a coordination signal that is naturally available to all partners and is integrated into the learning process to shape policies toward mutually predictable behavior.

Result: On three benchmarks—the custom Card Alignment Game (which isolates brittle convention formation) and the more complex Level-Based Foraging and OvercookedV2—agents trained with MATE achieve higher coordination performance with unseen partners than baselines, including state-of-the-art symmetry-breaking approaches. The empirical studies show consistent improvements in zero-shot teaming metrics, suggesting that joint-attention-based signals help agents coordinate more reliably when paired with independently trained or heterogeneous partners.

Conclusion: Incorporating a joint-attention-like mechanism into MARL via MATE provides a practical way to achieve robust zero-shot coordination. By promoting alignment of attention on salient environmental objects, MATE goes beyond merely avoiding bad conventions and instead supplies a shared, environment-grounded basis for coordination. The authors conclude that joint-attention-inspired signals are a powerful and general coordination mechanism that can complement and surpass existing symmetry-breaking methods in multi-agent settings.

Abstract: Joint attention - the human ability to share a common visual or cognitive focus with others - enables a meeting of minds that lets us coordinate even with unfamiliar partners. In this work we investigate whether equipping AI agents with a similar mechanism can enable such zero-shot coordination. We introduce Mutual Attention for zero-shot TEaming (MATE): a novel multi-agent reinforcement learning method inspired by human joint attention. MATE encourages agents to coordinate their actions by aligning their visual attention on scene-salient objects during the interaction rather than relying on arbitrary partner-dependent conventions established during training. Unlike symmetry-breaking approaches that merely prevent brittle conventions from emerging, MATE actively promotes coordination through an environment-grounded signal that is naturally shared across partners. We evaluate MATE on three benchmarks: our Card Alignment Game, designed to isolate brittle convention formation, and the more challenging Level-Based Foraging and OvercookedV2 benchmarks. Our experiments consistently show that a joint-attention-inspired signal improves coordination with unknown partners, underlining MATE's potential as a general coordination mechanism that complements and surpasses symmetry-breaking approaches.

</details>


### [336] [RocketAgent: A Long-Horizon Engineering Agent for Multidisciplinary Design of Liquid-Rocket Thrust Chambers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06044)
*Junxiang He,Runze Mao,Kun He,Teng Zhang,Liming Zheng,Ke Xiao,Zhi X. Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RocketAgent is an AI-based, long-horizon engineering agent that coordinates multiple tools and models to perform end-to-end, revision-aware preliminary design of liquid-rocket thrust chambers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Designing liquid-rocket thrust chambers requires tightly coupled, iterative analyses across multiple disciplines and heterogeneous tools, where downstream feasibility issues can force upstream design changes. Traditional workflows struggle to manage shared data, method choices, and dependency-aware updates, making it difficult to maintain consistency and traceability during design revisions.

Method: The authors build RocketAgent, a plan-owning coding agent that orchestrates specialized engineering skills for performance sizing, subsystem optimization, geometry generation, and multiphysics assessment. They introduce two core infrastructure elements: (1) a provenance-aware knowledge graph to track methods and support selection of appropriate analyses, and (2) a typed Design Intermediate Representation to hold shared parameters, artifacts, and decisions. They implement revision-aware checks that detect when changes invalidate prior results, automatically block superseded inputs from being reused, and require explicit engineering approval for consequential revisions.

Result: In a representative simulation-based thrust-chamber design study, RocketAgent successfully navigated from an initially infeasible cooling configuration through an engineer-approved operating-point change, found feasible subsystem designs, and then drove geometry generation and multiphysics analyses to support final configuration choice. Additional focused tests evaluated surrogate-model performance and nozzle adaptation, and a controlled comparison of two configurations over three scenarios confirmed that dependency invalidation and superseded-input blocking behaved as intended before solver runs.

Conclusion: RocketAgent can sustain coordinated, end-to-end multidisciplinary design of liquid-rocket thrust chambers while maintaining data consistency and traceability under revision. The provenance- and revision-aware mechanisms reliably manage dependencies and method choices, enabling robust automated support for complex, iterative engineering workflows.

Abstract: Liquid-rocket thrust-chamber design involves interdependent analyses in which downstream constraints can require earlier design decisions to be revisited. Managing these dependencies across heterogeneous tools requires consistent design information and coordinated updates throughout the workflow. We present RocketAgent, a long-horizon engineering agent for multidisciplinary preliminary design of liquid-rocket thrust chambers. A single plan-owning Coding Agent coordinates engineering skills for performance sizing, subsystem optimization, geometry generation, and multiphysics assessment. A provenance-aware knowledge graph supports method selection, while a typed Design Intermediate Representation maintains shared parameters, artifacts, and decisions. Revision-aware checks invalidate affected results and block superseded inputs, with consequential changes subject to engineering approval. In a representative simulation-based design, RocketAgent continued from an infeasible cooling search through an engineer-authorized operating-point revision, identified feasible subsystem designs, and coordinated subsequent geometry generation and multiphysics assessment to support final configuration selection. Separate module tests assessed surrogate predictions and nozzle adaptation. A two-configuration comparison across three controlled scenarios verified the expected dependency invalidations and superseded-input blocking before solver execution. The representative case demonstrates sustained coordination across a multidisciplinary design workflow, while the controlled tests establish the behavior of the revision mechanisms supporting that execution.

</details>


### [337] [Benchmarking Jailbreak Guardrails for Embodied Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06122)
*Xunguang Wang,Qingyue Wang,Yuguang Zhou,Zongjie Li,Wenxuan Wang,Shuai Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper evaluates how well different jailbreak guardrails actually protect embodied agents (robots) using LLM/VLMs, revealing trade-offs between safety, usability, and efficiency and giving guidance on guardrail design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Embodied LLM/VLM agents in the physical world can be jailbroken to perform harmful actions. Many guardrails have been proposed, but current benchmarks mostly test base agents, not how well different guardrails work in real embodied setups. There is no systematic, apples-to-apples comparison of guardrails across where they intervene (perception/planning/control), decision mechanisms, and modalities. The authors aim to fill this gap so practitioners can choose and design guardrails more effectively.

Method: They construct a modular evaluation framework where the embodied agent is fixed as a backend, and guardrails are plug-in components that can intercept at three stages: perception, planning, or control. They select six representative guardrails spanning different intervention stages, decision mechanisms, and input modalities. Using both template-based and automated jailbreak attacks, plus benign instructions, they evaluate each guardrail on: (1) defense effectiveness (bypass rate, hazard success rate in simulation), (2) usability (false-positive rate, task completion on safe instructions), and (3) efficiency (runtime latency overhead). They then compare results across guardrails and analyze how design choices influence trade-offs.

Result: Across extensive simulated experiments, none of the six guardrails dominates on all metrics. Some are highly effective at blocking hazardous actions but cause many false positives or substantial latency; others preserve usability and speed but allow higher jailbreak success or hazardous outcomes. The stage of intervention, the decision mechanism, and the input modality each materially affect performance. The framework exposes systematic trade-offs and makes differences between guardrails clear and quantifiable.

Conclusion: Guardrails for embodied LLM/VLM agents inherently involve trade-offs among safety, usability, and efficiency; a universal best guardrail does not exist. Evaluations must consider system-level behavior and the precise point of intervention in the agent pipeline. The authors’ pluggable evaluation framework enables fair comparison and helps identify which guardrail designs suit particular deployment needs. They provide practical recommendations for choosing and designing guardrails based on deployment priorities and constraints.

Abstract: Embodied agents powered by large language models and vision-language models are increasingly deployed in physical environments, but jailbreak attacks can induce these agents to perform physically harmful actions. A growing number of guardrail methods have been proposed to intercept dangerous behavior before it is executed, yet existing safety benchmarks evaluate the embodied models themselves, leaving it unclear how well these guardrails actually defend an embodied agent in practice. We present the first systematic evaluation of jailbreak guardrails for embodied agents. To compare guardrails under identical conditions, we build a pluggable evaluation framework that treats the embodied agent as a fixed backend and each guardrail as a module that can intervene at the perception, planning, or control stage. We subject six representative guardrails to template-based and automated jailbreak attacks as well as safe instructions, and assess them at the system level along three dimensions: defense effectiveness, measured by the bypass rate and the hazard success rate in the simulator; usability, measured by the false-positive rate and the task completion rate on safe instructions; and efficiency, measured by the latency overhead added at runtime. Experiments on guardrails that span different intervention stages, decision mechanisms, and input modalities reveal a clear trade-off among the three dimensions, and show that no single guardrail dominates in all settings. We further analyze how intervention stage, decision mechanism, and input modality shape safety outcomes, and we offer practical guidance for selecting and designing guardrails for embodied agents.

</details>


### [338] [On Impact of Loss Function on the Performance of Neural Networks in Melanoma Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06139)
*Morgan May,Pierpaolo Dondio,Simon Caton*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how different loss functions affect deep neural network performance and calibration for melanoma image classification under strong class imbalance, finding focal loss offers the best trade-off between accuracy (AUC) and uncertainty calibration (ECE).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Melanoma is highly lethal but more treatable if detected early; deep learning image classification can aid diagnosis but suffers on imbalanced datasets like SIIM-ISIC, where melanoma cases are rare compared to benign lesions. The authors are motivated to address degraded performance and poorly calibrated uncertainty caused by this class imbalance by exploring whether alternative loss functions can improve both classification quality and reliability of predicted probabilities.

Method: The authors train deep neural networks for melanoma classification on imbalanced datasets using three different loss formulations: focal loss, logit-adjusted softmax cross-entropy loss, and class-weighted softmax cross-entropy loss. They then evaluate models on standard performance metrics such as AUC and on uncertainty calibration metrics, especially expected calibration error (ECE), to compare how each loss impacts both accuracy and probability calibration.

Result: Across experiments, models trained with focal loss achieve competitive or superior classification performance (notably higher or comparable AUC) while also providing better-calibrated probability estimates, reflected in lower expected calibration error, compared with models trained using logit-adjusted or weighted cross-entropy losses.

Conclusion: The study concludes that among the tested loss functions, focal loss is particularly effective for handling class imbalance in melanoma image classification, as it simultaneously enhances discriminative performance and yields better-calibrated uncertainty estimates, making it a strong candidate for practical clinical decision-support systems on imbalanced medical imaging datasets.

Abstract: Melanoma is the deadliest type of skin cancer, whose early diagnosis is crucial for patients' survival. Image classification using deep learning models has shown promising results for melanoma diagnosis. However, the performance of these models on the melanoma datasets such as SIIM-ISIC melanoma classification dataset is a challenge due to the class imbalance. One of the methods to deal with this challenge is using loss function modifications. In this work, we have investigated the effect of different loss functions on the performance of deep neural networks. We trained these networks using focal loss, logit-adjusted softmax cross-entropy (CE) loss, and weighted softmax CE loss, and we report different metrics for evaluating performance and uncertainty calibration. Our results suggest that focal loss delivers a good combination of performance in terms of AUC and uncertainty calibration in terms of expected calibration error (ECE) simultaneously.

</details>


### [339] [Impact of Data Augmentation on Confidence Calibration in Melanoma Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06146)
*Morgan May,Simon Caton,Pierpaolo Dondio*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how data augmentation affects both performance and uncertainty calibration of neural networks for melanoma image classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In melanoma diagnosis, models must not only be accurate but also well-calibrated, so that predicted probabilities reflect true risk. Data augmentation is known to improve performance and handle class imbalance, but its specific effect on calibration in imbalanced medical datasets, especially melanoma classification, has not been well studied.

Method: The authors train neural networks on the SIIM-ISIC 2020 melanoma classification dataset in two settings: with and without various data augmentation strategies. They then compare the models in terms of area under the ROC curve (AUC) and expected calibration error (ECE) to assess both predictive performance and calibration quality.

Result: Models trained with data augmentation exhibit better calibration, as reflected in lower ECE, while also maintaining or improving predictive performance (AUC) compared to models trained without augmentation.

Conclusion: Data augmentation not only boosts performance on imbalanced melanoma classification tasks but also improves uncertainty calibration of neural network predictions, making it a useful tool for more reliable clinical decision support in this setting.

Abstract: Accurately quantifying the predictive uncertainty or improving model calibration plays an important role in medical image classification, in particular in melanoma diagnosis, where accurate uncertainty quantification can have significant implications for patient care. One of the methods for calibration improvement is data augmentation. In addition, data augmentation as a method for synthetically increasing the size of the dataset has been proven to improve the performance of models trained on imbalanced datasets. However, the impact of data augmentation, as a transformation of a part of the original data, on calibration of models trained on imbalanced datasets, in particular in melanoma classification is under-explored. We train neural networks on SIIM-ISIC 2020 melanoma classification dataset under two conditions: with and without data augmentation, and compare the differences in AUC and expected calibration error (ECE) in both scenarios. Our results shows improvements in uncertainty calibration using different augmentation methods.

</details>


### [340] [Auditable Clinical Timeline Reconstruction with Provenance-Aware Evidence Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06177)
*Judith Jeyafreeda Andrew*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They evaluate how well a synthetic patient-timeline QA system can be audited for its evidence, revisions, and abstentions, and how compression and NLP gates affect these properties.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Patient-timeline reconstruction systems for clinical notes must be auditable: answers should be backed by explicit text evidence, changes over time should be tracked, and the system should say “I don’t know” when the record is insufficient. Existing systems or heuristics often lose provenance, silently fail to answer, or rely on shortcuts. This paper aims to quantify and improve these aspects using a controlled synthetic dataset and formal evidence graphs.

Method: They construct a fully synthetic corpus of patient notes with explicit revision links and define 6,813 recency-based query points plus multiple control conditions where evidence is absent or ambiguous. They represent facts and their revisions in a temporally versioned, provenance-aware Evidence Graph. Two graph-compression operators are applied that preserve answer and mention links while reducing graph size, and are compared to a fixed-window baseline. To test abstention behaviour when evidence is missing or non-diagnostic, they use a BioClinicalBERT-based classifier and a zero-shot LLM as gates on ‘announcement’ controls and on marker-free controls. They also evaluate how well the LLM and a span-prediction head on BERT can localize and cite supporting evidence spans, comparing to 482 regenerated gold spans. All abstentions are stored as typed edges in the provenance graph to keep them queryable.

Result: The two provenance-preserving Evidence Graph operators reduced nodes-plus-edges to 67% and 63% of the original (about 77–78% of serialized size) while preserving all answers and mention links across 6,813 recency-answerable query points. In contrast, a simple fixed-window baseline failed to return answers for 53.4% of those points and did not flag these omissions. On controls where notes explicitly announced missing information, both the BioClinicalBERT and zero-shot LLM gates mainly reacted to the announcement cue instead of deeper reasoning about evidence. On marker-free controls, BERT never abstained (0/81 notes) and its accuracy dropped sharply from 93.8% to 59.3% across three relation types, showing poor calibration of abstention. The LLM’s coverage dropped from 75.6% to 27.7% on notes that its own model family had judged indeterminable, indicating inconsistent abstention behaviour. For evidence citation, the LLM achieved span recall 0.850 and precision 0.864 against 482 gold spans, whereas BERT’s span head, trained without explicit span supervision, failed to localize evidence usefully. The authors also identify a shortcut solution that reaches 0.651 accuracy on the clean task without full reasoning over provenance.

Conclusion: Provenance-aware, temporally versioned Evidence Graphs can substantially compress patient-timeline representations while preserving answerability and explicit evidence links, outperforming naive fixed-window baselines that silently lose many answers. However, both BioClinicalBERT and LLM-based gates show problematic abstention behavior, often keying on superficial announcements or failing to abstain when evidence is absent, and a non-trivial accuracy shortcut exists. LLMs can cite supporting spans with reasonably high precision and recall, whereas BERT without span supervision cannot reliably localize evidence. Overall, the work illustrates how to rigorously audit and instrument a synthetic patient-timeline QA pipeline, but the authors caution that the reported behaviors reflect synthetic data conditions rather than validated clinical performance.

Abstract: A patient-timeline reconstruction system is auditable only if it keeps the mentions behind each answer, records how facts were revised, and declines to answer when the evidence is not in the text. This study tests these three properties on a fully synthetic corpus (1,000 patients, 3,353 notes, 220 revision edges). Two provenance-aware Evidence Graph operators reduced the node-plus-edge count to 67% and 63% (77-78% of serialized size) while preserving every answer and mention link across 6,813 query points answerable by recency; a fixed-window baseline returned no value for 53.4% of points, unflagged. On evidence-unavailable controls that announce the omission, a BioClinicalBERT gate and a zero-shot LLM gate responded mainly to the announcement. On marker-free controls, BERT abstained on 0 of 81 notes while its accuracy fell from 93.8% to 59.3% across all three relation classes; the LLM's coverage fell from 75.6% to 27.7% on notes its own model family judged undeterminable. Against 482 regenerated gold spans, the LLM's cited evidence reached recall 0.850 and precision 0.864; BERT's span head, trained without span labels, did not localize evidence. A temporally versioned provenance graph stored abstentions as typed, queryable edges. The clean task admits a 0.651-accuracy shortcut, and results describe implementation behaviour on synthetic data, not clinical performance.

</details>


### [341] [Bridging the Evidence-to-Execution Gap:A Reflective Agent for Multi-Objective Peptide Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06190)
*Haosen Zhang,Yang Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EASER is a reflective LLM-based agent that connects literature-based reasoning with controllable peptide sequence generation via a learned property interface and iterative probe-and-steer feedback, achieving superior multi-objective antimicrobial peptide design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models can reason over scientific literature to suggest design strategies, but they struggle to directly and reliably implement these strategies at the level of biological sequences. Conversely, protein generative models can produce sequences but lack the ability to incorporate multi-step, evidence-based reasoning from the literature. This creates an evidence-to-execution gap: models can reason about what should be done but cannot reliably translate that into specific sequence edits aligned with experimental objectives and constraints. The authors aim to close this gap so that automated scientific reasoning can drive targeted, multi-objective sequence engineering, particularly for peptide therapeutics.

Method: The authors propose EASER (Evidence-Aware Sequence Engineering with Reflection), a reflective agent architecture that links scientific reasoning to sequence generation. EASER uses a learned property interface built from offline-trained, fixed low-rank matrices that approximate how sequence edits affect target properties. The agent retrieves relevant literature and contextual evidence, then composes these property matrices to steer a diffusion-based sequence generator. It formulates explicit intervention hypotheses specifying anchors (fixed regions), editable positions, and control coefficients for properties to optimize. A Probe-and-Steer mechanism first probes candidate interventions to validate predicted property responses and then allocates sampling budget to promising interventions. Outcomes from generated sequences are fed back into the agent’s reflection loop, influencing subsequent hypothesis formation and steering decisions. Components such as evidence retrieval, episodic history, reflection, and Probe-and-Steer are individually ablated to evaluate their contributions.

Result: On a multi-objective antimicrobial peptide design task (simultaneously maximizing antimicrobial activity while minimizing hemolysis and toxicity), EASER outperforms competing baselines that do not employ explicit reflective hypothesis formulation but operate under identical decision budgets. Explicit hypothesis-driven steering yields better multi-objective optimization metrics, including higher mean hypervolume and lower mean IGD+ over six repeated experimental trials on screened candidates. Ablation experiments demonstrate that removing evidence retrieval, episodic memory, reflective reasoning, or the Probe-and-Steer component degrades performance, confirming their importance.

Conclusion: EASER shows that equipping a reasoning agent with an executable property interface and a reflective, feedback-driven control loop enables effective translation of literature-grounded scientific reasoning into precise biological sequence edits. By combining evidence retrieval, structured hypothesis formulation, and probe-guided steering of a diffusion generator, the system achieves superior multi-objective peptide design. This suggests a general strategy for closing the gap between abstract scientific insight and concrete, property-targeted sequence generation in computational biology and drug discovery.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can reason over scientific literature to devise design strategies, yet fail to reliably implement them for biological sequences. While protein generative models learn sequence patterns, they lack the capacity to incorporate literature evidence for multi-step reflective reasoning, forming an evidence-to-execution gap between scientific reasoning and sequence manipulation. We present EASER (Evidence-Aware Sequence Engineering with Reflection), a reflective agent bridging reasoning and sequence generation via a learned property interface of offline-trained, fixed low-rank matrices. The agent steers a diffusion generator by combining these matrices, proposing intervention hypotheses (anchors, editable positions, control coefficients) grounded in retrieved evidence, sequence context and past results. A Probe-and-Steer mechanism validates interventions and allocates samples according to predicted property responses, with outcome reflection informing subsequent decisions. Evaluated on multi-objective antimicrobial peptide design (optimizing activity, non-hemolysis and non-toxicity), explicit hypothesis formulation delivers better multi-objective performance than direct action generation under identical decision conditions. Ablation studies verify the importance of evidence retrieval, episodic history, reflection and Probe-and-Steer. Over six repeated trials, EASER obtains the highest mean hypervolume and lowest mean IGD+ on screened candidates compared with competing baselines. Our work demonstrates how an executable property interface and iterative feedback link scientific reasoning to targeted peptide sequence generation.

</details>


### [342] [Copies or Sources? Measuring How LLM Aggregators Count Restated Evidence in Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06192)
*Jianxin Gao,Runze Li,Tianyi Yu,Liangwei Ren,Bohan Chen,Zining Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how multi-agent systems built on LLMs improperly double-count repeated statements as independent evidence, proposes a way to convert reported probabilities into an equivalent number of independent readings, and evaluates how different communication protocols and simple rules can reduce this overcounting and early overconfidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In LLM-based multi-agent systems, information is often forwarded, copied, and restated across agents and shared spaces. Naively aggregating these messages risks treating repetitions as independent evidence, leading to overconfident beliefs and premature decisions. There is a need for a principled way to measure how much independent evidence an aggregator is implicitly assuming and to design communication and prompting strategies that avoid double-counting while preserving genuine corroboration.

Method: The authors define a mapping from reported probabilities to an equivalent number of independent readings under Bayesian assumptions. This defines a 'copy weight' for restated messages: 0 if the aggregator fully de-duplicates sources, 1 if it fully counts each repetition as new evidence. They then run experiments on three controlled testbeds that keep the underlying evidence fixed but vary how it is restated: (1) message logs evaluated against an exact Bayesian oracle, (2) web documents with artificially appended copies, and (3) logs generated by LLM multi-agent teams under four different communication protocols. They compare reported beliefs to the oracle to infer the effective copy weight and detect cases of early commitment inconsistent with the oracle.

Result: Across four LLMs from three providers, forwarded copies are treated as only 0.06–0.42 of a truly new reading on average, showing partial but not complete double-counting. Nonetheless, a substantial fraction (5–40%) of logs in which a single reading is restated three times lead the models to beliefs that imply an early commitment the Bayesian oracle would never make. Models that are more robust to copy inflation on controlled message logs are likewise more robust on web-copy and agent-written logs, suggesting stable behavioral differences across models. Adding a short, explicit declaration about what a copy should contribute reduces copy weights on controlled logs to 0.08 or less. A protocol change that makes agents refer to prior readings instead of restating them cuts belief-implied early commitment from 11.2% to 1.1%, without suppressing genuine corroboration when truly independent evidence is present.

Conclusion: LLM-based multi-agent systems are prone to overweighting repeated information, leading to overconfident and prematurely decisive beliefs. The paper shows how to quantify this problem via an 'equivalent readings' framework and demonstrates that simple prompt-level interventions—explicitly specifying how to treat copies and encouraging reference to prior readings instead of verbatim restatement—substantially reduce double-counting and early commitment while retaining the benefits of additional independent evidence. This suggests that careful communication protocol and prompt design are critical for reliable multi-agent reasoning with LLMs.

Abstract: Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) restate observations as a matter of course: relays forward them, shared boards repeat them and discussion rounds echo them. An aggregator that pools such messages should count sources, not statements. We convert a reported probability into units of independent readings, which assigns every restatement a copy weight, 0 for an aggregator that counts sources and 1 for one that counts every statement, and yields the implied decision under any cost structure. Three testbeds hold the evidence fixed and vary how it is restated: message logs with an exact Bayesian oracle, web documents with appended copies, and logs written by LLM agent teams under four communication protocols. Across four models from three providers, a forwarded copy counts for 0.06 to 0.42 of a new reading, mostly because some replies count every statement. On 5% to 40% of logs that state one reading three times, the reported belief implies an early commitment that the oracle never makes. The models that count copies least and most on controlled logs do so on web copies and agent-written logs as well. A one-paragraph declaration of what a copy contributes brings the copy weight on controlled logs to 0.08 or less. A rule that has agents refer to readings instead of restating them cuts belief-implied early commitment from 11.2% to 1.1% and preserves genuine corroboration.

</details>


### [343] [AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06207)
*Amin Jalali*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a teaching framework that integrates AI as a core element in business process design through structured decision checkpoints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: BPM education and frameworks do not adequately prepare students to design end-to-end business processes that treat AI (LLMs, RAG, AI agents) as integral components rather than peripheral tools, creating a skills gap for future process developers.

Method: The authors define "AI-decision checkpoints"—structured points in the process development lifecycle for identifying AI-candidate sub-processes, evaluating their impact on key performance dimensions, and considering constraints. They instantiate these checkpoints in a fictitious customer onboarding process as a BPM teaching case organized into six lifecycle-based modules that chain outputs and inputs across process modeling, simulation, workflow execution with AI agents, and process mining. They then conduct a preliminary formative reflection based on instructor observations, student artifacts, and process maps mined from LMS logs.

Result: The teaching case and checkpoint framework were implemented and qualitatively evaluated via classroom use. Exploratory evidence from artifacts, logs, and observations indicates that students developed a clearer differentiation between where AI should automate individual tasks versus how it contributes to overall process value.

Conclusion: Integrating AI-decision checkpoints into BPM teaching via a lifecycle-spanning case can help students reason more systematically about AI in process design, promoting better alignment between task-level AI automation and end-to-end process objectives. The approach appears promising but needs more extensive evaluation.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and AI agents are increasingly embedded in operational business processes. Yet Business Process Management (BPM) curricula and frameworks still largely treat artificial intelligence (AI) as an add-on technology, leaving graduates (as potential future process developers) unprepared to reason about AI as a first-class design element of end-to-end processes. This paper addresses that gap by proposing \emph{AI-decision checkpoints}: explicit moments in a process development trajectory where process developers identify AI-candidate sub-processes, assess expected effects on time, cost, quality, and flexibility, consider legal and organisational constraints, and document a reasoned decision to adopt, constrain, or reject specific AI components. The checkpoints are instantiated through a fictitious customer onboarding process as a \textit{BPM Teaching Case}, embedded in a lifecycle-driven framework spanning six modules that combine process modeling, simulation, workflow execution with AI agents, and process mining, with each module's output serving as the next module's input. A preliminary formative reflection draws on instructor observations, submitted artifacts, and discovered process maps from learning-management-system logs. These exploratory observations suggest that the approach supported clearer distinctions between task-level automation and process-level value.

</details>


### [344] [From Papers to Mechanisms: An Evidence-Grounded Knowledge Substrate for Scientific Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06248)
*Qiuhui Chen,Yibo Liu,Tao Dai,Jiafan Lu,Zhenglei Zhou,Weimin Zhong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They build a structured, mechanism-focused knowledge base from sensor papers and show it helps language models answer scientific questions more correctly than standard text-based retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing scientific language models typically read papers as unstructured or weakly structured text chunks. This loses important functional and evidential structure—such as how materials, devices, and signals are mechanistically connected—which is crucial for answering mechanism-rich scientific questions. There is a need for a representation that makes mechanisms and their supporting evidence explicit and queryable.

Method: They design an evidence-grounded mechanism substrate that decomposes papers into small, provenance-linked evidence units, types all entities by their mechanistic roles, and connects them via directed mechanism paths. They instantiate this as MS^3, a Material-Sensor-Signal-System schema tailored to conductive-fiber flexible sensors. They populate MS^3 from 13,689 papers, yielding 131,083 evidence items and 26,648 mechanism objects. Then they build QA benchmarks (in-domain and with coverage shift) and systematically compare four setups—closed-book LMs, generic Web search, Raw-PDF RAG, and MS^3-based retrieval—across ten language models.

Result: Across these QA benchmarks, using MS^3 retrieval improves macro-averaged scientific correctness of answers versus baselines. It also yields better citation entailment, meaning cited sources more reliably support the claims, and it improves answer completeness. These gains hold across different language models and question regimes.

Conclusion: Structuring scientific literature as a mechanism-centric, evidence-grounded substrate like MS^3 provides a stronger representation layer for scientific LMs than raw untyped text or vanilla RAG. Such substrates help LMs generate more scientifically correct, well-supported, and complete answers. The authors propose a "source-repair" workflow: when the substrate lacks sufficient evidence, the system should selectively fetch and process the linked papers to repair gaps, instead of assuming users have pre-supplied the exact relevant PDFs.

Abstract: Scientific language models often access literature through untyped text chunks, which fragment the functional and evidential structure required for mechanism-rich questions. We introduce an evidence-grounded mechanism knowledge substrate that organizes scientific literature into provenance-linked evidence units, role-typed entities, and directed mechanism paths. We instantiate it as MS$^3$, a Material-Sensor-Signal-System schema for conductive-fiber flexible sensors, over 13,689 papers, 131,083 evidence items, and 26,648 mechanism objects. On in-domain and coverage-shift question-answering benchmarks, we compare closed-book generation, Web search, Raw-PDF RAG, and MS$^3$ retrieval across ten language models. MS$^3$ improves macro-averaged scientific correctness. It also improves citation entailment and answer completeness. These results support mechanism substrates as a reliable representation layer for scientific language models and motivate a source-repair workflow in which insufficient MS$^3$ evidence triggers targeted retrieval from its linked papers rather than assuming that a user has already supplied the correct PDFs.

</details>


### [345] [Evolving in Thought Space: Training a Small Model at Test Time Unlocks Better Discoveries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06269)
*Chonghe Jiang,Ao Qu,Siyuan Liu,Ruoyun Ma,Zijian Zhou,Dingyi Zhuang,Bo Liu,Han Zheng,Hanfei Yu,Baichuan Mo,Jinhua Zhao,Paul Pu Liang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Guidance-TTT is a test-time training framework that uses a small, trainable guidance model to make high-level strategic edits to candidate solutions, while a large frozen execution model implements full solutions, enabling efficient and powerful open-ended scientific discovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based scientific discovery methods like TTT-Discover adapt a large solution-generating model at test time using verifier feedback. This is expensive because it requires maintaining training states for big models while generating long outputs, and it makes credit assignment difficult since feedback conflates high-level strategy with low-level implementation quality. There is a need for a more efficient and better-structured way to leverage verifier feedback for iterative solution improvement.

Method: The authors introduce Guidance-TTT, which splits responsibilities between two models: a compact, trainable guidance model and a frozen large execution model. At each iteration, the system selects a promising previous solution, the guidance model proposes a high-level strategic modification, the execution model turns this into a full executable solution, and a verifier evaluates it. Only the guidance model is updated using an adaptive group-relative reinforcement learning objective based on the verifier feedback. This focuses learning on short strategic decisions while leveraging the strong but fixed implementation abilities of the large model.

Result: Without web access, Guidance-TTT achieves strong performance on four diverse domains: Polyomino Packing (combinatorial optimization), AHC058 (heuristic programming), Lasso (machine learning), and TriMul (GPU kernel optimization). On these benchmarks, it surpasses the best prior solutions reported in earlier work and remains competitive with state-of-the-art entries on public online leaderboards.

Conclusion: Separating high-level strategy learning from low-level solution execution via a small trainable guidance model and a frozen large execution model enables more efficient and effective test-time training for open-ended scientific discovery. Guidance-TTT improves over prior TTT-based approaches, offering a practical way to exploit verifier feedback while controlling computational cost and simplifying credit assignment.

Abstract: Open-ended scientific discovery often requires repeatedly proposing and evaluating candidate solutions. LLM-based systems can support this process by generating and refining executable solutions from verifier feedback. Methods such as TTT-Discover use test-time training (TTT) to update the solution-generating LLM from verifier feedback, adapting its generation policy to improve subsequent proposals on the target problem. However, this becomes expensive when reliable execution requires a large model, since training must maintain gradients, optimizer states, and policy statistics while repeatedly generating long, structured outputs. It also complicates credit assignment: outcome-level verifier feedback must jointly evaluate the high-level strategy and its low-level implementation. In this work, we introduce Guidance-TTT, which separates these roles. A compact guidance model is trained at test time to propose high-level strategic changes, while a frozen execution model implements them as complete executable solutions. At each step, the system selects a promising previously discovered solution, proposes a change, executes and verifies it, and updates only the guidance model using an adaptive group-relative RL objective. This concentrates test-time learning on short strategic decisions while retaining the implementation capability of a substantially stronger model without adapting it. Without web access, Guidance-TTT produces strong solutions across four distinct domains: combinatorial optimization (Polyomino Packing), heuristic programming (AHC058), machine learning (Lasso), and GPU kernel optimization (TriMul). Across these tasks, it outperforms the best solutions reported in prior work while remaining competitive with state-of-the-art results on public online leaderboards. Code is available at https://github.com/Human-Agent-Society/reef/tree/guidance-ttt-support.

</details>


### [346] [DPNL: A DPLL-based Algorithm for Probabilistic Neurosymbolic Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06270)
*Thomas Jean-Michel Valentin,Pierre Genev{è}s,Luisa Sophie Werner,Sarah Chlyah,Nabil Laya{ï}da,Nils Gesbert*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose a new, more scalable framework for probabilistic neurosymbolic learning that avoids fully computing logical provenance, and they show it makes more problems tractable while allowing approximate but certified inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing probabilistic neurosymbolic learning systems suffer from a major bottleneck: they must materialize the full logical provenance (all explanations/derivations) of a query before doing probabilistic inference. For complex tasks this provenance can become huge, making inference slow or infeasible. The authors want an inference approach that scales better while still supporting end-to-end learning from weak supervision (only final outputs, no intermediate labels).

Method: They introduce Dynamic Probabilistic Neurosymbolic Learning (DPNL), an oracle-guided search framework. Instead of eagerly computing all logical provenance, DPNL lazily explores the space of possible intermediate assignments. Oracles are used to certify that whole regions of this search space either always yield the target output or can never yield it, allowing those regions to be resolved or pruned without full enumeration. They provide conditions for the soundness and termination of this procedure. They also propose ApproxDPNL, which adds early stopping to the same search process while maintaining provable upper and lower bounds on the true output probability, giving controlled approximate inference. The framework is designed so that the oracle interface abstracts away the particular representation of the symbolic component, allowing custom problem-specific reasoning modules.

Result: Theoretical results establishing conditions under which DPNL is sound (produces correct probabilities) and guaranteed to terminate, plus approximation guarantees (probability bounds) for ApproxDPNL. Empirically, on multiple neurosymbolic benchmarks, both DPNL and ApproxDPNL can solve significantly larger or harder problem instances than prior probabilistic neurosymbolic inference methods that rely on full provenance materialization.

Conclusion: By moving from full provenance materialization to oracle-guided, lazy exploration, DPNL makes probabilistic neurosymbolic learning more scalable while preserving correctness, and ApproxDPNL adds efficient approximate inference with certified bounds. The oracle abstraction allows the same framework to be applied across different symbolic representations, and experiments demonstrate substantially expanded tractable problem ranges for neurosymbolic tasks.

Abstract: Probabilistic Neurosymbolic Learning (PNL) combines neural predictions with symbolic reasoning, enabling end-to-end learning from final-output supervision without labels for intermediate concepts. A central challenge is probabilistic inference: state-of-the-art approaches often rely on materializing the logical provenance of a query, which can itself become a major computational bottleneck. We introduce Dynamic Probabilistic Neurosymbolic Learning (DPNL), an oracle-guided framework that avoids requiring complete provenance materialization before inference. DPNL lazily explores the space of intermediate assignments, while oracles resolve entire regions that can already be certified to produce or exclude the target output. We establish conditions ensuring soundness and termination. ApproxDPNL extends the same search with early termination while maintaining certified bounds on the exact output probability, providing controlled approximation guarantees. The oracle interface decouples inference from the representation of the symbolic component, enabling problem-specific reasoning within the same framework. Experiments on several neurosymbolic tasks show that DPNL and ApproxDPNL substantially extend the range of problem instances tractable by probabilistic neurosymbolic inference.

</details>


### [347] [Teaching a Minimalist Machine to Discover Recursive Programs for Arithmetic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06304)
*Dominik Magiera,Christiane Wiebel-Herboth,Frank Jäkel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Minimalist Machine, a program synthesis framework that learns recursive arithmetic concepts from very few examples using a small Prolog-like language.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To model human-like conceptual learning, where people infer rich, recursive structures (like arithmetic) from sparse data, and to obtain transparent reasoning traces instead of black-box models.

Method: Use a constrained relational subset of Prolog with only facts and two-body Horn clauses. Run inductive program synthesis over this space, with recursion emerging by reusing the target predicate in clause bodies. Train the system over a human-curated curriculum of arithmetic concepts, starting from no prior knowledge and gradually introducing more complex predicates.

Result: The system incrementally learns structural predicates, successor-based state transitions, and then recursive programs for the core arithmetic operations—addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division—within the minimalist Prolog schema.

Conclusion: A tightly constrained, curriculum-trained program synthesis framework can learn recursive arithmetic concepts in a human-like, data-efficient manner, while producing fully interpretable inductive reasoning traces that mirror transparent conceptual learning.

Abstract: Humans can often acquire and synthesize complex, recursive concepts from minimal experience. Leveraging cognitive insights, we propose the Minimalist Machine, a framework for inductive program synthesis designed to model such conceptual learning. The system uses a compact relational subset of Prolog: Programs are searched within a fixed schema of body-free facts and two-body conjunctive Horn clauses. Recursion is not defined by a dedicated metarule. Instead, it emerges when a target predicate is reused inside the body of a learned clause. Inspired by a primary school curriculum, the model is taught through a human-curated, sequential introduction of new concepts in arithmetic. Starting from initially empty knowledge base, it first acquires simple structural predicates, then successor-based state transformations, and finally recursive programs for addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. Ultimately, this approach yields the fully transparent, inductive reasoning trace necessary for human-like conceptual learning.

</details>


### [348] [RollPlace: Improving Macro Placement via Monte Carlo Rollout Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06316)
*Qi Zhou,Guojun Liu,Guangzhi Qi,Ming Lu,Jiechu Liu,Zhongli Liu,Jianqun Yang,Xingji Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RollPlace is a two-stage macro placement framework for chip design that refines an initial placement using MCTS-based local search to outperform prior methods on standard benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL/ML-based chip placement methods typically generate a full layout in one pass and often need additional refinement; they are also constrained by sequential decision processes that can be inefficient and inflexible for large, complex designs. There is a need for a more general, scalable, and refinement-oriented framework that can improve initial placements from diverse sources while handling modern chip complexity.

Method: RollPlace uses a two-stage optimization pipeline for macro placement. First, it generates an initial placement using either learned models or heuristic strategies. Second, it refines this placement by selectively adjusting a subset of macros instead of regenerating the whole layout. The refinement process integrates Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to manage the exploration–exploitation trade-off and uses rollout-based local search to efficiently evaluate and improve candidate macro moves. This avoids the strict sequential placement of traditional RL approaches and focuses computation on the most impactful local changes.

Result: On the ISPD 2005 macro placement benchmarks, RollPlace achieves better performance than state-of-the-art methods, indicating superior placement quality and/or efficiency. In additional end-to-end experiments using the OpenROAD flow across 19 benchmarks, RollPlace shows improvements across multiple evaluation metrics, demonstrating its practical effectiveness within a realistic physical design toolchain.

Conclusion: RollPlace provides a robust, scalable macro placement framework that can plug into existing EDA flows, refine placements produced by various initial methods, and handle modern chip design complexity more effectively than prior RL-based sequential approaches. Its two-stage, MCTS-driven local refinement strategy leads to consistently improved placement quality across standard and end-to-end benchmarks.

Abstract: The application of Reinforcement Learning (RL) in Electronic Design Automation (EDA), particularly for chip placement, has attracted considerable attention in recent years. While existing machine learning (ML)-based approaches have achieved notable progress, they predominantly focus on generating optimal layouts in a single attempt, often producing solutions that require subsequent refinement. To address this limitation, we propose RollPlace, a novel and generalized macro placement framework. RollPlace adopts a two-stage optimization strategy: generating initial placement solutions via machine learning methods or heuristic-based strategies, and refining these layouts efficiently by adjusting specific macros derived from the initial stage. This strategy circumvents the sequential generation constraints inherent in traditional RL-based placement methods. Furthermore, RollPlace seamlessly integrates Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to balance exploration and exploitation, and employs a rollout mechanism for efficient local search. Extensive experiments on the ISPD 2005 benchmark demonstrate that RollPlace outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, end-to-end experimental results based on OpenROAD across 19 benchmarks show that RollPlace excels in multiple metrics. The proposed framework offers a robust and scalable solution for addressing the growing complexity of modern chip design challenges.

</details>


### [349] [CRAFTER: Causality-based Self-adaptation for Autonomous IoT Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06320)
*Houssam Hajj Hassan,Ajay Kattepur,Denis Conan,Georgios Bouloukakis*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CRAFTER is an automated framework that uses Causal Reinforcement Learning to design and deploy reusable, self-adaptive IoT systems, improving adaptation performance by 25% over state-of-the-art RL approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: IoT environments are highly dynamic, with fluctuating workloads and changing application demands, making it hard to maintain consistent QoS. Existing self-adaptation solutions are often domain-specific and not easily reusable across different IoT verticals, and there is a lack of automated methods to identify causal performance drivers for effective adaptation decisions.

Method: CRAFTER applies Causality as the core formalism for performance analysis of IoT systems. It automatically derives causal graphs that capture cause-effect relationships and dependencies between system components. These graphs then inform Causal Reinforcement Learning-based adaptation agents, which exploit the causal structure to select adaptation actions more effectively under dynamic conditions.

Result: Experiments show that CRAFTER can automatically generate meaningful causal graphs across multiple, diverse IoT use cases and that, when used to guide self-adaptive behavior, it improves adaptation performance by 25% compared to existing RL-based self-adaptation techniques.

Conclusion: By integrating causal analysis with reinforcement learning in an automated framework, CRAFTER enables reusable, more effective self-adaptive IoT systems across different domains, leading to better QoS maintenance in dynamic environments than conventional RL-based approaches.

Abstract: This paper presents CRAFTER, an automated framework for designing and deploying self-adaptive IoT systems using Causal Reinforcement Learning (CRL). As IoT devices increasingly populate pervasive computing spaces, smart environments are enabled with advanced monitoring and interactive services. The dynamic nature of these environments, such as fluctuating workloads and evolving application demands, poses significant challenges in maintaining consistent Quality of Service (QoS) levels of IoT applications. While existing self-adaptation techniques offer adaptive capabilities, they are often designed to deal with specific application domains, hindering the design of self-adaptive solutions that can be re-used across multiple IoT verticals. In addition, there is a lack of automated pipelines that act on identifying key performance drivers to take effective adaptation decisions. CRAFTER addresses these issues by using Causality as a formal framework for performance analysis of IoT systems. CRAFTER generates causal graphs to uncover dependencies among system components and guide adaptation decisions based on cause-effect relationships. Then, adaptation agents can leverage this knowledge to take more effective adaptation decisions in dynamic situations. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates how CRAFTER enables deriving causal graphs spanning diverse IoT use cases. Furthermore, we showcase how CRAFTER improves self-adaptation performance by 25% compared to state-of-the-art Reinforcement Learning-based approaches.

</details>


### [350] [ImproveAnyTask: An Autonomous Post-Training Harness for Iterative Model Self-Improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06347)
*Xingbo Yao,Xiaoman Wang,Zhengwu Lei,Tinghui Luo,YiLin Zhang,Yuefeng Wu,Yijie Xu,Tianfu Wang,Qingyuan Zhan,Ye Guo,Daoxin Zhang,Zhe Xu,Jian Liu,Hui Xiong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduce ImproveAnyTask, an autonomous post-training harness that systematically improves LLM task performance under limited compute.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Adapting general LLMs to specific tasks usually needs heavy manual effort in data design and training strategy, and becomes harder over time because model updates shift error patterns, forcing constant redesign of adaptation strategies.

Method: Design an autonomous post-training harness, ImproveAnyTask, that structures adaptation similarly to gradient-based optimization: (1) error attribution via metric- and case-level analysis to locate focal problems, (2) automated selection among research-backed adaptation strategies by weighing expected gains versus reproduction difficulty, and (3) translation of the chosen strategy into concrete training data and configurations, with small-scale sanity runs before full post-training. The system iterates: evaluate, adapt, select better model, and cache validated strategies/scripts for reuse.

Result: On 11 benchmark tasks, ImproveAnyTask yields mean performance improvements of 18.29 percentage points for Base models and 11.97 points for Instruct models, with maximum observed gain of 41.96 points, all within a 24-hour compute budget using resources equivalent to eight H20 GPUs.

Conclusion: An autonomous, gradient-inspired post-training harness can reliably and efficiently improve LLM performance on diverse tasks under realistic compute constraints, while also producing reusable adaptation recipes for future model updates.
