Abstract: Adapting general-purpose large language models to specific tasks requires substantial human effort in designing data and training strategies. Sustaining improvement is especially challenging because model updates change the error distribution, requiring strategies to be continually refined. We introduce ImproveAnyTask, an autonomous post-training harness that improves task performance under a limited compute budget. Drawing inspiration from gradient-based parameter optimization, the harness organizes adaptation into error attribution, update-direction selection, and executable model updates. It combines metric-level and case-level analysis to identify a focal problem, then investigates research-backed strategies and compares their reported gains and reproduction difficulty. The selected strategy is translated into training data and a training configuration, with small-scale execution checks preceding full post-training. Subsequent evaluation guides model selection and further adaptation, while validated strategies and scripts are retained for reuse. Across 11 tasks, ImproveAnyTask achieves mean gains of 18.29 and 11.97 percentage points on the Base and Instruct models, respectively, with a maximum gain of 41.96 points, under a 24-hour budget with resources equivalent to eight H20 GPUs.

</details>


### [351] [GraphDecide: Benchmarking System One Models on Graph Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06354)
*Xianliang Yang,Yapu Zhang,Li Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GraphDecide is a benchmark to evaluate how well option-selecting (System One) models like Jev make decisions on graph-structured tasks, revealing that basic edge recognition doesn’t imply deeper structural understanding or high-quality solutions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although large language models are being used for graph reasoning and decision-making, there is a specific class of models (System One / choice-based models like Jev) that only select from provided options instead of generating free text. Their actual ability to handle graph-based tasks—beyond simple edge recognition—is poorly understood. Existing benchmarks are not tailored to systematically analyze their strengths and weaknesses on graph decisions or to compare them fairly with standard LLMs.

Method: The authors design GraphDecide, a model-independent benchmark for graph decision-making. It uses (1) structural task profiles to cover different graph reasoning skills, (2) carefully matched graph-only vs graph+text input settings to contrast modalities, and (3) heuristic-proposal controls to ensure that tasks are not solvable by trivial heuristics. They then evaluate Jev and related choice-based models, as well as language-model baselines adapted to choice-based interfaces, yielding fourteen distinct model–interface configurations. The benchmark defines standardized task contracts, candidate-option interfaces, and scoring rules to enable consistent comparison across these systems.

Result: Experiments with Jev demonstrate three key empirical findings: (1) being accurate at recognizing graph adjacency (whether two nodes are connected) does not imply broader structural correctness on more complex tasks; (2) adding textual descriptions to graph inputs (joint graph-text input) does not reliably improve prediction quality; and (3) the fact that a model can feasibly construct answers in this decision format does not mean the resulting solutions are high quality. The benchmark successfully exposes these distinctions across models and interfaces.

Conclusion: GraphDecide provides a structured way to evaluate and compare graph decision-making abilities of option-selecting System One models and language models adapted to selection tasks. It shows that surface-level graph skills and straightforward interface designs are insufficient indicators of deeper structural reasoning or solution quality. The benchmark, along with released code and aggregate results, establishes a basis for more rigorous analysis and future improvement of graph decision capabilities in such models.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for graph understanding and decision-making, while System One models such as Jev select directly from supplied options. However, the capabilities of System One models on graph-related tasks remain unclear. We introduce GraphDecide, a model-independent benchmark that combines structural task profiles, matched graph-text input contrasts and heuristic-proposal controls to diagnose graph decision performance. We evaluate Jev and related choice-based models alongside language-model baselines, covering fourteen model-interface configurations. Jev's results illustrate the benchmark's central distinctions: accurate adjacency recognition does not guarantee broader structural correctness, joint graph-text input does not consistently improve prediction, and feasible construction does not establish high solution quality. Its task contracts, candidate interfaces and scoring rules support comparison across native selectors and language-model adapters. Code and aggregate results are available at https://github.com/VictorYXL/JevGraphBench.

</details>


### [352] [Capability-Driven Self-Evolution of Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06361)
*Yaoqi Chen,Yuru Feng,Qianxi Zhang,Baotong Lu,Jianan Lu,Zhirui Wang,Shusen Xu,Zewen Jin,Zengzhong Li,Cheng Li,Qi Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes PrisMem, a capability-driven memory self-evolution method that improves long-context memory programs by optimizing specific capabilities and integrating their complementary strengths, achieving significant gains on million-token history benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing memory self-evolution methods rely on holistic evolution guided by aggregate task feedback. This mixes signals from different capabilities (e.g., retrieval accuracy, reasoning over retrieved info, robustness), making it hard to see which parts are improving or regressing. As a result, promising directions for some capabilities may be discarded if overall performance does not improve, and capability-specific gains can be masked by regressions elsewhere. The authors want a more fine-grained, capability-aware way to evolve memory programs that better exploits feedback and scales to very long interaction histories.

Method: They introduce capability-driven evolution for memory self-evolution. Instead of optimizing a single monolithic score, they decompose performance into multiple capability dimensions and evolve specialized memory programs for each. PrisMem has three main components: (1) Dependency-aware capability selection, which chooses which capability to optimize next based on dependencies and the potential for cross-capability benefits; (2) History-guided diagnosis, which identifies failure cases from past interactions to refine these capability specialists; and (3) Trace-guided integration, which runs candidate programs on paired differential cases, compares their behavioral traces, and integrates complementary strengths into a unified memory program by preserving behaviors that perform better on each case. The overall process iteratively evolves and merges specialized programs using task feedback over long histories.

Result: On two long-context benchmarks, BEAM-1M and LongMemEval-M, both involving million-token histories, PrisMem significantly outperforms strong baselines that use holistic memory self-evolution or other memory mechanisms. Specifically, it improves performance by 10.54 percentage points on BEAM-1M and 7.83 percentage points on LongMemEval-M, indicating better handling of long histories and more effective use of task feedback for memory evolution.

Conclusion: Capability-driven evolution offers a more informative and efficient way to guide memory self-evolution than holistic approaches. By explicitly modeling and optimizing along capability dimensions, and then carefully integrating specialized gains, PrisMem achieves stronger and more robust memory programs, especially in long-horizon settings with million-token interaction histories. This suggests that future memory and tool-learning systems should consider capability-aware optimization and compositional integration of behaviors rather than relying solely on end-to-end aggregate performance signals.

Abstract: Memory self-evolution uses task feedback to iteratively improve executable memory programs that store and retrieve information from past interactions. Existing approaches typically adopt holistic evolution, deriving revision directions from mixed feedback and judging progress by overall performance. This can obscure optimization directions and hide capability-specific gains offset by regressions elsewhere, leaving promising directions underexplored. We introduce capability-driven evolution, which extends search guidance from overall performance to individual capability dimensions, preserving promising revisions and expanding exploration beyond the boundaries of holistic evolution. We propose PrisMem, which uses dependency-aware capability selection to prioritize targets with potential cross-capability benefits and history-guided diagnosis to refine capability specialists. Trace-guided integration compares evaluated programs on paired differential cases, using their behavioral differences to consolidate complementary gains into a unified memory program. Experiments show that PrisMem outperforms the strongest baselines by 10.54 and 7.83 percentage points on BEAM-1M and LongMemEval-M, respectively, demonstrating its effectiveness on million-token histories.

</details>


### [353] [CVIF: A Criticality-Driven Visual Intervention Framework for Geometric Diagram Understanding in MLLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06399)
*Jiahui Kang,Bifan Wei,Lingling Zhang,Tianwen Jiang,Qiuyong Xiao,Jihong Zhang,Jun Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose an inference-time, training-free framework (CVIF) that improves MLLMs’ understanding of geometric diagrams by steering attention toward visually critical evidence, significantly boosting F1 scores on geometry benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal LLMs perform well on many visual tasks but still struggle with geometric diagrams, where visual cues are sparse and symbols have ambiguous relations to geometric primitives. As a result, models over-rely on textual priors, sometimes contradicting what is actually shown in the diagram. The authors aim to reduce this mismatch by ensuring the model’s reasoning is grounded in the visual evidence rather than default language patterns.

Method: They introduce CVIF, a training-free, inference-time framework that intervenes inside MLLMs without retraining. First, the method identifies ‘critical layers’ where the model shifts from aggregating visual evidence to semantic decoding. At these layers, a Geometry-Constrained Local Relation Reconstruction (GCLR) module selects vertex-centered visual tokens and assigns them importance weights under geometric constraints. Then, an Adaptive Visual Steering Operator (AVSO) modifies the attention distribution to concentrate more mass on the selected visual tokens, effectively steering the model toward relevant geometric evidence while leaving the rest of the model intact.

Result: On two geometric problem benchmarks, PGPS9K and PGDP5K, applying CVIF to existing MLLMs increases Overall F1 from 77.85 to 85.58 on PGPS9K and from 75.23 to 82.84 on PGDP5K, showing substantial performance gains without extra training or data.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates that targeted, training-free visual interventions inside MLLMs can significantly improve geometric diagram understanding by aligning attention with critical visual evidence. CVIF establishes a new paradigm for inference-time visual steering, suggesting that similar approaches could generalize to other domains where models under-utilize visual signals and over-rely on textual priors.

Abstract: Despite significant progress in visual tasks by Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), geometric diagram understanding remains challenging due to the presence of sparse visual cues and ambiguous symbol-primitive associations. MLLMs may therefore rely on textual priors, producing interpretations that conflict with visual evidence. We introduce the training-free Criticality-Driven Visual Intervention Framework (CVIF), an inference-time method that localizes critical layers and executes visual interventions during the transition from evidence aggregation to semantic decoding. At these layers, a Geometry-Constrained Local Relation Reconstruction (GCLR) module selects and weights vertex-centered visual evidence, while an Adaptive Visual Steering Operator (AVSO) redistributes attention mass toward the selected tokens. Experiments on PGPS9K and PGDP5K show that CVIF raises Overall F1 from 77.85 to 85.58 and from 75.23 to 82.84, respectively, establishing a novel inference-time visual intervention paradigm.

</details>


### [354] [From Benchmark to Bench: Can Agents Survive Real-World Drug Discovery?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06411)
*Pierre Llompart,Levent Guner,Helen Lai,Alessandro Tibo,Yijie Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They build an open, modular AI agent (MAGI) that coordinates molecule design tools and show that, in real lead‑optimization projects, the main bottleneck is the accuracy/applicability of scoring models, not molecule generation or agent orchestration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic/LLM-based molecular design systems are being adopted but it is unclear which part of the stack (agent logic, generative model, or scoring models) actually limits performance on realistic drug-discovery projects. Current benchmarks often use toy setups and don’t reflect pharma workflows. The authors want to quantify where the true bottleneck lies and whether an agentic coordinator can integrate existing tools effectively while producing chemistry that looks expert-level to medicinal chemists.

Method: They design MAGI, a modular agent that: (1) writes optimization objectives, (2) launches and monitors multi-objective optimization runs, (3) interprets emerging structure–activity relationships, and (4) revises its design strategy iteratively. MAGI can generate molecules in two interchangeable ways: directly via an LLM or by delegating to REINVENT 4, with standardized scoring interfaces. They replay nine real-world retrospective lead-optimization campaigns from three pharma companies under fixed time cutoffs, comparing LLM vs REINVENT generations under various scoring models. They also conduct a blinded human evaluation where medicinal chemists compare MAGI’s proposed compounds and SAR narratives with held-out expert-designed compounds.

Result: Both LLM and REINVENT routes produced syntactically and chemically valid molecules. LLM-based proposals tended to remain closer to the existing chemotype while often achieving target primary activity in fewer steps; REINVENT explored a wider region of chemical space. Success in achieving campaign objectives correlated strongly with the accuracy and applicability domain of the predictive scoring models: once proposed chemistry drifted outside those models’ domains, optimization performance degraded sharply, regardless of generation method. In the blinded study, chemists generally could not distinguish MAGI’s molecules from human-designed ones, and considered MAGI’s SAR reasoning believable though not fully comprehensive.

Conclusion: MAGI works well as a flexible coordination layer that can be plugged into standard computational chemistry pipelines and can interface with different generative models and scoring services. However, in realistic lead-optimization settings, the limiting factor is the quality and applicability of the scoring models, not the sophistication of the agent or the choice of generative engine. Improving predictors and their applicability domains is therefore more critical than further tool orchestration for lifting performance ceilings in current AI-driven molecular design.

Abstract: Agentic systems increasingly coordinate molecular-design tools, but it is unclear which layer of the stack limits outcomes on real projects. We developed MAGI, an open modular agent that authors objectives, launches and monitors optimization, interprets structure--activity relationships, and revises its strategy accordingly. MAGI generates molecules either directly through the LLM or by delegating to REINVENT 4, with scoring services interchangeable behind a common contract. We tested it across nine retrospective lead-optimization campaigns from three pharmaceutical companies, replayed under fixed temporal cutoffs. Both routes produced valid structures: LLM proposals stayed closer to local chemistry and reached comparable or higher primary activity in fewer operations, whereas REINVENT explored broader chemical space. Whether a campaign met its objective depended on the predictive models, not on the generation route: attainment followed model accuracy on the chemistry proposed, dropping once that chemistry moved outside the model's applicability domain. Separately, a blinded evaluation asked whether the MAGI's output could pass as expert work: chemists were not able to discriminate agentic proposals from held-out compounds, and judged the SAR reasoning broadly plausible yet incomplete. Together, these results position MAGI as a coordination layer pluggable into existing computational chemistry workflows. The ceiling on real projects, however, remains currently set by scorer applicability rather than by tool orchestration.

</details>


### [355] [Multimodal Safety Evaluation Should Measure Controllability Beyond Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06452)
*Junhyeong Park,Hanwool Lee,DongGeon Lee,Dasol Choi,Yejin Son,Haon Park,Youngjae Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper argues that safety evaluation for vision-language models should go beyond classifying inputs/outputs and also assess whether internal safety-related states can be detected and controlled, introducing a “controllability profile” and demonstrating its use on implicit toxicity for two VLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current safety evaluations of vision-language models focus mostly on classifying whether inputs or outputs are safe/unsafe. This overlooks whether safety-relevant internal states exist in a form that can be accessed and manipulated, which matters for interpretability, governance, and reliable deployment. The authors want a framework that reveals not only whether a model behaves safely, but also whether its internal representations enable controllable safety interventions, especially in subtle cases like implicit toxicity.

Method: They define a controllability profile with four axes: (1) representation-level detectability (can safety signals be read from internal features?), (2) cross-modal specificity (are these signals tied specifically to safety content across text and image modalities?), (3) intervention sensitivity (do interventions on these features reliably change behavior?), and (4) benign-preserving selectivity (do interventions avoid harming benign behavior?). Using implicit toxicity as the test domain, they apply sparse feature decomposition methods to two VLMs, LlavaGuard and Qwen3.5, identify internal features related to toxicity, and experimentally probe and intervene on these features under different operators to measure their controllability profile.

Result: For LlavaGuard, they find localized internal “handles” (features) associated with toxicity that can be intervened on, but the safe operating range for such interventions is narrow, with only modest improvements in downstream safety while preserving benign behavior. For Qwen3.5, they observe that toxicity-related signals can be read out strongly at the representation level (good detectability), but their interventions cannot establish a similarly selective control regime: attempts to manipulate these signals do not yield reliable or benign-preserving changes in behavior under the tested intervention operators.

Conclusion: Internal representation-level safety signals and their controllability can diverge from external behavioral safety metrics. A model may encode safety-relevant information in its representations without offering a practicable way to manipulate that information to reliably and selectively improve safety. The authors propose that future multimodal safety benchmarks should therefore report not only behavioral safety performance but also a controllability profile, explicitly documenting whether and how safety-relevant internal features can be probed and safely intervened on within a validated operating range.

Abstract: VLM safety is commonly evaluated through input- and output-level classification. Such classification is necessary, but it does not reveal whether a safety state is accessible or controllable inside the model. We argue that multimodal safety evaluation should therefore report a \emph{controllability profile} alongside behavioral classification, separating representation-level detectability, cross-modal specificity, intervention sensitivity, and benign-preserving selectivity. Using implicit toxicity as a stress case, we instantiate this profile on LlavaGuard and Qwen3.5 with sparse feature decompositions. LlavaGuard admits localized handles with a narrow benign-preserving intervention range and modest downstream safety gains, whereas Qwen3.5 supports strong representation-level readout but no comparable selective-control regime under the tested operators. These results show that internal readout and controllability can diverge. Future multimodal safety benchmarks should therefore report not only behavioral safety metrics, but also whether safety-relevant internal signals can be intervention-tested and controlled within a validated operating range.

</details>


### [356] [Normality Constraint Learning: Adapting Foundation Models for Time Series Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06453)
*Xiaohui Zhou,Yijie Wang,Hongzuo Xu,Weixuan Liang,Guansong Pang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose NCL, a plug-and-play normality-constraint framework that adapts pretrained time-series foundation models for anomaly detection by constraining representations to a compact normal subspace, thereby amplifying reconstruction/forecasting errors on anomalies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pretrained time-series foundation models learn broad temporal patterns and can reconstruct or forecast both normal and rare anomalous patterns well, which reduces error-based anomaly scores and weakens anomaly detection performance. A method is needed to adapt such powerful but overly general models so that they emphasize normal behavior and highlight deviations without retraining or changing their parameters.

Method: NCL builds on a frozen, pretrained TSFM. It first collects a small set of patch features from normal time series segments and constructs a compact normality subspace. During inference, each patch feature from the TSFM is constrained and steered toward this subspace using contrastive constraints that encourage compact and discriminative manifolds for normal data. Features are calibrated within this normality manifold, aggregated to reinforce normal components, and then fused with the original model output. The final reconstruction/forecasting is thus biased toward normal patterns, increasing the error for truly abnormal observations.

Result: Across multiple TSFM architectures and anomaly detection benchmarks, NCL consistently boosts anomaly detection performance compared with using the raw TSFMs, indicating that the normality-constraint mechanism improves the separability of normal and anomalous data under error-based scoring.

Conclusion: By constraining the representation space of pretrained TSFMs to a compact normality subspace, NCL turns their broad modeling capacity from a liability into an asset for anomaly detection, providing a lightweight, plug-and-play, and general framework that improves anomaly detection performance without modifying pretrained parameters.

Abstract: Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) achieve strong generalization by learning to reconstruct or forecast broad temporal patterns from large-scale time series during pre-training. Yet this strength can become a weakness for anomaly detection: TSFMs may model rare anomalous patterns as effectively as normal ones, allowing anomalies to be accurately reconstructed or forecasted and thus diminishing their reconstruction/forecasting error-based anomaly scores. This paper proposes $\underline{\textbf{N}}$$\textbf{ormality}$ $\underline{\textbf{C}}$$\textbf{onstraint}$ $\underline{\textbf{L}}$$\textbf{earning}$ ($\textbf{NCL}$), a lightweight plug-and-play framework that adapts pre-trained TSFMs for accurate anomaly detection without modifying their pre-trained parameters. Our key insight is to constrain the broad pattern space of TSFMs to the normal structure of a target time series, preventing their broad modeling capability from obscuring abnormal deviations. Specifically, NCL constructs a compact normality subspace from a few normal patch features and adaptively steers each patch feature toward normality within this subspace, guided by contrastive constraints that form compact and discriminative normality manifolds. The calibrated features are aggregated to reinforce normal components and fused with the original TSFM output, amplifying the discrepancy between normal and abnormal observations for the reconstruction/forecasting error-based anomaly scoring. Extensive experiments across diverse TSFM families and benchmarks show that NCL consistently improves anomaly detection performance, providing a generalizable framework for adapting TSFMs to anomaly detection.

</details>


### [357] [AgentPrivArena: Evaluating and Auditing Real-world AI Agent Privacy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06454)
*Shouju Wang,Haopeng Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AgentPrivArena is a framework and benchmark to evaluate privacy risks of LLM agents using real tools and trajectory-level metrics, and AgentPrivAudit is a runtime auditing method that detects privacy violations during multi-step executions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents now autonomously use external tools and services, often handling personal data. Existing privacy benchmarks rely on simulated trajectories and only check final outputs, missing privacy issues that occur during multi-step execution such as unnecessary data access. There is a need for a realistic, tool-integrated, trajectory-aware way to evaluate and monitor privacy risks in agent workflows.

Method: The authors build AgentPrivArena, a reproducible environment that wires LLM agents to real MCP tools and self-hosted services. Within this environment, they define trajectory-level privacy metrics that track what personal or sensitive data the agent accesses at each step and measure unnecessary data exposure, not just what appears in the final response. On top of this, they develop AgentPrivAudit, a runtime auditing mechanism that observes agent-tool interactions as they occur and flags or quantifies privacy violations throughout the trajectory.

Result: Through experiments involving state-of-the-art LLM agents running in AgentPrivArena, the authors find significant privacy risks that prior evaluation setups failed to identify, especially involving superfluous personal data access during multi-step tool use. These results validate that trajectory-level monitoring provides richer and more critical privacy insights than outcome-only measures.

Conclusion: AgentPrivArena offers a more realistic and fine-grained way to evaluate privacy risks in LLM agents by focusing on trajectory-level behavior with real tools. AgentPrivAudit further enables online auditing of privacy violations during execution. Together, they show that trustworthy deployment of LLM agents requires monitoring and controlling not only final outputs but also intermediate steps and data accesses.

Abstract: The rapid advancement of LLM agents has enabled systems to autonomously perform complex tasks through external tools, but their growing access to personal data introduces significant privacy risks. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate LLM agent privacy through simulated trajectories and outcome-based metrics, limiting their ability to capture privacy risks arising during multi-step agent execution. In this work, we introduce AgentPrivArena, a framework for evaluating privacy risks in realistic LLM agent workflows. AgentPrivArena integrates authentic MCP tools and self-hosted services within a reproducible execution environment. We further propose trajectory-level privacy metrics that quantify unnecessary information access beyond final response leakage. Building on this framework, we introduce AgentPrivAudit, a runtime auditing approach for monitoring privacy violations during agent execution. Extensive experiments on state-of-the-art LLM agents reveal substantial privacy risks overlooked by existing evaluation paradigms, highlighting the importance of trajectory-level auditing for trustworthy agent deployment.

</details>


### [358] [GPlaceRL: An Open-Source Graph Reinforcement Learning Framework for Detailed Placement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06489)
*Pavlos Stoikos,Foteini Oikonomou,Christos Poulos,Maria Pantazi-Kypriou,Athanasios Tziouvaras,Christos Anagnostopoulos,Georgios Karakonstantis,George Floros*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GPlaceRL is an open-source graph-based reinforcement learning framework for detailed placement refinement in VLSI, showing significant HPWL improvements with compact GAT-based PPO policies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most learning-based placement methods target higher-level placement stages (floorplanning, macro, or global placement), leaving detailed placement refinement underexplored despite its impact on final layout quality. There is also a lack of standardized, reproducible environments to systematically study RL+GNN methods for detailed placement, including the effects of different graph encoders, policies, rewards, and local actions.

Method: The authors model legalized circuit placements as graphs and build GPlaceRL, a modular RL environment that lets researchers plug in various graph encoders, policy architectures, reward designs, and local placement actions. As a case study, they train proximal policy optimization (PPO) agents using graph attention network (GAT) encoders in a per-design optimization setup, and assess them via greedy evaluation on multiple benchmarks.

Result: On five placement benchmarks, the best learned policies yield half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL) reductions between 3.27% and 32.87% over the initial detailed placements. Empirical analysis shows that more compact GAT encoders and richer, flexible local action spaces tend to perform better for placement optimization.

Conclusion: GPlaceRL enables systematic, reproducible research on RL-based detailed placement refinement by providing a configurable graph-RL environment. The experimental study demonstrates that carefully designed GAT-based PPO policies and local actions can substantially improve detailed placement quality, motivating further exploration using this framework.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising approach for placement optimization, particularly when combined with graph neural networks (GNNs) that capture circuit connectivity. However, most learning-based placement approaches focus on floorplanning, macro placement, or global placement, while detailed placement refinement remains relatively unexplored. In this paper, we present GPlaceRL, an open-source graph reinforcement learning framework for detailed placement refinement. GPlaceRL represents legalized placements as graphs and provides a modular environment for studying graph encoders, policy architectures, reward formulations, and local placement actions. To demonstrate the capabilities of GPlaceRL, we conduct a systematic evaluation of proximal policy optimization (PPO) policies with graph attention network (GAT) encoders in a per-design optimization setting. Across five placement benchmarks, the best greedy evaluation results achieve HPWL improvements ranging from $3.27\%$ to $32.87\%$. The results highlight the importance of compact GAT architectures and flexible local action spaces for placement optimization. Overall, GPlaceRL provides a reproducible and extensible framework for systematic research on RL-based detailed placement refinement.

</details>


### [359] [polyview: A Python package for multi-view machine learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06491)
*Gwendal Debaussart-Joniec,Argyris Kalogeratos*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: polyview is a scikit-learn–compatible Python library for end-to-end multi-view learning workflows, covering embedding, clustering, fusion, augmentation, and incomplete views.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-view learning is increasingly important, but Python lacks a unified, actively maintained framework that supports complete multi-view pipelines with consistent APIs and easy integration with existing tools like scikit-learn.

Method: The authors design and implement polyview, a modular set of core classes and utilities that expose a unified interface for multi-view embedding, clustering, fusion, view augmentation, and handling missing views, with seamless composition of multi-view and single-view stages. They demonstrate its use on five real multi-view datasets and benchmark its canonical correlation–based components against two existing libraries.

Result: polyview successfully supports heterogeneous multi-view workflows within a scikit-learn–style API, handles incomplete views, and in empirical comparisons on five real datasets, its CCA-based components perform competitively with or better than those in two established libraries.

Conclusion: polyview provides a practical, extensible toolkit for implementing, benchmarking, and prototyping multi-view learning methods in Python, and offers a solid foundation for future research and method development in multi-view learning.

Abstract: Multi-view learning jointly exploits multiple complementary representations of the same data and has become increasingly important in machine learning. However, the Python ecosystem lacks actively maintained, unified tooling for end-to-end multi-view workflows. In this paper, we present polyview, a Python package that provides tools for multi-view embedding, clustering, fusion, and view augmentation, as well as for handling incomplete views, all compatible with scikit-learn. The library offers a unified interface for composing heterogeneous multi-view workflows, including seamless transitions between multi-view and single-view stages. It is built around a core set of classes and utilities that enable composition of different methods and straightforward implementation of new ones. We illustrate the package on five real multi-view datasets and compare its components based on canonical correlation analysis with those of two established libraries. polyview aims to be both a practical toolkit for benchmarking and prototyping multi-view methods and a foundation for future research and development in this area.

</details>


### [360] [You Changed Your Mind, The Model Didn't: Demystifying Intent in Multi-Turn Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06496)
*Junle Chen,Wei Chen,Zhengjun Huang,Zhoujin Tian,Yuxuan Liu,Kai Wang,Rui Chen,Xiaofang Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They identify that LLMs often get derailed by previously mentioned but later rejected or superseded user instructions, and introduce both a benchmark (Intent-Eval) to measure this and a training method (Intent-OPSD) to align models with the user's final active intent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To ensure that in multi-turn interactions, LLMs reliably follow the user's final, active intent rather than being confused by previously suggested but rejected or superseded instructions, which currently causes persistent errors.

Method: 1) Construct Intent-Eval, a benchmark with controlled multi-turn scenarios across tools, code, databases, and math where user intent evolves, including rejected proposals and superseded requirements; 2) empirically evaluate existing LLMs on this benchmark to characterize failure modes; 3) propose Intent-OPSD, an on-policy self-distillation framework where a frozen Teacher model, conditioned on the user's final decision, identifies active intent and supervises a Student model trained on full dialogues to follow only active requirements.

Result: Models frequently misinterpret rejected or outdated requirements as still active, leading to significant and sometimes compounding accuracy drops on Intent-Eval. Applying Intent-OPSD improves adherence to the user's active intent and mitigates degradation across turns on the benchmark.

Conclusion: LLMs conflate what has been mentioned with what remains in effect during multi-turn tasks, causing them to follow rejected or outdated instructions. Explicitly modeling and training on active user intent via Intent-Eval and Intent-OPSD substantially improves robustness, underscoring that future conversational systems must track and condition on evolving intent rather than raw dialogue history.

Abstract: When a large language model handles a multi-turn task and a user proposes a change but ultimately rejects it, the model should continue as if nothing changed. We find a surprising failure: merely mentioning a rejected change can derail task execution, even when the user's final intent remains unchanged. To systematically study language model behavior under evolving user intent, we introduce Intent-Eval, a controlled benchmark spanning tool actions, code, databases, and mathematics. Across diverse tasks, models are vulnerable to both rejected proposals and superseded requirements, consistent with mentioned-as-in-effect confusion: conversational content is treated as active requirements even after it has been rejected or replaced. Accuracy degradation can deepen or persist as interaction continues, highlighting the need to distinguish what has been mentioned from what remains in effect. Building on this insight, we propose Intent-OPSD, a decision-conditioned on-policy self-distillation framework with Teacher and Student initialized from the same model. The frozen Teacher provides active-intent supervision from the complete task matching the user's decision, training the Student on the full dialogue to follow active requirements reflecting user intent.

</details>


### [361] [ANT: A Multi-Granularity Network Traffic Dataset and Benchmark for Agents Behavior Auditing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06514)
*Fan Li,Xiangyu Gao,Zixuan Liu,Tong Li,Chuanpu Fu,Ziqiang Wang,Ke Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ANT is a labeled network-traffic dataset for LLM agents that enables auditing and analysis of agent behavior, risk, and tasks without inspecting private content.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents are increasingly used inside organizations, and security teams need ways to monitor and audit these agents’ behavior for risk and misuse. Direct inspection of prompts, outputs, or internal states may violate privacy or data-protection constraints, so there is interest in using network traffic as an indirect, privacy-preserving signal. However, it is unclear how much information about agent tasks, risk levels, and operational stages can be inferred from traffic alone, and existing datasets lack the detailed annotations (task, scenario, behavior stages) necessary to rigorously evaluate this. The paper aims to fill this gap so that more accurate and explainable agent auditing and forensic tools can be built.

Method: The authors construct ANT (Agent Network Traffic), a dataset where LLM agent executions are recorded together with detailed annotations of agent behavior. They define multiple granularities: risk (e.g., benign vs. risky workflows), scenario type, and fine-grained behavior primitives grouped into macro categories. They collect 3,114 execution episodes spanning 20 tasks under five scenarios, and log 276,417 bidirectional flows. These flows are segmented into 40,049 behavior primitive segments mapped to 47 macro groups. On top of this dataset, they design a benchmark suite covering three tasks: risk identification, scenario recognition, and behavior primitive classification from network traffic. They implement and evaluate 13 representative existing traffic analysis models/baselines on these tasks, comparing their performance and analyzing where they succeed or fail.

Result: The evaluated traffic analysis methods are able to recover some meaningful signals about LLM agent behavior from network traces, showing that traffic-based auditing is feasible to a degree. However, performance is uneven: models have difficulty detecting risk when malicious or risky workflows produce traffic patterns similar to benign ones; they also struggle to correctly classify scenarios that share overlapping or weakly distinguishable traffic signatures. For behavior primitives, classification accuracy is higher for macro groups that appear more frequently in the dataset and for those associated with distinctive traffic patterns, but performance drops significantly for rare primitives and for groups that are semantically or behaviorally similar in terms of network usage.

Conclusion: ANT offers the first large-scale, richly annotated network traffic dataset specifically targeting LLM agent behavior, enabling systematic study of what can be inferred about agent tasks, risk, and fine-grained operations purely from network traces. The benchmark experiments demonstrate both the promise and the current limitations of traffic-based auditing: existing methods can capture some behavioral cues but are unreliable for nuanced risk detection and for distinguishing similar scenarios or rare behaviors. By releasing ANT and baseline results, the authors provide a standardized foundation for developing and comparing more advanced techniques for precise, privacy-preserving auditing and forensic analysis of LLM agents within organizational networks.

Abstract: The growing adoption of large language model (LLM) agents creates a need for network administrators and security teams to audit agent behavior within organizational networks without inspecting private user content. Network traffic offers an observable source of evidence, but how much it reveals about agent tasks and operations remains unclear. Existing traffic datasets lack the joint task and stage annotations needed to evaluate this question. We introduce ANT (Agent Network Traffic), a dataset providing agent behavior information at risk, scenario, and behavior primitive granularities alongside network traffic. ANT contains 3,114 execution episodes across 20 tasks and five scenarios, comprising 276,417 bidirectional flows and 40,049 behavior primitive segments organized into 47 macro groups. We establish a benchmark for agent risk identification, scenario recognition, and behavior primitive classification using 13 representative traffic analysis baselines. The results show that existing methods recover useful but uneven behavioral signals. They struggle to identify risk when malicious workflows resemble benign tasks and to distinguish scenarios with similar traffic patterns. Primitive classification is more reliable for frequent macro groups and those with distinctive traffic patterns than for rare or semantically similar groups. ANT provides a common basis for developing more precise auditing and forensic analysis of agent behavior from network traffic. Our data and code are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ant-main-suite-7BC0/.

</details>


### [362] [Proof-Grounded Patient-Specific Clinical Explanations from Knowledge-Graph Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06549)
*Surajit Das*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They built and audited an explanation layer on top of a clinical knowledge-graph reasoning system, showing it can produce fully traceable, provenance-linked, and internally consistent decision-support outputs, but they did not test whether its clinical conclusions are correct or useful.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical decision-support systems often act like black boxes, offering recommendations without a clear, auditable path from patient data through knowledge to conclusions. This lack of transparency and provenance makes it hard to trust, validate, or regulate such systems. The authors aim to create an explanation engine that turns internal reasoning states of a clinical knowledge-graph system into explicit, checkable structures that can be systematically audited for correctness of implementation and traceability, independent of model training or clinical accuracy.

Method: They designed the CKG Clinical Explanation Engine as a downstream layer on top of a frozen, training-free clinical knowledge-graph reasoner. The engine transforms inference states and disease knowledge into structured typed facts, explicit rule-application traces, provenance-linked conclusions, and policy-licensed recommendations. The architecture explicitly separates three dimensions: (1) whether a measurement is available, (2) how completely it is represented, and (3) whether disease-specific logic is activated, so that zero-activation evidence is not conflated with missing data and partial representations are distinguished from unobserved evidence. Language generation, when used, is restricted to content that is symbolically licensed by the underlying reasoning. They then evaluated implementation and structural properties using five workbooks covering 6,720 patients and 20,160 patient-disease traces, examining IG-range validity, provenance, numerical cross-sheet consistency, and trace completeness across over a million feature-evidence rows. They also ran a separate seeded end-to-end audit on 25 patients with pre-specified checks for trace correctness, licensing, provenance, and state consistency.

Result: In the large workbook corpus, they achieved 100% validity of inference-generation ranges and 100% correctness of knowledge provenance. Numerical consistency across sheets was perfect (120,960/120,960 values matched), and all logical and report trace exports were complete (20,160/20,160 traces). Availability representation consistency was 99.7028% (1,018,404/1,021,440), with all 3,036 inconsistencies confined to three systematic feature-cohort pattern issues rather than random bugs. The data included 86,783 instances where evidence was observed but led to zero activation and 139,949 instances of observed but only partially represented evidence, illustrating the system’s nuanced handling of availability and representation. The 25-patient end-to-end audit ran without execution failures and met all pre-defined criteria for trace completeness, licensing constraints, provenance tracking, and internal state consistency.

Conclusion: The CKG Clinical Explanation Engine successfully provides structurally transparent, provenance-rich, and internally consistent explanations for a clinical knowledge-graph decision-support system. Their audits demonstrate that the engine’s reasoning traces, numerical handling, and representation of evidence can be systematically checked and validated at scale, establishing strong implementation and structural auditability. However, these findings explicitly do not address whether the underlying clinical reasoning or recommendations are medically correct or beneficial in practice; the work lays an infrastructure for trustworthy auditing rather than proving clinical effectiveness.

Abstract: Clinical decision-support outputs can lack an au- ditable link between patient observations, encoded knowledge, conclusions, and recommendations. We present the CKG Clinical Explanation Engine, a downstream layer for a frozen, training-free clinical knowledge-graph reasoner that converts patient inference states and disease knowledge into typed facts, explicit rule-application traces, provenance-linked conclusions, and policy-licensed recommendations. The design separates measurement availability, representation completeness, and disease-specific activation; consequently, observed zero-activation evience is not treated as missing and partial representation is distinct from unobserved evidence. Optional language generation is restricted to symbolically licensed content. Across five usable workbooks (6,720 patients; 20,160 patient-disease traces; 1,021,440 feature-evidence rows), IG-range validity and knowledge provenance were 100%, numerical cross-sheet fidelity was 100% (120,960/120,960), and exported logical/report trace completeness was 100% (20,160/20,160). Availability representation consistency was 99.7028% (1,018,404/1,021,440); all 3,036 disagreements were confined to three systematic feature-cohort patterns. The corpus contained 86,783 observed zero-activation and 139,949 observed partially represented instances. A separate seeded 25-patient end-to-end audit completed without execution failure and passed all pre-specified trace, licensing, provenance, and state-consistency checks. These results establish structural and implementation auditability, not clinical correctness or utility.

</details>


### [363] [Signature-Based Feature Learning for Human Activity Recognition: A Reproducible Machine Learning Study of Representation, Depth, and Model Choice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06553)
*Kamal Jarrar,Jacky Cresson,Christian Paroissin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper assesses whether mathematically grounded signature transforms improve human activity recognition compared to raw sensor signals, under a strict, leakage-aware evaluation on UCI HAR.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In HAR, performance depends heavily on how raw sensor time-series are represented, yet deep and handcrafted approaches often mix representation design with modeling choices, making it hard to isolate the value of the representation itself. Signature transforms, rooted in rough path theory, can encode temporal order and interactions across channels, but their practical benefit for HAR—and how it depends on implementation details like truncation depth and embedding—has not been systematically and reproducibly evaluated.

Method: Using the UCI HAR dataset, the authors build a fully reproducible, leakage-aware pipeline that preserves the original train–test split and employs subject-disjoint validation. They compare three input representations: (1) raw flattened signals, (2) time-augmented paths, and (3) lead–lag transformed paths. For the latter two, they compute path signature features at multiple truncation depths. All representations are evaluated with two classifiers—MLP and Random Forest—under identical preprocessing and validation procedures. They also faithfully reproduce a prior K-means-based feature reduction approach for baseline comparison.

Result: Signature-based representations substantially improve performance when used with Random Forest classifiers. The best setup—time-augmented six-channel signatures truncated at depth 6 with an entropy-based Random Forest—achieves 0.858 accuracy and 0.859 macro F1, outperforming the strongest raw-signal baseline accuracy of 0.816. Lead–lag embeddings perform competitively at moderate signature depths but do not surpass the best time-augmented configuration. MLP models, regardless of representation, fail to exceed the raw baseline performance.

Conclusion: Signature transforms can provide a beneficial representation for HAR, but their effectiveness is not universal; it critically depends on how the path is embedded (time-augmented vs. lead–lag), the truncation depth, and especially the downstream classifier. When well aligned with a suitable model such as Random Forest, signature-based feature learning yields measurable gains over raw-signal baselines in a rigorously controlled, reproducible setting.

Abstract: Human activity recognition (HAR) relies on transforming sensor signals into informative representations for classification. Although deep learning and handcrafted features are widely used, the role of representation itself is often not systematically isolated. Signature transforms provide a mathematically grounded way to encode temporal order and cross-channel interactions, but their value for HAR under a fully reproducible and leakage-aware framework remains unclear. To evaluate whether signature-based feature learning improves HAR performance compared with raw-signal baselines, and to assess the effects of embedding strategy, truncation depth, model choice, and sensor configuration. Experiments were conducted on the UCI HAR dataset using a fully reproducible pipeline with the original train--test split preserved and subject-disjoint validation to prevent leakage. Three representations were compared: raw flattened signals, time-augmented paths, and lead--lag transformed paths. Signature features were computed at multiple truncation depths and evaluated using multilayer perceptron (MLP) and Random Forest (RF) classifiers under identical preprocessing and validation procedures. A prior K-means-based feature reduction study was also reproduced for comparison. Signature-based representations improved performance when paired with RF models, the best configuration was time-augmented six-channel signatures at depth 6 using entropy-based RF achieving 0.858 accuracy and 0.859 macro F1, outperforming the strongest raw baseline (0.816 accuracy). Lead--lag representations were competitive at moderate depths but did not surpass the best time-augmented models. MLP models did not exceed raw baselines. Signature-based feature learning can improve HAR, but its benefit depends on alignment between representation design and classifier choice.

</details>


### [364] [HERA: Harness-Environment Co-Evolution for Reliable Agentic Abstention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06563)
*Han Luo,Bingbing Wen,Guang Yang,Zora Zhiruo Wang,Pan Lu,Lucy Lu Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents HERA, a co-evolution framework that jointly adapts LLM agent harnesses and environments to improve when agents correctly abstain on infeasible tasks while still solving feasible ones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents using tools in complex environments often attempt to solve tasks that are actually infeasible, instead of recognizing impossibility and abstaining. Existing abstention methods are usually tuned to a fixed task set and do not generalize to unseen failure modes, leaving a reliability gap for real-world deployment. The paper aims to systematically generate challenging abstention scenarios and adapt agent harnesses that generalize better across models and environments.

Method: The authors propose HERA, which has two main components: (i) an automatic pipeline that takes solvable tasks and applies controlled mutations to the environment or task configuration to create closely-matched pairs of feasible and infeasible tasks that are verifiable; and (ii) a co-evolution procedure where failures of the current agent harness on these tasks drive iterative adaptation of the harness and guide the generation of new environments and tasks that target prior weaknesses. This loop jointly evolves both the evaluation suite and the agent harness for improved abstention behavior.

Result: On held-out tasks, an agent harness evolved via HERA improves abstention accuracy from 61.7% to 83.3% and feasible-task completion from 68.3% to 76.7%, outperforming baseline methods on both metrics. Furthermore, the best-evolved harness transfers to 19 additional LLMs, improving abstention accuracy by an average of 15.3 percentage points without any model-specific tuning and allowing smaller models to reach the performance of stronger models at roughly 85% lower cost.

Conclusion: HERA’s harness-environment co-evolution approach yields more reliable abstention behavior in LLM agents, simultaneously improving recognition of infeasible tasks and success on feasible ones. Its learned harness generalizes across many different LLMs and reduces the need for model-specific optimization, enabling cost-effective deployment of smaller models with abstention performance comparable to larger models.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly capable of acting in complex tool-use environments, yet they often fail to recognize when tasks are infeasible and no valid solution exists. Recent work has formalized this reliability gap as the problem of agentic abstention, and existing approaches typically optimize a model or agent harness against a fixed set of tasks, leading to limited generalization to unseen failure modes. We introduce HERA, a framework for harness-environment co-evolution for agentic abstention. HERA consists of (i) a pipeline to automatically construct verifiable pairs of feasible and infeasible tasks by applying controlled environment mutations that transform solvable tasks into cases requiring abstention, and (ii) a co-evolution procedure in which performance failures on previous tasks are used to drive harness adaptation and generate new execution environments and tasks geared towards previous weaknesses. On held-out evaluation tasks, an evolved harness from HERA improves abstention accuracy from 61.7% to 83.3% while improving feasible-task completion from 68.3% to 76.7%, achieving the highest abstention and feasible-task completion among the compared methods. The resulting best harness transfers across 19 other LLMs, improving abstention accuracy by 15.3 percentage points on average without any model-specific optimization, and enabling smaller models to match the performance of more powerful models at an estimated 85% lower cost.

</details>


### [365] [DGA-Muon: Decoupled Geometry-Aligned Adaptive Scaling for Muon](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06578)
*Wenpeng Zhang,Runsheng Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They analyze why the NorMuon optimizer appears adaptive, show that its adaptivity mostly comes from orthogonalization geometry rather than meaningful gradient information, prove that better orthogonalization actually reduces its adaptivity, and then design a new optimizer, DGA-Muon, that decouples scaling from orthogonalization and aligns adaptivity with matrix shape, achieving better theory and practice.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: NorMuon performs well in practice but the source and nature of its adaptive behavior are unclear. The authors want to understand whether its adaptivity is truly optimization-relevant or merely an artifact of the orthogonalization step. They also aim to identify limitations in NorMuon’s design and to create a principled, better-performing adaptive variant of Muon with clear theoretical grounding.

Method: They perform a theoretical analysis of NorMuon’s scaling factors under exact and approximate orthogonalization, characterizing when they collapse to a global scalar and how their variation is induced by row-energy distribution and orthogonality residuals. They then study the geometric alignment between NorMuon’s row-wise scaling and the orthogonal structure of matrices of different shapes. Based on this, they distill design principles for a new optimizer and construct DGA-Muon with decoupled, geometry-aligned adaptive scaling, plus additional features like sum-based second-moment estimation, bias correction, and adaptive clipping. They further provide convergence guarantees and empirical experiments comparing NorMuon and DGA-Muon.

Result: They show that for square and wide matrices with exact orthogonalization, NorMuon’s row-wise scaling degenerates to a single global scalar, and for tall matrices, its variation stems from post-orthogonalization row-energy non-uniformity rather than gradient information. With approximate orthogonalization, residuals add artificial variation, leading to the Orthogonalization–Adaptivity Paradox: improving orthogonality reduces adaptivity. Their analysis reveals a geometric mismatch between NorMuon’s row-wise scaling and tall matrices’ one-sided orthogonal structure. DGA-Muon, built to follow their proposed principles, enjoys convergence guarantees and empirically outperforms NorMuon while matching the theoretical characterization of NorMuon’s scaling degeneration.

Conclusion: NorMuon’s apparent adaptivity is largely an artifact of orthogonalization geometry, and tighter orthogonalization actually weakens this adaptivity, exposing design flaws such as shape-misaligned row-wise scaling. By decoupling adaptive scaling from orthogonalization and aligning it with the polar factor’s shape-dependent orthogonal structure, the proposed DGA-Muon optimizer overcomes these issues, is theoretically grounded with convergence guarantees, and achieves superior empirical performance compared to NorMuon.

Abstract: While NorMuon has achieved strong empirical performance in large-scale pretraining by enhancing Muon with row-wise adaptive scaling, its underlying adaptive mechanism remains poorly understood. In this work, we provide the first systematic analysis of NorMuon's adaptivity, revealing that it originates primarily from orthogonalization-induced geometry rather than genuine optimization-relevant information. Under exact orthogonalization, the adaptive scaling factors degenerate into a single global scalar for square and wide matrices, while for tall matrices their variation arises from the non-uniform distribution of row energy after orthogonalization. Under approximate orthogonalization, the orthogonality residual introduces additional variation into the scaling factors, leading to the \textit{Orthogonalization--Adaptivity Paradox}: more accurate orthogonalization weakens adaptivity. We further show that NorMuon's rigid row-wise scaling is geometrically misaligned with the one-sided orthogonal structure of tall matrices. Based on the analysis of these limitations, we propose two core design principles that a desirable adaptive mechanism for Muon should satisfy. First, adaptive scaling should be decoupled from orthogonalization, with the scaling factors computed directly from raw gradients. Second, adaptive scaling should be aligned with the shape-dependent orthogonal structure of the polar factor, using row-wise scaling for wide matrices and column-wise scaling for tall matrices. By incorporating several other design considerations, including sum-based second-moment estimates, bias correction, and adaptive clipping of scaling factors, we obtain the Decoupled Geometry-Aligned Muon (DGA-Muon) optimizer. We establish convergence guarantees for DGA-Muon and empirically validate both our theoretical characterization of NorMuon's scaling degeneration and the superiority of DGA-Muon over NorMuon.

</details>


### [366] [The Review Lottery: Calibrating an Observational Estimator of Peer-Review Noise (ICLR 2017-2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06591)
*Feilian Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper estimates how often conference accept/reject decisions would change under a different set of reviewers, using statistical modeling of large-scale review data instead of running duplicate program committees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Directly measuring the randomness in conference decisions by running a second, independent program committee is the gold standard but is extremely costly and has been done only twice. The authors want a general, cheaper way to quantify how much decisions depend on which reviewers happen to evaluate a paper, and to study how this variability has changed over time and across reviewing setups.

Method: They build an observational estimator based only on existing review scores. First, they use a Bayesian ordered-probit model to decompose each numeric review score into an underlying latent paper quality component and a reviewer-noise component. Then, they fit a logistic model that maps these latent quantities to accept/reject decisions. Using posterior sampling, they simulate pairs of independent program committees of varying sizes (k=2,3,4 reviewers per paper) to estimate how often the two committees would disagree. They calibrate the estimator externally using NeurIPS 2021’s real duplicate-committee experiment and internally using ICLR papers with 4+ reviews by splitting reviewers into two groups and comparing real vs. simulated disagreements. They also perform longitudinal analyses to see how reviewer noise changes over time, examine the impact of different scoring scales, and run a breakpoint test around 2023 to explore possible effects of LLMs on review variance.

Result: Across nine years of ICLR data (2017–2025), simulated disagreement rates between two independent committees are about 23–30% when each committee has 2 reviewers per paper and 18–24% when each has 4; among accepted papers, roughly 30–50% would be rejected by the other committee. External calibration against the NeurIPS 2021 duplicate-committee experiment shows very close agreement: the estimated disagreement rate at k=3 is 23.3% vs. the observed 23.0%, with small errors in precision of acceptance and inter-committee correlations. Internal calibration using 2+2 splits on papers with at least 4 reviews also matches simulation within 1 percentage point for several years. Over time, there is no clear trend in reviewer noise from 2017–2025. The high flip rates in 2020 are largely explained by a coarse four-point score scale that created many ties and zero within-paper variance, while 2021’s high flip rates stem from particularly noisy reviews combined with many papers near the acceptance threshold. A breakpoint test in 2023 on within-paper variance finds no detectable change, but the test has very low power and key post-2022 data modalities are missing, so no conclusions about LLM effects are drawn.

Conclusion: A large fraction of conference acceptance decisions are unstable to the particular reviewers assigned: even with typical committee sizes, around one-fifth to one-quarter of decisions, and up to half of accepted papers, could flip under a different but equally qualified committee. The proposed observational estimator, validated against real duplicate-committee experiments and internal splits, provides a practical way to quantify this randomness using only score data. Reviewer noise has not clearly improved or worsened over time at ICLR, but design choices like coarse rating scales and thresholds crowded with marginal acceptances can substantially increase decision instability. Current data do not allow reliable inferences about the impact of LLMs on reviewing behavior.

Abstract: How much of a conference accept/reject decision would change if the same paper were reviewed by a different set of reviewers? Running a second independent program committee is the gold standard for answering this, but it is prohibitively expensive: done only twice (NeurIPS 2014 and 2021). We build an observational estimator of this quantity from public review data alone, calibrate it twice, and apply it to nine years of ICLR (2017-2025; 36,113 papers, 134,912 reviews). The estimator decomposes scores with a Bayesian ordered-probit model into paper quality and reviewer noise, maps scores to decisions with a logistic model, and simulates two independent committees (posterior draws B=1,000; committee sizes k=2,3,4). Estimated disagreement rates are 23-30% at k=2 and 18-24% at k=4; 30-50% of accepted papers would be rejected. External calibration: at the NeurIPS 2021 reviewer-count caliber (k=3), the simulated 2021 disagreement rate is 23.3% [21.7%, 25.0%] vs. reported 23.0% (bias +0.3pp); accept precision and committee correlation agree within 5pp and 0.04. Internal calibration: on 18,740 papers with 4+ reviews, random model-free 2+2 reviewer splits agree with the k=2 simulation within 1pp in 2018 and 2021-2025. Longitudinally, we find no robust time trend in reviewer noise over 2017-2025. The high accepted-paper flip rates of 2020 and 2021 have distinct mechanisms: the 2020 four-point scale compressed scores (23.7% of papers had zero within-paper variance), and a counterfactual shows coarsening the scale raises disagreement by about 7pp; 2021 instead combined the lowest signal-to-noise ratio in the sample with the most threshold-crowded acceptances. For the LLM era, a 2023 breakpoint test on within-paper score variance finds no break, but the design has almost no power, and no post-2022 review text or confidence data exist, so no LLM attribution is attempted.

</details>


### [367] [Can Agent Harnesses and Inference Engines Hear Each Other? The HEAR Protocol for Agentic LLM Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06597)
*Jiaqi Zhao,Haodong Chen,Jitai Hao,Wei Zhao,Jinghao Pang,Qiang Huang,Jun Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes HEAR, a standardized bidirectional protocol between an LLM agent harness and the inference engine to coordinate complex, multi-turn, tool-using LLM workflows more efficiently.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents now run complex workflows with multi-turn reasoning, tools, and multiple parallel agents. Efficient serving requires coordinated decisions between (1) the harness, which knows the workflow structure, context lifecycles, and goals, and (2) the inference engine, which sees queues, KV-cache states, and hardware/resource conditions. Existing interfaces do not expose or connect these complementary views in a principled way, leading to suboptimal, workflow-agnostic execution under realistic constraints like memory pressure and concurrency.

Method: The authors design HEAR, a bidirectional Harness–Engine Pairing protocol. HEAR specifies how the harness can express workflow intent, dependencies, and execution requirements to the engine, and how the engine reports back runtime state, capabilities, and outcomes. The protocol cleanly separates semantics (what is communicated) from optimization policies (how decisions are made), enabling different coordination strategies without changing workflows or model behavior. They instantiate HEAR in two concrete settings: (1) online, cache-aware runtime coordination that exploits KV-cache information and (2) workload-aware execution-mode selection tailored to different agent roles. They then integrate HEAR into an LLM serving system called Mooncake and evaluate on several multi-agent, conversational, and research-agent benchmarks under memory-constrained, concurrent serving conditions.

Result: Using HEAR within the Mooncake serving system, the authors report substantial performance gains on four benchmarks. Under constrained, concurrent serving, HEAR yields a 1.61× batch throughput speedup and a 2.23× reduction in median time-to-first-token on SCBench. On BrowseComp-Plus and DeepResearchBench, using workload-specific configurations enabled by HEAR gives 1.23× and 2.45× end-to-end speedups, respectively, with no observed drop in task quality.

Conclusion: HEAR provides a reusable, standardized coordination substrate that bridges the gap between workflow-aware agent harnesses and resource-aware inference engines. By enabling the harness to communicate intent and requirements and the engine to expose live state and capabilities, HEAR allows more efficient, cache- and workload-aware scheduling and execution for agentic LLM serving. The demonstrated speedups across multiple benchmarks and load regimes suggest that explicitly modeling this harness–engine relationship is key to scalable, efficient deployment of complex LLM agents without sacrificing output quality.

Abstract: LLM agents increasingly execute complex workflows involving multi-turn reasoning, tool use, and parallel agents. Efficient serving requires decisions that span two layers with complementary information: the agent harness understands workflow dependencies, context lifecycles, and execution objectives, whereas the inference engine observes request queues, KV-cache state, resource pressure, and execution capabilities. Existing interfaces do not systematically connect these views, limiting workflow-aware execution.
  HEAR, a bidirectional Harness--Engine Pairing protocol for agentic LLM serving. HEAR standardizes how the harness communicates workflow intent and execution requirements and how the engine returns runtime state, capabilities, and outcomes. By separating protocol semantics from optimization policies, HEAR supports diverse coordination strategies without changing workflow or model semantics. We instantiate HEAR for online cache-aware runtime coordination and workload-aware execution-mode selection for agent roles.
  Across four conversational and research-agent benchmarks under memory-constrained, concurrent serving, HEAR achieves a $1.61\times$ batch speedup and reduces median time-to-first-token by $2.23\times$ on SCBench. Mooncake shows that workflow intent and live engine state provide complementary benefits across load regimes. On BrowseComp-Plus and DeepResearchBench, workload-specific configurations yield $1.23\times$ and $2.45\times$ end-to-end speedups, respectively, without observed task-quality degradation. These results establish HEAR as a reusable coordination substrate for efficient agentic LLM serving.

</details>


### [368] [FREA: A Multi-Source Expert Benchmark for Reaction Feasibility Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06614)
*Botao Yu,Bo Zhou,Daniel Adu-Ampratwum,Frazier N. Baker,Ziru Chen,Reza Averly,Ye Liu,Wenhao Gao,Xia Ning,Huan Sun*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces FREA, a benchmark of expert-labeled reaction feasibility for diverse types of reaction candidates, and uses it to systematically evaluate and train feasibility verifiers, revealing that current verifiers behave inconsistently across candidate sources and that naive use of generated negatives has mixed benefits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative models and AI agents can propose enormous numbers of synthetic reactions, far more than human chemists can manually check. Feasibility verifiers are therefore critical gatekeepers, but it is unclear whether their decisions align with expert chemists across different kinds of proposed reactions, especially for both realistic proposals and systematically generated negative examples. There is a need for a standardized, expert-annotated benchmark and for understanding how negative supervision affects verifier performance and generalization to real model proposals.

Method: The authors build FREA, a benchmark of 751 chemical reactions that are labeled as feasible or infeasible by expert chemists under a clearly stated feasibility criterion. The reactions come from multiple sources: retrosynthesis model proposals, zero-yield reactions from experimental records, LLM-edited reactions, and several automated negative reaction generation methods. They then evaluate different feasibility verifiers, including forward reaction prediction models and LLM-based verifiers prompted only with the feasibility criterion, across these sources and in more detailed diagnostic tasks such as distinguishing infeasible alternative disconnections from feasible generated candidates. Additionally, they construct and release a large corpus of over 14 million recorded reactions and generated negative candidates, and run controlled training experiments where forward models are retrained with different mixtures and types of generated negative examples to study their impact on AUROC across reaction sources and on proposal screening behavior.

Result: No single verifier dominates across all sources of reaction candidates. LLM verifiers prompted only with the feasibility criterion can match or rival specialized verification models overall. Forward prediction models perform particularly well on screening retrosynthesis model proposals but perform poorly on other sources, such as feasible edits to recorded reactions, which they often reject at practical operating thresholds. In detailed analyses, both forward models perform below random chance at discriminating infeasible alternate disconnections from feasible generated reactions, indicating systematic weaknesses. Adding generated negative examples to forward-model training increases mean AUROC across candidate sources, but these improvements do not translate to better performance on actual retrosynthesis proposals. Moreover, certain negative generation strategies that yield the largest AUROC gains on generated candidates simultaneously degrade proposal-screening quality, showing a trade-off and poor transfer.

Conclusion: The study shows that current reaction feasibility verifiers are fragile and source-dependent: strong aggregate metrics can mask serious failures on specific, realistic kinds of candidates. LLMs can already be competitive with dedicated verification models when given clear criteria, but forward models in particular can mis-handle subtle distinctions such as alternative disconnections. Simply adding large numbers of generated negative reactions during training is not a universal fix; it can improve benchmarks involving similar negatives yet fail to help, or even harm, performance on retrosynthesis proposals. These results highlight the importance of evaluating verifiers on expert-labeled benchmarks drawn from diverse candidate sources and of carefully designing negative data so that improvements transfer to real model-generated proposals rather than overfitting to artificial negatives.

Abstract: As generative models and AI agents propose chemical reactions at a scale beyond expert review, feasibility verifiers decide which proposals enter synthesis planning. But do their decisions agree with chemists across different kinds of candidates? We introduce FREA, a benchmark of 751 reactions labeled by expert chemists under an explicit feasibility criterion, drawn from retrosynthesis model proposals, zero-yield experimental records, edits by large language models (LLMs), and five negative candidate generation methods. Our evaluation finds that no verifier leads across all sources: LLMs given only the criterion are competitive with dedicated verifiers, while forward models perform best on retrosynthesis proposals but reject most feasible edits of recorded reactions at the evaluated operating points. Looking beyond aggregate scores, both forward models perform below chance when separating infeasible alternative disconnections from feasible generated candidates. To study whether negative supervision addresses these weaknesses, we also release a corpus of over 14 million recorded reactions and generated negative candidates. In matched training comparisons, adding a mixture of generated negatives to forward training raises mean AUROC across sources, but these gains do not extend to retrosynthesis proposals. Varying the generation method further shows that the largest gain on generated candidates coincides with worse proposal screening. These findings motivate evaluating verifiers against experts across sources and designing negatives for transfer to model proposals.

</details>


### [369] [Collective intelligence through aggregation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06652)
*Franz Dietrich,Christian List*

Main category: cs.AI
