TL;DR: The paper studies how groups can intelligently aggregate individual judgments on interconnected, possibly multi-valued issues, and proves results about consistency, strategy-proofness, and truth-tracking of different aggregation methods, highlighting the median rule as comparatively robust.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Groups such as committees or expert panels must often make collective judgments about complex, interconnected issues that go beyond yes/no questions. Naively aggregating individual opinions (e.g., by averaging) can lead to inconsistencies, vulnerability to strategic manipulation, and poor accuracy in tracking the truth. There is a need for a systematic, formal analysis of what aggregation procedures can deliver collectively intelligent outcomes under these constraints.

Method: The authors use formal judgment-aggregation theory and social-choice-theoretic tools to analyze aggregation rules for multi-valued and interdependent issues. They define properties such as collective consistency, non-manipulability (strategy-proofness), and truth-tracking, and then derive impossibility and possibility theorems characterizing when these properties can be jointly satisfied. They pay particular attention to rules based on averaging or taking medians of individual judgments.

Result: They show that many seemingly reasonable aggregation methods can generate inconsistent collective judgments, can be strategically manipulated, or fail to track the true state of the world. New impossibility theorems demonstrate that some desirable combinations of properties cannot be achieved simultaneously, while possibility theorems identify restricted conditions or specific rules that can satisfy them. Among practical rules, the median-based aggregation method emerges as relatively strong, achieving a good compromise between consistency, resistance to manipulation, and truth-tracking performance, though it is not perfect.

Conclusion: No aggregation rule universally guarantees consistency, strategy-proofness, and optimal truth-tracking for complex, interconnected judgment problems; trade-offs are unavoidable. However, by clarifying these trade-offs and formally characterizing the performance of different rules, the paper shows how groups can approach collective intelligence more systematically. The median rule stands out as a comparatively robust compromise, and the framework is also relevant for designing decision rules for non-human systems such as algorithmic ensembles or multi-agent AI systems.

Abstract: Suppose a committee, expert panel, or other group is making judgments on some issues, where these may be not just yes/no-questions, such as whether a defendant is guilty, but also variables with many possible values, such as macroeconomic or meteorological variables or travel directions. Furthermore, there may be interconnections between different issues, as in the case of economic or climate variables. How can the group arrive at "intelligent" collective judgments, based on the group members' individual judgments? We investigate three challenges raised by this judgment-aggregation problem. First, reasonable methods of aggregation (such as defining the collective judgment for each issue as the average or median judgment) can produce inconsistent collective judgments. Secondly, many methods of aggregation are manipulable by strategic voting. Finally, not all methods of aggregation are conducive to tracking the truth on the issues in question. We prove new impossibility or possibility theorems on all three challenges, identifying what it takes to produce collective judgments in a consistent, non-manipulable, and truth-tracking manner and thereby to achieve collective intelligence through aggregation. Overall, the median method, though imperfect, performs reasonably well. We also note the relevance of our analysis for non-human group decisions.

</details>


### [370] [Conditional Rank Allocation for Taxonomy-Aware Medical Language Model Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06765)
*Guangyuan Dong,Ziwei Hong,Xuehao Zhou,Zidong Yu,Bingchen Liu,Kehan Liu,Chuang Liu,Rong Fu,Yuchao Hou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces ARBOR, a parameter-efficient, structured conditional adaptation method for medical question answering that selects rank-one components from a shared low-rank basis per question, outperforming standard LoRA and MoELoRA across multiple medical QA benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Medical question answering covers diverse specialties and clinical operations, so a single, fixed adaptation (like a standard LoRA update) may not capture the heterogeneity of tasks. The authors want a more flexible, conditional adaptation mechanism that can route parameter updates based on question content and clinical tags, improving performance without large parameter overhead. They also note that fixed low-rank updates hit an approximation floor when subtasks differ in structure, motivating conditional selection of low-rank components.

Method: The authors propose ARBOR, a parameter-efficient adaptation method that uses a shared low-rank basis of rank-one components. For each question, ARBOR selects and combines a subset of these components via an additive gating mechanism that takes as input the question representation, specialty tags, operation tags, and their interactions. A learned scalar coefficient scales the adapter residual added to the base model. They present an illustrative theoretical separation on synthetic orthogonal, equiprobable subtasks showing that conditional selection of rank-one components can avoid the approximation floor faced by a fixed low-rank update with the same active rank. They implement ARBOR on the Qwen3-8B model and train it across different numbers of medical specialties. They also conduct ablations with tag perturbations and atom masking, and analyze atom clustering, calibration, transfer behavior, and computational costs.

Result: On the CMB, CMExam, MedQA, and MedMCQA medical QA benchmarks with Qwen3-8B, ARBOR achieves a five-seed mean accuracy of 69.69%, outperforming standard LoRA with rank 16 and MoELoRA by 1.26 and 1.30 percentage points, respectively. The performance advantage over LoRA r16 increases from 0.08 to 1.94 percentage points as the number of training specialties grows from one to seven, indicating benefits in more heterogeneous settings. Tag perturbation and atom masking experiments show that routing via clinical tags is useful, and learned atom clusters correlate well with specialty labels, with an adjusted Rand index of 0.62. They also provide measurements of calibration, transfer, and computational cost, showing ARBOR is competitive and efficient, though specific numeric details are not in the abstract.

Conclusion: ARBOR demonstrates that structured conditional adaptation—using question- and tag-dependent selection of low-rank components—can improve performance for medical QA over standard low-rank and mixture-of-experts LoRA baselines, especially as the diversity of specialties increases. The method is parameter-efficient, benefits from explicit clinical routing signals, and yields interpretable structure in the learned atoms that aligns with medical specialties. However, the work remains at the level of benchmark evaluation; issues of clinical safety and real-world deployment are not addressed and are left for future study.

Abstract: Medical question answering spans specialties and clinical operations that may benefit from different adaptation directions. We propose ARBOR, a parameter-efficient method that selects rank-one components from a shared low-rank basis for each question. An additive gate combines question representations, specialty tags, operation tags, and their interaction; a learned coefficient scales the adapter residual. An illustrative separation under orthogonal, equiprobable subtasks shows how conditional selection can avoid an approximation floor faced by a fixed update with the same active rank. This result motivates the design without asserting a corresponding bound for medical corpora. On Qwen3-8B across CMB, CMExam, MedQA, and MedMCQA, five-seed experiments yield 69.69% mean accuracy across benchmarks, exceeding LoRA r16 and MoELoRA by 1.26 and 1.30 percentage points, respectively. The reported advantage over LoRA r16 increases from 0.08 to 1.94 points as training expands from one to seven specialties. Tag perturbations and atom masking support the usefulness of clinical routing, while atom clusters align with the supplied specialty labels (adjusted Rand index 0.62). Calibration, transfer, and measured costs further characterize the method. These findings support structured conditional adaptation for medical QA, while leaving clinical safety and broader deployment untested.

</details>


### [371] [Back to the Future: Rethinking EDA Infrastructure for Agentic Systems in Chip Design Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06790)
*Je Yang,Ivan Lobov,Thomas Karpati*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces BTTF, an agentic framework that converts large simulation dumps into a relational database and uses multi-agent orchestration plus SQL generation to answer natural-language verification queries for chip design, achieving 95.33% accuracy on a 150-query benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern AI chips are extremely complex Systems-on-Chip with billions of transistors, but verification workflows after simulation are still highly manual. While LLMs have been applied to EDA, most work focuses on generating RTL code rather than helping engineers analyze post-simulation data and waveforms. There is a gap in tools that can autonomously support verification and debugging using natural language interfaces over simulation outputs.

Method: The paper proposes Back-to-the-Future (BTTF), an end-to-end framework. It first ingests massive, unstructured simulation dump files and converts them into a normalized relational SQLite database. Then it uses a collaborative multi-agent system that parses natural language verification questions, generates schema-aware SQL queries, and reasons over the resulting data. The agents also correlate detected signal anomalies with version-controlled RTL repositories to support debugging. The whole system is evaluated on a standardized benchmark of verification queries.

Result: On a benchmark of 150 natural-language verification queries, BTTF achieves 95.33% execution accuracy, indicating that its SQL generation and analysis reliably produce correct, executable answers. This demonstrates that the system can practically support automated verification query handling over real simulation data.

Conclusion: BTTF effectively bridges a key missing piece in AI-accelerated EDA workflows by enabling autonomous, natural-language-driven analysis of simulation results and signal waveforms. The high benchmark accuracy suggests that such agentic, database-backed approaches can make post-simulation verification more efficient and less manual, pointing toward more fully autonomous chip verification flows in the future.

Abstract: The unprecedented computational scale of modern artificial intelligence depends on complex, multi-billion-transistor Systems-on-Chip, yet the workflows that verify these chips remain stubbornly manual. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have made rapid inroads into Electronic Design Automation (EDA), approximately 74.6% of existing studies target static Register-Transfer Level (RTL) code generation, leaving post-simulation verification and interactive waveform debugging largely untouched. We introduce Back-to-the-Future (BTTF), an end-to-end agentic framework that closes this infrastructural gap. BTTF distills massive, unstructured simulation dumps into a normalized relational SQLite database and couples it with a collaborative multi-agent orchestration engine that translates natural-language verification queries into schema-aware SQL while correlating signal anomalies with versioned RTL repositories. Across a 150-query benchmark, BTTF attains 95.33% execution accuracy, charting a practical path toward autonomous EDA verification.

</details>


### [372] [TasteVal: Measuring the Experimental Research Taste of AI Systems Against Human Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06824)
*Oliver Jaffe,Dane Sherburn*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TasteVal is a benchmark that measures how efficiently AI models design and interpret experiments on realistic AI R&D tasks, quantifying their “experimental research taste.”


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks focus on coding, reasoning, or problem-solving, but not on whether models have good “research taste” in experimental science—specifically, how well they choose informative experiments and interpret results under compute constraints. Since experimental taste effectively multiplies available compute and thus strongly affects AI progress, the authors want a way to measure and track it over time for frontier models.

Method: They define experimental research taste as compute efficiency: for a fixed research task, a model that achieves an expert-level score with fewer serial experiment-hours has proportionally higher taste. They build TasteVal, a suite of 8 challenging, open-ended tasks mirroring frontier AI R&D. To disentangle experimental design from coding, the evaluated model acts as a “Researcher” that only proposes experiments, while a separate fixed “Coder” agent executes the code and returns results. The Researcher can iterate until it hits either a 40 H100-GPU-hour compute budget or 120 wall-clock hours. Human experts (24 total, at least 2 per task) attempt the tasks, and the best expert run per task is used as the baseline. They then evaluate 20 frontier models (2023–2026), compute each model’s “compute multiplier” relative to the expert baseline, and fit trend lines for how this multiplier and final performance improve over time.

Result: The top model, Opus 5.5, surpasses the expert human baseline with a compute multiplier of 2.3x (95% CI 1.15–4.37), meaning it reaches expert-level outcomes using less than half the experimental compute, and it does so at about 1/30 the average per-run cost of the human baseliners. Across models, the compute multiplier on TasteVal has accelerated sharply: it doubled roughly every 14 months from 2023 to Dec 2025, but since Dec 2025 it has been doubling about every 3.0 months (95% CI 1.7–5.0). In contrast, normalized final task performance continues to improve at the older, slower pace, doubling roughly every 14.6 months, with no obvious trend break.

Conclusion: Experimental research taste, as quantified by compute efficiency on complex R&D tasks, is improving much faster than raw task performance in frontier models. Recent models not only match but can exceed human experts in experiment design and interpretation while using substantially less experimental compute and cost. Because this “taste” acts as a multiplier on experimental resources, it is likely to be a critical driver in future AI progress. To prevent training-time contamination and keep the benchmark predictive, the authors do not release the concrete TasteVal tasks.

Abstract: We introduce TasteVal, a benchmark to evaluate the experimental research taste of frontier models. We define research taste as the ability to pick interesting problems to solve, design experiments, and interpret experimental results. TasteVal measures the experimental component of research taste; given a fixed research problem, we measure how well a model iteratively designs experiments and draws conclusions from their outcomes. We operationalize experimental research taste as compute efficiency; a Researcher who reaches the same score as an expert human using half the serial experimental compute has twice the experimental taste. Experimental taste thus acts as a multiplier on experimental compute, making it a key input to forecasts of AI progress. TasteVal consists of 8 novel, challenging, open-ended tasks representative of frontier AI R&D. To isolate taste from coding ability, the model under evaluation acts as a Researcher that iteratively designs experiments while a fixed Coder agent implements them and reports their results. The Researcher executes until either the 40 H100 hour or 120 wall-clock hour budgets are exhausted. We recruit 24 human experts, at least 2 per task, and take the best expert attempt per task as the expert baseline. We evaluate 20 models released between 2023 and 2026. The best-performing model, Opus 5.5, exceeds our expert baseline, with a compute multiplier of 2.3x (95% CI 1.15-4.37), at roughly 1/30 of our baseliners' average per-run cost. On TasteVal, the compute multiplier of frontier models has doubled approximately every 3.0 months since December 2025 (95% CI 1.7-5.0), up from every 14 months between 2023 and December 2025. Measured by final normalized performance, frontier models show no trend break, doubling every 14.6 months. To keep TasteVal uncontaminated, we do not release the tasks.

</details>


### [373] [BiasFlow: Geometric Monitoring and Backbone Regularization for Spurious Feature Reliance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06846)
*Haojin Deng,Zhiping Lin,Yimin Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose BiasFlow, a toolkit and regularization scheme to analyze and shape feature-space centroids so that models are more robust to biased head retraining, complementing worst-group accuracy (WGA).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Worst-group accuracy only measures performance of a specific trained predictor and doesn’t reveal how the underlying feature backbone behaves when a new classifier head is trained, especially on biased data. There is a need for tools to diagnose and improve how features encode spurious attributes and how robust they are to biased retraining.

Method: They introduce BiasFlow, a hook-based feature-analysis toolkit that tracks class-attribute centroid alignment (IBMI), within-class centroid separation (W-IBMI), and sensitivity of features to projection. They also propose BiasFlow Regularization (BFR), a supervised, class-conditional centroid-alignment penalty added during training to shape the feature geometry. W-IBMI serves as a diagnostic verifying the quantity optimized by BFR, though it is scale dependent. They then evaluate these tools in multiple benchmark and stress-test settings, including freezing backbones and retraining heads on biased data, and a synthetic watermark experiment on ImageNet.

Result: On small-scale benchmarks, adding BFR generally improves or at least preserves mean worst-group accuracy, with improvements up to +26 percentage points on UrbanCars. In a main stress test on CelebA-Std where backbones are frozen and new heads are trained on biased data, combining BFR with GroupDRO increases WGA from 40.7% to 64.1%, while the accuracy of a Male attribute probe drops from 92.5% to 72.2%, indicating reduced reliance on that attribute. However, attribute information is still recoverable and cross-task results are mixed. In a synthetic watermark ImageNet setup, BFR improves watermark-shift accuracy by +23 percentage points under matched training conditions.

Conclusion: Evaluating and shaping the geometry of feature centroids—via IBMI, W-IBMI, and BFR—and testing resistance to biased head retraining provide valuable complementary information to worst-group accuracy alone. Within the tested protocols, these centroid-based diagnostics and regularization can substantially improve robustness to distribution shifts induced by biased training heads, though they do not completely remove attribute information from the features.

Abstract: Worst-group accuracy (WGA) evaluates a trained predictor but does not characterize how its frozen backbone behaves when a new head is learned. We introduce BiasFlow, a hook-based toolkit for monitoring class-attribute centroid alignment (IBMI), within-class centroid separation (W-IBMI), and feature-projection sensitivity. IBMI is confounded by class-attribute correlation and is not a measure of causal feature reliance. We pair these diagnostics with BiasFlow Regularization (BFR), a supervised, composable class-conditional centroid-alignment penalty. W-IBMI verifies the quantity BFR optimizes; it is scale dependent and does not independently establish attribute removal. Across the reported small-scale benchmarks, adding BFR improves or preserves mean WGA, with gains up to +26.0 pp on UrbanCars. The principal independent stress test freezes CelebA-Std backbones and trains fresh heads on biased data: BFR+GroupDRO improves WGA from 40.7% to 64.1%, while Male probe accuracy decreases from 92.5% to 72.2%. Attribute information remains recoverable, and cross-task results are mixed. A controlled synthetic-watermark ImageNet experiment additionally improves watermark-shift accuracy by +23.0 pp under matched training. These results support evaluating centroid geometry and resistance to biased head retraining alongside WGA, within the tested protocols.
